# The Legendarium of Dia-thìr — The Ancient Age (An Aois Àrsaidh)

# Chapter One: Of the Mason and the Lightning

*VE 1*

> *Bha teine sa chloich.*
> There was fire in the stone.

*The First Part: Of An Clachair's Fire, and the Covering of the Vein*

## I. Of the Dry Spring

This is told at the hearth, on Oidhche an Dealanaich, by whoever in the house is oldest, and it begins before the mason ever touched the wedge, in the season when his valley had no water.

The spring under the shoulder of the hill had fed that household and three others since before anyone living could say. It rose out of a fold of rock, cold even in high summer, and ran a hand's width wide down a groove worn into the stone by every year it had ever run. In the autumn of that year it failed. It did not fail all at once. It thinned through the wet months when it should have been running full, and by the dark of the year it was a trickle a child could stop with two fingers, and then some mornings there was nothing in the groove at all but a damp stain and a smell of old moss.

The valley did not starve. There were becks lower down, and the households sent their water-carriers a mile and a half with skins on their backs, morning and evening, in whatever weather the year gave them, which that year was mostly sleet. But a valley that carries its water on its back through a hard winter learns to want a well of its own, dug where the rock holds water even when the sky will not give it, and the households met at the flat stone below the failed spring and talked of digging one.

They did not choose lightly, for the digging of a well in that country was slow and cruel work, done with a wedge of hard stone and a maul of oak, a hand's depth of rock at a time, and the man who did it would be at it through the worst of the winter with his knees in the mud and his back to the wind. They chose Neachdan, because he was the best splitter of stone that any of the four households could put a name to, and because he had said, when the others were still weighing whether the spring might yet come back, that it would not, and had gone to look for a place to sink the shaft while the rest of them were still talking.

He was not yet thirty. He had split more stone in his life than most men split in two, walling folds and lining graves and setting the flat stones that floored every threshold in the valley, and there was not a household in it that did not owe him some doorstep or some byre wall. His father had taught him the trade and had been dead some years. His wife was Sorcha, and they had a house at the low end of the valley with a boy of six named Conall and three littler than Conall, and it was Sorcha who came out to the new-marked shaft on the first morning with a skin of water and stood a while watching him set the first wedge, and said nothing, because there was nothing to say that the wedge and the winter had not already said between them.

## II. Of the Wedge and the Rock

He began below the flat stone, on a rise a little east of the dead spring, where the older men of the valley said the rock ran true and would not crack sideways on him and waste his work. It was the dead of the year, past the shortest day, and the light he had to dig by was grey from first light to last, with sleet in most of it.

The way of it was this. He set the hard wedge into a seam of the rock with the flat of his hand, judged it true, and struck it with the oak maul, and struck it again, and went on striking until the rock gave along the seam or did not, and if it did not he moved the wedge a hand's width and began again. A day was perhaps two hand's-depths of shaft, if the rock ran kind, and less if it did not, and there were days that whole short winter when he came up out of the cut at dusk with nothing to show for it but split knuckles and a wedge blunted at the edge.

The cold did that to him before the rock did. His hands split at the big knuckle and across the base of the thumb, the way a mason's hands always split in a hard winter, and the cuts never had time to close between one day's work and the next, so that by the dark of the year his hands looked older than the rest of him, red-rimmed and cracked and always a little wet, whether from the wound or the weather there was no telling. He wrapped them in strips of hide when Sorcha made him, and lost the wrapping within the hour because a man cannot feel a seam in stone through a hide glove, and Sorcha stopped making him after the fourth time, and only rubbed grease from the sheep-fat pot into the cracks at night while he sat by their own small fire, which in those days on Dia-thìr was no fire at all: a heap of dark stones set out on the south face of the hill to take what sun the day had, and carried in at dusk wrapped in bracken, giving off a heat that was more memory than warmth by the time it reached the house.

There was no other kind of fire on the island. No one on Dia-thìr had ever seen one lit; there was the sun, and there was the lightning, which came and went and could not be carried, and there was the slow patient husbandry of sun-warmed stones and piled skins and bodies packed close, which was how every household on the island had always held off the worst of a winter, and none had ever held off all of it. Old people died of the cold in a hard year, and children died of it, and it was accepted as the weather was accepted, because there was nothing else to do about either.

By the fifteenth day of the digging the shaft was over Neachdan's head, and he worked now with a rope ladder of plaited hide and a leather bucket that Conall's cousin hauled up from the lip, full of chippings, forty and fifty times a short winter day. The rock had begun to run darker as he went down, a grey going to black, harder under the wedge than anything above it had been, ringing instead of cracking clean, so that he had to strike twice or three times where once had done. He did not think much of the darkening. Rock ran however it ran; he had cut through worse.

## III. Of the Black Break and the Colours In It

On the morning it happened the sleet had turned half to rain, which was in its way worse, since rain finds every gap in a cloak that sleet only sits on. He went down into the shaft before the grey light was properly up, because the household wanted water and every day he did not reach it was a day the carriers walked their mile and a half twice more.

A seam ran clean across the face of the cut, a hair's width of a line that his eye, trained on twenty years of stone, told him would open true. He set the wedge and struck.

It went with one blow, which in that hard black rock had happened perhaps twice in the whole digging, and the block came away in his hands heavier than its size promised, and he nearly dropped it. He turned it toward the little grey light that came down the shaft from above.

Every stone he had ever split in his life, in that valley or any other, had broken to the same thing: grey dust, grit, a dull grey face going to a duller grey the longer it lay in the weather. This did not. The break ran black, black as a wet crow's wing, and along it, where the maul had opened the vein, there was colour: a streak that lay gold when he tilted it, the way the sea takes the low sun at evening though he had never seen the sea; a scatter of small points that shone white as frost catches the light before frost has any business shining; a vein of dull red-brown like the true heart of an old oak split for a beam; a thread that ran silver and did not tarnish when his thumb rubbed across it; and, set apart from the rest, a piece that when he turned it slowly held colour after colour after colour, so that he could not have said what colour it truly was, only that it was every one he had a name for and some, he thought afterward, that he did not.

He knelt in the bottom of the cut with the rain running off the shaft's lip onto the back of his neck and turned the pieces over and over in his cracked hands until the cold had taken the last of the feeling out of his fingers and he could no longer tell by touch which piece he held.

He did not know what it was. No one on the island had ever seen coal, coloured or otherwise; there was nothing in any hearth-tale, any wall-lore, any word passed down from any grandfather, that gave this a name or a use or a warning to go with it. He knew only that it was beautiful, and that a man does not leave a beautiful thing in the bottom of a well shaft to be flooded over when the water comes in, so he opened the neck of his tunic and put the pieces inside, against his chest where his own small warmth might keep the rain off them a while, and went on working the seam until there was no more colour in it and only the plain grey-black beyond, which he left where it was, because a well is dug for water and not for stone.

Midday found him climbing out of the shaft with his tunic heavy and lumped against his ribs and the light no better than it had been at dawn, meaning to show Sorcha what he had found and go back down before the light went altogether. He never went back down that day.

## IV. Of the Storm at Dusk

The sky had been low and grey and giving rain in a steady, sullen way since before he woke, the kind of day that does not announce a change in it. The change came in the middle of the afternoon, while he stood at the lip of the shaft chewing a strip of dried mutton that one of the little ones had brought him, and it came the way weather comes on that coast when it means to be taken seriously: the wind backed round from its steady quarter and freshened all in a few minutes, and the low grey overhead thickened from the west into a darker grey that had a green cast at its underside, which the old people of the valley said was a colour a sky takes before it does something worth remembering.

He judged, watching it come, that there was no sense going back down the shaft into a storm; a man in a hole in the ground in a hard rain is a man waiting to be drowned in his own well. He gathered his tools, capped the shaft-mouth with the split boards kept there for it, and looked for shelter, and found it under the lip of a low crag a stone's throw above the shaft, an overhang no deeper than a man is tall, but dry, where the herders of that hillside sheltered their beasts in the worst of a summer squall.

The storm came up the valley like something walking. He watched it from under the crag: the rain-curtain moving across the far slope first, greying it out entirely, then the near slope, then his own; the wind driving hard enough to lean the heather flat and to find its way even under the lip of his shelter and set the rain slantwise against his legs; and the light going to a strange thick yellow-brown, nothing like the grey of an ordinary evening, that made the whole valley look, he said afterward, the way a bruise looks a day after the blow.

Then the sky broke.

There was no other way any teller of it, then or since, has ever said it. It did not thunder first and lighten after, in the ordinary way of a storm working up to its worst; it went from the yellow-brown stillness straight to a white light that filled the whole overhang he crouched in, so bright that for a moment he saw the black rock of the crag above him as though it were noon, and in the same instant a sound came that he did not hear so much as feel in the ground under his knees and in his own teeth, a single crack, as if the hill itself had been struck with a maul the size of the sky.

He was thrown back against the rock. When his sight cleared enough to see anything at all, he saw that the light had not simply flashed and gone, as lightning does. It had gone down. He had watched it, in the half-second his eyes could hold it, run down out of the cloud in a white line no wider than a spear-shaft, and strike the ground below the crag, on the very line of the capped shaft, and vanish into it.

For a long moment he did not move. The rain went on falling. The wind went on. Nothing in the valley below him showed any sign that the sky had just done a thing no one living had words for.

Then he saw the light.

It came up faint at first from around the edges of the split boards over the shaft-mouth, a low reddish glow, the colour a coal takes at the heart of an ember, and it did not fade the way an afterimage fades from a struck eye. It grew. By the time he had got his legs under him and come out from under the crag into the driving rain it was strong enough to throw his own shadow, black and long, across the wet heather in front of him.

## V. Of the Thing Alive in the Well

He came to the lip of the shaft with the rain running into his eyes and pulled the split boards aside, and the light came up out of the ground and struck him full in the face, and he knelt there at the edge with the rain hammering his back and looked down at what he had made, though he never afterward believed he had made it, only that he had broken it open and the sky had done the rest.

The whole face of the black seam, as far down as his eye could follow it in the murk of the shaft, was awake. It did not burn the way he imagined fire must burn, if he had ever tried to imagine such a thing at all; it moved low along the vein, a dark flame with red at its root, the colour of peat-water stirred up from the bottom of a bog and lit from within, and it breathed. That was the word he used all his life after, and no other word ever satisfied him or the people who heard him tell it. It swelled and drew in, swelled and drew in, as a chest does, and where it swelled the heat came up the shaft in a wave he felt on his face and on his hands before he felt anything else, a heat with no wind in it and no cold anywhere behind it, the first warmth any living thing on Dia-thìr had ever felt that did not come, however faintly, from the sun.

The rain fell into the shaft in sheets, straight down the sides where the boards had been, and struck the burning vein, and hissed, and the vein did not go out. Rain that should by every reason he had ever been taught have drowned the thing dead went on falling into it and coming off it as a thin white smoke that the wind took away over the hillside, and he could do nothing but watch it, a long while, unable to do anything else.

He put his hands over the shaft-mouth, not into it, only over it, the way a man holds his hands to a fire he has not yet decided to trust, and the warmth came up into his split and blackened knuckles and into the base of his aching thumbs, and something in him that had been clenched since the dead of the year, since the spring failed and the sleet began and his hands began to crack, let go all at once. He knelt in the mud at the lip of his own well with the storm going on over him and wept, not loudly, the way a man weeps who has been cold a long time and has stopped expecting to be warm again, and he was not ashamed of it afterward, though he did not tell it often, and it is the one part of the whole telling that the households of that valley have always agreed was surely true, because it is not the kind of thing a teller invents to make a tale better.

## VI. Of the Coal Carried Home

Kneeling there, he could not know whether the thing would live an hour or a year, and it was that not-knowing, more than anything else, that moved him. A wonder that might go out with the next gust was a wonder that had to be taken while it could be taken.

He found among his tools a flat stone he had set aside from the digging, one of the pale slabs meant for the new well's coping, and he went down the rope ladder into the shaft, into the heat and the strange breathing light of it, with the rain still coming down the sides in ropes, and he chose a piece of the vein near its edge, where the burning had not yet reached its full strength, and worked it free with the antler pry he used to lift split slabs, careful as a man lifting an egg from under a sitting bird. It came away whole, a fist-sized lump of the black seam with the dark flame still moving in it, throwing more heat in his two hands than the whole warmed-stone hearth of his house threw in a night.

He set it on the flat slab. He drew his cloak from around his shoulders, wet through as it already was, and folded it over the burning piece so that only a slit was left for air, the way, without ever having been told to do such a thing, a man's hands simply know to shelter a flame from wind and wet at once; and he climbed the ladder one-handed, Leac na Fèithe and its burden held against his chest with the other arm, and went out into the full weight of the storm to carry it the mile down the valley to his own door.

It is the walk that every teller of the mason's tale slows for, whatever else is passed over quickly, because it is the walk on which Teine a' Chlachair on Dia-thìr was nearly lost a dozen times before it was ever set on a hearth. He went slantwise down the hill so that his own body stood between the coal and the driving rain. He stumbled twice on wet stone and each time caught himself with his free hand and never let Leac na Fèithe tip. Once, crossing the beck that fed the failed spring, swollen now with the storm's own rain, he waded it rather than risk the stepping-stones in the dark, holding Leac na Fèithe high over the water with both arms, the cloak's wet wool steaming faintly where the coal's heat met the flood below it. He said afterward that he had not once, on the whole of that walk, thought about the water in the well or the winter or anything else the household had sent him out that morning to solve; he had thought only of the small red light under the cloak, and of keeping it.

## VII. Of the First Hearth

Sorcha had the door open before he reached it, because she had seen, coming down through the rain, a light where no light on that hillside had any business being, low and red and moving with him, like nothing that hillside had ever shown.

He came into the house stooped over Leac na Fèithe like a man carrying something asleep that he feared to wake wrong, and set it down in the centre of the floor, on the ring of bare-swept earth kept clear for the sun-stones, and drew back his cloak from it, and the household saw, for the first time in the history of anything that had ever lived on that island, what a flame was.

Conall, who was six, came close enough that Sorcha had to catch the back of his tunic, and the three littler than him stood behind their mother's legs and would not come close at all, and stared at the low red-black light with the wide unblinking look of children who cannot yet tell whether a thing is dangerous by anything but its strangeness. Neachdan told them, because he did not yet know better himself, that it would not hurt them if they let it be, and for that first night it was true, since none of them touched it and it did nothing but breathe its slow dark flame and give off a warmth that reached every corner of the one room they had, farther and steadier than any warmed stone had ever reached it.

He remembered the rest of the coloured pieces still in his tunic and drew them out, one by one, and set them by the burning one to see what they would do, and this is the part of the telling that every hearth in the hill country still gives the same way. Each piece, laid against the fire, caught. Each burned as the first had burned, low and dark-flamed, and as each caught, the colour went out of it: the gold sheen dulled to the same red-black glow as the rest, the white points dimmed, the red-brown vein and the silver thread and the last strange piece that had held every colour at once all burned down, in the end, to one same low dark flame indistinguishable from any other, so that within the hour there was nothing left in the whole burning ring to tell a man which piece had shone gold and which silver and which had held the rainbow.

Neachdan looked at that a long while, turning the last blackened lump with a stick, and he told his children, and told it again at every hearth-night after, that he had been sorry for it, a little, the way a man is sorry to see any beautiful thing spend its last; and that he had been glad all the same, more glad than sorry by more than any measure could set between them, because his household was sitting round a fire, red-faced in its light, with the rain still hammering the turf roof above them and none of them cold, for the first time since any of them could remember being alive at all.

## VIII. Of What the Fire Taught in One Night

It did not stay a simple wonder for long. A fire, once made, carries its own nature along with its light and its warmth, and that nature had to be learned in the same night it was given, by people who had never had reason to learn it before.

The first lesson came within the hour, when the flame at the heart of the ring began to sink and dull of its own accord. The roof kept the rain off it; it had simply nothing more to take. Neachdan understood, watching it fade, what none of the tellings that came before him could have told him, because there were none: that the thing ate. It had eaten the black rock it was born in, slowly, breathing its heat out of the burning stone, and now the coal he had carried was more ash-grey crust than the black it had been, and the flame under the crust was going the colour of a dying ember rather than the strong dark red it had shown at the shaft.

He broke the crust with the same stick, more from the instinct of a man cracking a nut than from any knowledge, and beneath it the coal still glowed, and the glow strengthened when the air reached it, and that told him a second thing, though he could not have put a name to what it told him: that the thing wanted feeding and wanted air both, and would not simply burn until it was done and stop.

It was Sorcha who fed it heather. No one told her to; there was dry heather stacked by the door for bedding, and a mother's instinct in a cold house is to put whatever will hold heat within reach of the thing giving it. She laid a handful of the dry stems against the failing coal, and the fire took them at once, faster and brighter than it had taken the stone, with a small crackling that made the littlest of the children cry out and back further behind her skirt; and the flame leapt up gold-white for a breath and then settled, fed, into a steadier light than it had shown since it left the ground.

That was the turn of the whole night, the one the tellers give weight to above all the rest: that the thing they had brought into the house could be fed, and could therefore also, if it was not fed, go out and die, as surely as a beast dies of hunger or a man of cold; and that it was theirs to keep or lose by their own care, in a way that the sun and the wind and the sea had never been anyone's to keep or lose. Neachdan understood it before he could have said it in so many words, and it frightened him more than the lightning had, because the lightning had come and gone in an instant beyond anyone's holding, and this, this small red thing on his own floor, could be lost through nothing worse than an evening's carelessness, and once lost, by everything he had seen and reasoned that night, might never be got again.

## IX. Of Sorcha's Hand

The second lesson cost more than the first.

Conall had been told, and told again, to keep his hands well back, and did, being six and old enough to be frightened as well as curious; it was Sorcha, feeding the fire a second time as the night wore on, who reached too far in setting a fresh knot of heather against the glowing heart of it and let her palm brush the crust of the coal itself, the ash-grey skin that looked, to every eye in that room, no different from any dead stone that had lain cold in a wall all its life.

She cried out and snatched her hand back, and for a moment the household froze, because none of them, not even Neachdan who had knelt at the shaft's mouth and put his own hands over the breathing vein, had yet understood that the thing could bite a hand that did not ask its leave first. Her palm reddened at once, and by the time Neachdan had her by the wrist in the low light to look at it, a welt was rising across the base of her fingers, and she held it against her own breast and would not at first let him touch it, more from the shock of the thing than from the hurt, though the hurt was real enough and lasted her the better part of a month.

He put grease from the sheep-fat pot on it, the same grease she had rubbed into his own cracked knuckles through the whole hard winter of the digging, and it was, he thought afterward, a strange turn that the fire she had helped bring alive should be the first thing in that house to need tending in the old way, with the same jar and the same hands.

From that night the household kept a rule that needed no telling twice: the fire was fed with a stick's length between the hand and the flame, and never, whatever the cold, with a bare palm laid flat against the glowing crust to test whether it still had heat in it. Sorcha herself taught it to the littler children before dawn, holding up her reddened hand for them to see, and it is said, though this the tellers admit they cannot swear to, that it was from that hurt and that teaching, given the very first night the fire lived in a house, that every hearth on the island since has kept its stick, its poker, its tongs, and has never once gone back to bare hands.

## X. Of the Household Red-Faced at Dawn

They did not sleep, none of the household, through the whole of that first night; there was too much to watch, too much still to be learned about a thing that had never before existed anywhere any of them or their fathers or their fathers' fathers had ever stood. The storm wore itself out somewhere in the small hours, the wind falling first and the rain going after it to a last thin drizzle and then to nothing, so that by the last dark before dawn the only sound in the valley was the low steady crackle of the fire and, further off, water still running high in the beck from all the rain the hill had taken.

Conall fell asleep at last sitting up against his mother's knee, close enough to the fire to feel it and far enough, by then, to be trusted there; the three littler ones slept in a heap under one cloak on the far side of the ring, their faces, when the flame caught a fresh piece of heather and leapt, going from shadow to sudden red and back to shadow as the light moved. Sorcha sat with her hurt hand wrapped and held loosely in her lap and watched the fire the way a woman watches a sick child through its worst night, not trusting it yet, not looking away from it either. Neachdan sat across from her with the last of the dark, half-burned lump of the rainbow-coloured stone turning slowly in his fingers, its colours long since gone the way of all the others, black and glowing at its heart like any other coal, indistinguishable now from the plainest grey chip he had ever split from a wall.

When the grey light of the true dawn came in under the door, thin and cold and utterly ordinary, the fire was still burning, banked low but alive, in the centre of the floor where no fire had ever burned before. Neachdan looked at it a long while, and then at his wife's bound hand, and at his sleeping children reddened by its glow rather than blued by the cold as every dawn of their short lives had found them until that one, and he said the only thing that any teller of Teine a' Chlachair has ever agreed he said, the words that are given, in the short form, before the long reciting of the fathers begins at every hearth on Oidhche an Dealanaich even now.

He said it must not go out.

He did not say it as an order given lightly, the way a man tells a child to shut a door; he said it kneeling by the fire with his cracked hand flat on the cold earth beside it, the way a man swears an oath over something he does not fully understand and is afraid, all the same, to lose. Sorcha, from across the ring, said that it would not, not while she had hands to feed it, and held up the one that had already paid the fire's first toll as though it were a pledge rather than a wound; and Conall, waking at the sound of their voices, looked from his mother's bandaged hand to his father's blackened knuckles to the low red heart of the thing between them, and asked, in the plain way of a child too young yet to know what a question like that would cost his whole line to answer, what it was for.

Neither of them had an answer for him that morning. It was nine hundred years, and thirty-four fathers after Conall, before anyone of his line stood in a grove far to the north and asked the same question of a stranger made of smoke, and got, at last, the beginning of one. But that telling belongs to another hearth-night, and this one, the tellers say, ends here: with the rain gone off the valley, the well still uncut to water, and a fire on a swept ring of earth that had not been there the morning before, and has not, by any hearth it was ever carried to, gone out since.

# Chapter Two: Of the Fire Given Away

*VE 1 – 71*

## I. Of the Vein Left Burning

The well-cut above the valley did not fill in. No one would let it. For a hand of years after Oidhche an Dealanaich the broken vein burned on down in the rock, low and dark, and the mason's household kept a path worn to it as a path is worn to a spring. It did not flare as it had flared under the rain; it lay in its crack like a sleeping thing, breathing a small heat, and whoever went to it went quietly, the way a person goes near a sleeping child, not to wake it wrong.

Neachdan would not let the well be filled, and would not let it be dug deeper either, though there were those who came from three valleys off only to look down into it and see the black stone glowing at the bottom like an ember under ash. He set two flat stones across the mouth of the cut, a hand's breadth apart, so that no one could fall in and no rain could quite put it out, and he told his children that the fire in the ground was the same fire as the fire on the floor, and that both must be fed and neither trusted.

There was no counting of the years then, not by anyone on the island, and the household did not say "the third year" or "the fifth". They said "before Ailbhe could walk" or "the spring the ewes came early" or "since the lightning," and let it go at that. But it is told that in the fourth spring after the well was struck, a girl was born to Neachdan and Sorcha at the hearth, so close to the flame that the women turned her a little sideways with their hands lest a spark should catch her hair, and that she was the first child of the island ever to open her eyes by firelight and not by the light of the sky alone. They named her Ailbhe. The hearth was already old enough by then that no one troubled to remark on the strangeness of a birth beside a fire; only the oldest women said, low, that a child born so would know the fire better than her own kin, and it was not meant unkindly, and it was not wrong.

The boy Conall was six when his father brought the first coal home under his cloak, and he grew through those years the way a boy grows near a thing he has been told never to let go out: watchful of it before he was watchful of anything else. He learned to read the fire the way another child learns to read weather. He knew the difference between the low steady red that meant it would keep till morning and the paler flutter that meant it was hungry, and he knew which wood answered it kindly and which spat and starved it, and long before he was a man grown he could tell, walking into a house from the cold, whether its fire had been fed with love or with laziness, by nothing but the smell of the room. His father set him, young, to watch the well-cut through the short nights of summer, when the household's own hearth needed less minding, and he would sit on the two flat stones with his knees drawn up and look down at the vein burning alone in the dark, and think, as a child thinks, that it did not need him at all, and was glad of him anyway.

It is the household's own telling, kept since, that no fire went out in Neachdan's house in all those first years, not once, not even in the wet spring when the roof let water onto the floor two nights running and every ember in the valley but theirs went dark. Whether that telling is wholly true no one now can say; households make of their own beginnings what they can bear to keep. But there is this much under it: that the fire the mason carried up out of the ground did not go out, that Conall watched it with more care than he gave his own hands in a cold winter, and that the vein down in the rock burned low and steady through all of it, unregarded by most of the valley and utterly regarded by one small household, waiting, though none of them yet knew for what.

## II. Of the Meat on the Stones

It was in the second winter after the lightning that the household first put meat to the fire on purpose, and the tellers of the high valleys, who give the carrying of fire and the hut on the heather their full weight, give this its own small place as well, because it changed what a household ate more than anything since the island was new.

They had eaten meat raw all their lives, as every household on the island ate it: cut thin and chewed long, or dried in strips on the wind in the summer and kept for the cold months, or pounded with fat and berries into cakes that kept longer still. No one had ever thought meat wanted anything done to it that the wind and a sharp flint could not do. It was Sorcha, again, who changed it, and by accident, as most of the first things of that household were done: she had hung a haunch of mutton from the roof-beam over the hearth to keep it from the dogs, lower than she meant to, and in the night the heat coming up off the fire browned the underside of it and set the fat dripping, so that the house woke to a smell none of them had ever smelled before and all of them, even the littlest, knew at once for food.

Neachdan cut a piece from the browned side with his flint and ate it standing, and stood a long while after with the taste of it in his mouth, and then cut a second piece for Sorcha and a third for Conall; and that was how the household learned that meat held over a fire was a different thing from meat held in the wind, softer and hotter and easier on an old tooth, and that a household with a fire need not chew all winter on strips as hard as leather. By the spring they were laying mutton and venison on flat stones heated in the embers, and turning it with a stick, and by the next winter a flat stone kept at the edge of the hearth for that one purpose had become as plain a part of the household as the hearth itself.

The neighbours learned it with the fire. It went out with the coal in Ailbhe's pot and in every pot after hers, so that a household begging fire from the mason's line got, along with the coal, the knowing of what to put over it and for how long; and it is told that the first thing a household ever did with a fire newly carried to it, before it thought to warm its hands, was to lay a piece of meat on a stone at the edge and wait to smell it.

There was grief in it too, the tellers say, though small. An old man of the household two doors along, who had lost the last of his teeth the winter before the lightning and lived since on broth of pounded meat and water drunk cold, wept the first time he ate mutton softened over the fire, because it was the first meat he had been able to chew in a year, and because his wife, who had pounded his meat for him every day of that year with her own two hands, had died of the cold in the week before the lightning came and never tasted it.

## III. Of the Night the Hearth Died

It went out at last in the fifth year, in the black hour before the earliest light, when Conall was eleven and the household had grown careless the way any household grows careless of a thing that has never once failed it.

There had been three days of rain driving sideways off the high ground, the kind that finds every gap in a roof of turf and heather no matter how well it is laid, and on the third night a gust came down the valley strong enough to lift a corner of thatch clean off the byre and lay it across the yard. Water came through where the thatch had been and ran along a rafter and dripped, patient as a slow thief, directly onto the hearth-stones. Neachdan was from home that night, gone two valleys off to look at a spring some other household hoped might be theirs to claim, and Sorcha slept heavily with the new baby at her side, and it was Conall who woke first, in the deep cold hour, to a darkness in the house that was not the ordinary darkness of night.

He knew before he was fully awake what it meant. Every night of his life he had slept within reach of a red glow on the floor, faint even through closed eyes, and its absence woke him the way a silence wakes a person more surely than a noise. His hand went flat on the hearth-stones and found them wet and cold, and when he raked through the black wet mess with his fingers there was no spark in it anywhere, not the smallest eye of red, nothing.

He did not wake his mother. He has told, since, that he thought of it, and did not, because he could not think what she would do that he was not already doing, and because some part of him, eleven years old and frightened in the dark, wanted the thing mended before anyone else knew it had broken.

The clay pot that stood by the door, the one his mother used for carrying water from the burn, went into his hands, and he went out into the rain in his bare feet with nothing over his shoulders but a fold of hide, and he ran. It was black as the inside of a closed hand and the ground was slick underfoot and he fell once, hard, on his knee on a stone, and did not stop to feel it. He ran the whole way to the well-cut by the path his own feet had worn to it, sure of it in the dark the way a hand is sure of a door it has opened ten thousand times, and he came over the two flat stones and looked down, and the vein was there, low and red and breathing exactly as it always breathed, indifferent to the storm and to him and to everything but its own burning.

He had never taken anything from it before. That had always been his father's work, or his father's father's, though there was no father's father now to remember. He lay flat on the wet stone with the pot in both hands and reached down into the cut as far as his arm would go, and the heat of it came up into his face, and he scraped a burning piece of the vein into the mouth of the pot with a scrap of slate, working fast because his arm was shaking with the strain of the reach and because the rain was trying to fill the pot before the coal could sit in it. He got one piece in, no bigger than a hen's egg, glowing through a crust of grey, and he packed cold dead ash from the rim of the cut in around it, the way he had seen his father bank a fire at night, and he held the pot against his chest under the fold of hide and ran home with it as he had run out, only slower now, every step careful, a boy carrying a small ember of a sleeping thing five years old and understanding for the first time that a fire need not stay in one place at all. It could be moved.

He tipped it out onto the wet hearth-stones and blew on it with his whole chest and fed it the driest tinder he could find by feel in the dark, a fistful of bracken kept dry under the roof-beam for kindling, kept dry, that one night, by nothing but luck. The fire caught slowly and then all at once, the way fire always does, going from nothing to a small red mouth to a flame standing up off the hearth in the space of a few breaths, and by the time Sorcha woke, roused at last by the light on the wall rather than by any sound her son had made, the hearth was burning as though it had never stopped, and Conall was sitting cross-legged before it with his knee bleeding onto the floor and the empty water-pot still clutched in both hands, and he did not know, himself, whether to be proud or ashamed, and so he said nothing, and let his mother think what she liked.

That hearth still tells it, and every hearth fire has reached since has told it too: that this was the night it was learned that fire need not stay where it is born, that it can be carried, a live coal in a clay pot banked round with its own ash, from one fire to light another. Before that night the household had thought of its fire the way it thought of the well-cut, a fixed thing, rooted in one place in the ground. After it, they held a small living thing that could be taken up and moved, and given, if they chose to give it, and a boy of eleven with wet feet and a water-pot had proved it could be done.

## IV. Of the Hut on the Heather

The first house to burn stood not half a mile off, at the near end of the same slope, the house of a household that had begged fire from Neachdan's hearth two winters before and kept it faithfully since, tending it as carefully as anyone tends a thing given by a neighbour rather than found by a father's own hand.

It went wrong on an ordinary evening, no storm in it, no blame that anyone could afterwards lay at any one door. The fire had been laid, as fire was laid in most houses then, on a bed of old heather packed down hard over years until it seemed as good as stone, because heather was what lay to hand on that slope and no one had yet been burned badly enough to think otherwise. A coal rolled, or a child kicked at it in play, or the wind found a gap under the door-hide and breathed on it too long while the household slept; which of these it was, the tellers never agreed, and in the end it did not matter. What mattered was that the packed heather under the fire caught from beneath, unseen, and smouldered there for the better part of an hour doing nothing that any waking eye would have marked, and then broke into open flame all along its length at once, under a roof of the same dry heather thatch, and the whole of it went up together, roof and floor and walls of turf, faster than the household inside could rightly understand what was happening to them.

They got out. That much was mercy: a mother, a father, three children, all out into the cold with nothing saved but each other and the clothes they slept in, and they stood in the yard and watched the one warm, dry, safe thing they owned burn itself to nothing in less time than it takes to walk to the burn and back, and the youngest child screamed the whole while, too small to fear the fire, only screaming because her mother's arms were gripping her too hard to breathe in.

Conall was among the first from the near houses to come with water, though there was nothing by then that water could do but wet the ground around the ruin and keep the fire from crossing to the dry grass beyond. Sixteen that year, a young man's height on him already, he stood in the yard in the smoke and the firelight and looked at the family gathered together in the ruin of their own warmth. His mind went to his own fire on its stones, with the two flat rocks laid over the well-cut a mile off, sitting always on ground that could never catch. Something his father had never quite put into words, though he had lived it every day since the lightning, stood plain before him now: a fire on stone can be fed and watched and trusted, and a fire on heather, however faithfully kept, is a fire lying on its own fuel, waiting only for a moment's inattention to remember what it is.

He said so, that night, to the household that had lost its roof, gently, for grief needs no scolding, and he said it again in the days after to anyone who would stand and listen, and he was young enough that some of the old men smiled at a boy telling them their business. But he had carried a coal alone through a storm at eleven, and there were those who had not forgotten it, and slowly, over that year and the ones after, the word went about the near hearths that a fire wants stone under it if it is to be trusted through a night, not the packed heather of the floor it stands on, and here and there a household began to lay flat stones gathered from the burn-bed beneath the hearth before it lit its fire there at all. It did not happen everywhere at once. Old ways die slowly on a hillside, and there were fires laid on heather for a generation and more after that night, in houses too poor in stone or too far from good rock to do otherwise. But the household that had lost its roof rebuilt on stone, and the near hearths that had watched it burn did the same, and it is from that year, the tellers say, that the custom began, stone under every fire the mason's line has ever given.

## V. Of Ailbhe and the Reach to the Northern Moor

Ailbhe grew up beside two fires at once, her mother's on the hearth and the vein's own down in the cut, and by the time she was old enough to be trusted with a pot in her hands she knew both better than any of her brothers did, for she had been set from her earliest years to watch the hearth while the others were sent to the herding or the digging, being the youngest daughter and thought too small yet for harder work. It was said of her, later, and said kindly, that she had learned to walk holding a coal at arm's length before she had learned to walk holding her mother's hand, which cannot be wholly true, but is not far from what those who knew her as a girl believed.

It fell to her, as she came into her growth, to be the one who carried the fire outward, because her brothers were needed at other work and because she had, from watching it so long, a steadiness with a live coal that older and stronger hands lacked. When a household two valleys off sent word that their own fire had died and they had heard, as everyone by then had heard, that the mason's people kept a fire that never failed, it was Ailbhe who was sent with a pot banked in ash and a fold of hide to keep the wind from it, walking the whole way herself, a girl not yet grown, carrying a small red heart of the family's fire out across country that most of the valley had never troubled to cross on foot before.

Neachdan never once refused it. That, too, is remembered and told, that though the fire had cost him a well he could no longer use for water and a debt of care his household paid every day of its life, he would not hear of keeping it back from any hearth that asked, and told his children plainly that a fire withheld from a cold house was a worse thing than a fire given away and never thanked for. So Ailbhe walked it, spring and autumn, summer when the light let her go further and winter when it did not, to the near valleys first and then, as she grew surer of the ground and the ground grew more used to her coming, further out: south along the slope to households that had only heard of Teine a' Chlachair by report, west to where the burn ran into wider country, and at last, in the year she came fully into her strength, north across the shoulder of the high ground to the edge of the moor that lay at the limit of any household's grazing, a day's walk each way and more if the weather turned.

It was slow work and it was not without its cost. A coal could die in the pot on a hard, wet crossing no matter how carefully it was banked, and there were journeys Ailbhe made twice over because the fire had gone out on her halfway and she would not turn for home without it lit, walking back to the last hearth she had passed to beg a fresh coal rather than arrive empty-handed at the one she was going to. There were households, too, proud or wary, that would not at first take fire from a girl of another valley, thinking there was some obligation in it they did not want to owe; but fire in a cold house wears down pride faster than argument does, and in the end every hearth that Ailbhe reached kept what she brought it and looked for her again.

By the time the fire had been carried, hearth by hearth, as far as the northern moor, no one could any longer say how many households now kept, on their own floors, a flame that had first burned in a well a day and more away. The mason's own fire had not multiplied by magic; it had simply been walked outward, one live coal at a time, by a girl who had grown up believing that a fire not shared was a fire not fully understood, and the valley that had once known one hearth in all its length now knew dozens, none of them less warm for the giving, and all of them, in the telling that mattered most to the households that kept them, still one fire.

## VI. Of Neachdan's Death and the Long Watch

Neachdan died by his own hearth, an old man by then for that hard country, in the year his grandchildren had begun to outnumber his children round the fire he had carried home under his cloak. In his last years he grew slow and would sit long hours by the flame doing nothing that any onlooker could call work, and those who watched him closest said he was listening to it, the way a man listens to a stream he has crossed his whole life and never once heard the same twice. Near the end he asked to be carried out one last time to see the well-cut, and they carried him, and he looked down for a long while at the vein still burning steadily in the dark of the rock, unchanged in all the years since the lightning had found it, and said, of it, only that it had outlasted him and would outlast his sons too. He was not wrong. That same night he died at the hearth he had lit, with the fire he had carried home burning beside him as it had burned every night of his life since, and the household kept it fed through the whole of the mourning without once letting it fall, because that, by then, was understood without needing to be said.

It was in the years after his death that Conall, grown into the eldest man of a household grown large, set down in words what he had first felt standing in the smoke of a burning roof: that fire belongs on stone and nowhere else, that no hearth in the valley should be laid on packed heather or bare turf if flat stone could be had and carried to it, and that this should stand, from that day, as every household's law that took fire from the mason's line. He said it standing, at a gathering of the near hearths in the dark half of the year, and though he had no more right to command another man's fire than any neighbour has, the households that heard him kept it, for they too had stood in the smoke of the burned roof, or had heard of it from those who had, and a rule that answers a fear already known is a rule that needs little enforcing.

Through all the years after, Conall kept the watch his father had kept before him, sitting by the well-cut through the dark half of every year when the fire in men's houses is most needed and most easily lost, and it became known among the valley's children, long before they knew why, that the two flat stones over the black cut were not to be gone near without an elder by, and that the old man who sat there through the cold months, saying little, watching the vein burn low and red in its crack in the rock, was not to be disturbed at his work, though no child rightly understood what the work was. He grew old at it. His hands, which had once reached down into the burning cut at eleven with a water-pot and a scrap of slate, grew stiff and slow, and in his last years it was his own son who carried the coals out to him and sat with him through the coldest nights, learning without being taught the same watchfulness his father had learned from his father before that.

Conall died as Neachdan had died, by a hearth, in the fullness of a long life for that country, with the vein in the well-cut still burning as it had burned since Oidhche an Dealanaich and showing, in all the years of his watching, no sign that it meant ever to stop. His son took the watch from him without any word of ceremony, the way a man takes up a tool his father has just set down, and sat that same winter through the dark half of the year on the two flat stones above the cut, and looked down at the fire that had now outlived two of the mason's line, and understood, as his father and his father's father had understood before him, that it was not his to let go out.

# Chapter Three: Of the Three Wells and the Slab

*VE 72 – 226*

## I. Of the Black Well and the Young Well

By the time Conall's son took up the watch of the well-cut, the fire in the vein was no longer a wonder to the valley. It was a fact of the place, the way the ridge above it was a fact, and the children who grew up within a day's walk of Tobar dhìreach had never known a world where it was otherwise. They knew the two flat stones set across the mouth of the cut, and the low red glow that lay between them if you looked down at the right hour of the evening, and they knew, because they were told it before they could well understand why, that the fire had come down out of a storm and into their great-grandfather's well, and that no other well on the island could say the like.

It was this last claim that other wells began, in those years, to dispute.

There was a household two valleys east that kept its hearth from a black seam of its own, cut into stone so dark it had never wanted for a name beyond the black well, and there was a household further east again, beyond the black well, whose well was young in the way that a spring is young, having been sunk only a father's lifetime before Oidhche an Dealanaich, so that everyone still living remembered its cutting. Both had taken fire from the mason's line in the early years, as every hearth for three valleys round had taken it, freely given and never grudged; and both, as the generations turned, began to tell a different tale of where that fire had first been struck.

The loudest of these tellers was a man of the black well named Tadhg, big in the chest and bigger in the voice, who had grown up hearing his grandmother swear that the crack of the lightning on the night it fell had come from directly over their own valley and no other, and who had turned that swearing, by the time he was a man grown, into something very near a certainty. He had never doubted it a day in his life. He did not doubt it now, at six-and-forty, holding up before a gathering at the black well a stone the size of two fists, dark along one face in a way that might have been fire and might, as well, have been nothing but the stone's own colour.

"There," he said, and turned it so the firelight ran along the dark face of it. "There is the mark of it. My grandmother's mother saw the sky open over this valley, not that one, and here is the stone that took the strike, kept in my family since before any of you were born to doubt it."

No one at the black well doubted it, or said they did not, for it was Tadhg's stone and Tadhg's voice, and both were large enough in that small gathering to leave little room for another opinion. Word of it went out along the paths the fire-bearers walked, as word of anything strange or proud will go, and by the following year there were those three valleys over, at hearths that had never seen the stone and never would, repeating that the black well had the truer claim, on the strength of a story told about a stone none of them had held.

The mason's own household heard it and did nothing.

This was remarked on, in its turn, almost as much as the claim had been. There were those at Tobar dhìreach who wanted to send someone east with the truth of the matter, since the truth of the matter was there for anyone to see: the capped shaft with its scorched lip, black to this day where the lightning had run down the rock, a mark no scattered stone could match for plainness. But the eldest of the household, Conall's son grown grey now at the work his father had left him, would not have it argued.

He had his own reasons, and gave them plainly enough to anyone who asked. He had seen, as a boy at his grandfather Conall's knee, how little a quarrel over a well had ever fed a hearth, and he held to the plain shape of the thing: theirs was the fire, and the fire had been walked out to a hundred houses that did not care two straws which valley the lightning had chosen, so long as it kept burning on their own floor. A dispute carried east would cost three days' walking and buy them, at the end of it, nothing warmer than an argument won. He would sooner spend the three days at the well-cut, teaching his own son the watch, than spend them proving a scorch on a stone to a man who had already made up his mind not to see it.

"Let Tadhg keep his stone," he said. "We keep the well. A man may say what he likes of a fire he did not carry home; it will not make the fire his, and it will not make ours less ours for his saying it." And when his own son pressed him, wanting to know why they should let a false thing stand unanswered, he said only that a fire spoken of by two households was a fire remembered by two households, and that this was no bad thing for a fire to be, however crookedly the remembering ran.

It was not long after that a second claim rose, quieter than Tadhg's and, in its way, harder to answer, for it came without a stone to hold up or a loud voice to carry it. At the young well an old woman began to tell, in the dark half of the year when such tellings are told, that her own mother had stood at the door of their house on Oidhche an Dealanaich and seen the light go down into their own well, newer sunk though it was, and that the mason had only carried fire from his cut because it lay nearer to hand for the carrying, and no other reason. She told it the way the old tell things they have turned over so long they no longer remember whether they were given it whole or worked it out themselves: softly, without heat, as a fact rather than a boast, which is why it travelled further than Tadhg's stone ever did, and outlasted it.

By then there were three tellings abroad in the high valleys, where there had once been one plain fact, and no way left for a stranger passing through to know which well the lightning had truly struck without walking to Tobar dhìreach and looking down at the scorch on the stone himself. Few did. It was easier, and pleasanter, to believe the well one's own grandmother had sworn by, and the valleys settled, without any of them quite deciding to, into three tellings held at once and never set against each other, the way three roads may run to the same market and each traveller swear his own the shortest.

The household at Tobar dhìreach let it stand so. They had the fire. Whatever else was said of it, at the black well or the young well or anywhere a telling might wander to, could not be carried home and put on a floor to warm a child's hands, and it was this, more than any argument, that the eldest man of the line held to when his son asked him, once more and for the last time, whether they ought not answer Tadhg. "Answer him with the fire," the old man said, "the way we have answered everyone else who ever came cold to our door," and after that the matter of the three wells was let alone at Tobar dhìreach, though it did not stop being told, east and south, for as long as there were hearths near enough to hear it.

## II. Of Muirne

The girl who would keep the vein through its last years was born at Tobar dhìreach some forty years after Conall died, a great-granddaughter of his line on the mother's side, in a household grown too large by then to count easily by the fathers alone. Her name was Muirne, and she was given, almost as soon as she could be trusted on her feet, to the woman whose task it had long been to see that the household's floor-fire never wanted for tending, so that she grew up as much at the hearth as in her own bed, and knew the sound a good fire makes settling for the night before she knew her letters, not that anyone in the valley had letters to know.

She was quick, and she was quiet in the particular way of a child who has been let sit still among grown talk from very young, listening more than she was listened to. By the time she was old enough to be sent to the well-cut on her own, an honour and a chore both, granted only to those the household trusted not to lean too far over the two flat stones, she had already spent half her short life near enough to fire to have opinions about it that older folk found, when she gave them, oddly sound. She said once, watching an aunt feed the floor-hearth with wet wood that hissed and sulked rather than caught, that the fire was not lazy, only hungry for the wrong thing, the way a person turns from bad bread and reaches for good, hungry all the while. The aunt, who had never thought of it so, laughed and told it about the valley as a child's saying, and it stuck to Muirne all her life, so that grown folk who ought to have known better than to ask a girl such things came to her, even young, wanting to know what a fire was hungry for, as though it were a question with an answer only she could give.

She grew, too, in a household that had by then forgotten what it was to be small. Where Neachdan had once fed a single hearth with his own hands and Conall had walked a coal to the nearest neighbour and thought it a long errand, the kin at Tobar dhìreach now numbered enough grown men and women that Muirne could go a full day without speaking to the same face twice, and the fire her forefathers had carried out to strangers was, by her childhood, burning in so many houses along the valley floor that no one troubled any longer to count them. She heard the old tellings at the hearth as every child of that household heard them, of the wedge and the storm and the burning well, and she heard them the way a child hears the lie of the land she was born on, already there before she thought to ask how it came to be.

She took up the true watch of the well-cut somewhat before she was grown, when the man before her, worn out at the work as men are worn by any long watching, began to leave more of the winter nights to her than he kept for himself. No one made a ceremony of it. She simply came to be the one who sat on the two flat stones through the dark half of the year, wrapped against the cold with her knees drawn up as every keeper before her had sat, looking down at the vein in its crack in the rock.

And it was Muirne, more than any who had watched before her, who first let herself see plainly what the fire was doing.

It had burned, by then, for the better part of a hundred and fifty years, Teine na Fèithe, down in the same broken seam the lightning had first found, fed by nothing but its own store since the night it was struck, for no one had ever thought to feed the vein the way a floor-hearth is fed; it was the floor-hearths that were fed from it, a hundred of them and more by then, walked out hearth to hearth across three valleys and the northern moor besides, each one a small child of that single fire. The vein only burned on, low and dark and steady in its crack as it had burned from the first, and no one who had not sat with it through many winters running would have marked the change in it from one year to the next. Muirne sat with it through many winters running.

She learned, in those years, the small offices of the watch as her forebears had learned them: to lay a broken branch across the mouth of the cut when the wind ran hard down the valley and threatened to worry the flame thin, though she never once fed the vein itself, for that was not the watch's work and had never been; to keep children back from the two flat stones with nothing sharper than a raised hand and a word, the way she herself had once been kept back; to sit still enough, on the coldest nights, that a fox might cross within a spear's throw of her and never know she was there. It was slow work, and lonely work for long stretches of it, and she came in time to prefer it to the crowded warmth of the floor-hearth, where a dozen voices talked over one another and no one voice could be heard clearly. At the well-cut there was only the fire and the wind and, eventually, her own thoughts, turned over slowly the way a knapper turns a flint nodule in his hand, and it was in that quiet, more than anywhere else, that she began to notice what she noticed.

She saw, where her father's father had seen only a fire that had never failed, that the glow between the two flat stones was a little lower each year than the year before. A man rarely marks his own child growing, seeing the same face at the same table every evening, and yet knows well enough, meeting a cousin's child after some years apart, how far the growing has gone; it was in that way, slow and sidelong, that Muirne came to know the vein was failing. She said nothing of it for a long while, for it was a hard thing to say to a household that had built its whole understanding of the world on a fire that did not go out, and she was young yet, and did not trust her own eye against the certainty of her elders. But she kept a private reckoning of it in her own mind, a habit of noticing she never spoke of to anyone, matching this winter's glow against her memory of the winter five years gone, and five years before that, until she could no longer doubt what she saw: that the vein, however slowly, was going the way of any fire that is not fed, and that there would come a night, though she could not have said which, when it would go the whole way and not come back.

## III. Of the Last Ember

The wet spring that finished it came when Muirne was near forty, in a year the whole valley remembered afterward for other reasons besides the vein, for the rain that spring stood in the low fields a hand's depth deep and rotted the seed in the ground, and there was hunger enough abroad that the fire's failing was, for once, not the worst thing spoken of at any hearth. But it was spoken of, and by Muirne first.

She had gone down to the well-cut on an evening when the rain had not let up in three days, gone the way she always went, without expecting anything different of the visit than she had found the evening before, and had found the glow between the two flat stones smaller than she had ever seen it and paler, a red gone the colour of an old bruise rather than the colour of living heat. She sat with it a long while in the wet, not moving, the way a person sits with someone they already know will not see the morning, and somewhere in that sitting, though she could not afterward say at what hour, the glow went out.

It did not go out all at once, with any sound or sign a teller could make much of. It simply, at some point in the dark and the rain, stopped being there, and when Muirne put her hand down into the cut, careful as she had been taught to be careful of a fire that might still bite, she felt only wet stone, cold under the rain the way any stone is cold, and knew before she climbed back up into the storm that the fire the mason had carried home out of the lightning, the fire that had burned in that one crack of rock since before her grandfather's grandfather was born, had burned itself out at last, quietly, with no one there to see the last of it go but her.

She told the household plainly, at first light, for there was no way to tell it that would make it smaller than it was. There was grief in the hearing of it, real grief, though every fire in three valleys still burned bright as it had always burned, fed from floor to floor and needing the vein no longer for its own life; the valley mourned that morning the mark itself, the sign of Oidhche an Dealanaich, gone from the world the way the night was already long gone, kept now only in the telling.

It was not many days before someone said what more than one had already been thinking, which was that the fire might be found again if the well were dug deeper, since a vein that had held fire once might hold fire again, further down where the coloured stone was said to run. It was a young man of the household who said it first, and others took it up quickly, for there is comfort in a task even a false comfort, and digging is a task any strong back can offer a valley grieving something it cannot otherwise mend. Muirne let them talk of it two full days before she spoke against it, and when she did, she spoke standing at the well-cut, with half the household gathered in the drizzle to hear her.

"The fire did not come to us out of the ground," she said. "It came out of the sky, into the ground, on one night only, and it is not for us to go looking after it down where it fell, the way a man goes looking for a knife he has dropped. What is down there now is stone the lightning never touched, and stone the lightning never touched will not answer a maul any better than it answered one before the mason ever struck this seam. We did not make the fire. We will not go digging to remake it."

Not everyone in the household believed her outright, that first morning, and there were those who thought, privately, that Muirne spoke more from fear of disturbing a holy thing than from any true knowledge of what lay under the broken rock. The young man who had raised the talk of digging said as much to her face, there in the drizzle, asking what harm a few strokes of the maul could do a stone already broken once by lightning. Muirne did not answer him with anger. She only asked him, in turn, whether he had ever known the vein to grow brighter for any care they gave it, in all the years of the watch, or whether it had only ever burned as it was struck and gone the way it was going now regardless of what hands were laid on it; and when he had no answer to that, the household took her silence for his and let the matter rest. Whether it was her word that stopped them, or only that the wet spring had left few backs strong enough to spare for a well no one could promise would give anything back, the digging was never begun, and within the season even the young man who had first proposed it had let it drop, the way most griefs are let drop once the worst of the winter that bore them has passed.

## IV. Of the Slab and the New Well

What the household did instead, in that same wet year, was what Muirne herself proposed once the talk of digging had died down: to leave the broken vein as it lay, and cover it.

They chose a stone for it from the same outcrop the mason had cut his own wedges from, long ago, a flat slab broader than a grown man lying full length, Leac na Fèithe that came after to be called Leac na Fèithe, and it took six of them the better part of two days to lever it up the slope and set it down across the mouth of the cut where the two smaller stones had lain since Neachdan's own time. Muirne stood by through all of it, past the years when her own back could have joined the lifting, but she watched each stone's fall as closely as she had once watched the fire, as though the setting of it mattered as much as the labour that set it.

When it was down, and the last gap along its edge packed with turf so that no rain would run in beneath it, she knelt and put her palm flat on the stone, in the drizzle, the way she had once put her hand down into the cut to feel for a living warmth that was no longer there. Leac na Fèithe gave back nothing but its own coldness, and the wet of the day, and she knelt there long enough that those waiting on her began to wonder whether she meant to speak. She did not. She only rose at last, wiped her hand on her skirt, and said that no water was ever to be drawn beside that stone again, not for beasts nor for washing nor for any use at all, and that this, from that day, was the whole of what the household owed the place: to leave it be, and remember it was there.

The black cut the mason had first sunk with wedge and oak maul, the well itself, gave the household no more water after that, though the water in it had not failed; Muirne simply would not have it drawn from so near the covered vein, fearing, though she never said so outright, that a bucket lowered too near Leac na Fèithe might one day come up holding something other than water. A new well was cut that same season, a stone's throw off across the yard, by men with strong backs and no memory yet worn thin enough to make the digging feel like anything more than an ordinary well-cutting, and it gave good water from the first day, cold and clean, the way any well on that ground gives water when it is cut with care. In time it was this well, and not the black cut under Leac na Fèithe, that the household drew from every day of its life thereafter, so that a stranger walking into the yard a generation on would have taken the new well for the old one, and never known, unless someone troubled to tell him, that the true well of Teine a' Chlachair lay a stone's throw off, sealed and silent under a slab no one drew water beside.

Word of the covering went out along the same paths the fire-bearers had walked for generations, though it travelled slower than the fire had once travelled, for a covering is a smaller thing to carry from house to house than a live coal in a clay pot. At the black well Tadhg's grandsons heard it and said little, for there was less glory to be had contesting a stone that gave off no light than there had been contesting a fire that had; and at the young well the telling of the light going down into their own cut went on being told regardless, since a story that had never needed the proof of a burning vein to be believed was not about to be troubled now that the vein no longer burned for anyone to compare it against. The three tellings held on, east and south, long after the one true well at Tobar dhìreach had nothing left to show but a flat stone and a household that would not draw water near it.

Muirne lived on many years after Leac na Fèithe was laid, long enough to see her own grandchildren old enough to be sent to the well-cut in their turn, though there was no fire in it now for them to watch, only the covered stone and the telling that went with it, which she made sure was told to each of them before they were old enough to forget it wrongly. She told it the same way every telling year after year, standing, as Conall had stood to give the rule of the stone, and by the time she was old her telling had become the one the household kept, unaltered, passed down after her the way the fire had once been passed hearth to hearth: a wonder found, and a wonder covered, and a well that gave water all the same.

In her last years she grew slow on her feet and could no longer walk out to Leac na Fèithe in the worst of the winter weather, and it fell to her grandchildren to go in her place and bring back word of the stone's condition, as though it were a sick relation that wanted visiting rather than a covered well that asked nothing of anyone. She would ask them, each time, whether the turf at the edge still held the rain out, and whether any fool had left a bucket standing near it, and was satisfied only when told the stone lay exactly as she had last seen it, unmoved and unvisited by anything but weather. It was, by then, less a duty to her than a comfort, the way an old woman finds comfort in hearing that a door she can no longer reach is still shut fast.

She died in the household's own house at Tobar dhìreach in the fullness of years the valley reckoned long for that country, and was buried, as the custom of the hill-folk was by then, in the ground near the house rather than carried anywhere else, with no coal and no fire laid beside her, for it was the vein's own fire she had kept, not any hearth's, and the vein's fire she had already given, whole and entire, back to the stone. What was left to the household after her was the telling, and Leac na Fèithe, and the new well giving water a stone's throw from the old, and for some years yet, until another keeper rose to take up the office Muirne had made her own, it was the youngest of her grandchildren who walked out to the covered stone in the dark half of the year, knelt, and laid a bare palm on the cold flat of it, the way she had taught them: for what the stone had once held, not for anything it gave back now, and because a place that has held fire is never quite the same, to those who remember it, as any other stone.

# Chapter Four: Of the Snow on the Mountains and the Oak in the North

*VE 227 – 505*

## I. Of Conn and the Rising Water

The Abhainn uaine ran narrower in Conn's grandfather's day, or so it was told at the hearths that summered along it, and narrower still in the day before that. No one who herded the high ground doubted it, for the proof of it lay in the gravel of the river's own bed for anyone who cared to walk it and look.

Conn was born to a household of the upper valley some two hundred and five years after Oidhche an Dealanaich, a fair way inland of Tobar dhìreach and higher up than any household cared to winter, and he grew, as his father and his father's father had grown, following sheep and a scatter of small dark cattle up into the high pastures each year as the snow drew back off them. It was slow, patient work, not glad work and not grim either, the kind that asks little of a man beyond a good eye for weather and the willingness to walk further than he is tired. He had both. By the time he was a young man grown he could tell, looking at the colour of the light on the tops before dawn, whether the beasts would want driving down before noon, and he was seldom wrong, and the older herders of his kin let him choose the ground more often than his years alone would have earned him.

The snow that mattered to Conn was the old snow, lying all the year round in the high corries under the shoulder of the central mountains and fed the river below with its melting, thin in winter when the frost held it fast and full and cold and loud in the first weeks of summer when the sun at last found it. His grandfather's telling held that the snowfields had once come down further, close enough that a man driving cattle to the high grass in an early year might still find drifts of it lying in the shadowed clefts as late as midsummer. In Conn's own boyhood the same clefts showed bare rock by the turn of spring, and every year of his growing the white seemed to draw back a little further up the mountain's shoulder, leaving more grass than before, and more water running down off it than the grass alone could well explain.

He did not think much of the reason for it. A young man following beasts has little use for reasons; he has use only for the ground he is on and the ground he means to reach before dark. But he noticed, the way a herder notices everything about the country he crosses year on year without troubling to ask why, that the river's own bed was widening under him, and that the banks he had walked as a boy were not always the banks he walked as a man.

It was in his twenty-fifth year, the year his kin reckoned by the wet spring that drowned half the low pasture, that Conn first laid hearth-stones on the gravel terrace above the river's summer bend, a day and more up from where the household wintered, in a stretch of ground his father had used before him and his father's father before that. He built the ring the way it had always been built there: a flat stone at the back to break the wind off the water, smaller stones set round in a half-circle, the whole of it a stone's throw above the river's edge and well above, so every herder before him had judged, any water the Abhainn uaine could reasonably be expected to send against it.
