He kept a coal there from the household's own fire, carried up in a clay pot banked in ash the way every fire on that ground was carried since the mason's day, and he slept by it through the short nights of high summer with the beasts grazing loose around him and the water running on below.

The river rose against him twice in the years he kept that ground. The first time was a small thing, a wet week in an ordinary summer that sent the water a few feet up the shingle and no further, enough to wet the lowest stones of his fire-ring and no more, and he moved his hearth back a body's length without much thought and built it again exactly as before. The second time was not small.

It came in his thirty-fourth year, in a summer that had begun hot and dry and then broken all at once into a run of days when the cloud sat on the high ground and did not lift, day after day, until even the oldest of the household said they could not remember its like. Conn was two days up from the winter ground with the beasts when the water began to climb. He woke on the third morning of the cloud to a sound under the ordinary sound of the river, a deeper note that had not been there the evening before, and came out from under his hide to find the water already at the lowest of his fire-stones, brown and thick with everything it had torn loose above him, carrying whole branches down at a pace no man could have outrun on the bank.

He had time, though not much of it, and he used it the way a man uses time he does not trust to last: he raked the coal out of the ring first, before anything else, into the clay pot, packed it round with cold ash from the rim, and only then began driving the beasts up off the terrace to the higher shelf behind it, shouting and slapping at the slowest of the dark cattle with the flat of his hand until they moved. The beasts he got up; the fire-ring stayed where it was, and by the time he turned to look back at it, from the higher ground with the pot held against his chest, the water had already taken the lowest stones under and was working at the second row, and by evening, when the cloud broke at last and the river began at last to fall, there was nothing left of the ring he had built at the start of that year but the flat stone at its back, half buried now in silt, with a scour mark on its face showing how high the water had stood.

He built again above it, on the higher shelf where he had driven the beasts, and that ring held through every summer he kept the ground after. But he did not fill in the lower one, and he did not let his sons fill it either, when in his old age he walked that stretch of the river with them and showed them where the water had been. He left the old stones where the flood had left them, half sunk in gravel a stone's throw below his own hearth, and beside them, further down still, a third ring older than either, that his father had shown him in the same way his father's father had shown it: three rings of fire-stones on three shelves of the one terrace, each a little higher than the last, each set there in its own year by a man who had judged, as carefully as Conn himself had judged, how far the water could reasonably be trusted not to come.

"The river climbs," Conn told his sons, standing among the three rings with the water a long way below them all that year, low and clear and ordinary, giving no sign that it had ever meant them harm. "It has climbed in my father's life and it climbed again in mine, and I do not know why, only that the high snow gives it more water each year than it gave the year before, and that a man who builds his fire by a river's edge builds it where the river was, not where the river is."

His sons kept the highest ring after him, and moved higher again in their own time, for the water climbed a little further even in their lives, though never again all at once as it had climbed against Conn. Conn died in his sixty-second year, an old man for that hard country, at the household's own hearth in the low valley. It was the high ground and the three rings on it that his kin remembered him by, and travellers who came that way in years after, following the same summer track up the Abhainn uaine, were shown the terrace and told, in as many words as the teller cared to give it, that a man once built his fire there three times over, each time a little further from a river that would not stay where a man could trust it.

## II. Of Eachna and the New Hearths

West of Conn's high pastures, down off the shoulder of the massif and out onto ground that opened flatter and drier than the herding country, there was in those generations no hearth at all. It was good grazing, level enough to run on without looking at one's feet, watered by a burn that ran clean the year round, and it stood close enough to Tobar dhìreach that a fast walker might cover the distance between dawn and midday. But no household had settled there, for a valley that has water and grass and no fire of its own is a valley people pass through on the way to somewhere else, and not a valley people stay in.

Eachna's household changed that, in the year she came into the fullness of her own judgement, some two hundred and eighty years and more after Oidhche an Dealanaich.

She was born to a household some way south of Tobar dhìreach, one of the many by then that kept a fire lit from the mason's own, carried to them hearth by hearth in the generations since Ailbhe had first walked it outward, and she grew up knowing the fire the way every child of that country grew up knowing it, as a thing fed and watched and never let go dark, without troubling to ask where the first of it had come from. What she wanted, from an early age, was ground of her own, good open ground for a household rather than a corner of her father's, and by the time she was a young woman she had already walked the flatter country to the west more than once, looking at it the way a woman looks at a thing she means, in time, to have.

She took her fire from Tobar dhìreach the year she went to settle it, walking the day's distance with a coal from the line's own hearth carried in a pot the way every fire on that ground had been carried since the mason first carried his. The household that gave it to her asked nothing beyond the giving; it had been the mason's own rule, kept by his son and his son's son after him, that a fire asked for was a fire given, and by Eachna's day the rule was old enough that no one thought to question it. What she did not carry away, and did not ask for, was any piece of an gual dathach. The line kept that apart, as it had kept it since the vein was covered: the fire it gave to other hearths was ordinary fire, burning ordinary fuel, Teine a' Chlachair and no other, and no hearth beyond the line's own ever burned, in those years, so much as a sliver of what Neachdan had carried home under his cloak.

Eachna's first fire on the new ground was laid on a bed of pine brought down from the higher slopes and heather cut and dried through a summer for the purpose, the pine for its quick catching and the heather to hold the heat once caught, banked the way every careful hearth by then was banked, on stone rather than bare turf, for that lesson too had gone out from the mason's own household by her day and travelled as far and as freely as the fire. Round the hearth, in the seasons after, lay the ordinary leavings of an ordinary household's fire: scrapers of grey flint worked from stone carried up from the burn-bed, split and cracked for the marrow in them, the bones of red deer taken on the moor above, a scatter of hazel shells from nuts roasted whole in the embers. No coloured stone lay among them, then or for a long while after, and any traveller who came to that hearth in the years after and dug in the ash of it would have found nothing to mark it out from any other fire of that age, save that it was well kept and long kept, the household growing round it year on year as Eachna's own children and their children stayed on ground their mother had chosen rather than moving on.

The place took its name from the ground before it took any name from Eachna, called simply the straight field by those who first worked it, for it lay level and true between the burn and the rise behind it in a way that little ground on that broken country did; and it kept that name, Achadh dhìreach, after the households round it had grown too many to count by any one head, well after Eachna herself was gone from it.

In her old age it was said of her household, once it had grown large enough to be spoken of as more than one woman's fire, that its hearths kept the beasts closer in at night than the herding kin further up the valley troubled to, for the deer that came down off the moor in the dark months to browse the low ground had grown bold in a country still thin of houses, and more than one calf had been lost to nothing worse than a beast wandering too far from the firelight in a black night. Eachna's sons took to hunting the deer by torch after dark rather than waiting on daylight, a burning brand carried low and a second man behind with a spear, working the herds back from the standing crop toward the burn where the ground was open enough to see them by; it was slow work and cold work, and it did not always answer, though it answered oftener than watching alone had, and it kept, through Eachna's own lifetime and some way past it, more calves alive through the dark months than the valley had thought to expect.

Eachna lived to see her hearth become three hearths and then five, the straight field filling the way a valley fills, household by household, as sons and daughters married out and stayed near rather than moving off, each new hearth lit in turn from the one before it, back in an unbroken line to the coal she herself had carried from Tobar dhìreach as a young woman with more will than patience. She died at Achadh dhìreach in her sixty-eighth year, by her own hearth among her own grown children, and the fire she had carried burned on there after her the way every fire on that island by then was expected to burn on, tended by hands that had never seen Tobar dhìreach and never would, and owing it nothing beyond the memory of where the first of it had come from.

## III. Of the Birch That Went and the Oak That Came

It is the grandmothers who keep this part of the telling, more than any single deed of any single household, for it happened the way the snowfields drew back on the high ground: too slowly for any one generation to say they had seen it happen, and plainly enough that three generations set together could see that it had.

The old women of the northern heath, in Eachna's day and after it, told it this way to their grandchildren, sitting by fires their own grandmothers had never known: that when their own grandmothers were girls, the ground north and east of the high valleys had stood thick with birch, pale-barked and quick-grown, and with pine among it on the drier rises, and little else beside heather and the low scrub that birch and pine will suffer to grow beneath them. Fuel from that country was thin fuel, quick to catch and quick to burn away, and a household that wintered near it kept its fire hungry through the cold months and grudged every armful it fed to the flame.

By the time those same grandmothers were themselves old, the telling went, the birch had thinned in places and gone from others altogether, and oak stood where it had stood, broad-crowned and slow-grown, with hazel thick beneath it wherever the light broke through, and the ground under both smelled different in autumn than it had ever smelled under birch alone, of leaf-mould and the sweet rot of fallen mast rather than the thin dry smell birch leaves give as they curl. Fuel from oak was better fuel, slower to catch but far slower to burn away, holding a fire through a night that birch alone would have starved by midnight, and a household that had oak within a morning's walk kept a warmer hearth for less carrying than a household that had only birch, or so every grandmother who told it agreed, whatever else she disagreed on.

No one could say, in Eachna's day or after, why the one tree should give way to the other over so wide a country, or how long the giving-way had truly taken, for it was not a thing any single teller had watched from its beginning to its end, only a thing each teller had watched a portion of and heard the rest from a mother or a grandmother who had watched the portion before. The northern grove that stood furthest into that changing country, far past any household's grazing, was oak already by the time any hearth-teller's grandmother could remember it, standing on ground that the oldest tellings held had once been open heath, bare and windswept, with nothing on it taller than a man's waist; and by Eachna's grandchildren's day it was oak grown tall enough that a man walking under it in summer could not see the sky for the leaves of it, and the ground beneath was thick with a mast of fallen acorns that no one troubled, in those years, to gather. That grove kept, among those few who spoke of it at all, the old name of Doire ghlas, though it lay so far to the north and so far from any hearth that most households of the high valleys had never seen it and never would, and knew it only as a word in an old woman's telling, a place where, it was said, the trees had once been different, and had changed themselves without asking leave of anyone.

What the change meant, if it meant anything at all, no teller of those generations pretended to know, and the wiser grandmothers did not pretend either. They told it as they told the snowfields drawing back on the high ground above Conn's country, as a thing the world did in its own time and by its own reckoning, neither for the comfort of the households that lived through it nor against them, only alongside them, the way the seasons went alongside a life without ever once asking how that life was going.

## IV. Of Luag and the Bare Horn

The households of the northern heath knew, by the time Eachna's grandchildren were grown, that the island did not go on forever in every direction the way a man might once have supposed, from ground he had never left, that it must. Herders following grazing further out than their fathers had troubled to go came back with word of a shore to the north that no fire could be carried past, and of a wind out there that took the warmth from a body faster than any winter in the high valleys, and the word travelled, as word did in that country, from hearth to hearth until it had gone further than any single herder's own feet had carried it.

Luag was the one who went to see, some four hundred and twenty-five years after Oidhche an Dealanaich, born to a household of the northern heath, near enough the changing country of birch and oak that he had grown up hearing the grandmothers' telling of it at every dark-of-the-year fire, and restless in a way that his own household found hard to account for, since nothing in his upbringing had marked him out for restlessness beyond any other young man of that country. He herded, as every young man of that country herded, but he herded further out each year than the year before, following the grazing past where his own kin were accustomed to follow it, until by his twenty-fifth year he had walked ground that no one of his household, so far as any of them could tell him, had ever walked before.

He set out for the horn in the spring of his twenty-sixth year, alone, with a coal carried in a clay pot the way every traveller of that country carried fire, and dried meat and a hide to sleep under, telling his household only that he meant to see how far the land truly went before it met the sea, and that he would be back before the grazing failed. It took him the better part of four days' walking, out past the last households his own kin had word of, out past the last stands of oak and hazel into country that thinned first to birch again and then to nothing taller than a man's knee, heather and low scrub and bare wet ground that sucked at his feet with every step, until on the evening of the fourth day he came up over a last low rise and saw, for the first time in his life, the open sea.

It was not the sea of the sheltered sounds that the herders of the north had told of, grey water with an island's shape somewhere against the far horizon to give the eye something to rest on. This was open water with nothing beyond it that Luag's eye could find, grey under a grey sky, running in long low swells that broke white on a shore of black rock with no beach to speak of, and a wind coming off it that found every gap in his hide cloak within the first few breaths of his standing there, colder than any wind he had felt in the high valleys even in the dead of winter.

He tried, that first night, to keep his fire as he had kept it every night of the journey out, banked in a shallow scrape with stones set round it for a wind-break. The wind came round the stones as though they were not there at all, and took the flame sideways along the ground faster than he could feed it, and by the third handful of dry heather he understood that the fire he had carried four days across the island to look at the sea was not going to live an hour on that ground, no matter how he built it or how he fed it. He let it go out rather than waste the last of his tinder chasing it, and spent that night in the lee of a rock with the hide pulled over his head and his body curled round the cold pot, colder than he had ever been in his life and too stubborn, or too curious, to turn back for it.

In the days he stayed there, walking the shore both ways as far as the light allowed, he found no hearth-stone, no scrap of charcoal, no sign anywhere on that ground that a fire had ever been kept there by anyone, hill-folk or otherwise, and no tree taller than his own knee standing anywhere he walked, though he went some distance along the shore in both directions to be sure of it. The ground was not poor ground exactly, for there was grass enough in the hollows out of the worst of the wind, and he saw the marks of deer on it and the droppings of hares, but it was ground that would not hold a household, he judged, walking it, no more than it would hold his own small fire, open on every side to a wind that never seemed, in all the days he stayed, to fully drop.

He stood a long while, on the last evening before he turned for home, on the highest rock he could find above the shore, looking west, for the wind that beat at that coast came off the water in that direction rather than from the north as the worst of the high-valley winters did, and it seemed to him, standing there with his hide cloak snapping about his shoulders, that whatever weather his own country knew, fair or foul, came first across that water from somewhere further out than his eye could reach. He had no word for what lay beyond it, and did not trouble himself hunting for one; that evening it was enough to stand at the edge of ground he could walk no further along without a boat under him, and know, in a way he had not quite known setting out, that the island his own people lived on had an edge to it, here as much as anywhere, and that this was where its edge lay bare to the weather with nothing between it and the open sea.

In the morning he turned for home, walking the four days back by the same track he had come, and relit his fire at the first hearth he reached, a herding household two days short of his own that gave him coal and a meal and asked, as everyone by then asked a traveller from a strange direction, what he had found out there. He told them plainly: no tree, no hearth, no shelter a household could keep a fire in, only rock and wind and grass in the hollows and, past it all, water going on further than a man could see. He told the same, in much the same words, at his own hearth when he reached it, and again at the gathering of the near households in the dark half of that year, and the telling went from there the way every telling of that country went, hearth to hearth, until most of the northern heath had heard, in one form or another, that the land ran out at last in the north-west, bare to a wind no fire could stand against, with nothing beyond it that any of them had ever seen or ever would.

Luag lived on at his own household's hearth for the better part of fifty years after, herding the nearer ground in his later life as his knees stopped wanting the long walks of his youth, and he was known to the end of his days, kindly rather than mockingly, as the man who had gone to the edge of the world to see what was there and come back with nothing to show for it but a burnt cloak and a telling. He died in his seventy-second year among his own grown children, an old man by any measure the high country kept, and the telling he had brought back outlived him easily, kept at hearth after hearth well after there was no one left who had heard it first from his own mouth: that the island had an edge in the north-west as sure as it had a middle, and that a man could walk to it and stand on it and feel, in the wind that never dropped there, how small a fire truly was against the whole breadth of the weather the sea sent in.

# Chapter Five: Of the Drowned Neck and the First Boats

*VE 506 – 750*

## I. Of Gràinne and the Drowned Neck

There was a time, the north-shore tellers say, when a household could walk dry-shod to Eilean dhubh at any tide of the year, and a time after it when the same walk could be made only at the ebb of the lowest tides, and a time after that when it could not be made at all. No one household watched the whole of that change. Gràinne watched more of it than most, for she was born on the neck itself and she died on it, or near enough to it that the difference hardly mattered to those who buried her.

Her people had kept a hearth on the low neck since before her grandmother's grandmother, on a shelf of dry ground between two arms of shingle where the crossing to the island was narrowest and firmest underfoot. It was good ground for the purpose it was put to: near enough the mainland pastures to run beasts on both sides of the water, and near enough Eilean dhubh itself, where deer grazed thick and unhunted in her great-grandmother's day, that a household settled there ate better in a hard winter than a household settled further inland ever managed. The neck was never a rich place to live, being low and salt-scoured and bare of any shelter but what a household built for itself, but it was never a hungry one either, and Gràinne's people had no reason, through all the generations before her, to think of leaving it.

She was born some eighteen fathers after the mason, as the line at Tobar dhìreach would have reckoned it, the youngest of a large household, and grew up doing what every child of the neck grew up doing: watching the tide. It was not a game to her, though it began as one. Her mother could read the run of a spring tide against the last one the way Conn's people, far south of her, read the colour of the light before dawn, and she taught Gràinne to read it the same way, walking the shingle with her at the top of every high water and setting a stone at the mark the sea had left, so that the next high tide could be measured against it. By the time Gràinne was a young woman she kept that watch herself, without her mother telling her to, because it had become a thing she did not know how to stop doing.

The stones told her what the household already half knew without wanting to say it aloud: that each year's highest tide came a little further up the shingle than the year before's, some years so little that only Gràinne's own eye could have caught it, and some years, after a wet season or a run of westerly gales, a stride's length further in one water than it had taken three ordinary years to gain. Her grandmother's telling held that in the grandmother's own girlhood a household could cross to Eilean dhubh on any day it pleased and get its feet no wetter than the mud always made them; by the time Gràinne was grown, the crossing could be made only within two hours either side of the lowest ebbs, and only then by those who knew which channels ran soft and which ran firm, for the neck no longer dried the same way in every place.

She married on the neck and buried a husband on the neck and raised children on it, and through all of that the sea kept its slow account against the shingle, a stride a year in the bad years and less in the good ones, and never once, in Gràinne's whole life, a stride backward. She would not leave. Her sons asked her to more than once, in the years when asking was still a thing that could be done gently, pointing out that the dry ground behind the shelf ran back further than the shelf itself and that a hearth moved a bow-shot inland would still be a hearth on the neck, still near enough the crossing and the deer and the shellfish beds her household had always worked. She heard them out each time and gave them the same answer each time: that she would move her hearth when the sea came into it and not a day before, for a hearth that ran from the water before the water had truly come for it was not a hearth kept by a people who meant to stay anywhere.

It came for it in her fifty-first year, in a spring of hard westerlies that piled water against the whole north coast for the better part of a month. Gràinne woke before dawn to a sound she had never before heard at that hearth, water moving under the floor of packed earth where her own feet had walked dry every morning of her life, and came out into a grey half-light to find the sea standing in the lowest corner of the house, black and cold and already a hand's depth deep, working its way toward the hearth-stones themselves with each small surge. She did not weep over it, or if she did the tellers do not say so. She raked the fire out into the clay pot her mother had raked fires into before her, and she carried it out past her own threshold for the last time, and she stood on the higher ground behind the shelf while her sons and their wives pulled what could be pulled from the flooding house, and she watched the water find the hearth-stones and put out, in a long hiss she said afterward she could hear over the wind, whatever of the old fire's ash had been left lying loose upon them.

They built the new hearth that same day, on the ground behind the old shelf that had stood dry through every tide Gràinne had ever measured, and she carried the coal to it herself out of the pot rather than let any of her sons do it, and lit it there before dark. She lived twenty-five years more at that second hearth, old even by the reckoning of that hard coast, and she kept the same watch on the tide out of the same habit as before, though by then it mattered less to her personally than it had, for the ground behind the shelf ran back far enough that no tide she lived to see came near it again. But she taught the watch to her grandchildren all the same, walking the shingle with them at every high water the way her own mother had walked it with her, and telling them, in words her household kept long after she was gone from it, that the sea did not forget an inch it had once taken, and that a household on that coast that stopped watching the water was a household asking to wake and find it already indoors.

The deer of Eilean dhubh, cut off from the mainland pastures once the neck stopped drying at all but the very lowest ebbs, grew smaller across the lifetimes that followed, penned as they were on ground too small to feed a herd that had once ranged the length of two islands as one. Hunters who crossed to the island by boat in Gràinne's granddaughters' time, when a boat had become the only sure way across, brought back carcasses lighter than their grandfathers' tellings had led them to expect, and said among themselves, without much wondering at it, that an island shrunk to an island fed its deer accordingly. Gràinne herself did not live to see that told at the hearth; she died at the second house, by her own fire, three fathers after her birth, as the line reckoned such spans, and was buried on the higher ground she had moved to rather than on the shelf that had been her people's for longer than any teller could reckon, which by then lay under the sea at every tide that came.

## II. Of Oisean and the Hide Boat

On the far side of the island, on the south shore where the water ran calmer and the land shelved gently rather than drowning by inches, a young man named Oisean grew up watching the sea for a different reason than Gràinne's people watched it. He did not care what it took. He cared what it held.

Oisean was born some seventy years after Gràinne, to a household of seal-hunters who worked the rocks and skerries of the mainland shore the way their fathers had worked them, waiting for the grey seals to haul out within reach of a spear thrown from dry land, and going home hungry on the seasons when the seals chose to haul out somewhere a spear could not reach. Oisean had watched, since he was old enough to be taken along and told to sit still, the greater number of seals that hauled out on Eilean mhin, the low island that lay off the south coast in plain sight of his own hearth on a clear day, further out than a man could wade and further out, so every hunter of his household had always said, than any boat of that coast could carry a man and bring him back.

There were no boats of that coast, in truth, worth much more than a log a boy might straddle to cross a burn in flood. Oisean's people knew hide, and knew how to stretch it and how to grease it against wet, for every hearth on that shore kept its winter cloaks of sealskin and knew the working of the stuff as well as any household on the island. What Oisean did, in his twenty-third year, was a thing none of his own people had thought to do with that knowledge before him, though afterward it seemed to every one of them a thing that should have been done long since: he built a frame of bent hazel, light and springy, shaped roughly to the outline of his own body doubled, and over it he stretched and stitched hides greased with seal fat at every seam, working alone at first, ashamed to be watched failing at a thing he could not himself have said would work.

It took him the better part of a season to make a hull he trusted to hold, and longer than that to trust himself to sit in it on open water rather than the calm inlet where he had first floated it and found, with some surprise, that it did not sink under him. His household thought him strange for the trying and stranger still when the trying went on past the point where a sensible man would have given it up; but no one stopped him, for it was known on that coast, as on every coast of the island, that fire and shelter were owed to any kin who asked, and a young man's strangeness was his own business so long as it fed no one badly.

He crossed to Eilean mhin in the calm of an early summer morning, alone, with nothing but the paddle he had shaped and a coil of plaited hide should the boat need mending on the far side, and he was gone from his own shore long enough that his mother had begun, by the tellers' account, to walk the beach and watch for him with a dread she did not speak aloud. He came back before dark with three seals lashed across the frame behind him and the boat riding low enough in the water that he had shipped a hand's depth over the gunwale more than once on the crossing back, and he stood on his own shore soaked to the skin and laughing, by every telling that has come down of that evening, in a way his household had not seen him laugh before.

It was, so far as any teller of that coast or any other has ever claimed otherwise, the first time anyone on Dia-thìr crossed open water on purpose, meaning to reach a place he could see but could not walk to, and meaning to come back from it the same day. What Oisean had proved, standing dripping on his own shore with three dead seals and a boat that had not failed him, was a thing simpler than any of his household at first understood it to be: that the water between two pieces of dry land need not be a wall. It could be crossed, if a man built the right thing to cross it in and trusted the building enough to sit inside it once it was afloat.

He did not stop at the one crossing. Within two summers he had built a second boat, larger, with room behind the paddler for a season's worth of dried meat and skins, and he began to camp on Eilean mhin rather than crossing and returning within a single day, staying out among the seal rocks for a stretch of good weather at a time and coming home only when the meat ran low or the weather turned against him. The camp he kept there, a low shelter of driftwood and hide pitched in the lee of a rise above the landing beach, came to be known among his own kin and the kin near them simply as the bothies, and it was kept a season at a time rather than year-round, for no household yet trusted itself to winter on ground with no fresh water of its own and no shelter but what could be carried across in a boat still small enough to overset in a bad sea.

Others followed him across in the years after, first his own brothers and then young men of neighbouring households who had watched the boats being built and reasoned, as Oisean himself had reasoned, that a thing built by hands could be built again by other hands. By the time Oisean was himself an old man, the crossing to Eilean mhin in the calm months was no longer spoken of as a strange thing a strange young man had once done, but as a thing the shore households of that coast simply did, the way they gathered shellfish or dried fish on racks, and the seal-bothies on Eilean mhin stood, each summer, ready to be thatched again and lived in until the weather sent the boats home. Oisean himself crossed and camped there most summers of his life, and died at last at his own hearth on the mainland shore, in his sixty-ninth year, with his grandsons already building boats of their own beside his, each one, so the tellers say, a little surer in the making than his had been, for they had his to look at and he had had nothing at all.

## III. Of Scàire and the Grey Bank

Further along the coast and further north than Oisean ever crossed, the water ran harder and the weather came in worse, and it was there, on the north shore, that a woman named Scàire took the boat further than any of her own people had yet trusted it.

She was born some sixty years after Oisean, into a household that had already, by her girlhood, taken up the making of hide boats after the manner that had spread up the coast from the south, though the boats of the north shore were built heavier and lower than Oisean's had been, for the water off that coast ran seldom calm and seldom warm even at midsummer, and a boat built light for a still southern crossing would not have lived an hour in it. Scàire grew up in those boats rather than merely watching them made, taken out by her father and her uncles from the time she was old enough to sit still and bail, and by the time she was a grown woman she handled a boat in a following sea as surely as any man of her household, which was, on that coast, saying a good deal.

The seals of the north shore did not haul out on any single island a man could reach and camp on in a day, as Oisean's did, but on a scatter of low skerries off Eilean fhada, bare rock standing clear of the water only at the ebb and swallowed whole at the flood, where the grey seals came each autumn in their hundreds to pup on ground no fox or wolf could reach. It was autumn work by its nature, for the seals came with the first of the year's gales and were gone again before the worst of the winter storms set in, and it was gale work by its nature too, for a crew that waited for calm weather to make the crossing waited, on that coast, for weather that autumn seldom gave.

Scàire went out with her father's crew from her sixteenth year, in boats that shipped water over the bow with every third or fourth swell and had to be bailed continually by whoever was not paddling, and she learned, the way every hunter of that coast learned, to judge by the smell of the wind and the run of the cloud which days would let a crew out and back before the gale that was always somewhere behind the weather caught up with them. It was not judgement any teller could set down as a rule, only as a knowing that a body earned by being wrong about it once or twice early and surviving the wrongness. Some years the judgement failed more often than others. The households of the north shore kept, without troubling to set it down as anything more than a shared memory, a rough reckoning of how hard a year had been by how many of its boats the autumn gales had held ashore rather than let out to the skerries at all, and the year Scàire turned thirty-eight stood, in the memory of anyone then alive, as the hardest of that kind: five boats out of every six kept on the beach the whole autumn through, and the seal harvest that year thin enough that more than one household went into the winter short of oil for its lamps.

She herself was master of her own boat and crew by then, her father dead some years and his place taken by her without much argument from anyone, for no one on that coast doubted, by that time, that Scàire read a north-shore sea as well as any man alive on it. It was on one of the crossings of her middle years, out on the skerries themselves with the seal-taking done and the crew waiting on the tide before the run home, that she climbed the highest of the bare rocks to look for the change in the weather her father had taught her to watch for, and saw, lying along the whole northern edge of the sea where sky and water ought to have met in a plain line, a grey that did not lift.

It was not fog as she knew fog, which came and sat on the land in the small hours and burned off with the sun. This lay always in the same place, along the same stretch of horizon to the north and, she came to notice on crossings after, along much of the eastern water as well, never closer and never further, a wall of grey that the brightest day never burned through and the hardest gale never blew away. She asked the older hunters of her own crew whether they had marked it before, and found that they had, in a loose way, the way a man marks a hill he has looked at all his life without ever once asking its name; no one on that coast had gone out far enough, or often enough, or with reason enough to look hard at it, to have made more of it than a grey bank that sat, as it had always sat so far as any of them could tell her, on the sea to the north and east and nowhere else.

Scàire looked at it a long while that day, from the highest of the skerries with the wind coming cold off it and the seal-blood still on her hands, and she did not go toward it, for there was nothing in the going that any purpose of hers required, and the boats she and her people built were built for the work they had, not for a water no one had yet had reason to cross. She told of it at her own hearth that winter and it went from there, as such things went on that coast, hearth to hearth along the shore until most who worked the northern water had heard some form of the telling: that there was a grey on the sea to the north that never lifted, that it stood always where it stood and moved for no wind, and that no boat of that coast, so far as anyone yet knew, had gone into it and come back to say what lay beyond.

She herself went out to the skerries most autumns of the rest of her life, gale years and calm years both, and grew old on that hard water the way Oisean had grown old on the gentle water of the south, dying at last at her own hearth in her sixty-third year, remembered by her own kin less for the grey bank, which by then every household of that coast had heard of and settled into simply knowing, than for the thirty-eight boats she had brought home whole across a working life on a sea that forgave very little.

## IV. Of the Weirs on the Abhainn ìseal

While the two shores learned the water each in its own way, a quieter change was working itself out along the banks of the longest river on the island, where it ran wide and slow through the low ground before losing itself in the sea.

The Abhainn ìseal had never, within any telling that reached that far back, run in quite the same bed for two generations together, spreading itself across the flat ground in wet years and drawing into a narrower, deeper channel in dry ones, until sometime in the years after Gràinne's death it settled, as rivers will when the ground beneath them has finally been worked to its own true shape, into the wide bed that the households along it came to know as simply the river, without further telling being needed to say which one was meant. It was in the side channels of that newly settled bed, the shallower cuts where the current ran gentler and the fish gathered thickest at certain seasons, that the first weirs of hazel stakes were driven.

No single teller is remembered as the one who thought of it, and no single household claimed the making the way Neachdan's household claimed Teine a' Chlachair; it was a thing that seems to have occurred to more than one household along that stretch of river at much the same time, once the bed had settled enough that a stake driven one autumn could be trusted still to stand there the next. The stakes were driven close together across the mouth of a side channel at the season when the fish ran thickest, angled to hold against the current, with gaps left for a man to reach in and take what the current had crowded against the barrier; and when the season's run was done the stakes were left standing rather than pulled, for a household that had once found the right place for a weir saw no reason to find it again from nothing the following year.

They were renewed rather than rebuilt, generation on generation, the households of that stretch of river driving fresh stakes into the same holes the old ones had rotted out of, so that a weir kept by a household thirty years on from its first driving stood, to any eye that measured it against the riverbank, on almost exactly the ground it had first stood on, though not one stake of the original driving remained in it. It became, without anyone remarking on it as a change worth remarking, the way that stretch of the Abhainn ìseal was fished, and children of those households grew up wading the shallows at weir-mending time the way children elsewhere grew up herding, knowing which hole took a stake easily and which fought it, long before they knew why the holes were where they were.

The salmon came up that river in their great runs each year at much the same season the seals hauled out on Scàire's northern skerries, and it was some twenty-eight fathers after the mason, the weirs by then old and well proven, that the households along the river first kept what came to be remembered as a feast of it rather than simply a harvest: households from up and down that stretch gathering at the largest of the weirs when the run was at its thickest, sharing out what the barriers had caught between more hands than any one household's own, and eating, by every account that survived of it, better in that one week than most of them ate in the whole of any other season. No single voice planned it, the tellers say; it grew the way the weirs themselves had grown, out of neighbours finding it easier to work a good run together than to guard it apart.

By then the neck where Gràinne had watched the tide lay drowned at every water, and the seal-bothies of Eilean mhin stood thatched each summer as a matter of course, and boats of one build or another put out from half the coasts of the island in weather that would once have kept every hearth ashore. A traveller of that year, walking the bank of the Abhainn ìseal at the height of the salmon feast, might have seen at the largest of the weirs a boy no older than six or seven wading out with his father's hand steadying him, driving a fresh stake into a hole worn smooth by stakes his father and his father's father had driven there before him, into water that ran, as it had run for longer than either of them could reckon, exactly where the river had chosen, at last, to run.

# Chapter Six: Of the Shell Mound and the Three Strokes

*VE 751 – 820*

## I. Of the Heap at Dunn

On the eastern coast, where the land breaks into low cliffs and the tide goes out a long way over flat rock, there was a heap of shell already old before any of this is told. No one living could have said how it began, and no teller of the hills, then or after, ever went near enough to ask, for the hill-folk and the people of that heap did not go about among one another, and what passed between them, if anything passed, is not told here.

A woman came down to the shore each morning while the tide was out, and worked the rock pools and the wet sand with a stick of bone worn smooth at the grip, and filled a woven bag with limpets prised loose one at a time, each with its own small crack and give, and with the flatter shells that lay half buried at the tideline, and with whatever crab or urchin the falling water had left behind in a hollow. She had done this since she was old enough to carry a bag of her own, following her mother down the same path over the same rock, and her mother had done it before her, and no one troubled to ask further back than that.

What she gathered she carried up a short rise above the shore to where the heap stood, and there she opened the bag and let the shell fall where the heap wanted it, working it in with her foot so that it lay level and did not slide, the way she had been shown. Bones went into it too, seal bones mostly, cracked for the marrow and picked clean and then given to the heap along with everything else, and weed burned black on a fire kept at the heap's foot went into it in its ashes, so that the whole mass of the thing was shell and bone and burnt weed together, layer under layer, each layer settled by the weight of the one above it.

The woman's mother had told her, as her own mother had told her before that, where each kind of shell was to be set and where the bone, and why the burnt weed went in thin and not thick, and why the whole was worked with the foot and never simply thrown; and the woman kept it as she had been given it, without asking herself why it should be kept in that order rather than some other, for it had always been kept so, and a thing kept so long needs no further reason than that.

The work took most of a morning and something of the afternoon too, in every season but the deepest of winter, when the household drew in closer to the fire and lived a while off what the summer and the autumn had put by. In spring the pools ran thick with young limpets easily taken, and the gulls came down onto the rocks in numbers to work the same ground a little behind the gatherers, so that a woman crouched at her work through half a morning might straighten to find the whole shore behind her white with birds, waiting on whatever she left uncovered. In the drier months of summer the low cliffs above the shore carried nests of their own, and eggs went into the bag along with the shell when a ledge could be reached, though never so many from one ledge that the birds did not come back to it the next year; that much, at least, every gatherer on that coast seemed to know without having been told it in words, the way a hand knows not to close entirely round a coal.

The fire at the heap's foot never went fully out. Who had first set it there, or how, no one now living could say, any more than they could say who had first carried a shell up from the shore and let it fall in that one place rather than any other; it was simply a thing the heap had, the way the shore had tide and the sky had weather, and it was kept the way anything is kept that a household cannot do without, fed through the wet months with driftwood carried up from the strandline and through the dry months with whatever scrub grew close enough to spare. In the worst of the winter gales, when the wind came in off the water hard enough to lay a grown man flat, two or three would crouch about it through the black hours with their backs to the weather, feeding it a stick at a time, and in the morning it would still be there, low and red under its own ash, however far the gale had driven the rest of them to shelter.

One such gale, in the woman's own girlhood, tore the roof from the low shelter her household kept behind the heap and drove the sea itself up over the rocks where the gathering was done, so that for three days no one went down to the pools at all, and the household sat close about the fire at the heap's foot with what little was left from before the storm, listening to the wind take whatever it could still find to take. When the gale broke and the water drew back off the rocks it left the shore scoured clean and strange, familiar pools filled with sand and new pools opened where none had been, and the gathering had to be learned freshly over that stretch of coast as though the sea had asked a question and expected the answer found again from the beginning. The fire, banked low and fed through all three days by whoever could be spared to crouch over it, had not gone out; and though nothing was said of that in any words the telling has kept, it was noticed, and it was remembered, the way a thing is remembered that a household has come near to losing.

By the time the woman had a daughter old enough to carry her own bag down to the shore, the heap already stood higher than the woman's own waist along its seaward face, and higher again where the older shell had settled hardest, grey with age and crusted with a growth the newer shell did not yet have. It smelled, on a still day, of the sea gone stale, of weed and old bone and smoke, a smell that clung to the hands and the hair of anyone who worked at it and that none of them, having grown up inside it, ever noticed until they had been away from the shore a day or two and come back to it.

## II. Of the Height of a Man

The years went by the way years go by for people who keep no count of them: by the return of the birds that nested on the low cliffs each spring and left again each autumn, by the runs of fish that came in close to shore at one season and out again at another, by the slow climb and fall of the tide against marks on the rock that every child of that shore learned before any other lesson. The woman's mother grew old working the pools in the cold months long after her hands had stiffened past any real use for the work, unwilling to sit by the fire while there was shell still to be carried, until one winter she did not come up from the shore at the day's end, and was found sitting against a rock with the tide already turning round her feet, gone as quietly as she had lived.

They buried nothing of her at the heap. What was done with her the telling does not follow, for it went on below the rise, among the household's own places, out of sight of anything that would carry the doing of it further than it was meant to go; only that after that day the woman worked the pools alone for a season, and then with her own daughter beside her, and the heap went on growing the way it had grown before, a little higher each year, as though it had not noticed, and in a sense it had not.

For that one season the woman went down to the shore before first light and came up from it after dark, working alone the ground she had always worked beside another, and those who watched her said afterward that she never once let the fire at the heap's foot go lower than she had kept it when there were two pairs of hands to feed it. She did not speak of her mother at the work, then or later; grief in that household, whatever shape it took, took it below the rise and out of sight, and what showed at the heap was only the steadiness of a woman going on with a thing that wanted doing whether she grieved or not.

The daughter, grown near a woman's height herself by then, found once, digging her stick down into an old shoulder of the heap to loosen a stubborn crust of shell, a tool of her grandmother's time worked into the mass below: a scraper of flint, broad and short and struck from the stone in a way that showed, to anyone who set it beside a tool freshly made at the heap's fire that same season, that the hand which had made it had held the stone differently, and struck it at a different angle, and finished its edge by a different kind of working altogether. It was not a strange thing to find an old tool in the heap, for tools went in with everything else once they were worn past use, but this one the daughter kept out a while before she let it go back into the shell, turning it in her fingers and running her thumb along its edge, which was blunted now but had once, by the set of it, been sharp along a line no one now living struck a stone to match. She said nothing of it to her mother that she is remembered to have said, and put it back where she had found it before the light went, and the heap took it in again the way it took in everything given to it.

The heap stood, by the year that the woman herself began to feel her own hands stiffen in the cold months as her mother's had, taller than any of them, higher at its crown than a grown man could reach with his arm stretched over his head, a long low mass along the rise above the shore that could be seen, on a clear day, from boats working the water some way off, a pale ridge against the darker ground behind it. No one had set out to build it to any height. It had simply grown, morning by morning, bag by bag, foot-fall by foot-fall, for as long as anyone could remember and a good while longer than that, until it had become, without any one person meaning it, the tallest thing that shore had.

The day it was first remarked on for its height, rather than simply worked at as it had always been worked at, was an ordinary one: a boy of the household, sent up from the shallows to fetch fire down for a smoking of fish, stood at the heap's foot and looked up its face the way he had never troubled to before, and said, to no one in particular, that a man standing at the top of it could see further out over the water than a man standing anywhere else on that stretch of coast. It was true, and no one had thought to say it before him, and after that it was said again from time to time, when a boat was overdue or a weather sign wanted watching for, that the top of the heap was the place to stand for it; and so the heap that had grown for no purpose beyond having somewhere for the shell to go came, without anyone setting out to make it so, to be used as a place from which to watch the sea.

On other shores of that same coast, in those same years, other households kept other heaps in the same slow way. None of them is this telling's business, save to say that the heap at the eastern shore was neither the largest of its kind on that coast nor the smallest, and that whatever moved the hands that heaped the others moved the hands at this one too, without any of them, so far as anyone can now say, ever comparing their work with any other household's along the whole long line of that shore.

## III. Of the Net-Maker of Cwen

Some way along the coast, where the land turned in on itself and made a wide bay sheltered from the worst of the open sea, another household kept a different trade, and a woman of it who is remembered only as the net-maker worked stone weights for her lines the way her own mother had worked them before her.

She took beach stones for it, rounded ones about the size of a fist, and pecked a groove about the middle of each with a harder stone struck again and again in the same place until the groove was deep enough to hold a cord without slipping, a slow careful work that ruined more stones than it finished, for a stone that split wrong at the wrong moment was no use to her and went back onto the beach with the others. When a weight was finished and true, she did one thing more to it before she judged it done: she cut three short strokes into the stone's face, close together, always in the same place and always in the same order, the first stroke a little longer than the two beside it, the whole no bigger than the width of two fingers laid flat.

No one asked her why she did it, and the telling carries no answer, for there is none to carry. Every stone she finished carried the same three strokes, no more and no fewer, whatever its size or its place on the line, always the same close order whether it was the first weight cut that season or the fiftieth. It was simply a thing she did to a stone once the stone was ready to be a weight and not before, the way a woman elsewhere might finish a pot with a rim pressed by her own thumb, or a scraper with one last stroke along its edge past the point where the edge itself needed it. Whether it was hers alone, or a mark that had come to her from someone before her the way the notching of the groove itself had come to her, no one now can say; only that every weight found afterward along that stretch of shore, however old, carried the same three strokes cut the same way, so that a stone worked a lifetime before her own could be told from a stone worked by any other hand only by the eye that had learned the small differences a lifetime leaves in even the same three strokes cut again and again.

The net itself was her mother's work as much as the weights, plant fibre twisted and knotted by hand into a mesh wide enough to let the smallest fish through and hold the rest, a labour of whole winters spent close by the fire with the cord running through fingers grown hard and quick at it, knot after knot after knot until the mesh lay in coils as tall as a child. For years the nets that household set were short ones, reaching only a little way out from the shallows on either side of the bay's mouth, enough to take a fair catch on a good tide but leaving the deeper water of the channel between them open, and through that gap, on the years the run was heaviest, more fish went than ever came against the line.

In the year the net-maker judged her mesh long enough at last to close the whole distance, she set it across the bay from shallow to shallow in one unbroken run for the first time in that household's memory, staking it through a low tide with every hand that could be spared, the net-maker herself wading the deepest stretch of the channel with the heaviest weights slung at her waist to sink the centre of the line true. The tide came in behind them as they worked, and they finished the last stake with the water already at their thighs, and stood back on the shingle in the dusk to see the whole long line of floats and weights holding steady from one side of the bay's mouth to the other, a barrier where there had never before been more than two arms reaching toward each other and failing to meet.

What came against that net in the days that followed was more fish than the household's smoking-racks could hold, and word of the catch went along the shore the way such word went, so that households some way off came to see the thing for themselves and went home again to lengthen their own nets by whatever means each knew, though none of them, so far as anyone remembers, ever matched the closed line at the net-maker's own bay in that same year. She set her nets across the mouth of the bay in every season after that the fish ran thick, staking the ends where the water shallowed and letting the weighted line hang between, low enough to sit just under the surface where the fish did not see it until they were already against it, work that wanted more than one pair of hands and drew the whole household down to the shallows at both ends of the day, wading out to their knees in cold water to set stakes and gather in whatever the night had brought against the line.

## IV. Of the Three Strokes

The net-maker had a daughter who came to the work early, as children of that shore came early to any work that wanted small quick hands, and who sat beside her mother through whole afternoons watching the groove deepen in stone after stone, the same patient strokes falling in the same place until the stone gave way and took the shape wanted of it. She learned to judge, before she was trusted to peck a groove herself, which stones would split true under the working and which would shatter wrong however carefully they were struck, a judgement her mother never troubled to put into words and that the girl came to only by watching enough stones ruined and enough stones finished to feel the difference in her own hands before she could have said what the difference was.

It was longer still before her mother let her cut the three strokes, for a weight badly grooved could be reworked or set aside with little lost, but the strokes were cut only once, on a weight already finished, and a bad cut there spoiled a stone that had cost a morning's careful work to bring that far. The girl watched her mother's hand do it a great many times before she was given a stone of her own and the smaller flint used for the cutting, and was shown, without being told in any words the telling has kept, where the first stroke began and how long it ran and at what small angle the two beside it were meant to fall, close enough together that a glance took in all three at once and none as its own mark apart from the others.

Her first attempts went wrong the way a child's first attempts at any close work go wrong, the strokes too long or too short or crossing where they should have stood apart, and each spoiled stone went back to the pile of stones not yet fit to be weights, without anger and without much comment, for every hand at that work had spoiled stones before it made good ones and the girl's mother had spoiled her own share in her time. The girl kept at it through a good part of a year, cutting the three strokes on stone after stone in whatever quiet hour her mother judged she could be spared from the heavier work of the nets, and each time she looked harder than the time before at the depth and the angle and the closeness of the cuts, holding the flint the way she had watched it held rather than the way that first came easiest to her own hand.

On a morning in the calm weather that closed one summer of that stretch of years, she cut three strokes into a finished weight and held it up to the light the way she had seen her mother hold a hundred stones up before her, turning it so the low sun caught the grooves and threw a small shadow along each one, and found nothing in it that her eye, trained now to the fault, could fault. Her mother took it from her without a word and turned it the same way in the same light, and gave it back, and said nothing more than what her hand did next, which was to take up another stone from the unworked pile and set it down before the girl for the next one.

From that stone onward she kept a way of turning a finished weight over in her hand before she set it down that her mother had never quite had, holding it a breath longer in the light than the work itself required, as though the three strokes, once she had learned to cut them true, had become a thing worth looking at for its own sake and not only for the weight's sake.

Her mother grew old at the work in the years after, her eyes going first, so that she gave over the finer judging of a stone's fitness to the daughter's sharper sight some while before her hands themselves failed her, and the daughter took up the whole of the weight-cutting in her own right well before she had any daughter of her own to sit beside her and watch the groove deepen in stone after stone. She kept the strokes as she had been given them, the first a little longer than the two beside it, the same close order every time, on every stone she ever finished from that year to the end of her own working life; and when in time she came to teach the cutting to a child of her own, she taught it exactly as it had been taught to her, without adding to it and without troubling to explain what, if anything, it stood for, for there was nothing more to give than the shape itself and the knowing of it complete.

The weight the girl had cut went onto the net with all the others that season, indistinguishable among them to any eye but her own and her mother's, one more small stone among a great many doing the same plain work at the edge of a bay that had held a household at that work for longer than either of them could reckon; and if it were possible to lay every weight ever cut on that shore out in a single row, the three strokes on each would run the same close order down the whole long line of them, stone after stone, hand after hand, the one mark on all that coast that any of them ever troubled to make the same way twice, for no other reason that the telling keeps than that it had always been made so, and that having a shape to give a finished thing was itself, it seems, a kind of answer to something none of them ever asked aloud.

# Chapter Seven: Of the Boy Who Asked

*VE 821 – 889*

> *Tha spiorad fa leth san speur, san talamh agus sa mhuir. Meascaich na spioradan agus bidh iad uile-chumhachdach.*
> The sky, the earth and the sea each carry their own spirit. Merge the spirits, and they become almighty.
>
> — Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich, as Clann a' Chlachair keeps it

*The Second Part: Of the Question in the Grove, and the Gold on the Sea*

## I. Of the Pot and the Bag

At Tobar dhìreach the hearth had not gone dark since Oidhche an Dealanaich, and after some thirty fathers no one troubled to say so any more, the way no one troubled to say that the sun rose. The household had grown the way a good field grows, year on year, until it was less one house than a scatter of houses about the old ring of stones where Teine a' Chlachair had been set down, and the line that kept the ring had a name in every mouth from the high valleys to the eastern hearths, though the name meant no more to most of those mouths than "the people who keep the fire and ask the question nobody can answer."

The fire itself was ordinary enough to look at: peat and birch and whatever else the year gave, banked low at night and built up at morning, the same as any hearth from the coast to the moor. What set it apart from every other hearth on the island, the household said, and had said for so many generations that the saying had worn as smooth as a much-handled stone, was that it had never once been struck new. It had come down, coal to coal, unbroken, from the storm that had put it into Neachdan's well; and to keep that unbroken thread alive, one woman of the line at a time kept a clay pot near the ring, banked with ash of its own, in which a single ember of the old fire was never let go out, so that even if the whole wide hearth should somehow die in the night — which it never had, but the women who kept the pot did not build a custom on what had never happened, they built it on what must never happen — there would still be, in the little pot, enough of the mason's own fire to light the hearth again from that one ember, and owe nothing to any neighbour's fire for it.

The pot had a name in the household, though not, in those years, one the wider hills had troubled to learn: they called it simply Poit an Teine, and the woman who kept it, the keeper of the pot, and both titles had passed, mother to daughter or aunt to niece as the fires of a household usually pass, through more hands than the household could easily number by then. In the year this telling opens, the keeper of the pot was an old woman known to her own kin only as the old woman of the pot, for she had outlived every teller who might have troubled to fix a better name to her; and it was into her charge, and after her into the charge of a woman named Fionnghuala, that the pot came down.

There was a second thing kept at Tobar dhìreach that the wider hills knew a little better, because children carried word of it home from visiting cousins the way children carry word of anything strange and bright. This was a leather bag, worn soft at the seams, that held seven pieces of stone unlike any stone dug from any other ground on the island. Black, one of them was, and took a polish like still water at night. A second had a sheen of gold on it, so that it seemed, held to the light, to hold a small still sea inside it. A third was flecked all through with points of white, like a hard black sky full of small stars. A fourth had a gleam of silver under its black; a fifth was the deep red-brown of an old oak's heart; a sixth held the colour of flame itself, red and gold together, moving in it as flame moves when it is turned; and the last was a colour no one at Tobar dhìreach had ever agreed how to name, for it changed as it was turned, gold to green to a blue no sky ever wore, and back again, never twice the same, the way oil sits on the top of still water and shows every colour there is without keeping any of them. This last piece the household called, when it called it anything, the rainbow piece.

The pieces had come home in Neachdan's own tunic on Oidhche an Dealanaich, part of the same breaking of stone that had let the fire into the world; and being pretty and being useless — they had been tried in the fire, long before, and had burned low and dark and given up their colour to the flame like any other coal, and no one troubled the trying twice — they had passed, in time, out of the keeping of the elders and into the hands of the children, the way a household's outworn treasures generally do. Every child born at Tobar dhìreach for as long as the pieces had been kept there had, at some point in a short and undistinguished life of being minded by an older cousin while the grown households worked, tipped the bag out on the hearthstone and set the pieces in a row, and turned them to the fire to watch the colours move, and lost interest in them by the time the next meal was called, the way children lose interest in anything that does not need feeding or chasing.

That was the whole history of the coloured pieces, so far as the household of Fionnghuala's girlhood understood it: a wonder found with the fire, tried once as fuel and found no better than any other coal, kept afterward because throwing away a thing that had come with the lightning felt, to every keeper who had ever considered it, an unlucky sort of economy. No one at Tobar dhìreach, in all the generations between the mason and the boy this telling is about, is remembered to have asked why the pieces were coloured at all, when the coal of the common hills was not; or if any had asked it, the asking had died with them and left no mark on the telling, the way most questions do.

## II. Of the Question

Diarmad was born at Tobar dhìreach some thirty-four fathers after Conall, the third child and second son of Fionnghuala, who was by then some four-and-twenty and not yet keeper of the pot, that office still resting with her own mother's sister, the old woman the household called, without much ceremony, the aunt. He was a quiet child by the account of those who remembered him quiet, and by all other accounts a child who asked more than his fair share of questions even for a child, which is a kind of creature that asks a great many; but the household had raised enough children by then to have a settled patience for it, and most of what he asked — why the geese went, why the salmon came, why the frost took some plants and spared others — got him a plain answer or an honest "no one knows that," and the matter closed there the way such matters generally close.

He was seven years old, in the summer of his seventh year, when he tipped the bag out on the hearthstone one wet afternoon with two cousins for company, and set the seven pieces in their row as every child before him had set them, and turned them, one after another, to the low grey light coming in at the door. It was a game he had played a dozen times before without it meaning anything more than an idle afternoon. This time, holding the black piece up and turning it so its polish caught what light there was, he asked the aunt, who was working wool by the same hearth and paying the children the same half-attention she paid the weather, why it was that this stone had colour in it and the coal from the cutting on the hillside, which she burned every day of her life, did not.

The aunt did not know, and said so without much thought, the way she would have said she did not know why the frost took some plants and spared others; and that, on any other afternoon with any other child, would have been the end of it. But Diarmad set the black piece down and picked up the gold-sheened one and asked the same question of that, and then of the silver one, and then, turning the rainbow piece so the colour ran gold to green and back, asked it of that piece hardest of all, for it seemed to him, he said afterward more times than the telling can count, the strangest of the seven and therefore the one most owed an answer. By then the aunt had given over three or four answers of the "no one knows that" kind and found the child unsatisfied with every one of them, and she said at last, not unkindly, only with the weariness of a grown woman whose wool has stopped taking her attention, that the stones were coloured because the sky had made them so on the night it sent the fire, and a boy who wanted a better answer than that could go and ask the sky.

It was meant, by every account the household later gave of it, as the kind of thing said to close a matter, not open one. Diarmad took it, by every account he himself is remembered to have given, as an answer worth pursuing.

## III. Of the Years of Asking

He did not go and ask the sky, being seven, and having some idea, even at seven, of where a question could sensibly be carried and where it could not. He went instead, over the years that followed, to everyone at Tobar dhìreach and beyond it who might plausibly know a thing that his own household did not, and asked each of them, in his own words and in his own time, why the coloured pieces held colour when no other stone on the island did.

The oldest of the line, a bent man who had buried more of his own kin than he had living, told him only that the fire had come from the sky and the pieces with it, and a thing that comes from the sky need not answer to a boy why it looks as it looks. The fire-bearers, the men and women whose office it still was, in those years, to carry a coal in a clay pot to any household that asked one, and who therefore travelled further and saw more of the island than most, gave him one true morsel among the rest: a woman among them had heard, from a household three valleys over, that colour in a stone was only the same colour the eye puts into a rainbow, no more real than a rainbow is, and vanishes the same way when you go close enough to look. This pleased Diarmad not at all, for he had gone close enough to look at the pieces a hundred times and their colour had never once thinned for the looking. Travellers passing through on their way to somewhere else, strangers with no stake in the household's pride and therefore, he reasoned, no reason to fob him off with an answer meant only to be rid of him, gave him, from most of them, either a shrug or a longer answer that amounted, when turned over, to the same shrug dressed in more words.

He took to carrying the rainbow piece with him, in a small bag of its own hung at his belt, from about his tenth year onward, and the household grew used to seeing him turn it in whatever light was going: the low red light of the hearth of an evening, the white light of noon on a clear day, the flat grey light of the rain, which he seemed, if anything, to prefer, for he was known more than once to sit out under the eaves in a shower with the piece held bare to the wet, turning it slowly, watching to see whether the rain drew the colour out of it or only lay on top of it the way rain lies on any other stone. It lay on top of it. He noted this, in the way a child notes a thing he means to come back to, and went on asking.

By his thirteenth year the asking had become, without his quite meaning it to, a settled feature of the household's talk, the kind of thing a family jokes about the way it jokes about an old dog's habits or an uncle's temper. "Diarmad's question," the valley began to call it, and the phrase travelled further and faster than any answer ever had; a fire-bearer from Tobar dhìreach arriving at a strange hearth with a coal in her pot might be met, before the coal was even set down, with someone asking, half in earnest and half to raise a laugh from the rest of the house, whether she had brought word yet of why the pieces were coloured, for the boy at Tobar dhìreach was still asking, was he not, and had anyone yet given him an answer that stuck. It was said, for the most part, the way a valley says most things about its own, with more affection in it than the words alone would suggest to a stranger. But it was said often, and a joke said often enough wears a groove, and by the time Diarmad was old enough to notice the groove for what it was, he had been the valley's fondest jest for longer than he could clearly remember not being it.

His mother did not always find it so fond. Fionnghuala had taken the office of keeper of the pot in her two-and-fortieth year, the aunt having died the winter before at a good age and by a quiet death, and she kept it, by every account, with the same close attention she had always given her son's asking, neither of which she was minded to have laughed at in her hearing. There is a telling kept at Tobar dhìreach still, worn thin with retelling, of an evening when a cousin by marriage, newly come into the household and not yet schooled in its ways, made the joke of the coloured pieces once too carelessly at the hearth, in front of a full house and in front of Diarmad himself, who by then was near enough grown to feel a joke land where a child does not; and of Fionnghuala setting down her work, and saying, in a voice the telling swears carried to every corner of the house though she never once raised it, that a question asked twenty years running by the same boy was not the same thing as a boy who could not let a matter drop, and that she would thank the house to remember the difference, for she had raised the one and would not sit easy hearing him called the other. The cousin, the telling says, made no more such jokes in that house again; the rest of the valley, having no such mother to answer to, went on making them a good while longer, though a little more quietly when word of that evening reached them.

Diarmad, for his own part, seems from every account to have taken the joke and the mother's defence of him both with much the same even temper, neither much stung by the one nor much comforted by the other, as a man goes on with a long walk regardless of whether the weather along it is fair or foul. He kept asking. He kept turning the rainbow piece to whatever light the day offered.
