And by the time he had passed twenty years, with the household's fire and the pieces' silence both unchanged since the day he first set them in a row on the hearthstone, he had begun, without much announcing it, to ask a narrower question than the one he had started with: not why the pieces held colour, which no one on the island seemed able to tell him, but whether there was anyone, or anything, on the island at all that might know.

## IV. Of the Herder of the North Moor

It was a fire-bearer, in the end, who gave him the first thread worth following, though she herself did not know she was giving it, and would have been surprised, the telling says, to learn what came of it.

In the summer of Diarmad's four-and-twentieth year she had gone on the longest circuit the household's fire-bearers still walked in those days, up past the last of the herding grounds and onto the high moor that lay north and a little west of the valley, where the households thinned to a scatter and a fire, once given, might not be asked for again for a generation. She came home some weeks later with little enough to report of the households she had found, for there had been few, and those few had wanted only the fire and no talk with it; but she mentioned, more in passing than as a matter she thought worth much, that one old herder on the moor, a solitary sort who kept more to his sheep than to any hearth, had told her, when she asked the way onward, to keep well clear of a grove of oaks a further two or three days north, for the wind in it, he said, did not blow the way wind blows anywhere else, and a man who camped near it on a bad night might hear it say things a wind has no business saying.

The fire-bearer told it as she had heard it, as an old herder's fancy, the kind of tale every solitary keeper of a lonely ground tells to anyone who will listen, more to hear his own voice than to be believed; and most of the household who heard it that evening took it exactly so, and forgot it by the next day's work. Diarmad did not forget it. More than once over the following weeks he asked her to say again exactly what the herder had said, and exactly how he had said it, until she grew tired of the asking and told him plainly that she had already told him everything there was in it, three times over, and that he would do better to go and hear it from the herder's own mouth if he wanted more than that.

He took the suggestion more seriously than she had meant it. Over the two years that followed he sought out every traveller who passed through Tobar dhìreach from the north and west and asked each of them the same thing: had they heard, in their own travels, of a grove where the wind spoke, or of the old herder who kept sheep near it, or of anything at all that a teller might set beside such a tale. Most had heard nothing. A few had heard something, thinner scraps mostly, an old woman's warning to keep no fire lit within sight of a certain stand of trees, a half-remembered saying that the birds would not roost in it though the ground round it was as good as any for nesting; and one traveller, an old man himself, said he had passed near enough to see the tops of the oaks from a distance once in his youth, standing taller and greener than any wood he knew elsewhere on the moor, and had felt no wish at all to go nearer, though he could not, when Diarmad pressed him, say what exactly it was he had felt or feared.

None of it, set together, amounted to much that a careful man would have called evidence of anything beyond a lonely moor's fondness for its own stories. Diarmad set it together anyway, the way a man who has been asking one question for twenty years learns to set together whatever scraps come his way, for he has long since given up waiting for a whole answer to arrive complete. What struck him, he is remembered to have said at the hearth more than once in those years, was not that the wind in a grove might speak, for winds say a great many things to a lonely ear and he did not think himself fool enough to build much on that alone. It was that of all the tellings he had chased in near twenty years of chasing them, this was the first that had not simply shrugged the coloured pieces off as a matter closed, the sky's business and no one else's. A grove where something spoke, whatever it was, was at least a place where a question might be put and an answer, of some kind, might come back.

## V. Of the Walk

He was seven-and-twenty in the late winter he finally went, old enough by the reckoning of that country to have long since taken a wife and a household of his own, which he had not, being by then a man the valley had grown used to thinking of chiefly as the boy who still asked the question, and finding, most of them, little enough reason to change the habit of thought even though the boy had grown, in every other respect, into something closer to a settled man. His mother was the first of the household he told what he meant to do, for he judged, rightly, that she alone among them would neither laugh at it nor try seriously to talk him out of it; and she gave him, in place of either, the rainbow piece to carry loose in his hand rather than shut in its bag, saying that if he meant to ask his question of a wind in a grove, he had best have the thing itself before him while he asked it, and not only the memory of its colours.

Diarmad set out on a clear morning in the month of the lambs' first coming, walking light, with a small clay pot banked round a coal from the hearth, a small store of food, a cloak against the weather, and the rainbow piece carried, as his mother had told him, loose against his palm inside the fold of his cloak, where his thumb found it without his troubling to look. The way north and a little west from Tobar dhìreach ran first through country he knew, herding ground and the thinning edge of it, and then, by the second day, through country he did not, where the households grew as few and as far between as the fire-bearer had found them, and the moor opened wider on every side than any ground he had walked before.

The weather held fair through the first day and turned, on the second, the way weather turns on a high moor without much warning given for it: a wind coming up out of the west in the early afternoon, cold and steady, and clouds massing behind it faster than a walking man cares to watch. He camped that night in the lee of a fold of ground with what shelter he could find, and woke before light to a wind grown harder still, and pushed on regardless, for he had counted the days of his walking against the little food he carried and knew he had no days to spare for waiting out weather on open moor.

By the third afternoon he could see, some way ahead across the last stretch of open ground, a dark line along a low rise that was neither heather nor bare rock but stood taller than either, and greener even at that distance and in that light than anything else the moor showed him; and he knew, before any traveller's telling could have told him so for certain, that this was the grove he had walked three days to find.

The gale was on him in full by the time he came under the first of the trees, a wind such as he had not felt even on the open moor, for the moor at least let a wind run clear and did not throw one gust back against another the way the oaks now did, roaring in their high branches and flinging down showers of last year's leaves and small broken twigs in the gusts between. He put his back to the nearest broad trunk he could find, a great old oak fallen half over and caught against its neighbours, and crouched in what lee it gave him, and got, after long blowing at the coal from his pot with his hands shaking from the cold and the wet, a small fire of gathered twigs going in the shelter of the fallen wood, low and guttering and streaming sideways in every gust that found its way through to him.

He sat with his back to the trunk and the rainbow piece turned to the small unsteady light of his own fire, watching the colour run in it the way he had watched it run a thousand times before at the hearth of Tobar dhìreach, while the gale went on through the branches overhead with a sound that was, he thought, turning it over afterward as he turned over every part of that night for the rest of his life, less like any wind he had ever camped under and more like a great many voices speaking all at once and none of them quite loud enough, or quite close enough, to be made out.

Whether that was the truth of the place or only the tiredness of three days' walking working on a mind that had waited twenty years to come this far, he did not yet know. He meant to sit up and listen, all the same, for as long as the fire held and his strength with it, and see what the grove, if it had anything to say, would say to a man who had come this far to ask it.

# Chapter Eight: Of the Keeper in the Grove

*17 an Gearran, VE 890*

## I. Of the Fire Under the Oaks

Three days he had walked, north and west, out of the high valleys where every hearth knew his face and his question both, and into a country that grew stranger the further he went from Tobar dhìreach: the heath thinning, the birch giving way first to hazel and then, on the last day, to oak, standing thick and old in a hollow where the wind funnelled down off the moor above it and never seemed to rest. He had gual bogha-froise loose in his palm inside the fold of his cloak, as his mother had bidden him, though for most of his life he had carried it in a small bag at his belt, and his food was three days gone and his feet were three days blistered, and he came down into the grove at Doire ghlas in the last light with the gale already roaring in the crowns of the oaks over his head.

He had meant, that first evening, only to find shelter and go on looking in the morning, though he could not have said what he thought there was to find. A herder of the northern moor had told him once, in the way men tell a thing they do not quite believe themselves, that there was a grove far to the north-west where the wind talked if a man sat still enough to hear it, and Diarmad had carried that the way he carried every scrap anyone would give him, turned it over on the long road the way he turned the coal over in his hand, and come, in the end, because it was the last thing left that no one had yet laughed him out of trying.

He had been asking since he was seven years old, and he was seven-and-twenty now, and in that whole span he had learned exactly one thing worth the learning: that a question asked often enough stops sounding like a question to the people who hear it and starts sounding like a habit, the way a limp stops sounding like pain to those who have watched a man walk with it for twenty years. The fire-bearers who carried the flame from Tobar dhìreach out to the last farm before the moor only shrugged when he asked them, and said the fire was the fire, colour or none, and warmed a hand the same either way. Travellers who came up from the eastern farms with salt and hides to trade looked at him the way a man looks at a child who asks why the sky is up. The old women at his own hearth, who kept every other telling of the valley word for word back past memory, had patted his head when he was small and, later, when he was not small any longer and went on asking, stopped patting it and started laughing instead, not unkindly, the way a house laughs at the one habit of its own that it has stopped expecting to outgrow. Only his mother had never laughed. She had never had an answer for him either, but she had never once told him to stop asking, and it was the memory of her face, more than any hope of an answer, that had kept the question alive in him after every other mouth in the valley had worn it smooth with repeating.

The trunk of a fallen oak lay along the hollow's lowest ground, its roots torn up in some older storm into a wall of black earth and white wood taller than a man, and in its lee the wind dropped enough that a small fire might live if it was fed with care. He gathered what dry twigs the ground gave him, oak mostly, snapped short, and built them up the way his mother had taught him when he was small enough to sit at her knee and watch her hands do it before his own were old enough to be trusted with the work, a little tent of the driest first and the damper laid to catch after. No new fire was struck. He had carried an ember the whole way, in a clay pot packed with moss, the way the fire-bearers carried it to every hearth from the northern moor to the eastern farms, and he tipped it out now into the twigs and blew until they caught, and sat back on his heels with his hands out to the small heat of it while the gale went on tearing through the oaks above him as if the grove were a thing to be pulled apart.

He took gual bogha-froise out of its hide and held it up before the little flame, the way he had held it up before every fire he had ever sat beside since he was seven years old, turning it slowly so that the colours ran across it and would not settle into any one of them, gold sliding into red and red into a blue he had no better word for, and none of it staying long enough to be named. It burned black-flamed like any other coal when it was thrown into a fire whole, the way the whole seven had burned black the first night the mason ever fed his own fire from the vein; every hearth in the high valleys knew that story, and every hearth had heard, sooner or later, that Diarmad of Tobar dhìreach still asked why the colour went out of it. He thought of none of it now, sitting there warm at last after three cold days on the road, his mind gone as empty as a man's mind goes when the walking is done and the fire is caught; and it was in that thoughtless moment, with the coal turning in his fingers and the small fire streaming sideways in the wind that came down through the roots, that he looked up and found someone standing across the fire from him.

It was the height of a tall man, and it was made of grey smoke, such as a peat fire gives when it is banked low and burns slow through a wet night, and it stood in the middle of the gale and did not stir. Diarmad's own little fire streamed flat along the ground under the wind's hand, the flame laid nearly sideways, the smoke of it torn away as fast as it rose; and the figure across from him stood in that same wind as still as a standing stone, its grey unmoving, no fold of it lifting, no edge of it fraying into the air the way smoke frays into air everywhere else in the world. The oaks roared. The dead leaves went past between them in streams, low along the ground, and not one passed through where the figure stood; they went round it, the way water goes round a rock in a stream, and came together again on the far side.

He did not run. The tellers make much of that afterward, when the tale is given at the hearth in the dark of the year: that a man alone at night, far from any house he knew, with a shape out of nowhere standing in his own fire's light in a wind that should have scattered it to nothing, did not run. He had asked his question too long and been laughed at too often to let a wonder pass him by unquestioned, whatever it cost him to stay and ask it; or perhaps, and this is also told, he was too weary from the road to find the strength for fear. He sat where he was, with the coal still warm in his closed hand, and looked at it a long while before he found his voice, and when he found it, it did not shake as much as he had thought it would.

"What are you?" he said.

"I am Coimhdeach na Fine," it said. Its voice was quiet and very clear, and the wind did not carry it away, though it carried away everything else in that grove that had a voice to carry, the crack of the fire, the roar of the oaks, his own breath when he let it out. "The keeper of the kin. I watch over the people of this island for the one who made them."

"Are you a god?"

"No."

"A ghost, then."

"Neither. I was made out of the smoke of the first coal he woke. I have watched your line since the mason." It was still a moment, the grey of it neither settling nor stirring, and then it said, "You have a question. Ask it."

Diarmad held up the coal in his hand, so that what little light his fire still threw caught the edge of it and the colours moved across Coimhdeach na Fine's stillness the way they moved across everything else he had ever held it up to. "Why are there colours in it?" he said. His voice had steadied now, and there was something in it that had not been there when he asked the boatmen and the fire-bearers and the old women at every hearth from his own valley to the last farm before the moor, something that had learned, over twenty years of being laughed at, not to hope for an answer and to ask anyway. "What are they for?"

## II. Of the Telling

Then Coimhdeach na Fine told him.

It did not tell it the way a teller tells a tale at a hearth, with the shape of a beginning and an end laid out for the listener to walk between. It came to him instead the way a fire comes up in a room full of smoke, all at once and everywhere, so that afterward he could never say in what order he had learned it, only that by the time the grove went quiet around him again he knew it whole, the way a man knows his own name.

He saw sparks flying wide from a coal broken open in a god's hand, and the sparks did not fall. A cold came over him in that seeing, though his own small fire still burned at his knee, the cold of the dark before there was any world to be warm in, and he watched the sparks hang and catch and become, one by one, the very stars that hung now over the roaring oaks above his head, so that when he looked up in the middle of the telling he found himself looking at the same fire twice, once remembered and once real. The weight of hills pressed up out of a black coal by two thumbs was in his own hands as he felt it, though his hands held nothing but gual bogha-froise, no bigger than an egg. A grey sea opened before him with no land in it anywhere, and a last coal held up over the water and let burn, and drops of fire falling from it one at a time into the grey, each drop hissing and hardening where it struck, until a rock stood in the sea, and then a hill, and then mountains he knew the shape of from every ridge he had ever walked, though he had never once thought before to ask how they had come to stand there.

He knew, without being told it in any order he could afterward have set down, that there was more folded into the coal in his own closed hand than the black weight of the ground alone: a colour for the sea and a colour for the air, a colour for the running water and a colour for the blood in a living thing, and last of all the one he held, that took every colour and kept none, holding whatever the other six were only once they were together. He did not see each in its turn the way a teller lays out a telling for a child, one thing and then the next; he felt them the way a man feels the separate aches of a body he has driven too hard on a long road, all at once, none of them waiting politely for the others to be named first. The names came to him afterward, in the days and years he had left to turn them over; that night in the grove he had only the feeling of a great deal folded very small, the way a whole winter's warmth is folded small into one banked coal under its blanket of ash.

He saw people come up out of the heather like grass after rain, blade after blade, too many to count and each its own, blinking in a light they had never yet opened their eyes to, the soil still on their bare feet. He had heard old women call the folk of the island the green grass of the island all his life and thought it only a manner of speaking, the kind of thing said at a hearth because it had always been said; now he saw it, or something that was not seeing and was not less than seeing, and understood for the first time that it had once been meant whole: that the people of Dia-thìr had grown up out of the island itself as grass grows, root and blade together, and that this was the oldest ground of the saying every hearth on the island knew without asking where it came from: *we did not come; we were here*.

And then, somewhere in the telling, though he could not have said where the joy of it turned, he felt something close and hot behind his own eyes that was not the fire's heat, and knew it for shame before he understood what he was ashamed of. He was seeing a hillside torn open by a flood, long before the mason, long before any fire burned on the island at all, and a child of the old godfolk standing in the raw bank with her cloak filled with stones that shone where no stone should shine, gold and silver and white-flecked and red-brown and the black that took a polish like still water at night; and he watched, helpless in the seeing the way a man is helpless in a bad dream, while that whole valley turned the stones over in the sun and struck them together and broke a tooth on one and cut a shape into another and threw it down in disgust, and called them, in the end, the droppings of the mountain, fit for children to play with and no one else, and let the heather grow back over them until there was no one left alive on the island who remembered they had ever been found. It was his own blood in that valley, though bloodlines meant little enough in days before any line was counted; it was his people, whatever people meant so long before there were hearths to keep the count of a people at all, and they had held the whole of what he had spent his own life since he was seven years old asking after, held it in their two hands in the sun, and let it fall back into the ground unasked.

"Was he angry?" Diarmad said, when he could make himself say anything at all. His voice came out smaller than he meant it to, a boy's question more than a man's. "The one who made it. Was he angry, that they let it lie?"

The grey shape across the fire did not answer at once, and when it did there was something in the stillness of its voice that might, in a living face, have been the ghost of a smile. "He was not," it said. "He watched it from his father's hall, and he laughed, as a father laughs who sees his child set aside the finest gift of the feast to play with the wrapping instead. A gift that is not opened is still given. He could wait. The coal was in no hurry, and neither was he."

All that Coimhdeach na Fine told him that night Clann a' Chlachair kept after, word for word, and carried it in time to every hearth in the hill country that would listen, so that within a few lifetimes there was hardly a fire lit from the northern moor to the eastern farms where a child could not say some part of it back before he was old enough to understand what he was saying. It is not told twice here. What is told is only this: that it was long past the middle of the night before the telling was done, and that Diarmad sat afterward without speaking for longer than he had sat in silence in the whole of his walk north, while his fire burned down to a red eye in grey ash and the gale went on unwearied above him, and that when at last he did speak, it was the one question that had followed him three days north and would follow him three days home again.

## III. Of the Riddle

"He hid it," Diarmad said at last. "Why would he hide a gift?"

"So that it would be found," said Coimhdeach na Fine. "He said to me once: a gift that is not opened is still given."

"Then how is it opened? The mason burned the coals and they burned like any coal. We have burned them since, at every hearth in the valleys, and the colours go out of them every time, and nothing is left but heat like any other fire's heat." He held up gual bogha-froise again, though there was little enough light left in his own fire to show its colours by now, only the last red glow under the ash. "How is it opened?"

"Because you burn them all in the one fire," said Coimhdeach na Fine, "and none of them in its own."

Diarmad waited, but nothing followed that could be called an answer to it, not at once; Coimhdeach na Fine only stood as it had stood the whole of that long night, grey and upright and unmoved by the wind that moved everything else in that grove, and after a moment it spoke again, and this time it spoke slowly, the way a man speaks a thing he means another man to carry away whole and unbroken, first in words Diarmad did not know and then again in the tongue of his own hearth, so that he might keep both:

> *Tha spiorad fa leth san speur, san talamh agus sa mhuir. Meascaich na spioradan agus bidh iad uile-chumhachdach.*
> The sky, the earth and the sea each carry their own spirit. Merge the spirits, and they become almighty.

He said the words over once in his own mouth, haltingly, the strange ones first and then the plain ones, to be sure he had them, and Coimhdeach na Fine did not correct him, which he took, rightly or not, for a sign that he had them right. Then he sat with them a while longer, turning them the way he had turned the coal all his life, looking for the seam in them that would open, and found none.

"That is no answer," he said.

"It is the one I was given to give," said Coimhdeach na Fine.

And the wind, which had gone round it all that long night without once so much as stirring the grey of it, went through the place where it stood as though there had never been anything there to go round, and there was nothing there.

Diarmad sat alone by the last red eye of his fire with the two coals of the night in his two hands, the rainbow one that would not light and the three words that would not open, and above him the oaks went on roaring at a wind that had, for the whole of that long telling, seemed to be listening as hard as he was, and now seemed only a wind again.

## IV. Of the Two Days Alone

He did not leave the grove in the morning. When the grey light came up cold and wet through the black branches and found him still sitting where Coimhdeach na Fine had left him, he told himself he would go on looking in the morning; and when the morning had come and gone he told himself the same of the next, because he could not make himself walk away from the one place on the whole island where the answer had stood across a fire from him and spoken, even though it had told him plainly that it had no more to give.

He tried Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich against everything the grove offered him, the way a man tries a key in every lock he can find rather than admit the one door it was cut for is shut to him. Up through a gap in the oaks where the gale had torn the crown from one of them he held gual bogha-froise to the sky, turning it so that whatever light came down through the grey cloud might find it, the way a man holds a thing up to catch the sun; nothing in it changed. Into the black wet earth at the fallen trunk's root he knelt and pressed it, deep as his hand would go, and left it there through the better part of a day, and dug it out again in the failing light no different than he had buried it, cold, dark, and itself. Into his little fire it went, alone this time, none of the other six with it, and it caught black-flamed and low as any other coal, the colours going out of it exactly as they went out at every hearth; he raked it out again with a stick before the flame had eaten more than its edge, and it lay scorched and dark on the leaves, and the colours came back into it only slowly as it cooled. Sky, and earth, and fire; he had none of the sea to try, so far from any shore, and no way, alone in an empty grove with one small coal in his hand, to know what it would mean to try the three at once even if he had had them all.

On the second morning he tried it once more, a way that had not occurred to him the first day: he set the coal down bare on the black wet bark of the fallen trunk and knelt over it and spoke the words aloud into it, both the strange ones and the plain ones, close enough that his breath stirred the ash of his dying fire beside it, as though a thing that had answered to sea-water and open sky and buried earth in the telling he had heard might answer also to a voice alone, if the voice said the right words over it in the right place. The coal lay where he had set it and did not so much as warm. A wren came down out of the fallen trunk's roots while he knelt there, hopped along the bark to within a hand's breadth of the coal, looked at it and at him with its head cocked first one way and then the other, and went off again about its own business in the undergrowth, entirely unconcerned with a god's hidden fire or a man's twenty years of asking after it; and something in the plainness of the bird, going about a wren's morning in a grove where he had spent a night talking with the smoke of the first coal ever woken, struck Diarmad harder than any of his failed trials had, and he sat back on his heels and did not try again that day.

By the second evening he understood, in the flat tired way a man understands a thing his heart has known since the wind first went through the place where Coimhdeach na Fine had stood, that nothing he did alone in that grove was going to open Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich for him. The story was his now, whole and unbroken, more of it than any living soul on the island had ever been given in one night, and the three lines of Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich had been turned over so many times in two days that he could no longer tell whether he was still hearing Coimhdeach na Fine's voice in them or only his own. An answer was not among what he had, and Coimhdeach na Fine had told him, as plainly as it had told him anything, that it had none left to give him.

So he banked what was left of his little fire under turf, the way a man banks a fire he means to leave and come back to, though he did not think, walking away from it, that he would ever stand in that hollow again. Then he took up his coal, wrapped it back into its fold of hide against his chest where it had ridden the whole way north, turned south with the wind now at his back instead of in his face, and began the three days home.

The words came out of him the whole of that first day, aloud where the road let him and under his breath where it did not, the strange ones and then the plain ones, over and over, the way a man says a name again and again on a road so as not to lose it before he reaches the house he means to carry it into: *tha spiorad fa leth san speur, san talamh agus sa mhuir; meascaich na spioradan agus bidh iad uile-chumhachdach*; the sky, the earth and the sea each carry their own spirit; merge the spirits, and they become almighty. By the second day the words had worn a way into him the way a path wears itself into a hillside, so that he no longer had to reach for them; they were simply there, turning under his walking the way the coal turned under his fingers, and he found himself, without quite meaning to, already shaping in his mind how he would say them at his own hearth, and to whom, and what face his mother would make when he told her he had not found an answer after all, only a longer question than the one he had carried north.

The weather turned kinder on the way south than it had been on the way north, as though the grove had kept the worst of the gale for itself and let him go with only ordinary wind and ordinary rain, and he was glad of it in a way he could not quite have explained, glad of the plainness of it, the mud that was only mud and the wet that was only wet, after a night in which nothing had been only itself. He slept the first night on the road under a fold of rock, as he had slept coming up, but he did not sleep well; he woke twice with the sense of a grey shape standing just outside the reach of the small fire he had built, and both times there was nothing there but hazel scrub and the ordinary dark, and both times he lay a long while afterward with the coal held tight in his closed fist before he could make himself sleep again. He thought, walking the second day through country he had barely marked on the way up, so intent had he been then on reaching the grove, how strange it was that a man could carry the whole shape of the world's making folded into him and still feel his feet ache and his belly want feeding exactly as they had before he carried it, as though the story and the body it lived in had agreed to go on about their separate business without troubling each other overmuch.

More than once on that second day his mind went back to the six coals he had not brought north at all, the rainbow alone having gone with him: the black one and the fire-red one and the white-flecked and the silver and the red-brown, all of them kept at the hearth in the leather bag the children still played with when they were small enough not to know better, and it came to him, somewhere on that road, that whatever Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich meant, it was not a thing one man could finish alone with one coal in an empty grove, however many days he gave to trying. It would want the whole bag, and the whole line, and more roads walked than the one under his own two feet; and though the thought should perhaps have weighed on him as one more failure laid on top of the first, it did not weigh that way. It sat in him instead the way the fire itself had sat in the mason's well before anyone thought to carry it home, a thing not yet begun rather than a thing already finished and found wanting, and for the first time since the wind had gone through the place where Coimhdeach na Fine stood he found himself walking a little faster on the road south.

He came down at last into the high valleys on the evening of the third day, footsore and hollow with hunger, with hazel giving way to birch and birch to the bare heath he had grown up on, and somewhere on that last stretch of road, with the smoke of known hearths rising thin and grey against a sky he had walked three days under without once seeing it clear, he stopped saying the words aloud and let them go quiet in him, the way a coal goes quiet under ash and is not gone. He had gone north with one question and come home with a story no one else on the island had ever heard and a riddle he could not open, and he did not yet know, walking down into the valley in the last light with Tobar dhìreach's own smoke rising ahead of him among all the rest, which of the two the hearths would find harder to believe.

# Chapter Nine: Of the Counting of the Fathers

*VE 890 – 950*

## I. Of the Telling at the Hearth

He came down into Tobar dhìreach on the evening of the third day with mud to the knee and his feet gone past aching into a kind of numbness he no longer noticed, and the household that had watched him walk north with a stone in his shoe of a question came out to watch him walk south with something in his face none of them had a name for. His mother reached him first, and old as her eyes had gone she saw before she asked that he had not found what he went for, and something else besides, and she put both hands to his face the way she had done when he was small and fevered, to feel whether the heat in him was sickness or only walking.

"What did you find," Fionnghuala said, the words shaped less to draw an answer out of him than to steady the hand that held his face.

"I found what there was to find," Diarmad said, and said no more of it that night, even to her. He sat by the fire eating what was put in front of him without tasting it, gual bogha-froise still wrapped against his chest under his cloak where it had ridden the whole way, until the household had gone one by one to their own sleep and only his mother sat up with him in the low light, waiting the way she had always waited, without pressing.

It was two nights more before he told it, and when he told it he told it standing, the way a man stands to say a thing he means the house to keep. He had thought, on the road home, that he would tell it the way it had been told to him, but he found before he was three sentences in that no mouth could carry the whole of what had come into him that night in the grove, the sparks that did not fall and the sea with no land in it and the grass-people blinking up out of the heather, not in an evening, not in a hundred evenings; so he told instead the bones of it, the making of the island out of drops of fire let fall from a broken coal held over grey water, the forgotten gift buried in the ground and dug up and thrown away by a valley of grass-people who did not know what they held, and the smoke shape that had stood across a small fire from him in a grove three days north and told him all of it in a single long night without once sitting down. He told them Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich last, because it was the only part of it he had by heart word for word, having said it over to himself the whole road south until the strange tongue and the plain tongue had worn a single path through him: the sky, the earth and the sea each carry their own spirit; merge the spirits, and they become almighty.

There was a silence after it of the kind a house keeps after a death, and then someone at the back, one of the young men of Tadhg's line by marriage who had never once in his life let a chance for laughter go by unused, said that Diarmad had walked three days into an empty grove and talked to the wind, and the wind, being an accommodating sort of listener, had told him whatever he most wanted to hear; and the laughter that followed was not unkind, exactly, it was the same laughter the valley had always kept ready for Diarmad's question, worn smooth from years of use, the laughter of people glad to have their world handed back to them the shape it had always been. Diarmad did not argue it. He had expected the laughter, had walked three days home turning over how he would meet it, and he only said that he had told them what he had been given to tell, and that they might keep it or let it go as they pleased, and sat down again by the fire, and let the talk move on to other things the way talk always does when it has worn out the one thing it came for.

It was his wife who would not let it go, though not, at first, in his favour. Niamh had married him four years before, a strong-handed woman of a hearth two valleys east who had heard of Diarmad's question long before she ever met the man who carried it, and had thought, in the way of a young woman weighing a match, that a man known the length of the high valleys for a single stubborn foolishness might at least be a man of some substance under the foolishness, which had proved true enough in the small ways a marriage tests it, in patience and in temper and in the work of two hands against a hard year. But she had not married a man who talked with the smoke of the dead, and when he told her, alone, what he had not told the whole hearth, the telling in full this time, sparks and grass-people and the shame he had felt for a valley of grass-people he had never met, she heard him out to the end and then said, plainly, that three days alone on an empty moor with too little food and too much cold in his blood could put a great many things into a man's head that had no business being in it, and that she loved him, and that she did not believe a word of it.

He did not press her either. He had learned, in twenty years of asking one question to a valley that had no answer for it, that pressing only wore a thing smoother without changing its shape underneath, and he let her keep her unbelief the way he let the young men of Tadhg's line keep their laughter, and went on saying Aithris a' Chruthachaidh at the hearth, a little more of it each time as he found the words for pieces of it he had not had words for the first night, until there were nights when even Niamh sat and listened without leaving the fire, arms folded, her face giving nothing away, and other nights when she did not.

## II. Of the Fathers' Names

What changed the house was a second thing Diarmad set himself to beside Aithris a' Chruthachaidh, in the second year after his return, a thing that asked for no belief at all, only memory. He began going hearth to hearth among the kin, the near kin and every household further out besides, from the high valleys to the northern moor, any that could claim so much as a grandmother married into the line, and at each one he asked the same plain question he had once asked about the coal, save that this one had an answer if only enough mouths could be found to hold it between them: who was your father, and who was his, and how far back could the house say the names before the names ran out into "an old man" and "before my grandmother's time" and silence.

It was slow work and unglamorous, nothing like a night in a gale with a god's smoke across the fire from him, and for that very reason it won him a hearing Aithris a' Chruthachaidh itself had not. A man who talks to spirits in a grove is easy enough to laugh at over a fire in company; a man who sits at your own hearth of an evening and asks patiently after your grandfather's grandfather, and writes nothing down because there is no writing to be had, only carries the names away whole in his own head the way a fire-bearer carries an ember in a pot of moss, is doing a kind of work every house in the valleys understood and most of them, once they thought about it, wanted done. Old women who had never once troubled themselves over Diarmad's question about the coal turned out to have kept, unasked, four and five names of fathers back, the way a house keeps a worn tool it has stopped using but cannot bring itself to throw out, and were glad enough of someone willing to take the names off their hands and carry the weight of remembering them onward.

He worked at it three years, off and on, between the ordinary work of a household that still had to be fed and warmed whatever a man's head was full of, and at the end of it he could stand at his own hearth and say, without a pause anywhere in it, the whole of the line back to Neachdan who broke the vein and Conall who carried it burning to the first hearth beyond his own, father and father and father, thirty-six names in all, and the few deeds that were remembered with them, Conall's watch over the burning vein and Leac na Fèithe laid over it in the days of his sons' sons, on down to his own father's father's name and his own; and where a house's memory ran out before it reached him, he said so plainly, rather than filling the gap with a name invented to make the line look longer than it was, which his mother told him, when he asked her once whether he should, was the one thing that would make the whole of it worth nothing at all.

He fixed the saying of it, in the end, as a thing said once a year, standing, on the darkest night, rather than told loosely by the fire on whatever evening someone thought to ask for it, the night every household in the high valleys already kept in its own smaller way as the night Teine a' Chlachair first came into the world; and it was on that night, in the year that made five years since his walk to the grove, that he stood at his own hearth with the whole household gathered and every kin-house that could reach them in one evening's walk besides, and said the fathers' names from Neachdan to himself without a stumble, and after him, because he asked it of her before he began and she had not said no, Niamh stood and said Aithris a' Chruthachaidh after him. She had not come to believe it; she said afterward only that a house ought to hear the whole of what its head carried, belief or none, and that a wife who would not say a hard thing for her husband when he asked it of her once in a marriage was no wife worth the name. The recital had no name that night beyond "the fathers' names" or "the Line," said plainly, and the name it bears, Sloinneadh a' Chlachair, came to it only slowly, as names come; but the shape of it was set that night and never afterward broken: the fathers named standing, on Oidhche an Dealanaich, in the order they had lived, with no name added that a house could not answer for.

## III. Of the Trials That Failed

Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich did not sit idle in him all those years, though it did no better for the waiting. He had come home from the grove with six coals still dark in the leather bag at his hearth, the black and the fire-red and the snowflake white and the silver and the red-brown, none of them tried even once against their own element the way the rainbow had been tried against sky and earth and buried ground alone in the grove, and it seemed to him, turning the words over through those same years he spent gathering names, that a riddle which spoke of three spirits and their merging could hardly be answered by one man trying one coal alone, and that the line owed it more than his own two hands could give while those two hands were also busy carrying names from hearth to hearth.

So when the kin gathered for the standing of the Line, in the years after that first telling of it, they tried the coals as well, together, the whole bag of seven emptied out onto the flat stone before the fire while half the valley watched. They put four of the dark ones into a driving rain one autumn, laid out bare on the hillside through a night of it, on the thought that rain was as much the sky's water as the sea's, and found them in the morning only wet and cold and themselves, no different for the soaking than any stone left out in weather. They carried the bag up onto the ridge above Tobar dhìreach on a night the wind came hard and steady off the moor, thinking that if earth and sea each had a spirit to answer to, the sky's own spirit might answer to nothing gentler than its own true weather, and held the coals up bare-handed into the gale until their arms ached with the cold of it, and the wind went through their fingers and around the coals and past them into the dark, indifferent as wind always is to what it passes over. All seven went into the one fire together another year, on the reasoning that if merging was the word of Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich, perhaps it meant only that the coals themselves must be merged, thrown into one flame rather than kept apart in the bag or tried alone one at a time; they burned down black and ordinary together exactly as each had burned alone at every hearth since the mason first fed his own fire from the vein, no brighter for the company. And because word of Oisean's boat and Scàire's skerries and the salt taste of the wider sea had reached even so far inland as Tobar dhìreach by then, Diarmad sent to the south shore for a skin of true sea-water, carried the long way home on a man's back and poured over the coals in a stone basin at the hearth itself, the nearest any of them could come, that far from any coast, to trying the sea without walking to it; and the sea-water did to the coals exactly what the rain had done, wetted them and left them cold, and was tipped out afterward onto the ground the way any spent water is tipped, and soaked away into the same earth that had already refused the black coal its own trial twice over.

None of it worked, and none of it surprised him, by the third or fourth failure, though he did not stop trying for that. He came, in those years, to a kind of patience with Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich that was not quite belief that the answer was near and not quite despair that it would never come, a patience his mother, before she died in the second year after the first standing of the Line, told him was the only sensible way to hold a question too large for one lifetime to finish: to carry it the way a man carries a full pot on a long road, minding it without staring at it every step, and letting it crush none of the ordinary days under it. Fionnghuala died in her own bed with Poit an Teine within reach of her hand, as she had asked, and was buried the way the valley buried its own, and Diarmad took up the keeping of the pot himself, that year, alongside the keeping of the names and the keeping of Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich, three weights on the one back, and carried all three without once, in any hearth's telling of him afterward, being heard to complain of the load.

## IV. Of the Telling's Going Out

Aithris a' Chruthachaidh itself, meanwhile, had begun to do what no argument of Diarmad's could do for it: it travelled. A fire-bearer who had heard it three times at Tobar dhìreach on his rounds carried it, unasked, to a hearth on the northern moor where he stopped each winter to trade, and told it there in his own halting way, missing pieces and mixing others, so that the version that reached the moor had the sparks becoming stars but lost the grass-people entirely and gained, from somewhere in the fire-bearer's own head, a line about the god's laughter that Diarmad, hearing it come back to him years later from a traveller who had it from the moor in turn, did not recognise as his own telling at all until the laughter itself gave it away. He did not correct it. He had learned by then that a telling, once it left his own mouth, belonged as much to the mouth that carried it onward as to the one that first shaped it, the way a coal passed hand to hand at a fire-begging keeps the shape of the pot that last held it more than the shape of the hearth it came from, and that a thing told at every hearth from the high valleys to the northern moor could not, and perhaps should not, come back sounding exactly as it went out.

It went east as well, slower, because the eastern farms traded less with Tobar dhìreach than the moor did and had their own tellings already, of deer and dogs and the salmon runs, that made room grudgingly for a new one. But it went, carried by traders who came up for salt and hides and went home with more than they had bargained for, and by the thirtieth year after Diarmad's walk to the grove there was hardly an eastern hearth that had not heard some shape of it, sparks or grass-people or Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich itself said wrong in a dozen small ways and right in the one way that mattered, that the coal held a gift no one had yet found how to open. Diarmad heard, once, from a trader newly down from the east, a version of his own riddle so garbled that the sea and the sky had traded places in it and the earth had dropped out entirely, replaced by a line about fire answering to fire that made no sense at all set against what he himself had heard in the grove; and he sat a long while after the trader left, turning that over, not troubled by the wrongness of it so much as struck by how far a true thing could travel and still be carried, however badly, by people who had never doubted for a moment that it was worth the carrying.

He grew old carrying all of it, the names and the pot and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich and the slow spread of Aithris a' Chruthachaidh east and west of him, and the household watched him go from the man who had walked north at seven-and-twenty with one question and come home with a longer one, to a man they no longer laughed at even the young men of Tadhg's line, though few enough of them, in the end, said outright that they believed him. Niamh believed him at last in the tenth year after his return, though she never told him so directly; she told their daughter instead, one evening when she thought Diarmad out of hearing, that a woman could live a long while beside a strange thing without believing it and then find, on some ordinary evening with no sign to mark it, that she had come to believe it without ever once deciding to, the way a path comes to lie worn into a hillside without any single footstep being the one that made it a path; and Diarmad, who had in fact been within hearing the whole time, said nothing of it to her that night or ever after, and kept what he had overheard the way he kept the coals, quietly, and did not try to open it further.

## V. Of Diarmad's Death and the Daughter Who Kept It

He died in his seventieth year, an old man by the reckoning of the high valleys though no age at all beside Coimhdeach na Fine's long night, sitting up in his own bed with Poit an Teine near enough to touch and the leather bag of six dark coals and one that would not stay any colour long enough to be named laid on the floor beside him, and the last thing the household heard him say, to Niamh, who sat with him through that last night as she had sat up with him through so many nights of trying and failing before it, was that he was sure now the answer was near, nearer than it had ever been in all the years of the trying, though he could not, when she asked him plainly what he meant by it, say what had brought the nearness home to him beyond a feeling he had no better word for than the feeling a man gets on a long road when the smoke of a known hearth first shows over a rise he has not yet crested. He was not able to say whether he meant Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich would be answered in his son's time or his son's son's, or only that a question carried long enough and honestly enough could not, by its own weight and the weight of everyone who had come to carry it alongside him, go forever unanswered; and Niamh, who had spent forty years learning not to press him for more than he had to give, did not press him for that either, and let him die with the nearness unexplained, the way she had once let the whole of Aithris a' Chruthachaidh itself sit unbelieved in her for ten years before it settled.

It fell, in the end, to his daughter to keep Aithris a' Chruthachaidh whole, where his sons had not. Deirbhile was thirty-seven when her father died, old enough by then to have heard Aithris a' Chruthachaidh said at the hearth every darkest night of her own remembered life and young enough still to have the whole of it by heart in a way her older brothers, busy with the herding and the ordinary work of the household, had never troubled to make theirs; and where her father had told it a little differently each time, finding new words for pieces that had never quite settled into words the first time, Deirbhile set herself, almost from the week of his burial, to saying it the same way every time, word for word, the sparks and the grass-people and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich in the exact order and the exact phrases her father had used in the last years of his telling it, on the reasoning she gave her own children when they asked her why she was so strict about it: that a telling which changed with every mouth that carried it would, given enough mouths and enough years, end up saying nothing at all that the first mouth had meant, the way a coal passed round a whole valley of hearths comes home, if it comes home at all, cold and unrecognisable; and that if her father's question was ever to be answered by anyone, that someone would need the words as he had first been given them, not as forty years of retelling had worn them.

She taught it the same exacting way she kept it, sitting each of her own children down in turn once they were old enough to hold a long telling in their heads without losing the thread of it, and making them say it back to her a section at a time until they had it as clean as she did, and she taught it, besides her own children, to any of the wider kin who would sit still for the whole of it and promise to keep it as strictly as she asked; and by the sixtieth year after Diarmad's walk to the grove, there was no longer any single mouth in the high valleys that alone held Aithris a' Chruthachaidh, but a scattering of them, cousins and cousins of cousins, each one able to say it clean from the first spark to the last plain line of Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich, so that the thing Diarmad had carried home alone on his own two feet from an empty grove now walked the valleys on a dozen pairs of legs at once and could not, any longer, be lost by the death of any single one of them.

## VI. Of the Telling at an Eastern Hearth

It was said, that year, at a hearth three days' walk east of Tobar dhìreach, by a woman who had never met Deirbhile and had it instead from her own mother, who had it from an aunt who had sat once, as a girl, at Deirbhile's own knee and taken the whole of it down clean; three mouths removed from the keeper who had fixed it, and further still from the mouth of Diarmad himself, and further again from the grey shape that had first given it, word for word, across a small fire in a grove no one at that eastern hearth had ever seen or would ever see. The woman said it standing, on the darkest night of that year, to a household that kept no fire-pot and no bag of coloured coals and no claim at all on Sloinneadh a' Chlachair beyond the bare fact of being kin to kin to kin who had once married into it three generations back, and she said it the way Deirbhile had taught her mother to say it, the sparks that did not fall, the grass-people blinking up out of the heather, the sky and the earth and the sea each carrying their own spirit, and the words she gave last, because they were the words she herself had been given last and had never once heard explained: merge the spirits, and they become almighty.

A child at that hearth, hearing it for what he could not have known was the first time in his own short life though it would not be the last, asked the plain question every child who ever heard it seemed, sooner or later, bound to ask, the same question that had once sent a boy of seven at Tobar dhìreach out to badger every fire-bearer and elder and traveller within a day's walk of his own hearth: what did it mean, to merge a spirit. The woman who had told it did not know, no more than her mother had known, no more than the aunt three mouths back had known, no more, in the honest end of it, than Diarmad himself had known on the last night of his life with the nearness of the answer sitting unexplained in him like a smoke he could smell but not yet see the fire of; and she told the child, as her own mother had told her when she asked the same thing at the same age, that it was a question for An Clachair's own line to answer, if any line on the whole island ever answered it, and that a household three days east of Tobar dhìreach had only to keep the words themselves whole and hand them on, the way a fire is handed on in a pot of moss from a hearth that lit it to a hearth that did not, asking of the coal only that it stay lit long enough to be carried, and trusting that whoever received it at the far end would know, better than the bearer ever could, what to do with the fire once it arrived.

# Chapter Ten: Of the Mole and the Steps

*VE 951 – 1,169*

## I. Of the Mole at Skell

On the first day of the warm month the old man walked the bank of the river at Skell from first light, looking at nothing anyone else would have troubled to look at, and by mid-morning he had chosen his stone.

He had judged stones on that bank for longer than anyone at Skell could remember him not judging them, walking the shingle at every fall of the water with his hands loose at his sides, turning one boulder with his foot and letting the next lie, so that the younger men who worked at his word had long since stopped asking what marked the ones he chose from the ones he left. It was not size alone, for he passed by boulders bigger than the one he took that morning, and it was not shape alone, for the one he took was no rounder or flatter than a dozen others within reach of it; it lay, when he had finished with it, in the current's edge with its broadest face turned upstream and its weight sitting low and sure against the drag of the water, and that was the whole of what could be said of his judging by anyone who watched him do it and never learned to do it himself.

They rolled it down to the water's edge on green logs cut for the purpose, six men to a stone that size, with the old man walking beside it the whole way and saying nothing until it came to rest where he wanted it, at which point he would put out one hand, flat, and the log-bearers would know to stop, and the stone would go into the current from there, walked the last length on its own logs until it dropped with a sound that carried up the bank and settled into the silt the river had already given it. Then the old man would stand in the shallows with the water at his shins, turning his head one way and then the other at the stone half-sunk before him, and either nod, once, and send for the next, or shake his head and set them to shifting the one already placed a hand's width this way or that, which was harder work by far than the placing of it, for a stone once let go by the current did not want to be moved again.

It went on so through the whole of that warm season and into the wet one after it, boulder after boulder rolled and set and sometimes shifted, walked out from the bank a little further with every stone that held, so that by the time the leaves turned there was a low ridge of rock standing above the water even at the flood, running out from the bank at a slant the old man had set on the first day and never once changed, though he changed everything else about the work as it went. Boats that had beached on open shingle, dragged up clear of the water by main strength at every landing and dragged down again at every setting-out, began instead to come in under the lee of the stone and lie there quiet while the current went past outside it, and by the second winter there were boats enough sheltering there of an evening, a dozen at a time on a bad night, that the households along that stretch of bank had stopped thinking of the beach below their houses as open water at all.

The wet season after the first stones were set brought a flood the like of which the old man said he had not seen at Skell in all his years on that bank, the river coming up brown and fast and carrying whole trees down from higher ground, and the boats that had not been hauled well clear of it went where the water took them, out into the main current and away downstream past where any of them could follow on foot before dark. One boat went that flood, a small one, with nothing worse lost than the boat itself and the fishing gear in it, for the man who owned it had had the sense to leave it rather than go after it into that water; but the mole itself, the low ridge of stone the old man had been building through two seasons, took the flood's whole weight against its upstream face and held, and when the water fell back within its banks the ridge stood there still, scoured cleaner than before and not a stone of it shifted from where he had set it.

After that flood the old man was not troubled for stones. Households that had watched the work from a distance, minding their own boats and their own beaches, came now and asked to have their landings brought under the same lee, and he took them at their word and set them to the rolling and the placing exactly as he had taught the first of them, walking beside every stone still, right hand out flat when it had come far enough, until the ridge that had begun as one man's slow work along a hundred paces of bank had become, by the years his own grandsons were grown men rolling stones themselves, a long low wall of unmortared boulders reaching further out into the river than any one household could have built in a lifetime working alone.

He did not live to see it reach as far as it would go. What he did live to see, in the last summers when his legs no longer let him walk the bank at first light but only sit above it and watch others do the walking, was a whole season's boats come in of an evening one after another under the lee of the stone he had first set with his own hands, riding easy in water that would have driven every one of them onto open shingle in his own father's time, and it is told that he sat above the river on those evenings and counted the boats coming in the way another man might count anything else worth the counting, though what he made of the count, or whether he made anything of it at all beyond the pleasure of watching it grow, the telling does not carry, for it went with him below the rise where the households of that shore keep what is theirs alone.

There was a boy among the old man's grandsons who took to the water in those years the way some children take to it and others never do, and who is remembered, by whoever it was that first told this of him, for standing chest-deep at the mole's outer edge on the calmest days of high summer with his feet braced against the last stone set, letting the current push at him and push at him without once giving ground, as though the stone under his feet had lent him some part of its own stubbornness against the river. His grandfather, watching from the bank with the patience of a man who had spent a lifetime watching water move against stone, said nothing to him about it either way, neither calling him in nor praising him for staying out, and the boy grew to be one of those who rolled the furthest stones in the old man's last working years, walking beside them exactly as he had watched his grandfather walk, right hand ready to go up flat the moment a stone had come far enough.

The foot of the mole he set that first warm month lies under the water still at the lowest fall of the river, and every landing built out from that bank in all the years since has stood, in the end, on stone he chose and placed with his own hand and eye, though none now living could point to which stones were his and which were set by the hands that came after him, for a wall of unmortared boulders holding back a river gives up that kind of memory the moment the current has run over it a single winter.

## II. Of the Steps at Bral

On the far side of the island, where the land fell to the sea in a cliff of raw rock rather than a shore of shingle, a household that kept its beasts on the grazing above the water had for longer than anyone could reckon gone down to the shingle by whatever crack and ledge a man's feet could be trusted on, a scramble that wanted both hands free and was not to be tried at all after rain, when the rock ran wet and the safest holds turned treacherous under a boot.

It was a woman of that household, in a year no one troubled to fix, who first set her shoulder to a slab loosened already by frost and worked it, over the better part of a season, into a step at the foot of the worst of the scramble, wedging it level with smaller stones packed in beneath it until it took her whole weight without rocking. She had no thought, that first year, of doing more than the one step, for the one step alone saved the worst stretch of the climb, the stretch where a slip meant the shingle thirty feet below rather than a bruised hip on the rock; but a step once cut asks, in its own way, for the step above it, and by the time her own daughter was old enough to carry a bag of shellfish up from the shore unaided, there were a dozen slabs set one above another where before there had been only the crack and the ledge.

The work went on as such work goes on among people who keep no count of years, in the odd hour between the beasts and the shore, in the slack season when the grazing wanted less watching, a slab worked loose and dressed rough with a harder stone and set and packed and tried under a full load before the next was begun. Some years saw three steps cut, some years none at all, for the stone did not always give a slab where a slab was wanted, and a household with sickness in it or a hard winter behind it had neither the hands nor the heart to spare for cutting stone that would still be there, unset, the following year. No one who worked at it ever spoke, so far as the telling carries, of finishing the climb entire; each worked the stretch in front of them, the stretch that made the going hardest that season, and left the stretch above or below to whoever came to it next with strength and time enough.

By the time the third generation of that household was grown, the steps ran unbroken from the shingle at the cliff's foot to a shelf perhaps a third of the way up, wide enough there that two could pass without either turning sideways, and the scramble that had once wanted both hands free and a clear head began, above that shelf, all over again. A boy of that generation, sent down for shellfish on a morning when the tide was right and the household short-handed, is remembered to have run the whole finished stretch without once setting a hand to the rock, down and up again both, laughing at the top of it in a way that made the older women watching from above laugh with him, for none of them, not the woman who had cut the first slab nor any who came after her, had ever gone down that stretch without at least one hand out for balance until that morning.

The steps above the shelf took longer than the steps below it, for the rock there ran harder and gave up fewer slabs willing to be freed by frost or fire-cracking, and more than one worker of that household spent a whole season on a single stretch of a dozen feet that yielded, in the end, three steps and no more. It is told that when the full climb was at last finished, two hundred and twelve steps from the shingle to the grazing above, cut by hands that had never once all worked together in the same season, the household that had begun it was three generations removed from the woman who set the first slab, and not one of the three generations between had known her, though every one of them had grown up going down to the shore and up again by steps she had begun and none of them had finished.

The treads of the lower steps, the ones cut soonest and used longest, wore hollow in their middles long before the upper steps had worn at all, a shallow dish worn by bare feet and sandalled feet alike, by the young going down light and the old coming up slow with a full bag, by beasts driven down once in a while to graze the weed left uncovered at a low spring tide and driven up again bawling at every unfamiliar step under their hooves. No one now living could say how many feet, over how many years, it had taken to wear stone that hard into a hollow a thumb's width deep, and none of that shore, so far as the telling carries, ever tried to reckon it; the steps were there, and were climbed, and wore as anything wears that is used every day by every hand and hoof a household has, and that was the whole of what needed saying about them.

An old woman of that household, late in the years the steps took to finish, is remembered to have sat some evenings on the shelf a third of the way up, where two could pass without turning, and to have run her hand along the edge of the topmost step then cut, the one nearest the unfinished stretch above it, the way another woman might run a hand along the rim of a pot she had shaped herself. She had not cut that step, nor any near it, her own working years being long behind her by the time the climb reached that height, but she had carried stone up to whoever did cut it, in her turn, as her own mother had carried stone before her, and she is remembered to have said, of the unfinished rock above, only that it would come when it came, in the tone of a woman who had learned, over a long life on that cliff, not to trouble herself over work that was not hers to finish.

## III. Of the Recital Kept Idle

At the hearth of Clann a' Chlachair the fire that had once broken living out of the rock burned now, as it had burned since before any of the fathers now spoken could remember otherwise, in a pit dug and stone-ringed and fed with heather and split wood the way any hearth on the high valleys was fed, no different to look at than the hearth of any household a day's walk off, save for the clay pot set always at its western edge and the leather bag kept always within reach of whoever tended it.

The recital that Diarmad had fixed, standing on Oidhche an Dealanaich with the fathers' names running back through him to Neachdan who had broken the vein, was said now by hands that had never known Diarmad living, taught mouth to mouth from a woman of his line to a granddaughter of hers, and from that granddaughter on again, each keeper holding the words as she had been given them and giving them on unaltered, for a word changed in the telling, however small, was held to be a word lost, and no keeper of that hearth wished to be remembered as the one under whose watch a word was lost. It was said standing, every year, on the dark-of-the-year night, to whatever household had gathered for it that season, and it was said also, more quietly, to a child of the line old enough to hold still through the whole of it, the first of many such tellings before that child grew old enough to say it back whole and unbroken.

Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich that had come with Aithris a' Chruthachaidh, the sky and the earth and the sea and the three spirits that must somehow be brought together, was said too, every year, in its place after the recital of the fathers, but it was said now the way a thing is said that has been tried and has failed and is not, for the present, being tried again. In Diarmad's own day, and after him in his daughter's, the coals had been carried to a rain that would not stop falling, sunk in sea-water fetched home in skins from a shore three days off, set together seven at once in the hottest fire the line's hands could build, and had come out of every trial the same dull stones they had gone in, no brighter and no darker, giving up nothing of what Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich asked of them. After the third such failure, or the fourth, the telling does not keep the count exact, the trying was let rest, the way any hard work is let rest when the hands that might do it have other work in front of them that wants doing first, a hearth to keep fed and children to raise and beasts to see through a winter; and by the years the mole was rising at Skell and the steps were being cut at Bral, the leather bag of coloured coal hung at the hearth of Clann a' Chlachair much as it had hung for two generations already, opened sometimes for a child to turn the pieces over in wonder at their colours and closed again after, tried against nothing.

It was not that the line had given up Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich, for no keeper of that hearth, asked outright, would have said so; it was only that Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich had become, in those years, a thing that was kept rather than a thing that was worked at, said each year in its proper place the way the fathers' names were said in theirs, waiting on whichever of the line's children might yet take it up again with a strength or a notion the ones before had lacked. More than one traveller passing through the high valleys in those years heard the recital said at that hearth and asked, afterward, whether anyone had tried this or that against the coals, some new way that had occurred to the traveller on the spot, a fresh idea offered in good faith by someone with no stake in the failures already behind it; and the keeper of the hearth, whoever she was in that year, would hear the traveller out and thank him for it and set the bag away again unopened, for a household that has tried the sea and the rain and the fire together and failed at all three has little patience left, most years, for a stranger's fresh idea got in an afternoon.

So the recital was kept whole, word for word, said standing every dark-of-the-year night whether the household that heard it that year troubled to ask for it or not, for by then the saying of it had become, in its own right, a thing the line did because it had always been done, in much the way a mole of stone is added to because a mole of stone has always been added to, and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich rode along inside it unanswered, carried forward from keeper to keeper the way the recital's own words were carried, waiting on a hand that had not yet been born.

In the year the crossing to Bral's higher shelf was first made without a hand out for balance, though the hearth of Clann a' Chlachair knew nothing of that crossing and never would, the recital was said, as it was said every year, to a gathering that had come that season without being sent for, walking up from the lower valleys of their own will on the strength of a saying passed hearth to hearth that the night was near; and the keeper of that year, a granddaughter's granddaughter of the woman who had first fixed the words in her own memory, stood and said the fathers' names from Neachdan down to her own father without once being asked to begin, for by then no asking was wanted, the gathering's own silence being asking enough. She said Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich after, as she said it every year, and closed the bag again after, as it was closed every year, and if she felt any want in herself to be the one who opened it in earnest rather than merely kept it, the telling that survives her does not carry so much as a hint of it.

## IV. Of the Dead of Vell

On the low headland in the island's south-east, where the shore ran flat enough for a boat to be launched at any state of the tide, a household kept its own dead the way it kept everything else it valued: apart, and facing the water.

When one of that household died, whether old at the work or young to a fever that came up sudden from the marsh air, the body was washed and wrapped in the household's own way, which the telling does not follow past the wrapping, and carried down to the shore on a litter of poles, and set into the broadest of the hide boats with two rowers to take it out. The crossing to the low island off that coast took less than an hour's pull in calm water, and it was never made light of even so; the rowers went out at first light, before the day's other work began, and came back before the sun was high, and no household of that shore, so far as anyone now can say, ever sent its dead across in bad weather, waiting instead however many days the sea gave them no choice but to wait, the body kept meanwhile in a place apart from the household's own hearth-fire.

On the island the graves were boxes of set stone, four slabs and a lid, raised a little above the ground and packed round with rubble so that the whole would stand against weather and time both, each one built by the household of whoever it was to hold before that person died, if there was time for it, or built in haste after if there was not, by whichever hands could be spared from the rowing. Every box, without exception, so far as the telling carries, was set to face the same way: not toward the open sea beyond the island, where a dead man's household might have thought to send him on to wherever the drowned or the departed were held to go, but back across the strait toward the mainland shore, toward the low headland and the shore and, beyond it, whatever fires still burned in the households that had rowed the boxes' occupants out.

Why the dead of that shore were made to look back rather than out, no teller of that coast, in all the years the telling ran, is remembered to have said, and none of the mainland's own tellers, who came no nearer that shore than any hill-folk came to any of Seann-Dhaoine' places, ever learned enough of the matter to guess at it either. It was simply the way it was done: a box was built, and a box was set, and the lid that closed it faced always toward the mainland and never toward the open water, whatever the last months of the person inside it had been spent looking at while they lived.
