The rowing itself fell, in most households of that shore, to whichever two were fittest for it in a given season, and it was not held to be grim work, or at least not spoken of as grim work by anyone the telling remembers, though a woman who had rowed her own mother out one autumn and her own daughter out the spring after is said to have gone to the boat, after that second crossing, with a face that told those who watched her go that this was not, for her, a labour like any other, whatever it might have been for a rower sent out with someone else's dead. She rowed it all the same, for the household wanted two hands at the oars and hers were among the fittest still, and came back before noon as every crossing came back before noon, and took up the day's other work as though the morning's had been no different from any other morning's, which the telling holds to have been, for her, the greater part of what there was to admire in her.

The stone for each box came from the island where the ground gave it up, or was carried across in the same boats that carried the dead when the island's own rock ran short, a labour spread across whatever days the household could spare from its other work, so that a box begun the week of a death was not always finished the week after, and more than one family of that shore is remembered to have gone back and forth across the strait a dozen times over a season, ferrying slabs one or two at a time, before the four walls and the lid stood true over the one they were meant to close in. The lid itself was always the last stone set, and always the heaviest, wanting every hand the crossing boat could carry along with it, and it is told that no household of that shore ever let a grave stand open through a night, whatever the state of the work, choosing rather to lay a covering of brush and stone across an unfinished box until the true lid could be brought than to leave the dead exposed to weather even for the span of a single dark.

The island filled slowly, box by box, over more lifetimes than any one household on that shore could reckon by its own memory alone, each new box set a little further along the low ground than the one before it, following the same face-the-mainland rule without deviation, so that a person walking the length of the island, had any hill-folk ever gone there to walk it, which none ever did, would have found row on row of stone boxes all looking the same way, at the same low headland, out of which every one of their occupants had once been rowed. The households of that shore, so far as anyone now can say, kept some rough sense among themselves of how many boxes stood there, though the telling that survives them does not say by what means they kept it, whether by a mark cut somewhere or simply by the kind of memory a small close-knit shore keeps of its own dead without needing to write any of it down; and it is told, of the year the crossing that closed out these years came, that the box set that season was counted, by whatever reckoning the household used, the fortieth to stand on that low ground, its lid laid and its face turned, like every lid before it, back toward the water it had been rowed across and the shore its household had never once let it out of sight of.

# Chapter Eleven: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff

*VE 1,170 – 1,330*

## I. Of the Gate in the Rock

At Toll, where a shelf of grey rock ran down into the Abhainn uaine and broke the river's push into two channels before it could reach the sea, a household kept a gate cut into the rock's own body rather than standing open on it, a channel worked into the stone with a wattle gate set only into the channel's narrowest place.

The cutting had been begun long before any of them now living could remember its beginning, a groove picked out stroke by stroke with a harder stone against the softer, following a crack that already ran most of the way where the channel was wanted, so that the work was less a making from nothing than a widening of what the rock half offered on its own. It ran from the still water above the shelf down to a pool below it that filled and drained with the river's own rise and fall, a channel a man's stride across and knee-deep at its shallowest, worn smooth along its floor by the water that had gone through it every year since before the cutting was finished, so that no one could any longer say which of the smoothness was the river's work and which the first workers' own.

At the channel's narrowest place, where the rock pinched in on either side close enough that a man could touch both walls with his arms half spread, a slot had been cut into the stone on each side, deep and true, running from above the water's highest mark down below its lowest. Into the slots, when the river ran low and the pool below wanted emptying, a woven gate of wattle was let down and driven home with a mallet of oak until its foot sat hard against the channel's floor and no fish of any size could pass either way through the gap it closed.

The dropping of the gate was a household's whole work for the better part of a day, from the first light in which the water could be judged low enough to try, through the fetching of the gate from where it hung, dried and mended, under the eaves of the shelter above the shelf, to the driving of it home stroke by stroke with the mallet, one man in the channel to guide its foot true and two above with their weight on the mallet's haft, until the gate stood square in the slots and the water above it began, almost at once, to climb a hand's width against its face where before it had run through unchecked.

Behind the gate, in the pool the channel fed, the fish that had come up with the last high water and not gone back down again with the ebb were left penned in a stretch of water no deeper, at its lowest, than a woman's knee, and it was there, once the gate stood driven and the pool's level had settled, that the real work of the day began: wading in with woven baskets and bare hands both, working the pool's whole width from the gate down to its lower lip, taking what the day's need called for and leaving the rest to swim on when the gate was drawn again with the next rise. It was slower work than a net across open water and it took more hands, but it took fish from a stretch of river where no net could be strung, in a channel the household had made for no purpose but this, and it took them dry-shod but for the one man in the water, which on a cold morning of the wet season counted for something the tellers of that shore never troubled to say aloud, for it did not need saying.

A child born to that household in the years the channel was already old learned to walk its length before she learned to walk the shore proper, led by the hand along the smoothed floor at low water while the elders worked, and learned before she was fit to lift the mallet herself which stretch of the channel's floor stood firm underfoot and which gave a little where the current had worked beneath it, a knowledge no one troubled to teach her in words because there were no words in that household's use fit to carry it, only the leading of a small hand along the same stretch of rock, season after season, until the feet themselves knew what they stood on without asking the eyes.

The slot into which the gate was driven wore, over the years the channel was worked, a groove of its own inside the groove first cut for it, the wood's own foot working the stone a little smoother, a little truer, with every dropping and every drawing, until an old man of that household could set the gate's foot to the slot in the near dark and feel, through the haft of the mallet, whether it sat true before it was more than halfway home. What the river gave in one wet season and withheld in the next, the channel and the gate together took in whatever measure the season allowed, penning a little where a little was there to be penned, and standing open and unremarked the rest of the year while the current ran through the gap the gate had left, carrying down to the sea whatever the rock had not been cut to catch.

There were years the river did not fall low enough, or not for long enough, to make the dropping of the gate worth the day's work, and those years the household lived on what the sea gave a little further down, and on what small game the woods above the shelf held, and did not trouble the gate at all from one wet season to the next; and there were years it fell so low and stayed so low that the gate was dropped twice or three times before the autumn rains filled the channel again, each dropping taking the same day's labour as the last, so that a household's whole late summer might be measured out, in the telling that has come down of it, by the number of times the gate had been driven home and drawn again since the water first began to fail, a count kept in place of any count of days. It was not the same gate from one generation to the next. Wattle rotted where it stood driven into wet slots, and a gate that failed at its foot in the pull of a high river was mended where it could be mended and remade whole where it could not, so that the shape of the gate outlasted any one weaving of it, each in turn gone back into the reed bed it was cut from, the way the channel persisted though no two floods left its floor carrying quite the same silt.

A boy who lost two fingers of his left hand to the mallet's swing, misjudging the moment his own weight ought to come off the haft and leaving it a breath too late, went on working the gate in the seasons after with the hand that remained him and the stumps of the other tucked close against his palm out of the mallet's way, and was neither pitied for it nor spared the work on its account, for a household that lived by the channel wanted every hand it had, whole or not, and the boy himself, so the telling carries, came in time to set a gate's foot into its slot as true by feel as any man of that shore with both hands unhurt.

## II. Of the Road Across the Reeds

Some way to the west, where a wide loch lay cupped among low hills and its western shore ran out into a reed marsh a full mile across before the ground rose firm again, another household turned, generation on generation, to a slow work of shell laid upon reed and mud, a little each season, until what had been water underfoot for half the year became, at last, ground a person could walk dry across without once feeling the marsh reach for the foot.

It began, as such things begin on that shore, without any one person setting out to make a road. A family whose gathering-ground lay on the firm rise beyond the marsh had worn a path through the reeds by the plain repetition of walking it, a soft track that held for a season and sank again with the winter's water, so that every spring the same feet found the same reeds standing where the path had been the autumn before, as though the marsh forgot each year what had been asked of it. What changed it was the shell.

The household that worked the loch's edge gathered a great deal of shell from the shallows there, freshwater mussel mostly, and had always let the broken and the empty shell fall back near the water where it was worked, the way any household lets its waste fall near its work. Someone among them, one wet season when the reed track had sunk further and sooner than most years, began instead to carry the broken shell out along the worst of the sunken stretch and let it fall there, underfoot, rather than by the water where it did no one any good; and where the shell fell and was trodden in, the reeds beneath it held firmer through the following winter than the reeds a stride to either side.

It is not told which season this began in, nor whose hands first carried a basket of shell out onto the reeds rather than leaving it by the shallows, for the telling that has come down of it keeps no name and asks for none. What is told is that it was done again the next season, a little further along the same stretch, and again the season after that, until the carrying of shell out onto the worst ground had become, without anyone deciding it should, a thing the household did each year as part of its ordinary work at the loch's edge, the way the net-menders of other shores mended nets each spring because the nets wanted mending.

The shell was crushed before it was carried, broken small underfoot on a flat stone kept by the water for the purpose, for whole shells worked loose and slid where crushed shell packed and held; and it was carried in the same woven baskets that carried the day's gathering home, so that a basket that went out full of mussel in the morning might come back in the evening full of its own broken shell, emptied onto the reeds on the way out and refilled with the day's take on the way back, two errands made of one walk. Over years enough that no one household's own memory held the whole of it, the crushed shell built up along the worst of the marsh a hand's depth at a time, packed down by every foot that crossed it and topped again the next season where the winter water had worked it thin, until the track that had once sunk under every autumn's rain stood instead a good forearm above the reeds on either side, pale with shell against the dark water, a raised way running the better part of a mile from the firm rise to the loch's own shallows.

A girl of that household, grown just old enough to be trusted with an errand of her own, was sent one autumn to carry word to the loch's edge that the boats were wanted in before the light failed, and went the whole way out along the shell road at a run without once setting a foot into the reeds on either side, the first, so far as the telling remembers, to cross the whole finished length of it without the older habit of testing the ground first with a toe before trusting it with a step. She came back the same way, still at a run, and it was some while before anyone thought to remark that the road, worked at by so many hands over so many years that none of them had set out to build a road at all, had that day carried a child at a run from one end to the other and not once given way beneath her.

The marsh on either side of the shell road kept its own way through all the years the road was built, standing wet and reed-thick and treacherous to any foot that stepped off the packed shell, so that the road did not drain the marsh or change it, only crossed it, a single dry thread laid over ground that remained, on both sides of that thread, exactly what it had always been. Boats still went out from the shallows at the loch's edge to work the deeper water, and the reed-cutting for thatch and for matting still went on along the wet margins either side of the road, and the road carried nothing more than feet and baskets and, on the days the catch was heavy, fish strung on cords over a shoulder; it asked for nothing and gave nothing but the one dry way across, and the household that had built it without meaning to kept it, once built, the way any household keeps a well or a hearth, mending the low places each spring with a fresh basket of crushed shell before the winter's washing had quite worn them through.

It was not the only crossing of that marsh, for the household beyond the firm rise had, in the years before the shell was ever carried out, waded the reeds at need the way any household wades a marsh it must cross, wet to the thigh and watching for the softer ground that would take a leg to the knee if a foot found it unlucky; and even once the road stood finished, a hand at least a forearm above the water on either side, those who worked the reed-cutting close along its edges went on wading as they always had, for the road served the crossing and not the cutting, and no one thought to lay shell out over ground that only wanted standing in a while and not walking across. The two ways of using the marsh went on side by side the whole time the road was building, the wet way and the dry, neither troubling the other, and a child of that household might grow to a grown height knowing both, the firm shell under the sole for an errand to the far rise and the cold reed-water at the shin for the cutting, without ever once thinking the one had made the other less needful.

In the autumn a family from further round the loch's northern shore, whose own crossing lay a longer way about over higher ground, came down one year to see the road for themselves, having heard of it from a household that fished the loch's open water and had watched the shell-carrying from their boats for seasons without once setting foot on the finished road themselves. They walked its length from the firm rise to the water's edge and back again, the whole family together, saying little that the telling has kept, and went home the long way about all the same, for the road belonged, in whatever unspoken reckoning that shore kept of such things, to the household that had built it, and a stranger's foot on another household's shell was not a thing lightly done, however plainly the shell lay open to any foot that wanted to try it.

## III. Of the Signs on the Cliff

Far along the same coast, where the land rose in a line of pale cliffs above a shore too broken with rock for any mole or any road, a household of a different trade turned, in the years the gate was worked at Toll and the road was laid at the loch, to a labour that left behind it neither a channel to catch fish nor a way to walk dry-shod, but rows of small cut marks on the standing rock, and nothing else that the telling has ever been able to say the marks were for.

A man of that household is remembered, though not by any name, for the care of his hand at the cutting, a care that others of the same trade along that cliff did not always trouble to match. He worked with a chisel of flaked flint, held close to the eye and struck with a small stone hammer no bigger than could be closed in one fist, and he cut each sign the same careful way: a line begun at one point and carried through without lifting the chisel until the whole shape of it stood cut, then a second line crossing or joining the first as the shape called for, each stroke of the hammer light enough that the chisel bit only a little at a time, so that a single sign that a careless hand might have cut in a dozen blows took him, by the count of a boy who once sat a whole afternoon watching him at it, the better part of two hundred.

The signs he cut, and the signs others of his trade cut beside his along the same stretch of cliff face, ran in rows, one row above another where the rock stood high enough to carry more than one, each row running some way along the face before it stopped, sometimes at the rock's own edge and sometimes, it seemed, at no edge at all, simply where the cutter had judged the row done. No two rows ran the same length. No two signs within a row, to an eye set beside them and asked to judge it, looked quite the same as any other, though each carried some kinship with its neighbours that the eye caught without being able to say in what the kinship lay, the way a hand knows one household's pot-rim from another's without being able to say which curve of the thumb made the difference.

The careful man was watched, more than once, by others of his own household standing a little off while he worked, and none of them, so far as the telling carries, ever asked him what the rows said, for there was no word in any of their use for what a row of cut signs on a cliff face might be asked to say, any more than there was a word for what the three strokes on a net-weight far along the coast might be asked to say. He worked at his rows in whatever hours the tide and the weather left him free of the trade that fed his household, some days cutting three signs and some days none, and when a row was as long as he judged it wanted to be he began another above it or beside it, without troubling, so far as anyone watching him could tell, to look back at what he had already cut before he began the next.

Not every row on that cliff stood as its first cutter had left it. Here and there along the face a run of signs had been gone over a second time, the first shallow cutting deepened and widened by a later hand until the old shape beneath it was lost under the new, or cut across at an angle that broke the row's own line into two halves that no longer read, if they had ever read, as one thing. The tool that did this second cutting was of the same kind as the first, a flint chisel struck with a small hammer, and the care taken with it was, where it could still be judged, of the same order as the care taken with the first cutting it undid; whoever went back over an old row worked it with the same patient stroke-by-stroke care that had made the row in the first place, neither careless nor hurried nor angry at the stone. Why the second hand undid what the first had made, the telling does not carry, and no one now living, on that shore or any other, has ever claimed to know.

The rain that fell on that coast in every wet season found the new-cut rows before it found anything else on the whole exposed face, running down into the fresh grooves and darkening them a shade the older, weathered signs around them had long since lost, so that for a little while after every cutting a row stood plain against the paler rock about it, sharp-edged and dark-lined, before the weather over the following seasons drew it down toward the same pale, softened grey as everything cut before it. The careful man cut on through his own years at the trade regardless, adding row to row along a stretch of cliff that already, by the time a boy watched him at it for an afternoon, carried more rows than any one person standing at its foot could take in with a single turn of the head; and when in time his own hand grew too unsteady for the fine work of it, it is not told that anyone else of his household took it up in the same close way, or that the rows he had already cut were ever added to again by any hand as careful as his own.

The boy who watched him that one afternoon came back more than once as he grew, drawn to the foot of the cliff on days his own work left him free, and stood looking up at the rows the way he had once sat and watched them made, though he himself never lifted a chisel to the rock in all the years the telling follows him. He came to know, by looking alone and by no other means, which rows the careful man had cut and which belonged to other hands of the same trade working the same stretch of cliff in the same years, for the careful man's own signs kept, to an eye grown patient enough to find it, a straightness in the line and an evenness in the spacing that the others' did not quite match, however close they came to it; and this knowing he kept to himself, for there was, in that household's whole use of words, none fit to carry it further than the looking had already carried it.

Below the rows, where the cliff's foot ran down into a shingle no different from any other shingle on that coast, the same household that fished and gathered the tideline there went on with its ordinary work the whole time the signs were being cut above them, hauling boats up past the high-water mark and mending nets and splitting driftwood for the fire, most of them never once climbing the short scramble up to where the rows stood, for the cutting was the careful man's trade and not theirs, the way the gate was the Toll household's trade and the shell road the loch household's, each a labour one people took up for reasons the telling has never been asked to give, and each left, by every other people near it, entirely to the hands that had begun it.

## IV. Of the Rain on the New Signs

It fell to a woman of the household at Toll, in the years the gate had been worked at longest and the slot wore its own groove within the first, to walk the coast one summer on an errand that is not told, and to come, in the course of it, along the cliff where the signs stood cut in their rows, and to stand a while at their foot looking up at them the way the boy had once sat and watched the careful man cut them, though her own eyes found only what was already finished and could say nothing of how it had been made.

She had never seen the like before, for no household of the river-gate or the marsh-road cut anything into stone beyond what bare use demanded, a groove for a gate's foot, a notch for a cord; and she stood at the cliff's foot a while in a rain that had begun while she walked and had not yet decided whether to lift, watching the water run down into the freshest of the rows and darken it against the older signs around it, and then she went on the way her errand called her, and the telling, which follows her only that far, does not say that she ever spoke of it at either of the two households she came from or came to.

The rows stood after her as they had stood before her, taking the rain the same way they had always taken it, darkening under it and paling again as it dried, without asking of any hand that passed beneath them, hers or another's, more than the looking she had given them; and along the whole of that coast, where the gate was dropped and the road was mended and the rows were cut a little longer every season they were worked at, no telling passed from the gate's household to the marsh's, or from the marsh's to the cliff's, so that what was made at each stood, so far as the tellers of that shore have ever carried it forward, entirely on its own, known to no household but the one whose hands had made it.

# Chapter Twelve: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea

*VE 1,331 – 1,442*

## I. Of the Boy Who Had Not Seen the Sea

Aodh was born at Tobar dhìreach a good many fathers after Diarmad had first brought Aithris a' Chruthachaidh down out of the grove, into a hearth that had by then told the same three lines so many times over that the youngest child at it could say them before it could walk a field alone: the sky, the earth and the sea each carry their own spirit; merge the spirits, and they become almighty. He learned the words the way every child of that line learned them, from his mother's mouth before he had teeth enough to say them back whole, and he grew up knowing the sky for the wind that came down off the moor and the earth for the black ground his own feet stood on and the wool his own hands helped card, and knowing the sea, when he thought of it at all, for a word.

He was nine years old before it troubled him that a word was all it was. A traveller up from the eastern farms, resting a night at the hearth on his way to trade salt for hides, said something in passing of a grey water without a far shore to it, and Aodh, sitting close by the fire with the leather bag of the seven pieces in his lap as every child of the line was let hold it once the elders judged the small hands careful enough, asked the man plainly whether he had seen it himself. The traveller laughed and said he had, more times than he could count, from a headland a day's walk past his own farm, and that it went on flat and grey to the very edge of the sky and gave nothing back to a man's eye but more grey water. Aodh turned that over the whole of the next day, and the day after asked his mother how far off the sea might be found, and she told him a day's walk north, more or less, past the last hearth any of their kin kept, and that she had never gone to see it, having had no cause.

He had cause enough of his own by then, though he could not yet have said what it was. Every recital of Aithris a' Chruthachaidh that he had sat through since he was old enough to sit still for one ended the same way it had ended since Diarmad first brought it down out of the grove: that gual òir held the sea, and had never yet been carried to the sea itself, only wetted in Diarmad's day with sea-water fetched home in skins, because no one of the line, in all the generations since, had carried it the day's walk north to try. The old women who kept the recital word for word said this the way they said every other part of it, as a fact long settled and long past troubling anyone new, the way a household says a well has always run dry in a hard summer and always filled again after; and it was some while before Aodh understood that what the old women called long settled, no one living had actually gone and done.

He asked why, the way Diarmad had once asked why the stones had colours, and got much the answer that first Diarmad had got: that the sea was a day's walk and more for a household with beasts to tend and a hearth to keep, and that a coal thrown once and sunk was a coal thrown, and there were six pieces left in the bag that answered to nothing anyone had found yet, and the line had waited five hundred years already and could wait a season or two longer. It did not strike him, at nine, as a good answer, though he had not yet the years to say so to anyone who would listen; and the thought sat in him after that the way the grove had once sat in Diarmad, waiting on nothing but a body old enough and free enough to go and do it.

## II. Of the Growing of the Question

The recital raised him the way a trade raises another boy, said standing at every gathering of the fathers' names, at Oidhche an Dealanaich when the whole kin turned out under the dark of the year to say the Line from Neachdan down, and at the lesser tellings besides, when a traveller asked to hear it or a child was born and the elders judged the new soul owed the whole of the story before it was a season old. Water was carried and peat was cut and the shape of every field his household worked came to him the way it comes to any child of a hearth, the black soil that gave the barley and the wet ground that did not; and under all of it he carried, the older he grew the more rather than the less, the one plain fact that troubled him: that he had heard the sea named at every recital of his whole life and had still, at fifteen, at twenty, never once stood before it.

His own mother had little patience left for the trouble by the time he was grown, having heard it out of him since he was nine and judged it, by twenty, a habit more than a hope; but his mother's aunt Muirgheal, who kept Poit an Teine at the hearth and had Aithris a' Chruthachaidh word for word as Deirbhile's teaching had fixed it, had a longer patience for it than anyone else at Tobar dhìreach, a woman of few words who could say Cunntas nan Athraichean back further than most cared to follow; and it was Muirgheal who did not laugh when Aodh at five-and-twenty said aloud, at last, what he had carried quiet since he was nine, that he meant to walk north and try gual òir against the sea himself before another generation let it lie.

"Your grandfather's grandfather said the same," Muirgheal told him, "and never went. It is easier to mean it than to walk it."

"Then I will walk it," Aodh said, "and find out which I am."

She did not answer that at once, and when she did it was not to forbid him, only to say that a thing waited five hundred years bore waiting a little longer yet, until the barley was in and the beasts settled for the dark months, so that a household could spare the hands his going would cost it; and Aodh, who had waited sixteen years already since the trouble first took him, found he could wait one more season for the sake of an old woman's asking. He worked the harvest that year with more will in him than any harvest before it, the way a man works faster at a thing he means to leave behind him clean, and when the last of the barley was under thatch and the beasts driven in from the high pasture, he told Muirgheal he would go with the first clear spell of weather, and she nodded and said nothing more against it.

## III. Of the Walk North

He went in the season the leaves were down off what few birches grew that high, when the moor above the valley stood the colour of a bruise under a sky the colour of ash, and he carried the leather bag with all seven pieces in it against his chest under his cloak, in the same fold of hide Diarmad had once carried an gual dathach alone. The night before he left he had asked Muirgheal whether he ought to carry the gold piece alone and leave the other six safe at the hearth, and she had told him no, that Aithris a' Chruthachaidh said the seven were cast at the mason's own fire together and ought, in her own reckoning if in no other's, to go together wherever one of them went, so that whatever answered would answer among its own. He did not ask her how she came by that reckoning, and she did not offer to say more of it, only wrapped the bag in a second fold of hide against the weather and pressed it into his hands the way a mother presses bread on a son going to a fair, as though the wrapping were half the gift.

The moor rose steadily under him the whole first hour, heather giving way in patches to bare black peat where the wind had scoured it, and he walked it alone, for no one else of the hearth had cause to go and he had not asked anyone to come; this was a thing he meant to do with his own two feet and no other's, the way Diarmad had gone alone into the grove eighteen fathers before him. The wind came harder as the ground climbed, the last cold breath of the season before the true dark months shut the moor entirely, and twice he stopped in the lee of a rock to eat a little of the bread he carried and to feel, through the two folds of hide, that the bag still sat close and whole against him.

He crossed no hearth he knew the whole first day, for the last of his own kin's fields lay behind him before noon, and the ground past them belonged to no household he had ever heard named, bare moor cut here and there by a burn running fast and brown off the high ground, cold enough at the fording that his feet ached the length of the far bank before feeling came back into them. Once, on the highest stretch, he startled a flock of small dun birds up out of the heather at his very feet, so sudden and so many together that his heart went hard in his chest before he understood what had frightened him; and once he passed the bleached ribs of some beast long dead, sheep or deer he could not tell by then, picked clean and half sunk into the peat, and gave it no more than a glance, being in no mind that day to read a sign into every bone the moor happened to show him.

It was past noon of that first day, with the moor's highest ground behind him and the land beginning at last to fall away north, that he smelled it before he saw it: a coldness in the air different from the moor's own cold, carrying something in it he had no word ready for, salt and weed and a wideness that seemed, even before his eyes found anything to confirm it, to have already got into his breathing. He came over the last rise with that smell thick in his throat and stood a long moment looking down at grey water running flat to the edge of the world, exactly as the trader long ago had said it would, and found that sixteen years of imagining it had prepared him for nothing at all. It moved. That was the thing no telling at any hearth had ever thought to say plainly, that the sea did not lie still the way a loch lay still on a calm day. It heaved from edge to edge, slow and grey and endless, a live thing breathing under a skin too wide for any eye to take in whole.

He stood there long enough that the cold began to work into his feet before he remembered to go on, and came down the last slope to a shingle shore where the land gave out at last into the water proper, waves running up the stones in long grey folds and drawing back with a sound like a held breath let go, over and over, without ever once resting between one and the next.

## IV. Of the Casting

He did not throw the coals that first evening, though the light still held enough for it. A day and more of walking lay behind him now, and something in him, once he stood at last on the stones with the bag warm against his chest, wanted the doing of it done properly and not rushed at the tail of a long walk with his legs still shaking under him from the climb; so he found a hollow above the tideline out of the worst of the wind, ate what bread was left him, and lay through a cold night listening to the sea work at the shingle below him, a sound he had never once heard in his life until that day and thought, lying awake under it, that he might never afterward be able to sleep easily without.

In the morning, with the light come up grey and even over water that ran the same colour as the sky above it, he went down to the water's edge and opened the bag.

The seven pieces lay in his palm the way they had always lain in the leather bag at the hearth, small and dull and unremarkable to any eye that did not know what they were, none of them showing, in the flat morning light, more than the plain black of any coal broken from any vein. He held each in turn a moment before he threw it, the way a man says a word over a thing before he lets it go, though he had no fixed form of words for the doing and made none up on the spot, only stood at the water's edge with the cold coming up through his boots and let each piece go into the swell as it rose to meet his hand.

The first sank without a mark of any kind, gone under the grey water as plainly as a common stone would have gone, and the second went the same way, and the third and fourth after it, each swallowed into the sea's own colour before the ripple of its falling had even smoothed away. He had known, standing there, that six of the seven were not the sea's to answer and had told himself as much on the whole walk north, so that he felt less each time than he had feared he might, only a small settling disappointment, familiar by the fourth piece, that this one too had been only a coal. The fifth went the same way. The sixth.

The seventh he held longest of all, though he had meant to hold none of them longer than another, for his hand seemed, of its own accord, unwilling to let it go; and when at last he did throw it, no differently than he had thrown the six before it, out into a swell rising grey and slow toward the shingle, it did not sink.

It took fire on the water, a small bright gold flame standing up out of the swell where the coal had struck, no bigger than a hand's span and burning steady in a wind that would have snuffed any ordinary flame in a breath; and it rode the rise and fall of that one swell the whole way in toward the shore, burning gold on grey water under a grey sky, until a breaker further out gathered itself and rolled over where the small flame stood and put it under in a single fold of white water, and it did not come up again.

Aodh stood at the water's edge with the empty bag hanging loose in his hand and watched the place where the flame had been, though there was nothing left to watch, the sea already smoothing back into the same grey heave it had shown him the evening before, giving no more sign that a coal had burned gold on its face than it gave of the six that had simply gone under. He stood there long enough that the cold reached past his boots into his legs before he remembered himself, and when at last he turned from the water he found he was weeping, though he could not afterward have said, when the old women at the hearth asked him, whether it was for the five hundred years the answer had waited or for the small span of a morning that a fire had burned and then had not.

## V. Of the Telling at the Hearth

He walked home slower than he had walked out, for the weather had turned against him and the ground was heavier with rain underfoot, so that a day and more going became the better part of two days coming back; and he came into the valley at last gaunt and salt-stained and empty-handed but for the leather bag, which he had folded and carried home though there was nothing left in it that answered to anything.

Muirgheal was the first to hear it from him, sitting by the fire she had kept since before he was born, and she made him say it twice over, once plain and once again slower, before she would let herself believe the whole of it: that six had sunk as any coal sinks, and the seventh, the gold, had taken fire on the swell and burned there, riding the water, until the sea had put it under. When he had said it the second time she sat a long while without speaking, her hands still in her lap, and when at last she did speak it was to the fire rather than to him, in the voice of a woman working out a sum she had carried unfinished a very long time.

"Nearly five hundred years," she said, "since the grove." And then, to Aodh, "Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich is true, then. Each answers to its own."

Word of it went out from Tobar dhìreach faster than Aodh himself had walked home, carried by whoever first heard it told and could not sit still on the hearing, so that by the second evening households a half-day's walk off in every direction had sent someone to ask whether it was true, and by the third Poit an Teine's own door stood open near the whole of the daylight to let in one more household wanting to hear it from Aodh's own mouth rather than a neighbour's telling of it. He said it over so many times in those first days that the words wore into the same shape each time, the six that sank and the one that burned, until he no longer needed to search for how to say it and it came out of him as easily as the fathers' names came out of the old women at a recital; and he noticed, saying it the tenth time and the twentieth, that no one who heard it laughed, not once, not even the youngest children who had laughed at every other wonder a grown man ever told them.

She wept that night at the hearth before the whole gathered kin, an old woman who had buried a husband and two children of her own without more than a dry eye shown for either, weeping now over a fire lit gold on a grey sea a day's walk from where she sat; and when she was asked why, by those too young to have carried the weight of it themselves, she said only that she had said Aithris a' Chruthachaidh word for word since she was a girl, and had never once let herself believe, in all her years of saying it back word for word, that she would live to hear it proved even once. The recital that night ran longer than any within living memory, for the fathers' names were said as always down from Neachdan, and then, for the first time since the mason's own well, a new line was added after them, plain and short: that in that year gual òir was thrown into the northern sea by Aodh of the line, and took fire there, and burned gold until the water put it under. It is from that night that the piece was first called, at every hearth Aithris a' Chruthachaidh reached after, *gual òir*, gual òir, a name it has kept at every recital since.

## VI. Of the Six That Would Not Answer

Aodh did not let the matter rest with the one answer given him. He went back to the northern shore twice more in the years after, though the bag now held only six pieces and no eighth chance for the gold, and threw each of the six in turn from a different height and a different ground each time he went, from the hilltop above the shingle where the wind stood hardest, from the black peat of the high moor dug open to the bare ground beneath, from a shallow pool of standing rainwater he found once in a hollow and thought, for want of any better guess, might stand close enough to the sea's own element to serve. Nothing answered him. The coals lay in whatever ground or water he set them in the same dull black they had always shown, and he came home from each of those later walks with nothing to tell the hearth but that the six were still six, and the gold still one, and the answer, whatever shape it would take for the rest, was not going to be hurried by a man's own wanting it hurried.

He did not stop trying for that. In the years he had left he carried the six pieces to every high ground and every water within a hard day's walk of Tobar dhìreach that he could reach and return from before the season turned against him, and tried each against ground and water and once, in a hard frost, against the bare air, held up on an open palm the way Diarmad was said to have held an gual dathach up to the sky in the grove; and each time he came home to say, to whoever still troubled to ask him, that the ground had not answered and the water had not answered and the air had not answered, only the sea, only once, and that he did not yet know what any of the rest were waiting on. Muirgheal did not live to hear the last of these failed tryings. She died an old woman by then even by the reckoning of a household that buried most of its own well short of her years, and the recital that told her death added, after the fathers' names, only that she had lived to hear the sea answer and had wept for it, and that she was carried out and laid as her own mother had been laid before her, with the fire kept burning at the hearth the whole night through as it had never once been let go out since the mason first carried it home.

Aodh himself did not live to see any of the six answer either. He kept the trying up until his own strength for the walking gave out under him, and died in his own bed at Tobar dhìreach at eight-and-sixty years, a long life by the reckoning of that hearth though not the longest the line had known, with the leather bag of six unanswered pieces still under his own hand where he had kept it close through all his last years the way another man might keep a tool he had not yet finished the work he meant it for. The recital that told his death said what it had said of every keeper of the line before him, the fathers' names down from Neachdan and then his own name added after them; and it said, besides, what no recital before his had ever had cause to say of any man of that line, that in his one lifetime the sea had been answered where it had waited five hundred years unanswered, and that six waited yet, and that whoever came after him would have to carry them further than he had, or find some ground he had not thought to try.

## VII. Of the New Pieces from the Stream-Bank

It fell, in the years just after Aodh was laid in the ground, to a boy of his own house too young to remember him clearly, out following a strayed goat along the bank of the stream below Tobar dhìreach where the water had cut a fresh notch into the earth after a hard season of rain, to find the black vein showing bare in the cut bank exactly as the mason's own crack had once shown bare in the rock of the well, a seam no wider than two fingers laid together, dark and dull in the wet earth. He did not know, at first look, what he had found, only that it was not the ordinary black of the peat around it, and he carried a broken piece of it home in his fist the way any child carries home a thing that has caught its eye, meaning to ask someone older what it was.

The elders of the hearth knew it at once for what it was, and more than one of them wept a second time that autumn, more than forty years after Muirgheal had wept at the gold, to see a bare showing of the vein found again after so many generations of the line had known it only as seven old pieces kept close in a leather bag and never renewed. They went out themselves to the stream-bank in the following days and cut what fresh pieces the notch would give them, careful of the bank's own crumbling the way the mason had once been careful of his well, and brought the new coal home to lie beside the old seven in the bag the children still played with, so that for the first time since Neachdan's own day the line held more pieces of the vein than the seven it had counted and recounted for five hundred years, with no more certainty than the mason himself had ever had of what any of the new ones might answer to, or when, or in whose lifetime the answer would come.

They said the recital that year with the new pieces passed hand to hand around the gathered kin before the fire was banked, an old custom half remembered and half made new on the spot, so that every soul at the hearth might hold, once at least, a piece of the vein not yet tried against anything at all; and it is told that the youngest child there, no older than Aodh himself had been the year the trader first spoke to him of the sea, held one of the fresh pieces up before the fire the way every child of that line had done since Diarmad first turned an gual dathach in his own small hand, and asked, in a voice too young yet to know how old the question was, what it was for.

# Chapter Thirteen: Of the Kilns, the Ramps and the Houses on the Water

*VE 1,443 – 1,669*

> *Dhìrich Fearghas gu mullach an eilein, agus ghabh an gual sneachda teine san adhar.*
> Fearghas climbed to the top of the island, and gual sneachda took fire in the air.
> — from Sloinneadh a' Chlachair

*The Third Part: Of the White Coal on the Height, and the Walls of Seann-Dhaoine*

## I. Of the Kilns at Morn

At Morn the beach ran shingle to a bay of grey water, and above the shingle, where the ground rose enough to stand dry of the highest tide, a household of the Seann-Dhaoine had for longer than any of its own living members could number dug pits into the turf and lined them with flat stones set on edge, so that each pit stood like a shallow box sunk into the ground with its rim just proud of the grass. Seven such pits stood there by the year the kilns are first told of, though the household said, when asked, that there had once been fewer, the way any household says of a thing it keeps adding to as the years and the catch allow.

Each pit had, cut into the turf at its lower side where the ground fell a little toward the shingle, a short channel no wider than a forearm and no deeper, through which a fire lit at the channel's mouth drew its smoke the length of the pit and out through gaps left along the stone lining, so that the whole pit filled with a slow smoke thick enough to hang a hand's blackness on a strung fish inside a morning and a night. It was not, the household would have said had there been anyone of another trade to ask it, a fire built to warm a body or cook a meal; it was built low and kept low and fed sparingly, on purpose, for its work was smoke and not flame, and a pit that flared was a pit whose keeper had misjudged the peat.

The keeping of the fires fell, in the years this telling holds, to a woman of that household who is remembered by no name but by the plain fact of her trade, the keeper of the kilns; and hers was a day unlike any other day kept on that shore. She rose before the light to walk the seven pits in turn, laying a palm flat an inch above each smoking bed to feel whether the night's fire had held or guttered, and where it had guttered she fed it a little dry peat from a store kept dry under an overhang of turf for that single purpose, never green peat and never wet, for green peat flared where dry peat only smoked, and a flare in a kiln full of the day's catch could undo in a morning what a season's fishing had built. Where the fire had held steady through the night she did nothing at all, for a kiln left alone in good order was a kiln doing its work, and it was, she had been taught and taught in her turn, no part of the trade to trouble a fire that troubled no one.

The catch itself came down to her from the boats each evening, strung on cords through the gills the way every household of that coast strung a catch, and she laid the strings across green withies set from rim to rim of each pit, low enough that the smoke closed over them but high enough that no fish hung near the fire's own heat, for a kiln was reckoned well kept when a hand laid flat on the fish by evening found it no warmer than the smoke around it. A fish taken out too soon spoiled within days despite the smoking; a fish left too long in a pit whose fire had crept too high dried hard and lost its worth at the trading; and between the two lay a length of days that the keeper of the kilns judged, so far as the telling can say, by no measure but the one in her own hand and eye, laid on the fish itself each morning and each evening, cord by cord.

It is told that in the years the seventh pit was dug, the smoke of Morn's kilns stood some mornings thick enough over the bay to be seen from the high ground a half day's walk inland, a grey column standing where no cooking-fire's smoke had ever stood long enough to be marked, and that herders of the inland hearths who saw it took it, for a while, as weather of some kind particular to that stretch of coast, a mist that rose from the sea on certain still mornings and no other. It was some years before the herders understood, by what road the telling does not say, that the column was smoke and the smoke was a fire kept on purpose, low and smouldering, day upon day, for no warmth and no cooking and no light against the dark, but only to dry a fish that would keep through a season no boat could fish in.

No hearth of the hills built the like of it in all the years this telling has followed either shore, for the hearths of the hills had no catch to keep in such a quantity that a single winter's eating could not see it through, and a fire built and fed and never let flare, day upon day, for the sake of what it did to meat rather than what it gave to the people standing near it, was a use of fire the hill-folk had not yet had reason to think of. It is the first building raised on Dia-thìr, so far as the telling has ever traced, for a trade and not for a hearth to sleep by or a hearth to lay a body near in death; and the keeper of the kilns, whoever she had been in the years before this telling opens, or her mother before her, or whoever it was first thought to dig a pit and line it and lead a channel of air into it rather than simply hang a string of fish over an ordinary fire and hope the smoke found it, left no name behind for the thinking of it, only the seven pits themselves, and the eighth begun before the telling loses sight of that shore, and the ninth begun after.

It is told of one summer, a good way into the years this telling has followed the kilns, that a night's rain drove in sideways off the bay and put out the fire in the fourth pit before the keeper had made her last round of the evening, so that she came to it at first light and found the withies bare, no smoke standing over them at all, the fish upon them cold and wet and already turned in their smell. She did not relight that pit that day, for a fire started fresh under a full load of soaked fish would have flared before it settled, and a flare would have cost her the load twice over rather than once; she carried the spoiled strings down to the tideline instead, where the gulls of that shore had long since learned to wait on such mornings, and let the pit stand cold and empty until the stones inside it had dried enough, by her own judging hand, to take a new fire without weeping steam back into the smoke. It is the only loss of a whole pit's load that this telling has kept a memory of from all the years the kilns are told of, and it is kept, so far as can be judged, only because the keeper herself is said to have spoken of it once, in her age, to a niece she was teaching the trade to, as the one morning she had ever stood at a kiln and found it had nothing at all to give her.

The niece kept the telling of it, and kept also, from the same teaching, the rule the keeper drew from that one wet morning: that a kiln in a gathering rain wanted watching past the hour a keeper would otherwise have gone to her own bed, for a fire low enough to smoke and not flare was, by that same lowness, a fire near enough to going out that a hard rain could take it before a keeper's next round found it gone. Whether every keeper of Morn's kilns who came after held to that watching in every wet night of her own years, the telling does not say; but the ninth pit, dug in the last years this telling follows that shore, stood a little higher on its rise than the first seven, its channel a little longer and angled a little more against the wind that drove rain in off the bay, as though whoever dug it had learned something from a pit dug lower and had no wish to learn it twice.

## II. Of the Ramps at Brenn

On the north coast, where the land ran down in long shelves of flat pale stone toward water deep enough close in that a boat could float within an oar's length of dry ground, another household of the same people had for its own long span of years built and launched and mended the skin boats common to every shore of the island, each hide stretched on a light frame of bent wood no bigger than two or three grown people could carry between them down to the water and back. In the years this telling now turns to, that household began a work no other shore had yet attempted: they laid, down the same shelving stone their boats had always launched from, long ramps built up of flat slabs set edge to edge and levelled with smaller stone packed beneath the low places, running from well above the highest tide down into water deep enough to float more than a skin boat's draught.

The first of the ramps was the work of more seasons than the telling can count with any confidence, for the slabs were heavy beyond what two or three hands could set true, and each one had to be walked and levered into its place a hand's breadth at a time, tried with a loaded sledge dragged its length, and lifted and reset where the sledge caught or rocked. It is told that the ramp stood finished, its whole length from the turf above to the water below laid true enough that a sledge run down it met no check from the first stone to the last, some years before anyone of that household had cause to build, upon it, anything heavier than the boats they had always built.

What was built there afterward, and drawn down that ramp and launched from its foot into the deep water, was a hull of a different make than any hide boat: a frame of timber built up plank upon plank rather than skin stretched over bent wood, shaped and pegged and caulked with whatever that household used for the purpose, and raised the whole length of the ramp on rollers cut from young trunks, a crew of them at the ropes and more at the rollers, walking it down by inches while the tide stood at the height the ramp was built for. A boy of the household, sent down at first light to see that no roller had shifted in the night, is the only person the telling names as standing close by it in its last hour ashore; the rest of the household came down as the light rose, and stood along the ramp's edge, and did not go into the water themselves.

The hull went down slower than any load the ramp had carried before it, checked twice on rollers that bit unevenly and freed each time with the same patient shifting of weight that had built the ramp in the first place, and took the water at last with no more sound, so far as anyone standing on the shore could afterward agree in the telling, than the ordinary slap of a wave against stone. It floated low and steady, riding in water deep enough that no one standing on the ramp's foot could any longer see its keel, and hands already aboard it, for someone had gone aboard before it left the rollers, though the telling has never agreed how many nor which of the household, took up oars of a length no skin boat's crew had ever needed and worked it out past the last shelf of stone into open water.

No season that the household could later fix a year to brought it back to that shore, so far as this telling has followed the household afterward; and of where it went, or what it was built to reach, or whether it reached it, nothing is told. The household went on building at the ramp after it, wider each time and longer, and launched hulls from it in the years that followed the way any trade repeats what it has learned once it has learned it; but the first hull, and the water it went out into, and the coast it may or may not have raised on some horizon no one of Brenn ever stood close enough to see confirmed, belong, in every telling that has come down of it, to the sea alone.

Of the first ramp's own building, before ever a plank was laid to make a hull for it to carry, more is told than of the hull that came after, for the ramp stood a long while as a thing seen and stepped over by the whole household before it became a thing that launched anything at all. Twice, in the years the telling follows its laying, a slab set well enough by daylight was found in the morning to have settled crooked in the night, the packed stone beneath it having given under its own weight where the ground below ran soft, and both times Leac na Fèithe was levered up again with poles of green oak braced against driven stakes, the low place packed afresh with smaller stone rammed hard by hand and by heel, and Leac na Fèithe let down a second time onto ground that had, by then, been tried and found wanting once already. The household that did this work is not told to have cursed the crooked stone or hurried its second setting; the telling that has come down of it says only that it was done again, the same careful way, as many times as the ground asked for it.

A dog of that household is remembered, though not by name any more than the boy who watched the last rollers or the hands that first went aboard, for lying across the finished ramp on warm days in the last summer before the first hull was framed above it, so that more than one of the household is said to have stepped over or around it on the way down to the water rather than move it, the ramp by then being as ordinary a part of that shore's ground as the shingle either side of it. Whether the dog lay there on the morning the hull was finally walked down to the water, and was moved for that one day only, or was kept well clear of the work for longer than a single morning, the telling has not troubled to say; it is remembered only for the many ordinary days before, lying full length on stone that had cost the household more labour than anything else that shore had ever raised, exactly as it might have lain on any bare patch of turf.

## III. Of the Houses on the Water

Inland from either shore, where the land folded down into a loch called Loch chrom, ringed close about with reed and alder, a scatter of low platforms stood out over the water on legs of oak driven down through the shallows into the firmer ground beneath, each platform joined to the shore, and each to its nearest neighbour, by a walk of split planks laid end to end and lashed to crossbeams below. Whether the platforms were the work of the Seann-Dhaoine, whose kilns smoked on one coast and whose ramps grew on another in those same years, or of some other people who left no other mark the telling has since been able to point to and say *these were theirs and no one else's*, is not a thing this telling, or any telling that has come to it, has ever been able to settle; the oak legs, driven and trimmed and lashed at their tops to bear a floor of split timber, say only that hands did it, and are silent on whose.

The platforms stood a little apart from one another across the loch's shallower reach, each with its own low house of wattle and turf raised on the floor above the water, and the walks between them ran narrow enough that a laden basket carried along one had to be carried square to the body or knocked against the low rail lashed along either side. Beneath the floors, in the water and the mud between the piles, eels gathered in numbers no open bank of that same loch ever drew them to in such close reach of a hand or a woven trap, for the shade of the platforms and the stillness the piles made in the current suited them better than open water did, and the households above learned, within what the telling reckons a very few years of the first platform standing, to lower baited traps through gaps left on purpose in the plank floor rather than working the open shallows from a boat as they had before.

A child of one of those households, too young by the household's own reckoning to be trusted alone on the open walks, was set nonetheless, on a morning this telling has kept though it has kept no name to go with it, to carry a basket of the day's eels the length of the longest walk, from the furthest platform to the shore, while the grown hands of the household were occupied at the traps. The child went the whole distance at a careful walking pace with both hands full and the basket's strap looped twice about a wrist against the chance of a slip, watching the planks underfoot rather than the water on either side, and set the basket down on dry ground at the walk's landward end without once losing footing on planks that another child, a season or two younger, would not yet have been trusted upon at all.

It is told, though not by any teller close enough to the loch to have seen it done, that the child was watched the whole way by an elder of the household standing at the shore end of the walk, arms folded, saying nothing, neither calling encouragement nor warning of a loose plank, for the crossing was by then, in that household's own reckoning of such things, an ordinary errand and not a trial; and that when the child set the basket down at last, the elder only turned back to the day's work at the traps without remark, the way a household turns back to its work once an ordinary thing has been ordinarily done. What the telling has kept of that morning, it has kept for the crossing alone, and not for anything the child or the elder is remembered to have said of it.

The platforms stood on their piles through wet years and dry, mended plank by plank as planks split or piles settled, longer than any one household's memory held whole; and the eels taken from beneath them, smoked or eaten fresh or carried inland on the same slow roads that carried word of the smoke at Morn, fed households that never set a plank of their own over that water nor asked whose hands had first driven a pile into its mud.

The driving of a new pile, when one was wanted, in place of an old one worked loose by years of current and weight, was reckoned the heaviest labour any of the loch's households undertook, heavier by their own account than the raising of a wattle wall or the cutting of a season's reed, for it asked four or five hands working together where most of that shore's other work asked one or two. A trimmed trunk of oak, its foot cut to a rough point and charred a little in a low fire to harden it against the wet ground it would stand in, was walked out along the nearest finished platform on rollers of its own, upended over the gap where the old pile had failed, and driven down by a weighted beam of the same oak, swung and dropped from a frame lashed above the gap, blow upon blow, until a hand laid flat against the standing trunk could no longer feel it give at the strike. It is told that the driving of a single pile in firm ground took the better part of a day, and in soft ground, where the trunk wanted driving deeper before it held, the better part of two; and that the households of the loch counted a new pile driven and holding as an occasion worth a shared meal on the nearest platform once the frame was struck down and the mud had settled around the new wood, though the telling has kept no word of what was eaten or said at such a meal, only that it was held.

The walks between platforms, no less than the platforms themselves, wanted mending against the same wet years that worked the piles loose, for a plank laid flat across open water and walked upon by every foot and every laden basket of a household's daily round wore thin at its centre long before its lashed ends gave way, and a worn plank was watched for and replaced before it broke rather than after, by households that had, by the years this telling holds, come to know the sound a sound plank made underfoot and the slightly different sound a thinning one made, a knowledge kept in the foot and the ear rather than in any word for it. A child too small yet to be trusted with a basket, but old enough to be sent along a walk on no errand heavier than its own feet, is remembered to have been set, more than once, to walk the length of every plank each morning before the grown hands went out to the traps, listening for the sound of a plank gone thin beneath its own light weight before a grown foot, heavier and less patient in its listening, might find the same plank the hard way.

## IV. Of the Shore Grown Bold

Three shores, in the years this telling has followed them, each took up a work heavier and stranger than any before it: pits dug and lined and fired for smoke alone; stone laid the length of a shelf to carry a hull the sea itself would swallow the memory of; timber driven down through water to raise a floor where no floor had stood. None of the three households that raised them knew, so far as any telling carries, what the others were about on their own stretch of coast in those same years, for word between shore and shore travelled slower in those days than smoke rose from a kiln or a plank was laid across a pile, and each work stood, while it was building, as its own household's own matter and no one else's.

Yet a single thing had changed along every coast the telling has followed in this age, and the telling, looking back from beyond it, can call the thing by its right name though none of the three households then building could have called it by any name at all: the sea, which had for so long been taken as it was found, waded and fished and rowed across in a skin no bigger than a boat's own crew, had begun in these same years to be worked. Ground was dug for it that had never been dug before. Stone was laid for it that would outlast the hands that laid it. Water was driven timber into, and floored over, and made to carry a household's own floor above its own depth. The shore that had once only received what the sea gave it had begun, in three places at least, and likely in others the telling has not followed, to shape the meeting place between land and water to its own purpose rather than take that meeting place exactly as the tide had always left it.

Inland at Tobar dhìreach, where the fire that had come down out of the storm still burned as it had burned since before any of these three shores had cut a kiln-pit or laid a ramp-slab or driven an oak pile, the line of the mason kept its seven pieces in the leather bag and told, at every recital, of a gold coal that had taken fire on the sea and six that had not; and no word had yet come to that hearth, in the years this telling holds, of kilns or ramps or platforms on any coast, for the hills and the shore-trades of the Seann-Dhaoine kept, in this age as in every age before it, each to its own doings and its own silence toward the other. What passed between the fire-keeping line of the hills and the smoke-keeping, water-working households of the coasts was carried, when it was carried at all, no faster than a traveller's own two feet, and a traveller with reason to cross from one to the other was not yet, in these years, a common thing on any of the island's roads.

The last that is told of the hull launched from Brenn is the small dark shape of a sail it is said to have carried, seen once, by no name the telling has kept, from high ground some distance along that same coast, standing out against the grey of the water and growing smaller with every count of the watcher's own breath until it could no longer be told from the water it stood on. Whether that sail belonged to the hull raised at Brenn, or to some other hull of some other shore's building that this telling has not followed, is not settled and was not settled then; but the watcher who saw it, whoever that watcher was, is remembered for one thing only, which is that they stood and watched until there was nothing left to watch, and then turned and went back down to whatever work the day still asked of them, the way every shore of that age turned, in the end, back to its own work once the sea had taken what it was going to take and shown what it was going to show.

# Chapter Fourteen: Of the Whale, the Round Houses and the Tower

*VE 1,670 – 1,950*

## I. Of the Whale-Ribs at Dunn

Below the southern Dunn, where the land broke down from turf to shingle in a single short fall a man could jump without troubling to look for a path, a whale came ashore in an autumn gale out of the west, driven in on a sea already grey and heavy long before the wind that carried it had properly begun, so that the household nearest the shingle heard the surf change its voice before first light and were down on the stones, half dressed, before the sky had greyed enough to show them what the noise had brought.

It lay the length of six grown men end to end, and longer, stranded above the ordinary reach of the tide and beyond any hope the next high water might carry it off again, and it lived through that first day and into the next, its one visible eye following the household as they stood off from it at a careful distance, not yet knowing what a thing of that size, breathing still, might do if it heaved. By the third morning it had stopped its breathing, and by then word had gone along the shore both ways, on the two feet of whoever could be spared to carry it, and other households besides the one that had heard the surf change came down to Dunn to see what the sea had put ashore.

The cutting of it was work for every hand the shore could gather, and took the better part of a half-month, the meat carried off in loads no single household could have eaten before it turned, salted where salt could be got and smoked over slow fires where it could not, shared out by a reckoning none of the tellings that have come down of it have troubled to set out in full, save that no household that had come down to help went home again with an empty basket. The blubber was rendered in clay-lined pits dug back from the shingle, the oil skimmed and kept in bladders and in the same clay pots the shore already used for water, and burned afterward in stone lamps through two winters at least by more hearths than the one household that had first heard the whale come in.

What was left, once the meat and the blubber and the skin had all been taken and the gulls and the foxes had begun on what remained, was the frame of it: ribs longer than a man is tall, curved the whole of that length, white already before the flesh had wholly gone from them, and too heavy for fewer than four hands to lift any one of them clear of the shingle. It is told that no one set out, in the first days after the whale came ashore, to do anything with the bones beyond let the sea and the gulls have them back in their own time, the way any household let a carcase go back to the shore once it had given what it could give; and it is told, just as plainly, that before that first winter had closed, the ribs stood upright in the turf a little back from the high-water mark, driven in at their thicker ends and lashed together in threes and fours at the crown, so that three round houses stood where, a season before, there had been only shingle and the smell of rendering.

The turf that roofed them was cut in long strips from the ground a little above the shingle and laid across the curve of the ribs the way turf was laid across any lighter frame of bent wood or driven stake, but the ribs held a wider span and a taller crown than any house the shore had raised before, so that a grown man could stand upright in the middle of one of the three without his head troubling the roof, a thing not every household's own house allowed him. The households that took up the three whale-rib houses that first winter are not named in any telling that has reached this one, save that they were of the shore nearest the shingle and had first cause, by the plain fact of having heard the surf and come down to look, to whatever the sea had left behind once every other hand had taken its share.

The bone did not last as the driven stake and the bent branch of an ordinary frame lasted. Salt and rain and the slow work of years told on it faster than they told on green wood, and a rib that had stood four winters was found, on the fifth, cracked through where the weight of the turf bore hardest, and had to be shored with a driven stake lashed alongside it or taken down before it brought the roof with it. The three houses stood, in the shape the whale had first given them, the better part of ten years before the last of the original ribs failed past shoring; and when they were rebuilt, it was on whale-bone again, for by then a second stranding, smaller than the first but of the same kind, had come ashore some way along the same stretch in the years between, and the household had learned, from the first building, how a rib wanted setting and lashing and how deep its foot wanted driving to stand the winters it could be made to stand.

It is told that the frames were raised a third time in the years this telling now follows, on bone from neither of the first two strandings but carried, this third time, some distance along the shore from a whale that had come ashore further west and been cut there by a household with no thought yet of building anything from what it left behind; word of usable ribs travelled, by then, faster along that coast than word of the strandings themselves had once travelled, for the shore had come to know what a length of whale-bone was worth to a household that wanted a house taller and wider than turf laid over branch could give it, and did not wait, the third time, for the bone to come ashore of its own accord below their own stretch of shingle.

Between one raising and the next, the rotted ribs that were taken down rather than shored were left where they had stood, unburned and uncarried, half sunk already into the turf that had grown up thick around their feet, so that a child of the third household to build there, digging one spring for no purpose sharper than a child's own digging, turned up a length of bone gone soft and dark with the years it had lain buried, and could not at first say what kind of thing it was, until an elder, called over, named it for what it had been: the foot of a rib from the first house, sunk and near forgotten under turf that had by then grown as thick over it as over any ground the whale had never touched at all.

The shingle below the three houses kept, through all the years of the first and the second and the third raising, a scatter of smaller bone the cutting had left behind and no one had ever troubled to clear, vertebrae the size of a grinding-stone and finger-bones no bigger than a child's own thumb, worked by the tide and the years into the ordinary stones of that shore until a stranger walking the shingle for the first time might have crossed the whole stretch below the houses without once marking that half of what lay underfoot had come from the sea's own flesh and not from the island's own rock. A household living there long enough came to know one from the other without looking, by the heft of a stone in the hand and the give of it underfoot, the bone always a little lighter for its size than the true stone lying beside it, though none of that household is remembered ever to have found a word to say why.
