Of the second stranding, smaller than the first and further along the same stretch, less is told than of the first, save that it came ashore in calm weather with no gale to announce it, found by a household out at low tide for shellfish rather than woken to it by any change in the sea's own voice, and that the cutting of it, being a smaller thing altogether, was the work of the finding household alone, with no call sent along the shore for other hands to come and share the reckoning. What that household kept from it, beyond the meat and the oil every stranding gave, was the whole set of ribs entire, and it is these, more than the first whale's bones already once rebuilt and once failed, that a household of the third raising is remembered to have chosen, judging bone that had not yet stood a single winter driven upright in wet ground to be worth more than bone twice already shored and twice already failed.

## II. Of the Round Houses of the Eastern Vell

A different shore, a good way to the east and south of Dunn, held nothing so strange as a whale's own bones for a roof, but raised, in these same years, a cluster of houses in stone the whale-rib builders never troubled to lay: fourteen round houses of dry-built stone, walls two courses thick and near shoulder height before the roof began, set close enough together on the ground the eastern Vell held that a household leaving one door could all but touch the wall of its neighbour's without crossing open ground at all.

The stone there was got from a scatter of loose slabs and boulders lying thick enough on the ground above the shore that no one household needed to quarry fresh rock to raise a wall; the labour lay instead in the choosing and the fitting, a wall built without mortar of any kind, each stone set and reset until it sat true against its neighbours on every side, the courses above holding the courses below without any binding but their own good fit. A wall raised this way asked more patience than speed of the hands that raised it, for a stone set badly low down was not found out until the courses above it had grown too heavy to lift off again without bringing half the wall down with it, and the households of the eastern Vell are remembered, in what has come down of their own telling, for unbuilding a wall's top courses more than once rather than build on over a stone they had begun, too late, to mistrust.

Each house was raised round rather than square, the walls curving in a little as they climbed until the last courses could be closed over with flat slabs laid corbel-fashion, one edging in past the one below it, until an opening no wider than a man's two hands together remained at the crown, closed at last with turf and a single flat stone laid over the whole. Inside, the floor was sunk a little below the ground outside the door, and at its centre a hearth-pit cut deeper again than the floor around it and lined with smaller stone set on edge, so that the fire burned below the level a draught from the door could easily trouble, and the smoke found its own way up past the corbelled roof and out through whatever gaps the fitting of the last stones had left open at the crown, for no house of that cluster is remembered to have cut a hole on purpose for it.

What the eastern Vell's builders are remembered for beyond the walls and the sunk hearths was a channel cut under the wall at its lowest point, lined the same way the hearth-pit was lined, running out from beneath the floor to open ground some way beyond the house, so that water that gathered on the sunk floor in a wet season, whether rain found its way in past an ill-fitted door or the ground simply rose wetter than usual under the winter's rain, had somewhere to go that was not simply where it happened to lie until it was trodden into mud by every foot that crossed the floor. It is told that not every one of the fourteen houses was given such a drain from its first raising, and that the households without one, watching their neighbours' floors stand drier through a wet winter than their own, took their own floors up in the following dry season and cut the channel in afterward, working it in under a wall already standing rather than build it in from the first course, a harder labour by every account that has come down of it than laying the channel before the wall went up, but done all the same, house by house, until by the years this telling now closes on, every one of the fourteen had its own dry outfall and its own drier floor to show for the labour.

The fourteen houses stood close enough, and were raised near enough in the same years, that no single telling has kept which household raised which first, or in what order the cluster grew from one house to fourteen; what has come down instead is the cluster whole, as a thing already finished and already lived in, doors facing every way the ground allowed rather than all one way, so that a child born into that press of near neighbours grew up knowing, before it knew much else, which door led to which household's hearth and which threshold belonged to kin close enough to walk in on without first calling from outside. A woman of the cluster is remembered, though not by name, for having been born in one of the fourteen houses, married into another three doors along without ever leaving the same cleared ground the fourteen stood on, and buried at last, by her own household's telling, within sight of both thresholds, the one she was born to and the one she kept; and it is said of her, in the one line the telling has kept whole, that she never in all her years needed to ask a stranger's door twice which household's hearth lay behind it.

The ground between the fourteen doors was worn, within a few years of the last house standing finished, into a hard-packed yard no grass ever troubled again, criss-crossed with the paths every household's own errands wore into it, to the well the cluster shared at its centre, to the midden each kept a little apart from its neighbour's, to whichever threshold a child had been sent to borrow fire from on a morning its own hearth had gone out overnight. A dog loose in that yard on an ordinary day might be fed from three or four hearths before the day was done, none of the fourteen households troubling to ask whose dog it was so long as it answered to being driven off a threshold it had no business lying across; and a stranger come to the eastern Vell for the first time is remembered to have stood some while at the yard's edge before venturing in, unable at first glance to tell, among so many low doors set so close, which belonged to the household with the elder he had been sent to find, until a child playing in the packed yard was asked and pointed the way without stopping its own game.

## III. Of the Tower at the North-Western Skell

Further north again, on the coast the north-western Skell held at its farthest and least sheltered reach, a household raised a single tower the like of which no other shore of the island had yet built: round like the fourteen houses of the eastern Vell, but built with a wall thick enough to be hollow through its whole height, an inner face and an outer face of dry-laid stone with a stair let into the gap between them, climbing the wall's own thickness in a tight turn from the door at the foot to an open crown at the top, so that a person could go up inside the standing wall without once crossing open floor.

Why that household chose to build hollow rather than raise a plain thick wall as the eastern Vell had done, the telling that has come to this one does not say, save that the ground the north-western Skell held there ran out to open water on three sides at once, and a household settled at such a place had cause, more than most, to want a height from which the sea in every direction could be watched without a climb up onto an exposed roof that the wind off that water might not have let a person keep their footing on for long. The tower's crown, once the stair had climbed the whole height of the wall to reach it, stood open to the sky, ringed by a low parapet no higher than a standing man's waist, and from it the water to the west lay open to the edge of sight on a clear day, with nothing between the tower's foot and the horizon but the sea.

The building of it, by what the telling has kept of the labour, went slower than the raising of any single house of the eastern cluster, for two faces of wall had to be carried up together, course matched to course on either side of the stair's gap, with cross-stones laid at intervals through the gap to bind the inner face to the outer and keep the whole from leaning apart as it climbed; and it is told that the household lost the top of one half-finished stair to a winter storm before the tower stood a third of its final height, the outer face alone thrown down while the inner held, and had to clear the fallen stone from the gap and set the cross-stones closer together through the whole climb of what remained before they trusted the wall to carry a stair any higher.

The first night any of that household spent at the tower's crown, once the stair stood whole and the parapet was laid, fell in a season of clear cold weather with little wind, and is remembered, in the one line of it the telling carries whole, for the plain fact that whoever climbed up that night saw more of the sea at once, by starlight alone, than any of that household had ever seen from any roof or headland they had stood on before, the water running unbroken from directly below the tower's foot out to where the dark of the sea and the dark of the sky no longer could be told apart. What was said on the crown that first night, if anything was said at all beyond what the climb and the sea's own width might draw from a person standing where no one of that shore had stood before, the telling does not carry; it keeps only that the climb was made, and that it was made again, by other hands of the same household, on other clear nights in the years that followed, until the crown of the tower had become, for that household, as ordinary a place to stand of an evening as any threshold or any strand.

The tower asked more of its household than the fourteen houses of the eastern Vell had asked of theirs, and the keeping of it once raised was the harder half of that asking, for a stone worked loose high in either face wanted setting again before the next storm found the gap it had opened, and the climb to reach a loose stone near the crown was neither short nor easy; and it is told that the household kept, from the first years the tower stood finished, a habit of walking the whole stair from foot to crown after every storm hard enough to have been worth remarking at all, feeling with a hand along both faces as they climbed for any stone gone slack in its bed, a labour that fell, in the years this telling has followed that household, to whichever of them had the surest foot and the least fear of the narrow dark of the stair, rather than to any one person by right of age or of standing.

The stair was dark through nearly its whole climb, lit only where a gap left on purpose in the outer face let in a narrow blade of daylight at two or three turns of its rise, so that a person climbing learned it as much by the hand trailing the inner wall and the foot's own count of the turns already taken as by anything the eye could make out in the gloom between one blade of light and the next; and a child of that household, sent up for the first time without a grown hand ahead of it to follow, is remembered to have stood some while at the foot of the stair before starting up, and to have counted the turns aloud the whole way, a habit that stayed with the child into a grown age, muttering the count of the stair under its breath even on climbs it no longer had any real need to count.

The household kept, besides the walking of the stair after storms, a second use for the tower beyond the evening climbs to its open crown: when a wind rose out of the west hard enough to make the open water dangerous to any boat still out on it, whoever of the household could be spared went up to the crown and stood watching the water below for as long as the light held, not for any one boat known to be out, for the household's own boats stayed ashore on such days, but on the chance that some other shore's craft, caught further out than its own crew had judged wise, might be seen making for whatever shelter the coast below the tower could offer it; and it is told, though the telling names no year for it, that a boat not of that household's own shore was once seen from the crown standing in toward the rocks below in weather that would have driven it onto them blind, and that a fire was lit on the parapet in time for its crew to see the coast they were running for and bear off from the worst of the rocks before the light failed altogether; where the boat and its crew went once they had borne off, the telling does not carry.

## IV. Of the Huts at Toll and the Sand

Far to the north, on the other coast of the island, where the land ran low into dune country and the wind off the sea had built the sand, over years longer than any telling could set a number to, into ridges taller than a standing man, a household of Toll built a scatter of stone huts in the lee of one such ridge, low-walled and turf-roofed, set close against the dune's own slope so that the ridge's own bulk broke the worst of the wind before it ever reached a wall.

The huts stood some years in the shelter the dune gave them, the dune troubling them no further, the sand that blew loose off its crown in an ordinary autumn gale settling no deeper against the walls than a household's own broom could clear from the threshold each morning, a small and steady labour so ordinary to that shore that no telling has troubled to remark it as labour at all, any more than a shore further south remarked the daily emptying of a fish-trap. Children of that household are remembered for having been set, almost as soon as they could be trusted to swing a broom, to clear the night's blown sand from the door each morning before the grown hands of the household turned to any other work, a task light enough for small hands and steady enough that a child too young yet for heavier work could be given the whole of it and trusted to see it done.

In the year this telling now comes to, a wind rose off the sea that did not settle in a night as the ordinary gales of that coast had always settled, but held through a full day and into a second, driving sand off the dune's whole exposed face in a haze thick enough that a person standing at one hut's door could not, by what the telling has kept of it, make out the next hut along with any certainty, the air gone the colour and near the heft of the ground it carried. The household worked at first as it had always worked, clearing what blew against the walls as fast as the wind piled it there, but the sand came faster than any number of hands could clear it, mounting against the windward wall of the first hut in the row until, by what the telling has kept of the second day's reckoning, it stood higher than the wall itself and had begun to press in over the turf of the roof.

It is told that the household left the huts before the second night of that wind closed on them, carrying what could be carried in the arms and on the back in the little time the sand's own rising gave them warning to judge by, and went inland to higher ground the ridge itself had always sheltered them from having to think about before, waiting out the rest of the storm under whatever cover the higher ground could give a household that had brought no shelter of its own with it. No one of that household is remembered, in any telling that has reached this one, to have been lost in the leaving of the huts, nor hurt beyond what a hard walk through blown sand in the last light of a bad day might be expected to cost any household that made it; the huts themselves are the only thing the telling says the sand kept.

When the wind fell, on the third day, and the household came back down from the higher ground to see what the storm had left them, the row of huts they had built in the dune's lee was not there to be seen at all: the dune had moved forward the whole width of the huts and some way beyond them, and stood, where the huts' doors and thresholds had opened onto level ground the morning before, as an unbroken slope of new sand, paler and looser underfoot than the ridge's older face, with nothing above it to show that a household had ever raised a wall or laid a roof on the ground it now covered. The household dug, in the days that followed, at the edge of the new sand where they judged the nearest hut's door might lie, and found, by what the telling has kept of the digging, enough of a wall and enough of a roof-turf still in place beneath the fresh sand to know that the huts stood yet, whole, under the weight that had come over them, before the digging itself was given up as asking more than it could return, and the household turned instead to raising new walls a little further inland, on ground the dune had not yet claimed and might, by their own reckoning of how the wind and the sand had always worked on that coast before, be trusted not to claim again for longer than any of them now living could expect to see.

Four shores, in the years this telling has followed them, each found its own shelter against what the sky or the sea or the ground itself might otherwise have taken from a household unhoused against it: bone raised against the open air at Dunn, stone and a hidden channel against the wet ground at the eastern Vell, a hollow wall and a climbing stair against the wind and the watching sea at the north-western Skell, and, at Toll, walls that in the end kept out neither wind nor sand, but were themselves kept, whole and unbroken, under the one thing they had never been raised to hold back. The household that built there last turned its face inland and did not trouble the buried row again; and the dune that had taken it stood afterward as it stood on the day the digging was given up, its new paler face already beginning, before that year was out, to darken and settle into the same weathered grey as the ridge behind it, with the roofs of Toll's first row lying still and undisturbed beneath it.

# Chapter Fifteen: Of the Lean Years of the Line

*VE 1,951 – 2,097*

## I. Of the Kilns in the East

At the eastern landing the fires were never all lit at once and never all dark at once, for a household that dried its whole catch on the same night had nothing to eat the night the wind failed and the boats came in empty. So it had been kept since before anyone tending the pits that year had first crawled to them on hands and knees to feel the heat off the stones, and so it was kept still: three kilns fed while three stood cold and swept, the ash from the cold ones carried down to the shingle and given to the tide, the short flues drawing peat-smoke up through racks of split fish laid belly-down until the flesh went the colour of old rope and would keep a season without turning.

The one who minded the middle kiln that year had minded it, in one turn or another, for longer than the youngest of the household could remember any other hand at it, and had in that time worn a path in the turf between the drying racks and the door of her own house that no grass had troubled to grow back over. She judged the smoke by its smell more than by its colour, holding her face low over the flue's mouth at first light and again at dusk, and she judged the fish by the give of the flesh under one finger, and neither judgement had she ever put into words that anyone remembered, teaching it instead the way it had been taught her, by standing a child at her elbow through enough dryings that the child's own hand learned what her mother's had learned before it.

A day's rowing up the coast, along a shore that showed nothing but grey water and grey sky to anyone who did not already know the set of it, another household kept the same three kilns and three, the same racks and the same flues, built by whoever had first carried the way of it between the two landings, in a trade or a gift or a theft the telling of neither shore has ever kept. The two places knew of each other the way a household knows of a cousin's household two valleys off: seldom seen, never in doubt. A boat went between them now and again with dried fish traded for something the one place had and the other lacked, a bundle of sinew, a stone good for scraping hide, and came back before the light failed, for neither crew cared to be caught between the landings after dark on a coast where the current ran stronger than it looked.

The woman who minded the middle kiln had a granddaughter old enough that year to be trusted with the racks alone through a whole low tide, and it was this granddaughter, and no one older, who first noticed that the smoke off the middle kiln ran a shade paler than the smoke off the two beside it, some seasons, without the fire beneath it being fed any different. She said so to her grandmother, expecting to be told what it meant. Her grandmother looked at the flue a long while, and then at the girl, and said only that the smoke told her what the smoke told her, and set the girl to turning the racks, which was answer enough for a child who had asked the question mostly to be spoken to.

That same winter a boat came up from the south with word, passed on the way word travelled between the two landings, that a beast had come ashore dead below the southern kilns and been cut up for its oil, and the eastern household sent back, by the same boat when it turned, a share of dried fish it could ill spare that season, for the giving and the taking between the two places ran both ways over the years and no one there kept any closer account of it than that. The woman who minded the middle kiln put the fish into the returning boat with her own hands, and stood on the shingle watching it go until it was a shape and then nothing against the water, and went back to her racks without a word to anyone about how long she had stood there watching an empty stretch of sea.

## II. Of Gormal and the Kin That Went Down

Six hundred years, near enough as the reciters kept it, had gone by since Aodh stood to his knees in the northern sea and watched gual òir ride the swell before a breaker took it under, and in all that span only the sea had answered. The gold burned in the tellers' mouths at every recital, bright as the night it was seen; the other six lay in the leather bag at Tobar dhìreach dark as any stone off any hillside, tried against the rain and the wind and the fire together and giving up nothing for the trying.

Gormal had grown up on the trying. She had heard Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich said standing before she could say the fathers' names back whole herself, had turned the six dark coals over in her own hands as a child the way every child of the line had turned them, and had watched, as she grew, more of the kin lose patience with a question that answered no one in a life or in three lives together. By the time she was keeper of Poit an Teine in her own right, past thirty and past the birth of the one daughter who lived, she had buried a father, an aunt and two of her own age who had gone to their graves saying the sky-coal would never light and the line was fools to keep hoping otherwise.

She had been a plain child, by her own later telling of herself, neither the quickest of the kin's daughters nor the slowest, and had come to Poit an Teine only because the aunt who kept it before her had no daughter of her own living and had taken a liking to the girl who sat nearest the hearth without fidgeting through a whole recital. What Gormal had, that the aunt saw in her before anyone else troubled to look, was a memory that did not let a word go once it had taken it in, and a temper that would not let a thing drop merely because it had gone unanswered a long while. She learned the fathers' names from Neachdan down at nine years old, standing them over to the aunt every evening for a whole winter until not a name came out of its place, and she learned Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich the same way, and asked, the first time she heard it whole, why no one had simply tried the thing from higher ground; and the aunt, who had heard every manner of fresh notion offered by children and travellers alike over a long keeping, only smiled at her and said that the hills of the high valleys had all been climbed already by hands with the same notion, and that Gormal would learn, given time, how much a hill could be climbed and still leave the question standing.

She would not let the recital go slack for that. It was Gormal's rule, said first to a gathering that had come more out of habit than hope, that the fathers' names and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich after them be said standing every dark-of-the-year night whether any soul under that roof cared to hear it or not, for a thing kept only while it was believed was not a thing kept at all, and a hearth-keeper who let the saying lapse one year would find it harder, not easier, to raise it again the year after. Some of the kin thought her stubborn for it. She let them think so.

Her own daughter, Sìomha, grown to a woman with children of her own by the time the branch made ready to leave, had more than once told her mother to her face that the young of the kin no longer sat still for Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich the way they had once been made to, and that a keeper who wanted the words carried on after her would do better to soften them, to let a child leave the fire once the fathers' names were done rather than hold him through Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich after, when half of them were asleep on their feet before the last line was out. Gormal heard her through and answered that a child who slept through Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich at nine would wake to it at nineteen or at forty, the words being in him whether he had listened with his eyes open or shut, and that she herself had slept through the greater part of a good many recitals as a girl and could say every word of them back all the same. Sìomha did not trouble to argue the point a second time, though she went on saying it, in her own house, to her own children, in gentler words than her mother's.

It was in those same years, while the argument between mother and daughter went on being had and never quite settled, that word came up from the eastern slopes of a good harvest two years running, and then a third, and the branch that had been drifting down in ones and twos for two generations began drifting faster.

That branch was cousins three and four times removed from Gormal's own line, kin all the same by the reckoning that mattered at a hearth, and it had for two generations been walking down to the lower ground where the farms of the eastern slopes gave a man back more than the high valleys ever had for the same digging, the high valleys being stone under thin soil at the best of times and a wind off the moor for most months of the year. Twenty years into Gormal's keeping, the last households of that branch still on the high ground made ready to follow the rest down for good, and when they went they went with a coal from no one's hearth but their own daily fire, carrying not one splinter of the mason's vein with them.

Gormal walked out to meet them the morning they loaded the last of their gear onto two ox-sledges, and stood in the yard while the sledges were lashed, and said what she had come to say plainly, without asking them to stay, for she had asked that of others before and had learned it did no good.

"You go with no coal of the vein in your hand," she said. "In all the years the line has kept the bag, no household has gone from it empty before."

The man who answered her, a grandson of her own grandfather's brother, did not stop lashing the sledge while he spoke. "We have carried the dark coals up every hill within a day's walk of here, grandmother's kin, and thrown them off every one, and they have come back dark every time. What is there left in a stone that will not answer for six hundred years?"

"You have thrown them from every hill you could reach in a day," Gormal said. "You have not thrown them from the highest ground this island owns, and no two of you agree, even now, which ground that is."

That checked him, though only for a breath. "Then let whoever agrees on it climb it," he said. "We have farms waiting that do not care what the sky thinks of us." And he went back to the lashing, and within the hour the sledges were moving down the track east with the whole branch walking behind them, children and dogs and all, and none looked back at the high valleys they left, so far as anyone watching from Tobar dhìreach that morning could see.

Gormal did not let the matter drop merely because the branch had. She raised it at more than one recital after, standing at the fire with the leather bag in her lap and the coals laid out on a cloth before her, sky and earth and sea, and put to whoever would hear her the same thing she had put to the man at the sledges: that the sea had been thrown into by a man who had never before seen it, and had answered at once, on the very shore where he first laid eyes on it; that the sky, by the same reasoning that had served the sea, ought to be tried from the ground that stood nearest it, and that no ground on the whole island stood nearer the sky than the highest of it, wherever that proved to be. She named three hills she herself judged for the honour, one south of the black well, one west toward Achadh dhìreach, and the third, the one she came back to oftenest in her last years, a bare shoulder of moor she had walked to once as a young woman and never forgotten the wind of. The old men of the kin argued each for a different one of the three, and some for a fourth she had not named, and none of the arguing settled anything in her lifetime, for no one among them had climbed all of the candidates and come down able to say with a clear conscience which had stood highest under his own feet.

She kept Poit an Teine and the bag until the year she died, in her seventy-fifth year, and on the last recital she stood for, her voice gone thin but the words unfaltering, she said Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich as she had said it every year of her keeping and then added, which was not in the fixed words and was never repeated by the reciters after her exactly as she said it, that the line had thrown the coals from every hill it could be troubled to climb and had still not thrown from the one that mattered, and that whoever first agreed with his own eyes which hill that was would do the line more good in an afternoon than the branch that had gone down to the farms would do it in ten generations of easier digging. She died that winter in the house she had kept Poit an Teine in her whole life, with Sìomha at one side of the bed and a granddaughter at the other, the fire fed and the leather bag within her reach though she no longer had the strength to lift it on her own. Near the end she asked to have the six dark coals laid out on the blanket where she could see them, and lay looking at them a long while without speaking. When Sìomha asked if she wanted Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich said once more, she shook her head; she had said it enough times in her own life, she told her daughter, that saying it again over a dying woman's bed would only ease the living, not answer the sky. It needed saying to someone who still had years enough left to climb a hill in. The bag and the question passed, as the recital passed, to hands that had heard her say both enough times to say them back the same way, and the three hills she had named were argued over at more than one hearth for years after, without the argument once coming nearer an end than it had stood the day she named them.

## III. Of the Oyster Beds in the South

On the southern coast, where a long low headland ran out into water shallow enough that a child could wade past a man's height of it before the bottom dropped away, one shore had built its whole living on a shellfish so plentiful there that no other trade had ever taken firm root beside it. The oysters lay thick along the headland's whole seaward face, packed close enough in places that a rake drawn once through the shallows at low water came up heavier than two hands could easily carry, and generation on generation of the same households had done little else with their days than rake them, open them, eat what could be eaten fresh and dry what could be dried, and pile the empty shells where the tide would not soon take them back.

The pile they made of it, by the time anyone now living there could remember, ran the whole length of the headland and stood, at its oldest and thickest end, higher than a tall man could reach with his arm above his head, whiter at its crown where gulls had picked it clean and greyer with age the deeper a hand dug into it. Children of that shore were set, almost as soon as they could be trusted not to cut themselves on a broken edge, to carrying the day's empty shells up to whichever part of the mound was that season's dumping-place, and grew up thinking of the heap the way a hill-country child thought of the hill behind its own house, a thing that had simply always stood there and would go on standing after they themselves were gone from the shore.

The lowest layers of that mound, where the oldest shells lay, held oysters bigger by half than any taken from the same water in the memory of the raking households still living, broad as a spread hand and thick-shelled enough that opening one wanted a harder blow than a fresh catch ever needed. No one on that shore troubled over why the old shells ran larger than the new; the water gave what the water gave, in whatever size it chose to give it in a given generation, and a household that had raked the same beds for as long as any of them could reckon had learned not to ask questions of a tide that answered none of them. There was little else to that shore beyond the raking and the eating and the piling: no ramps for hulls, no kilns for drying fish, no mole against a current, for the water there ran shallow and gentle the whole year and gave up its harvest to a rake and a strong back with nothing else asked of anyone. A household that wanted a hull for deeper water went without rather than build one, for there was little enough deep water within reach of that shore to make the building worth the trouble, and a family that wanted dried fish traded a basket of oysters for it at whichever landing further along the coast had fish to spare, walking the trade there on its own feet rather than by any boat of its own.

The rake itself was the one tool that shore troubled to make with any care, a length of bent wood with a row of teeth lashed along its lower edge, each tooth shaped and fitted by whichever household's hands were freest that season, and a rake once well made was kept and mended rather than replaced, passed on at a death to whoever in the house had the surest arm for using it. A woman known along that shore for the truest rake anyone there could remember had made it as a girl under an aunt's eye and used no other through a life long enough to see her own granddaughters raking beside her with rakes of their own making, and when she died the rake went to the granddaughter judged strongest in the arm, who used it in her turn until it wanted mending past any mending and was laid, by a custom none of that shore explained to anyone who was not of it, on the mound rather than burned or thrown back to the sea.

An old woman of that shore, whose own hands had raked oysters from the same stretch of headland for longer than she herself cared to count, was known to sit some evenings on the crown of the oldest part of the mound with a broad shell from its lowest layer turned over in her lap, running a thumb along its ridged outer face the way another woman might run a thumb along the rim of a well-used bowl, and to say nothing at all about it to whichever grandchild had come to sit with her, for there was nothing in it that wanted saying beyond what the shell already said by its own size and weight, and a shore that had lived on the same harvest for longer than its own oldest teller could reckon had long since stopped feeling any need to say more about it than that.

## IV. Of the Second Landing

Far to the north-east, along a stretch of coast none of the shore's own tellers ever set beside the first without a pause, a household laid slabs of flat stone edge to edge down the shelving shore into deep water, wide enough for hulls greater than any hide boat, and walked hulls down them exactly as another household had done, generations before, on the northern coast far to the west, at a landing that bore, by whatever chance carried a name across so much land and water, the very same name as this one.

Whether the two households had ever been one people, split by some journey or some quarrel too old for either shore to keep in its own telling, or whether only the name had travelled between them, carried by a trader or a wanderer who had seen the first ramps and given the second place its word without ever giving it the people who built the first, no teller of either coast, then or after, was ever known to say, and none of the hill-folk who might otherwise have puzzled over it ever came near enough that shore to ask.

The work went as such work always went: a slab judged and levered and set, a length of green log laid and greased with fish-oil and left to season under a spread of brush until it would bear a hull's whole weight without splitting, a first small boat walked down the finished ramp on a still morning with half the household standing along the bank to watch it take the water clean, no different in the taking than the first hull had taken the water at the western landing so long before that not one soul now living at either place had any memory, or any telling handed down of a memory, of which ramp had gone into the water first.

The old man who judged the stones for this second set of ramps had learned the judging, as every hand at that work learned it, from another who had learned it before him, back through a line of judging hands that ran further than the household's own memory could reach, so that no one now at the second landing could have said whether the way of laying a ramp down into deep water had been carried whole from the first landing in one crossing, brought by some ancestor who had rowed or walked between the two in a single lifetime, or had grown up new at the second place out of the same sea and the same need working on hands that had never once seen the first ramps with their own eyes. He himself favoured neither telling over the other when a grandchild pressed him for one, saying only that a ramp that carried a hull was a ramp that carried one, wherever the knowing of it had first come from, and that a boy more interested in where a thing came from than in whether it worked would make a poor judge of stones.

By the second summer there were two ramps standing side by side where there had been one, and a household grown confident enough in the work to let its youngest hands set the smaller stones under the old ones' eyes rather than under their hands, and by the third there was a third ramp begun a little apart from the first two, for a household with hulls enough now to want more room than two ramps gave it. A boy of that household, sent one autumn morning to carry word along the bank that the tide had turned, is remembered by whoever first told this of him to have stood a long while at the water's edge before he ran his errand, looking at the two, and then the three, long pale ramps running down into the same grey water that had carried away, out of any memory the shore now kept, whatever hands had first thought to lay stone into the sea in that particular way; and he ran his errand at last, as he had been sent to, and said nothing to anyone of what he had stood looking at, for it was, to him as to every other soul on that coast, no more than the ramps his own household used every day of the boating season, twin to another set of ramps on a shore he had never seen and never would, and no cause, so far as that shore's own telling ever carried it, for a boy already late on his errand to stand and wonder over it any longer than he did.

# Chapter Sixteen: Of Fearghas on the Height

*VE 2,098 – 2,240*

## I. Of the Two Brothers and the Three Hills

Gormal had been five generations in the ground before anyone climbed for her. The bag with its six dark coals hung where it had always hung, in a niche cut in the wall above Poit an Teine at Tobar dhìreach, and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich was said standing at every dark-of-the-year recital exactly as she had left it, sky and earth and sea, and no one born since her death had thrown a coal from anywhere higher than the shoulder of moor she herself had once favoured and never climbed. The three hills she had named went on being argued at hearths that had never known her, the argument outliving the woman who had started it, the way a fire outlives the hand that first struck it.

Fearghas grew up on that argument the way every child of the high valleys grew up on it, hearing it before he could walk to the door on his own legs and forgetting to be surprised by it long before he was grown. He had it from his mother, as the recital had kept it since Gormal's day, and he heard it said the same way every year at the recital: the sea answered when a man who had never seen it stood on its shore and put a coal into it; the sky, by the same reckoning, wanted the ground nearest it, and no ground on the whole island stood nearer the sky than the highest, wherever that proved to be. He turned the six dark coals over in his own hands more than once as a boy, the way every child of the line turned them, weighing nothing in his palm but stone, and put them back in the bag without either of the wonder or the doubt that older mouths brought to the same handling.

His brother Mathan was three years the elder and had none of Fearghas's patience for sitting still through the whole of a recital, but he had a longer stride and a surer foot on wet rock than any of the kin his own age, and it was Mathan, not Fearghas, who first said aloud what the two of them had each been turning over apart for a year or more: that a question asked since the grove was not going to answer itself while the line sat arguing at its own hearth which hill among three it had never troubled to climb was the one that mattered. Fearghas was nine and twenty that summer, Mathan two and thirty, and neither of them had climbed higher than the ridge behind Tobar dhìreach where the sheep went in the hard months.

"Gormal named three," Fearghas said, "and none of the three agreed with the other two."

"Gormal never climbed further than her own doorstep to name them," said Mathan, who had never had much reverence for a woman five generations dead. "She named what she could see from where she stood. We have legs."

They went first to the hill south of the black well, the nearest of Gormal's three, on a morning fine enough that half the kin thought it no more than an outing, and stood on its crown by midday with the wind pulling at their cloaks and the whole run of the high valleys laid out below them, brown and green and grey, and Mathan looked west and said that the shoulder of moor Gormal had favoured stood plainly higher than the ground they were standing on, and Fearghas, looking the same way, was not sure he agreed, for a hill seen across a valley cheats the eye as often as it tells true, and a man standing on one height has no sure way of judging another he has not stood on himself. They argued it there on the crown until the light began to go, and came down no wiser than they had gone up, save that they had learned between them that Gormal's three hills could not be judged one against another from any one of the three, and that the only honest way to settle it was to walk to each in its turn and stand on it, and then walk on to whatever ground beyond it still looked higher, and keep walking until no ground anywhere in sight looked higher than the ground they stood on.

It took the better part of two years, the walking. They went out in the fair months and came back before the hard ones, for neither of them was fool enough to be caught on open ground in a Dia-thìr winter with no more shelter than a cloak, and each season's walking carried them a little further south than the season before, past hills that had looked from a distance like the last word on the matter and proved, once climbed, to have a taller neighbour standing behind them all along, hidden by the very ridge that had seemed, from below, to be the whole of the sky's edge. More than once they stood on a crown certain they had found it at last, only to see, once the low haze burned off toward noon, a paler shoulder of rock further off still, standing clear over everything nearer, and to know without needing to say it to each other that the walking was not done.

They quarrelled the whole way, as brothers will who are agreed on the errand and disagreed on every step of it. Mathan wanted to trust his eye and be done; Fearghas wanted to trust nothing he had not stood on with his own two feet, and would not let a hill go unclimbed merely because it looked the lesser of two from where they already stood, for he had seen enough by then to know how often the eye lied on ground it had not walked. More than once Mathan called him stubborn to his face, and Fearghas answered, more than once, that a stubborn man who climbed every hill in his path would find the true one eventually, and a quick one who trusted his eye might die old on the wrong summit and never know it.

In the second summer they fell in with a herder driving a small flock along a saddle of moor neither of them had crossed before, an old man with a dog and a stick and a face burned dark by more winds than either brother had yet walked into, and when they told him what they were about, in the plain words the whole high country used for it by then, he stood a while chewing on nothing and looking south past their shoulders before he answered. He had grazed that ground man and boy, he said, and every ground a day's walk from it besides, and there was a shoulder further on, past a burn he named and a stand of stunted thorn he named after it, that his own father had sworn stood higher than anything nearer the valleys, though the old man himself had never gone to prove it, having sheep enough to mind without chasing his father's notions over open moor. He gave them the way of it as well as he could, pointing with the stick, and went on after his flock without asking why two young men of Clann a' Chlachair wanted such ground, for the line's long business with the coals was known well enough by then that a herder needed no telling of it twice.

They found the burn and the thorn on the fourth day after, and beyond them the shoulder the old man's father had sworn by, and stood on it in a driving rain that let them see nothing at all of what lay further south, and came down soaked through and short-tempered with each other over whether the climb had been worth the wetting. It was three days more, the rain cleared and the ground drying under them, before they climbed it again in better weather and saw, from its crown, the same bare grey summit with the cloud on it, which by the third summer they had proved beyond doubting to be the one true height; but that first sight of it, small and far off and half hidden in its own weather, taught Fearghas, he said afterward, more of patience than the whole two years before had taught him, for a man who had climbed a hill in the wet only to find a truer one waiting beyond it, still half a season's walking off, learned either to give the search up for good or to trust that the walking itself would end somewhere, in its own time, whether he could yet see the end of it or not.

It was in the third summer, walking a ridge neither of them had gone near before, bare rock breaking through thin turf and the wind already colder than it had any right to be so early in the season, that they came out from behind a shoulder of stone and saw, standing clear above every other height in every direction the eye could reach, a bare grey summit with cloud dragging along its top like smoke off a hearth that would not settle. Neither of them said anything for a while. Then Mathan said, low, that they had found it, and Fearghas, who had learned by then not to trust a first look, said only that they would know when they had stood on it and looked from there, and not before.

## II. Of the Climb

They went up for it at the turn of the summer in the third year of their walking. He was thirty-two that year, Mathan five and thirty, and both of them had grown lean and hard-legged on three summers of walking ridges, so that the climb, when they came to it at last, felt to Fearghas less like a beginning than like the last stride of a road they had already been three years on.

They carried the six dark coals in the leather bag, wrapped in a fold of hide against the wet, and Fearghas carried it himself the whole way, slung from his shoulder under his cloak the way Neachdan was said to have carried Teine a' Chlachair home under his, though no one at Tobar dhìreach had made that likeness aloud before Fearghas set out, and he did not make it aloud either, only felt the weight of the bag against his hip on every stride and thought of it once or twice without meaning to.

They set out from the camp they had made at the foot of the climb on the first evening of an t-Sultain, meaning to sleep an hour or two and go up with first light, but the wind came on hard after dark and neither of them slept much, lying in the lee of a boulder with their cloaks pulled tight and the coals in their wrapping between them, and so it was still black night, the second of an t-Sultain not yet an hour old, when Mathan sat up and said there was no more sleep to be had lying still and freezing for it, and they might as well be climbing.

The lower slopes went easily enough, turf and loose scree and here and there a burn to cross by stepping-stone, and they climbed in the last of the dark and the first grey of the morning without much need of speech between them, each finding his own footing by feel where the light was not yet enough to see it. Higher up the turf gave out and the rock came through bare, and the wind, which had been at their backs on the lower ground, found them from every side at once as the ridge narrowed, so that Fearghas felt it less as a wind from any one quarter than as a thing that had been waiting for them on the height and now had them where it wanted them.

The cold on the summit, when they came out onto it at last with the sun not yet clear of the eastern sea, was a cold that got into the back of the jaw and made the teeth ache, a cold neither of them had felt on any of the lower hills they had climbed the two summers before, though the season below was still warm enough for haymaking. Fearghas stood a while with his hand over his mouth before he trusted himself to speak, and when he took the hand away his breath went out of him in a plume that the wind tore apart before it had gone the length of his arm.

There was no growing thing on that top, not so much as the toughest moor-grass, only bare stone scoured pale by weather that never let up on it, and a scatter of loose rock at the summit's crown where frost had been working at it longer than any teller could reckon. The two of them stood at the highest point of it, where the ground fell away on every side, and turned slowly on their heels, and saw the sea.

It stood at every edge of the island at once, shining where the early sun caught it, grey-gold to the east and a deeper grey to the north and west where the light had not yet reached, and between the sea and the two of them lay the whole of Dia-thìr laid out below in one sweep neither of them had ever seen it in before, valleys and ridges and the pale threads of rivers, and away to the north, small and grey and impossibly distant, a shoulder of higher moor that Fearghas knew, without needing to be told, for the ground where the mason had struck his wedge into the rock two thousand years before. He had never in his life thought of Tobar dhìreach as a small place. From where he stood it looked no bigger than a thumbnail held at arm's length.

Mathan spoke first, and his voice came out thinner than Fearghas had ever heard it, the wind taking half the words before they had gone a yard. "There is nothing higher than this on the whole island. Nothing anywhere in sight stands over it."

"No," Fearghas said, and found his own voice no steadier. "There is nothing."

He unwrapped the coals with hands that had gone stiff and clumsy in the cold, kneeling at the steep southern edge of the summit where the rock fell away in a long broken slope toward the lower ridges, the wind trying the whole time to take the hide wrapping out of his fingers and carry it off over the drop. Mathan crouched beside him and said nothing more, and for a while there was only the wind and the small sounds of Fearghas working the knots loose, and somewhere below them, very far off, a bird crying over open ground.

Fearghas took the first coal out, the one with the gleam of silver under its black, and held it a moment in his open palm, feeling nothing from it but its own cold weight, and then let it fall from the height of his own arm, out over the drop, the way a man drops a stone into a well to hear how deep it goes.

It struck the slope some way below and lay still. He let the second fall, and the third, watching each all the way down to be sure, and each struck and lay as dark and cold as it had left his hand. The fourth went the same way. Mathan had stopped speaking altogether by then, watching the drop with his jaw set, and Fearghas found that his own hands had begun to shake, not wholly from the cold.

He took out the fifth, the one flecked all over with small white marks like stars caught in dark water, and held it a moment longer than the others, turning it once so the flecks caught what light there was, and then opened his hand and let it go.

It did not fall far.

Fearghas watched it turn once in the air, no more than the height of two men below the edge, and then it was burning. There was no smoke first, no slow catching such as a hearth-fire takes from tinder; one moment it was a falling stone and the next it was a small fierce whiteness in the grey morning air, white as nothing Fearghas had ever seen a flame be, sharp-edged against the dull rock behind it like a star fallen out of its place and still burning where it had no business to burn, with no fuel under it and nothing around it but empty air and the fall. It struck the slope below still alight and did not go out on the striking, and lay there among the cold grey stones burning white and steady in the wind that could not put it out any more than the rain, so long before, had put out the vein in Neachdan's well.

Neither of them moved for a long moment. Then Mathan let out a sound that was half a laugh and half something with no name to it, and gripped Fearghas by the shoulder hard enough to hurt, and Fearghas found that he was on his knees at the very edge of the drop with the cold stone biting through his knees and had no memory of kneeling there, only of watching the small white fire below him and feeling, for the first time in his life, that the thing the whole line had been asking after for twelve hundred years was a true thing that answered, when a man found the right way to ask it, and no mere story told at a hearth.

"It is the sky's," Fearghas said, when he had breath enough to say anything. "Gormal was right. It only wanted the right ground under it."

They climbed down to where the coal lay, a slower going than the climb up, for the cold had stiffened their hands and the drop was steep and loose underfoot, and stood over it a long while before either of them would touch it. It burned on, small and white and even, giving off no smoke that either of them could see and no more heat than a man might feel from a hearth-coal held at arm's length, and it did not sink into ash the way a burning thing should, only went on burning, as steady on the third hour as it had been on the first.

They left it there. Neither of them said so to the other in so many words, but each knew without asking that the coal had found its own place and its own element and had no more business being carried home in a pot than gual òir, so long before, had had any business being fished back out of the northern sea. Fearghas gathered the four cold coals from the slope, and let the sixth fall after them for the sake of the telling, and it struck and lay as cold as the rest; and he wrapped all five again in the hide, and the two of them climbed back to the summit and stood there a last while with the sun well up now and the whole island bright below them, and Mathan, who had never in his life been given to solemn gestures, stooped and set one loose stone from the summit's crown atop another, a small cairn no higher than a man's hand, and said nothing over it, and Fearghas understood the doing of it without needing the saying.

## III. Of the Naming and the Cairn on the Height

They came down off the height in two days, going carefully on legs that had gone stiff with the cold and the standing, and reached Tobar dhìreach on the evening of the second day with the five cold coals in the bag and nothing else to show for a climb of three summers' finding and two days' doing, and yet the whole household knew before either of them had said a word that something had answered, for Fearghas came through the door with a look on him that no one at that hearth had worn coming back from any hill before.

He told it standing, as the telling of such things was always told at that hearth, with the bag open on the floor before him and the five dark coals laid out on a cloth for anyone to see and turn over who wanted to, and the household sat late into the night hearing it twice through, once from Fearghas and once, because Mathan would not be left out of the telling of a thing he had climbed for as long and as hard as his brother, from Mathan, whose telling ran shorter and rougher but agreed with Fearghas's in every particular that mattered. The old women who kept Gormal's saying at the recital wept at the hearing of it, the same weeping the old women were said to have wept the night Aodh came home from the northern sea, eight hundred years before, and by morning the telling had gone out from that hearth to every household within a day's walk, carried by whoever had heard it first and could not keep from carrying it further.

The summit took the kindred's name before that first winter was out, called Binnean a' Chlachair from the first telling of it and by no other name after, Binnean a' Chlachair, though no one household could afterward say for certain who had first called it so; it was as if the name had been waiting on the height the whole two thousand years since the mason struck his wedge into the rock, needing only a household willing to climb high enough to claim it. Herders of the high valleys who drove their flocks anywhere within sight of that grey summit began, within a few years of the telling, to leave a single stone on its crown whenever their own way brought them near enough to climb it, a small stone laid without much ceremony on the little cairn Mathan had begun, so that within a lifetime the crown that had been bare rock scoured clean by weather carried a heap of stone a man could see from some way off, each stone laid by a different hand and none of the hands ever troubling to say why, beyond that it seemed a poor thing to stand on such ground and leave nothing of oneself there.

Fearghas went back to the height himself twice more in his life, once with his own son grown old enough to make the climb, to show the boy the white fire still burning steady among the cold stones of the slope below the summit, unchanged in every particular from the morning he had first seen it catch, and once alone, in his last years, when his legs were no longer what they had been at two and thirty and the climb took him the better part of three days each way instead of two. He found the coal burning that third time exactly as he had left it every time before, and stood over it a long while in the cold, an old man now, remembering a morning when his own hands had shaken with more than cold, and left a stone of his own on the crown before he climbed down for the last time.

## IV. Of the Years After

Mathan did not live to see his brother's second climb. He died in his fifty-sixth year, of a fever that came on him in a wet spring and would not break, and was buried at Tobar dhìreach with the small cairn stone he had kept from the summit's crown, the very first one he had ever set there, closed in one hand at his own asking, for he had told his wife, in the last days when he could still speak clearly, that he wanted something of the height with him in the ground, having given the height, as he put it, three summers of his legs and the best notion he had ever had in his life. Fearghas stood over the grave and said nothing that the household later remembered as fit for the recital, only that his brother had trusted his eye from the first day on the ridge and had been right from the first day, whatever the walking after had cost either of them to prove it.

Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich went on being asked at every recital after, for five of na Seachd Guail still lay dark, the earth and the blood and the river and the fire, and the rainbow last of all, still to be found by hands not yet born, and the line did not grow easy merely because the sky had answered where the sea had answered before it; if anything, Fearghas himself was heard to say more than once, an old man by then, that a question answered twice in twelve hundred years was no cause for slackness, only for the patience to keep asking it a third time and a fourth. But something had changed at that hearth all the same, in a way none of the kin could easily have put into words. A household that has thrown one coal into the sea and had it answer, and thrown a second from the height of the whole island and had it answer too, keeps the other five with a different weight in its hands than a household that has only ever heard the throwing told as another household's story.

Fearghas himself lived into his sixty-second year, an old man by the standards of the high valleys though not the eldest anyone at that hearth had known, and he kept his own hand steady enough to turn the five remaining dark coals over by his own fire almost to the last, saying to whoever sat with him in those final months that he had climbed the highest ground the island owned and stood there with his own two feet under him, and a man who had done that once in his life had no great cause to fear a bed.

He was buried within sight of Leac na Fèithe that covered the mason's own vein, as every keeper and every finder of the line had been buried before him, and at the recital said over his grave that winter, standing as every recital of the fathers was said standing, the reciter gave the fathers' names down from Neachdan and Conall and Diarmad and Aodh, thirty-one fathers whose names the line no longer gave to strangers, down to the last of them, who was the father of Fearghas; and after his father's name the reciter said Fearghas's own, and told, in the fixed words that would be said the same way at every recital after, how he had climbed to the top of the island with his brother beside him and let the six coals fall, and how the snowflake had taken fire in the empty air and struck the stones below still burning, and how the summit bore the kindred's name from that day for as long as anyone should climb it. The old among the household, who had heard Gormal's own three hills argued over at that same hearth every winter of their childhood, stood through the whole of it with their heads bent, and when the reciter came to the naming of the height, more than one of them was heard to say the name back under their breath before the reciter had finished saying it aloud, as though the word had been waiting in them the whole long while since Gormal first named her hills, needing only someone to climb high enough to give it a place to stand.

# Chapter Seventeen: Of the Cliff-House and the Curved Mole

*VE 2,241 – 2,523*

## I. Of the Long House at Tarr

At Tarr, in the north-east, where the cliff broke back on itself into a cleft wide enough for a household to stand upright in and deep enough that the wind off the water lost most of its strength before it reached the innermost wall, a household built a single long house against the living rock rather than free of it, so that the cleft's own back became the house's back, and no wall needed raising where the cliff already stood higher than any wall a household could have built for itself. The floor they levelled with beach shingle carried up in baskets a load at a time, and the walls that closed the cleft's mouth were laid dry, stone on stone, no higher than was needed to keep out what the cliff itself did not already keep out, so that from the sea the house showed as little more than a darker line across the cleft's opening, easy to pass without marking at all unless a boat came close enough in to see the smoke.

The hearth they set against the rock face itself, a little back from the door, where the draught that found its way past the stones outside would not trouble a low flame, and it burned there through every season the household kept the house, fed on driftwood gathered along the shingle below and on whatever the sea gave up after a hard blow, so that in time the rock above the hearth blackened with soot to the height of a tall man standing, a stain no scrubbing ever lightened and none of the household ever tried to lighten, for a blackened stone over a hearth was no more remarkable to them than a blackened pot, and told only that the fire had been kept a long while in the one place. A child of that household, grown old enough to be sent for wood on her own, is remembered to have measured her own growing by that stain, standing back to it each year at midwinter to see how much further up the rock her own crown now reached, until the year she stood as tall as the soot itself and was told, by whoever stood the measuring with her, that she had grown past what the fire alone could tell her.

The winter that gave the household its hardest year came some years into their keeping of the cleft, when the wind held out of the north for the better part of two months without once swinging round to give the coast a day's rest from it, and the sea below the cliff ran white from the rocks out to as far as the cleft's mouth let anyone see, so that no boat put out from Tarr that whole stretch and the household lived on what it had already dried and salted and on shellfish gathered at low water between one gale and the next, work that fell hardest on whoever's hands were quickest and least troubled by the cold, for a slow hand on the rocks in that weather came back with less than the tide alone would have given it and sometimes did not come back with fingers it could feel at all. The driftwood ran thin before the wind did, and toward the worst of it the household burned what it could spare of a broken boat-frame kept those several years against just such a want, stripping it plank by plank rather than let the hearth go cold, and is remembered to have argued, in whatever words that argument took, over how much of the frame could be burned before there was not boat enough left in it to mend once the weather turned.

It turned at last a little before the shortest day, the wind dropping out of the north in the space of a single night and swinging round to a quarter that let the sea inside the cleft's mouth lie flat enough by morning for a hand to be put over the side without the cold of it stopping the breath outright, and the household is remembered to have gone down to the shingle that morning before the light was properly up, wanting nothing from the calm so soon beyond the standing in it, a place out of the wind at last where they could feel, for the first time in two months, a stillness that did not mean the storm was only drawing breath before it came again. What they found on the tide that morning, driven in against the rocks below the cleft, was a run of small fish thick enough to be taken by hand from the shallows, more than the household could eat fresh or dry before it turned, and it is told, in the one line of that winter's telling that has come down whole, that no year after was reckoned as hard as that one by anyone of Tarr who had lived through it, however hard a later winter might in its own turn have seemed while it was being lived.

The house stood the better part of that household's years in the cleft, mended where the sea reached it and left alone where the cliff already stood firm enough to need no mending, and a household coming after them kept the same hearth against the same blackened rock rather than clear the stain and begin again, holding, by whatever reasoning shaped it, that a fire already so long fed in one place burned the readier for being lit again where it had always been lit, and that a hearth moved even the width of the house lost something of what the years already spent there had given it.

Outside the one door the cleft allowed, a shelf of rock ran a little above the tide's ordinary reach, wide enough for a man to stand and cast from without wetting his feet, and the household kept its lines there through every season the fish ran close enough in to be worth the casting, coiling the wet cord each evening on a peg driven into a crack in the cliff face rather than carry it inside where the damp of it would trouble the floor. A boy of the household, sent out one still morning to draw water from a pool the tide filled and left standing among the rocks below the shelf, is remembered to have called the whole household out at a run for what he took at first sight to be a seal hauled up close under the cliff, and to have been laughed at gently, once the thing was seen plainly for a length of drifted timber turned dark and round-backed by the sea's own working of it, though the timber itself was kept afterward and split for firewood rather than thrown back, the fright it had given him judged no reason to waste good wood.

Winters lighter than the hardest one still asked their own toll of the household, for the cleft that broke the worst of the wind also kept the sun from the door through the shortest months, the cliff standing high enough on either side that the shingle floor saw direct light for no more than an hour at midday even on a clear one, and a household living so many years in that half-dark is remembered to have kept, without any of its own tellings troubling to say who began the custom, a second small fire lit just inside the door on the darkest days, fed lighter than the great hearth against the rock and let burn low, more for the little more light it gave the doorway than for any warmth the great hearth further back did not already give the whole house.

## II. Of the Vell on the Abhainn Bheag

A day's walk and more to the west of Tarr, where the Abhainn bheag ran down to the sea through banks steep enough on either side that a household building close to the water needed to cut its own level ground into the slope before it could raise a wall at all, a small Vell grew up a short way above the river's mouth: four houses set close along the cut ground, and beside them, nearer the water than any of the four, a boat-shed roofed the same way as the houses but longer and lower, built to keep a hull dry and out of the weather between one season's use and the next rather than to shelter anyone sleeping in it. No dwelling of the Seann-Dhaoine on the whole of that coast stood further to the north-east than the four houses at this Vell, a fact none of the four households troubled to remark on in any telling that has come down of them, for a household living at the world's furthest edge in its own day rarely knows itself to be living there, and knows only that its own water runs cold and its own reach up the coast finds nothing further before the shore itself gives out.

The river gave the Vell what the open sea further along the coast could not always be trusted to give: eels taken in wicker traps set where the current ran slow enough near the bank for a trap to hold its place, and salmon in their season, run thick enough some years that a household needed only to wade into the shallows with a spear and strike without much troubling to aim, the fish crowding past in such numbers that a poor cast found another target within the same breath as a good one missed its first. The boat-shed held one hull built for the river's own quieter water rather than for the open sea beyond its mouth, flat enough in the bottom to be poled up past the first rapids in a dry season when the current ran low, and the household that built it is remembered to have gone further up the Abhainn bheag in that boat than any of the four households had gone on foot, coming back with word of ground upriver that none of them, in the years that followed, ever troubled to walk out and see for themselves, holding the word of the boat's own crew good enough without the seeing.

A child of the Vell, born into the youngest of the four households in the years the boat-shed still smelled of its own new-cut timber, grew up knowing the river before she knew the sea it ran to, and is remembered, once grown, for having gone down to the river's mouth on a still evening and stood a long while looking out past it at the open water beyond, water wider and greyer than anything the river itself had ever shown her, before turning back up the bank to the four houses without going any further down the shore to see what lay beyond the mouth in either direction. It is told that she never went that further way in all her years at the Vell, holding, when asked, that a mouth was as far as a river's own child had any business going before the river's own water gave out under her, and that what a boat might carry a person to beyond that mouth was the boat's own business and not hers.

The four houses stood close enough to the water that a hard spring flood, coming once in a run of years when snow high on the central massif melted faster than the ground could carry it away, rose far enough up the bank to reach the boat-shed's lower course and stood there the better part of a day before falling back, leaving the shed's floor silted with river mud that took a household the best part of a week to clear, working the mud out in baskets the same way the shingle at Tarr had once been carried up in baskets, though no one at the Vell on the Abhainn bheag ever knew, or had any way to know, that a household so far along the coast from them was that same year carrying the same kind of load for much the same reason. After that flood the boat-shed was raised a course higher on its uphill side, and no later flood, however high the snow-melt ran, troubled the hull kept inside it again in the years this telling follows.

The four households ate well enough in most years to spare a share of their eel-catch and their salmon both, dried and smoked over slow fires built for no other purpose, for kin further down the coast who kept no river of their own and were glad of a fish that did not taste of salt water in every bite; and word of what the Vell on the Abhainn bheag could spare travelled, by whatever slow paths word travelled along that shore, far enough that a household from two days' walk to the south is remembered to have come up once in a lean year with nothing to trade but a good store of dried seaweed and a promise of help at the next boat-launching, and to have gone home again with more dried fish than the promise alone seemed to the Vell's own households worth, given all the same because a household that asked plainly for help in a lean year was not, by the Vell's own reckoning, a household to be sent away counting.

The eel-traps wanted mending every season the willow they were woven from dried and split in the sun between one setting and the next, and the weaving of a new trap fell, in the years this telling follows, mostly to an old woman of the youngest household who had learned the pattern as a girl from hands older still than her own, and who is remembered to have taught it in turn to two of the Vell's children, a boy and a girl both, holding that a pattern known only in one pair of hands was a pattern one bad season from being lost to the whole Vell, whatever a river running full of eels every year of a person's own life might tempt that person to believe.

## III. Of the Second Mole at Skell

On the northern coast, far from the river mole the Seann-Dhaoine had laid out into the Abhainn naomh at the great Skell many generations before, a household of a second Skell took up the same work for its own stretch of water, laying stone on stone out from a low headland; but where the river mole ran straight against a current, this one was given a curve against the open swell, so that a boat standing off in rough weather with that headland in sight could find, by the shape of the stone alone, water calmer than the sea running past it on either side.

The work went slower than the first mole's own telling remembers its own laying to have gone, for the household at this second Skell had fewer hands to spare from the ordinary work of the shore than the builders of the first mole are remembered to have had, and carried the stone for their own curve down from a scree a little back from the water rather than quarry fresh rock, choosing each piece for its fit against the pieces already laid rather than for the ease of carrying it, so that some years the curve grew by no more than a boat's length of new stone and other years, when the scree gave up pieces that fitted well one against another, by a good deal more. A household further along the shore, watching the curve grow from one season's visit to the next, is remembered to have said of it only that stone laid slow stood no less firm for the slowness, a saying that outlasted, in the tellings that have come down, the names of whoever first said it.

The curve was carried far enough out, by the year this telling now reaches, to break the swell for the length of shore behind it that the household judged worth the sheltering, and no further, for a longer mole asked more stone than the scree behind the shore was ever likely to give up and more years than any one household expected to have hands enough to spend on it.
