A boat brought in behind the finished curve on a day the open sea beyond it still ran hard rode easier at its mooring than any boat of that shore had ridden before the mole stood finished, and a household that had lost gear more than once to a swell running in past an unsheltered mooring is remembered to have moved its own hull inside the new curve within the same season the last stone was laid, without waiting to see a full year's weather prove the shelter good.

The two moles, the river mole far to the south-west and this curved one on the northern coast, were never joined in any telling that has come down, each household knowing its own stone and its own stretch of sheltered water and little enough, beyond the bare fact that another such mole stood somewhere along the same coast, of the other's. It is told that a boy of the second Skell, grown to a man and travelling some way south-west over the land on an errand this telling does not trouble to name, came once within sight of the first mole and stood some while looking at it before going on, saying to whoever asked him of his travelling, on his return, only that the stone there was laid the same way as the stone he had grown up watching laid at home, stone for stone, though built, so far as either shore ever came to know, without one household ever having set eyes on the other's work before it was finished.

The choosing of the stone asked more of the households than the carrying did, for a piece taken from the scree without care for its shape as often sat loose against its neighbours as true, and a wall of loose-fitting stone standing against an open swell failed sooner than the swell itself troubled to test it fully, so the household that kept the work longest is remembered for a habit of laying each new piece dry against the course already set before committing it, working it back and forth by hand until it sat without rocking, and setting it only then, a slower way of building than simply piling what came to hand but one that let the second Skell's own curve stand, by the time this telling reaches it, through more winters of hard weather than the household that began it had thought, at the outset, the work would ever need to answer for.

One autumn a swell rose out of the north-west harder and longer than any the second Skell had yet tried its unfinished curve against, breaking clean over the stone at its furthest point and running white the whole visible length of it for the better part of two days, and the household that had laid the most recent courses went down each morning of that swell expecting to find its own work of the past several seasons scattered back along the shore the sea had taken it from; it found instead, when the swell dropped at last, every stone still where it had been set, moved perhaps a hand's width here and there but nowhere thrown clear, and took the finding as proof enough of the slow way of laying it had kept to that no household of that shore, in any telling that has come down, is remembered to have argued for a quicker one after.

## IV. Of the Pits in the Western Dune

On the western shore, where the Seann-Dhaoine had long kept a Vell among the dunes a little back from the open beach, a household began, in these same years, to dig a line of pits into the dune's own slope rather than raise anything above it, each pit cut down past the loose upper sand to ground firm enough to hold its shape, lined round with clay carried up from the river mouth a short walk to the south and beaten smooth against the sand walls before it dried, and closed at last with a slab of flat stone heavy enough that no fox working at it in the night could shift it clear.

What went into the pits was whatever the shore gave more of than a household could eat in the season it was taken: fish salted and dried past the point a gull or a fox would trouble to dig for it, shellfish packed in their own liquor and sealed while it still ran fresh, and in a lean season the last of a stranded catch too much for any one household's ordinary stores to hold. A pit once filled and lidded was left alone through the season it was meant for, opened only when the shore's own ordinary catch had run thin enough that a household judged the stored season's food worth more, taken now, than left sealed against a leaner year still to come, a reckoning each household made for itself and is not remembered to have agreed on with its neighbours, so that one pit might stand opened in a season another, dug the same year and filled the same way, was left sealed through.

A woman of the western Vell, whose own hands had dug the first of the line and lined it before any other household of that shore had troubled to dig one of its own, is remembered to have argued, in the years the line of pits grew from one to a scatter of a dozen and more, that a pit dug too near another drew damp from its neighbour through ground neither clay lining alone could wholly stop, and to have set her own later pits a full body's length apart from the first for that reason, a spacing the households that came after her on that stretch of dune are remembered to have kept without troubling to test, for themselves, whether her reasoning held.

Some of the pits, opened after longer than a season had passed over them, gave back less than had gone in: fish bones picked clean of anything a household might still have wanted from them, the flesh gone and the bones themselves gone soft with damp that had found its way past even the best-laid clay in the end, and a household opening such a pit learned, from the finding, to trust the clay less far into a second year than into its first, and to empty a store before the season turned rather than let it stand sealed on the chance a leaner year might still make use of it.

The clay itself was not always got without argument among the households that shared the walk down to the river mouth for it, for a bank cut too often in the same place slumped in the next high water and gave up no good clay at all until a season's rain had settled it back into a workable bed, and the woman who had dug the first pit is remembered to have kept, in her own head if nowhere any telling has set down, a kind of turn among the households as to which bank each might cut in a given season, a turn she never once wrote or marked in any way this telling can point to, holding it only in memory and in the asking, each spring, of whoever meant to dig that year where the last digging had been. A younger household new to the dune, not yet knowing the turn she kept, once cut a bank two others had already agreed between themselves to leave a season fallow, and gave over, when the disagreement that followed reached her, one full pit's worth of its own dried catch to the household whose turn it had truly been, a settling neither side is remembered to have thought unfair once it was made.

The lids themselves were not all of one stone. Some were slabs carried whole from a low reef bared at the lowest tides a little south along the beach, flat enough on both faces to need no working before they were set; others, where no slab of the right size could be got whole, were built up of two or three smaller stones fitted edge to edge and packed round with clay the same way the pit's own walls were packed, a harder seal to keep sound than a single slab but one that let a household close a pit dug in a season the reef gave up nothing of the size it wanted. A pit closed with the pieced lid asked checking, once or twice through a long winter, that the clay between the stones had not dried and cracked enough to let a fox's nose in at it, a small chore that fell, in most households, to whichever child was old enough to walk the dune alone and young enough still to be given so plain a task without complaint.

In these same years a quiet came over that shore that none of its households ever put a plain reason to in any telling that has come down whole: doors that had for generations faced the open water without a second thought began, in one household after another, to be set a little more toward the dune at their backs than toward the sea in front, and a family that had always kept its hearth nearest the door that looked seaward moved it, without remark, nearer the wall that looked inland instead. No teller of that shore ever said what the eyes had begun to look for in that direction, or whether they found it, and none of the households that turned their doors is remembered to have said so themselves; only that where a threshold had once opened straight onto the beach, it came, in those years, to open a little sideways from it, toward the rising ground behind. The last pit of that season was dug, lined and lidded before the first hard frost, Leac na Fèithe set and the sand banked back over its edges the way every pit before it had been closed, and the shore settled, as it had every year before, into the waiting that a sealed store and a closed season together asked of it, though what else it had begun, in those same years, to wait for, none of its own tellings ever say.

# Chapter Eighteen: Of the Outpost and the Three Rings

*VE 2,524 – 2,678*

## I. Of the Wall on the Spur

For as long as any hearth of the Seann-Dhaoine could tell of itself, its people had kept to the shore. They dressed stone at Morn, dried fish over peat smoke in the seven pits of the kilns, launched hulls down the ramps at Brenn, raised round houses over a stranded whale's ribs, and buried pits of clay-lined store against the lean months, but whatever they raised, they raised within a morning's walk of salt water, and no telling of that shore said why, only that it had always been so. In the year the spur was first climbed, that had already stopped being true a season or two, though none of the diggers who broke ground on it that spring could have said when the stopping began.

The spur stood a day's walk inland from the nearest kiln, a shoulder of higher ground thrown out from the southern lowland where the grass thinned to gorse and the wind lost the salt smell it carried everywhere nearer the water. A household that had fished three generations out of the same cove sent its two eldest sons up first, to look before anyone thought to build, and what they came back saying was that a man standing on the spur's crown could see the whole lowland laid out below him the way a gull sees it, and see, too, any thing that moved across that lowland long before it reached the cove. Whether that was reason enough to raise a wall so far from the water, no one now living could tell straight, but a wall went up all the same, through two summers of carrying stone on sledges dragged by hand up a slope steep enough that more than one load went over sideways and had to be gathered again from where it had rolled.

The mason who set the first course, a woman past the middle of her years and known on that shore for the evenness of her fitting rather than for her name, chose to dress the stones only on the face that would show outward, leaving the inner face rough as it came from the ground. Asked why, by a younger man who thought it a waste of good stone to leave any of it unworked, she said only that a wall need be smooth where an enemy's eye would run along it looking for a hold to climb by, and rough where a friend's hand would rest on it going up the inside steps, and that a stone dressed on both faces for no reason but tidiness was a stone whose labour had gone begging. The younger man had no answer to that beyond a shrug, and the wall rose the rest of its course the same way, smooth without, raw within, and stood so through every season it was kept.

The gate they set to face inland, away from the sea the whole people had always kept its face toward, and this choice more than any other is remembered to have been argued over at length before the first lintel stone was lifted into place. One old man, who had fished the same cove as the mason's own kin and had never in his life built anything higher than a smokehouse, said plainly that a gate looking away from the water was a gate built by people who had forgotten what the water had always been to them, and that no good would come of turning a whole household's door from the one direction the sea had never yet failed to feed it from. The mason answered him, not unkindly, that the sea had never yet come up the spur to trouble anyone standing on it, and that whatever a gate here needed watching against would not come rowing. The old man went home unconvinced and is not remembered to have climbed the spur again in the years he had left, though he sent his own grandsons up to help finish the carrying whenever the work asked for more hands than the spur's own people could spare.

Through that first winter Làrach an Dùin-fhaire held no more than a handful of families, enough to keep the wall's steps swept of snow and a watch kept from first light to last, and it is told that the watch in those early months was kept less for any thing seen approaching than for the keeping's own sake, as though the people who had built so far from the water needed some task to fill the silence a coastal hearth never knew, the silence of ground that gave back no tide sound and no gull cry, only wind moving through gorse and, some nights, nothing at all. A woman who kept that first winter's watch longer than anyone else of her household, because sleep came harder to her than to the rest, used to say afterward that the quiet up there had a weight to it unlike any quiet the shore ever gave, and that she had grown, before the winter was out, almost to prefer it to the sea's own noise, a preference she never fully explained even to those who asked her outright what she meant by it.

By the second summer the gate itself was hung, a heavy door of oak planks pegged edge to edge and swung on a socketed post that two strong men together could just move on its hinge, and the day it first swung shut on its own weight without needing a shoulder to help it home is remembered as a small feast day among the households that had given hands to the work, though no telling now living can say which household first thought to mark it so, or what exactly was eaten or said. What is remembered plainly is that the old fisherman who had argued against the inland gate came up that day unbidden, stood at the threshold a long while without going either in or out, and at last put his own hand flat against the swung door and said nothing at all, a silence the young folk who saw it took, rightly or wrongly, for a kind of blessing withheld and given both at once.

Cattle were driven up the spur that same summer for the first time, a slow business of coaxing beasts used to level grazing up a slope steeper than any they had climbed before, and more than one animal balked outright at the gate itself, planting its feet and lowing until a rope round its horns and three men's shoulders together got it through. Once inside, though, the beasts settled to the thin grass within the wall readily enough, and a boy set to herd them there through that first season used to say the cattle seemed, within a few days, no longer to miss the sea grass they had grazed all their lives, a settling he thought stranger, in his own way, than anything the people themselves had done in coming up.

The steps that ran up the wall's inner face on both sides of the gate were cut narrow and set close, each no deeper than half a foot, so that a watcher could go up or down them at a run in the dark without needing to look at his own feet to find the next one, and it was the boy who herded the cattle, more often than any grown watcher, who was sent up and down them fastest, carrying word between the gate and whoever stood the height at any hour, since a boy's legs tired less of the running than a grown man's did and a boy could be spared from other work more readily than a man who was needed, besides, at the wall itself or out among the beasts. He came, before that first year was out, to know every uneven tread in both flights of steps by the feel of it under a bare foot, and is remembered to have said once, when an older cousin asked him how he never once stumbled going up in full dark, that his feet had simply learned the wall the way a hand learns a rope it has hauled on every day for a year, without his ever once sitting down to learn it on purpose.

It was that same boy, in the second autumn of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire's keeping, who first raised the cry that brought every watcher on the wall to the gate side at a run, for what he saw, coming across the lowland from the west in the last low light of an evening, was a line of shapes he took at first for a herd of deer moving faster and more evenly together than any deer he had ever watched cross open ground. The watch was called and held through that whole night, torches kept burning along the inner steps though no one on the wall could say for certain, once full dark had come down, whether the shapes were still out there or had never been more than deer after all, moving as deer sometimes did in a hard year when a whole herd shifted ground together ahead of an early frost. By first light nothing showed on the lowland at all, no track a careful eye could find once a party went down to look, and the matter was let go without ever being settled either way, though the boy himself held to his first telling of it all his life, and Làrach an Dùin-fhaire's watch, from that autumn on, was never again let lapse to a single pair of eyes the way it had sometimes been let lapse before.

## II. Of the Cistern and the Three Rings

Some distance off, on a height nearer the south-eastern coast, a greater work was rising in those same years, and the two crews that raised it never once, in any telling that has come down whole, met at either site or knew in full what the other built, so that each held for a long while to its own account of what was going up on the far height, some saying it no more than a second watch-wall like their own, others saying it something larger they could not picture without having seen it. It was, in the end, larger by a wide measure: three walls, ringed one within the other round a hilltop broad enough, once the innermost ring was closed, to hold four hundred people at once with their beasts and their stores besides, a scale no single household on that coast had ever raised to before.

The crew that raised it worked under a woman the tellings give no name to beyond what her own people called her, the one who reads the ground, for it was said of her that she could stand on a rise and see, before a single stone was laid, where a wall would hold and where the same wall built a spear's length to either side would slide with the first hard winter's frost, a reading she never once explained beyond saying that the ground told her plainly enough if a body only stood still long enough to be told. Under her eye the outer ring went up first, broad and low, more a barrier to slow an approach than to stop one outright, and behind it the middle ring rose higher and thinner, and behind that again the innermost ring stood tallest of the three, tall enough that a man standing at its base and looking up could not see over it without stepping well back.

The cistern was cut into the bedrock at the hill's own crown before either ring was finished, a basin hollowed by hand and fire together, heated stone after heated stone cracked loose from the rock with water thrown on while it still glowed, a labour that is remembered to have taken the better part of two whole seasons and to have blistered more hands than the rest of the building together. The woman who read the ground stood over that digging as closely as she stood over the walls, and is remembered to have said, when a digger asked how deep the basin need go, that it should go deep enough to hold water through a summer no rain fell in, though none then living had seen such a summer, and that a cistern cut shallow to save a season's labour was a cistern that would fail exactly the year it was most needed.

It filled for the first time the spring the innermost ring was closed, a slow filling from a spring found seeping through a crack near the basin's foot that no one had marked until the digging opened it wider, and the day the water stood a hand's depth over the basin's floor a child of one of the building households was let climb down on a rope to fetch up the first drawn measure in a skin, more for the wonder of the thing than for any thirst the height's own people yet had. The woman who read the ground tasted that first measure herself before anyone else touched it, held it in her mouth a long moment, and said only that it tasted of stone, which everyone standing by took as high praise from her, whatever it might have meant from anyone else.

Cattle were driven inside the rings that same year, a longer and steeper climb than the spur had asked of its own beasts, and more animals were lost on the way up, over loose scree that gave without warning under a hoof, than the spur's herders had ever lost driving theirs. A woman who lost two of her own household's beasts that climb is remembered to have said afterward that whatever the three rings kept out, they charged dear enough for what they let in, a saying repeated on that height for years after by anyone minded to grumble at the work the rings' upkeep still asked of them.

The inner buildings went up more slowly than the walls, round houses set close along the innermost ring's inner face, roofed in turf cut from the hill's own flank so that from a distance, before smoke rose from any of them, the whole crown of the hill showed as one unbroken slope of green, the houses hidden in the ground's own shape the way a bird's nest is hidden in a hedge. A household that moved up from the shore to take one of the first of these houses is remembered to have found, its first winter within the rings, that the wind that reached them there, filtered three times over by wall after wall, was gentler by far than any wind the same household had known at the water's edge, a mercy none of them had thought to look for in coming so far from the sea, though it was thought a poor trade by more than one older voice among them, weighed against all that the sea itself was no longer at hand to give.

The woman who read the ground grew old within the rings she had raised, and in her last years she took to walking the innermost ring alone each morning before the rest of the height was awake, a slow circuit with a stick to lean on that had once needed no stick at all, and more than one of the younger builders who saw her at it took to walking a length of the wall with her, for she said little on those mornings, but to be shown, by nothing more than where she chose to stop and rest a hand flat on the stone, which stretches of the three rings she still judged sound and which she had begun, in her own private reckoning, to distrust. She never said outright that any stretch of wall she had herself set was failing, only that a wall, like a person, aged unevenly, some lengths of it good for a hundred winters and others, laid the very same season by the very same hands, good for a good deal less, and that a height meant to hold four hundred people needed someone always walking it who could tell the difference before the ground told it plainer, in a wet spring, by giving way.

She died within the innermost ring in a season the tellings give no exact count of years for beyond saying she was old, and her own people buried her, at her own asking made long before, not outside the rings among the dead of the households that had come up from the shore, but within the second ring's shelter, close under a stretch of wall she had named to more than one listener, in her last winter, as the soundest work of her whole life. A cairn was raised over her there small enough not to trouble the ground the cattle grazed, and it is told that for as long as the height was kept, no herder let a beast graze close against that particular cairn, though none of them could have said, pressed for a reason, what harm they thought a hoof might do to stones that had already stood so many winters undisturbed.

## III. Of the Kerbed Way

Between the spur and the height a stretch of lower ground ran, marsh in its wettest reaches and stony moor in its driest, ground that had never before carried more traffic than a herder's own two feet, and it was across this ground, in the years Làrach an Dùin-fhaire's wall stood finished and the rings' innermost course still rose course by course on the height beyond, that a track was laid the like of which the Seann-Dhaoine had never built away from the shore in all the generations the tellings hold.

It began, by most accounts, as no more than a line of trodden ground worn by the few who had reason to go between the two rising works, a path that grew muddier each season as more feet used it, until a household living along its worst stretch, tired of hauling loads through ankle-deep mire every time the rain held more than a day, laid a scatter of flat stones across the softest ground simply to keep its own feet dry, with no thought, at the laying, of any greater work to follow. Others saw the dry going those few stones gave and laid more beside them, each household adding what it could spare of its own labour to the stretch nearest its own door, so that the track grew the way a shoreline midden grows, one household's contribution at a time, with no single hand ever holding the whole plan of it from one end to the other.

It was only some years into this scattered laying that anyone thought to kerb the edges, setting upright stones along both sides of the trodden way to hold the paving in place against the ground's own slow spreading, and the first stretch so kerbed held so much better through a wet winter than the unkerbed stretches on either side of it that the practice spread along the whole track within a few more seasons, each household that had laid its own piece coming back to add the kerb its neighbours had shown the worth of. A cart, once the kerbing held firm enough over a long enough stretch, could be dragged its width without a wheel sinking to the axle, and it is told that the first load ever so dragged, of stone meant for the height's own innermost ring, went across in a single day where the same load, hauled the old way over open moor, had once taken the better part of three.

The paving itself was never of one stone throughout, for each household cut what its own nearest quarrying gave, so that a traveller walking the whole way in one going would have passed, in a single day's walk, over pale stone and dark, over slabs broad as a door and stretches of smaller stones fitted edge to edge like the pieced lids of a storage pit, the whole track a record, to anyone minded to read it so, of every household that had ever laid a hand to it, though none of those households, laying its own short stretch, is remembered to have thought of the work as anything grander than keeping its own feet dry between one season and the next.

A cart was driven the whole length of the track for the first time in the year the last of its middle stretches was kerbed, laden with dressed stone meant for the height's outer ring and drawn by two yoked oxen a household near the spur had raised from calves for no other purpose, and the driver of that first cart, a young man who had never before taken a load further than the short haul from his own quarrying to his own household's wall, is remembered to have walked the whole way at the oxen's heads rather than ride, watching the wheels for any give in the paving that might tip the load, and to have found, at the far end, that not one stone of it had shifted the whole way, a steadiness he called out to the height's own people before he had so much as unyoked the beasts, as proud of the road's holding as he might have been of a wall he had raised himself.

The last stretch to be laid ran up the final rise toward the height itself, steeper than any ground the track had yet crossed, and the crew that closed it set its final slab, by every account that has come down whole, tilted a little rather than level as the rest of the track had been laid, so that the paving's whole run, seen from below, seemed to lift the eye up the slope and on past the height itself toward the high country further inland, the central mountains standing pale and distant beyond the nearer ground the way they stood on every clear day from anywhere on that coast, though no teller of that laying ever said the tilt was meant to point there, only that the stone was set so and has lain so ever since, unmoved by any season that has passed over it, and that whoever set it last, whether by design or by nothing more than the ground's own lie under that final slab, is not remembered by any name the tellings have kept.

## IV. Of the Turning

What passed between the households of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and the households of the three rings in the years both works stood finished, no telling that has come down whole says plainly, for the two never worked one crew and kept, even after the track joined them, more to their own hill each than to any single people shared between the two heights. But it was of both together, and of no other work the Seann-Dhaoine had raised before them, that the shore hearths first began to say the thing that afterward became a saying repeated the length of that coast: that a people who had always kept their faces to the sea had, in those years, without any single voice among them ever quite deciding it aloud, turned their faces from it instead, toward the ground behind them and the high country beyond that ground, a turning no shore mother ever fully explained to a child who asked why the family's own door, that had opened on the water three generations running, now opened instead on the path inland.

It was not that the sea was given up. The kilns at Morn still smoked through every drying season, the ramps at Brenn still launched their hulls, and the households of the two new heights sent down, every year, kin enough to keep a hand in the old work and bring back dried fish and traded shell for a hearth too far from the water to gather its own. But the gate that had once seemed, to the old fisherman who mistrusted it, a strange thing to build facing away from the only direction that had ever fed his people, no longer seemed strange to anyone climbing the spur by the year the last slab of the track was laid, and a child born within either ring of the height, or within the spur's own wall, grew to walking age never once having slept in a house that heard the tide.

The last stone was set into the kerbed way's final stretch on a still morning with no wind off the sea to carry any salt smell up that high, and the small crew that set it, having no more stone of its own to add and no further stretch left unpaved between the two heights, stood a while looking back the way the track had come, down across the lower moor toward the shore neither height could any longer see from where they stood, and then turned, without any word the tellings have kept, to look instead the other way, up the track's own tilted last slab and past it, toward the high pale country that had stood at the edge of every clear day's sight for as long as any of them had lived, and had never before that morning seemed a thing worth walking toward.

# Chapter Nineteen: Of the Altar and the Shafts

*VE 2,679 – 2,800*

> *Na las teine far am faic e thu.*
> Light no fire where it can see you.

*The Fourth Part: Of the Black Coal in the Ground, Uilebheist na Mara and Marbh-bheò*

## I. Of the Platform in the Eastern Hills

The last slab of the kerbed track had lain a bare season before the households of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and Làrach an Dùin began, without any telling saying which of them first raised a hand to it, a work higher into the hills than either wall or ring: a platform of fitted stone built up in steps on a shoulder of ground in the eastern hills, each step no higher than a man's knee and wide enough along its whole run for two people to walk abreast, so that a climb up its face went easier than a climb up any hillside near it, though no telling says why so gentle a climb was ever wanted there in the first place. On the topmost step, set back from its outer edge by rather more than a stride, a single great block of stone was laid and dressed flat on its upper face, and it is this block, more than the steps that carried a person up to it, that the tellings of the hills came in time to mean when they spoke of Làrach an Teampaill.

The stone for the platform was quarried some way off and dragged up on rollers of trimmed timber, the same labour that had raised Làrach an Dùin-fhaire's wall and Làrach an Dùin's three rings, and a household that had helped haul stone for either of those earlier works would have known this hauling for the same kind of work, only carried higher and further than either. What set the altar block apart from every other stone Seann-Dhaoine had ever cut and laid, in the eastern hills or on any shore before them, was not its size, for stones as large had gone into Làrach an Dùin's walls, but the line its face was cut to lie along, for while every mole, every ramp, every kiln and every round house Seann-Dhaoine had ever raised faced the water that fed it, salt or fresh, near or by sight, the top of this one stone was squared instead to the great mountains standing in the middle of the island, a good many miles off and out of sight of any sea at all from where the block was set.

Who first laid a level along that line, and by what means, no telling that has come down says, and none of the households that climbed the platform's steps in the years that followed ever troubled, in any word remembered of them, to ask. A woman old enough to have climbed those steps as a girl and again as a grandmother said only, of the one time she was asked by a stranger why the great stone at the top looked where it looked and not where the sea lay, that the stone had always looked that way and that a thing so set before her own grandmother's grandmother was no more hers to question than the shape of her own hand.

In the first years of the platform's standing, before habit had worn a clear path up its steps, a household of the southern lowland is remembered to have gone up at first light on the shortest morning of the year, carrying nothing between them that any telling names, and to have stood some while about the great stone as the sun came up over the sea behind them and its first light ran along the top of the block and out toward the mountains it was squared to, touching, for the little while the sun stood low enough to throw a light so far, the same line the stone held. What was said at that standing, if anything was said, has not come down; what has come down is only that the household went up again the next year at the same season, and the year after that, and that others of the lowland, seeing them go, began in time to go up too, until the shortest morning of the year found more households climbing the steps together than any single household could have climbed alone.

A boy of one such household, sent up for the first time old enough to be trusted on the steps without a hand held out for him, is remembered to have asked, on the climb, what it was they were going up to see, and to have been told by whoever climbed beside him only that they were going up to see the light meet the stone, an answer that satisfied him well enough at the time and that he is remembered, grown old in his turn, to have given in the same words to a child of his own asking the same question on the same climb. No one of the eastern hills, in any telling that has come down whole, ever said more than that of what the standing was for, or what, if anything, the mountains the stone looked toward were held to hold. A crowd need not know why it gathers each year at the same season to watch a light meet a stone; the tellings remember the gathering, kept and passed on, far more surely than they remember why it began.

The rite, once it had settled into a yearly thing, kept always to the one morning and never to any other, whatever the weather made of that morning, so that a year came, within living memory of those who told of it after, when cloud lay thick over the eastern hills from the day before the shortest morning until well past it, and no light reached the stone at all that year for any household to see meet it; and it is remembered that the households climbed the steps all the same, in the dark and the cold, and stood about the great stone through the whole of the morning it would have taken the light to cross it, and went down again when the hour had passed without a word of complaint at what the cloud had cost them, holding, so far as the telling says anything of their holding, that the standing was owed whether the light came to be seen or not.

None of the households that kept the rite, in all the years this telling follows, ever cut so much as a single mark into the great stone, though marks were being cut in those same years on the cliffs of the eastern coast by hands of their own people, and the stone stood at the century's end exactly as it had been dressed at the century's start, bare of any sign but the flatness of its own face and the squareness of its own cut. A woman who kept, among her own household's things, a small carved bird of the kind the Seann-Dhaoine of the shore sometimes carved and buried with their dead, is remembered to have carried it up once and set it at the stone's foot rather than take it home again, and to have gone down without it; whether this was the rite's own custom or a thing she alone did, no telling that has come down can now say, for no second such bird, and no third, was ever found at the stone's foot by anyone who came after her.

The steps themselves asked more years to finish than the great stone atop them asked to raise, for a household laying flat stone into a slope worked slower than a household piling wall on open ground, each slab bedded and levelled before the next was set above it, and the work was carried on, by the tellings that name it at all, mostly in the months between one planting and the next, when the hands that dug and hauled were not also wanted for the ground below. A man who gave the better part of his own years to the laying of the upper steps, where the slope stood steepest and the stone wanted the most patient setting, is remembered to have refused more than once to let a slab go into place before he had knelt on it himself and rocked his own weight across it, holding that a step a person's foot could feel give, even by a hand's width, was a step that would, given the years, throw someone from it, and that the platform's whole worth lay in a climb no one troubled to watch their own feet upon. The last step, laid some years after the great stone had already stood on its own step above the unfinished work below it, closed the run at the bottom flush with the moor's own ground, so that a person coming to it from level walking felt no more than the least catch underfoot before the climb began, and it is this last, easiest step, rather than any higher and harder-won one, that the tellings of the households nearest the platform remember best, for it was the one every child among them first learned to find with a bare foot in the dark, going up before dawn on the one morning of the year the climb was made.

A stranger to the eastern hills, come up from the southern lowland on some errand the telling does not trouble to name, is remembered to have stood at the platform's foot one year on an ordinary day, neither the shortest morning nor any day near it, and to have asked of a woman drawing water nearby what the great stone at the top was raised for; and she is remembered to have answered him, in words a granddaughter of hers repeated to others, that a stone which had stood before her grandmother's grandmother needed no raising explained to a stranger who had not troubled to be born to it, and to have gone on with her drawing without looking up again at either the stranger or the stone. He is not remembered to have climbed the steps himself, that day or any other, nor to have come back a second time; and no telling of the eastern hills, from that year to the end of this one, names him again.

## II. Of the Shaft at the Eastern Toll-dubh

Some years into the platform's keeping, and some way off from it, at a place in the south-east the hills already called Toll-dubh before any hand had touched it, a household began a work of a wholly different kind: not up, as the platform went, and not out along a shore, as every mole and every ramp before it had gone, but straight down into the ground, on level moor where no well and no quarry had ever yet been cut.

The first cut was no deeper than a well's own depth, and for the better part of a year it might have passed, to anyone who came upon it without knowing better, for a well begun and left, the kind of half-finished digging a household abandons when the water it hoped for does not come. But the digging went on past the depth any well on that moor had ever needed to reach, and it went on straight, cut round and true as a well is cut, but with its walls worked smooth by hand long after the digging alone would have left them rough, an old man of the household standing at the lip each evening with a lamp let down on a cord to judge, by the reach of its light along the walls, how far the smoothing had been carried and how much of the day's work still wanted doing before the light gave out on him.

The baskets that came up out of the shaft, full of the broken rock the digging threw off, were carried away each evening over the rise at the moor's edge by whoever's turn it was to carry them, and were not, by any telling that has come down of that household, brought back empty the way a basket carried only a little way is brought back; and no heap of the rock so carried was ever afterward found anywhere near the shaft's mouth, nor anywhere on the moor about it that anyone troubled to walk out and look. Where rock enough to fill so many baskets went, over years enough to sink a shaft so deep, no telling that has come down so much as guesses at; the telling gives only the carrying, evening on evening, and the going, and lets the rest lie where the household itself let it lie.

A woman of that household, grown old in the years the digging went on, is remembered to have said to a granddaughter asking after the rock's going, only that some work is carried and some work is asked after, and that a household did well to know which was which before it went asking the wrong question of the wrong work. The granddaughter, so the telling says, never asked again, though whether from being satisfied by the answer or from knowing, by the way it was given, that no better answer would follow it, the telling does not say either.

The lamp was let down further with each year the shaft went deeper, on a longer length of the same plaited cord each time, and it is remembered that a length was added to the cord on three separate occasions before the digging stopped, each addition marked, in the one telling that names it at all, only by the household gathering at the lip on the evening a new length was first paid out, to watch the lamp go down further than it had ever gone before and come up again still burning. On the last such evening the telling names, the lamp went down so far that its light, by the time it reached the bottom, showed no more of the walls around it than a small round patch no wider than a man's two hands held apart, the rest of the shaft's depth standing dark above and below that patch alike, and it was on this same evening, or very near it, that the digging is remembered to have stopped, though no telling says in so many words that the two things were one and the same, or that the small patch of light was the reason the digging went no further.

A stone let fall from the lip on an evening after the digging had stopped, by a hand the telling does not name, gave back no sound of striking anything below, though the household that let it fall stood listening a good while after it left the hand, in a silence that the telling remembers as longer than the silence any of them had kept for anything else in all the years of that digging, well or ill.

The work was not without its cost to the hands that did it, for a shaft cut so narrow and so straight gave a person let down into it no room to fall wrong without striking the wall on the way, and a young man of the household, sent down one autumn on the cord to free a basket that had caught against a shoulder of unworked rock some way below the lip, is remembered to have come up again with a gash along one forearm that kept him from the heaviest carrying the better part of a season, and to have gone down again the following spring all the same, the cord tied about him the same way it had always been tied, as if a single wound was owed no more weight in the reckoning than a blister from the oar or the mattock. The cord was renewed twice in the years the digging went on, the old length kept afterward rather than thrown aside, coiled and hung inside the household's own door, so that a visitor coming to that threshold afterward might see, without being told what it had once measured, two lengths of worn hide cord hanging where another household might have hung a net or a snare.

Winter closed the shaft each year before the ground froze hard enough to trouble the digging, for the lamp burned poorly in the damp that gathered in the depth once the air above turned cold, and guttered more than once, in tellings that name the guttering at all, before it could be drawn up again; and it became the household's own custom, kept without any single year's telling saying when it began, to lay a flat stone loosely over the shaft's mouth each year at the first hard frost and lift it again only when the days had lengthened past the shortest, a covering meant, so far as the telling says anything of its meaning, to keep a wandering beast or a careless foot from the lip through the months no one went down to work it, rather than to shut anything already below away from anything still above.

## III. Of the Shaft at the Western Toll-dubh

Far across the island, on ground the western households likewise called Toll-dubh before the digging began, a second shaft was cut in these same years, by a household that had no more knowledge of the eastern one, by any telling that has come down of either, than the eastern household had of it. The two shafts were never, in the whole of this telling, said to have been begun at the bidding of one crew working both, or of any word carried between the two households that cut them; each is remembered only for its own digging, by its own people, on its own ground, and it is left to whoever hears both tellings together, side by side, to wonder at how closely the one work answers the other.

The western shaft went down the same way the eastern one had gone, straight and round and smoothed by hand past the depth the digging alone would have left rough, and its baskets were carried off in the same manner, evening on evening, by whoever's turn the carrying fell to, and were never brought back to be tipped where any later hand could find what they had carried. A man of the western household, past the age when the heaviest carrying still fell to him, took instead to keeping the lamp trimmed each evening for whoever went down to judge the smoothing, a smaller work than the digging but one the telling remembers him for all the same, as though the wick kept even and the oil kept full mattered to that household as much as the depth the digging reached that day.

A girl of the same household, young enough still to be sent for water rather than set to carrying, is remembered to have asked her mother, on an evening the lamp came up burning low from further down than it had gone the evening before, whether the shaft would be dug all the way down to wherever the mountains kept their roots; and her mother is remembered to have answered only that the ground kept its own matters, and that a household did well not to ask them aloud, an answer that told the girl nothing of what the shaft was truly for, and that the telling gives, in the end, as the nearest any teller of the western shore ever came to saying why the digging was begun at all.

The western shaft, like its twin in the east, was carried down until the lamp at its bottom showed no more than a small patch of smoothed wall with darkness standing above and below it, and it too, so far as any telling says, stopped there and went no further, though which of the two shafts reached that depth first, or whether they reached it in the same year or years apart, no telling that has come down troubles to say, holding them, in the manner of the tellers of that coast, as two halves of one thing rather than as a first and a second.

It fell to a boy of the western household, the youngest old enough to be trusted with the lamp's own cord, to let the last stone go on the evening the digging there, too, was given over, and he is remembered to have counted, under his breath, the whole time it took the stone to leave his hand until he judged, by his own counting, that it must by then have struck bottom somewhere below him; and when no sound came up to him at the number he had reached, nor at any number after it that the household, standing about him in the last light, troubled to go on counting to, he is said to have looked up at the faces around him rather than down the shaft, as if the listening, and not the stone, was the thing that mattered to be seen doing.

The western household kept, through the years of its own digging, a habit the eastern telling does not name for its own shaft: each evening the lamp came up, whoever had carried it down that day set it, still burning, on a flat stone laid for the purpose a little back from the lip, and let it burn there untended until it went out on its own, rather than snuff it the moment the day's work was done, a small wastefulness of oil that the household never once, in any telling that names it, troubled to give a reason for keeping. A grandmother of that household, asked once by a grandchild why the lamp was left to burn out above ground when it had already done its work below, answered only that a light let go out on its own was no more trouble to anyone than a light snuffed by a hand, and that some things, once begun, were better let run their own course than stopped short by whoever happened to be standing nearest when the stopping crossed their mind; whether she meant the lamp alone by this, or the digging with it, the telling does not say, and the grandchild is not remembered to have asked her to say more.

The two shafts stood after that, east and west, neither filled nor covered, each with its own household keeping, in its own way, a distance from the mouth that the digging had never kept, so that a person of either coast coming near either shaft afterward is remembered to walk wide of the lip rather than close to it, and to let a dropped stone, if a stone was ever again dropped there by anyone, go down into a silence that by then no household troubled any longer to break by listening after it. The platform in the eastern hills went on being climbed each year at the one morning it had always been climbed; the two shafts went on standing where they had been sunk, unfilled and unexplained, the rock that came out of them gone wherever it had gone, and no household of that age, on either coast, is remembered to have asked, aloud and before others, where either people had learned to dig so straight, or so deep, or why, having dug so far down into ground that had never before answered any question anyone had put to it, they let the digging stop at all.

Of the three works this telling has followed, one reaching up toward the mountains and two reaching down past every depth a well or a grave had ever asked of that ground, no single teller of the shore or the hills ever set them side by side in one telling while any of the three still stood unfinished; each was kept, in its own years, as its own household's own matter, told by its own people in its own words, the platform's climbers knowing nothing, so far as any telling says, of the shafts' diggers, and the diggers of the one shaft knowing as little of the other. It is only from the far side of those years, gathering what three separate hearths each kept whole in their own way, that a listener comes to see the one thing plainly enough to be surprised by it: that in these same generations, on three pieces of ground far enough apart that no single pair of feet is remembered to have walked between all three, Seann-Dhaoine stopped building only along the water that had fed every other work of theirs before, and turned instead toward the high ground and the low, the mountains that no boat had ever needed and the dark that no net had ever asked for, as if the shore, for those years, had come to hold less than it once had for the reaching.

# Chapter Twenty: Of the Steersman

*VE 2,801 – 2,860*

## I. Of the Word of the West

On the north-west shore, where the household hearths sat back from the water among stunted thorn and the wind never quite stopped, they kept Aithris a' Chruthachaidh the same as the high valleys kept it, but they kept it differently too. The recital of the Line went out to them father by father, the way it went out to every hearth on the island, and they knew it as well as anyone who had never seen Tobar dhìreach: the sky and the earth and the sea, each with its own spirit, and the coal that would answer only its own element. A shore household hears a telling with the sea at its back, though, and what it takes from the telling first is neither the sky's part nor the earth's. Sky was the sea's business one day in a hundred, when the weather turned; earth was under the feet and gave the peat and little else in that stony ground. The sea was at the door every day of a life, grey most mornings, green when it wanted to be kind, white when it did not, and the shore hearths listened hardest to the part of Aithris a' Chruthachaidh that spoke of what lay past it.

That part did not come from Coimhdeach na Fine's own mouth, or none said so. It came, the old women said, from further back than the mason, from an Dia-shluagh's own children before there was fire at all, and it had ridden into Aithris a' Chruthachaidh the way a stray dog rides in among a flock and is let stay because no one has the heart to drive it out. It said that west over the open sea, past the edge of sight and further than any hide boat had gone, there lay a green land that had no equal on Dia-thìr: Tìr nan Òg, and Magh Meall beside it, Magh Meall, where nothing grew old and nothing grew sick and the fruit hung ready in every season at once. And further off again, to the south-west, on a rock the sea went round and round without ever quite reaching, stood Taigh Dhuinn, the house of the lord of the dead, where those who did die on Dia-thìr went over water at the last, whether they had ever set foot in a boat in their lives or not.

Bran was born into that hearth in a year the household counted, later, as a year of good fishing, though he did not remember it, only that his grandmother spat into the fire for luck whenever the year was named. He grew up with the sea a stone's throw from the door and was in a coracle before he could say his own name straight, sitting in his father's lap with both small hands round the withy frame, howling with delight at every dip of it. His father, Fearadhach, was himself a fisher of the middling sort, careful rather than bold, and it was a puzzle to him all his life where the boy's restlessness came from, since nothing in his own blood or his wife's had ever looked past the next day's catch.

By the time Bran was a man grown he was the best boatman on that whole stretch of coast, and everyone on it, kin and stranger alike, said so without being asked. He could read a swell before it broke and tell, by the particular grey of the sky to the west at evening, whether the next day would let a boat out or keep it ashore, and he was right about it far oftener than he was wrong. He took seal and fish for his own hearth and for three others besides, and he mended the hide of every boat on that shore that needed mending, because his stitches held where other men's let the sea in. Neighbours brought him boats from half a day's walk along the coast rather than trust their own kin's needle, and he never once asked payment beyond a share of what the mended boat brought home after. Of an evening, when the tide had turned and there was nothing left to do at the water, he would sit with the other boatmen of that shore mending net or line by the last light, and the talk there was of seal grounds and the run of the mackerel and which headland kept a boat dry in a north wind and which did not, talk that filled a whole life for most of the men who traded it. Bran traded it as freely as any of them. It was only afterward, alone or with his mother, that the other listening began.

Such a man did not sit easily at the fire once the meat was eaten, the way some boatmen were content to, glad of the work and glad to let the rest of the world alone. Bran listened instead. He listened to Aithris a' Chruthachaidh every time it was said, the same words he had heard a hundred times, the way another man might listen for the note in a bowstring that told him it would break before it broke. What he wanted he could not himself have said clearly, only that when the recital came round to the part about the land past the sea's edge he sat forward with his hands gone still in his lap, and his mother used to say, once the matter had stopped being a thing said lightly, that even as a small boy he had looked west at the closing light with an attention no other child on that shore gave to it.

Once, when he was near ten, she found him standing at the tideline in the last grey of an evening, long after he should have been called in, and asked him what he thought he was looking at out there with nothing to see. "The place where it stops being water and starts being something else," he told her, and would not say more, and she did not press him, taking it for a child's fancy that would wear off with the years the way most fancies did. It did not wear off. "It is only a telling," his father told him once, when Bran was near a man and had asked, for the third or fourth time, whether anyone now living had ever gone out past the point where the swell ran long and slow and the gulls thinned to nothing. "The sea is the sea out there the same as it is here, only colder and longer, and a man who goes into it far enough does not come back to say what he found. The telling means no more than that. It is a way of saying: don't."

Bran said nothing to that. He did not forget it either, though, and it never once did the work his father had meant it to do.

## II. Of the Boat He Stitched

He was six-and-twenty, unmarried still though not for want of asking, when he began to gather hides that were not for mending. At first he told no one what they were for, and his kin took it, for a season, as a boatman's habit: a man who works hides gathers hides, and no one thinks to ask why a net-mender keeps cord by him. Only the toughest bull-hides would do, cured longer than any hide he had cured before, worked soft with fat and smoke until they would bend without cracking and hold water without weeping. He cut ribs of bent hazel and ash, more of them and set closer than any boat on that shore carried, and lashed each joint with sinew twisted so tight it sang when he plucked it, the way a good bowstring sings.

He worked through two winters at it in the lee of the house, out of the worst of the wind, most evenings after the day's fishing was done and most of the dark months when the sea kept him ashore anyway. Neighbours came by at first out of no more than a boatman's interest in another boatman's frame, and stayed longer than they meant to, turning the ribs over with their hands and asking, at first idly and then less idly, what water he meant such a hull for. He gave no straight answer for a long while, only that a bigger boat could carry a bigger catch, which was true enough as far as it went and satisfied most of them. By the second winter it satisfied fewer, for no man building only for a bigger catch builds a bow so high, or decks half the length of his hull with skins stretched and sealed against green water, or sets his ribs closer than three fingers' width apart when a hand's width has always served.

By the second spring the thing standing on its trestles in the yard was no coracle and no boat any of his kin had a name for: broad in the beam, high enough at the bow to climb a real sea rather than ride over a river chop, built, though none but Bran yet said so aloud, for water that meant to fight back. His mother asked him straight out, at last, what he meant to do with a boat built for more sea than any man on that coast had ever needed to cross, and he told her straight back.

"I mean to go and see if Aithris a' Chruthachaidh is true."

She did not weep, or not where he could see it. She had half known, she said afterward, since he was the boy who stood too long at the tideline in the failing light. What she said to him that evening, standing at the door of the boat-yard with her arms folded against the wind, was only this: that Aithris a' Chruthachaidh never once said a living man had gone and come back to say what he found, and that a telling with no one to bring it home was not a telling to build a boat on.

"Then I will bring it home," he said, "and it will be a telling with someone to bring it, after."

He found his crew easier than he had looked to, which surprised even him. Four men came, none of them fools, all of them known on that coast for steady hands: two who had fished with him from boyhood and trusted his eye on a swell over their own judgement of it; one older man, a net-mender of that shore, who had buried a wife the year before and said, when asked why he would go, only that there was less now to keep him ashore than there once had been; and last a boy not yet a man, not seventeen, whose name the tellers who kept the hushed part of this telling never gave, saying only that he was Bran's sister's son and had begged so long and so hard to come that his mother let him go at last rather than have him hate her for keeping him. Blàthnaid was that sister, three years the younger, and she alone of the whole kin neither wept over the boat nor argued against it. She asked her brother only one thing, the night before he put out: to tell her the truth of what he found, whatever it proved to be, if ever the chance came to tell her anything at all. He promised her that. It was the promise she held to for the rest of her long life, though there was soon no one left to ask it of.

They put out on a morning in high summer when the sea lay flat and green almost to the edge of sight and the wind, such as there was, sat steady out of the north-east, which Bran judged would carry them long and even without driving them off whatever line he meant to hold. Out past the last skerries to the north the sky carried the grey bank that never lifted off that stretch of sea in any season, the same grey that every boatman on the coast knew to leave well alone; Bran held his bow south of it from the first hour, west and a little south, away from the grey and into open blue water where no boat of that coast had held a course before. He stood the whole of that first morning at the steering-oar himself and let no other hand take it, watching the grey bank fall away astern on the right hand until it was only a smudge and then nothing at all, and the household came down to the shingle to see the five of them off. No one sang, for there was no telling yet of what a voyage like this one ought to be sung with, and the tellers say the silence of that leaving was remembered longer on that shore than any of the words that were said in it.

## III. Of the Boy Who Came Back

What passed on the water in the days that followed, no one on Dia-thìr can tell with a whole mouth, for only one of the five that went out ever stood on the shingle of that coast again, and he was past whole telling by the time he stood there.

He was found near the end of the same summer, a season and a little more after the boat put out, lying below the tide line on a stretch of coast two days' walk south of where he had left, as though the sea itself had carried him round and set him down gently at a place he had never asked to be brought. A woman gathering shellfish found him and thought him drowned until she saw his chest move. He was burned dark by a sun harder than any that fell on that coast, thin as a stripped willow-wand, and his mouth was too cracked to make more than a whisper for the better part of a day after they carried him in and gave him water a little at a time, as a man returning from a long fast must be given it, for fear the giving itself would kill him.

When the whisper came, it came in pieces, and the pieces did not always agree with one another, which the tellers say is only what is to be looked for of a boy half out of his wits with thirst and grief both. He said they had sailed many days, more than he had kept count of, west and a little south as Bran held the course, with nothing before them but water going out flat to a rim that never came any nearer for all they sailed toward it. He said the food ran thinner than they had reckoned and the water thinner still, and that there were whole days none of them spoke, because a man's mouth was too dry to waste on anything but the oar. Then, he said, his voice dropping so low that those who sat by him had to lean in close to catch it, as though he were telling something he half believed himself and half thought he must have dreamed in his thirst, they came on a land.

It rose green out of the water on a morning when none of them had strength left to hope for it, he said. It was a green such as none of them had ever seen on any hill of Dia-thìr, a green that seemed to hold its own light apart from the sun rather than only catching what the sun gave it. There was fruit on the trees down almost to the tideline, and a spring of sweet water broke out of the rock not a stone's throw from where they beached the boat, and they drank until their bellies ached and slept where they fell and woke with strength in them they had not carried since they left home. He said the people of that land came down to them without fear, neither young nor old to look at, none of them marked by time the way every face on Dia-thìr was marked by it, and that they were made welcome as though welcome cost that land nothing at all, because there was more of everything there than anyone could use in a life, and more life, it seemed, than any of them had ever thought to ask for.

He said his uncle would not leave.

That one thing at least, the tellers say, had stayed whole in the boy's mind through everything else the sea had done to it, and he told it plainly where the rest of his telling wandered. Bran had stood on that shore, he said, and looked back once at the boat drawn up on the sand, and told the boy he was free to go home if home was what he wanted, and that no one would think the less of him for wanting it. He himself had followed a question the whole length of his life to get to that shore, Bran told him, and he would not turn from it now that his feet were standing on the answer.

Of the other three men nothing certain is told. Some say they stayed beside Bran of their own will; some that the sea took them on the way home and only the boy, youngest and lightest of the five, lived to be carried the whole way back on whatever swell or storm set him down again on his own coast. The boy himself could not say which was true, and would not guess at it even when pressed. What he did say, more than once and always the same way, was that his uncle had held him by both shoulders on that green beach and told him: go home, and tell them the truth of it, and no more than the truth, and let them believe what they will of it after. Bran had put him back in a small boat alone, with water and dried fish enough for the crossing, though how a small boat crossed what the great one had barely crossed, and how a boy alone found his own coast again when five men together had needed the better part of a summer and Bran's own eye on the swell to find that other shore, none of the tellers who kept this after him have ever been able to say, and none of them pretend to.

The household that carried him home did what could be done for a body so far gone in thirst and sun, and for the first two or three days thought they might yet keep him. They laid him nearest the fire and gave him broth before water, a little at a time through the night, and one or another of the kin sat by him at every hour so that he never once woke to an empty room. Word of him went along the coast faster than any of them could stop it, and by the fourth day there were strangers at the door asking to see the boy who had crossed the western sea, and had to be turned away for his own quiet.

He lived eleven days after they carried him in from the shingle, long enough to say what he said to his mother, and to Blàthnaid, and to two or three others who sat with him by turns, and no longer. He grew quieter each of those days rather than stronger, and on the last of them asked that the door be left open so he could see the water from where he lay. The failing light of that evening was the last he saw, and the last thing he was heard to say, more than once in those eleven days, was that it had not been an unkind land, and that his uncle had not looked afraid.

## IV. Of Blàthnaid's Hushing

What the boy said did not stay in one mouth. It could not; too many had sat by him in his dying to keep it to themselves, and a telling of that kind does not wait to be asked for before it goes from hearth to hearth. Within a year it had gone the length of that coast and some way inland besides, gathering, as every telling gathers in the going, a little more certainty than the boy himself had ever claimed for it. Men who had never been within sight of the boat spoke of the land in the west as though they had walked on it themselves. Boys not yet grown talked, the way boys do, of building craft of their own and finding it for themselves, and one household lost a fifteen-year-old for the better part of a night before he was found sitting on the shingle in the dark with a coracle he had no business taking out, only looking west, and was brought home and beaten and wept over in the same evening.

It was after that night that the elders of the shore, kin of Bran's household and of two others besides, sat together at a fire none of the young were let near and agreed, without much argument, that the telling had done all the good it was going to do and would now only do harm. They did not forbid the speaking of it outright; a thing forbidden is a thing every young man on a coast wants to hear twice over. They let it fall instead the way a fire is let fall when no one feeds it. No one told it new to a child who had not already heard it. No one who came asking after strangers' talk of it got a straight answer. Within a generation there were households on that same shore whose children had never heard Bran's name at all, and grew up knowing only that some kin of theirs, long ago, had once built an over-large boat for reasons nobody now troubled to remember, and had lost it, and that was thought reason enough to build no other like it. A boy of that later generation who asked his grandfather why no one on that shore built boats bigger than the seal grounds needed was told only that a big boat once went out and did not come back, and that the sea did not reward greed in a hull any more than it rewarded greed in a net, and the boy took the answer for the whole of the matter and never asked again.

Blàthnaid alone did not let it fall all the way. She kept the promise she had asked of her brother the night before he sailed, though he was never there again to be asked anything further of, and she kept it, in the years after, the only way left to her: by holding the whole of it in her own mouth and giving it out, once, to one person only, long after the shore's common fire for the telling had been let die. She was an old woman by then, and the daughter she told it to was near grown herself, and the two of them sat alone at a hearth Blàthnaid had banked and covered rather than let its light show through the door, the way that shore had by then come to keep its fires of an evening when a telling not meant for every ear was going to be said over them. The whole of it she told her daughter as the boy had told it to her: the green land, the spring, the welcome that cost nothing, the uncle who would not turn from a question he had followed his whole life to answer. She did not tell it as a warning, the way the elders' hushing had meant it, in the end, to be kept. She told it, her daughter said afterward, the way a woman tells a thing she has been keeping warm a long time against the day someone would finally ask to hear it.

"And his name," she said, when the telling was done and the fire had sunk to nothing under its covering stone, "was Bran."

She died some twenty years after, an old woman by any count that shore kept, and what she had told her daughter that one evening went on after her from mother to daughter in the same low voice at the same covered fire: further, with each telling, from the shore's common talk, and closer, in its way, to what a thing becomes when only one mouth at a time is trusted to carry it. It was kept dim on that coast rather than forgotten outright, and it was never again said where the young could hear it start.

# Chapter Twenty-one: Of Brian and the Buried Five

*VE 2,861 – 2,936*

## I. Of the Man Who Dug the Graves

Seven hundred years had gone by since Fearghas let the white-flecked coal fall from the height of his arm and saw it catch fire halfway down the rock and lie burning on the stones like a star come down before its time. Since then the summit had taken the kindred's name and kept it, and herders left a stone on the top when they passed, and at Tobar dhìreach the recital was said every year on Oidhche an Dealanaich with two colours answered and five still dark in the bag: the black, the red-brown, the silver, the one that woke at a snap of the fingers, and the rainbow that held them all and answered to none. Children of the line grew old hearing it and died leaving it no further on than they had found it. It had come to be said, among households that were not of the line and had no cause to be kind about it, that An Clachair's people would go on asking the same question until the island wore down to the sea.

Brian was born into that waiting and paid it little mind. A plain man, thought plain by those who knew him, he wore the word without complaint. He dug the graves of the valley. It was not an office anyone had given him; his father had done it before him, a little, alongside his proper work of herding, and Brian had found in himself a steadiness for it that others lacked, and by the time he was two-and-twenty it was understood that when a death came to any of the hearths above Tobar dhìreach, someone went for Brian.

He was a big-shouldered man, slow to speak and slower to laugh, with hands scarred across the backs from stone he had turned in a hundred diggings. He kept his own counsel about the dead, the way another man kept his counsel about a debt. When a child of the black-well household died of a fever in his twentieth year he dug through frozen ground for the better part of two days without once cursing it, and when he had finished he sat by the raw earth a while before he would take the food that was brought to him, though no one asked him to and he never said why. Those who worked beside him said only that he was good at it, and better than good, and let it go at that, for it is not an easy thing to praise a man for burying your dead well, and the valley had not found the words.

He married Caoimhe in his one-and-twentieth year, before the whole valley had settled on calling him for its dead. She was of a herding household two valleys east, a quick, sharp-tongued woman who could set a whole hearth laughing with a single word and who had, more than one of her kin said, married beneath her wit if not beneath her worth. She used to say of Brian, to those who would listen, that he had courted her the way he dug a grave: without hurry, without noise, and with his eyes down at the ground the whole time, so that it was three seasons before she was sure he had meant it. It was fondly said, and truly.

They had no children who lived past their first winter, three of them, one after another, and this the valley also understood without being told, in the way a valley understands most things about its own people, and let alone. Caoimhe kept a hearth that was warm to visitors and cold to pity. Brian dug on.

It was work that gave a man time to think, more than most, for the labour of it did not fill the mind the way herding or splitting stone filled it, being slow and repeated and requiring no more of him than his back and his hands, hour on hour, in earth that did not care how carefully he opened it. He had grown up, like every child of the high valleys, on the telling of the mason and the lightning and Coimhdeach na Fine in the grove, said at his own hearth and at every hearth he visited, for it belonged to no one household by then; it was the valley's own tale, told to strangers before the strangers had finished sitting down. He had heard Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich a thousand times before he understood it was a riddle and not merely a saying:

> *Tha spiorad fa leth san speur, san talamh agus sa mhuir. Meascaich na spioradan agus bidh iad uile-chumhachdach.*
> The sky, the earth and the sea each carry their own spirit. Merge the spirits, and they become almighty.

Two of the seven had answered already, long before any grandfather now living could remember, and further back than that: the sea had taken gual òir on the swell of the northern shore, and the sky had taken the white-flecked coal in the empty air above the height that bore the kindred's name now. Of the sea and the sky Brian knew only what every hill-child knew, which was little, for he had never gone so far as either; he had walked as far as the market at Àth gharbh once in his life and no further. What he knew, and knew better than most men in the valley knew anything, was the earth. He had put his hands into it more times than he could count, and taken more out of it than he had put in, if a body counted for anything; the tellers said it did not, and Brian left such reckoning to them.

## II. Of What a Plain Man Thought

The line still kept the five dark coals in the leather bag that had held all seven once, and still tried them, though less often than it had, for the trying had worn down a great many hopes across the generations and left less each time to spend.
