They had been thrown into rain and left in it a season; they had been carried down into the wet air above the black well and the young well and held there through a whole spring; they had been laid in one fire all together, on the reasoning that if each answered its own element perhaps all together they might answer each other, and burned dark as any stone burns, giving off nothing but the ordinary red glow of heat and none of the promised fire. Diarmad's own grandchildren had tried carrying them in skins of sea-water home from the northern shore and pouring the water over them at the hearth, which struck most of the valley, when it heard of it, as a fair example of how far a household could go on an idea that had already failed once.

Brian had never gone near the bag. It belonged to the eldest women of the line, kept as it had been kept since Fionnghuala's day, and a man who dug graves for his bread had no more claim on it than the herder two valleys off. He heard the trying discussed, as everyone in the valley heard it discussed, at every gathering and every recital, the older folk arguing over which shore, which height, which season, as though the failure of seven hundred years could be mended by trying the seventh height instead of the sixth. He listened the way he listened to most talk, without much to say, turning it over slowly the way he turned a spade in unfamiliar ground, feeling for where it gave.

What struck him, when it struck him, was not clever. He said so himself, afterward, more than once, to those who wanted to make more of it than there was. He had been standing at the edge of a fresh-dug grave, waiting on the kin to bring the body down from the hearth, on a grey morning in his seven-and-twentieth year, and he had looked down into the black earth he had opened and thought, the way a man thinks of an ordinary thing without meaning to think of anything at all: *this is where the dead go, and the dead lie still, and the earth takes them and does not give them back.* And on the heel of that thought, without his calling for it, came another: *the sea took its coal by being waded into. The sky took its coal by the coal being thrown into the sky's own air, from as high as a man could climb. If the earth is to take a coal, the coal must go where the earth is deepest, and be left to it, the way a body is left to it.*

He was a slow man with an idea, the way he was slow with everything. He finished the grave he was digging, and saw the dead put into it, and stood at the edge with the rest of the valley while the words were said over it, the same words said over every grave in the high valleys, asking the ground to hold what was given it gently. Three days went by before he said anything to Caoimhe, and a fortnight more before he said anything to the eldest of the women who kept the bag, an old widow named Sireadh who had held it longer than Brian had been alive.

"You want to bury them," she said, when he had got it out, plainly and without much art, the way he said everything.

"I want to try it," Brian said.

"It has been tried," said Sireadh. "In the rain. In the wet air by the wells."

"Not this," Brian said. "Deep, and left there. The whole night through."

The old woman looked at him a long while, the way she might have looked at a piece of ground she was deciding whether to trust, and at last she said what many of the line had said before her, across the generations, to one idea or another: that it could do no harm, since the coals were dark already and had been dark as long as anyone living had known them, and a man who spent his days putting things into the ground might, for once, know something the rest of them did not.

## III. Of the Grave Beside the Slab

She would not let him take the whole bag, nor all seven, for the two that had answered were not hers to risk on a guess, however good the guesser; but she gave him the five that were left, wrapped in a fold of undyed wool, and told him to bring them back whole, whatever came of it.

He chose the ground beside Leac na Fèithe. It was the plainest choice in the world to him and he never understood, afterward, why anyone should think it strange; Leac na Fèithe at Tobar dhìreach was the one place on the island where the earth was known, past doubting, to have held fire once, for the vein still lay under it, covered these seven hundred years and more, and if the earth had a spirit at all it seemed to Brian no more than sense that the spirit should be nearest where the earth had already shown it could hold such a thing. No one drew water beside Leac na Fèithe, and no house was built near it, and the ground there was given over to grass and to the recital that was said standing on it once a year; it was as close to consecrated as any ground in the valley came, though that word belonged to no one yet.

He dug on an evening in the middle of an t-Sultain, when the barley was in and the light was going early and there was a smell of turned earth and woodsmoke over the whole valley. He dug it the depth of a grave, no more and no less, for it was the only depth he trusted himself to judge by feel, and he lined it, as he lined the graves he was known for, so that the sides would not fall in on what was laid there before morning. Caoimhe came out to watch him at it, wrapped against the evening cold. Neither of them held digging to be woman's work, and she offered him no hand with it, but she stayed the whole while, sitting on an old quern-stone near Leac na Fèithe with her knees drawn up, watching her husband dig what half the valley by then, having heard the word of it, was calling the sixth grave he had dug for the line, though nothing of the line's was dead.

"They will say you have buried it," she told him, once, into the quiet. "The hope of it. However this comes out."

"Let them," Brian said, and went on digging.

Others came, in ones and twos, as the light failed, drawn by the word the way word always drew a valley to anything out of the ordinary: an old man of the north hearths who had tried the coals in his own youth and failed with them and had opinions still; two of Sireadh's grandchildren, sent to watch and report back what was done, since the old woman's knees no longer let her stand at a graveside past dusk; a boy who had no business there at all and was sent home twice and came back a third time and was let stay, since by then Brian had stopped noticing who watched him and who did not. The talk among them was low, and one voice did not agree with the next. Some held that burying the coals was no different, in its bones, from throwing them in the sea or the rain, one more trying among many, no likelier to answer than the rest. One or two, more sourly, said that a grave-digger ought to know better than most what the earth did with things put into it, which was nothing, which was keep them, unchanged, or eat them slowly down to nothing at all, and that neither keeping nor eating was the same as answering.

Brian heard all of it and answered none of it. When the hole was as deep as he wanted, he climbed down into it himself, though it came near to his shoulders, and Caoimhe passed the five coals down to him one at a time, unwrapped now from the wool, dark and ordinary-looking in the last of the light, five pieces of blackish stone that might have been swept up off any hearth in the valley. He laid them at the bottom close together, the way a mason sets stones that must bear together, and stood over them a moment with his hands still dusty from the digging.

"I don't know the words for this," he said, half to Caoimhe, half to no one. "There are no words for burying a stone."

"Say what you say over the dead," said the old man of the north hearths, not unkindly. "It cost nothing to try."

So Brian said, standing in the grave he had dug for five coals as he had stood at the edge of a hundred graves he had dug for the valley's dead, the same words, asking the ground to hold gently what was given it; and no one there thought it strange, though the tellers, shaping the night into a telling of its own, would make much of how well the words fit.

He climbed out and filled the grave himself, working by the last light and then by starlight, tamping the earth down the way he tamped it over the dead, firm but not hard, so that the ground would settle true and not sink hollow later. Caoimhe brought him a brand from the hearth to see the last of it by. When it was done there was nothing to mark the place but turned earth, no different to look at from any grave in the valley, lying in the grass a stone's throw from the flat slab that covered the vein.

The watchers went home in twos and threes, most of them saying, in one way or another, that they would come back in the morning to see. Sireadh's grandchildren ran the word back to her before they were properly indoors. Brian and Caoimhe stayed longest, sitting by the fresh earth as the night came down cold and clear, the kind of clear that comes after a warm harvest day, with more stars out than either of them troubled to count, until Caoimhe said at last that there was nothing more to be done by sitting, and they went in.

Neither of them slept well. Brian never said, after, what he had thought through that night, lying awake beside his wife with the ordinary sounds of the valley outside the door, a dog somewhere, the wind working at the thatch; but Caoimhe, old now and telling her own small part of a larger telling, said more than once that she had asked him that night in the dark whether he believed it would work, and that he had been quiet so long she thought him asleep, and then he had said: "I believe the earth keeps what's given it. I don't know if that's the same as answering." And she said that was the truest thing anyone in the whole long history of the question had said about it, though she never said it to his face, not wanting to spoil him with praise he had no use for.

## IV. Of the Black Coal Warm in the Ground

He went out at first light, before Caoimhe was properly up, and by the time she came out to him he had already opened the grave down to where the earth was undisturbed by frost, working carefully now, with his hands more than his spade, the way he worked when he came near a coffin he did not want to mark. Word had gone round the valley faster than either of them, and by the time the five coals were bare in the bottom of the hole there were a dozen people standing at a respectful distance, among them Sireadh, who had got herself out that far on a grandchild's arm and would not be talked out of it.

Brian knelt and lifted them out one at a time, the way he had laid them, and laid each on the flat of his palm before he set it down on the grass beside him.

Four were cold. Cold the way any stone out of cold ground is cold, cold with the whole night's chill still in them, no different to the hand than they had been the evening before, dark, ordinary, dead.

The fifth was the black one, *gual dubh*, black as a wet crow's back, the same black the mason himself had first seen in the broken vein seven hundred years and more before that morning. Brian's hand closed round it out of habit, the same motion he used lifting any stone from a grave, and he had it half out of the earth before he understood what his hand was telling him, which was that it was warm.

He said, afterward, that he thought at first it was only the ground's own warmth, held over from some trick of the night, and it was Sireadh, watching from her grandchild's arm, who called out to him to hold it up so she could see, for she had kept coal and fire-pot both across sixty years and knew better than any living soul what a thing ought to look like when the earth had merely warmed it and what it ought to look like when it had not.

He held it up. In the grey of the morning, with the sun not yet over the eastern shoulder of the valley, a line of red crept across the black surface of the coal where the air first touched it, slow, the way the last coal of a banked fire creeps back to life when the ash is stirred from it, and then widened into a glow, deep in the black, red going toward gold at its heart, and a thread of smoke came up off it into the cold air, and it smouldered in his open hand the way a coal smoulders that has been fed all night and is only waiting to be blown on.

It did not burn him. He said that too, afterward, more than once, for it was the thing people asked him first: did it burn you. It did not. It lay in his palm warm as another man's hand is warm, no hotter, though it went on glowing and smoking gently the whole while he knelt there with it, and the four cold coals lying forgotten in the grass beside him, and the dozen people at the graveside gone entirely silent, so that the only sound in the whole waking valley, for what Caoimhe swore afterward was the length of a held breath and longer, was the small tick and whisper of a coal breathing.

"The earth took it," Sireadh said at last, into the silence, in a voice that had gone thin with more than age. "The answering came at the rising out of the ground, not the lying in it."

It was the truest word said that morning, and it held. The line had tried the coals in rain, and the rain had done nothing, for rain was the sea's business, not the earth's; they had held them in wet air, and the wet air had done nothing either, being neither one element nor another; but the earth, given the whole slow dark of a night to work in, undisturbed, had done what the earth does with anything laid deep in it and left, which was change it, patiently, from beneath, the way a seed is changed, or a body, though a body's changing goes the other way. The black coal had waited seven hundred years for someone to think of asking the earth for that much time, and Brian, who had spent his life giving the earth exactly that much time with everything he laid in it, had been the one man in all the valleys who thought to ask.

He did not go home first. He went, still kneeling, still cradling the warm coal in one hand and the four cold ones gathered up in the crook of the other arm, to Tobar dhìreach itself, to the hearth where Poit an Teine was kept, and there before the eldest of the line and half the valley that had come running at the word, he set the black coal down among the embers of the mason's own fire, the fire that Clann a' Chlachair held to have burned, hearth to hearth, unbroken, since Oidhche an Dealanaich; and it caught there the way any coal catches, low and steady, and burned on, red-hearted, the whole of that day and into the night, and did not go dark again.

## V. Of the Long Keeping

Afterward he kept it in a plain clay pot of his own making, fired for the purpose, with a lid of turf he cut fresh each season to fit it; the pot of the line was another woman's charge, its own long watch, and no part of his to hold. He fed the coal wood and heather as any hearth is fed, and carried it with him, in the pot, banked and covered, wherever the year's work took him, so that for the better part of forty years there was not a night in the high valleys that Brian's black coal was not burning somewhere within a day's walk of Leac na Fèithe.

More times than he ever troubled to count, he was asked whether he thought he had answered Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich, whether the black coal's burning meant the earth's spirit was in it now and no further finding needed. He always said the same thing, in one form or another, and Caoimhe used to say it word for word behind his back to make the children of the valley laugh, though there was no unkindness in it: that he had only asked the ground a question it was willing to answer, and that whether the answer was the whole of what Coimhdeach na Fine meant, or only a part of it, was a matter for cleverer heads than his, and he had graves to dig.

He went on digging them. The valley did not let a man of sixty stand at every graveside as it had let a man of thirty, and in his last years the heavier digging fell to younger hands he had himself taught the trade to, watching over how deep they went and how they lined the sides, for he held, and said often, that a grave badly dug was a poor last gift to give anyone; but he kept the black coal himself, banked in its pot by his own hearth, until the year he died.

He was three-and-sixty that year, worn more by the work than by any illness the valley could name, and Caoimhe, who outlived him by nine years and never remarried, said that he went the way he had put every one of the valley's dead into the ground before him: without complaint, and with his eyes on the work in front of him almost to the last, which in his case was nothing more than sitting by his own hearth watching the black coal glow.

They buried him beside Leac na Fèithe, near the ground he had first opened for the five coals, for it seemed to the valley, and to Caoimhe, that there was nowhere else so fitting; and the pot with the black coal in it was set beside the grave through the length of the burial, still burning, banked low, so that the last thing said over Brian, grave-digger of the high valleys, was said by a fire that owed its life to him and to no one else in the whole history of the question. When the words were finished and the earth given, Caoimhe herself lifted the pot and carried it home, and kept the coal burning at her own hearth the rest of her days, and after her it passed, as such things do, into other hands, banked and fed and carried on, one more small fire added to the fires the mason's line had already kept unbroken for the better part of three thousand years.

At the recital that was said on the next night of the lightning, the reciter of the line, coming to the old count of the coals, said it new for the first time in living memory: the sea had taken the gold, the sky had taken the white-flecked coal, and now the earth had taken the black, *gual dubh*, slowly, in the dark, the way the earth takes everything it is given time enough with. Four remained unanswered: the red-brown, the silver, the one that would wake, if it woke at all, to no more than the snap of a hand, and the rainbow that held every colour and answered to none of them yet. It was, by every count the line still kept, some seven hundred and fifty years since the sky, and more than fifteen hundred since the sea, and no one standing at that recital thought the finding of the fourth would come soon; but it was said at that recital, and at every one since, that the earth's answer had come the way Brian himself had lived, without hurry and without noise, out of a man who asked it no more than the plain question a plain man asks, and waited, the one night through, for the ground to tell him what it knew.

# Chapter Twenty-two: Of the Stakes in the Mud and the Watcher in the Sea

*VE 2,937 – 3,146*

## I. Of the Stakes in the Mud

The north-western point ran out low and black into the sea, a spine of rock worn smooth by a tide that came and went twice in a day and left, at its lowest ebb, a wide shelf of mud the colour of a bruise. The households that fished that stretch of coast knew the shelf the way a man knows the floor of his own house in the dark, by feel and by long habit rather than by looking, for it was seldom worth looking at: grey mud, grey stone, grey water going out to a grey sky, and nothing in any of it to hold the eye. They went out on it at the low tides to gather cockle and razor-shell, and to see to their own stakes, the short hazel posts driven into the firmer ground above the mud-line where the coracles were tied of an evening against a rising tide that would otherwise have carried them off to wherever the sea carried things it was given.

It was a boy minding his family's stakes, in the year the households later reckoned as some four generations back from Criomthann's own time, who found the others.

They lay further out than any household drove its own, in a line so straight that no eye could mistake it for anything the tide had arranged by accident: a row of posts, most of them broken off at the mud's surface and a few standing a hand's height proud of it, and caught about the base of one, worked down into the silt until only a corner of it showed, a scrap of hide gone black and stiff as old leather left in a byre. The boy dug it free with his fingers and brought it home, and his father turned it over by the fire that evening and could make nothing of it beyond what his own eyes told him: that it had been stitched once, along one edge, with a neat close seam no different in kind from the seams every boatman on that coast sewed into his own hide boats, though finer than any hand on that shore now living could match.

Whose posts they had been, and what boat or boats they had once held against what tide, no one on that coast could say, then or after. They were not new work when the boy found them; the wood was grey through and through, and the hide had the look of a thing the sea had been working at for longer than any single life could account for. Some of the elders said the posts were old kin's work, driven by grandfathers of grandfathers no one living had known to speak to. Others said, in the low voice a man uses for a thing he does not care to say loudly, that the stakes were not kin's work at all, that no household on that coast had ever driven a mooring so far out into water no coracle of theirs had cause to sit in, and that whoever had rowed there had rowed from somewhere else and gone back to it, or not gone back at all. The mud gave up nothing further to settle it either way. It kept the stakes, half of them still standing after all those generations, and it kept its silence about the rest, and the households of that shore learned, the way they learned most things the mud and the sea would not answer, to let the not-knowing stand rather than fill it with a telling that pretended to more than it had.

They called it only the stakes, after that, when they had cause to speak of it at all, which was seldom; a landmark for the low tide, no more remarked than the black spine of rock itself. Children were shown it once, usually by an older cousin rather than a parent, with a shrug rather than a story, and grew up knowing it the way they knew the shape of the point, without ever quite wondering at it the way a stranger might have wondered. It sat in the mud below the north-western point for as long as anyone's telling ran back, half swallowed, patient, asking nothing and answering nothing, until the year Uilebheist na Mara was first seen from that same stretch of water.

## II. Of the Watcher

The crew that saw it were four men out after mackerel in the grey hour before a summer dawn, working a net between two coracles lashed gunwale to gunwale the way that shore fished a big shoal, with the net paid out between them and the fish already knocking against the hide in numbers enough to make the morning's work a good one. The sea that morning lay flatter than any of the four had known it lie in a lifetime of going out on it, flat and pewter-coloured under a sky not yet decided whether it meant to clear, and it was into that flatness, off to the north where the water ran deep and no boat of that coast had reason to go, that the eldest of the four, a man near fifty who had fished that water since before any of the others were born, happened to look up from the net.

What he saw, he said afterward, more times than he ever wanted to say it again, was a back. Not a wave, not a rock, for there was no rock on any chart the coast kept in its head for that stretch of open water, and not a whale either, though it was the shape his mind reached for first and fastest, because a man's mind reaches always for the shape it already knows. It was too long for a whale and it broke the water wrong, rising without the roll a whale's back gives as it comes up to breathe, rising instead the way a low island might rise if an island could rise, smooth and dark and glistening where the light caught it, and it held above the surface for longer than any breathing thing he had ever watched hold, long enough that he had time to call out to the others and have all three turn and see it too before it went down again, without spray, without sound, the water closing over it as quietly as it had opened.

None of the four could afterward agree on how long it had shown itself, whether the span of ten breaths or the span of a hundred, which the tellers of that coast came in time to take as its own kind of proof, on the reasoning that a true wonder unmakes a man's count of things the way an ordinary sight never does. What they agreed on, all four, without needing to put their heads together over it first, was the size of the thing: bigger, by every man's reckoning, than the biggest whale any of them had brought a story home of, bigger than anything that had business being in water that shallow so close to shore, though none of them could afterward say with any confidence how far out it had lain, for distance on a flat morning sea is a hard thing for even a practised eye to judge.

They rowed home without finishing the net, which no man on that coast did for any lesser cause, and they told what they had seen before the fish they did bring in were so much as gutted, and within the day it had gone from that one household to every hearth within a morning's walk, growing, as such things grow, a little surer and a little larger in every mouth that carried it onward. By the second telling the thing had a name it kept from then on, though none of the four who saw it first ever claimed to have coined it: Uilebheist na Mara, *Uilebheist na Mara*, as though the old women who first fixed the name to it had reasoned, in the space of a single evening's talk, that a thing so patient in its rising and its going under again could only be watching, and had been watching, likely, for longer than any of them had been alive to know it.

Not every hearth believed the four had seen what they said they had seen. There were fishermen on that coast, in that first year and in every year that followed it, who held the whole telling to be nothing more than four tired men and a trick of flat light on deep water, and said so, sometimes to the four men's faces, in the blunt way one fisherman tells another he thinks him a fool without quite using the word. But the four did not change their account under any pressing, not that year and not in all the years after, and one of them, the youngest, carried the telling of it word for word into his own old age and told it to his grandchildren exactly as he had first told it to his own father, without adding to it or taking from it, which the coast came in time to count for more than any argument the doubters brought against it. Believed or doubted alike, the water off the north-western point went, from that year forward, by a name it had never needed before: Uilebheist na Mara's water.

## III. Of the Beacon

Criomthann was born on that shore some five-and-twenty years after the four men saw what they saw, into a household of net-menders and boatmen no different in its trade from any other on that stretch of coast, though different in one particular that shaped him before he had any way of knowing it had: his mother's mother had been kin, at some remove no one troubled any longer to trace exactly, to the household that had once sent a great hull and five men west over the open sea and got back only a dying boy and a telling that was, by the time Criomthann was old enough to hear any of it, kept low and close and spoken of, when it was spoken of at all, at a covered fire rather than an open one. He grew up knowing the shape of that older grief without ever being told the whole of it plainly, the way a child on that coast came to know most things that mattered, by the silences round a subject rather than by anyone sitting him down to explain it, and it left him, from very young, with a caution about open water that some of his cousins mistook for want of nerve and none of them, in the end, ever managed to shame out of him.

He was not, by his own account and by every account his neighbours gave of him afterward, a bold man in any way that coast measured boldness. Never once, in all his years on that shore, did he build boats bigger than the water called for, or express the smallest wish to see what lay past the edge of sight to the west. What he had instead, and had in a measure none of his kin quite matched, was a steadiness that showed itself first in small things: a net mended so that it held a season longer than any other man's, a boy pulled from a rip current by Criomthann's own hand while three grown men still stood arguing on the shingle about the best way to go after him, a hearth kept banked through a winter storm that put out every other fire in the household's row of huts. By the time he was a young man grown, the shore had come to trust him with the kind of trust that is given seldom and taken back almost never, the trust given to a man who does the plain necessary thing before anyone has finished discussing whether it needs doing.

He was a score of years old, married a year and with his first child not yet walking, when the second of the great losses came to that shore, though it did not yet come from the water Uilebheist na Mara had been seen in. A boat working close in below the point, in weather no worse than any boat on that coast went out in twice a week, went over in a swell that rose from nowhere any of the watchers on shore could afterward account for, and two men drowned within sight of their own hearth smoke, in water shallow enough that a third man, hauled out half-drowned himself, stood afterward and could point to the very patch of sea where his companions had gone under. It was not laid to Uilebheist na Mara, not by anyone, for the water was the wrong water and the drowning had the ordinary shape of any drowning that coast had known before the four men's telling ever began; but it happened in a year when Uilebheist na Mara's telling was still young enough on that shore to colour everything, and Criomthann, standing on the shingle with the rest of the household watching the third man dragged in, found himself thinking, not for the first time and not for the last, that the sea gave a man very little warning of the exact moment it meant to take something from him, and that a warning given late was no better than no warning at all.

He said as much to his wife that night, by their own hearth, with the child asleep between them, and she asked him what warning a man could give the sea that the sea would trouble itself to answer to. He had no answer for her then. It was another seven years before he had one, and when it came it came, by his own telling of it afterward, less as a thought arrived at than as a thing he found himself already doing, the way a man sometimes finds his hands at work on a task before his mind has finished deciding to begin it.

What he began, on the last headland of that coast, the one that stood highest and looked furthest out over the water where the four men had seen the back rise, was a fire.

It was not, at first, meant as anything more than what any fire on any headland might have been meant as: a mark for boats working late to steer home by, no different in kind from a dozen such fires kept on a dozen headlands the length of the island, wherever a household wanted its boats to find the shore in failing light. Criomthann fed it himself, most evenings, climbing the last steep pitch of the headland with an armful of driftwood and gorse after his own day's work was done, and for the first season or two no one on that coast thought it any more remarkable than a careful man's habit. It was only in the second year, when he began to keep it burning through the daylight hours as well, in fair weather when no boat needed a mark to find its way home by, that his own kin began asking him plainly what the fire was for.

He told them, when he told them at all, in few words, and the words changed from telling to telling while the sense of them held steady: that a man who watched water long enough came to feel, in his own body before his mind had properly reasoned it out, where the water changed its temper, and that the stretch off that headland, ever since the four men's telling, had felt to him like water that wanted watching rather than water that wanted trusting. He never once claimed to have seen Uilebheist na Mara himself, in all the years the fire burned, and when pressed on it he always said the same thing: that he had not needed to see it to believe four men who had no reason between them to agree on a lie, and that a fire cost him little enough to keep, set against what it might, one day, be found to have saved.

The word he settled on to go with the fire, the word he began calling down to any boat that worked too far out into that stretch of water, came to him worn smooth over several seasons, the way a saying is worn smooth by repeated use, until only the truest, shortest form of it was left standing. By the time he had said it enough evenings running that his own children could say it back to him in their sleep, it had settled into the few short words every household on that coast came in time to know as well as they knew Aithris a' Chruthachaidh itself:

> *Tionndaidh air ais. Chan ann dhutsa an t-uisce seo.*
> Turn back. This water is not for you.

He called it down from the headland to any boat he judged had strayed too far into Uilebheist na Mara's water, in a voice pitched to carry over wind and surf both, a voice his own sons said they could still hear plainly enough asleep in their own beds a full night's memory away. Most boats that heard it turned without argument, for a warning shouted from a headland by a man known the length of that coast for steadiness rather than fancy was not a warning easily laughed off, whatever a man might privately think of Sea-Watchers and old women's tellings. A few did not turn, in those first years, and came to no harm for the not turning, which some on that coast took as proof the whole fear was overblown and others took as no proof of anything at all, since a warning given need not be answered by disaster every time it goes unheeded in order to be a true warning.

The fire burned on. Criomthann tended it himself for close on forty years, through every season and every weather that coast gave him, adding wood and gorse and, in the leanest winters, peat cut specially for the purpose from a bank his own household kept aside and touched for nothing else, so that the fire on the last headland was never once let go dark in the whole span of his tending it. He was three-and-sixty, and had been a widower nine years by then, his own wife carried off by a fever that took half the young children of that shore with her in the one bad season, when his own strength began, at last, to fail the climb; and it was his eldest son, and after him his son's son, who kept the fire fed from the year Criomthann's legs would no longer carry the wood up the last steep pitch, so that the flame he had first lit for no reason he could fully put into words burned on above the water long past the reach of his own life.

He died at four-and-sixty, in his own bed, with three generations of his own kin about him, having outlived, by then, every one of the four men whose telling had first sent him up that headland with an armful of driftwood in his arms. His own asking was to be buried on the lower slope of the headland itself, apart from the household's other dead, within sound, his sons said afterward, of the fire he had kept; and the fire went on being kept above him, generation folding into generation the way fire on that coast was always kept, fed by hands that had never seen Uilebheist na Mara and never once doubted that there was good cause to feed it.

## IV. Of the Widows of Ros ruadh

It was Criomthann's grandson who was tending the fire, some years into his own turn at the keeping of it, when the season came that the whole of that coast afterward reckoned the worst it had known.

It began, as the worst seasons on that coast most often began, in weather that gave no warning at all of what it meant to take. A calm settled over the water in early summer of the kind fishermen prayed for and seldom got in full measure, day after day of flat grey-green sea and a wind too light to trouble a coracle's balance, the sort of run of weather that filled a household's stores for a whole winter if a crew worked it hard enough while it lasted. The boats of Ros ruadh, a fishing settlement some way down the coast from the headland where the fire burned, close enough that its own boats had heard Criomthann's call turned back more than once in his lifetime and his grandson's after him, went out harder that season than any season in living memory, for a calm like that one was not a thing a fishing household let go to waste.

The first boat did not come back from an evening's work that any of the watchers on shore could afterward point to as different, in any particular they could name, from a hundred evenings before it. It had gone out with three men aboard, working water well inside what any household on that coast called safe, in sight of the shore for most of the day, and it simply did not come home with the tide, and no wreckage of it, then or ever after, washed up on any shingle the length of that coast for anyone to find. A second boat went the same way eleven days later, from a different household and a different stretch of that same calm water, with two men aboard this time, and again no wreckage, again no storm any watcher on shore had marked, again only the tide coming in as it always came in and the boat that should have ridden it home simply not among the boats it brought.

By the time the seventh boat failed to return, in a season that had by then gone on calm for longer than any fisherman on that coast could remember calm holding, there was no household left at Ros ruadh untouched by it, for seven boats lost from one settlement in one season, out of the handful that settlement kept afloat at any time, meant there was scarcely a hearth in the place that had not lost a father, a son, a brother, or all three together, to water that showed no storm, gave up no bodies, and left no boat's timber behind to say what had taken it.

The widows of that season were the ones who first said, plainly and at every hearth that would let them say it, what half the coast had until then only thought and not spoken: that Uilebheist na Mara had taken them. It was not the four men's telling, grown old and half-doubted by then in some mouths, that gave the widows their certainty; it was the plain fact, turned over at every hearth in Ros ruadh through that whole terrible summer, that seven boats crewed by careful men working water they knew like their own hands had gone under, one after another, in a season with no storm in it to blame, in water that lay within a morning's row of the stretch a headland fire had been kept burning against for two generations by then. What else, the widows asked, and asked in a way that was less a question than a naming, could take seven boats from calm water and leave nothing behind to say how, if not the very thing the fire on the headland had been lit to warn against in the first place.

It was the first time on that whole coast that a loss had been laid at Uilebheist na Mara's door by name rather than only feared in its shadow, and once said it was not unsaid again. The tellers who carried the telling onward in the years after gave the widows themselves the naming of it, and said, more than one of them, that a fear kept general and nameless for two generations had needed only one bad season, and the plain grief of women who had buried nothing because there was nothing left to bury, to become a fear with a name fixed to it for good.

The fire on the headland burned harder that year than in any year since Criomthann first lit it, fed, the tellers say, not only by his grandson's hands but by kin from three households besides, men and women who climbed the headland of an evening with what wood they could spare, as though a fire fed by more hands might somehow answer for what seven boats' worth of careful seamanship had not been able to answer for. It went on being fed, year on year after that season, long past any living memory of the seven who had been lost in it, banked by night and built up by day, tended by hands that had themselves been born after the worst of that summer and grown up knowing the fire only as a thing that had always burned there and always would, until its ash, heaped and shifted and heaped again on the same patch of ground for lifetime after lifetime, stood a man's own height deep on the headland where it was kept, deep enough that a boy sent up to feed it could stand in the hollow of it and be seen from below only from the shoulders up.

Of the seven boats themselves nothing further was ever told. No wreck came ashore in any season after to close the account, no drowned man's body was ever found on any shingle to be carried home and buried where the rest of Ros ruadh's dead were buried, and the coast, having no better answer to give and having by then a name it trusted to stand for whatever the true answer was, let the not-knowing settle the way it had let the stakes in the mud settle two generations before, without pretending afterward to know more of it than it did. What Ros ruadh kept, in place of graves it had no bodies to fill, was the empty places on its own shingle where seven boats had once been drawn up of an evening among all the rest, spaces the households marked for years after by habit rather than by any need, walking round them at the tide's edge the way a man walks round a grave he does not mean to stand on, until the shingle itself, shifted by enough winters' tides, no longer held even the memory of where the seven boats had lain, and only the fire on the headland, and the telling the widows had first given a name to, remained to say that they had ever gone out from that shore at all.

# Chapter Twenty-three: Of the Lee of the Headlands and the Writing in the Hills

*VE 3,147 – 3,303*

## I. Of the Boats That Kept the Land Close

For two generations after Criomthann's fire the boats of the north-west still went out by the old marks, keeping the headland on the left hand and the open water on the right, the way their fathers had gone before Uilebheist na Mara had a name to be feared by. It was not fear alone that turned them in the end, or none of the tellers of that coast ever said so outright; it was the slow arithmetic of empty boat-places on the shingle, which any fisherman can do without being taught it, and which comes, in time, to the same answer as fear does.

The change was not a single season's work. A crew that had always worked the open water off the northern point began, without much said about it, to work the water in the lee of the headland instead, where the swell broke early and a boat could see the whole of its ground at once; and the next season two more crews did the same, and by the time a boy born the year the fire was first lit had grown old enough to take an oar himself, there was hardly a hide boat left on that coast that put out past the last headland while the light held. The change carried its own cost, which the shore hearths counted as carefully as they counted the empty places: seal thinned where the old grounds had always given seal, at Ros ruadh and along the outer skerries, and the middens that had grown for generations at those grounds grew slower, and in some years did not grow at all. But in the sheltered water south of the headlands, and along the strait where the tide ran quiet between the mainland and the near skerries, the middens of Bothan a' Chaolais rose faster than they had ever risen, shell on shell and bone on bone, until the oldest of the bothy folk said that a man might build a wall as long as a house out of what a single winter left there.

It was the strait folk themselves who first said it plainly, at a gathering that had no more purpose than the mending of nets and the telling over of who had lost whom that year. An old steersman of Bothan a' Chaolais, whose father had fished the outer grounds all his life and never once seen what his son now feared without having seen it either, put it the way it was afterward remembered: that the sea had not grown smaller, only that the island's hand had drawn back from the part of it a man could no longer trust, the way a hand draws back from a fire that has burned it once, without waiting to be burned a second time to learn the lesson again. No one at that gathering disputed him, and no one thanked him for saying it either, for there is little thanks going in a fishing camp for a man who says aloud what everyone has already done without discussing it.

The strait was not without its own dangers, for no water on Dia-thìr was without danger, but its dangers were the old, known kind: a squall coming down off the mainland heights faster than a boat could run from it, a rip where two tides met at the narrows, a rock that showed at low water and did not show at high. Against these a fisherman could set his knowledge and his oar and win more often than he lost. Against the other danger, the one that lay off the open coast and showed itself perhaps once in a generation and was never once proved false by any wreck brought home to argue with, there was nothing to set but distance, and distance the strait gave freely. So the boats came in from the open water, and the seal bones thinned at the old grounds and thickened at the new, and a whole coast learned, within the span of two lifetimes, to call a stretch of open sea its neighbour's water and not its own, though no one on it had ever seen the neighbour, and no one who had seen it had lived long enough to be believed twice.

## II. Of Eimhir and the High Pastures

South of that coast, and a long day's walk inland from it, the land climbed into a country of thin soil and thinner grazing that the hill folk called, among themselves, the green grove country, for the oaks that had once stood there thick enough to darken a hillside, though by the time this telling opens the old grove itself had gone back to scrub and bracken and only the name remembered what it had been. It was harder country than the shore, and harder again than the broad valley where Clann a' Chlachair kept its fire and its recital twelve miles to the north, and the households that worked it were fewer and kept closer to their beasts than to each other, each family holding its own stretch of high pasture through the summer months and coming down only for the worst of the winter.

Into one such household, some three hundred years after the black coal was warmed in the ground at Tobar dhìreach, though the hill folk reckoned their years less carefully than the valley did and would have said only that it was long since, a girl was born who was given the name Eimhir, and who grew, as most children of that country grew, first at her mother's hearth and then, as soon as her legs were long enough to keep pace with a flock on a slope, out on the high ground with the sheep and the cold and the wide grey sky. She was not a remarkable child by any account that survives her, quick enough with a crook and a whistle, slow to anger and slower to forget a slight, more comfortable, by most tellings, in the company of beasts than of people, which is no rare thing among those raised to that work. She knew the recital, as every hill child knew it, in the broken, half-understood way it reached households that stood twelve miles from the hearth where it was said whole, and she could recite the count of the coals — gold, white, black, and the four still unanswered — without being entirely certain, if pressed, which coal was which, or why the count mattered so much to the valley folk who came up now and then to trade wool for salt and talk of nothing else.

What she knew better than the recital was the ground itself: every fold of it, every seep and outcrop and stand of gorse for three valleys in either direction, learned the way any herder learns a country, through the soles of the feet more than through the eyes, over years of walking it in every weather the sky could send. By the time she had seen twenty summers she could have walked the whole of her family's grazing blind, and often did, in the grey light before dawn when the flock needed moving before the day's heat brought the flies up from the bog.

It was in the course of that walking, and no more than that, that she came, on a morning in the season when the bracken was just turning, upon the face of rock that would give this telling of the hills its name.

## III. Of the Cutting on the Stone

A ewe had strayed in the night, as a ewe will, up a narrow defile where the family did not usually take the flock, being poor grazing and awkward footing both; and Eimhir went after it before the light was properly up, more from habit than from any great worry for one animal among many, following the beast's own track through wet bracken into a fold of the hill she did not remember walking before, though she had thought she knew every fold within a day's reach.

The ewe she found easily enough, caught by a bramble and glad enough to be caught by a person instead. It was on her way back down, with the animal on a rope and the light coming up grey and slow behind the eastern ridge, that she stopped, for no better reason at first than that something in the corner of her sight did not sit the way stone usually sits.

The rock face rose sheer on her left hand, a grey scarp perhaps twice her own height, weathered the way every outcrop in that country was weathered, lichened in patches of orange and pale green. But across the lichen, where the surface had been struck away to bare stone beneath, ran lines: not the crack and tumble of frost-split rock, which she had seen a thousand times and would have known blind, but lines cut with intent, straight and angled and joined to one another in shapes that repeated, here and there, close enough to be the same shape said twice, the way a word is the same word said twice in a telling. They ran the height of the rock and along it for longer than her own arm span, more of them the further along the face she walked, the ewe forgotten on its rope behind her.

She had seen carved stone before. Every household in that country marked its boundary posts, and Clann a' Chlachair itself, she had been told, kept the count of the coals by mouth at Tobar dhìreach and said it standing, though she had never gone to hear it. But those marks she knew, plain notches and simple figures a person could learn in an afternoon. What ran across this rock face was neither plain nor simple, line after line of it, in a hand — if a hand it was, and not some older weather she did not have the word for — that she did not know at all, and had never heard any teller in her own hearth's memory claim to know either.

She stood a long while before she touched it. When she did, running two fingers along one cut line from where it began to where it stopped, she found the stone at the bottom of the groove smoother than the weathered face around it, as though wind and rain had not yet had the years to roughen what the tool had first laid bare; and yet the lichen at the edges of some of the cuts was old lichen, thick and long-established, telling her without words that whatever hand had made these marks had not made them yesterday, nor in her grandmother's day either.

And there was this, which she noticed last and remembered longest: in three places along the face, a passage of the cutting had itself been cut across, the clean lines broken by a second working, rougher than the first, done — she would have sworn it, standing there, though she could not have said how she knew — with the very same kind of tool, as if whatever hand had written the lines, or another hand that knew the same trade, had come back afterward, deliberately, to strike part of the writing out.

She left the ewe to find its own way home, which it did, being a sensible enough animal on level ground, and went down off that hill faster than she had come up it.

## IV. Of the Word Going Down

She told her mother first, at the family's own hearth, in the plain, halting way a person tells a thing they themselves do not yet believe, and her mother, who had lived sixty years in that country and buried a husband and three of six children in it, did not laugh at her, which Eimhir noted and was grateful for long after she had forgotten most of what was actually said that morning. Instead her mother sent word, by the boy who carried salt between the hill households and the valley, to the two or three elders of that country whose opinion still carried weight beyond their own hearths, and within the week a small company of them had climbed the defile behind Eimhir to see the thing for themselves.

They were longer at it than she had been, and quieter. One of them, a bent man named for a grandfather three generations dead whose own name this telling does not keep, put his palm flat against the stone the way a person tests a beast for fever, and held it there a good while before he took it away again and said nothing at all, which unsettled the company more than any word he might have offered. Another, a woman who had outlived two husbands and kept, besides her flock, a longer memory of the hill country's own small tellings than anyone else living in it, walked the length of the writing twice, once each direction, and then said, in the flat voice of someone stating a fact rather than offering an opinion, that she did not know the hand, and did not know anyone, living or lately dead, who had ever claimed to know it, and that in her long experience a thing no one in a small country claimed to know was, more often than not, a thing that country would come, in its own time and by its own means, to know anyway.

She was right, though not one of the company standing at the rock face that morning could have said how she knew to say it, or how the knowing would come. It did not come as a telling handed down from someone who had read the marks, for no one on that hill, then or after, ever claimed to read them; the lines stayed as unreadable to the last hill-born child of that generation as they had been to Eimhir on the morning she first laid two fingers against them. It came the way certain things come to a small country that lives close together and talks at its hearths through the long winter evenings with little else to talk of: slowly, by no one path that could afterward be traced, gathering itself out of dreams two or three people swore, independently and without having spoken to one another first, that they had dreamed in nearly the same shape; out of a half-remembered scrap some old woman recalled her own grandmother saying, without recalling where her grandmother had had it from; out of the plain, wordless dread that settled, before any of it could be put into a sentence, over anyone who stood alone at that rock face after dark. By the time two winters had passed, there was not a hearth in that country that could not have told a stranger, if a stranger had ever come asking, what the cutting on the stone was held to say: that something had once walked those hills that did not breathe as a living thing breathes, and that it fell upon whoever lit a fire where it could see the light of it burning.

No one could say why breath and fire, of all things, should be bound together in the telling, and the hill folk, being practical people more given to watching their flocks than to turning over the whys of their own fears, mostly left the asking alone. It was enough, for most of that country, that the fear had come, and had come to more than one hearth at once, and agreed with itself too closely, dreamer to dreamer, to be set aside as one old woman's fancy.

## V. Of the Cutting-Over

What none of the company at the rock face could account for at all, that first morning or in the years after, was the second working: the passages of writing struck across and spoiled by a hand using, as near as anyone with an eye for stonework could judge, the very tool that had cut the writing in the first place. Two thoughts went about the hearths concerning it, and neither ever won out fully over the other.

The first was that whoever had written the warning had come back to unwrite parts of it, out of some purpose no hill teller could guess at: to hide a name, perhaps, or a place, or some part of the telling too dangerous even for a warning to carry whole. The second, favoured by the woman who had walked the stone twice that first morning and by most who thought as she did, was harder and colder, and it was this: that the very thing the warning spoke of had done the defacing itself, offended, in whatever way such a thing could be offended, at having been written down and named where the light could fall on it. A hand that could scar stone the way another hand had first cut it was not a hand a sensible person went looking for after dark.

Eimhir herself, in the many years she lived after that morning, was asked more than once which of the two she held to, and by every account that survives her she never answered plainly either way, saying only, when pressed, that she had touched the smoothed groove of the first cutting and the rougher groove of the second with the same two fingers on the same morning, and that her fingers had told her nothing at all about which hand she should fear, only that both hands had been in earnest.

## VI. Of the Years Between

The finding of the writing did not empty the hills, nor did it stop the flocks going up to the summer grazing, for a country that lived by its beasts could not afford a fear that kept it from its work, and the hill folk, whatever else is told of them, were not a people who let fear idle their hands for long. What it did, slowly, over the better part of two decades, was change the shape of the days: fewer households sent a child alone to the far pastures after the finding than had sent one before it, and fewer still let a fire burn low and unwatched through the small hours on a night when the wind came off the high ground with nothing in it a person could put a name to. The defile where Eimhir had found the ewe was given a wide berth by common unspoken consent, though sheep still strayed into it now and again, and were fetched, though never after dark and never by a child sent alone.

Eimhir herself went up past that rock face more times than she ever troubled to count, for a herder's country does not rearrange itself around one bad morning, and in time the going grew almost ordinary to her, the way any fear grows ordinary that a person must live alongside rather than flee. She married into a neighbouring household two valleys over. Of her husband this telling keeps only that he was a quiet man, steadier with beasts than with words, and that he outlived her by eleven years. She raised children on the same slopes she had herself been raised on, and taught them, as she had been taught, to read the weather and the ground and the temper of a flock before they were old enough to read anything else. What she taught them of the writing on the stone she kept plain and short, by every account: that it was there, that no one read it, that the hills had their own sense of what it meant, and that a fire built where the ridge could see it was a fire built carelessly, whatever else a person believed or did not believe about why.

Twice in those years word came up from that country of a thing seen on a ridge at dusk by travellers with beasts to drive home and the light failing on them before they were ready for it: an upright figure, unhurried, walking the crest against the last grey of the sky, with no breath standing in cloud above it though the night was cold enough to hang breath from every mouth and muzzle below. Both times the ones who saw it lived to tell it, and both times the telling agreed on the one particular that the hill folk came to hold above all others: that neither party had had a fire lit or a light shown on the path, and that this, and nothing else they could name, was why they had come home to tell it at all.

## VII. Of the First Covered Hearth

It was in the sixtieth year of Eimhir's own life, by the hill country's rough count, that a household two ridges to the east of her own — new to that ground, having come up from a lowland valley to take a grazing left empty by a family that had died out — dug its cooking fire down into a pit for the first time and roofed it over with a flat slab lifted on two low stones, so that no flame showed above the ground at all, only a slot of red light and a thread of smoke escaping sideways into the dark. They had heard the telling of the writing from their new neighbours within a season of arriving, as any newcomer to that country heard it soon or late, and had chosen, being cautious people in a country new to them, to give the fear more credit than a life's habit, and dig accordingly.

They were mocked for it a little, in the way any first departure from custom draws a little mockery before it is judged either foolish or wise, and one or two of the older households said openly that a family which had not lived in that country long enough to lose anyone to it had no business teaching the country its own fears back to it. But no one stopped them digging, and within the year two more households on the eastern side had done the same, more from watching the first family's fire burn on, unremarked and untroubled, through a whole hard winter, than from any argument put to them in words.

Eimhir watched the pit dug from a little way off, on the day the eastern family first cut it, and said nothing to anyone about it that this telling keeps, though her daughter, many years after, remembered her mother standing longer at the sight than the digging alone seemed to call for.

## VIII. Of Eimhir's Own Hearth

She did not dig her own fire down, that year or in any year that followed it, though she lived to see a fourth household and then a fifth take up the covered hearth after the first three, each a little more readily than the one before, the way any new custom gathers speed once enough hands have tried it and not been burned for the trying. Her own hearth stayed as her mother's had been and her mother's mother's before that, a ring of stones on the open floor of the house, the fire built up each evening and banked each night under its own ash, giving its light up through the smoke-hole in the roof for any ridge in that country to see, had anything been walking the ridges to see it.

Her daughter, grown and married with children of her own, asked her once, late in her life, why she had never dug the fire in, when half the hearths of that country had done it by then and the other half were talking of doing it before the next hard winter. Eimhir was an old woman by that time, by the standard the hill country kept for old, her hands slower on a crook than they had once been and her eyes gone milky at the edges, but her mind, by every account, no less her own than it had been on the morning she followed a strayed ewe up a defile she did not remember walking before.

She gave no answer at once, but sat, when the question was put to her, on the low stool she had used at her own hearth for the better part of forty years, with the fire built up before her the way she had always built it, open to the room and open, through the smoke-hole above, to whatever sky lay over the roof that night; and she looked at it a long while, the way a person looks at a thing they have looked at every evening of their life without, perhaps, ever once looking at it quite so closely, before she said what she said, which her daughter kept, and which is the last of Eimhir's own words this telling has to give: that she had touched the writing on the stone with her own two fingers before any hearth in that country had thought to cover itself against it, and that whatever the writing meant, and whatever walked the ridges when it chose to walk them, she was not going to spend the years she had left hiding her fire from the sky that had watched every fire her family had ever kept, on the chance that the sky had turned against her only now, in her own old age, after keeping faith with her the whole of her life before it.

She said no more than that, her daughter's telling has it, and went on looking at the fire, and the fire went on burning the way it always had, open to the room and to the roof and to whatever, if anything, watched from beyond it.

## IX. Of the Years After

She died two years on from that evening, some sixty years after the finding of the writing, of no illness or misfortune the country could put a name to beyond the plain wearing-out of a long life honestly spent; and she was buried, as the hill folk buried their own, on a slope above her family's grazing, with no marker but a stone set on end and no telling but the one her children and her children's children carried on afterward at their own hearths.

Her own fire went out with her, banked for the last time by her daughter's hand and never built again in that house on the open floor; for her daughter, though she had defended her mother's choice to every questioner who asked it of her in Eimhir's own lifetime, dug the family's hearth into the ground within the year of the burial, and said, when asked why she had not done it while her mother lived, only that a daughter does not take a fire from a living mother's floor, whatever she herself might choose to do with her own.

By the time forty years more had passed over that country, the covered hearth had spread from household to household and ridge to ridge until an open fire, built up on the bare floor the way Eimhir had kept hers to the last, was a rare enough sight in the Doire uaine hills that a child born into a household that still kept one was asked about it by every other child at every gathering, the way a child is asked about any household custom that has become, elsewhere, a thing of the grandparents' time. It had not yet become the whole country's law, nor would it, this telling must own, for some years longer than either Eimhir or her daughter lived to see; there were households still, scattered along the country's quieter edges, that kept the old open floor through habit or stubbornness or a plain want of belief in a fear no living soul could any longer claim to have seen with their own eyes. But the hills had begun, by the century's turning, to keep their light low and covered more often than they kept it open, and to watch their ridgelines at dusk the way they had once watched only the weather; and what had begun on one morning with a strayed ewe and two fingers laid against a cut stone had become, by slow and uneven degrees, the shape of how a whole country lived after dark.

# Chapter Twenty-four: Of the Covered Hearths and the Nine

*VE 3,304 – 3,407*

## I. Of Laoghaire and the Hearth Under the Slab

Forty-two years had gone by since the herder-girl who found the defaced lines on the rock faces of the Doire uaine hills had died an old woman with her own hearth still open to the sky, unwilling in the end to live any other way, though she had lived the last of her years knowing what the hills now knew and could not unknow: that the lines running for yards across the stone, cut over and cut over again by the same hand or the same kind of tool, told of something that walked without breathing and fell upon whoever lit a fire where it could see. On the eastern side of that country the first household to dig its own fire into the ground and roof it with a slab had by then been dead two generations, and most of the hearths that side of the hills had long since followed it below the turf. But the custom had come slower, and less certainly, to the quieter western valleys, where the ground ran higher and stonier and a household's neighbours were a morning's walk apart rather than a shout across a field; and it was there, in a valley that still kept as many open hearths as covered ones, that the argument the eastern side had already half settled went on being argued still. Two of the earliest pits dug on that side had shown, on windless nights, a thread of glow at the smoke-vent that had frightened the households that dug them nearly as badly as an open fire would have, and it had left a fair part of that country unsure whether the ground itself had made them any safer or only given them a new way to be careless.

Whether a fire kept low was fire enough hidden, whether the walker minded smoke or only flame, whether a people that had carried its light from hearth to hearth since before any of them could count backward should now go creeping about in the dark of its own valleys like thieves in another man's house: all of it was argued over again, that western valley's own way, at every gathering.

Laoghaire was no thinker on the matter, by his own telling of himself and by everyone else's telling of him after. He was a digger of ditches for the water off the high pastures, a big slow-spoken man with a spade-shaped scar across one forearm from a fall on wet rock as a boy, and what he brought to the question that had worn a generation thin with talking was a habit of hands rather than any answer. He had spent half his life putting things into the ground where the weather could not get at them: seed corn against the wet, the hides of slaughtered beasts against the crows, the small store of hazelnuts his household kept for the lean months, sunk in a clay-lined pit and lidded with a slab no fox or badger had ever worked loose. It was his wife, by the account the hills kept longest of the two of them, who said it to him first, more in weariness than in hope, on an evening when the argument had gone round the fire circle for the hundredth time and got nowhere: that the eastern hearths had already shown a fire could be put into the ground, and that if theirs still glowed at the vent on a still night, then the fault lay in the digging and not in the notion, and a man who could sink a pit for hazelnuts that no fox nor badger had ever worked open ought to be able to sink one for a fire that no eye on a ridge could ever find.

He did not answer her that night. He sat a long while with the fire between them going down to embers, turning the notion over the way he turned a stone over before he set a spade to it, looking for the grain of it. "A pit for hazelnuts keeps out crows," he said at last. "It does not keep out cold, or breathe, or want a way down a man can walk without breaking his neck." His wife said only that she had not told him it would be easy, and went to bed, and left him sitting by the fire a good while longer, watching the low light of it climb the smoke-blackened roof-poles and thinking, by his own account to his sons, that a fire seen from above at that hour would carry a very long way over open ground.

He went out at first light instead, alone, to a shoulder of ground below his own house where the soil ran deep enough for a man to dig his own height without striking rock, and he began.

It was harder work than any pit he had cut for corn or hide, for a fire could not simply be dropped in and lidded; it wanted air to breathe by, and a way down to it that would not throw light where light could be seen. He dug a hole a man's height in depth and near two men's lengths across at its widest, and cut into one wall of it a slanting shaft no wider than his own shoulders, angled so that a man going down it went down blind, with the last stretch bent enough that no glow from below could climb it straight to the surface. At the bottom he laid a floor of flat stones and built his hearth upon them as any hearth was built, wood and peat and a coal carried down in a clay pot from the household fire above, and over the whole pit, resting on a low kerb of stone he had set into the sides for the purpose, he laid a great flat slab dragged down from the scree on a hide sledge by himself and his two elder sons, with a gap left at one corner no wider than a man's forearm, for the smoke to find its own slow way up through a crack in the turf a good ten paces off, where it thinned in the heather and told nothing to anyone looking down from above.

The digging took him the better part of three days, working alone through the first and calling his sons to the slab-dragging on the third, and there was a moment on the second evening, kneeling at the bottom of his own half-finished pit with the light gone from the sky above him and nothing but a hand's width of grey dusk showing at the top of the shaft, when he owned afterward to a fright that had nothing to do with any beast that walked the ridges: the plain, ordinary fright of a man who has dug himself into the ground and cannot, for the length of a held breath, remember which way the shaft bends. He came up that evening faster than he had meant to, and said nothing of it to his wife, and went down again the next morning as though the moment had not happened, for a man who dug ditches for a living did not let one bad breath in a hole turn him from a job half done.

He slept beside it the first night it was whole, in the pit, on the excuse of tending it, though everyone who knew him understood well enough that he wanted to be the one below if the thing he had built proved no better than the two glowing pits on the eastern side that had failed to settle anyone's mind before him. On his back on the packed earth with the fire's small light moving on the underside of Leac na Fèithe above him, close enough to touch if he reached, and listened, he said, for a long time to nothing at all: no wind, for the pit took the wind clean away, no voice, no step on the turf overhead that the earth might have carried down to him, only his own fire's small talk and his own blood in his ears. Nothing came. He came up at first light with soot on his hands and grass seed in his hair from the crawl up the blind shaft, and told his wife only that it had held its heat through the dark better than any open hearth he had ever slept beside, which was true and was also, everyone agreed afterward, not the whole of what he had gone down to learn.

It was the whole of what he could tell them, and it proved, in the end, to be enough. Word of the blind bend and the offset vent went from his own hearth to the next and from that to the next again, the way any useful thing went in those hills, carried by whoever had seen it and told plainly, without ornament, to whoever asked; and within the season the two families whose own pits had glowed at the vent came and stood at the lip of his, and went home, and dug theirs afresh on his pattern. Within two years there was a scoffer's name for anyone west of the ridge still keeping an open fire on the old pattern, and within five it was the open hearth that wanted explaining and the covered one that needed none. Laoghaire himself dug three more in the years that followed, one for a widowed sister and two for households that begged the digging of him outright rather than trust their own hands to the angle of the shaft, for he alone among them seemed to hold in his head, without ever setting it down as a rule anyone could repeat back, exactly how far the blind bend had to run before no glow climbed it, and how wide the vent had to be to draw the smoke away thin and slow rather than in a column any eye above could follow to its root.

He was six-and-sixty, and had outlived two of his own children and buried them under no marker louder than a plain heaped stone, when he died in his own house on a night no different from any other, his wife said afterward, save that he had gone to check the pit himself before bed as he had gone every night of his life since the first, out of a habit by then worn as smooth and as unremarked as breathing. He was buried, at his own long-standing wish, not beside the pit he had dug first, which his sons kept in use for another three generations after him, but on the shoulder of ground just above it, where he had stood the morning he began to dig and looked down, his wife said he had told her once, at nothing more than a patch of bare soil that had not yet become anything.

## II. Of the Hearth That Would Not Be Covered

At Tobar dhìreach, a long day's walk to the north, the fire that had come down from the mason's own well had never once, in all the generations since Diarmad first carried Aithris a' Chruthachaidh home from the grove, been put under a slab or a skin or anything else that stood between it and the open sky. It burned where it had always burned, in the low stone ring at the centre of the line's own house, with the clay pot that held what the line called the mason's first fire set always within an arm's reach of it, and the leather bag of the six dark coals and the one that would not darken hung on its peg above, and no household of Clann a' Chlachair, in all the years the covered hearth spread through the hills to the south, so much as dug the first spadeful of earth to make one of its own.

It was not that the word had failed to reach them. Travellers carried it, as travellers carried everything, and kin by marriage from the Doire uaine households brought it plainer still, standing in the doorway at Tobar dhìreach with soot still under their nails from a pit dug that same season and asking, some of them gently and some of them not, why a people who kept the mason's own fire, of all the fires on the island, should be the one household too proud or too stubborn to learn from its neighbours.

The man who kept the pot in those years — his name is not given here, for it is a rule older than any single teller that the fathers of the line between Brian and the one the hills came in time to call Cormac of the Misstrike are kept by the recital and given to no stranger who asks, and a telling carried beyond the hearth is a stranger before it is anything else — heard the question put to him more than once at his own hearth, and gave, by every account that has come down of it, the same answer each time, in words that varied a little from telling to telling but held to the one shape.

The fire in this house, he said, was not kept for warmth alone, nor even chiefly for warmth, though it warmed them as any fire warmed any house. It was kept because the mason's own hands had carried the first of it out of the ground on a flat stone under his cloak, and because every fire on the island, the pit-fires of the Doire uaine hills not excepted, traced back through some chain of borrowed embers to this one ring of stones and no other. A fire that had never once, in all those generations, been let go dark could not now be hidden without becoming, in the hiding, a fire like any other fire that a household banked low against its own fears; and the line held, rightly or not, that Teine a' Chlachair was owed better than to be treated as though it were no different from a peat-stack fire on a hillside that had reason to be afraid.
