There were those at Tobar dhìreach, in those same years, who thought this reasoning proud rather than wise, and said so, and one branch of the kin did in the end dig a covered hearth of its own, apart from the line's own house, keeping the open fire only for the recital nights and banking the household's daily fire below ground the rest of the year, a compromise that satisfied neither the boldest nor the most fearful among them and was, by most tellings, quietly let drop again within two generations. But the line's own hearth, the one ring of stones the pot and the bag were kept beside, stayed open through every year of the trouble that follows in this telling, and stays open, so far as any teller of the hills can say, to this day.

## III. Of the Nine

There was a hill camp in those years in the south of the massif, a scatter of huts where three or four households wintered their beasts close together against the worst of the weather, no larger and no smaller than a dozen such camps the hills kept, and no more remarked. It kept its fires the old open way still, being far enough from Laoghaire's own valley and young enough in the custom that the pit under Leac na Fèithe had not yet been dug there, and no ill had come of it in all the winters the camp had stood, so that its households had come, as households will, to hold their own distance from the trouble a lucky thing rather than a borrowed grace.

The shepherd who found it, from a neighbouring valley and kin by marriage to one of the camp's three households, had gone up on an errand no more solemn than the borrowing of a ram, and noticed the lack of smoke only as a man notices any small wrongness, a thing his eye caught before his mind had troubled to ask why. He stood a while at the foot of the last rise looking up at a sky with nothing rising into it from any of the huts, on a morning cold enough that his own breath hung white before his face, and told himself, walking up, three or four reasons a camp might let its fires go low on a still night that had nothing to do with anything worse. None of the reasons held by the time he reached the gate. He found it standing open to a silence he said afterward he had felt on his skin before his eyes had told him anything was wrong.

Nine people lay inside it, about a hearth burned down to fresh grey ash and no further, none of them fallen as a man falls in a struggle, none marked by wound or blood or any hurt a living eye could find on skin or bone, lying instead as though the sleep that had taken them at the fire's side had simply not let them up again. The shepherd did not go in past the doorway. He went for the nearest kin the camp had, and they did not go in either, not that day nor any day after, and the hut was left standing with its dead inside it and its door swinging, until in time the wattle rotted and the roof went down over them and the grass came up through the collapsed thatch and no one from that day to this has ever gone in to bury what the roof by then had already covered.

What had been burning in that hearth, on the night whatever came for the nine had come, no one who found them could afterward say with certainty, though the ash was fresh enough, the shepherd swore, that the fire could not have been out above a day when he climbed to the camp and found the smoke gone. Whether it had been a fire kept open on the old pattern by householders too newly come to that ground to have learned the custom of their neighbours, or a covered hearth whose smoke-vent had for some reason shown more than it should have on a still night, the hills never settled, and the tellers who carried the account onward after gave it, in the end, no answer at all, only the one plain fact that stood at the centre of every version: nine people, a fire gone cold in an ordinary way, and not a mark on any of them to say what had stopped their breath.

The camp was never resettled. Other households, in the years that followed, drove their beasts wide of that shoulder of hill at the season the trouble had come, and in time the ground took on the kind of name that needed no telling to explain it, spoken of by herders passing near it, when it was spoken of at all, in the same low voice a man on the north-western shore might once have used for a stretch of water he had cause to keep clear of, though on the hills that voice had learned to speak of ground rather than water, for it was ground, and not the sea, that the hills of Doire uaine had come to fear.

## IV. Of the Hut That Burned Empty

Some thirty years after the camp was left, a family new to that country came up from the eastern farms to take grazing on a slope the hills had by then gone a long generation without settling, drawn by grass that had grown thick and unclaimed in the years since the neighbouring ground was given up. They were kin of a line that had never lived among the Doire uaine hills and had heard the custom of the covered hearth only as a thing travellers spoke of, half believed and half thought a hill people's fancy, the way any custom sounds when it is heard secondhand from a people one does not yet know well enough to trust.

They built their first house that summer on the old pattern, with the hearth open to the roof-hole as every hearth of their own kin had always been built, and it drew comment from the nearest neighbours before the roof-thatch was even finished, comment given, by every account, kindly enough and more than once, in the plain hope of sparing strangers a grief the hills themselves had already paid for. One old woman of the next valley over, who had herself dug her own pit-hearth as a young wife in the years the custom first spread, walked up twice that summer to say her piece plainly at their door: that she had lost no kin herself to the walker, and knew no one now living who had seen it, and would not for that reason claim to know its mind; only that a people did not go on digging into their own ground for a hundred years over nothing, and that a stranger new to a country did well to take an old fear from its own people at their word before learning, the hard way, what the word had been worth. The family thanked her for it, both times, and kept their fire open through that first autumn all the same, being, as newcomers to any custom often are, readier to hear a warning than to act on one they had not yet felt the weight of themselves.

It was in the dark of that same winter, on a night none of the near households could afterward fix more exactly than "hard frost, and still," that a boy sent at dawn to borrow fire, his own household's having gone out overnight in weather too cold for even banked coals to hold, came down again from the new family's door faster than he had gone up it and could not, for some while, get out more than that the door stood open and no one had answered his call.

Those who went up with him found the hut as he had found it: the door open to a morning white with frost, the beds slept in and thrown back as a bed is thrown back by someone rising in haste or in sleep, and every soul of that household gone from the place without a trace of where or how, no blood, no sign of a struggle, no track in a fresh fall of snow that had come in the night to say which way, if any way, they had gone. And on the hearth, banked the night before by a hand that plainly meant it to hold till morning, the fire burned on into the empty house exactly as it had been left, low and steady and untended, warming a room that held, by the time the neighbours reached it, no one left alive to feel it.

## V. Of the Walker on the Ridge

Twenty years more went by, the ash on the abandoned camp's cold hearth long since blown into the heather and the empty house on the eastern slope fallen in the way any house falls in once no one is left to mend its roof, before two herders of that country, a man and his sister-in-law out after strayed ewes on the ridge above the old camp in the last light of an autumn day, saw what Eimhir's own generation had once seen and lived to tell, and what few enough had seen since to keep the telling fresh: a shape moving along the skyline, at a distance neither of them could afterward agree on more closely than "far enough that we should have felt safe, and did not," that walked as a man walks and was not a man.

It went, they both said, at an even pace neither hurried nor slow, following the line of the ridge the way a shepherd follows a track he knows without needing to look down at his own feet, and it gave off, in the failing light, no breath they could see rise from it into the cold air, though the evening was cold enough by then that every sheep on that hillside stood wreathed in its own small cloud of it. Neither of them called out. Neither of them, by their own account given many times after to kin who asked and to kin who did not, so much as spoke to the other until the shape had passed beyond the shoulder of the ridge and out of sight, and it was only then, with it gone, that the man found he had been holding his sister-in-law's arm the whole time without either of them noticing when his hand had closed on it.

They had, that evening and every evening before it on that slope, no fire lit anywhere near them, their own hearth banked and covered a good half-hour's walk below, and it was this, more than anything either of them could put into clearer words, that both came to believe afterward had let them come home at all: that whatever walked the ridge that evening had passed by two people with no flame anywhere about them for it to find, the way it had passed, in every telling the hills by then kept of it, by every hearth that gave it nothing to see.

It was the last such sighting the hills kept any close account of, though not, in the tellers' own admission, because the walker was never seen again, only because by then there was little left for a sighting to prove that the hills had not already settled among themselves beyond arguing. The pit with the blind bend and the offset vent, the pattern Laoghaire had worked out on the shoulder of his own ground close on a hundred years before, was by the year the two herders came down off that ridge with their flock and their unspoken fright no longer spoken of household by household as it spread, east side or west, nor a scoffer's mark against whoever still kept the old pattern, but simply the way a hearth was built in that country, so plainly and so completely that a child born in those hills in that year would grow to be an old woman herself without ever once, in the whole span of her life, seeing an open fire lit under any roof but the one at Tobar dhìreach, where the mason's own flame went on burning, as it always had, in the one house the hills had long since stopped expecting to change.

# Chapter Twenty-five: Of the Uncut Woods

*VE 3,408 – 3,639*

> *Tha blas eile air an uisce seo seach uisce na mara.*
> This water tastes different from the sea water.

*The Fifth Part: Of the Coal of Life, the Silver in the River, and the Shore*

## I. Of the Wood That Knew Itself First

In the east of that country, a long way past the last of the covered hearths and the last of the arguing that had gone with them, there stood a wood that no household living could say who had first set apart. It was not a young wood. The oaks in it had the girth of three men's arms linked, and the ground beneath them lay dim even at noon of midsummer, the light coming down in coins rather than sheets, and every family whose fields ran up to its edge told the same telling of it, passed down as plainly as the shape of the hills: the trees knew it first, and the people after.

No one could say what that meant, put to the question straight, and no one who lived by that wood ever put it to the question straight, for it was not the kind of telling that wanted testing. It meant, near enough, that the wood had been holy before anyone had thought to hold it so, the way a well is cold before anyone thinks to call it cold; that a household new to the country, walking its dogs along the treeline for the first time and feeling the hair rise on its own arms without cause, was feeling a thing the wood had always done and not a thing the older families had taught it to feel. Sadhbh's grandmother had told it to Sadhbh's mother in those words, sitting at the hearth with the shutters closed against an autumn gale, and Sadhbh's mother told it to Sadhbh in turn on a morning much like any other, when the girl was six years old and had asked, the way children ask, why the wood-carriers went the long way round instead of through.

The long way round was no small thing to choose, in that country. The nearest true fuel-wood outside the holy trees lay the better part of half a day's walk beyond them, over a shoulder of open ground that gave no shelter from weather and less from the walking, so that a household cutting its winter store made two journeys where one would have served it, had it been willing to put an axe to anything standing within the wood's own bounds. No one was. Sadhbh grew up watching her father and her uncles set out before light with the cart and the two dogs, swinging wide of the treeline by a field's width even where the ground made the wide way harder, and she grew up too watching the charcoal that came into the household's own hearth arrive black and ordinary from a dozen kinds of tree and never once, in all the years she kept count without meaning to, from that one.

There was talk, now and again, among the younger of the households, of what a wood that size might spare a family in a hard winter if only one tree of it, one, were felled and split and burned like any other. It came up most often at the end of a bad season, when the wood-carriers had made their third or fourth double journey of the month and a man's back had good cause to grumble at the extra mile. Sadhbh heard her own uncle say it once, half in jest and half not, leaning on the cart in the last light of a short winter afternoon with the load still short of what the household wanted: that a tree was a tree, whatever ground it stood in, and a fire did not ask where its wood had grown before it burned warm. No one answered him that evening, not with argument and not with agreement, and by the next wood-carrying he was walking the long way round with the rest of them as though he had never said it, for it was the kind of talk that a household let pass without rebuke and without repeating, the grumble of a tired man rather than a settled wish, and no one in Sadhbh's lifetime, whatever was said at the end of a hard month, ever put an axe within the wood's own bounds to test what the trees or anything behind them might have to say to it.

It was not forbidden in the way a thing is forbidden when someone has said the word aloud and set a penalty behind it. No elder stood at the treeline turning axes back. It wanted no guard, her father told her once, hefting the cart's shaft onto his shoulder on a cold morning with his breath standing white before him, because a thing that wanted guarding was a thing a person might still be persuaded to try, and no one in that country, so far as living memory or the memory before it could reach, had ever tried. He said it without heat, the way a man says a thing he has never once had cause to doubt, and Sadhbh, walking at his side with a hand on the cart's rail to keep her feet in the frozen ruts, understood before she had words fit to hold the understanding that this was the whole of the custom. No law kept it. It was a thing simply not done, the way a person does not eat the fire that warms them.

She asked once, being a child and not yet grown past asking the plain question aloud, what would come of a man who cut there all the same. Her father was quiet long enough that she thought he had not heard her over the cart's creaking, and then he said only that no one had ever found out, and that he for his part had no wish to be the first, and turned the talk to the state of the ground ahead, which was as much of an answer as she got from him that day or any other. It was, she came to see as she grew, the whole hills' answer to the same question, offered in one shape or another by every elder ever asked it. None of them could point to a harm done. What held them back was a caution kept so long and so evenly across so many households that it had worn a path into the ground the way any path wears, needing no one's word to keep it and no one's memory of why it was first walked.

## II. Of the Stag at the Wood's Edge

Sadhbh was past twenty and already a hunter in her own right, known across the eastern households for a steadier hand at the gully-drives than most of the men who worked beside her, when the wood gave the country the telling that outlasted every other telling that came out of it.

It happened at the gully the hunters called Gleann nan Damh, a deer-drive run down along the wood's own southern shoulder where the ground narrowed between a fall of scree on one side and the first outlying trees on the other, close enough to the holy ground that a beast driven hard down it sometimes broke for the treeline rather than the open flats below, and no hunter had ever yet followed one in. Sadhbh had worked that drive a dozen years by then, knew the wind of it and the footing of it as well as she knew her own threshold, and had never in all those years so much as raised her bow within a spear's throw of the trees, out of the same unspoken caution every hunter in that country carried with them the way they carried their knives.

She was posted that morning at the narrowest turn of the gully, waiting on the drive that two of her cousins were bringing down from higher ground, when a stag broke from the treeline rather than from the open hill, which was a thing she had not seen in all her years at that post and did not, for the length of a held breath, know how to read. It was white: white the way new snow is white before any foot has crossed it, from the muzzle back along the whole run of its flank to a tail that flicked once, catching what little light came down through the trees at its back, its antlers standing up out of that white like something carved rather than grown.

It stood at the treeline a long moment, close enough that Sadhbh could see the working of its ribs with each breath and the dark, unhurried eye it turned on her, not the wild white-rimmed eye of a beast that has just broken from a drive in fright, but a look she found no better word for after, in all the tellings she gave of it in her own long life, than steady. Her bow was in her hand and half drawn before she had thought to draw it, the plain reflex of a hunter's body outrunning her own mind, and it was her mind that stopped her hand where it was, though she could not afterward say what thought had done the stopping, only that the drawing felt, of a sudden, like a thing her body had begun on its own account and her whole self refused to finish.

Two others saw it with her that same morning, her cousin Ruadhan coming down late off the high ground and a boy new to the drive whose name the hills did not trouble to keep, and neither of them drew either, though both had clean sight of it and time enough, by their own later telling, to have loosed and struck. The boy said afterward that his hands had simply gone slow on him, the way hands go slow in a dream where a person means to run and cannot make the legs answer; Ruadhan, older and less given to saying more than he meant, said only that he had looked at it and known, without working out how he knew it, that it was not a thing his arrow had any business touching. The stag held its ground a breath or two longer, long enough that all three of them stood frozen in the same unspoken accord, and then turned, unhurried as it had come, and went back into the trees, and none of them heard so much as a snapped twig to mark its going.

They told it that evening at the nearest hearth, plainly and without much dressing, the way any hunting tale was told in that country, and it went from that hearth to the next the way every tale went, gathering a little colour at each telling but losing nothing of its bones: a white stag at the wood's edge, and three hunters who could not, between them, say why none of the three had drawn. Some of the older women, hearing it, said it was no beast at all, something the wood had put out to be seen, and let the matter rest there; others said only that a beast so marked belonged to no drive that had ever been run in that country and ought, on that ground alone, to be let go by whoever met it. No one that first year put a name to it, god or spirit or anything between. Sadhbh, asked more than once as the years went on whose creature she took it to have been, always gave the same answer: that she had looked it in the eye and known only that it was not hers to kill, and had never wanted to know more than that.

In the years between the first seeing and the second, the tale did its own quiet work on the country's custom without any elder ever setting it down as a rule. Hunters who ran the gully after that first year went to the post at its narrowest turn already carrying the tale with them, so that a drive that broke for the treeline, whatever beast led it, was let go with less argument than it might once have needed, on the plain chance that among the ordinary deer some one unlucky shot might catch the wrong beast in a bad light and bring down on the whole country a grief no one could afterward undo. It cost the households something real, in meat foregone at the wood's edge over years enough to count, and none of them, asked whether the cost was worth the caution, answered the question as though it were a hard one.

It came back. Twenty-two years on, when Sadhbh was past forty and had given the gully post to younger hands, word came down from a fresh pair of hunters, neither of whom had been born the first time it was seen, that a white stag had stood at the same treeline and let itself be looked at a long while before it turned back into the trees, drawing no arrow and taking no harm from any that were there. It was, by every account the hills kept afterward, the same beast, or one enough like it that no one troubled to argue the difference, and from that second seeing on it left off being one hunter's tale carried at one hearth and became a thing the whole country held between them, spoken of at the gully-drives before any beast was run, so that a hunter posted where Sadhbh had once been posted went to that ground already knowing what she might meet and what she was, by the country's own unspoken law, to do about it, which was nothing at all.

## III. Of the Second Wood

Many days' walk to the west, past the southern hills and out into the middle country, there stood a second wood that few of the eastern households had ever seen, though the hearths about it knew it as well as the east knew its own, though every one of them could point the way to it without hesitating.

It was older in its bearing than Coille Naomh Muileann chiar of the stag, or seemed so to every eye that fell on it, though no one living could have said by what mark they judged the age of a tree they had never gone close enough to touch. The ground about it rose in low, broken folds, and out of those folds the trees stood taller and closer-set than any wood a household had ever felled and let regrow, with a floor beneath them that no foot, so far as any telling reached, had ever walked from one side to the other. Three paths ran toward it, worn by generations of feet that had gone that way for water, for grazing, for the plain human want of walking to the edge of a thing and looking at it, and all three paths, without a single household ever having met to agree on it, stopped short of the trees at the same low line of set stones.

The stones themselves were nothing grand to look at, no taller at their highest than a man's knee, running in a broken course that dipped and rose with the ground rather than holding to any straight rule a mason might have set, so that a stranger coming on them without knowing their name might have taken them for no more than the kind of stone a field turns up on its own and a farmer piles at its margin out of the way of the plough. But no field lay behind them. Beyond the line the ground was not worn at all, not by foot nor by hoof nor by anything a person could point to and say a beast had passed this way, and every one of the three paths, worn smooth and hard-packed right up to the stones, went no further than the stones themselves, as though the feet that had made them, generation on generation, had walked to that exact mark and turned back without a word ever needing to pass between them as to why.

The hearths called that country the sìth's, though none of them, pressed on it, could say when the naming had begun or who had first said it aloud. It was the same shape of telling as the first wood's, near enough: no fear anyone could point a finger at and give a cause to, only a thing worn so evenly into the custom of the country that asking after its beginning got a shrug more often than an answer. The sìth, the hearths said, were the people of the hills and the mounds, who had held that ground before ever a household of the mason's own kind set a fence-post in that country, and who kept, by every account, to the far side of any line their own custom or their own leaving had drawn, so long as no one was foolish enough to draw it back the other way.

Children were told it early and told it plainly, the way children in that country were told which mushrooms killed and which fed, with no more ceremony than the telling wanted: go as far as the stones and no further, and if a ball or a stray lamb or a wandering hound crossed the line ahead of you, let it go, for whatever was lost that way stayed lost, and no household in living memory had gone in after anything and come out again the better for it. It was not, most families found, a hard rule to keep. A line of low stones asked little of a child beyond the asking, and the wood beyond it offered nothing a child's eye found it hard to leave alone: no berries grew close along that edge that did not grow just as freely on the near side, no game ran thick enough there to tempt a hunter's arm past caution, and the trees themselves, seen from the stones, gave back only the same dim, unbroken green that every other stand of old timber in that country gave back, holding out no promise a person might be fool enough to chase.

## IV. Of Muireall

Muireall was nine years old in the year the hills lost her, the youngest of four and the only girl among them, a quick, sharp-eyed child who had been told the rule of the stones as plainly and as often as every other child of that country and had, so far as anyone could afterward swear to, kept it as well as any of them until the one afternoon that undid the keeping.

It was late in the summer, the households out at the hay in the low fields a good way off from the second wood, and the children of three families left, as children of that country were often left on a fine working day, to their own charge on the near ground with an older cousin's half an eye on them. Muireall had gone with the others to the line of stones to watch for the deer that sometimes crossed the open ground beyond it in the evening light, a game the children of that country played often enough and thought little of, for the deer kept well clear of the trees themselves and a child standing at the stones to watch them was no closer to any harm than a child standing at its own threshold.

What drew her past the line, none of the other children who stood with her that afternoon could afterward say with any certainty, though every one of them was asked the question more times than any of them, by their own account, cared to be asked again. The eldest among them, a boy of twelve who carried the guilt of that afternoon a long way into his own grown life, said only that he had turned to call the younger ones back from the drop of a gully nearer the stones, and turned again a breath or two later to find Muireall gone from where she had stood, with no cry, no rustle in the bracken, nothing at all to mark which way she had gone save a small, easy gap in the undergrowth at the near edge of the trees, no wider than a child makes passing through without troubling to hold the branches back.

They called for her first among themselves, the way children call for a playmate they think has only wandered off to tease them, and it was some while, by the boy's own shamed account, before the calling turned to fright and the fright sent the eldest running for the hay-field at a pace that left him unable, when he reached it, to get out more than her name and the word gone before her mother was already past him and running the other way.

The search that followed held nothing back that the country had to give it. Every household within a half-day's walk came, men and women both, with torches cut and lit before the light was fully gone, for none of them, whatever they told each other of the sìth's own custom, could bring themselves that first evening to leave a nine-year-old child to a dark wood without at least the trying. They went up the three paths together, all of them, calling her name in a chorus that carried, by every account, a long way over the still evening air, and they reached the line of stones with the last of the daylight still holding in the west and stood there, the whole company of them, in a silence that none who were present that night ever fully found words to fill afterward.

No one crossed the line. It was not spoken of aloud, that first evening, as a thing decided; no elder stood forward to forbid it, and no household voice was raised in argument for going further. It happened the way the custom had always happened, without a word needing to pass between them: torch after torch came up to the stones and stopped there, the light of each one falling a little way into the trees beyond and showing nothing but more trees, and no foot, of all the dozens gathered on that ground that night, went past the line the child had crossed a few hours before. Muireall's mother stood at the stones longer than any of them, past the point where her own kin had begun, gently, to draw her back by the arm, and it was said afterward, by more than one who stood near her, that she asked the wood, once, in a voice pitched low enough that only those closest to her caught the words, to give the child back, and that no sound came from the trees in answer beyond the ordinary small movement of leaves that any wood gives back to any question put to it.

They searched again the next day, and the day after that, working the ground on the near side of the stones as thoroughly as any ground in that country had ever been worked, turning every fold and hollow within a stone's throw of the line on both flanks of the wood, in case the child had strayed along the edge of it rather than in, and found nothing: no print in ground soft enough to hold one, no scrap of the plain wool she had worn, no sound of her voice carried back on any wind that blew those two days from any quarter. On the third day the search narrowed to the stones, and stopped there. No household had tired of looking. There was, by then, nowhere left to look that did not mean crossing a line that no one in living memory, not even for a lost child of nine, had ever yet crossed and come back whole to speak of.

The hearths said afterward that the sìth had taken her, in the same plain, worn way the hearths said everything of that country's own custom, offering it neither as comfort nor as blame, only as the one telling that fit what the ground had shown them: a line long kept, a child who crossed it, and nothing on the near side of the stones, search it as thoroughly as they had, to say she had ever come back across. Muireall's father dug no grave, for there was no body to lay in one, and the household kept instead, in the years that followed, a small stone of their own setting near their own threshold, not at the wood, bare of any mark, so that whoever asked after it, whenever they asked it, would be told, in as many or as few words as the asking seemed to want, of a child who had gone as far as a line of set stones on a fine summer evening and had not, for all the searching the whole country gave her, ever been found on the near side of it again.

The rule of the stones, which had asked little of any child before that year and had been kept, in the main, without any household troubling to test how hard a rule it truly was, was kept a good deal more plainly after. No elder needed, in the years that followed, to remind a child twice of where the near ground ended, and no household ever again let its children stand watching for deer at that particular stretch of the line without a grown hand somewhere near enough to close on a small arm before it could slip free. The torches that had halted at the stones on the night Muireall was lost halted there still, in every telling the hills gave of that summer afterward, a whole country's worth of light standing at the edge of a wood it had searched to the very limit it would allow itself, and going no further.

Sadhbh lived to hear the telling of it many times over before her own death, an old woman by then and long past any drive of her own, sitting at hearths that were not her own household's and were asked, more often than she cared to count, to set the white stag she had once met at the gully's turn beside the child the second wood had taken, as though the two tellings answered each other. She never granted the two woods a common cause, not once in all the years she was asked it. The stag's wood had given nothing but a look and a going, she said, and had taken from the country only the meat it might otherwise have lost at a hunter's hand; the wood of the stones had taken a child outright and given nothing back at all, not so much as a mark in the ground to say which way she had gone. They were two uncut woods holding to two different silences, she told whoever asked her plainly enough that few asked her twice, and a country that meant to go on living beside either of them would do well to leave the working-out of why to those with more patience for it than a hunter had ever needed.

By the year the households about that wood counted, later, as the year the search finally stopped being spoken of at every gathering and became instead a thing simply known, the way the covered hearths of the southern hills had become a thing simply built, the line of stones had stood a full generation as the one mark on that country's ground that no household crossed and no household argued the crossing of. Children born in the years after Muireall's going grew up knowing the rule before they knew the reason for it, in the same worn, unquestioned way their grandparents had grown up knowing to carry their fuel the long way round Coille Naomh Muileann chiar far to the east, two customs kept by two countries far apart for two griefs that had never, in all the years since, given either of them cause to test what lay beyond either line.

# Chapter Twenty-six: Of Cormac of the Misstrike

*VE 3,640 – 3,719*

## I. Of Cormac and the Four Dark Coals

It was going on eight hundred years since Brian had dug his hole beside Leac na Fèithe and found the black coal warm in the morning, and in all that time the line had answered nothing further. Four coals still lay dark in the leather bag: the red-brown, the silver, the one that would wake, if it woke at all, to no more than the snap of a hand, and the rainbow that held every colour and answered to none of them yet. Three had spoken, out of the sea and the height and the ground, each in its own slow year, and the households of the high valleys had grown so used to waiting on the fourth that they had stopped remarking on it, the way a family stops remarking on a debt so old it has become a kind of furniture.

Cormac was born into that waiting at Tobar dhìreach, the eleventh child and the fourth son of a household that had held the bag and Poit an Teine and the recital, father to father, since Neachdan's own well. He was not the eldest, and by the custom of the valley that ought to have kept him at the plough and the herding and let an older brother stand for the line at the hearth on Oidhche an Dealanaich; but his two elder brothers died within a season of each other in his fifteenth year, one of a fever that took half the valley's children that winter and one of a fall on the scree above the black well, and so it came to Cormac, whether he wanted it or not, to learn the recital word for word from his father and to be the one who, when his father died, took the leather bag down from its shelf and untied the thong and counted the four dark coals into his own palm, one by one, the way every keeper before him had counted them.

He was a big man, wide through the shoulders, with a temper that came on him early and that his mother had spent his childhood trying, without much success, to teach him to keep behind his teeth. He never raised his hand to man or beast, and no one in the valley ever called him unkind. But he was quick to anger at a thing that would not go the way he meant it to go, a gate that would not latch, a rope that slipped, a lamb that would not be caught, and he had been known, more than once, to put his fist through a hurdle he had spent the morning building rather than mend the one weak lashing that had let it sag. His wife, Aoibheann, of a household two valleys west, used to say that Cormac could split more stone in an afternoon of temper than another man could split in a week of patience, and that the trick of living with him was never to be standing near the stone.

He grew up on the recital the way every child of the line did, said standing at the hearth on Oidhche an Dealanaich, the fathers named back to Neachdan and Conall, the tale of the boy who walked to the grove and came back with a riddle and no answer, the sea that had taken the gold, the height that had taken the white-flecked coal, the grave beside Leac na Fèithe that had taken the black one slowly, in the dark, overnight. He had heard it so many times before he was grown that he could have said it in his sleep, and did, once, to Aoibheann's laughing report, waking the whole house with the line about Fearghas and the height. It was a story he loved the way a man loves a thing he has never once had to work at loving. What he did not love, what caught at him worse each year he held the bag, was the four dark coals themselves, lying cool and ordinary in his palm at every year's telling, giving nothing back.

He tried, as every keeper before him had tried, the things that were known to have failed: rain, wind, the sea a second time in case the sea had merely been careless the first, the coals together in one fire in case the spirits, once woken, might wake each other. Nothing answered. He tried things no one had thought to try before him, because he was not a patient man and patience was what the line had mostly brought to it until then: he buried the red-brown one a second time, deeper than Brian had buried the black, thinking perhaps the earth wanted more of it; he carried the silver one to three different rivers in one summer, thinking perhaps the Abhainn ghorm alone had been asked and had said no for reasons of its own. He came back from each of these journeys with the coal as dark as he had carried it out, and each time the temper in him grew a little worse before it settled, and Aoibheann learned to have the supper ready and to say nothing until he had eaten.

It was in his thirtieth year, some three years into his keeping, that he came to the idea of the grove. He had heard, the way every child of the line heard it, that Diarmad had gone north to a place where the wind talked and come back with the whole Telling and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich both; that Coimhdeach na Fine had stood there once, in the smoke of an oak-twig fire, and had not been seen since by any teller the line kept. It seemed to Cormac, turning it over through a wet spring while the lambs were born, that a place with that much of Coimhdeach na Fine's business behind it might hold some leaving of whatever the smoke-figure had been, in the ground there, that would answer a coal the way the earth at Tobar dhìreach had answered Brian's. He said so to Aoibheann one evening, expecting her to laugh at him, as she laughed at most of his notions before he had finished having them.

She did not laugh. She looked at him a long while across the fire, the way she looked at a beast she was deciding whether to trust with a lamb, and said only that if he meant to go he had better go once the hay was in, and that she would keep Poit an Teine fed and the bag's thong tied while he was gone, and that he was to come back whether the coal answered him or not, for she had buried two brothers-in-law already and had no wish to add a husband to the count on the strength of a story.

## II. Of the Month Under the Oaks

He set out on a grey morning at the turn of autumn, with the four dark coals wrapped each in its own scrap of hide inside the leather bag, and a second bag of oatcake and dried mutton over his other shoulder, and no company but his own, for he had asked no one to come and no one had offered, the valley holding by then that a man's business with the coal was his own to carry. It was three days' walk to the grove, north and a little west, over ground that grew wilder the further he went from the last hearths he knew: up out of the high valleys onto open moor, down again through birch scrub into a country of standing water and rushes where he lost the best part of a morning finding a way round a bog that had not been there, or that he had not heard tell of, the last time anyone from Tobar dhìreach had gone that way. He slept the first night under an overhang of rock with a small fire of heather roots, the second in the lee of a fallen birch with no fire at all, for the wood was too wet to catch and his temper was too short by then to spend an hour coaxing it. He came to the oaks on the evening of the third day, footsore and hungry and in a worse humour than he had left home in, and stood at the edge of them a while before he went in, the way every teller said Diarmad had stood, though he did not think of that until afterward.

The grove was as the tellers described it and larger than he had pictured it: old oaks, wide-spaced, their crowns meeting high overhead so that the light under them came green and broken, and a stillness in the air that owed nothing to the wind, which he could hear moving in the crowns without ever feeling it move at ground level. He found the fallen trunk the tellers spoke of, or one he took for it, grey and half sunk into the leaf-mould, and made his camp in its lee, and built a small fire there of oak-twigs as Diarmad was said to have built his, more out of habit than hope, for he did not truly expect Coimhdeach na Fine to come for the asking.

It did not come. He sat by the little fire the first evening with the four coals laid out on a flat stone in front of him, watching them, as if watching hard enough were a kind of work, and nothing answered him but the small sounds of the wood settling into night, an owl somewhere off to the west, the creak of a branch finding its own weight. He told himself, that first night, that a place needed time to notice a man in it, the way a dog needed time to notice a stranger was not going to hurt it, and that he would give it a week.

A week became a fortnight, and a fortnight a month. He kept the little fire burning most nights, fed on fallen wood, for the grove gave him that much without complaint, and he ate through his mutton and then through what he could find, the last of the hazelnuts, rowan berries, once a wood pigeon he brought down with a stone after two days of trying. He walked the whole grove end to end more times than he could afterward have counted, laying each of the four coals in turn at the foot of every oak he thought looked older or stranger than the rest, leaving them a night, coming back for them in the morning as dark as he had left them. Thinking the ground here, so near whatever Coimhdeach na Fine had been, might succeed where the ground at Tobar dhìreach had not, he tried burying them again as he had at home; it did not answer him any better. He tried speaking to the grove outright, once, standing in its centre in the grey hour before dawn, asking it plainly what it wanted of him, and felt so foolish afterward, alone under the oaks with his own voice still hanging in the air, that he did not try it again.

The temper that Aoibheann knew so well, and that three years of failed rivers and a second grave had already worn thin, did not improve on a diet of hazelnuts and disappointment. By the third week he had stopped laying the coals out gently at the feet of trees and begun setting them down hard, as a man sets down a thing he is angry at, and by the fourth he had begun to talk to himself in the grove the way another man might talk to a stubborn beast, short words, no patience in them. He knew, some clearer part of him knew, that the coals could not hear him and would not answer him faster for being cursed at, and he went on doing it anyway, because there was no one else in the grove to curse at and a man alone for a month with a failure grows less careful of himself than he would be watched.

It was near the end of the fourth week, with the hay long in at home for all he knew and Aoibheann's patience, he suspected, wearing thinner than his own, that he came to the end of whatever restraint the month had left him.

## III. Of the Misstrike

He had carried, among the little he brought from home, the same maul and stone wedge his father had used for splitting stone, more from habit of a travelling man than from any plan to use them, for there was no well to sink in the grove and no wall to raise. On that last morning, waking stiff and cold and hungry to a fire gone to ash overnight, he took the red-brown coal from its scrap of hide and looked at it a long while, turning it over in his fingers in the grey light, a plain dull stone the colour of old blood dried on wood, giving no more sign of a spirit in it than the pebbles under his boots.

It came to him, in the flat, stubborn way an idea comes to a tired and angry man, that he had never once tried to break the coal open. Every trial the line had made, his own and his father's and his father's father's back to Aodh, had been a trial of where the coal was put, the sea, the height, the ground, the hearth. No one, so far as the recital told it, had ever asked what might be found inside one, whether the spirit, if it was there at all, lay hidden under the surface the way the colour had lain hidden in the vein before the mason's wedge went in and struck it open. It was not a clever thought, and some later part of him, telling it afterward at the recital, allowed as much; it was the thought of a man who had run out of patience and still had a hammer in his hand.

He set the red-brown coal on a flat stone at the foot of the fallen trunk, the same stone he had watched it on every night of the month, took up the maul in his right hand, and struck.

The coal was harder than any stone he had split in his life, harder than the granite of the well his own grandfather's grandfather had sunk, and the maul came down on its curved, unyielding face and turned in his grip, glancing sideways off the surface instead of biting into it, the way an axe turns on a knot no one saw in the wood. He had swung with the whole of a month's temper behind it, not thinking to guard against a miss because he had not truly believed, in the part of him that still believed anything, that the coal could turn a blow struck that hard. The head of the maul came round and down across the back of his left hand, which had been steadying the coal on the stone, and laid it open from the base of the thumb to the first knuckle, deep, to the white of the bone.

He did not cry out. He said afterward that the pain came a breath behind the blow, the way it always does with a true wound, and that in the space of that breath, before the pain had caught him up, he watched his own blood run off his fingers and fall, three drops, four, onto the red-brown coal still sitting where he had set it.

Where the blood touched, the coal caught.

It came up slow at first, a thread of colour spreading out from where the first drop had fallen, the way a stain spreads in cloth, and then all at once, a flame standing up out of the stone, the exact colour of the coal, red-brown, deep, low, not bright the way the gold had burned on the sea or fierce the way the white-flecked coal had burned in the fall through open air, but warm, close, the colour of firelight seen through the grain of oak, or of blood held up to a lamp. No sound came with it, and no spark. It stood there on the flat stone, burning quietly in the green morning light of the grove, while Cormac knelt with his ruined hand still open and dripping in his lap and stared at it.

He said, afterward, that he had no thought in his head for a long while but the plain fact of it burning, and that the pain of his hand, which by every reckoning should have driven every other thought out of him, did not reach him at all in that first stretch of time; he knelt there in the leaf-mould with the blood running unheeded down his wrist and into his sleeve, watching the small red-brown flame stand up out of a coal that had lain dark in a bag on his shoulder, and in his father's before him, and in every father's before that, back thirty generations to Brian, and he did not move, and did not bind the hand, and did not think to.

The other three coals lay forgotten on the ground beside him. He did not touch them again that morning.

## IV. Of the Bound Hand

How long he knelt there he could not afterward say with any certainty, though he guessed, from the light, that it was the better part of the morning. The flame burned steadily the whole while, fed by nothing he could see, taking neither larger nor smaller as the hours went, and it was only when it began at last to sink, guttering low the way any fire sinks when it has burned through what feeds it, that Cormac came back to himself enough to notice his own hand, stiff and swollen and crusted black with dried blood to the elbow, and to understand, with something between shame and wonder, that he had knelt beside a fire lit from his own body for the better part of a day and never once thought to stop the bleeding.

He bound it then, tearing a strip from his shirt and winding it tight over the wound, wincing for the first time since the blow had fallen, as though the pain had been waiting politely for his attention and came on all at once the moment he gave it. By the time he had the binding knotted the flame on the stone had gone out entirely, leaving the coal lying dark again where it had lain, save that its surface, when he picked it up at last with his good hand, felt warm still, faintly, the way a hearthstone stays warm long after the fire on it has died.

He gathered the other three coals, and the red-brown one now gone quiet, back into the bag, and broke his camp that same afternoon, though the grove had given him nothing but the one answer and he might, by the letter of what he had set out to prove, have stayed and tried the rest of the summer against the oaks as he had tried the first month. He did not. Telling it after, he said that something in him understood, kneeling there with his hand torn open and the small flame standing over his own blood, that the grove had answered nothing; that whatever had spoken had spoken out of him, out of the wound and not the wood, and that there was no more sense in staying under the oaks to ask the same question of his other hand than there would have been in staying under the roof of any house merely because a good thing had once happened inside it.

The walk home took him four days instead of three, for the hand slowed him and would not let him use it, and twice he had to stop and rebind it when the old binding worked loose and the wound, still raw, began again to weep. He came down into the high valleys on a cold evening with the bag over his shoulder and his left arm held stiff against his chest, and Aoibheann, who had been watching the northern track for the better part of a week without telling anyone she was watching it, saw him coming from a long way off by his walk before she could see his face, and went out to meet him at a run.

He was thirty that year. Standing in the yard before he would go in to the fire, he told her the whole of it: the month, the hazelnuts, the last morning, the blow, the blood, the flame that had burned quietly over his own hand for the better part of a day while he knelt and watched it and forgot, in his wonder, to save the hand at all; and she looked at the binding, already soaked through again, and said nothing about the coal at all, only that he was a great fool and that she would look at that hand properly before he said one more word to anyone.

The scar it left him ran the width of his hand, thick and pale, the bone beneath it never quite straight again, so that from that day he could never again close that fist all the way and had, more than once, to ask another man to draw a stubborn peg for him. He wore it, once the shame of the misstrike had worn off him, the way another man wears a mark he is secretly proud of, and let it be seen, and the valley, which had laughed at Diarmad's question near three thousand years before and long since stopped laughing at anything the line brought home from the grove, did not laugh at Cormac either. What they called him, from that year to the end of his life, was Cormac of the Misstrike, and he answered to it without complaint, saying once, when a nephew asked whether the name shamed him, that a man ought to be glad of any name he is given for having done a thing no one else in the world had ever done, whatever the manner of the doing.

At the recital that was said the next night of the lightning, he stood at the hearth at Tobar dhìreach with the bag counted out before him as every keeper counted it, three cold, one gone quiet after its burning, and held up the scarred hand for the whole gathered valley to see before he spoke the new line into the telling: that the sea had taken the gold, the sky had taken the white-flecked coal, the earth had taken the black slowly in the dark, and now a fourth had answered, quick, out of a man's own blood, the colour of firelight seen through oak. The kindred took to calling it *gual donn-ruadh*, and, more often, simply the coal of life, for it seemed to them, turning the word over at hearth after hearth that winter, the rightest name a coal could have that had wanted nothing of sea or sky or ground, and had wanted only a living man, and the hurt of him.

Cormac kept his keeping some forty years more, the temper in him gentling, Aoibheann said, a little each year, though never so far gentled that she stopped keeping the supper back until he had eaten it in peace. He tried the silver in three more rivers before he gave it over to a younger cousin to try in his stead, and lived to see that trial fail as his own had failed, and to laugh about it, which the valley took as proof enough that the misstrike had done him some good beyond the scarring of one hand. He died in his two-and-seventieth year, at his own hearth, with Poit an Teine burning near him as it had burned near every keeper of the line before him, and Aoibheann, who outlived him by six years, told it afterward that his last clear word, before the fever took his sense from him, was a complaint that his hand ached in the damp, the old scar aching the way old scars do, long after the wound is a story told and not a wound felt.

They buried him near Leac na Fèithe, as Brian had been buried, and the leather bag with its three remaining coals, silver and the one that had never yet been tried by fire and the rainbow that answered to none, passed to a younger kinsman of the line, whose name the recital keeps but does not give to strangers, as it does not give any name between one finder and the next. For some years after, at the hearths above Tobar dhìreach, children of the valley were shown the trick of it, an old scar on an old man's hand held up in the firelight and the story told again, of the coal that would not break and the blood that lit it anyway, until it had passed, the way every wonder passes in a valley that has already had three thousand years of them, into a thing everyone knew and no one any longer marvelled at, save on the one night of the year when the recital brought it round again, and the reciter's hand, whoever then held the office, was raised at the telling of it, empty of any scar, in memory of the one that had once been shown there.

# Chapter Twenty-seven: Of the Dogs, the Geese and the Farthest Reach

*VE 3,720 – 3,921*

## I. Of the Glen of the Stags

Dubhghall was twenty-five the autumn he first stood at the gully's throat, and he had been driving it in someone else's shadow since he was old enough to hold a stake upright. Gleann nan Damh lay east of the households, a fold of ground the red deer had used, by every telling the old people gave, since before any teller now living had a grandmother. Dubhghall's own father had walked it, and his father's father, laying the same lines of stakes and cut brush in the same low places each autumn to turn the herd's running into one running, funnelled down through birch and bramble to the narrow throat of the gully where men waited with spears braced against their own weight and the weight of what was coming.

It was plain work, and no one who did it thought otherwise. It wanted patience in the setting and nerve in the standing, and both of those Dubhghall had in the ordinary measure his people had, no more. He set his stakes where his father had set stakes, cut brush from the same low thickets so that the thickets kept their shape year on year and the deer, coming down off the high ground in the first cold, ran the path their mothers had run without knowing there was any other path to run. A drive was a slow thing to build and a fast thing to spend: half a day of quiet labour with mallet and knife, and then, some grey morning when the wind sat right, a noise raised from three sides at once, and the whole autumn's work gone by in the length of time it took a frightened animal to cross a gully.

He stood that first year at the narrow end with his uncle at his shoulder, close enough that Dubhghall could smell the wet wool of the older man's shoulder over the deer-smell coming down the wind ahead of the herd itself. Frost had whitened the bramble in the night and gone soft and dark by the time they took their places, so that the ground underfoot was greasy where the sun had not reached it and hard as bone where it had. The noise began somewhere up the glen, thin at first, then thickening as it was taken up along the line: sticks beaten on sticks, a dog's short bark cut off, a man's voice pitched high and wordless. Dubhghall's hands were cold on the spear-shaft and his knees, he would say afterward, had no more strength in them than a boy's, and then the first of the herd was on him, a hind with two calves close behind her flank, and past before he had thought to move at all.

The stags came after, and it was for the stags the whole day's labour had been spent. His uncle took the first, a big beast with a head like a low branch of oak, catching it low and letting it run itself onto the spear rather than driving the spear at it, which was, his uncle told him after, sitting on a wet stone with the blood still steaming off his hands in the cold air, the whole of the craft and the only part of it that could not be taught by watching. "You can be shown the stand," the old man said, working the feeling back into his fingers, "and you can be shown the throw. What you can't be shown is the moment you let the beast do the work for you instead of doing it yourself. That comes or it doesn't." Dubhghall's own throw went wide and struck a young stag in the shoulder rather than the throat, and the beast went down thrashing not twenty paces past him, bawling in a way that put the hair up on his arms worse than the cold had, and it took his uncle and two others to finish what his bad aim had begun. He was ashamed of it for a season, turning the throw over in his mind on nights when sleep was slow to come, and practising alone through the winter against a bundle of brush hung from a birch, until by the spring his arm knew the throw the way it knew the shape of his own name. No one else thought the wide throw worth remembering past the day it happened. That was the mercy of a household that lived close to its own failures: it forgot them quickly, having too many of its own to keep count of another's.

The antlers of the greatest stags were carried apart from the rest of the cutting and set up together at the mouth of the gully, a stand of them leaning one against another so that from a little way off they looked, in half-light, almost like a thing standing on its own account, a beast made of the parts of other beasts. No one had ever said why this was done, and Dubhghall did not ask his uncle, who would not have known either. It was the shape a good drive took at its end, the meat carried home and the horn left standing where it had fallen, a mark of what the glen had given that year set apart from what had been taken away and eaten. In a hard autumn the stand was thin. In a good one it grew tall enough that a boy could stand in its shadow at noon and cast no shadow of his own that reached past it.

Dubhghall drove that gully for thirty years, first at his uncle's shoulder and then, when his uncle's knees would no longer hold a standing man through a whole autumn morning, at the head of the line himself, setting the stakes where the stakes had always been set and teaching younger men the throw that let a beast run onto the spear rather than the other way about. He was not a hard teacher, by the accounts that outlived him, though he was exacting in the one thing that mattered: he would let a young man's aim go wide a dozen times before he said a word of blame, but he would not let a young man stand carelessly, feet planted wrong or weight back on his heels, because a badly planted man was a man the glen might yet take instead of giving to. He buried his uncle at the last of those thirty autumns, an old man by then, worn thin by winters, in ground close enough to the gully's mouth that the old man's grandchildren could point to the low rise from the stand of horn and say, without needing to walk the distance, that he lay just there. Dubhghall stood afterward at the mouth of the glen with the season's antlers stacked fresh beside the grey weathered horn of years before, and thought, as much as he thought anything so plainly, that the glen would go on taking its deer and giving its meat when every man now living at its mouth had gone the same way as the horn: standing a while, whitening a while, and then down among the rest, indistinguishable from what had come before it.

## II. Of the Dog at Cnoc fhionn

It was Dubhghall's own grandson, a boy called after no one living, who first buried a dog the way a person is buried, and it was done at Cnoc fhionn, the hill households east of the glen where Dubhghall's daughter had married into a family with fields of their own. The dog had been the boy's from a pup, one of a litter got off a bitch that ran the drives at the glen, and it had grown into the kind of dog that is loved past all reckoning of its use, little good for herding or hunting either one: it herded nothing well, killed nothing bigger than a rat, barked at strangers and at its own shadow with equal conviction, and slept across the boy's feet every night of its life from the week it was weaned, so that the boy learned early to sleep with his knees drawn up rather than disturb it.

It died old, as dogs that are loved past their usefulness are sometimes let to do, lying down one evening by the hearth after a day no different from any other and not rising the next morning. The boy, who was near a man himself by then, found it stiff and cold in the grey light before the household was properly awake, and sat with his hand on its flank a long while before he told anyone, as though the telling would make the thing truer than it already was. When he did tell it, his mother said only that it had been a good dog and a long-lived one, and went back to the morning's work, for a dog's death, however loved the dog, was not a thing a household could stop its day for. The boy dug it a grave the length of a dog and not the length of anything smaller, on the low rise above the house where the ground was dry and did not flood in a wet spring, working through the morning with a mattock too big for the job and getting blisters for his trouble that he did not complain of. He laid the dog in on its side, the way a sleeping dog lies, its legs drawn up as they had been drawn up every night of its life across his own feet, and before he closed the earth over it he set a shell at its head, a sea-shell some trader or fire-bearer had carried up from the coast years before and given to the boy as a boy's trinket, kept on a shelf by the hearth and turned over in idle hands on winter evenings but never used for anything until that morning.

No one told him to do it. That was the thing the household spoke of after, when the story of it had gone round the near hearths and come back changed a little in the telling, as such things do: that the boy had not asked anyone, not his mother, not old Dubhghall, whether a dog might be given a shell and a grave the way a person was given a shell and a grave, but had simply done it, on his own reckoning that the dog he loved deserved no less a leaving than the grandmother he had loved before it, who lay not far off on the same rise. Some of the older women thought it strange, even a little wrong, to put a beast's death alongside a person's in the same ground and by the same rite, and said so plainly enough at the next gathering of the near hearths, one of them going so far as to ask the boy, not unkindly, whether he meant to put a shell at the head of every lamb the household lost too. The boy had no ready answer for her, being young and not much given to argument, and only said that the dog had slept at his feet for nine years and a lamb had not, which the old woman allowed, after a pause, was answer enough. Others, and among them Dubhghall himself, thought it strange only that no one had done it sooner, dogs having slept at hearths and died at hearths since long before any teller now living had a telling of Teine a' Chlachair itself. "A thing that shares your fire that long," the old man said to his daughter, turning the matter over as he was given to turning things over in his last years, "and never once asks for more than it's given, earns more than being left for the crows."

Whatever was thought of it, it was done, and it was done again. Within a few years two more households near Cnoc fhionn had buried dogs the same way, a shell at the head and the grave dug proper, one of them a hunting dog that had put up game for its household for a dozen seasons and the other a pup that had lived scarcely a year before a fever took it, and the custom travelled on quietly, hearth to hearth, the way any custom does that answers something people already feel and only wanted shown how to say. No beast had been given a grave on the island before that boy dug the first one; afterward it was not thought remarkable at all, only ordinary, the way the covered hearth had gone in one lifetime from a strange new digging to a thing no household in those hills would think of doing without.

Dubhghall did not live to see the custom old. He died at Cnoc fhionn in his sixty-fifth year, among his daughter's family and near the hill where the dog and, before long, his own grandson's grandmother lay, an old man by the reckoning of that country though not, by the reckoning of the line at Tobar dhìreach, any great age at all; his people did not live long lives, and did not look for them, and thought a man who had kept his knees and his eyesight into his sixties had been given a fair measure and no cause for complaint. It was said of him at his own leaving, by the same grandson who had dug the dog's grave, that he had never in thirty autumns of driving the glen lost a man to a stag's horn or a fall on wet ground, a modest enough praise as such things go, and in that country no small thing to be able to say, and the grandson set a shell at his grandfather's head too, the last of a small store he had kept since the dog's burying, saying that a man who had taught him the throw that let a beast do the work deserved no less a shell than a dog that had only ever slept across his feet.

## III. Of the Geese of Eilean ghorm

West of the last of the households, off the coast no hearth-kindred had ever settled, there lay an island the tellers called Eilean ghorm, and to it, every year with the first hard storm of autumn, came the grey geese. No one now living could say when the geese had first been noticed rather than merely seen, the way no one could say when the wood in the east had first been held sacred rather than merely walked around; but by Dubhghall's day, and long before it, it was a thing every hearth from the glen to the northern moor could tell a stranger without needing to be asked twice: that the geese came to Eilean ghorm with the first storm and left it with the last, and that in all Cunntas nan Athraichean no one had ever gone out to that island to take them.

It was not, by any telling that survived, forbidden in the way the second wood was forbidden, with its line of set stones and its children taught early to stop at it. No household kept a law against the taking of the geese, because no household had ever needed one; it had simply never been done, the way a well is not fouled and a hearth-fire is not fed with green wood, a thing so plainly against the grain of how things were kept that the not-doing of it wanted no telling to hold it up. A boat could be built to reach the island easily enough, and boats far harder to build had crossed to islands far further out for seals and for less. But the geese came in on the storm-wind with a noise that carried for miles on a still evening, ragged lines resolving into order as they came down out of a sky already darkening toward the season's first real weather, and went out again months later the same way, their going almost always a day or two ahead of whatever storm would be the year's last, so that a household that watched them close enough could read the turn of the whole winter in it. Between the coming and the going the island was theirs and no one's else, and that was held to be simply how the geese and the island stood to one another, needing no more reason than the tide needs a reason to come in.

A young man of the northern moor, some years before Dubhghall's own time, was said to have gone out to Eilean ghorm all the same, in a season of want when the store of dried meat had run low before spring and a household counted every goose it saw fly over as meat it did not have. He built himself a small hide boat over a hard winter, telling no one what it was for, and put out from the shore alone one grey morning with the geese still on the island in their thousands. What happened to him the tellers did not agree on even then, and agreed on less as the years carried the story further from anyone who might have set it straight: some said he found the crossing harder than he had judged and never reached the island at all, his boat found stove in on the rocks below the point a week after; others said he reached it and came back with nothing to show for the going, the geese having risen off the water before his boat was within a bowshot and not settled again while he stayed; a few, and these were the tellers most given to saying more than they knew, held that he had reached the island, and that something on it had turned him back before ever he raised a hand toward a goose, though what, they could not say, having no more of the tale than the bare bones any teller starts from. Whichever of it was true, and none now living could sort the true from the added, the young man was not spoken of afterward as one who had found a rich hunting-ground and kept it to himself. He was spoken of as a warning, the kind of warning a country keeps by instinct, from one hard example, with no need to understand the danger it points at.

Dubhghall himself, in his last years, used to stand on the rise above Cnoc fhionn of a still autumn evening and watch, when the wind was right, for the first grey lines of geese going over high toward the west, and count it, in the way a man counts a thing he cannot number, as the true turning of the year quite as much as any telling of the cats' crossing or the salmon's run. When his grandson asked him once, as a boy asks, why no one hunted them there when the meat on so many birds together would have fed a household through half a winter, Dubhghall thought a while before he answered, watching the last light go off the water, and gave the boy no better answer than any other man of his country would have given, but gave it plainly: that some things were left because a people had always left them, and a people that stopped leaving what it had always left was not, any longer, quite the people it had been. The boy did not press him further, being at an age when a grandfather's plain answers were still answer enough, and the two of them stood together until the light was gone and the geese, if they had come that evening, had come and settled and could no longer be told from the darkening water.

## IV. Of Skell at Its Height

Far to the west, on a coast none of Dubhghall's kin had walked and none of their tellings named, the people of the landings had by those same years come to hold every shore of the island there was to hold. From the northern moor's edge to the southern lowland, from the eastern cliffs round to the far side of the western capes, there was no stretch of coast left where they had not, at one time or another in the long count of their own years, set a landing, laid a mole, driven a mooring-stake into the mud, or dug a kiln to dry the catch over peat-smoke; and the islands off those coasts were theirs as well, the near ones worked for seal and bird and the far ones rowed to for the dead.

Of all their landings the greatest stood where the Abhainn naomh ran down toward the western sea, at Skell. The mole that the old stone-judge had begun there in the time of the first boats of that river had by then stood some nine hundred years, mended and added to season on season until it ran further out into the current than any one lifetime could have carried it, and behind it, in the still water it made, lay more hulls at once than any person of that landing could have numbered without losing the count and beginning again.

A woman of Skell, who had the keeping of the mole's stones in those years as her mother had kept them before her, walked its length one autumn evening at the turn of the tide, as she walked it every evening, looking for any stone the day's current had worked loose. The river was full of boats. They lay three and four deep along the mole's sheltered face, skin boats and plank hulls together, some come in that day from the coast north and south with dried fish and seal-oil and cut shell, some waiting on the morning's tide to go out again; and on the shingle above them the smoke of more hearths than she could set a number to went up into a still sky, so thick and so many that the air over the river's mouth hung grey the whole evening long, like a low cloud that never moved and never rained. Children ran the mole's top the way children run along any wall built for other purposes, and were shouted off it, and ran along it again the moment the shouting turned away.

She found no loose stone that evening. She stood a while at the mole's far end instead, where the river's push met the stone and turned aside, and looked back along the whole of it: the moored hulls, the landing, the smoke, the people moving among the boats too many to be watched one by one; and then she turned and walked home along it in the last of the light, for the mole was sound and the tide was making and there was nothing more that evening that the stone asked of her.

The hills kept their own count of things, the drive at the glen and the shell at the dog's grave and the grey geese coming in on the storm, and the landings kept a count of their own that no hearth of the hills ever heard. At Skell that autumn every mooring was taken, and the smoke stood over the river from dawn to dark, and the mole held the current off the boats as it had held it for longer than any keeper of it could reckon.

# Chapter Twenty-eight: Of the Warm Springs and the Walled Gate

*VE 3,922 – 4,123*

## I. Of the Springs Under the Mountain

On the southern flank of the central mountains, where the ground drops in broken steps toward the lowland and the rock runs red when the evening light is on it, there is a place where the water comes up warm. It rises out of three low mouths in the hillside, one above another, at a heat a hand can bear for no longer than a slow count of ten, and runs down in a steaming thread over rock stained orange and green by its passing, and in the cold months the steam of it stands over the hillside like the smoke of a hearth that is never let go out. Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh, are called so still.

The people of the landings came to it in the years when their reach inland was widest, when their walls stood on the spur above the southern lowland and their three rings on the height near the south-eastern coast, and the kerbed way ran between the two; and what they built there was the plainest of all their works away from the sea. Below the lowest of the three mouths they cut the rock back to make a shelf, and on the shelf they set stone basins, slab fitted to slab and the joints packed with clay, three of them in a row, so that the water fell from the hill into the first and ran over its lip into the second and from the second into the third, cooling a little in each. In the first a hand could not be held. In the third a body could lie to the chin.

The woman who kept the basins in the years the telling first follows them had come up from the coast as a girl with a brother whose foot had been crushed under a hull at the launching, and had stayed, because the foot had mended and she had watched it mend. She was not young now. Her hands had gone red and soft at the fingertips from a lifetime in warm water, and she could tell by the colour of a wound, and by its smell when the dressing came off, whether it wanted the second basin or the third or neither, and she did not explain the telling of it to anyone, for she had no words for it that were not the thing itself.

They brought the sick to her from every coast.
