A man came in on a litter of poles and hide with his leg broken below the knee, the bone through the skin in two places, carried four days by six of his kin in turns, and the kin set him down at the lip of the shelf and stood back, the way people stand back from a thing they have carried a long way and no longer know what to do with. The keeper of the basins looked at the leg a long time. Then she had him lifted into the third basin on a frame of woven withies that held him off the stone floor, and she set the bone herself with her own two hands under the warm water, pulling and turning until the ends met as they had met before the fall, and bound it with wet bark and cord, tighter than any healer of the coast would have dared bind a broken leg for fear of choking the foot; and she turned him twice a day for a whole season, morning and evening, and changed the binding, and fed him broth from a horn spoon, and did not once let the wound-mouths go dry or foul.

He walked out on a stick before the winter turned. He walked without it inside two years, and lived to be old, and when he died he was brought back and buried on the slope below the basins at his own asking, with the other dead of the springs, where the ground was warm under the turf all winter long. The bone of that leg, if any hand had ever turned it up again, would have shown the old break as a thickened ring round the shaft and nothing more, knitted clean and straight. So would the bones of a good many of those who lay on that slope in the years that followed: arms and legs and ribs and, once, the bones of a child's skull, all broken, all mended, lying quiet in warm ground with the steam of the springs going up above them.

It was the first place on the island where the sick were brought to be made well. Before it every people had nursed its own hurts at its own hearths, with what skill each hearth had and no more. After it, among the people of the landings, a broken body had somewhere to be carried.

The keeper of the basins grew old at the work. In her last years she sat on the shelf beside the first basin, where the heat was fiercest and her old bones liked it best, and watched a younger woman do the turning and the setting and the binding, and said nothing unless something was being done wrong, which was seldom. When she died they buried her on the slope with the others, nearest the water, and the young woman went on with the turning the next morning, because there was a man in the third basin with a crushed hand who could not be left.

## II. Of the Young Keeper and the Child's Skull

The young woman who took up the turning after the old keeper died had come to the springs as a girl of twelve with a father whose ribs a falling spar had stove in, and had stayed on after he walked away mended, because the old keeper had seen her watching and set her to the carrying of the clean bark before she could decide whether she wanted to be set to anything. She had carried bark for nine years, and cord, and broth, and had turned the sick in the third basin when the old keeper's back would not let her, and she had never once set a bone with her own hands while the old woman lived. On the morning after the burying she set three.

It was not the setting that frightened her. She had watched it done so often that her hands knew the pull and the turn before she had ever made them, and the first bone, a boy's forearm snapped clean across in a fall from a boat's gunwale, went back into its place under the warm water with a small grinding she felt in her own teeth, and lay true when she bound it. What frightened her was the choosing. The old keeper had known, by a look and a smell, which hurt wanted the second basin and which the third, which wound would take the heat and knit and which would take the heat and rot; and the young woman, standing over the fourth that morning, a man whose leg had gone black below a crushing, did not know, and knew that she did not.

She put him in the second basin, where the water was hotter, and watched him through two days and two nights without sleeping more than an hour at a time on the shelf beside him, and on the third morning the black had not spread, and on the fifth it had drawn back a finger's width from where it had been, and by the time the moon came round again the man could bear his weight on the leg with a stick. She never knew whether she had chosen right or only been lucky, and she said so, when she was old, to the girl who by then carried bark for her; and she said that the not knowing had made her careful for the rest of her life in a way that knowing might not have, and that she did not wish it on the girl, and did not wish her spared it either.

The child came to her in her fifth year at the basins. It had fallen from the top of a kiln wall onto the stones below and struck its head, and it was carried in senseless by its mother, who had walked two days with it in her arms and would not give it to anyone else to carry. The bone above its ear gave under the young keeper's fingers like the shell of an egg that has been dropped and not quite broken. She had never seen such a hurt mended. The old keeper had spoken once of a man who lived for a season with a broken skull and died when the season turned, and of another who lived and never spoke again, and of none who had lived and been whole.

She did not put the child in the water. She laid it on the shelf beside the first basin, where the steam rose thickest and the stone was warm to the touch all night, and she cut the hair away from the broken place and washed it with water carried from the lowest mouth of the spring, which was the cleanest, and bound a pad of moss over it and did not bind it tight. Then she and the mother sat by it. They sat by it for three days, turning it as the sick in the basins were turned, twice a day, gently, and dripping broth between its lips from a twist of cloth; and on the fourth morning it opened its eyes and looked at its mother and asked, in a small cracked voice, for something to eat.

It grew up. The bone above its ear knitted with a ridge in it that could be felt under the hair all its life, and it was slow in the tongue for a year or two and then was not, and it lived to be a grandmother at a landing on the south coast, and when she died her own people carried her back to the springs to be buried on the slope, because she had asked it, and because it was known at that landing that she had been given back once and it seemed right that the place which gave her back should have her at the last.

The young keeper, who was not young by then, buried her herself, nearest the water, and said nothing over the grave that anyone remembered, and went back to the shelf where a man with a broken collarbone was waiting to be turned.

The keepers of the basins did not all come from the same landing, nor from the same kin, as the keepers of a hearth come; each was a girl or a boy who had come up with someone hurt and had stayed, because the keeper of that year had seen them watching. It was the one office among the people of the landings that passed by watching and not by blood, and it passed that way for as long as the basins were kept. In the dry summers the water ran lower from the three mouths and the basins cooled, and the keepers learned to lay flat stones heated in a fire into the third basin to bring it back to the warmth the sick needed; in the wet winters the water ran so hot and so full that it steamed over the shelf like a fog and the keepers worked in it half blind, feeling for the frames of withies under the water with their feet. In every season the sick came, fewer in the years when the heights were full and the landings far, and more again as the landings filled and the roads to the springs were walked by more feet; and in every season the slope below the basins took its share of those who did not mend, and those who mended and came back at the last, until the turf there lay over more dead than any other ground the people of the landings had given to the dead, save only the island off the south-eastern coast where the stone boxes stood in their rows.

## III. Of the Youth Sent Down

In the south-east, some days' walk from the springs, the eastern shaft at Toll-dubh had stood open since before any grandmother of that coast could remember its making: a hole sunk straight down through the living rock, its walls tooled smooth as far as any lamp had ever shown them, with no spoil heap beside it and no telling of where the stone had gone. Children dropped pebbles into it and listened, and heard nothing, and ran off laughing to hide how the nothing had frightened them. The grown people of that shore walked wide of its lip and did not drop anything into it at all.

The year the youth went down, it was the people of the south-east who plaited the rope. They made it of hide, cut in long strips from the skins of three oxen and plaited four-strand the way a mooring line is plaited, and it took two women the better part of a month, and when it was done it lay coiled on the turf by the shaft's mouth higher than a sitting child. Who first said that someone should go down, and why it should be that year and not some other, the telling does not say. It says only that the youth asked to be the one, and that no one argued with him long.

He was not yet grown to his full height. He sat on the lip of the shaft on a grey morning with the rope knotted under his arms and across his chest, and a lamp of fat in a hollowed stone in his lap, and the wind came up out of the hole, cool and smelling of wet stone, and lifted the hair off his forehead. The men who were to pay out the rope stood behind him with their heels dug into the turf. The women who had plaited it stood a little apart. No one spoke to him. He looked down into the dark a long while, and then he looked round once at the faces behind him, and then he slid off the lip and hung, turning slowly, and they began to let him down.

The lamp went down with him. That is the part of the telling that has been kept most carefully, and it is kept in the same words every time: the lamp went small. It burned as steadily as any lamp burns, and it did not go out, and it only grew smaller and smaller as the rope paid out hand over hand through the men's fists, a yellow point on the smooth wall, and then a smaller point, and then the dark closed over it and there was only the rope going down, creaking through the hands, and the wind coming up out of the hole past the watchers' faces.

The rope ran out to its last knot. They held it there. It hung straight and heavy from the lip and gave no sign, no jerk, no slackening, and the men holding it stood with their arms trembling from the weight and did not let go, and the women stood behind them, and no one said anything at all for so long that a woman at the back began, very quietly, to weep, and was not hushed.

Then the rope jerked twice, and they hauled.

They brought him up slowly, as he had been let down, hand over hand, because a thing that has hung a long while on a rope in the dark is not to be jerked back into the light as if it were a bucket, and because no one wanted to be the one who hurried whatever was on the end of it. It took longer to bring him up than it had taken to let him down. When his head came over the lip, the lamp in its stone was still in his hand, and it was out, and his face was the colour of ash.

He did not speak. They lifted him onto the turf and untied the rope from him and he sat where they set him, and his mother put her hands on his face, and he let her, and looked past her at nothing. They asked him what he had seen. He shook his head. They asked him again, gently, that evening, and the next day, and in the days after, and he shook his head each time, and in the end they stopped asking.

He never said what was at the bottom, not then and not in all the years he lived. He took a wife from a landing two days south, and had children, and worked a boat, and was known on that coast for nothing strange except that he would not let a lamp burn low in any room where he was; he would rise in the night to trim it or put it out altogether, and never said why a failing light troubled him. After him no one went down again. The rope was cut up for mooring lines, and the shaft stood open as it had always stood, and the grown people of that shore walked wider of its lip than before.

## IV. Of the Last Stone Set

On the spur above the southern lowland, where Làrach an Dùin-fhaire had stood with its one gate facing inland for longer than any watcher on its wall could count back, a season came when the gate was closed.

It was closed from within. The telling of it follows one man inside, and follows him only so far, and it is given here as far as it goes.

He carried rubble to the gate through the last of a short day. There had been others with him at the start, carrying and fitting, and one by one as the light went they had gone to some other part of the work within the walls, and he was left alone at the gate with a heap of broken stone and a lamp. He set each stone into the gap that was left with the same care a mason gives a wall that is meant to stand, turning it in his hands to find its best face, trying it, taking it out and turning it again, and packing the smaller stuff in behind it with the heel of his hand. The gap narrowed. Outside it, through the last of the opening, he could see the kerbed way running down off the spur toward the lowland in the dusk, pale and empty, and beyond it the dark line of the hills. He did not stop to look at it.

The lamp burned low beside him on the packed stone. It had been filled that morning and he had not filled it again, and he did not hurry because of it; he worked by its thinning light as he had worked by the full light of noon, and when the gap had shrunk to the width of his two hands he fitted the last stones by feel as much as by sight. The flame had sunk to a blue bead in the fat. He took up the last stone, a flat piece the size of a loaf, and turned it, and tried it in the gap, and it would not go; and he turned it the other way and tried it again, and it went, and he pressed it home with the flat of his hand and held it there a moment as if it might fall out again when he let it go.

It did not fall. The lamp beside him went on burning, very low.

There the telling stops. It does not say where he went after, or whether there was anywhere to go.

## V. Of the Empty Places

Làrach an Dùin-fhaire stood empty after that. No smoke rose from within the wall on the mornings when smoke had always risen, and no watcher stood on the steps inside the gate, and the kerbed way that ran down off the spur went unwalked, so that within a few years the grass had crept in over the slabs from the edges and the kerbs showed through it like the bones of a thing half buried. The gate stayed as it had been left, choked from within with rubble packed so tight that a hand could not have worked a single stone of it loose. By then there was no one to try.

Whoever had closed it had gone out of it some other way, or had not gone out. The wall ran unbroken round the whole of the spur, and no ladder had been left leaning against it, and no rope hung over it; and inside, among the footings of the houses where the roofs had fallen in, the grass grew as tall and as undisturbed as grass grows anywhere no foot troubles it.

On the height near the south-eastern coast the three rings still stood, and people still lived within them, and drove their cattle in at the gate of the outer ring at dusk and out again in the morning, and drew their water from the great cistern cut in the rock at the crown of the hill. It had served four hundred people and their beasts through summers when no rain fell, as the one who read the ground had meant it should when she stood over its digging. It served them still.

The woman who went to draw from it one morning, in a year a long while after Làrach an Dùin-fhaire fell silent, went early, before the rest of the household was up, because the water was sweetest at first light and her father was ill and wanted it. She carried two skins and a rope. She came to the lip of the cistern in the grey half-light and let the first skin down, and it did not go down. It struck something a little below the lip, something that gave under it and did not splash, and she drew it up again and looked, and in the grey light she saw what it had struck.

The cistern was full of cattle. They had been thrown in whole, unbutchered, beasts with their hides on and their horns on, heaped in the water on top of one another so that their backs and their bent legs broke the surface, and the water between them had already gone dark. There were more of them than the household she belonged to had ever owned, and more than the household beside it. She did not count them. She stood at the lip with the empty skin hanging from her hand and the smell coming up at her, and then she let the skin drop on the stone and went back to her father's house, walking, not running, and woke her brother, and told him what she had seen, and he went and saw it too.

No one of the three rings could say who had done it. No one had heard the beasts driven to the crown of the hill in the night, or heard them bellow, or heard the fall of so much weight into so much water; the watch on the outer ring had seen nothing come in at the gate. The cattle were beasts of the rings, and some of those who looked into the cistern that morning knew their own among them by the set of a horn or a mark on a flank, and said nothing of it, and went away.

They did not draw from the cistern again. No one would, not that year and not in any year after, though a people living on a dry height has no easy water but what it cuts into the rock for itself, and the carrying of water up from the springs of the valley below was a whole morning's labour for every household every day. They carried it. The cistern they left as it was, full of bone under water gone black, and they laid no cover over it, and walked round it as they walked round a grave.

What had gone wrong in the high places, in the years when Làrach an Dùin-fhaire's gate was closed and the cistern of the three rings was fouled, the people of the landings never said, not to one another in any telling that has been kept and not to anyone else. On the coasts their kilns still smoked and their boats still went out, and Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh under the mountain still ran, and the sick were still carried up to the basins on litters of poles and hide and turned twice a day in the third basin by a woman whose hands had gone soft at the fingertips. But on the heights the people who had turned their faces from the sea found that the ground they had turned toward had begun, one silence at a time, to give them nothing back but the rain.

# Chapter Twenty-nine: Of the Empty Rings and the Stripped Altar

*VE 4,124 – 4,195*

## I. Of the Last Fire in the Rings

The three rings of wall on the height near the south-eastern coast had held fire along their circuit for longer than any hand still living within them could say it had first seen one lit. In the last winter that fire burned there it burned no differently than it had ever burned: a chain of small fires set along the inner face of the middle wall, each tended by whoever was nearest when it wanted feeding, so that a watcher standing at the gate could look along the curve of the rampart on a clear night and see a string of low lights going away from him in both directions until the wall's own bend hid the rest.

That winter there were fewer hands than fires. Since the cistern was found full of bone, every household had carried its water up from the valley springs on its own back, a whole morning's labour every morning, and some had grown tired of the carrying before they grew tired of the height, and gone down. Those who were left let the farthest fires go dark first and fed what peat they had toward the fires nearest the gate, so that the string of lights grew shorter at both ends and thicker in the middle, like a rope fraying from its outer strands inward toward the one core that still held.

A woman who had tended the second fire from the gate for as many winters as she could count on both hands was the last of them awake on the last night. She had buried, in the two years before, more of her own kin than she had watched grow old: a husband who went from a cough to a grave inside one wet spring, a sister's whole household taken by the same spring or by the thin harvest after it, no one troubling any longer to say which. The rest of her blood had gone down the track from the gate one by one, some saying they went only for the winter and meaning it, and none of them had come back.

She had gone as far as the gate herself, more than once, on mornings when the track looked less like a way down than like the only sensible answer to a question the height had stopped troubling to ask. Each time she had turned back to her fire. A wall built to hold four hundred ought not to be left holding none, she had told herself, and her staying was a kind of tending too, no different from the peat she fed the flame each evening, only harder to see burn.

She fed it that night from the last of the store beside her, peat cut two summers before by hands that were no longer there to cut more, and sat with her back to the wall and watched it take. The wind came up off the valleys below as it always came after dark, carrying turf-smoke from some hearth low down that was still lit, and wet stone, and the cold clean breath of ground that never quite dried between one shower and the next. She sat in it a long while doing nothing more than any woman does at her own hearth on an ordinary night, and fed the fire again when it wanted it, and sat on.

In the morning she went the length of the middle wall to see what other fires wanted tending, as she had gone every morning of those two years, and found every one of them dark. Some had been banked to nothing by careful hands. Some were simply out, the peat beside them untouched, as though whoever had tended them last had walked away in the middle of the tending. She walked the whole circuit before she let herself believe it, out past the far bend where the ground fell away and the wind came harder, and found the same cold stone and the same untouched peat everywhere, and stood there a while looking out over the valley rather than back at the wall.

She did not light the far fires. She went back to her own, which still held a little heat under yesterday's peat, and sat by it that day and the day after; and on the third day, finding no one left to share the tending and no reason she could give herself to go on keeping a fire in a ring of wall that no one else needed, she spread the last of the embers thin across the stone, the way a fire is spread when a household means it to die and not to smoulder on unwatched, and walked out through the gate and down the track her kin had gone down before her, carrying nothing but what she had carried in.

The fires along the middle wall were not lit again. The gate she walked out through was never afterward closed by any hand, and stood open through every season that followed, and within a few winters grass had found a footing in its threshold, where the feet of four hundred had once kept the stone worn bare.

## II. Of the Ones Who Went Down

They went down in ones and in small kin-groups, over years and not in any one season, and none of the landings that took them in ever spoke of a single day when the high places emptied, only of finding, season on season, more faces at the shore fires than the shore had raised, and fewer questions asked of where a face had come from than might have been asked in an easier time.

A boy of one of the western landings, too young to remember the height his grandfather had come down from, grew up knowing only that the old man did not speak of the hills the way the landing's other old men spoke of the sea, with a store of small sure facts about a place they had spent their whole lives in. Asked what the height had been like, his grandfather would say only that it was cold there in a way the shore never was, a wind that found a man through wool doubled over wool, and that a fire there wanted feeding oftener than a fire anywhere he had lived since. He would not say why he had left, or when, or whether he had meant at the leaving to go back; and once, when the boy pressed harder than he usually dared, the old man said that a place could go on being a man's own long after it had stopped wanting him in it, and that this was not a thing a boy who had never lived on a height would understand, nor one he wished his grandson ever to have cause to.

It was the same at landing after landing along every coast: old men and old women who had come down from one height or another in their youth, settled among kin who had never gone up at all, and keeping whatever they kept of the high years to themselves. Some brought down small things the height had let them carry, a worked stone, a tool no one on the shore had a use for and no one asked the use of, kept on a shelf afterward or laid in the stone box with its owner when the time came. Some brought down nothing but what they stood in, having judged that a height given up was a height to be left whole and not picked over on the way out. The middens at the southern landings grew faster in those years than in any years before them, and a landing that had once counted its households by the dozen came, within two lifetimes of the last fire in the rings, to count them by the score.

None of the shore's own people ever gave a reason for the coming down, beyond the plain fact of it. What was said, by more than one old mouth at more than one fire, was only this: that a thing begun wants explaining and a thing given up does not; that a people troubles itself over why it went somewhere, and lets the coming back stand.

## III. Of a Household Come Down to the Kilns

One household that came down from the rings in those years came down to Morn, where the seven kilns and the eighth and the ninth still stood above the shingle as they had stood for longer than anyone at that landing could say, and it is told of that household more than of most, because it came down with nothing and had to learn the shore again from the beginning.

There were five of them: a man and his wife, both past the middle of their lives, and their son, and the son's wife, and a girl of eight who had been born inside the innermost ring and had never in her life seen the sea. They came down the old track from the height with what they could carry on their backs and one ox, and the ox died of a fall on the scree below the outer ring on the first morning, so that they came the rest of the way with only their backs. It took them nine days. The girl asked, on every one of the nine, how much further the sea was, and on the ninth her grandfather lifted her onto a rock at the top of the last rise above Morn and turned her to face it, and she looked at it a long while and said nothing at all, and then asked whether it ever stopped moving.

The landing took them in. There was no telling afterward of any argument over it; a household come down with nothing was a thing every landing on that coast had seen by then, some years more than one, and the ground above the shingle had room in it for another roof. What the landing did not do was feed them for nothing, for no landing on that coast had ever fed a strong back for nothing, and within the month the man and his son were out in the boats with the landing's own crews, sick over the side for the first week and then not, and the two women were set to the kilns under the eye of the woman who kept the middle kiln that year.

It was here that the household's learning went hardest. On the height a fire was a thing a person fed to keep warm and to cook by, and fed well, and was glad of when it blazed; and the keeper of the middle kiln, watching the son's wife build up a kiln-fire on her first morning until it roared under the racks, took her by the wrist without a word and led her to the next kiln, where the peat lay smouldering so low that the smoke came up thick and white and no flame showed at all, and held her hand flat over the rack there a long while, until the young woman understood by the heat on her palm what she had been told three times in words and had not understood. The fish on the racks above her own roaring fire had begun to cook where they should have been smoking, and were fit that evening for eating and for nothing else; and that was the whole of the lesson, and it was not given twice.

The older woman learned it faster, having less pride to lose in the learning, and it was she, in the end, who kept the eighth kiln for the rest of her life, and was known on that shingle as a keeper as good as any born there, save that she would never feed the fire from the landward side of the kiln but always from the seaward, and would not say why, and the landing let her have her way in it because the fish she smoked kept as well as any fish on that coast. Her husband never grew easy in a boat. He took to mending nets instead, and sat through the long evenings on the shingle below the kilns with the cord running through his fingers, looking up now and again at the dark line of the hills inland where the height stood that he had come down from, and he did not speak of it, and no one of the landing asked him to.

The girl who had never seen the sea grew up on that shingle as though she had been born to it. She learned to gut and to rack and to feel the heat of a kiln with the flat of her hand before she was twelve, and to handle a small boat before she was fifteen, and when she was grown she married a man of the landing whose people had kept the fourth kiln since before anyone could remember, and bore him children who were never told, by anyone, that their mother had been born inside three rings of wall on a hill above the southern lowland, because by then no one at Morn thought it a thing worth the telling. She told them herself once, when she was old, on an evening when the wind came off the land and not off the sea and carried a smell of heather down onto the shingle; and they listened politely, as children listen to an old woman's tale, and asked her whether the sea could be seen from there, and she said that it could not, and that she had not known, until she came down, that it was a thing a person could be without.

## IV. Of the Prising of the Altar

The temple on its stepped platform in the eastern hills was tended some years after the rings had gone dark and Làrach an Dùin-fhaire's gate had been closed, by fewer people each year, and by the end by no more than one kin of the valley below it, who went up on the shortest morning as their grandparents had gone up, and stood about the great stone while the light came over the sea behind them and ran along its top toward the mountains, and went down again.

Three of them climbed the steps with prising-bars on their backs on a grey morning at the fall of the year, with a thin rain in it, and the bars were long lengths of seasoned oak, shod at their ends with bone, the kind a household uses to lever a boulder out of a field. One of the three was the eldest of that kin, a man past sixty who had climbed the steps on the shortest morning every year of his life that he could remember, and he went up slower than the other two and did not ask them to wait for him.

They worked at the altar's top stone for the better part of the morning. The block had been set into the step below it in two sockets cut deep into the rock, and bedded there with clay and small stone so long ago that the clay had gone as hard as the rock around it, and the two younger men had to break it out a finger's width at a time with the points of the bars before they could get any purchase at all. The old man did not work the bars. He stood at the stone's far edge with both hands flat on its top, where the light used to run on the shortest morning, as if he were holding it steady against a shifting it had not yet begun to make.

It came free a while past noon. It canted first to one side, groaning in its sockets, and then with a shift of the bars it lifted clear of them and was lowered, not dropped, onto the step, and lay there whole. The three of them stood over it without speaking, as men stand over a thing whose weight has only just left their hands and whose next weight, the carrying of it on, they have not yet taken up.

They carried it down. They slung it between them on the bars in a net of hide rope and took it down the steps one step at a time, resting at every third, and out across the hillside below toward the west, where the ground fell away into the valley; and a little before dark they went over the shoulder of the hill with it, all three together, walking slowly under the weight, and the platform behind them stood with its top step empty.

The telling goes no further with them, and the stone was never found. On the top step the two sockets were left standing open, sharp-edged where the bars had broken out the old clay, and they did not soften with the years as a path softens or a doorsill, for a socket cut to hold a great weight keeps its edges as long as the rock around it keeps its shape. What had been cut on the top of the stone, if anything had been cut there, went with it.

## V. Of the Cairn on the Steps

After the stone was gone no one of that kin climbed the steps on the shortest morning again. The grass came in between the fitted slabs where it had never been let grow, and the last step, the easy one that every child of the valley had learned to find with a bare foot in the dark, was lost under turf within a few years, so that the climb began now with a stumble where it had once begun with no more than the least catch underfoot.

Some years after the prising, the old man who had stood with his hands on the stone while the others worked the bars went up alone. He was very old by then and went up slowly, a step and a rest and a step, with a stick; and at the top, below the empty sockets, where a person climbing would set his last foot before the platform, he built a small cairn. He built it out of the loose stones the prising had broken from the edges of the sockets, and out of others he gathered from the scree below, fitting each one to the one beneath it and tapering the whole of it toward a flat cap-stone set square on top, as square as the altar had been set. It took him most of a day. Then he went down again, and did not go up after.

He did not say what the cairn was for, to his kin or to anyone, and no one asked him, for it was plain enough to those who watched him come down with his hands scraped raw that he did not mean to be asked. It stood below the empty sockets after he was dead, kept by no one and added to by no one, weathering as unmortared stone weathers, a little of its shape lost to every hard frost, until in the end it stood no higher than a man's shin, and to an eye that did not know to look for it might have passed for a fall of loose stone off the step above.

## VI. Of the Rain in the Sockets

So the temple stood stripped, though it was not yet wholly forsaken; now and then someone of the valley still climbed its steps, and stood a while by the empty sockets, and came down again. The platform stood as the old man had left it: grass thickening between its stones, the small cairn below the top step, and the two sockets holding, in place of the stone that had been set square to the central mountains, whatever the sky over the eastern hills chose to put in them.

It was rain, oftener than anything. That country's weather was mild and wet and seldom dry for long between one shower and the next, and on any day after rain the two sockets held a little standing water apiece, dark with whatever had blown into them, and if the light fell right and the water lay still, the sky lay open in each of them, cut to the square shape the stone had once filled. From a little way off they looked less like two holes than like two small mirrors set into the hill, giving back whatever passed over them and keeping nothing of what had stood there.

In the south-east the shaft at Toll-dubh stood open as it had always stood. Under the mountain Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh ran on, and the sick were still carried up to the basins, though by fewer hands each year, for the landings they came from were further off now than they had been when the heights were full, and the way up was long. Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and the rings stood empty, and the temple stripped, within a few days' walk of one another, each left to the weather in its own year and its own way; and on every coast the landings filled, and the smoke of more hearths went up over the shingle than the shore had ever carried, and a people who had gone up into the hills came down to the sea again and did not say why.

# Chapter Thirty: Of Eòghann at the River

*VE 4,196 – 4,274*

## I. Of Eòghann's Keeping

Five hundred and fifty years had gone by since Cormac stood at the hearth of Tobar dhìreach with his ruined hand raised for the valley to see, and in all that span the bag had grown no lighter. Three coals lay in it still, cold and ordinary as the day the mason first tipped them out of his tunic: the silver-sheen, the one that would wake, if it woke at all, to no more than the snap of a hand, and the rainbow, which held every colour the eye could give a name to and answered to none of them. Keeper had followed keeper in that time, more of them than the recital troubled any longer to number separately, each carrying the three dark coals down to whichever water or fire or ground seemed to that keeper's own eye most likely, and each handing them on unlit to the next. The valley had long ago stopped remarking on the waiting the way it had stopped remarking, generations before that, on the waiting for the black coal and the red-brown. A thing five centuries unanswered ceases to feel like a question at all, and becomes instead a kind of furniture the household keeps because it has always been there, dusted at intervals and otherwise let stand.

Eòghann was born into that furniture at Tobar dhìreach, the second child of the household that held it, some five hundred and twenty-five years after Cormac's misstrike. He was not raised to think the keeping strange, any more than a child raised beside a hearth thinks the hearth strange; the bag hung on its peg above Poit an Teine from his earliest memory, and he had counted the three coals into his own small palm long before anyone asked it of him in earnest, turning them over the way another child turns over river stones, for the plain unremarkable pleasure of a smooth thing in the hand. His elder sister was the one looked to carry the keeping forward, by every custom the valley held to, and Eòghann grew up free of it in a way few before him had been free, watching the bag rather than answering for it, until his sister died of a fever in her nineteenth year and the keeping came to him instead, whether he had been raised to it or not.

He was twenty that year, and he took the bag down from its peg and untied the thong with his own hands for the first time on the same evening his father was carried out to be buried beside Leac na Fèithe, and he said afterward, when he was old enough to be asked such things and patient enough to answer them, that the two griefs had come so close together in his mind that for a long while he could not think of the coals at all without also thinking of his father's hands, which had counted them out the same way for thirty years before his own.

He was not a man of Cormac's temper. Where Cormac had struck at a thing that would not go his way, Eòghann turned from it and walked, and the valley came in time to know him by his walking the way it had known Cormac by his scar: a keeper who thought best with his feet moving, who would set out at first light with the bag over one shoulder and be gone three days, four, a week, and come back saying little of where he had gone or what he had tried there, only that it had not answered. His mother, who lived to see him grown into that habit and shook her head over it more than once, used to say that her son had been given a question too large for any one valley to hold him while he carried it, and that a body restless in that way was better let walk than penned to a hearth to grow sour on its own waiting, as she had watched other keepers before him grow sour, in households not her own, on years of counting the same dark coals into the same idle palm.

He married, in his twenty-fourth year, a woman of the lake-shore line named Dearbhail, who kept his fire-pot fed and his supper warm through absences that grew, as the years went on, neither shorter nor less frequent, and who used to say of him, laughing to her own kin about it, that she had married a man who would sooner walk to the edge of the island and back than sit still with a question he could not answer. She did not come to Tobar dhìreach ignorant of what she was marrying into; her own grandmother had kept a fire-pot for a lesser household two valleys off, and Dearbhail had grown up knowing, in the plain way a hill child knows which crops fail on which ground, that a keeper's household ran on a different clock than other households did, its comings and goings set less by season and herd than by whatever the bag's silence had lately driven its keeper to attempt. She never once, in all the years the valley afterward remembered of her, asked Eòghann to give the keeping over to some other line, though it was hers by no blood of her own and she might, by the custom of in-marrying wives elsewhere in the hill country, have been forgiven for wishing a quieter husband; she said only, when she was asked, that a man who walked was easier kept than a man who sat and brooded, and that she would rather feed a keeper his supper cold three nights in ten than feed a bitter one his supper hot every night of the year.

He tried, in his first years of keeping, most of what the recital told him earlier keepers had tried, and a good many things it did not trouble to tell, for every keeper before him had added some private trial of his own to the bag's long history and not all of them had thought their failures worth passing on. He carried gual airgid to the Abhainn ghorm below Tobar dhìreach, where his own great-grandfather's generation was said to have first carried it, in case the water nearest the hearth had simply never been given its fair turn against the water of strangers' valleys. Two other rivers he tried besides, north and east, in the same summer, and a mountain tarn that was no river at all but held, by the telling, water enough to be worth the asking. None of it answered him. Over those years he grew into the particular patience of a man who does not expect an answer and goes on asking anyway, less from hope than from the plain fact that the bag was his to carry and a thing carried wants somewhere to be carried to.

It was old custom in the valley, older than Eòghann's grandfather could say with any certainty, to carry the dark coals down to the northern shore from time to time and throw them into the sea, in memory of the gold that had answered there and out of the stubborn belief, held longer in some households than in others, that water was water and the sea might yet be asked again what the small rivers had refused. Eòghann did not put much store in it himself; he had heard his father call it an old man's habit kept past its use, water thrown after water, and had heard his father do it all the same, twice in Eòghann's own boyhood, because a thing done by every keeper before him was not a thing a keeper lightly let drop, whatever he privately thought of it. Eòghann kept the custom too, in his turn, the way a man keeps a saying he no longer quite believes because his father said it and his father's father before him, and in his twenty-ninth year, with nothing else newly occurring to him and the bag's three coals lying as dark against his palm as they had lain the day they came to him, he took them down to the shore once more.

## II. Of the Northern Shore

It was two days' walk north from Tobar dhìreach to the coast, over the shoulder of the massif and down through birch and open moor into country that grew rockier and windier the nearer it came to salt water, and Eòghann went it alone, as he went most of his errands with the bag, telling Dearbhail only that he would be back inside the week and that she was not to trouble Poit an Teine on his account, for it burned as well without him standing over it as with. He slept the first night in the lee of a boulder with a small fire of heather roots, as every keeper before him had slept on that same road, and came down to the shore on the evening of the second day with the wind already rising and a grey swell running in long unbroken lines from somewhere far out past the edge of what any teller on the island had ever claimed to have seen.

He knew the place. It was the same stretch of shingle his father had brought him to as a boy, a low curve of grey stone below a line of dunes, with nothing on it but the wrack the tide had left and a scatter of driftwood too salt-soaked to burn well, and a scatter, further up the beach, of the low stone hearths the seal-hunters of the near bothies built and abandoned season by season, cold now and half filled with blown sand. He had stood on that same shingle as a boy of nine or ten, holding his father's hand while the older man went through the same plain motions Eòghann went through now, and he remembered, standing there again with his own bag open, that he had thought nothing of it then beyond the ordinary wonder a child brings to any errand of his father's, salt spray and grey water and the strangeness of a coast after a childhood spent inland among hills. It did not feel strange to him now. It felt, if anything, like a duty discharged rather than a wonder attempted, the way a man goes through the motions of a rite whose meaning has worn thin with the keeping of it and finds that the going-through has become a kind of comfort in its own right, whatever it does or does not accomplish.

He stood there in the last of the light with the bag open on his palm, gual airgid and the untried one and the rainbow lying together the way they had lain together on every such evening for five hundred years, and threw them, one after the other, out past the breaking water into the grey swell beyond it.

He did not know, standing there, quite what he expected to see. No keeper's telling that had come down to him described the sea giving back anything more than the plain fact of its own indifference, a coal sinking, or washing back in on the next wave to be found again among the wrack, cold and wet and no different for the wetting; and that was what he found now, wading out to his knees in the falling light to gather them back before the tide could carry them beyond finding, three coals as dark in his palm as they had been dark in the bag, the salt water running off them the same as it ran off any stone on that shore. He stood a while longer than he needed to, watching the swell come in, less because he thought a longer watching would change anything than because a man who has walked two days to be disappointed is in no great hurry to turn round and walk two days back to say so.

The wind had backed round to the north-east by the time he set out for home the next morning, carrying rain in from somewhere further out than the eye could follow, and he walked the first day of the return in a steady wet that soaked through his cloak by noon and left him, by the time he found shelter for the night under an overhang he remembered from his boyhood travels with his father, colder and wearier than the walking alone accounted for. He did not think, that first night, in any words he could afterward have set down, about the coals at all; he thought, as a tired man thinks, of the fire he did not have and the dry clothes he did not have and the distance still between him and his own hearth, and slept badly, and woke stiff, and went on.

The second day the rain eased into the kind of fine wetting mist the hill country called no more than a greening day, not worth a cloak's trouble, and Eòghann walked through it with the bag closed again over his shoulder and his mind, so far as he afterward could say, on nothing more than the ground in front of his own feet, one stride and then the next, the way a man's mind goes when a body has been walking longer than it wants to and has stopped troubling itself with anything beyond the next mile. He came down off the moor by the middle of the afternoon into country he knew well, the birch scrub thinning into the upper reaches of the high valleys, the shoulder of the massif rising grey and wet-shouldered ahead of him, and somewhere in the last hour of that day's walking, with the light already going and his own thirst grown sharper than he had troubled to notice until then, he heard, before he saw it, the particular voice of moving water that meant the Abhainn ghorm, running full and brown-clear with the two days' rain, in the cut below the last rise before Tobar dhìreach.

## III. Of the Abhainn Ghorm

He came down the bank at the place where the path always crossed it, a shallow reach where the water ran clear and quick over grey stone and a man could kneel at the edge without wetting more than his boots, and he knelt there now without much thought behind the kneeling, the way a thirsty man kneels at the nearest water without weighing whether it is the water he means to make a study of, and cupped both hands and drank.

It was cold, colder than he had thought it would be so far downhill from the height, and it ran clean and sharp against a throat gone dry with two days of salt wind and rain, and he drank a second time before he sat back on his heels with the water still on his chin, and it was only then, sitting back with his hands still wet and the last of the day's light lying flat and grey along the surface of the river, that some part of him not given to remarking on such things noticed, the way a man notices a change in weather before he has troubled to look at the sky, that the water sat differently in his mouth than the water he had waded through two nights before, and he said it aloud, to no one, the way a tired man will say a thought aloud simply because there is no one nearer than the water to hear it and correct him.

"*Tha blas eile air an uisce seo seach uisce na mara,*" he said. This water tastes different from the sea water.

It was not, when he turned it over afterward at the recital and in all the years after that, a thought he could claim any cleverness for. He had not walked two days home turning the silver's long failure over in his mind and arrived, footsore, at some conclusion worth the saying; he had knelt, and drunk, and been thirsty, and the words had come out of him the plain unplanned way a true thing comes out of a tired man, before he had troubled to think whether it was worth saying or to whom. But he sat back on his heels a while after he had said it, with the bag still over his shoulder and the coals inside it as cold and unregarded as they had been all the way down from the shore, and something in the saying stayed with him longer than the words had taken to say, the way a thing said aloud sometimes settles in a man's mind more firmly for having been given a voice than it would have settled left silent.

He did not reason his way to what he did next, not by any account he ever afterward gave of it. He untied the bag's thong there on the bank, with the light nearly gone and the water running loud over the stones in front of him, and took out the three coals, and without weighing the sea's long failure against this one river's long failure, without any thought that this crossing had been tried before by his own great-grandfather's generation and had answered no better than the rest, he threw them, one after another, into the current in front of him, the way he had thrown them into the sea two evenings before, save that this time he did not wade in after them, being too tired, or too little minded to trouble, to go looking for what the river might do with them before it had done it.

Gual airgid took the current a hand's breadth below the surface and did not sink further, held for a moment turning in the flow the way a leaf turns caught on a stone, and then it caught.

It came up from beneath the water rather than from its own surface, a thread of pale fire spreading out along the coal's underside first, silver-white, the colour of moonlight on moving water, and then whole, a flame standing in the current and burning there, under the surface, fed by nothing the eye could account for and quenched by nothing the river could bring against it, the water running over it and through it without troubling it any more than the wind troubles a hearth-fire built in a sheltered lee. It lit the riverbed beneath it, the grey stones there showing pale and trembling through the moving water, and it lit, faintly, the underside of the current's own surface, so that a man kneeling on the bank, as Eòghann now knelt, saw not only the flame but its light thrown up and scattered across the whole width of the river in front of him, broken and re-made a thousand times over by every ripple that passed above it.

He knelt there a long while, by his own telling of it after, watching a fire burn under water that had never in all the tellings he knew burned under anything but open air, and did not at first think to look for the other two coals at all, the untried one and the rainbow, which the current had rolled on past him into the dark; he found them at first light the next morning, wading the shallows below the crossing, lodged cold and dark against a bar of gravel a stone's throw downstream, and carried them home in the bag as dark as they had gone into the water. The silver burned on where it had caught, through that whole night and, so far as anyone at Tobar dhìreach was ever after able to say, through every night since, a low pale light under the current at the shallow crossing below the height, that any traveller might kneel at the bank and see for himself on a dark evening when the water ran clear.

## IV. Of the Recital

He came into Tobar dhìreach some while after full dark, wet through, empty-handed but for the bag which now held only what the river had left him, and found Dearbhail still awake by Poit an Teine, who took one look at him standing in the doorway, soaked and hollow-eyed and saying nothing, and thought at first that some harm had come to him on the road before she thought to ask about the coals at all. He told her the whole of it standing there in his wet clothes before he would sit to the fire, the two days at the shore and the nothing they had brought him, the walk home in the rain, the kneeling at the crossing, the taste of the water and the words that had come out of him unbidden, and the fire that had stood up under the current and gone on standing there while he knelt on the bank and watched it, and Dearbhail, who had heard him come home disappointed from that same errand more times than either of them troubled any longer to count, said nothing at all for a long moment, and then only that he had better sit down before he told the rest of it, for he was shaking, though whether from the cold of the road or from what he had seen at the crossing he could not himself have said with any certainty.

At the next telling of the Line, on Oidhche an Dealanaich, Eòghann stood at the hearth of Tobar dhìreach with the bag counted out before him as every keeper before him had counted it, one coal gone from three to two, and spoke the new line into the recital before the gathered valley: that the sea had taken gual òir, and the height the white-flecked, and the earth the black slowly in the dark, and a man's own blood the red-brown, and now the river had taken the fifth, not thrown to it in trial as every coal before it had first been thrown, but given to it, he said, by a man who had done no more than kneel at its edge, thirsty, and tell it the truth of what he tasted. The valley took to calling it *gual airgid*, gual airgid, and some among them, turning the telling over at hearth after hearth that winter the way every new wonder was turned over before it settled into a thing everyone knew, said that of the five coals now answered, this was the only one that had asked nothing of the man who woke it beyond the plain truth he would have told anyway, to no one, at the edge of a river he had crossed a hundred times before without once expecting it to answer him.

There were those at the recital that first winter who pressed him afterward, at his own hearth and at others, to say again exactly what he had tasted in the water that made it different, hoping perhaps to learn some sign by which another man might know a river worth kneeling at before he troubled to throw a coal into it, and Eòghann, patient with them as he was patient with most things, told it the same way each time he was asked and owned, each time, that he could not have set the taste into words that meant anything beyond the plain fact of its being different, no more than a man could say in words what told him one face from another he had known all his life. It was not a taste he had gone looking for, he said, and he did not believe, however often he was pressed on it, that a man could go looking for it and find it any sooner than he himself had, kneeling tired and thirsty at a crossing he had waded through a hundred times without once thinking to drink from it slowly. Some among the valley's older hearths took that for a kind of answer on its own, that the coals had never once been woken by a man who set out meaning to wake them, and said so at their own firesides that winter, though none of them said it at Eòghann's hearth, judging it unkind to tell a keeper, however gently, that his own long walking might have counted for less in the matter than his own thirst.

Travellers came to the crossing below Tobar dhìreach in the years that followed, more than had ever troubled to pass that way before, kneeling at the bank in the last light of an evening to see for themselves the pale fire standing under the current, and some of them, the recital afterward kept, knelt and drank from the same water Eòghann had drunk from, though none of them, so far as any teller ever carried word of it back to the hearth, found the water tasting to them any different from water anywhere else on the island. Gual teine and the rainbow lay in the bag as dark as they had lain in it for five hundred years and more, the one that would wake, if it woke at all, to no more than the snap of a hand, and the one that held every colour and answered to none; and Eòghann kept the bag some thirty years further, walking still, though less far and less often as the years wore on him, and in that long stretch of his own keeping tried gual teine against flint more than once, without ever striking from it more than the ordinary spark any stone gives a blade, and let it be, at the last, telling Dearbhail that some things wanted a hand he did not have and would come, if they came at all, to a keeper not yet born.

He died in his six-and-sixtieth year at his own hearth, with Poit an Teine burning near him as it had burned near Cormac and near every keeper of the line before either of them, and Dearbhail, who outlived him by some years at Tobar dhìreach, told it afterward that his last words, before the fever took his sense from him, were of the crossing, not the coals, asking whether the water still ran clear there and whether the light could still be seen under it on a dark evening, as though the one answer his long keeping had ever been given mattered to him, at the end, less as a wonder accomplished than as a place he wished, one last time, to be told was still there. The bag passed from his grave to a younger kinsman of the line, as it had passed from Cormac's, carrying two coals still dark and a keeping not yet finished; and the crossing below Tobar dhìreach kept its pale fire under the current through every season that followed, so that a traveller coming down off the height on a clear night might see it a long way off, a low still light lying under moving water, and take it, before ever he was told otherwise, for no more than the moon caught and held a moment on the stones.

# Chapter Thirty-one: Of the Shore, the Sea-Way and the Godkin

*VE 4,275 – 4,474*

## I. Of the Empty Sockets

The last of the people of the landings who climbed to Làrach an Teampaill in that age was a woman whose name did not come down with her, and what she went up to do there, in the last year anyone is known to have gone up at all, no telling carries either. She climbed the steps of the platform alone in the early light, past the small cairn below the top step that the old man had built, with nothing in her hands, and she came down the same steps at evening with nothing in her hands, walking no differently than she had climbed. Whatever had drawn her up there that day she carried away from the hill entire, and she did not come back to it, and no one after her came in her place.

The platform had stood stripped for the better part of a hundred years by then, ever since three men of the valley below had gone up with prising-bars and come down with the altar's top stone slung between them and carried it over the shoulder of the hill to the west. The temple had not been given up all at once on that day. It had gone on being climbed to, now and again, by ones and twos who still held some errand there, as a household goes on setting a place at table for a while after the one who sat in it has stopped coming, before it stops setting the place at all. The stripping of the stone was the wound. The woman with empty hands was only the last visit the wound was paid.

What had lain on the altar's top before the stone was prised away, if anything had, her people did not say. The two sockets on the top step had nothing more to tell for being looked into: two square hollows cut clean into the rock, deep enough to have held the stone fast against any weather the height could throw at it, and holding now only what the sky put into them, rain in the wet months and a skin of ice in the cold ones and, in a dry summer, a little blown grit that the next rain washed out again.

After her no one climbed. The grass that the occasional foot had kept short between the fitted stones grew up thick, the sockets filled and emptied with the seasons, and the height became, for the landings below it, a place spoken of the way any finished thing is spoken of, without the reaching forward that a live question gets.

## II. Of the Middens at Cwen and the Landing-Stones

Whatever had turned the coast-people back from the high places in those years, Làrach an Dùin abandoned to its choked cistern and Làrach an Dùin-fhaire's one gate blocked from within by hands no telling ever named, the turning held. No new work of theirs went up again anywhere out of sight of salt water, not in the years the temple stood emptying nor in the long stretch after it, and the shore took back, little by little and without any single year marking the change, all the labour that the high ground had for a while drawn away from it. A people that had once spent its strongest hands cutting steps and shafts and standing walls into rock spent them now on nets and hulls and the long patient business of a midden, which is only a household's leavings kept in one place across more years than any single household lives to see the whole of, and which grows, for that reason, at exactly the pace a people's numbers grow, no faster and no slower.

At the southern landing of Cwen the midden that had stood modest and slow-growing for as long as the oldest tellers' grandmothers could account for it began, in the years after the temple's last climbing, to thicken season on season in a way that outpaced every midden near it, Dunn's included, which had for a lifetime and more held the name of the largest heap of shell and bone and burnt weed the coast could show. It grew the plain way any midden grows, one household's supper at a time, limpet and whelk and the split bones of whatever the nets and the low-tide gathering brought in, laid down and covered and laid down again across more years than any one pair of hands could claim credit for; and it grew faster at Cwen than anywhere else along that shore for the plain reason that more of the coast-people had come to live and eat and leave their leavings there than had ever gathered in one landing before, drawn down out of the abandoned heights by ones and families and, in the last years of the drawing-down, by whole kin-groups at once, until a landing once counted by the dozen came, within the span the tellers reckoned by, to be counted by the score, and the midden below it rose to match.

It was at that same landing, or near enough to it that the coast-people who kept the one kept the other without troubling to draw a line between them, that the lane of stones was worked hardest and kept plainest: a string of flat landing-slabs laid along the shallow water of the south-east coast a day's rowing apart, grooved deep in places by the passage of keels hauled up across them season after season, running from the river mouth below Dunn round the long cape and on to the sheltered bay that lay beyond it. No single hand had set the whole of it down; each slab, by the plainest reading anyone gave it, had been laid by whichever household found that stretch of shore convenient to its own comings and goings, and the lane had grown, stone by separate stone, into a single continuous way only because each household's convenience happened, by the shape of the coast, to fall a day's rowing from the next household's. It asked no one's leave to be called a road, and no one's labour to keep it one beyond the ordinary wear of use; a keel dragged often enough across the same stretch of stone wears its own groove into it, the way a path wears into a hillside underfoot, and the lane along that coast wore in the same way, by nothing more than the daily habit of people going where they had always gone.

A rower working that lane in the years the middens at Cwen were thickest could put a name to every landing-stone on it without troubling to count the miles between them, the way a man who has walked one road his whole working life comes to know it by its ruts and its particular trees rather than by any measure of distance a stranger might ask him for. He knew which stones took the tide well and which wanted a careful eye at the ebb, which stretch of open water between two landings ran calm on an ordinary morning and which turned ugly if the wind came round from the north before a boat was clear of it, and he knew, without needing telling, that the lane he worked had a beginning at the river mouth below Dunn and an ending at the sheltered bay beyond the cape, and nothing at either end that any teller of his acquaintance had ever claimed lay further. He rowed it, in the season the tellers afterward remembered best of him, with a boy of his own household in the bow to watch the water ahead and call the stones as they came, and he taught the boy the lane the only way it had ever been taught, by rowing it with him stone by stone until the boy's own eye could find the next landing before his father's voice named it, the same teaching a father gives a son the whole run of that coast, before and after, whatever the boat or the cargo or the year.

The lane was not without its own dangers, and every rower who worked it carried a private list of them the way a shepherd carries a list of the ground where a beast might founder. A stretch below the cape ran shallow over a bed of weed that could foul an oar in calm weather and turn a boat broadside in anything rougher, and every rower of that coast learned to feel for the change in the water's colour before his own eye had properly picked it out, the way a foot learns a familiar floor in the dark. Further north, where the lane left the shelter of the cape and ran a while in open water before it found the next landing-stone, a wind out of the north could come up faster than a laden boat could answer to it, and the tellers of that coast kept, among their older sayings, a plain word of caution for any rower new to the stretch: watch the gulls before you watch the sky, for the birds leave that water a good while before a man standing in it feels the first of what is coming. A boat caught there in a quick blow had no landing nearer than the stone it had last left or the one it was making for, and more than one crew, in the tellers' keeping, had spent a hard night pulling for whichever of the two seemed the less far, with nothing to show afterward for the night's work but a boat brought in whole and a story told quietly at the next gathering of boats.

He was rowing that lane, in the last summer the tellers gave him a season at all, when a boat coming the other way hailed him at a landing neither of them had reason to linger at, and the two crews sat their boats together a while in the calm water off the stone, trading nothing more than the news each carried, which was, that season, mostly news of the shore filling: more households at Cwen than either boat's crew could remember from a single year before, and a landing further north near empty of the families that had worked it a generation back, gone down, by every account either crew had heard, to the same swelling numbers at the southern shore. Neither rower troubled to wonder aloud why the pull toward that one landing had grown so much stronger than toward any other; it was enough, for the telling either of them carried home, that the shore was filling where it was filling, the way a valley's herds drift of their own accord toward the better grass without any single beast leading the rest to it, and the two boats parted at the landing-stone with nothing settled between them but the plain fact traded and carried on, each in its own direction, along the lane that neither of them had ever thought to give a name beyond the shore's own word for it: the old way of the sea, worked as long as either crew's memory reached, and older, by every account handed down to them, than that.

## III. Of the Dead Laid in the Ground

In the high valleys about the crack, in those same years, the households laid their dead in the ground as they had always laid them, and it is worth telling how, since it was by this more than by any other thing that the valleys afterward knew themselves.

When one of a hearth died, the women of that hearth washed the body with water drawn that morning and wrapped it in a cloak of its own, or in a hide if there was no cloak to spare, and laid it on its side with the knees drawn up, as a sleeper lies on a cold night. The men dug. They dug on ground near the hearth, or on a rise the household had always used, never on the green mounds of the valleys, which were the sìth's roofs and not to be broken, and never near Leac na Fèithe at Tobar dhìreach, where no one drew water and no one dug save the line itself. The grave went down to the depth of a man's waist, or deeper if the ground was soft, and the body went into it with its face toward the central mountains, and with whatever the household judged it would want: a knife, a comb, a string of shells, oftener nothing. Then the earth went back over it, and the turf over the earth, and a stone was set on end at its head, a plain stone, uncut, and that was all.

No mark was put on the stone. The valleys cut no signs, and did not wish to. A household knew its own dead by where they lay, and by the shape of the rise, and by the stone at the head, which was a stone and not a word; and when there was no longer anyone living who knew whose grave it was, the grave was left alone all the same, because it was a grave. A child of the valleys learned this as it learned which way the burn ran, before it could have said why: that the ground was full of the dead of the valleys, laid in it since before any father's name could be counted back, and that the living walked over them every day and did not break them.

It was this that Rathnait's people meant, afterward, when they said they had not come. The dead of the valleys lay in the valleys, under the turf, facing the mountains, as far back as anyone could dig; and there was no telling at any hearth of any other place they had ever lain, or any water they had crossed, or any shore they had come from. They were in the ground because they had grown out of it. Aithris a' Chruthachaidh said so, and the ground agreed.

## IV. Of the Name Said Aloud

Rathnait was not of An Clachair's own line, nor of any house that kept a fire-pot or a bag of dark coals against its own hearth, but she was of the valleys about the crack all the same, born the third child of a household two ridges east of Tobar dhìreach, and she grew up hearing Aithris a' Chruthachaidh the way every child of those valleys heard it, a little at a time, from whichever hearth she happened to be sitting at when some elder took it into their head to say a piece of it. She was not, by her own account given later in her life, a woman much given to wondering over the coals themselves, dark as they had lain in their bag for longer than any living teller could put a plain number to; what she wondered over, from a fairly young age and without ever quite settling the wondering, was the plainer question of what a household was, set beside all the other households of the valleys, and what a person owed to the ones near her blood as against the ones merely near her hearth.

It was a question that came to a head, for Rathnait as for a good many of her generation, on the night the valleys kept as the darkest of the year, the night the recital called Oidhche an Dealanaich, when every household that could reach another in a single evening's walk gathered at whichever hearth was that year's turn to hold the gathering and heard the fathers' names said standing, from the first spark to the mason's own line down to the living, and heard after it the older riddle of the sky and the earth and the sea that no one any longer troubled to try against the coals in earnest. Rathnait had sat through that gathering every year of her life she could remember, first on her mother's knee and then on her own two feet among the other children let stay up past their ordinary bedtime for it, and she had never, in all those years, heard the gathered households called by any single word that named the whole of them at once; each hearth was known by its own place and its own kin, this house of the eastern ridge or that house of the ford, and Aithris a' Chruthachaidh, when it named the people it spoke of, named them only as the mason's kin or the valleys' own, never by any word that drew a line around the whole gathering and set it apart from whatever lay beyond the line.

In her five-and-twentieth year the gathering fell to a household on the western side of the crack, larger than most and closer by half a day's walk to two other valleys besides its own, so that the crowd that came in for Oidhche an Dealanaich was thicker that year than Rathnait had seen it in any year before, hearths she barely knew sitting shoulder to shoulder with hearths she had known her whole life, all of them come for the one telling and the one riddle and the one night's watch against a dark that every valley of that country kept in exactly the same way. She sat that year not among the children, being grown enough by then to be counted among the women who kept the fire fed through the long recital, and she watched the crowd rather than the speaker for a good part of the evening, the way a person newly grown into a gathering often watches the gathering before she troubles to listen closely to what it has come together to hear.

It was in the stir after the fathers' names were said and before Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich was taken up, the crowd loosening for a while into its own smaller talk the way any long-held silence loosens once the thing it was held for has been said, that Rathnait heard a man of the western household, older than her own father and known to her only by sight, answer a stranger's question about who these people gathered here were, all told, with a word she had never heard given to the whole of them before. Clann nan Dè, he said, Clann nan Dè, and said it plainly, the way a man says a thing he has turned over long enough in his own mind that it no longer feels new to him in the saying, though it plainly felt new enough to the stranger who had asked, and new enough, too, to more than one of the near hearths who caught the word and turned to hear it repeated. He gave no long account of where the word had come from, only that it seemed to him, and to others he had spoken with, a truer word for the gathered valleys than any word tied to a single ridge or a single ford, since what held the valleys together on a night like this one was neither ridge nor ford but the fathers' names and Teine a' Chlachair and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich that had come down with them, a thing shared by blood or by hearth or by both at once, in a way no single valley's own name had ever quite managed to say.

Rathnait asked him, when the talk had opened enough for a young woman to put a question to an elder of another household without seeming forward in it, where the households said they had come from before Teine a' Chlachair was given them, whether from some shore beyond the water, and the old man answered her without hesitation that they said no such thing of themselves; the households of the valleys held no telling of any coming at all, only of having been there, in the ground they buried their own dead in and cut no mark upon, for as far back as any father's name could carry a listener. The valleys' dead went into the ground itself, he said, under the same earth the living walked over, and the households that buried them that way had never, in any telling Rathnait's own elders could carry back to her, claimed to have arrived from anywhere at all; and the households called themselves, when they troubled to call themselves anything beyond their own ridge or ford, the children of the gods Aithris a' Chruthachaidh spoke of, and let whoever asked further make of that claim what they would.

The word went round the gathering that night the way any new word goes round a crowd already loosened by a long recital and a full fire, tried out first in ones and twos at the edge of the firelight and then, as the night wore toward its coldest hour and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich was taken up in its turn, said more freely by more mouths, until Rathnait heard it a dozen times before the gathering broke for the households to find their own places to sleep out the rest of the dark.
