She said it herself before the night was done, trying the shape of it in her own mouth the way a person tries a new word to see whether it sits well or ill on the tongue, and found, without quite deciding to find it, that it sat well enough; she was of no house that kept a fire-pot, and no line that counted fathers back to the mason himself by name, but she was of the valleys about the crack, buried her own kin in the same ground as every other hearth of that country, and had never in her life claimed to have come from anywhere but the place she stood in. Not every hearth at that gathering took to the word so readily. An old woman of the ford, sitting nearer the fire than her years strictly wanted on so cold a night, was heard to say to her own daughter that a name was easily enough taken up in one warm evening's talk and just as easily let drop again once the frost of the walk home had cleared a person's head of it, and that she herself had heard other words tried at other gatherings in her own long life, words that had seemed, for an evening, to fit the valleys as well as any word could, and had none of them lasted so much as a season past the fire that first warmed them into being said. She was not unkind about it, and she did not trouble to argue the man of the western household out of his word; she said only, when her daughter pressed her on why she would not use it herself, that she had buried too many hearths' worth of new names already in her own lifetime to grow fond of one before it had proved itself against more than a single cold night, and that she would wait, as she had waited before, to see whether the word was still being said the next time the valleys gathered, and the time after that, before she troubled to let it sit easy in her own mouth.

Rathnait did not have an answer ready for the old woman that night, being young enough still to feel the weight of an elder's doubt without having any settled reply to set against it, but she carried the doubt home with her all the same, turning it over on the walk back to her own household's hearth the way she turned over most things that unsettled her without quite convincing her. It seemed to her, turning it, that the old woman was right about one thing and wrong about another: right that a word tried once at one fire was no sure thing, and wrong, or so it came to seem to Rathnait across the seasons that followed, in judging this one word by the run of words that had gone before it, for she found herself using it still at the next night of the lightning, and heard others near her using it too, hearths that had not been at the western gathering at all and could only have had the word carried to them by some mouth that had, the way a coal is carried from one hearth to a cold one three valleys off. By the time Rathnait was old enough to sit among the elders at her own hearth's turn to hold the gathering, the word she had first heard tried out at the edge of a stranger's firelight had settled into ordinary use across the valleys about the crack, said as plainly and as unremarked as any of the older words for a single ridge or a single ford, and she herself, asked once by a child of her own household where the households of that country had first got the name they called themselves, could only say what the old man of the western hearth had once said to her: that it seemed to her, and to others she had spoken with, the truer word for what held the valleys together, and let the child make of that what she would.

Clann nan Dè, she said it to herself once more, low, with the fire between her and the western hearth's crowd still finding new mouths to carry the word further, and it was still in her own mouth, unremarked and untroubled, when the gathering at last went down to sleep and left the name standing, for the first time that any teller after ever cared to mark, said aloud.

# Chapter Thirty-two: Of the Sliver at Àth gharbh and the Name of the Line

*VE 4,475 – 4,671*

> *Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann.*
> We did not come; we were here.

*The Sixth Part: Of Clann na Ceiste, and the Seventh Coal*

## I. Of the Sliver at Àth gharbh

Barabal was five and thirty years old the spring she burned the sliver, and she had carried it in a fold of her own girdle, on and off, since she was a girl young enough to be given a bright stone for a plaything and old enough to remember, all her life after, exactly where she had been given it.

It had come to her the way small things come to children who are not watched every hour: a boy of the households nearest the crack, one of the many who ran errands between the high valleys and were fed at whatever hearth they stopped at, had shown it to her at a ford four miles from her own door, turning it in the light to make her see the colours run, and had then, tiring of her wonder or wanting to be free of his hands for the game they were playing, pressed it into hers and told her to keep it, as boys will give away in an idle hour what they would fight to keep the next. Where he had it from he did not say and she did not ask, being at that age more taken with the having of a bright thing than with the history of it, and by the time she was old enough to wonder where a stone with a rainbow shut inside it might have come from, the boy himself was long gone back to his own valley and grown, for all she knew, into a man who no longer remembered giving it. She kept it the way a woman keeps the small relics of her own childhood, in a fold of cloth at the bottom of a box, taken out now and again to be looked at and put away again, and told no one at Àth gharbh what it was, chiefly because she did not herself know.

She knew only Aithris a' Chruthachaidh, which every hearth of the valleys knew by then, of the mason and the fire out of the sky and the coloured stones that had gone into it and burned dark like any other stone; and she knew, because every child of that country was told it before it was told anything else worth telling, that Clann a' Chlachair kept a whole bag of such pieces yet, unburned, and turned them over every so often at the hearth on Oidhche an Dealanaich, trying this shore and that height against a riddle none of them could answer. It had never once occurred to Barabal, in all the years she kept her own small piece folded away, that what she held was of a kind with what the line kept; it was to her a pretty stone a boy had given her at a ford, no more sacred than a good flint or a well-turned spindle-whorl, and if she thought of Aithris a' Chruthachaidh at all when she took it out to look at it, it was only the way a person thinks of any old story while handling any old thing, without troubling to draw the two together.

What put the drawing-together into her head, in the end, was nothing more than an idle evening and a low fire. She was five and thirty, married eleven years, mother by then of three living children and one buried, and it was the wet edge of a spring that had been hard on the peat-stacks; she had gone out in worse weather than she liked to cut what she could from a bank already half drowned, and had come in cold to the bone with her hands raw from the wet turf, and sat that evening turning the little bright stone in her fingers by the low fire the way she always did when her hands were tired and wanted something small to do. She had wondered, not for the first time, whether it would burn like any other stone if she put it in, and had never once tried it, out of some half-formed care for the pretty thing that she could not have named a reason for. That evening, with the peat smoking low and green from the wet bank and giving off more smoke than heat, she thought: it is only a stone, and stones do not care what is done to them, and set it, before she could talk herself out of it, on the coals at the fire's edge.

It did not vanish, and it did not shine. It caught the way any coal catches, slow at first and then all at once, a small black-flamed fire no bigger than a thumbnail, burning low and steady exactly as the peat around it burned, giving off the same dark smoke and the same middling heat, so that a person coming in from the yard and finding it burning there would have seen nothing in the fire worth a second look. Barabal watched it the whole while it burned, waiting for some other thing to happen, some flare of colour or some voice out of it such as Aithris a' Chruthachaidh gave to the mason's own finding, and none came; it burned down to a black cinder exactly as a lump of ordinary coal burns down, and went out, and by morning was cold ash mixed in with the rest of the hearth's ash, indistinguishable from it.

The hearthstone under where it had lain, though, had taken a stain through its whole thickness, a colour gone down into the grain of it the way water goes into a dry cloth, no soot-mark for a hand to rub away, faint gold at the stone's heart and paling to nothing at its edges. No scrubbing Barabal gave it in the weeks after ever brought the stone back to plain grey. She showed her husband, and her husband, who had no more patience for wonders than any man with peat to cut and cattle to see to, said only that it was a strange stone and she had best not go setting any more strange stones on his hearth without asking him first, and left it there. It was her husband's mother, an old woman who had outlived two households and remembered a good deal of the valleys' talk from further back than most, who said, turning the stained stone over in her own hands by the daylight of the door, that she had heard tell, once, long ago, from a teller who had it from a teller before her, that Clann a' Chlachair kept coloured stones just such as this, and that no one outside that line had ever, in any telling the old woman knew, been fool enough or curious enough to try one on an ordinary hearth.

Barabal did not think herself either a fool or unusually curious, only a tired woman with cold hands on a wet evening who had wanted to see what a pretty stone would do, and she said as much when word of the stained hearthstone began, as such things do in a country where every hearth knows every other hearth's business within a season, to travel beyond her own door. It travelled slowly at first, carried by whoever happened to stop at Àth gharbh and see the stone for themselves, and it travelled, in the main, as a curiosity rather than a wonder, a strange small thing that had happened to one household and might never happen to another, since no one else at Àth gharbh or the households near it had a piece of an gual dathach to try, nor any notion of where one might be got. It did not reach the line's own ears, so far as anyone ever afterward could say, for some years, and when at last a fire-bearer of the old carrying custom, passing through Àth gharbh on his way to a hearth further north, heard the tale told over a cup and carried it home with him among the ordinary gossip of the road, the line's own hearth at Tobar dhìreach took it, by every telling that survives of that day, with less astonishment than Barabal herself had felt at the first burning. The old woman who then kept the bag and the pot, whose name the recital does not give to strangers, is said only to have listened to the fire-bearer's telling of the stained stone through to its end, and to have said, when he had done, that a piece thin enough to fit in a boy's palm was thin enough to lose, and that she was neither surprised nor sorry that one had gone astray somewhere in the many years since the mason first filled his tunic with more than he could ever afterward account for.

Barabal lived seven and thirty years more after the burning, long enough to become, in her own valley, less the woman who had done a strange thing once than simply an old woman among her grandchildren, as every woman who lives long enough becomes; she died in her two-and-seventieth year, at her own hearth, with nothing more said over her going than is said over any grandmother's, and the stained stone, by then split at last by some later hand trying to see whether the colour ran all the way through, was kept afterward at Àth gharbh as a plain curiosity, shown to travellers who asked after it and to children who did not, for longer than any single teller's memory could afterward account for.

## II. Of the Stained Wool of Achadh dhìreach

Giorsal was born at Achadh dhìreach fifteen years after Barabal set her stone on the coals, in a household ten miles west of the crack that kept no fire-pot and counted no fathers back to any mason, and grew up, as every child of those hearths grew up, on Aithris a' Chruthachaidh and on the plainer, harder business of getting a living out of ground that gave up its crops grudgingly and its dead, in the way of all ground, without asking leave of anyone.

It was the dead that Giorsal came, in time, to know better than most women of her valley knew them, for she was the one her household turned to when a burial had to be seen to properly, the washing and the wrapping and the choosing of what went into the ground with a body and what stayed behind for the living to use, work that fell more often to the women whose own hands had steadied enough of their kin's dying to have lost their fear of the office. She had buried, by the time she was five and thirty, more of her own blood than she cared to count aloud, and a good many besides who were no blood of hers at all but had no one left of their own to see to them properly, and she had come, across all that burying, to a private habit that she never troubled to explain to anyone who did not ask, and that not many did.

She rubbed a little broken coal into the wool a body was wrapped in before the ground took it.

It was not a custom she had invented outright; there was, at Achadh dhìreach as at a scatter of other hearths along that stretch of the valleys, a scrap of broken coloured stone kept in a box much as Barabal's had been kept, come to that household by some road no living teller could any longer trace, whether traded for a good hide or given by a passing kinsman or simply picked up, once, by some forgotten hand, from a place it had no business lying. Giorsal's own grandmother had shown it to her as a girl, calling it only the bright stone and saying nothing of what it was, and Giorsal had grown up handling it the unremarkable way a child handles any small treasure kept in a household box, until the year she first stood over a grave with the wrapping in her hands and found herself thinking, without quite meaning to think it, that the dead ought to carry something of worth into the ground with them, and that a stone worth keeping in a box for three generations was as fit a thing as any to give.

She broke off no more than a sliver's dust each time, rubbed between finger and thumb into the coarse wool at the breast of the wrapping, where a mourner's own hand might rest a moment before the ground closed over it, and she did it seldom, by her own later account, from no rule she had ever set herself, only from the plainer fact that the stone was small and the dead of Achadh dhìreach were, in an ordinary year, more than it could ever have served had she rubbed it into every wrapping that passed through her hands. She judged, in some manner she never put fully into words even to the daughter she taught the office to after her, which graves wanted it and which did not, choosing perhaps one burial in thirty across the whole span of her working years, so that most households of that valley, asked afterward whether their own dead had gone into the ground with any of the coloured stone about them, could say only that they did not know, or that they supposed not, the office being Giorsal's to judge and not theirs to ask after.

The wool took the colour the way Barabal's hearthstone had taken it, a stain gone down through the fibre, no smear for time or damp to wear away, streaks of a hue that no plant Giorsal or anyone else of that valley had ever set to dyeing wool could match, gold in some threads and a deeper red-gold in others depending, it seemed to her, on nothing she could ever predict from one grave to the next. She never dug a wrapping up again to look at it, that being no fit thing to do to the dead for the sake of a woman's curiosity, and so she never knew, nor did any who came after her, whether the stain held in the ground the way it held in the moment of the rubbing, or faded, or spread, or did anything at all once the earth had closed over it; she knew only what her own eyes saw in the last moment before the closing, and she kept that knowledge to herself and to the daughter she taught, telling her only that the stone was a good thing to give the dead and that she would understand, in time, which graves asked for it, the same understanding having been given to her without much explaining by the grandmother before.

Word of Giorsal's habit travelled less far than word of Barabal's burning, partly because a wrapped body going into the ground offers less of a spectacle than a stained hearthstone shown at every passing traveller's asking, and partly because Giorsal herself, being a private woman about the office in every other particular, saw no reason to make more of this one particular than of the rest. It reached the ears of the line, when it reached them at all, by much the same slow road the tale of Barabal's stone had travelled, carried by a fire-bearer or a trader who happened to hear it told at some hearth along his way and thought it worth the telling further, and the line, by the time it heard, had already had some fifteen years to grow used to the plainer fact that its own long-kept treasure was not, after all, the only coloured stone the valleys held between them. Giorsal died in her seventieth year, at Achadh dhìreach, of a wasting that took the better part of a winter to finish its work, and was buried, her own daughter saw to it, with a sliver of the stone rubbed into her own wrapping in her turn, the office passing that once, as it must, from the hand that had always given it to the hand that had only ever received it before.

## III. Of the Bright Thing on the Midden at Bral

Far to the west, on the shore the coast-people called Bral, a woman going over the midden below her own household's huts in the low light of an autumn morning found, among the ordinary wrack of shell and burnt weed and the split bones of whatever the tide and the nets had lately given up, a small hard thing that was neither shell nor bone nor any stone she had ever turned up out of that heap before.

It caught the early sun the way wet slate never caught it, a gleam with more than one colour folded into it, and she turned it over in her fingers a good while, the way a person turns over any small unaccountable thing found where it has no business being, before she did with it what she did with most such finds: she carried it up to the huts and showed it to the others of her own household, who turned it over in their turn and were, by every account the shore afterward kept of that morning, no wiser for the turning than she had been. No one of that household could say how long it had lain among the midden's ordinary leavings before her own eye found it, whether it had come down with that season's shell and bone or lain buried some years already under layer on layer of the heap's slow growing, and no one troubled the question long, a midden being, by its nature, a place where things arrive by more roads than any one household can keep account of: by its own hands, by trade struck at some other landing and carried home, by a stranger's leavings washed up with the tide and taken for the household's own, or by some smaller, quieter road that no one at Bral that morning cared, or was able, to put a name to.

It was not burned. No one at Bral that season, or any season the shore's own tellers afterward reached back to, is known to have set it to any fire, cooking or otherwise; it was handled the way the coast-people handled any bright find that served no plain use, admired for a morning or two and then set aside among the household's other small keepings, a shell too fine to throw back, a bone worked smooth by the sea, a stone that caught the light. Whether it lay afterward in some box or niche of that household's own keeping, or was lost again in its turn to some later midden or some child's careless hand, no telling of the shore or the hill country either one ever afterward claimed to know; it passed, as most small bright things pass, out of the particular notice that had first found it remarkable and into the general keeping of a household that had a great many other things to attend to besides one stone among its trinkets.

The hill country never heard of it. Whatever the bright thing at Bral was, and however it had come there, by gift or by trade or by theft, it remained a thing the shore alone half-wondered at for a season and then let go, the way the shore let go of a great many small unaccountable things the sea and the land between them brought to its notice and never troubled to explain.

## IV. Of the Name Taken at the Gathering

By the year Colla came to the keeping of the bag, it was known across the whole breadth of the valleys about the crack, settled by then into the ordinary stock of things everyone knew rather than kept as any marvel, that an gual dathach did not belong to Clann a' Chlachair alone; that a stone had been burned once at a hearth of Àth gharbh and had stained the very rock it burned on; that a woman of Achadh dhìreach had, for a working lifetime, given slivers of it to the dead; and that here and there, at this hearth or that, some household could show a scrap of its own, come by gift or trade or simple finding, and could tell a version of the tale, more or less true to the first telling, of how it had come to them. None of it troubled the line's own long keeping in the smallest degree, the bag at Tobar dhìreach holding still, that year, the two coals that had never yet answered any trial given them, gual teine and the last, the coal of every colour together that the reciters had taken, since Diarmad's own day, to calling the rainbow; but it had changed, all the same, something in the way the valleys spoke of the line, for a people who had once been the sole and singular keepers of an unaccountable wonder were by then one household among several that held a piece of the same wonder, distinguished from the rest chiefly by how much of it they held and how long they had gone on asking what it was for.

It was this, more than Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich itself, that a wit of Àth gharbh named Oscar took up, half in jest, at the gathering that fell that year to a hearth two ridges from his own, on the night the valleys kept as the darkest, when every household that could reach another in an evening's walk came together to hear the fathers' names said standing and the old riddle taken up again and laid down again unanswered. Oscar was five and forty that winter, a man well known in his own valley and a good many neighbouring ones for a tongue that found the loose thread in any solemn thing and pulled it, gently enough that most who felt the pull laughed along rather than took offence, and he had, by his own later telling, no plan at all when he opened his mouth that night beyond the plain wish to say something that would make the hearth laugh before the cold walk home.

The recital had been said, the fathers named back through Eòghann and the fifteen whose names the line kept from strangers to the one then living at Tobar dhìreach, a man named Colla, five and thirty years old that winter and new enough to the keeping of the bag that more than one elder present remembered his father's own turn at the reciting better than they yet knew his. Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich had been taken up after, as it always was, and laid down again, as it always was, for no one that night had brought forward any new trial to try against it, the sea and the sky and the earth and the blood and the river all having long since answered, and the two dark coals lying, as they had lain for longer than anyone at that gathering had been alive to remember otherwise, exactly as dark as the day the mason first burned their fellows.

It was in the loosening after, the crowd breaking into its own smaller talk the way any long-held silence loosens once the thing it was held for has been said, that Oscar, standing near enough the fire to be heard by a good part of the gathering without troubling to raise his voice, remarked to whoever was near him that the line ought by rights to be given a better name than the mason's children, seeing as how the mason's own trade of splitting stone had gone clean out of the family more generations back than anyone could count and been replaced by nothing so much as the steady, unhurried business of asking the same question of the same two coals and getting, every time, the same silence back. He called them, that night, for the first time that any teller after ever troubled to fix a year to, Luchd-ceasnachaidh a' Ghuail Dhìomhair, the long questioners of the secret coal, saying it slow and a little grand, the way a man says a thing he means partly to be funny and partly, though he might not have owned to it that night, to be true.

The hearth laughed, as Oscar had meant it to, and a good part of the gathering with it, the name being long enough and grand enough set against so plain and patient a business to strike most ears there as exactly the joke Oscar intended; but it did not die with the laughing, the way most jests of a cold night die by morning, for a name that fits a thing, however it is first meant, has a way of being said again by mouths that never heard the first saying of it, carried the same slow road any word travels in a country of scattered hearths, from this fire to that one, until it no longer belongs to the man who first shaped it. Colla himself, asked some months after by a traveller passing through Tobar dhìreach what his people called themselves, is said to have given the long name back without any of the laughter that had first carried it, adding only that the short form most mouths found easier was Clann na Ceiste, the children of the question, and that either would serve, his own line having asked one question, in one form or another, for longer than it had done any other single thing worth the naming.

He was five and sixty when he died, having kept the bag some thirty years by then and handed the keeping on before the end to a son whose name, like every father's before and after him along that stretch of the line, the reciters kept from strangers; and it was under his name, said standing at the recital the winter after his death, that the older name of the line, the mason's children, was heard for what the tellers afterward reckoned the last time spoken as the line's own name rather than as an old thing remembered. The households of the valleys had, by then, taken to calling the line simply Clann na Ceiste in their ordinary talk, the way a name settles into use long before anyone troubles to mark the day it settled, and the reciters, who kept the older forms alongside the new the way they kept every name the line had ever answered to, said both that winter at the gathering, the mason's children and the children of the question together, before letting the newer name stand alone in every recital after.

Rathnait's own word for the whole of the valleys, spoken first at a gathering not so many years before Oscar's jest and settled by then into as ordinary a use as any name the hearths had ever taken up, was said that same night alongside the line's new name, Clann nan Dè and the children of the question both, two names taken up within one generation of each other, the one by the valleys and the other by the line, which shared, that winter, the one gathering and the one fire and, though neither troubled to remark on it, the one long habit of the valleys: that a name tried once at a cold hearth, if it fitted the thing it was given to, outlived the fire that first warmed it into being said, and was carried on, from mouth to mouth and gathering to gathering, long after the man or woman who first shaped it had gone, in their own turn, into the ground.

# Chapter Thirty-three: Of Fire in the Stone

*VE 4,672 – 4,850*

## I. Of the Stone New in the Grass

Lughaidh was two and twenty the year he first drove his flock up the western slopes past the ford where the two burns met, following the ewes further than his father had ever troubled to follow them, on the reasoning, which was his own and which he never explained to anyone who did not first ask, that grass eaten short by one summer's flock was grass a man wanted to leave a season or two before he brought his beasts back to it. He was a patient shepherd rather than a clever one, the kind neighbours spoke of as steady before they spoke of him as anything else, and it was this steadiness, more than any restlessness of his own, that carried him that year to a fold of the western grass no one of his own hearth had grazed in living memory.

He came on the stone in the last of the day, when the light lay long and gold across the tussocks and every small rise threw a long shadow ahead of it. It stood alone on a low shoulder of ground where nothing else stood, no cairn near it, no path worn to it that he could see, a single upright slab taller than a man with his arm raised, grey where the lichen had not yet taken it and green-grey where it had, leaning not at all, so square to the ground that Lughaidh's first thought, looking at it across the darkening grass with his dog gone quiet at his heel, was that no weather he knew of stood a stone up that straight on its own.

He did not go to it that evening. He counted his ewes instead, the way a shepherd counts before anything else, and made his fire a good bowshot off, on ground he knew, and ate what he had carried and lay down with the dog against his side and did not sleep well, waking twice to look toward the shoulder of ground where the stone stood black now against a paler dark, telling himself both times that a stone was a stone and had never yet troubled a sheep or a man, and neither time quite believing himself enough to sleep sound on it.

In the morning, with the light coming up grey and then gold behind him and the stone standing plain and ordinary in it, he walked over.

It was new. That was the thing he could not afterward make anyone who had not seen it for themselves believe: new in the way of a thing lately made, the cut faces of it sharp-edged still, unrounded by rain, the grass at its foot not yet grown back over whatever digging had set it, a bare collar of turned earth no wider than a hand's span all round the base, greening at the crumbled edges and black and raw at the centre where no green had reached at all. Lughaidh had seen old stones before, the low grey teeth of them scattered here and there about the high ground the way old stones are scattered on any hill a people has walked long enough, softened at every corner, sunk a little into their own hollows, grown into the land until a man half forgot they had ever been raised. This one had begun no such forgetting. It stood the way a new-cut post stands in a fence line before its first winter, still telling, to anyone who looked close, exactly how lately a hand had set it there.

He put his own hand flat against the face of it, for no reason he could have given beyond the reason any man puts a hand to a strange thing, and found it warm from the morning sun and rough under his palm in a way that was not all weather; and looking closer, with his eyes now used to the light, he saw that the roughness ran in lines, a shape laid on the stone by some other hand than weather's, a single running line of signs cut into the upper face from one edge near to the other, in a script he did not know and had never seen, and that no one of his people cut or read. It ran level, and it stopped clean at both ends, as though whoever had cut it had known exactly how much they meant to say and said no more and no less.

He did not touch that line again once he had seen it plainly. But lower down the face, where the stone narrowed toward its foot and the full morning light now fell square upon it, he found a second cutting, shorter, four small clusters of signs set close together, cut narrower and shallower than the line above by what he judged, turning his head to catch the shadow in the grooves, a finer tool and another hand. He could no more read them than the line above. He stood a good while with his hand near the stone and not on it, looking from the narrow lower cutting to the broad line above and back, turning over in his own slow way the plain fact that here were two hands where he had at first looked for one, and that neither hand had left any other mark on the hillside, no footprint the grass had not already swallowed, no ash of a fire, no litter of chips such as a mason leaves at his work. The stone stood finished. Whoever had raised it had raised it and gone.

He brought his flock down off that ground within the week, going a longer way round than the ground asked, and keeping the stone in sight over his shoulder the better part of the descent, as a man keeps a strange dog in sight rather than turn his back on it first. That night, at his own hearth, with the fire built up higher than a shepherd's supper called for, he told what he had found to his father's household, and was made to tell over again the shape and the place of the lower cutting, how many clusters, how close, how deep; and his father, an old man by then and slower to wonder than his son, asked only whether the boy had left anything of his own behind him up there, a mark, a stone moved, anything the ground might afterward be made to answer for, and Lughaidh, a little stung that this should be the first question asked of him, said he had moved nothing at all, which was true, and remained true the whole length of his life after.

The tale went from that hearth to the next inside the week and further before the season turned, gathering as it went, the way any tale gathers: that the stone stood taller than a man with his arm raised became, by the third or fourth telling, taller than two men stood one on the other's shoulders; that Lughaidh had found it in the last light of evening became, in some mouths, that he had found it by a light of its own, which Lughaidh denied plainly and without heat whenever the telling reached back to him. And by the next winter every hearth that told of the stone told also what its four low words said, *Bha teine sa chloich*, there was fire in the stone, though no one of the valleys could read a sign, and no one could say whose mouth had first given the words to the marks. How that came to be known is a riddle, as the knowing of the lines in the Doire uaine hills had been; known it was, and said the same way in every mouth, as though a saying that fitted so well the felt shape of an old wonder needed no hearth's embroidering to carry.

What the line made of it, Lughaidh himself never troubled to learn in any close way, being a shepherd and not a keeper, and the keeping of stones not being work he had ever been asked to take up; but it came back to him, in the way things came back along that same slow road, that the fire the second saying spoke of was held by Clann na Ceiste to be their own fire, Teine a' Chlachair, though who had cut the words, and when, and by what right a hand not of the line's own reckoning had come to speak the line's own matter in stone, none of them could say any better than Lughaidh could say who had left the older, wider line above it. The line took the lower words for their own. The upper line they left as Lughaidh had left it, unread, and it stayed unread by every eye that came after his, the whole length of Lughaidh's own life and long past it, a single running mark on a stone none could account for standing above four words that everyone, in the end, agreed to.

Lughaidh kept his flock on those slopes and the others near them for the better part of fifty years after, growing old the way a steady man grows old, and he is remembered, where he is remembered at all beyond his own hearth, as the shepherd who found the stone new. He died in his seventieth year, at his own hearth, the same year, as it happened, that a young man of the line standing at that season's gathering said the four words aloud for the first time to a crowd that had come to hear the fathers named; and whether Lughaidh, failing by then in his last illness, ever heard that they had gone so far, no one troubled to say.

## II. Of the Two Hands on the One Face

The line did not leave the stone in the west alone once it had taken the four low words for its own. A woman of Clann na Ceiste who had the recital better than any of her generation, and who was troubled, as the line had always been troubled, by any question left standing, walked west to it in the second summer after Lughaidh's finding with two of her sons to carry the food, and sat before it three days.

What troubled her was the order of the two hands. The broad line of unread signs across the upper face and the four narrow words below it had not been cut at one time, nor by one tool; any eye could see that much, and hers was a sharp eye. But which had come first she could not tell, and it seemed to her, sitting in the grass with her back to the wind and the stone standing over her, that it mattered a great deal which. If the broad line had been cut first, then some hand of the line's own people, or of a people who spoke as they spoke, had come afterward to a stone already cut by another and set its own saying beneath the older one, as a man might set his own mark beneath a stranger's on a gatepost to say that he had passed that way too. If the four words had come first, then some other hand had come afterward and cut its own saying above them, in signs no one of the valleys could read, over the head of a saying they could.

She looked for the answer in the grooves. She ran her fingers along the upper line and along the lower words, morning and evening, when the light came across the stone low enough to throw a shadow into every cut, and she felt the edges and the floors of the grooves and the lichen at their rims, and she could not tell. The upper cuts were broader and the lower narrower, and the lower were cut with a finer tool; but the lichen had not yet taken either, the stone being so new, and the weather had worked no more on the one than on the other. She said, when she came home, that she had sat three days with the two hands and they had both kept their counsel, and that she would not guess which had come first, since a guess said at the recital would be a guess remembered as a thing known.

The line kept to that. At every recital after, when the stone in the west was spoken of, it was said that the four low words were the line's own saying and the fire in them Teine a' Chlachair, and that the broad line above them was unread; and it was said, too, that when the second hand came to the stone is not known. The woman's sons, who had carried the food and sat the three days with her and grown very tired of the grass, said privately to their own children that their mother had known perfectly well which hand came first and had simply refused to say, because she did not like to be wrong in front of the recital; but their mother, asked it straight out on her own deathbed by a grandson who had heard the story, said she had not known then and did not know now, and that he might ask the stone himself if he doubted her, since it had answered her exactly as plainly as it would answer him.

It was the first of the island's stones to carry the marks of two hands on one face. The line said, and it is told still, that this was fitting, for Teine a' Chlachair had come to the island by two hands also, the sky's and the mason's own, and neither of them had asked the other's leave.

## III. Of the Second Stone

The second stone stood a good day's walk from the first, further into the hills where the ground rose broken and stony and the grass thinned to tussock and bare rock between, on ground no shepherd of Lughaidh's own valley grazed at all, being poor feed and further than any flock needed driving for it. It was found later than the first, by how much later no telling ever fixed with any certainty, though the line came to reckon it a matter of some years rather than many, and it was found, as such things are found on ground that few walk, by a traveller rather than a shepherd, a man of no particular note who left no name behind him in any telling and who is remembered only as having said, when he brought the word down to the nearer hearths, that he had near enough walked into the thing before he saw it, so little did it stand apart from the broken grey rock all about it.

This stone was shorter than the first and plainer, no line of unread script upon it at all, only the one cutting, three words only, in the same narrow, sure hand that had cut the four words low on the other stone, or in a hand so like it that no one who compared the two, then or after, could swear to any difference between them:

*Cuimhnich an teine.*

Remember the fire.

Who was bidden to remember, and what exactly they were bidden to remember beyond the plain word, no telling that came down from that hillside ever said, and the line at Tobar dhìreach, asked by more than one traveller over the years whether the second stone spoke to them any plainer than the first, gave the same answer each time: that the fire was theirs to remember whether the stone bade them or no, and that a command cut in rock to no one in particular was, for all that, a command they were glad enough to take as meant for them, there being no other hand on the island that kept a fire so old or minded so hard to be told to keep minding it.

It was some years after the second stone's finding that the four low words of the first stone were said, for what the tellers held to be the first time, standing, before a whole gathering rather than at a single hearth. The young man who said them was of the line, new enough to speaking before a crowd that his voice caught once in the saying and had to be steadied, and he said them as a thing come down to him, by the same slow road as everyone else, from a traveller who had had it from a traveller before him, back, though no one at that gathering could have traced the whole chain of it, to the first hearths that told of the stone, fifty years gone. The gathering took the words up the way the valleys took up any saying that fitted a felt thing, repeating it after him at the fire until it had passed into the ordinary stock of what was said at every gathering after, alongside the recital of the fathers and the old unanswered riddle of the coals.

## IV. Of the Ring at the Second Stone

Mòrnait was born at Tobar dhìreach into Clann na Ceiste, though not into the narrow line of fathers that kept the bag from father to son, her own household being one of the many that had gathered, over the generations since Oscar's jest first took, about the line's own hearth without ever holding the coals themselves. She grew up on Aithris a' Chruthachaidh as every child of the valleys grew up on it, and on the newer sayings besides, the four words and the three, said so often at so many gatherings by then that a child of her own age could not have told anyone which she had learned first or from which mouth, the sayings having become, by the time she was old enough to say them back, simply part of what was known, the way the shapes of the hills were known, without a first telling anyone troubled to remember.

She was a woman of no particular office among the line, keeping no bag and reciting no fathers, but she had, from a girl, the kind of restlessness that finds its own work where none is asked of it, and what she found, some years into her own married life, was the stone of the three words, Colbh Cnoc chiar, and the poor, broken ground about it, which she took to visiting at first out of no more than the wish to see for herself a thing so much spoken of and so seldom looked at, the valley's own folk being no readier to walk a hard day into stony hills than the shepherds before them had been.

The walk was no small undertaking for a woman with a household of her own to keep, a full day out over broken ground that gave a walker nothing easy underfoot the whole way, rising steadily from the last of the good grass into country where the path, such path as there was, picked between slabs of bare grey rock split by frost into edges sharp enough to cut a soft boot-sole, and where the wind, coming off the high ground with nothing to break it, found a traveller from every side at once rather than the one side a valley wind came from. She went in fair weather when she could choose her day and in weather no fairer than most when she could not, carrying the coal wrapped in its damp moss inside a second wrapping of oiled hide against the wet, and food enough for the two days the walk there and back and the sitting between them asked of her, and she came home each time, her own husband said afterward, looking as though the ground itself had had something to say to her on the way that she had not yet finished turning over.

Asked once, by a niece of her own household who thought the whole business a strange use of a grown woman's days, what she meant to prove by it, Mòrnait is remembered to have said that she meant to prove nothing, proving being the line's own long business at Tobar dhìreach and none of hers; and asked a second time, more gently, by an old woman of a neighbouring hearth who had herself walked the long road once and found nothing at the far end of it but a stone and cold rock, what she hoped to find there that the older woman had not, Mòrnait said only that she went to leave something rather than to find anything, a fire, where a stone had asked for one to be remembered, and that whether the stone or anyone behind it ever marked her leaving it was not, in the end, greatly her business either. What she did, once she had made the walk a second time and a third, she never afterward explained in any way that satisfied everyone who later asked her why, saying only, when pressed, that a fire kept meant more than a fire spoken of, and that a stone bidding her remember seemed to her, however the stone had meant it, ill remembered by words alone. She carried fire up from the pot at Tobar dhìreach, the coal wrapped close in damp moss the whole hard day of the walking so that it lived to the far end of it, and she built, on the bare stony ground about the foot of the second stone, a ring of fire-cracked stones gathered from the broken rock all round, and in the ring she laid and lit a fire the size of any ordinary hearth-fire, no bigger, and sat by it until it had burned down to nothing, and then she went home.

She did this again the next year, and the year after, at first alone and then, as word of it went about the valleys the way word of anything went about them, with others who came to sit by the fire with her a night or a day before going their own ways home, so that by the tenth year of her keeping it the ring at the stone had grown a worn path to it where before there had been none, and the ground within the ring had taken the hard-trodden, ash-blackened look of ground that has held fire and feet upon it many times over, no different in the end from the ground about any hearth kept a working lifetime, save that no house stood by it and no one lived there and the fire, once built and burned down, was left to go out on its own rather than banked to keep till morning.

Nothing came of it beyond the keeping, no wonder shown, no answer given, the fire she built behaving exactly as any fire behaves that is fed dry wood and left to burn, no coal of the vein ever brought to that hillside to be tried against the stone's own bidding, for Mòrnait held, and said so to anyone who asked whether she meant the fire as some trial of Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich, that the stone had asked only to be remembered and not to be questioned, there being questioning enough already given to the two dark coals by better keepers than herself over more years than she had been alive to count. She built her fires instead the way a woman keeps any old duty that has come to feel, over years of keeping it, less like a duty than like her own: because the ground asked for it, and because a stone that had stood so long bidding anyone at all to remember deserved, she thought, at the least, to see that someone had.

The ring was kept the whole of her own life after, walked to every year she was able, her steps growing stiffer with the walking as the years told on her the way years tell on any woman, until in her own sixty-fifth year she made the walk for what turned out to be the last time, her own household by then grown used to letting her go alone and expecting her back within the fortnight as she had always come back before. The fire she lit as she had always lit it, and sat by it as she had always sat by it, and it is told, by the few who came that year to sit an evening with her before going on their own ways, that she said, watching the flame go down toward the last of its light, that she did not know what the stone remembered, only that she had kept it as well as she knew how, and that whoever came after her would have to find their own way of keeping it if they meant to keep it at all.

She died that same year, at her own hearth at Tobar dhìreach, some weeks after her return from the last walk, of no illness anyone could name beyond the plain wearing-out of a long life, and her own daughter, and after her the daughter's own children, took up the walk to the stone in her stead, less often than Mòrnait herself had kept it, yet often enough that the ring did not go cold in any one man's lifetime after hers, the ash of each new fire laid down over the ash of the last until the ground within the stones held, in its blackened depth, more years of keeping than any single teller could any longer count from the top of it.

Of an evening, in the years after Mòrnait, a traveller crossing that stony ground toward dusk might still come on the ring at the second stone with a fire newly lit and low in it, and a face or two beside it he did not know, keeping, without much to say for themselves beyond the plain fact of the keeping, a fire that answered no riddle and proved no coal and asked, of anyone who sat by it, nothing at all but to remember; and the stone stood over them as it had stood over Mòrnait and over the traveller who first found it before her, plain and grey and three words deep, giving no more account of itself in the last light of any one of those evenings than it had given in the first.

# Chapter Thirty-four: Of the Column

*VE 4,851 – 4,904*

## I. Of the Third Stone

Ciannait was one and thirty the summer the third stone was found standing where no stone had stood the year before, on a low rise of open ground two days' walk south-west of the crack, where the hill households of that country brought their beasts down each autumn to graze the stubble before the frosts came. She had made that same drive every year of her grown life, her own hearth lying a half-day short of the rise, and she had crossed that same ground a hundred times without there being anything on it to cross toward beyond the one thorn tree the drovers used as a mark; so that when her brother's boy came running back along the track that year shouting that there was a great stone standing on the rise where the thorn tree stood alone, she took it at first for a boy's way of making an ordinary walk into something worth the telling, and only went to look because the beasts were slow that morning and there was time enough to spare for looking.

It stood taller than the thorn tree beside it, a single squared pillar of the pale blue-grey stone the hill country called only the blue rock, for want of any better word, set so true to the level ground that a plumb line hung from its top would, by the account of the first men to lay hands on it, have kissed the earth at its foot without a hair's width to spare either way. No cairn stood by it. No path led to it, not yet, though within the year there would be one worn plain enough by the feet of those who came to see it that even a stranger new to that country could have found the rise by the track alone, without ever being told which way to look.

She came up to it with her brother's boy at her heel and the rest of the drove already scattering out over the stubble behind her, and she did what everyone who came to it that first summer is remembered to have done: she put her hand flat to the stone's face, low down where a hand reaches without stretching, and found it warm from the morning sun and rough under her palm with the lines of a cutting she had heard tell of but never yet seen with her own eyes.

The words ran the whole breadth of the lower face, more words than either of the two stones further north had carried, cut in the same narrow, sure hand, or a hand so like it that no one who set the three sayings side by side, then or after, could ever swear to any difference between them:

*Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann.*

We did not come; we were here.

Above the saying, where the stone narrowed toward its shoulder, ran a second line in the older, wider script that no one on the island had ever read and no one on the island ever would, the same running, level mark that had stood over the first stone's four words and, fainter and shorter, over the second stone's three; and it was this, more than the new saying below it, that told the hill folk who came to look that whatever hand had cut the older line meant the three stones to be read, if they were to be read at all, as one long saying rather than three short ones, though what that whole saying was, taken together, no one at Achadh a' Chalbh that summer, or in any summer after, ever agreed on closely enough to fix it in words of their own.

Ciannait could no more read the cutting than anyone of her people could read a sign; yet before that first summer was out every drover who stood at the pillar said what its lower words were, as the words of the other two stones had come to be known, by no mouth anyone could name. She said them herself that autumn at the stone's foot, and heard her own voice go out over the stubble and come back thin off the one bare rise, and stood a while with her hand still on the stone after the saying was done, turning over in her own slow way what it meant to be told, by a hand no living person had seen at its work, that her own people had not come from anywhere at all.

Her brother's boy asked her, when she came away from it at last to see to the beasts, who had cut it; and she told him, because it was the only true answer she had to give him, that she did not know, and that no one living knew, and that it did not seem, from the plain freshness of the cutting and the bare turned earth still black at the stone's foot, that whoever had cut it had troubled to wait about afterward to be asked.

He asked her a second question that she liked no better for having no better answer to give it, which was whether the stone would still be standing come morning, boys of his age having heard enough, by then, of the walker on the ridge and the covered hearths of the hill country to wonder whether anything found new on open ground was safe to be left overnight; and she told him only that a stone was not a fire, and had never yet been known to go out, and that they would see for themselves soon enough, the drove being due back over that same ground within the fortnight whether the stone had a mind to bide there or not. It was there when they came back, exactly as they had left it, the bare turned earth at its foot a little more weathered and no wider, and it was there again the fortnight after that, and every fortnight and every season after, so that within that one year's turning the households of the drove had stopped asking, among themselves, whether it would stand, and begun asking only what, besides its own two sayings, it might yet be found to mean.

## II. Of the Field of the Column

Word of the third stone went out from that rise the same slow road the first two sayings had gone, hearth to hearth and gathering to gathering, but it went further and it went faster, for by the year it was found the four words of the first stone and the three of the second had already had the better part of a lifetime to settle into the ordinary stock of what every hearth in the hill country knew, so that a saying come new from a third stone, and a longer one besides, found ears already listening for it in a way the first two sayings had never found when they were new. Within two summers the rise had a name of its own among the households that gathered there, Achadh a' Chalbh, and within five it had a worn ring of bare earth about the stone's foot where feet had stood so often and so long that no grass had troubled to come back into it, much as the ring at the second stone had worn bare under Mòrnait's own feet a day's walk to the north.

It was at Achadh a' Chalbh, in the third summer after the stone's finding, that Ciannait heard the whole saying said standing, before a gathering of some thirty households come together at the dark of that year to keep Oidhche an Dealanaich together on ground none of them had kept it on before, the recital of the fathers being said, as it was said at every such gathering, by whoever among them had it best by heart; and it was an old woman of a hearth two valleys east of Ciannait's own, a woman near her eightieth year whose name went into no telling that outlasted her own grandchildren, who rose when the fathers had been named and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich laid down again unanswered, and said the three sayings of the three stones together for the first time that Ciannait, or anyone else at that gathering, had ever heard them said as one.

She said the four words of the first stone, and the three of the second, and then, turning to face the pillar where it stood pale in the firelight with its own shadow thrown long across the trampled ground, she said the words of the third: *Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann.* And she said after it, in words that were her own rather than any stone's, that Aithris a' Chruthachaidh every hearth in the hill country already kept, of the young god who had made the island of his last coal and the first people who grew up out of its ground like grass, meant a plainer thing than most tellers troubled to draw out of it: that a people grown from the ground they stood on had no other ground to have come from, and no other root than the one under their own two feet, and that the stone said only, in fewer words than Aithris a' Chruthachaidh used, what Aithris a' Chruthachaidh had always said.

Ciannait was four and thirty that night, old enough by then to have children of her own standing at her side and young enough still to remember, plainly, what it had been to put her own hand to the stone the summer it stood new; and she said afterward, to those of her own hearth who asked her what she made of the old woman's words, that she did not know if the god had meant the saying or only the shape of the telling had come to fit it, but that she had stood a long while that night looking at the pillar with the fire between herself and it, and had felt, for the length of that looking, that the ground under her own feet had a name it had not had before the saying was said over it.

The gathering at Achadh a' Chalbh was kept again the next dark of the year, by more households than the first, and again the year after that, until within Ciannait's own lifetime it had become, for the hearths of that whole stretch of country, the one gathering-ground of the year that every household within two days' walk turned toward as the days shortened, in much the way that other households further north turned each year toward Tobar dhìreach to hear the fathers named at the line's own hearth. No house was built there in Ciannait's time, nor for long after it, the ground about the pillar being kept, by a custom no one troubled to set down as a rule because no one thought it needed one, for the fires and the standing and the going home again rather than for living; but it had, by the time Ciannait's own hair had gone from dark to grey, what neither of the two older stones had ever had on their own bare hillsides, which was a name that every child of that country learned before it learned to walk the day's ground to earn it, and a fire built there, at the very least, once in every year that the dark of the year came round.

The crowds that gathered twice a year, once at the dark of the year and once at the height of summer when the drove-roads were driest and easiest walked, brought with them, as any crowd of that size brings, more business than the saying alone; and it was out of the standing and the going home again, rather than out of any plan laid by any one household, that a market grew up on the stubble about the pillar's foot in the years of Ciannait's own middle life, hides traded for salt and salt for wool and wool for whatever a household further off had to spare, the traders setting out their goods on hide cloths spread over the same trampled ground the fires were built on, and taking them up again within the day, for no one yet thought to leave anything standing there overnight beyond the stone. Ciannait traded there herself more than once, wool off her own beasts for salt she could not get nearer than three days' walk any other way, and she said of it, once her hair had gone grey, that she had gone the first few times for the salt and kept going, in the end, as much for the crowd and the fire and the saying said over it as for anything a trader could set out on a cloth.

## III. Of the Fire Coal in a Child's Hand

While the saying at Achadh a' Chalbh was still new enough that most who heard it had heard it first from someone who had themselves heard it only at second or third remove, a child was born at Tobar dhìreach into the narrow keeping of the bag, the son of the tenth father after Colla, whose name the reciters have never given to any stranger who asked it of them; and that child, a boy named Seathan, had gual teine in his own hands, by every account that came down from that hearth, before he was old enough to be trusted with anything else his household kept.

He was not yet six the first summer a fire-bearer passing through the valley on his way north carried with him, along with the ordinary coal for the hearths that had let their own go out, the word of the third stone and its saying, new enough then that even at Tobar dhìreach it was still told as news rather than as a thing everyone already knew; and the boy sat that evening at the edge of the household's fire with gual teine turned in his fingers, as he turned it most evenings for no reason beyond the plain unremarkable comfort of a smooth stone in a small hand, listening to the fire-bearer tell of the pillar and its shadow and the old woman's words without troubling, at that age, to understand more of it than that somewhere two long days south a stone stood that people walked a long way to look at, much as his own hearth was a place people sometimes walked a long way to hear the fathers named.

He asked his mother, when the fire-bearer had gone on his way, whether the coal in his own hand had come from the same place as the stone's saying, and she told him, in the plain way the women of that hearth answered such questions of their children, that the coal had come from the mason's own vein under Leac na Fèithe, and the stone's saying from no one anyone living could name, and that the two were not, so far as she or anyone else of that house had ever heard, the same matter at all, though both were things the valleys had come, in their own way, to keep.

His father, whose own name the reciters have kept from strangers as they had kept the nine fathers' before his, said less of it than his mother had, being a man of few words even at his own hearth, but he took the boy's chin in his hand that same evening and turned his son's face up to his own and told him only that the bag on the peg had waited longer than any stone in the south had waited, and that a thing worth keeping was worth keeping without asking each year whether the keeping had yet come to anything. The boy took it gently, said gently as it was, and kept it in mind ever after, by his own account given late in his own life, better than he remembered most of what either of his parents said to him in those years, for it was the first time anyone had told him plainly that the waiting, and not only the answer waited for, was a part of what the bag asked of whoever held it.

The coal did nothing that evening it had not done every other evening of the boy's short life: it lay black and cool in his palm while the hearth-fire threw its light across the backs of his hands, unburning and unchanged, the way it had lain in every hand of that household since the mason's day, while its fellows one by one answered to the sea and the height and the earth and the blood and the river, and this one and the rainbow were left over, unanswered, in the bag on its peg. The boy set it back in its place when his mother called him to his supper, and thought no more of the stone at Achadh a' Chalbh, by his own much later account, than a child thinks of any far country he has been told of once and has no cause to think of again; and it would be the better part of forty years, and the household grown old and passed to his own keeping, before that same coal gave him any cause to think of it a second time.

## IV. Of the Word Carried North, and Ciannait's Children

The saying of the third stone went further north than either of the two before it, carried, some twenty years after the stone was found, by a woman of the northern shore who had come south to trade hides for salt at one of the market days the valleys about Achadh a' Chalbh had lately begun to keep on the strength of the crowds the gathering-ground drew twice a year; she heard the saying said at the stone, standing among strangers with her own bundle of hides still on her back, and carried it home with her the whole long walk north the way she carried the salt, meaning at first, by her own later telling, only to have something worth the telling to set against the hides she had got for her trouble.

She had walked the better part of ten days to come so far south, by the drove-roads and the fords where the hill households kept the stepping-stones renewed, carrying her bundle of hides the whole way down and her sack of salt the whole way back, and she said afterward, to whoever at her own hearth asked her whether the walking had been worth the trading, that the salt alone would not have answered for it. Never in her own life had she stood among so many strangers at one fire as she stood among at Achadh a' Chalbh, nor heard so many households at once say the same four words together as though they had rehearsed them, which, in a manner of speaking not one of them would have owned to, they had, each in their own valley, for a lifetime before that night.

She said it first at her own hearth on the northern shore, to a household that kept no stone of its own and no gathering-ground within any number of days' walking, and it went from that hearth to the next the way any saying went among people with little enough new to tell one another, until within a handful of years a shepherd of the far north-western moor, asked by a trader what his own people held of where they had come from, could answer him with four words he had never once walked south to hear at any stone, and answer him as though the words had always been his to answer with.

Ciannait lived to see that much of it, though she never herself walked further north than the drove-roads her own beasts had always used, and she said, in the last years of her own life, to the children she had raised at her hearth two days short of the pillar, much what the old woman of that first gathering had said to her when she herself was four and thirty: that Aithris a' Chruthachaidh every child of the valleys already knew, of the god who had made the island last of all his makings and the people who grew out of its ground like grass, said the same thing the stone said, in older and longer words, and that a saying found new on a hillside was no less true for having waited so long to be said, any more than a well was less good water for having been dug only last spring rather than in the mason's own day.

She said it to them by her own hearth-fire on more evenings than any of them troubled to count while she was living to say it, and she said it to them once more, plainly and without much dressing beyond the words themselves, in the last winter of her own life, sitting close by the fire with a granddaughter's hand in her own because the cold had by then got into her joints past any warming; and it is this last saying of it, rather than any of the summers she had walked to Achadh a' Chalbh in her own strength, that her own children kept longest and passed on furthest, so that the words came down, in that one household at least, less as a stone's saying than as an old woman's, said at her own fire in her own last winter to the children who would carry it after her.

She told the granddaughter whose hand she held that winter, when the girl asked her why the words mattered so much to an old woman who could no longer make the walk to hear them said at the stone, that a saying did not need a body able to walk to it in order to go on being true, any more than Teine a' Chlachair had needed the mason himself still living to go on burning from hearth to hearth long after his own death; and she said that the girl might live to see the stone herself, or might not, and that it would be true either way, standing there with its two sayings and the one above them no one could read, whether any of Ciannait's own blood ever stood at its foot again or never did.

Ciannait died that same year, at her own hearth, in her one and seventieth year, and was buried on the ground her own people had always buried their dead on, without any coal of the vein given her in the ground, that custom never having reached so far south-west in her own lifetime; and her children kept the walk to Achadh a' Chalbh after her, some years and not others, much as Mòrnait's own daughter had kept the walk to the second stone, so that the fire at the pillar's foot did not go long unlit in any one generation's span, and the saying she had given them at her own hearth went on being said, at that fire and at others, by mouths that had never once stood at the stone themselves and never once doubted, for all that, that the words were theirs to say.

In the years after her death the pillar at Achadh a' Chalbh stood as it had stood the summer Ciannait first put her hand to it, its lower face no less plain for all the years of firelight that had played across it, its upper line no better read; and the boy who had once turned gual teine in his fingers by a fire far to the north, hearing a fire-bearer's first telling of a stone he had never seen, was by then a grown man keeping that same coal in a bag on a peg above his own hearth, walking nowhere with it, waiting, without much hope left in the waiting, for a day he did not yet know was close upon him.

# Chapter Thirty-five: Of Seathan's Snap

*VE 4,905 – 4,950*

## I. Of the Fire Coal in Seathan's Keeping

By the time the saying at the column had gone the length of the hills and back, so that a shepherd of the Doire uaine could say *Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann* to a stranger from Àth gharbh and be understood without a word of telling first, the bag at Tobar dhìreach still held two coals unanswered, and had held them so long that the households nearest the hearth had stopped troubling to ask after them at all. Five of the seven had been given up by then to the sea, the height, the earth, a man's own blood and the river below the house, each in its turn and each after its own long waiting, and the recital that named them had grown so familiar at the fire on Oidhche an Dealanaich that children said the fathers' names along with the reciter before they were old enough to know what a father was. What was left in the bag was gual teine, *gual teine*, and the coal that held every colour and answered to none, *gual bogha-froise*, the rainbow; and of the two gual teine was reckoned, by most who troubled to reckon it at all, the likelier of the pair, since fire was a thing the line already kept and fed and carried from hearth to hearth every day of its life, and it seemed a smaller step from keeping a fire to waking one than from nothing at all.

Seathan was born into the keeping of it, at Tobar dhìreach, the only son of a father whose name the reciters do not give to strangers, being one of the ten they keep back between Colla and himself; and he had gual teine in his own two hands, by his own account, before he could well remember not having it, turning it over as every child of that hearth turned it over, black and ordinary to the eye but for the faint sheen that ran through it when the light caught it a certain way, like the last colour left in an ember that has gone from red to grey. His father kept the bag until Seathan was twenty, walking with it as every keeper before him had walked, to the sea twice in Seathan's own boyhood and to the high moor once, and coming home each time with nothing to show for the walking but the same two dark coals and the same tired shrug he gave the household at the door, so that Seathan grew up, as Eòghann had grown up seven hundred years before him and Cormac five hundred years before that, watching a grown man's failure become, by long repetition, no more remarkable than the weather.

He took the bag over on his father's death, in his own twentieth year, and did not, in the years that followed, walk with it the way his father had walked. He had watched enough walking from the doorway of that same house to have formed, without ever quite saying so to anyone, a private opinion that the walking answered nothing, that a coal carried a hundred miles and thrown into water was no likelier to catch than a coal held quiet in a man's own palm by his own hearth, and that the recital's telling of five lightings — the sea taken by a man who had never before seen it, the height by a man who reasoned his way up to it, the earth by a man who buried it like the dead, the blood by a man's own hurt, the river by a man too tired to reason at all — argued, if it argued anything, that no manner of asking had yet been tried twice with the same result, and that a man might as well ask in the way that came naturally to him as go hunting after some other man's manner that had happened, once, to answer. So Seathan kept gual teine near him rather than carrying it abroad, put it into the household's own fire on the night he took the keeping and on every night since when the old fire was rekindled from the pot after some absence, watched it lie in the flame with the wood and the peat about it, unburning and unchanged while everything around it blackened and fell to ash, and took it out again each time no worse for the fire than it had gone in, and set it back in the bag, and waited.

He had put it, by his own count, into the pot once, into the fire the line held to be the mason's own, carried unbroken from hearth to hearth since Oidhche an Dealanaich; and it had lain in that fire as it lay in every other, dark and cool to the eye though the flame stood all around it, and Seathan had watched it a long while that night with the household asleep behind him, and gone to his own bed no wiser than he had sat down. He did not, after that, expect very much of any fire he put it into, though he went on putting it into fires all the same, the way a man goes on doing a small habitual thing less from any hope in it than from the discomfort of leaving off something that has become, over enough years, a part of how an evening is spent.

Seathan married, in his six-and-twentieth year, a woman named Caitir, of a household two valleys to the east that kept no coal and no telling beyond the ordinary one every hearth in the hill country now knew by heart, and she came to Tobar dhìreach knowing, as every woman who married into that house came knowing, that she was marrying a keeper and not only a husband, and that the bag on its peg above Poit an Teine was a third presence in the household that no wife before her had ever managed to be rid of, however she might in time come to be fond of it. Caitir was neither so patient with the waiting as Dearbhail had been at Eòghann's hearth seven hundred years before, nor so impatient with it as some wives of other keepers were remembered to have been; she said of Seathan, to her own kin when she visited them, that she had married a man who thought a great deal and walked very little, and that she would sooner have him sitting where she could see him of an evening, turning a black stone over in his fingers and saying nothing, than have him gone a week at a time over hill and shore the way his father had gone, and if the coal never woke at all she judged that no great loss set against a husband who came home to his own supper every night of the year.

They had children, three of whom lived past their weaning, and Seathan told Aithris a' Chruthachaidh to each in turn as it had been told to him, Coimhdeach na Fine in the grove and the smoke that stood still in a gale and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich of the three spirits, and watched each of his children, in the way of every child of that house before them, take up gual teine from its bag on some idle evening and turn it in the firelight, half in earnest and half in play, the way a child handles any wonder it has grown too used to to be properly afraid of. The years went by him in that house in much this manner, gual teine in its bag or in his hand or in some fire that could not touch it, the recital said each year on Oidhche an Dealanaich with his own name given now among the fathers who came after Colla, and no more happening in all that span, by his own reckoning of it, than happens to any man who keeps a hearth and raises children and grows, without quite meaning to, into the settled middle of his own life.

## II. Of the Warm Evening

It was the sixteenth day of an t-Ògmhios, and the evening had come on warm and still after a day of full sun, the kind of evening the high valleys got perhaps a dozen times in a good summer, when the heat stood in the ground and the midges hung thick over the burn and no one troubled to build up the hearth-fire before dark because the warmth of the day had not yet gone out of the walls. Seathan sat in the doorway of his own house with the last of the light on his hands. He had no particular business there; the doorway caught what air moved on such an evening, and the inside of the house did not.
