Gual teine was out of its bag, as it often was on a quiet evening, and he turned it in his fingers less to test it than for the plain unremarkable comfort of a smooth stone in the hand, the way another man might turn a whetstone or a knife-hilt while his mind ran on something else entirely.

He was not, that evening, thinking of gual teine at all, whatever the recital afterward made of the moment. He was thinking, so far as he could ever afterward say what he had been thinking, of the mason, and of the well the mason had been sinking on a morning nearly five thousand years further back than any living man could properly picture, and of the lightning that had come down into that well out of a storm and set a vein of black stone burning that had lain unburning under the hill since before there were hearths on the island to burn anything at all. It was an old thought, one he had turned over at that same doorway more evenings than he could count, and it came to him now, as it had come to him before, that Teine a' Chlachair had needed nothing carried to it and nothing thrown into any sea; it had simply come, in a single crack of light, out of nothing that any man beforehand could have named as its cause, the way a dry year ends in one afternoon's storm and no man can say, watching the sky the morning before, that this was the day the rain would come.

His fingers turned the coal as he thought it, working at it the way a man works absently at a thing his hands have long since learned to handle without his mind's leave, pressing and turning until the coal's outer face, dried by thirty years of handling and by that day's own sun on the doorstone, began to crumble under his thumb into a fine black dust that caught in the lines of his palm.

He did not decide to snap his fingers, and said so every time afterward that he was asked, and he was asked a great many times in the years that were left to him: his hand had done it the way a hand does a thing it has done ten thousand times before, without asking the rest of the man whether this time was different from the last, a boy's trick, a man's idle habit, the small dry crack a finger and thumb make when they are pressed and loosed the right way, and he had done it perhaps a hundred times that same summer alone, at that same doorstone, with dust of one kind or another on his fingers and his mind on something else.

He snapped his fingers.

The dust on them took fire.

It went up off the back of his hand in a small quick rush, no larger than the flare a dry twig gives when it first catches, and it was the colour of gual teine itself, a clear red-gold, brighter by a good measure than any hearth-flame he had sat beside in all his years of keeping it, and it lit the doorway around him for the length of a breath the way a struck spark lights a dark room, so that Caitir, coming to the door from within at the sound he made, saw his whole face for a moment lit from below as if he held a small sun cupped in his hand.

He shouted, more from the shock of the light than from any hurt, and beat his hand hard against the front of his coat the way a man beats out a spark that has caught in dry cloth, and the flame went out under the blow as quick as it had come, and he stood a moment with his hand still pressed to his chest before he brought it away and looked at it in the last of the daylight.

There was not a mark on it. The skin lay whole and unreddened across the back of his hand and along each finger, no different than it had lain that morning, and the black dust that had covered his fingers a moment before was gone entirely, burned away to nothing that even a careful eye could find on him.

He stood looking at his own open hand for what Caitir afterward said was a good deal longer than the thing had taken to happen, turning it front and back in what light was left, and then he sat down heavily on the doorstone where he had been sitting before, and began to laugh.

He laughed, by Caitir's telling of it, in a way she had not heard from him in all the years of their marriage: a long helpless laughing, far past the short dry laugh he gave at some jest of an evening, that bent him forward over his own knees and would not let him straighten to answer her when she asked, twice and then a third time, standing over him in the doorway with her hands still floury from the evening's baking, what in the world had come over him. Between one fit of it and the next he got out that the fire had been in his hand the whole time, that he had carried it thirty years in a bag on a peg and walked nowhere with it and asked nothing of sea or height or earth, and it had been sitting the whole while in the one place he had never once thought to ask, which was his own two hands doing what his own two hands had always done. Caitir understood perhaps a third of what he was telling her and none of why it should be so funny; she sat down on the stone beside him at last and took his hand in both of hers and turned it over herself, front and back, to see with her own eyes that there was truly no mark on it.

## III. Of the Telling at the Hearth

Word of it went from that doorway to every hearth within a day's walk before the week was out, carried first by the children, who had seen their father laughing on the doorstone in a way none of them could account for and had run to tell their mother's kin of it before they had rightly understood what there was to tell, and then by Caitir herself, who found, once she had turned the thing over in her own mind a night and a day, that she believed it a good deal more than her first hearing of it had let her believe, and said so plainly to whoever asked. Seathan told it himself at the recital that same year, on Oidhche an Dealanaich, standing at the hearth of Tobar dhìreach with the bag counted out before him as every keeper before him had counted it, one coal now gone from two to one; and he told it, by every account that came down from that telling, in much the plainer words he had used to Caitir on the doorstone, without dressing the thing up in any manner beyond the bare truth of it, that the fire had been in his own hand the whole time he carried it, in the hand and in the snap of it, the way the lightning had been in the sky the whole time before the mason ever set his wedge in the seam that woke it, and that a man could go looking a long way off for a thing he had carried on him from birth without once thinking to look there.

The old women of the line who remembered the silver's lighting in their own girlhood, and had heard from their own mothers of the black and the red-brown before that, wept a little at the telling, the recital says: no grief in it, only the plain accumulated weight of four thousand years since the grove, now come round again to a sixth answer; and there were those among the younger households, who had grown up thinking the two remaining coals no more likely ever to wake than Leac na Fèithe was likely to lift on its own, who came away from that telling with a new respect for the bag on its peg that their own fathers had not troubled to give it. The valley began, that same winter, to call the coal *gual teine*, gual teine, in the telling that had before called it only the sixth or the last-but-one, and some among the households furthest from Tobar dhìreach, hearing the tale at one remove and then at two, told it back with small changes of their own, so that within a very few years there were tellers who had Seathan snapping his fingers a-purpose, meaning to try gual teine that way as a fisherman tries a new knot, and had to be corrected by those nearer the hearth who had heard it plain from Caitir's own mouth, that there had been no purpose in it at all, only a man thinking of the mason with dust on his fingers.

There remained, after that telling, only the rainbow, *gual bogha-froise*, the coal that held every colour the eye could give a name to and had answered, in all the four thousand years since the grove, to none of them; and it was this coal, and not gual teine's own waking, that the household at Tobar dhìreach turned its mind to in the years that followed, for a man does not sit easy with one question answered while a second sits unanswered in the same bag on the same peg. Seathan, for his own part, said more than once at his own hearth that he had come to doubt any single manner of asking would serve the rainbow as it had served none of the rest by the same means twice; the sea had taken the gold, the height the snowflake, the earth the black, a man's blood the red-brown, the river the silver, and his own idle hand the sixth, and no two of those six had come by the same road, so that a man hoping to wake the seventh by copying any one of them was, to his mind, hoping against the very pattern the other six had already shown him.

He carried it to the northern shore himself, in the second year after his own coal's waking, more out of the old custom that every keeper before him had kept than from any real expectation in it, and threw it into the same grey swell his forebears had thrown coals into for generation on generation, and waded in after it in the falling light to find it exactly as dark and salt-wet as it had gone in. He carried it, the following year, down to the crossing below the house where the silver still burned under the current as it had burned since Eòghann's day, a pale fire any traveller might kneel at the bank to see, and held the rainbow a long while over the water without throwing it at all, reasoning that if the river had already taken one coal it might, given the chance, take a second without the trial of a throw; and when nothing in the water's own light or sound gave him any sign that it meant to answer, he threw it in as he had thrown gual teine's dust into nothing, and fished it out again some way downstream the next morning, cold and ordinary among the wet stones. Caitir went with him on both of those journeys, the recital says, the only keeper's wife of the line remembered to have gone rather than stayed by Poit an Teine at home, and it was she, by her own later telling to her daughters, who first said aloud what afterward became a saying among Clann na Ceiste, that the rainbow held every spirit and so belonged wholly to none of them, and might in the end be a coal no single element would ever claim for its own, whatever the line went on doing with it.

## IV. Of Seathan's Death and What Was Left

Seathan kept the bag some fifty years in all, from his father's death to his own, and in that whole span only gual teine answered him, and it answered him, as he never tired of telling it, on an evening when he had gone looking for nothing at all. He grew old at Tobar dhìreach in much the way his own father had grown old before him, the household about him thickening with grandchildren as his own children married into neighbouring hearths and brought husbands and wives back to sit at his fire, and he told Aithris a' Chruthachaidh to each new face that came into that circle as he had told it to his own children, word for word as his father had given it to him, the smoke that stood still in the gale and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich of the three spirits and the six lightings that had gone before his own; and he told, along with it now, the seventh telling that was his to give and no other man's, of the dust on his fingers and the snap and the light that had shown his own wife his face from below in a doorway at dusk.

He died in his three-and-seventieth year, at his own hearth, with Poit an Teine burning near him as it had burned near every keeper of the line before him back to Conall who first kept the vein alight; and Caitir, who was with him at the end, said afterward that his last clear words left the rainbow alone, though it had beaten him as it had beaten every keeper before him, and asked instead for gual teine, that she bring it to him from its place in the bag so that he might hold it once more in his own hand while there was still warmth in that hand to hold it with. She brought it to him, and he held it a while, saying nothing further that she could afterward make out, and was found at first light with it still closed in his fingers, cold as it had always been cold, though the hand that held it had by then gone cold as well.

The bag passed from his grave to his eldest son, a quiet man who had never expected, by his own account, to be given so great a charge while his father's hand was still warm; and Caitir stayed on at Tobar dhìreach some six years further, keeping Poit an Teine fed as she had kept it fed through the whole of her marriage, and telling, to whoever asked her at her own hearth, the same plain telling of the doorstone that Seathan had told at the recital, growing no fonder of the dressed-up versions that had gone about the valley than she had been the first year she heard them. She tried the rainbow herself once more in that time, at the river below the house, more for the comfort of doing something with it than from any hope she troubled to name, and it lay in her palm afterward as dark and unmoved as it had lain in Seathan's, and she put it back in the bag without any great disappointment in her face, by the account of those who were there, for she had long since ceased, she said, to expect that coal to answer to a woman who only wished it well and asked for nothing in return.

She died in her three-and-seventieth year also, the same age her husband had reached before her, and was buried beside him near Leac na Fèithe, and the bag by then held only the rainbow, one coal against the six that had gone before it, in a leather grown soft and dark with the handling of more generations than anyone could count since the mason first filled his tunic with it in the rain. The keeping passed on from her son's hearth in its turn, as it had passed from every keeper's hearth before, carrying the one coal still unanswered into years that Seathan and Caitir did not live to see; and the households of the high valleys, telling it over at their own fires in the winters that followed, said of gual teine what they had not troubled to say of any of the five before it, that it alone among the six already answered had asked of its keeper no long journey and no hard trial, only a tired man's idle hand on a warm evening, doing a small thing it had done ten thousand times without ever once, until that evening, being asked to answer for it.

# Chapter Thirty-six: Of the Gatherings and the Rows of the Dead

*VE 4,951 – 5,169*

## I. Of the Crowd at the Column

The saying at Calbh Cnoc ghorm had been a thing spoken to whoever stood near enough to hear it said, in the years after the column was first raised: a shepherd passing, a household come to leave an offering at the older stones nearby, a handful of children sent to fetch water from the spring below the hill who lingered to hear an old man say the words over because the words pleased them, whether or not the sense of them had yet come home. By the time Seathan's snap had been told a few winters over, that had stopped being true. Word of gual teine's waking in Seathan's hand had gone out from Tobar dhìreach faster and further than any telling before it, carried by kin visiting kin and by traders who had no kin in the matter at all but liked a good tale on the road, and it reached Achadh a' Chalbh already grown in the telling, so that some who heard it there believed the fire had come down a second time out of a clear sky rather than out of a tired man's own hand on his own doorstone. Whichever way they had heard it, they came to the column to hear the saying said properly, by someone who could be trusted to have it right, and they did not come one or two at a time any longer.

They came in tens, and then, on the nights the reciters chose for the telling, in what the households of Achadh a' Chalbh afterward judged to be some hundreds, walking in from every quarter of the hill country and camping about the stone for a night or two before they walked home again. No one had built anything at Calbh Cnoc ghorm before that; the column had stood alone on its rise with the grass growing up to its foot and nothing near it but the older markers that no one now living could say the meaning of. The first shelters went up in the year the crowd first overran the grass around the stone and trampled it to mud in a wet spring, low walls of turf and stone roofed with branches and hide, built by whoever had walked furthest and meant to stay the longest, and taken down again when the telling was over because no one yet thought of the column as a place a person lived. They were built again the next year the crowd came, on the same ground, because it was easier to raise a wall where a wall had stood before than to choose new ground and clear it; and within a lifetime there were shelters enough about the rise, rebuilt so many times over on the footings of the ones before them that a household coming for the first time could see, in the worn hollows and the packed earth between the walls, that other households had stood there before it and would stand there after.

The telling changed with the crowd, though no one who told it would have said they had changed anything. Where a single household's fire had once heard the recital from whichever elder of the line was nearest, the crowd at Achadh a' Chalbh wanted a voice that could be heard past the first ring of listeners, and got, in time, a manner of telling suited to it: slower, with a pause held after each father's name long enough for those at the back to catch it passed forward from mouth to mouth, and a way of standing on the rise above the column, with the crowd below it, that no single hearth had ever needed. Clann na Ceiste sent one of its own to Achadh a' Chalbh for the great tellings now, in the years after Seathan, a duty that fell in turn to whichever of the line could be spared from Tobar dhìreach and had the voice and the patience for it; the recital says only that it fell first to a nephew of Seathan's, a man the reciters keep among the names they do not give to strangers, and that he stood on the rise at the telling that named gual teine among the six already lit and told it, as Seathan had told it at his own hearth, without dressing the matter up beyond the bare truth of a man breaking coal-dust with his fingers on a warm evening.

He was a young man for the charge, by his own later account, and had stood the whole day before the telling watching the shelters fill and the cook-fires start up across the trampled ground, sick with a fear that had nothing to do with the words themselves, which he had known since boyhood, and everything to do with the number of faces he would have to say them to. An old woman of Achadh a' Chalbh, who had walked to every telling at the column since she was a girl and meant, she said, to walk to this one though her knees no longer thanked her for it, found him sitting apart from the fires with his hands pressed together between his knees, and asked him plainly whether he meant to lose his supper before he had given the hill country its telling. He told her he had never spoken the recital to more than a household's worth of listeners in his life, and that Seathan's telling belonged, by rights, to Seathan's own kin at Seathan's own hearth, not to a hillside of strangers who would carry it home and change it in the carrying. She said, and the recital keeps her words as it keeps few from outside the line, that a story kept in one hearth was safe from changing and safe from nothing else, and that a story given to a hillside might come back altered in a hundred mouths but would not, this way, die in the one mouth that first held it. He stood on the rise the next evening and gave the telling, and did not lose his supper, and the crowd, by every account that came down from it, wept a little at that telling as the old women of the line had wept at Tobar dhìreach, and went home in the days after and told it themselves at their own hearths with such changes, large and small, as every telling gathers in the mouths of those who were not there to hear it first.

By the middle years of that century the gathering at Achadh a' Chalbh had become, without anyone deciding that it should, a thing the hill country reckoned its year by nearly as much as it reckoned by the seasons: a night when households that never otherwise met walked toward the same rise from every quarter of the country, slept a night or two in walls that had stood, in one shape or another, longer than any one of them could remember building them, and heard a name spoken that every hearth in the hill country now knew before it left home. Some among the older households said the column had grown too crowded for its own good, and that a saying was worn thin by so much handling; more said nothing against it at all, and came again the next time it was told, and brought their children so that the children too could say they had stood under the stone and heard it.

## II. Of the Rainbow Passed Hand to Hand

In one of those years, at the great telling at the column, the keeper of the bag who had come down from Tobar dhìreach to say the Line did a thing no keeper had done before him at any gathering: when the fathers had been named and the six lightings told, and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich said, he untied the thong of the bag and took out gual bogha-froise and gave it into the hand of the woman standing nearest him in the front of the crowd, and told her to look at it and pass it on.

He had not told anyone at Tobar dhìreach that he meant to. He said afterward that he had not known he meant to until the coal was in his hand, and that it had come to him, standing on the rise over so many faces, that the coal had been kept in a bag on a peg in one house for longer than anyone could count, and tried by the hands of that house and no other, and that there were hundreds of hands on that hillside that had never touched it, and that it did not seem to him a thing any keeper could be sure of, that the coal would not answer some hand that had never been let hold it.

So it went round. It went from the woman in the front to her husband and from him to a boy beside him, and on through the crowd in the dark by the light of the fires, hand to hand, each person holding it a little while and turning it so that the firelight ran the colours across its face, gold and green and a blue that no sky wore, and passing it on. Some held it a long while and some hardly a breath. Some said something over it, low, and some said nothing. An old man who had walked four days to be there held it against his forehead with his eyes shut, and would not say afterward what he had asked of it. A girl of five, lifted up by her father to take it, put it in her mouth before anyone could stop her, and took it out again, and said it tasted of nothing, and was laughed at, not unkindly, by everyone near enough to hear.

It took the better part of the night to go round the whole crowd. The keeper stood on the rise the whole while and did not sit down, watching for it in the dark, following it from fire to fire by the stir it made where it passed; and near dawn it came back to him, carried up the rise by the same woman who had first taken it, who had gone round the crowd behind it to see that it was not lost. He took it from her and looked at it. It was as dark as it had been when he untied the thong, and as cold.

He put it back in the bag. He said, when he stood to speak again in the grey light, that the coal had been held that night by more hands than had held it in all the years since the mason, and had answered none of them, and that he did not know whether to be sorry for it or glad; for it seemed to him that a coal which would not answer to a whole hillside of hands asking it together, each in its own way, was not a coal that wanted asking at all, in the way the line had always asked, but something else, which he could not name. The crowd went home in the morning and told it at their own hearths, how they had held the seventh coal in their own hands and it had done nothing; and it was told for a long while after, by those who had been there, as the one night of their lives on which they had held the mason's vein, and it did not seem to any of them, telling it, that the coal's silence made the holding any less.

## III. Of the Burial Ground No One Had Made

Two days' walk and more to the south-east of the column, near the southern shore, on rising ground above a burial hill the hill country called Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, the dead of that country had for longer than any telling could account for been laid in the ground without ceremony that any teller thought worth keeping. No one living could say who had first chosen that hill over any other for the purpose, or why; the graves nearest the crown of it were older than the oldest names that could still be read there, and no name at all could be read there, for no hand on the island yet cut a name into stone for the dead any more than it cut one for the living. The thorn grew thick over the older mounds, and the households nearest the hill let it grow, holding that ground once given to the dead was not ground to be cleared again for any other use, though none of them could have said which ancestor had first laid down that rule, or whether it had ever been laid down in words at all rather than simply done, once, by someone whose reasons died with him, and kept ever after because no one saw cause to do otherwise.

The dead of the hill country went into that ground in the plainest way the households knew: wrapped in a cloak or a hide, laid on their side with the knees drawn up as though asleep, and covered over without marker or word beyond whatever was said at the graveside by whoever had loved them, which the reciters at Achadh a' Chalbh never kept and never claimed to keep, holding that a hearth's own grief belonged to the hearth and not to the column's telling. A few of the dead went into the ground with something of their own beside them, a knife worn smooth with handling, a comb, a string of shells from the western shore that had come to the hill country by trade a generation back and further; most went with nothing at all but the cloak they were wrapped in, for the hill country did not hold, as a rule, that the dead had need of what the living still had use for.

It was into this ground, some six score years after Seathan's snap, that a household from a hearth two valleys from Tuam Cnoc dhìreach carried a child too small to have been given more than a season's worth of a name among its own kin, and laid it in a grave dug at the western edge of the ground where the older mounds gave out into open turf.

## IV. Of Aoife's Child

Aoife had been married four years to a man of that hearth when the child was born, her first living child after two that had not lived past their first winter, and she had carried this one, by her own later telling of it, with a fear she had not let herself speak aloud to her husband or to her own mother, having buried enough already that she had stopped trusting a full nine months to mean what it seemed to mean. The child lived through its birth and through the first hard days after it, and lived through its first winter besides, thin and quiet but breathing steadily enough that Aoife's mother, who had raised six of her own and buried three, said at the turn of the year that this one, at least, she judged would live to walk. Aoife let herself believe it that winter, for the first time since the first of the two she had already lost, and she sewed, in the last of the cold months, a small coat cut to the child's own growing rather than handed down from an older cousin as its clothes had been until then, a thing she had not let herself do for either of the children before it.

It did not live to walk. The child sickened in the spring, in the way small children of that country sickened and sometimes did not recover from, without anyone being able to say afterward what the sickness had been or why it had taken this child and spared another, two houses along the same valley, that had shown the same fever in the same week; and it died in Aoife's own arms on a morning near the end of that spring, quietly, without the crying-out that had marked the deaths of the two before it, so that she said afterward she had known, before she was willing to know it, that this death was not going to be like the others.

She kept, from the leather pouch her own grandmother had left her, a sliver of an gual dathach no larger than a fingernail, black-veined and streaked through with the same gold and white and red-brown a hundred hearths in the hill country kept a piece of by then, broken long ago from some larger fragment traded down from household to household until no one troubled any longer to ask which of the seven colours it belonged to or whether it belonged to any. She had kept it as a child keeps a bright stone, without much thought of what it was, turning it over on quiet evenings the way every household with such a piece turned its own over; and on the morning the child died she took it from the pouch, without asking her husband and without, by her own account, quite deciding to do it in any way she could afterward explain, and closed it into the small cold hand before the wrapping was done, so that it went into the ground with the child rather than staying in her own keeping.

Her husband's mother said, when she heard of it, that a hearth ought not to give away a piece of an gual dathach to the dead when the living still had use for it, and there were words between the two households over the matter that neither side afterward cared to keep in the telling. Aoife did not take the sliver back, and would not be moved to, saying only, when she was pressed on it, that the child had held nothing else of its own in the whole short span of its life, no toy worn to its shape by its own hand, no coat cut to its own growing but the one small coat she had sewn it that last winter and that had gone into the ground with it besides, and that she would not begrudge it the one small dark thing that had been, for the little while it lived, given wholly to it and taken back from no one. The household buried the child at the western edge of Tuam Cnoc dhìreach with the sliver closed in its hand as she had closed it, and those who lowered it into the ground saw, before the last of the cloth was drawn over, a dark stain already spreading through the wrapping the shape and size of a small closed fist, though what had stained it, the coal or the child's own body or the two together, none of those standing at the grave could rightly say.

No other grave in all that ground, before that spring or after it through the whole span the recital covers, is remembered to have held any piece of the vein. Aoife's own mother said, in the years that followed, that she doubted any other household in that country could have done what Aoife did even if it had wished to, for want of a piece to give rather than want of the grief to give it with; An gual dathach had by then gone thin in its scattering, worn down and lost and handed on so many times over since the mason first filled his tunic with it that whole valleys held none of it at all, and a household that had kept even a sliver this long, and had not already burned it or lost it or traded it away, was rarer by that century than it had been in Colla's day. Aoife kept nothing else of the coal after that morning. She had given the one piece her house still held, and did not, so far as the telling knows, ever trouble to ask after another.

She went back, in the years after, to the western edge of Tuam Cnoc dhìreach more often than her husband's kin thought a woman ought to trouble herself with a grave already closed and grieved, walking the day's distance alone when she could spare it and sitting a while by the small mound with nothing in her hands, and she said, to the one or two who ever asked her outright what she went there to do, that she went to see whether the turf had settled evenly and to pull the thorn back before it could reach the child, which was, by that country's own reckoning, no more than any mother owed a grave, however far the walking. It was on one of these walks, in a year the recital does not trouble to fix, that she first noticed the new graves beginning to keep to a line along the western edge where before they had been scattered as the ground allowed, and remarked on it to no one, having by then grown used to watching that particular stretch of turf more closely than most.

## V. Of the Rows That Bent

The graves at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach had for longer than living memory been laid without much order beyond the plain custom of the ground: a family buried its dead near its own earlier dead where it could, and elsewhere where it could not, and no one had troubled to lay one grave square with another by any rule a stranger walking the hill could have named. That began, in the years after Aoife's child was buried at the western edge, to change in a way no single household could claim to have started and every household, once it was pointed out to them, admitted they had somehow fallen into. The newer graves, dug further out from the old crowded crown of the hill where the thorn grew thickest, began to be set in something like a line, each new grave a body's length from the last and facing the same way, heads toward the great mountains that stood blue and unreachable on the northern skyline from every part of that ground; and the line, once two or three graves had been laid to it, drew the next grave to itself the way a worn path draws the next foot that crosses that ground, until a household bringing its dead to Tuam Cnoc dhìreach a score of years after looked for the row before it looked for empty turf, and laid its own dead into the row's own line without being told to.

The rows held straight where the ground let them. Where an older grave stood in a row's path, a low unmarked swelling in the turf that no one now could put a name to but that every household knew, by long custom, not to open or to build across, the new row bent around it rather than through it, and straightened again on the far side, so that a stranger walking the ground while the thorn still allowed the rows to be seen whole could read in the bending of them the shape of every old grave that the newer dead had been laid to honour without a name to honour it by. The bending was not planned by anyone; the recital is plain on that, and every household questioned afterward agreed on it. A grave was dug in the row where the row ran, and if an old swelling stood in the row's way the diggers went round it because no one among them, not the most impious of the young men who sometimes grumbled at the extra work of the going-round, would put a spade to ground that had held a body long enough for its memory to have gone out of the world entirely. One young man of a hearth near the hill, digging his own grandfather's grave in those years and finding an old swelling square in the line he had meant to keep, said aloud to the two kinsmen working beside him that they might as well level the thing and be done with the awkward turning it cost them; and his uncle, who had dug more graves at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach than any other man then living, put down his own spade and told him plainly that a man who could not say whose grave he opened had no business opening it, grandfather's grave or no, and that the going-round cost an afternoon's awkward digging and no more, against a debt to some stranger's bones that no living man could reckon in years and had therefore no business trying to pay off with a spade. The young man dug the grave round the swelling, as every grave before his had gone round it, and did not raise the question again.

The rows grew, year on year through that century, out from the crowded crown of the hill toward the open turf at the edges where Aoife's child lay, each new row a little further out and a little more given to bending than the one before it, until the whole western face of Tuam Cnoc dhìreach showed, to anyone who stood back far enough to see the whole of it, no longer straight lines but a slow curved weaving, row folding round row folding round the swellings that no living hand had made and no living memory could explain.

Clann na Ceiste, through those same years, did not let the rainbow rest. The bag that had passed from Seathan's grave to his son passed down the line of fathers, and one of them, whose name the recital keeps from strangers, carried the one coal left in it, gual bogha-froise, north to Doire ghlas, meaning to try it in the grove where Coimhdeach na Fine had first given Diarmad Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich and where no keeper of the line, so far as the recital knew, had thought before to bring it. He walked the whole way north on his own feet, a journey of three days from Tobar dhìreach by the tracks that then ran, telling those who asked him along the road only that he went to the grove because every other ground the line had tried had failed the coal and the grove alone, of all the places the recital named, had once answered a question with more than silence. He found the oaks much as the tellings described them, tall and old with the wind loud in their crowns, and he built a small fire in the lee of a fallen trunk much as Diarmad was said to have done, and sat with gual bogha-froise turning in his hand through the evening and on into the dark, watching the firelight run the colours across its face and waiting, by his own later account, for anything at all: a smoke that stood still, a voice, even a wind that blew wrong. Nothing came. He held the coal to the coals of his own small fire until the fire burned down around it, and it lay black and cold among the ash in the grey of the morning, no likelier to catch than it had been the evening before, and the grove gave him, in a whole night's waiting, nothing that any teller afterward thought worth calling an answer.

He carried it home again, and told, at the next great telling at Achadh a' Chalbh, that the grove itself had answered him nothing, so that the crowd who had begun to hope, on hearing where he had gone, that Coimhdeach na Fine might speak again as it had spoken to Diarmad, went home disappointed of that hope along with every other. The line tried the coal again after him, at the sea and at the river and once, by one keeper's own idea, buried a night in the earth as the black coal had once been buried; and it answered none of them, through all the years the recital covers in this telling, any more than it had answered Seathan or Caitir before them.

Aoife lived on at her own hearth some forty years past her child's burial, raising two children born after it who lived to grow, and telling, to those of her own kin who asked her, the plain account of the sliver and the small stained cloth, growing no fonder with age of the versions that went about the valley with more grief dressed into them than her own telling ever gave it. She died in her seventieth year, and was carried to Tuam Cnoc dhìreach and laid in the row nearest the western edge where her child already lay, the row bending a little as it reached her grave to keep clear of the old swelling that had stood there, unnamed and unopened, since before either of them was born.

# Chapter Thirty-seven: Of the Panther Roads

*VE 5,170 – 5,299*

## I. Of the Cats That Kept Their Own Time

Beithir had herded on the high shoulders of the central mountains since he was a boy too small to carry a full crook, and he had never in all those years thought the great cats of the passes kept anything that could be called a custom, any more than the weather kept one, or the frost. They were there in the high country the way stone was there, a thing a herder learned to walk around rather than a thing that came and went by any order he could set his own days by. His own father had lost a ewe and a half-grown lamb to something on the high ground in a single bad summer of Beithir's childhood, and had said afterward only that the high pasture took its toll the way any pasture with a drop and a river and a hungry winter took its toll, naming no one thing above the rest as the cause of it. It was in the twenty-second year of a life spent among those shoulders, in a winter cold enough that the sheep's breath hung about them like a second, whiter fleece, that he first let himself believe otherwise.

He had gone up past the last shieling with two dogs and no company to look for three ewes that had wandered from the flock in the days before, and he found, in a saddle of ground between two peaks where the snow lay unbroken from one week's end to the next, a line of prints going through it that were not sheep and not deer and not his own dogs: broad, round-toed, sunk deep, spaced in the long easy stride of something that had not been hurrying and had not needed to. He had seen such prints before, singly, here and there over the years, and thought no more of them than a man thinks of a single crow. What stopped him now was that the line ran straight, from the saddle's western lip to its eastern one, as though the ground between held nothing to turn a beast aside for, and that when he cast about he found the same line, worn a little into the frozen turf as though feet before these had gone the same way, running on both sides of the saddle as far as the fall of the ground let him see it.

He did not find his ewes that day, and did not go looking for them the day after either, for the same track, followed a short way east with the dogs close at his heel and their hackles up the whole time, brought him within scent, though not within sight, of what had made it: a smell low and rank on the wind that put both dogs flat to the ground with their ears back before he had done more than take three steps past the last drift. A long while he crouched at that distance with his hand on the older dog's neck, more to still his own breathing than the animal's, and saw nothing move against the white of the slope above him, though the smell came and thinned and came again on the wind as if whatever carried it were pacing rather than standing still. Turning home without argument, he told what he had seen and smelled to the oldest man of his own hearth, who heard him out over the evening fire without any great surprise in his face, and said only that his own father had told him the same of that same saddle, in a different year, and that his father's father was said to have told it before him: that the great cats of the mountains did not wander the high ground at every season as a man might wander it, but crossed it, at some times of year and not at others, along lines they seemed to hold in the same regard a shepherd held a path.

No one in that country could have said, that year or for long after it, what set the times the cats kept, only that they were kept; that the same saddle, and others like it further along the spine of the mountains, lay empty of that smell and that track through most of the year and thick with both at two turns of it, once when the year climbed toward its warmest and once when it fell back toward its coldest, and that a household with beasts on the high pasture in those weeks did well to bring them down before the smell came, and ill to leave them up after it had. Beithir lived to be an old man himself, and told the saddle's prints to his own sons and their sons after him, and by the time he died the households of that country had begun to reckon those two turns of the year as surely as they reckoned the salmon run below or the geese going over, without any one of them being able to say, any more than his own father's father had been able to say, why the cats kept the roads they kept, or what walked them, or where.

## II. Of the Signs on the Gateposts, and the Thirty Head

The custom that grew up around the cats' crossing was not decided in any one place or by any one household, any of those who kept it agreed, when they were asked; it grew the way the rows at a burial ground grow, each household falling into the shape the households before it had already worn into the ground. Within a lifetime it had a shape plain enough that a stranger walking from one valley to the next in the crossing weeks could read it on every gatepost he passed without being told what it meant: a mark cut fresh into the wood at the turn when the smell and the track first came back to the high saddles, and scraped away again, flat and pale against the weathered grain around it, at the turn when both were gone.

It was not, so far as any teller of that country ever claimed, a mark that spoke to the cats themselves, or asked anything of them, or warded anything off; it spoke to the household's own kin and to whatever traveller might pass the gate in those weeks, saying plainly that the high ground behind this post was closed for the season, in the same way a low branch bent across a path said that the ground beyond it belonged, for the time being, to something better left alone. A woman new-married into a hearth on the eastern side of the mountains, coming from a valley too far south to lie under the cats' road at all, asked her husband's mother, the first crossing season she kept there, why the mark was cut so deep it scarred the post rather than simply chalked or tied on with a strip of hide as she had seen other warnings given in her own country; and the old woman told her that a mark meant to be scraped off again wanted cutting deep enough to still be read in the scraping, so that a household coming late to a gate already marked and already half cleared would know, from the pale scar under the fresh growth of weather, that the season had been kept there before and would be kept there again, whether or not the wood itself still carried the cut.

The camps in the high passes emptied with the same regularity the gateposts marked. Shielings that stood full through the warmer half of every year, herders and their dogs and their fires among them from the last frost to the first, stood bare through the two turns the cats kept, walls standing, hearths cold, the paths worn to them by summer's traffic left to close over with grass the herders themselves had trampled flat only weeks before. A boy sent up in error one crossing season, his own father having lost the count of days in a wet spell that blurred one week into the next, found the shieling he was to have wintered sheep at already stripped and shuttered by households further along who had read the signs aright, and came down again the same evening with nothing worse to show for the mistake than a scolding and a night's walk wasted, which the country afterward told as the mildest lesson the crossing season ever gave anyone, set against what it gave others.

Not every household held by the custom with the same care, and the country did not let the ones who broke it forget what it had cost them. Some years after, a man of the lower slopes, whose grazing ran further up into the passes than most and whose herd had grown large enough that the high pasture's extra weeks of grass had come to matter more to him than it had to smaller households, judged that the crossing that year had come early enough in its own turning that he could risk another ten days on the height before he brought his cattle down, the gateposts of his neighbours already scraped and closed while his own stood freshly cut and, in his own reckoning, cut too soon. His wife had asked him, the evening before, why he trusted his own count of the year over the marks his neighbours had already made of theirs, and he had told her that a man who grazed that ground summer on summer knew its temper better than any post cut by a household two valleys off, and that ten days of good grass was ten days he did not mean to give away for nothing.

He was not a fool by any account the country kept of him afterward, only a man who trusted his own eye over the mark on another man's post, and who had grazed that same high ground long enough without incident that the custom had come, in his own mind, to look more like caution than like law. He brought the cattle down himself on the tenth night, later than any neighbour would have risked it, driving them by torchlight down a track he could have walked with his eyes shut, and found in the morning that thirty head of the herd he had driven up whole had not come down with the rest, scattered wide of the track in the dark and never called back to it, though the drovers with him swore they had heard nothing in the night beyond the ordinary complaint of beasts unsettled by a strange path in the dark. What they found, searching the ground above the track by daylight two days after, when the smell that had kept them from searching sooner had at last thinned enough to risk it, the recital does not dwell on past the bare count: thirty head, and not one whole carcass among them worth the skinning, the ground about them torn in a way no wolf of that country tore ground.

He kept cattle after that, and grazed the lower slopes as every prudent household of that country grazed them, but he never again cut a gatepost sign later than his neighbours, and the tale of his thirty head was told at hearths a long way from his own for longer than his own name was, so that by the time Cairbre was a grown man on the southern shore, a full week's walk and more from the slopes where it had happened, the count of thirty head lost in a single crossing season was a thing every household along that coast could recite though few of them could have said whose herd it had first been lost from, or in which of the mountains' many high passes it had happened.

## III. Of the Cats That Turned Back

It was given, among the tellings the country kept of the crossing season, that the cats themselves might be read for a sign, though no one professed to know what mind, if any, lay behind what they were seen to do. In a later year, in a crossing that had begun ordinarily enough, with the smell coming up to the high saddles at the turn it always came and every gatepost along that stretch of the mountains cut fresh in its own week, a family watching from a rise above the track by daylight, at a safe remove and for no better reason than that the rise gave the clearest view of weather coming in from the west, saw the line of beasts that had begun crossing toward the eastern passes turn, without any cause the watchers could see, and go back the way they had come, down off the road and away toward the foothills on the western side, where by every account that country kept, the cats did not commonly linger once the crossing season had called them onto the high ground at all.

The family that saw it told it plainly, without dressing the matter in more meaning than the bare sight gave it: that the beasts had turned, that they had gone down rather than on, and that no one among the watchers could say why, since nothing in the weather or the ground that day looked to a human eye any different from a hundred crossings before it that had gone through to their own end without a turning. It was the households further along that stretch of country, hearing the telling in the weeks after, who first said aloud what the family who had seen it had been careful not to say themselves: that a sign so plain, and so far outside anything the crossing season had shown before, ought to be answered rather than merely watched, and that a hard winter was coming on the strength of it whether or not the turning cats had meant to say so.

They stored double that autumn against a want that had not yet shown itself in any other sign, peat cut and stacked higher than any household along that stretch had troubled to stack it in living memory, grain and dried meat laid by past what the ordinary count of mouths at each hearth called for. Households further off, who had the turning only at second hand and no rise of their own to have watched it from, stored single as they always had, and some among them said afterward, when word of the hard winter reached them too, that they envied their neighbours nothing so much as a rise with a clear view west and a family willing to trust their own eyes over an unbroken habit. The winter that came on after that autumn proved, by the time it broke, hard enough that snow lay to a grown man's waist in drifts along the lower valleys for the better part of two months, and every household that had stored against it said afterward it had been worth the extra cutting and the extra carrying, and not one of them claimed to know any better than before why the cats had turned, only that they had turned, and that the winter had come as if in answer.

## IV. Of Cairbre and the Eleven

Cairbre was thirty-two years old, and had led men of his own hearth on lesser errands into the foothills often enough that no one on the southern shore thought twice about it when he said, one autumn, that he meant to take ten with him up past the last of the low pastures to bring back a household of kin that had settled two valleys further in than any of the shore's own people commonly went, and whose harvest that year, word had come down, had failed badly enough that they would not see the winter through unhelped. His wife stood at the edge of Teallaichean a' Chladaich the morning the eleven set out, with their own two children at her skirts, and asked him only how many days he judged it, so that she would know when to begin watching the track for them; he told her twelve at the most, ten men's worth of harvest to carry down and no cause in the world to linger once it was loaded, and kissed her once before he took the path inland with the others behind him in single file, each carrying less on the way up than he meant to carry on the way down.

It was not, by his own reckoning and by the reckoning of every man who went with him, a crossing-season errand. The geese of the coast below Teallaichean a' Chladaich had not yet gone over in their numbers that autumn, and the shore held, as it had always held, that the geese going over marked the turn of the year toward the cold reliably enough to set a household's own calendar by; and the geese, that particular autumn, held later on the southern water than any of the eleven men setting out could remember them holding in their own lifetimes. Cairbre had said as much himself, the evening before, to an old man of the shore who asked him only in passing whether he had thought to reckon the mountain's own time against the coast's, and not against the season the geese were keeping that year down on the water; Cairbre answered, not unkindly, that the geese were the surest clock the shore had ever kept faith with, and that he saw no cause to trust a stranger's gatepost over a sign his own household had watched every year of his life.

They went up in good order, by the account the search that followed them later pieced together from what could be read of their camp-sites and their fire-scars along the way, keeping to the lower ground as long as the lower ground offered a path and climbing only where the valley they followed narrowed and left them no choice but the higher slopes. Cairbre had grazed no cattle in the high passes himself and knew the gatepost signs of that country only as a traveller knows another country's customs, by report rather than by his own hand on the wood; he read, at the last hearth before the true height, a post scraped bare of any mark at all, which he took, as any stranger reading it without a local tongue to ask, for a plain word that the season the mark was cut against had already come and gone. What the bare post did not tell him, because no post along that whole stretch of mountain was cut to tell it, was that the scraping that year had come early, the household who kept that gate having read the geese's own lateness as the country's other households read it, and judged, wrongly as it turned out, that a season slow to come would also be slow to hold, and cleared their post a full ten days before the smell that should have kept it standing came back up to the saddle above them.

Cairbre and the ten who went with him climbed into ground that the crossing had, in fact, already claimed for that turning of the year, reading the empty shielings and the bare posts around them as leave to go on rather than as the same closed season written in a hand they had not learned to read. They did not come down again. No household of that country, questioned afterward by the searchers who came up from the shore once the errand's length began to trouble those left behind, could say they had seen the eleven pass, or heard anything in the high ground in the nights the errand must have crossed it beyond what every household in the crossing season heard and had long since stopped remarking on. The kin two valleys in, whom Cairbre had set out to help, waited through that autumn and into the winter for a party that never reached them, and came themselves in the spring down to the shore to ask after men they had begun, by then, to fear they would never see arrive.

Cairbre's wife kept the twelfth day and the thirteenth and the fourteenth without word, and told herself, as any wife of that shore would have told herself, that a household two valleys in might have kept the eleven a few extra days over some kindness owed for the carrying, or that the track down was slower loaded than the track up had been empty. She watched the path from the same rise she had stood on to see them go, morning and evening, through a fifteenth day and a twentieth, and by the thirtieth day had stopped telling herself anything at all, and only watched. No household along that shore sent word up into the hills after them that autumn, for none of them knew, any more than Cairbre himself had known, which valley among several the eleven had meant to reach, or by which of several tracks; and winter closed the higher ground before any search could have been made of it in any case, so that the shore was left, through that whole first winter, with nothing to do but wait for a spring thaw that might, at least, let a search be tried.

The same year, at Tobar dhìreach, a son was born to the household that kept Poit an Teine and the bag of coals, a big child from his first week who closed his hand round a finger held out to him and would not readily let it go, so that they said of him, as they would go on saying of him, that he had been born holding on. He was given the name Suibhne, and grew, in the years the shore still watched for word of Cairbre and found none, into a boy old enough to be sent with the herds and old enough, when Poit an Teine's keeping fell to him in his own turn, to hear the whole of the Line said over him standing, as every keeper before him had heard it. A search was tried in the spring after the eleven went missing, and again the spring after that, men of the shore and of the two valleys both walking the ground the errand should have crossed as far as the season allowed them, and both times came down again with nothing to show for the walking but blistered feet and a country too wide, and too indifferent to a searcher's want of answers, to give up eleven men for the asking.

## V. Of the Bones Along the Road

It was eighteen years before anyone found what had become of Cairbre and the ten who had gone with him, and it was chance, by every account, and not any renewed search, that found it at last: a household driving cattle down off the high pasture at the proper close of the crossing season some eighteen years after, keeping well within the marked track as every household of that country had always kept it, came on a scatter of bone some way off the track itself, where the ground fell steeply enough on one side that a man losing his footing in the dark might easily have gone down it without meaning to. The drover who found the first of it took it at a glance for a deer's remains, weathered white and half sunk into the turf, and might have driven on and thought no more of it had one of his own dogs not worried a length of it out of the ground with a fixed intent no deer-bone had ever raised in the animal before, and set it down at his feet whole and unmistakable for what it was.

They found more, over the days that followed, spread wider than any one fall could account for, some of it gathered close in twos and threes as though the men it had belonged to had stood together at the end and some of it strung out along a line that ran, when the whole of it was at last laid out and looked at together, roughly the same course the cats themselves were known to keep between one saddle and the next. Nothing that had been carried with the eleven, no strap or blade or scrap of the harvest they had gone to fetch, was found among the bones or anywhere near them, so that the searchers who gathered them could not even say for certain, past the count of the bones themselves, that this had been the whole of the party and not some lesser part of it.

Nothing about the bones themselves said plainly what had killed the men they had been, and no one who found them claimed afterward to know for certain; the households of that country, hearing the tale carried down from the shore where word of it travelled fastest, said only what they had always said of that ground in that season, that eleven men had gone up into it at the one time of year no one went up into it by choice, and that the road itself, whatever walked it, had not troubled to leave more of an answer than the bones gave. A young man from Tobar dhìreach, eighteen years old that year and newly given the keeping of his own household's fire though not yet the full charge of the Line, walked with the search that carried word of the find back down from the passes, and came home from it saying little, by the account of those who knew him, beyond the plain fact of what had been found and where.

The southern shore buried what could be gathered of the eleven where they were found, high on the mountain's own ground rather than carried the long way home, for no household among them could say with any certainty which bones had belonged to which man, and it seemed to the country a lesser wrong to lay eleven men together where the road had taken them than to guess wrongly at dividing them among eleven separate graves. Cairbre's own name outlasted the rest in the telling, as a leader's name will outlast the men who followed him, but the shore kept, alongside it, the plainer fact the whole country had already made of the matter before his bones were ever found: that the cats' road asked to be read by its own signs and no other's, that a gatepost cut for one household's season could not be trusted by a stranger's eye, and that the crossing months, whatever walked them and for whatever reason, kept a count of their own that no household's calendar, however carefully watched, had yet learned to keep exactly with it.

# Chapter Thirty-eight: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne

*VE 5,300 – 5,324*

## I. Of a Child Born Slow to Speak

Suibhne was a boy of eighteen, born the same year Cairbre and the ten who had gone with him into the hills in the crossing season failed to come home, when he walked with the search that at last found their bones strung out along the cats' road at wide distances, as if the men had scattered from one another at the end rather than kept together. He carried nothing of the vein with him on that walk; there was no custom of it, and none of the households along the road had ever heard that fire of any kind would serve against what kept that road at that season. He came home from it saying little, by the account of those who knew him, and it was some years after, in his own house at Tobar dhìreach with a wife new to the keeping, that his son was born.

Ailean was a big child from the first week, heavier in the arm and the leg than any infant the women who helped at his birth could readily match against their own memory, and slow to close his hand round a finger held out to him and slower again to let it go once he had closed it, so that his mother said of him, half in complaint and half in something nearer pride, that he had been born holding on. He was slow with words as he grew, keeping to single ones while children a season younger than him at the neighbouring hearths were already stringing sentences, and there were those among his own kin who wondered aloud, in the way kin will wonder aloud over a child too young to answer for himself, whether the line had at last thrown up a son too plain to be trusted with the keeping; his mother put a stop to that talk wherever she heard it, saying that a slow tongue was no mark against a steady hand, and pointing to his hands themselves, broad already at six years old and thickening year on year after, as proof enough of what sort of man he would be.

He had, from as early as anyone could afterward call to mind, an interest in Poit an Teine that went beyond a child's ordinary fascination with flame. Other children of that hearth had been drawn to the coloured pieces in the leather bag as toys, turning them over for their colours and their smoothness and losing interest once the colours proved to give nothing back to the hand; Ailean, from the age he could sit upright unsupported, would be found by the pot for whole mornings together, not reaching for it or troubling it, only sitting near enough to feel what heat came off it, watching the low steady flame the line had kept without a break since the mason first carried it home under his cloak. His father found him there so often that he came in time to leave the boy be, saying to his own wife that a child could do worse than keep company with the one thing in the house that had outlasted every one of their forefathers, and that if the boy meant to sit and stare at it until the staring had taught him some sense, there was no harm and might be some good in letting him.

He grew into a young man built along the same broad lines as the child had promised, tall by the reckoning of the high valleys and heavier through the shoulder than his father, with hands that the old women of the household said, more than once and not always meaning it kindly, were the mason's own hands come round again after five thousand years, hands shaped for a wedge and a maul rather than for the small close work the keeping of the coals more often asked. His speech never fully caught the pace of other men's; he answered slowly, and thought visibly before he did it, so that strangers meeting him at the recital sometimes took his slowness for dullness and were corrected only once they had put a question to him worth a real answer, for what he gave back, when he gave it, was seldom the thing a quicker man would have said first. Among his own kin this was known well enough not to need remark, and the reciters who taught him Sloinneadh a' Chlachair found him no slower a pupil for it than any other, only one who wanted the words said over more times before he would trust himself to say them back whole.

## II. Of the Rainbow That Would Not Light

Suibhne kept the bag of two coals from his own father's death, a fire coal grown ordinary through generations of handling since Seathan's day and a rainbow no keeper between Seathan's household and his own had ever once coaxed into flame; and he kept, as every keeper before him had kept, the custom of trying it, some years with more hope in the trying than others. He was not, by nature, a man given to running after a thing that had already refused him a dozen times, and there were long stretches in his own keeping, a decade together on occasion, when the rainbow sat untouched in the bag while he gave his mind to the herds and the hearth and the long slow business of a household growing round him; but the recital came once a year, and every year at the recital the reciters gave the tellings of the six lightings in their order, and every year, hearing his own forefathers named one after another, Suibhne felt the old itch return to try the seventh again himself before the next telling came round.

The height he tried first, in the second year of his keeping, climbing to Binnean a' Chlachair in a morning wind that near took him off the summit and dropping the rainbow from the height of his own arm over the same steep side Fearghas had dropped the snowflake from, watching it fall the whole way to the stones below without so much as a flicker in it. The river he tried the year after, kneeling at the same crossing Eòghann had knelt at, and threw it into the current where the silver still burned beneath the water in its low steady flame, so that for a breath the rainbow lay beside a coal that was already alight, dark against bright, before the current carried it on downstream to be fished out cold some way below the house. The sea he tried once, on a hard grey autumn when the household could spare him a week for the walk, wading to his knees in water cold enough to numb the foot and throwing it out past where the gold was said to have taken fire on the swell in Aodh's day, and watched it sink without a mark on it the same as every coal before it that had not been the gold.

He tried the earth twice in different years, once digging a hole no deeper than a man's knee and once, in the year he judged himself old enough to know better and dug it anyway, a hole as deep as the grave Brian had dug for the black coal near two and a half thousand years before, laying the rainbow in it and covering it over and going back for it the following dawn to find it cold as the clay around it had been cold. By blood he would not try it; that trial he left alone all his life, saying to his own wife once, in a rare unguarded moment by the fire, that a man ought not go looking to open his own hand for a coal that had already shown him six times over that it wanted no single element and no single hurt, and that he had no wish to carry a scar for nothing the way Cormac had carried his for good cause. The small idle way that had served gual teine he never once thought to try, for that way, by its nature, could not be gone looking for; a man does not set out with a purpose to stumble on a thing by accident, and Suibhne, trying the rainbow at all, was always trying it with a purpose, which was, though he never said so in these words, half the reason it never answered him.

He was four-and-forty years old, going grey at the temple and thicker through the middle than the man who had climbed Binnean a' Chlachair in his youth, when he took the rainbow north to Doire ghlas for the first and only time in his life, walking the three days alone with the coal wrapped in a fold of cloth inside his shirt against his chest, reasoning, as his son would reason after him though by a longer road, that the place where Coimhdeach na Fine had first spoken might hold some virtue the shore and the height and the river did not. No fire did he build in the grove, having nothing to ask that a fire would serve to ask it with; he only sat under the oaks a night and a day with the coal held loose in his open palm, watching it for any change of colour or warmth that his own eyes might have missed a hundred times before in duller light, and saw none, and walked home again three days further with it cold in the same fold of cloth it had travelled north in.

He told the household, on his return, that he did not think the rainbow meant to answer to him, and that he did not know, past a certain point, whether a man ought to go on asking a question that had by then been asked in every way a man's own life could think to ask it. He said this at his own hearth and not at the recital, for he had never been a man to trouble a crowd with his own private failures, and it was among the last things of any length that Ailean, then sixteen years old and sitting near Poit an Teine as he had sat by it since infancy, ever heard his father say on the matter. Suibhne died two years after, in his forty-sixth year, of a fever that came on him hard in a wet spring and took him inside a fortnight, quick enough that there was no long dying to make a telling of; Ailean, eighteen years old and already the broadest man at that hearth though not yet its keeper by any word said over him, sat with his father through the worst of the last nights and heard nothing from him about the rainbow at all, only the ordinary things a dying man says to a son he trusts to carry on the herd and the house without him.

## III. Of Lìobhan and the Thought That Came

Ailean had married the year before his father died, taking Lìobhan of a household two valleys west that kept no coal of its own and had never, by her own telling, expected to marry into a keeping at all; she had known him three summers at the recital before either of them said anything of marriage, drawn, as she told her own daughter, less by his slow careful speech than by the way he sat with animals and small children alike, as a man sits who has never once in his life needed to raise his voice to be minded. She came to Tobar dhìreach a bride of fifteen, young even by the valley's own reckoning, and found herself within the year keeping house at the hearth of Poit an Teine, learning from Suibhne's own widow, in the short time that remained to teach her, how the pot was fed and how the bag was kept and what was and was not said of its contents to a stranger at the door.

Their daughter was born the same year Suibhne died, in a wet autumn that the household afterward remembered chiefly for having buried one keeper and welcomed one child within the turn of a single season; they named her Gormshuil, for the colour of her eyes at birth, which Lìobhan's own mother swore had never once in all her years attending births looked so blue so soon. Ailean was eighteen that year, a father and, by his father's death, the keeper of the bag as well, though he did not think of himself in those words for some time after, going on much as he had gone on before, minding the herd and sitting his evenings by the pot with his daughter more often than not asleep against his shoulder.

He tried the rainbow himself, in the first years of his keeping, much as his father had tried it before him, though with less patience for the long solitary journeys his father had made of it; he threw it in the river once and dropped it from the height once and dug it into the earth once, in each case finding it as cold afterward as his father had always found it, and came away from each trial a little more short with himself for having expected, however faintly, some different end to it than the end six generations of keepers before him had already reached. It was Lìobhan, by her own account given years later to her own grandchildren, who first said aloud to him what he had by then half thought and not yet let himself say: that a coal made, by Coimhdeach na Fine's own telling, of every colour together might not be a coal that any single element, taken alone, would ever own as its own, any more than a man born of two households could be said to belong wholly to either one.

Ailean turned that thought over through the better part of a winter, by the fire and at the herding and on the long walks a shepherd takes alone with sheep for the only company, and it grew in him slowly, the way his own words had always grown in him slowly, until it had settled into something nearer a certainty than a guess: that the six coals had each answered a single spirit because each of them, sea and sky and earth and blood and river and the small fire in a man's own hand, was a thing wholly on its own; the seventh held all six spirits at once, and so could not be woken, he came to believe, by offering it to any one of them alone, any more than a man could satisfy six hungry guests by setting a single dish before whichever one happened to be nearest the door. If the rainbow held every spirit, he reasoned, then it wanted every spirit answered at once, brought together in the one place and the one hour, so that whatever bound the coal shut might hear all six speak to it together rather than one after another across a hundred separate years.

He said as much to Lìobhan on an evening in his three-and-twentieth year, turning the rainbow over in his own broad hand by the fire while Gormshuil, five years old by then, slept curled against her mother on the far side of the hearth, and Lìobhan, hearing him say it slowly and carefully as he said everything, told him only that it sounded to her like a thing worth the trying, since nothing else in six generations had been. He did not go to the recital that year with any announcement of what he meant to do; he told the reciters only, when his turn came to stand and give his portion of the Line, that he meant in the year ahead to light the six again himself, one by one, by each one's own old way, and carry them living to wherever the seventh might at last be answered, and the reciters, who had heard bolder claims than this from keepers before him come to nothing, said only that they would wait to hear how it went before they put any new line into the telling.

## IV. Of the Six Kindled Again

Ailean began with the gold, in the last warmth of that same year, walking the day's road north to the shore with a fresh piece of the vein's colour carried loose in his palm the whole way, as Aodh had carried the seven before him, and a clay pot slung at his hip with a lid of green turf cut that same morning to fit its mouth. The northern sea in that season ran grey and short-tempered, breaking hard on the shingle under a sky the colour of wet slate, and he stood a long while at the water's edge before he waded in; it was the plain cold of it that held him back, and no fear of what would happen, for no telling of Aodh's day had ever troubled to mention the cold. Then he threw the coal out past the breaking water with an underhand cast that sent it further than a smaller man could have managed, and watched it strike the swell and take, exactly as the telling gave it, a flame the colour of its own sheen that rode the heave of the sea bright gold until a wave rolled over it; only this time, where Aodh had let it burn out on the water and gone home with an empty hand, Ailean waded in after it to the waist, careless of the cold, and caught it up still burning between his cupped hands the way a man catches a moth without crushing it, and carried it, dripping and alight, back up the shingle to the waiting pot, where it went on burning under its lid of turf all the long walk home, fed each evening with driftwood he gathered as he went.

Before the winter closed the height he climbed to Binnean a' Chlachair, carrying the second pot on his back beside the first, and stood in a wind cold enough to make his own teeth ache exactly as it had made Fearghas's teeth ache, and let gual sneachda fall from the height of his own arm as his forefather had let it fall, and watched it catch fire halfway down the steep side and burn white against the grey rock in the failing light. Going down after it took him longer than the wading had taken, the ground there being steeper and the light worse; he found it still burning where it had fetched up against a shelf of stone, and lifted it with a flat piece of slate into the second pot, and carried both fires down off the height together in the last of that day's light, the gold and the white swaying against each other in their pots on his shoulders with every step.
