The black he woke at home, needing no journey for it, digging a hole beside the old slab as deep as a grave in the last week before the ground froze hard, and laying the third coal in it and covering it over as Brian had covered his five, and going back to it at first light the next morning to find it warm in his hand and glowing at its heart the dark red Brian's own telling had given it, so that he had three fires burning in three pots under his own roof before the shortest days of that year were out, and Lìobhan said afterward that the house that winter never once in her memory stood so bright of an evening, with three low flames instead of one keeping the dark back from the walls.

He woke the red-brown in the early spring, alone in the yard behind the house on a morning grey with the last of the frost, setting the fourth coal on a flat stone as Cormac had set his and striking it with a hammer meant for splitting kindling, and the hammer turned on the coal's hard face as it had turned on Cormac's and came down across the back of his own left hand, laying it open near to the bone; he stood a long moment watching his own blood run down over the coal on the stone before the pain of it reached him at all, and where the blood touched the coal a flame came up the colour of the coal, deep and warm as firelight seen through oak leaves, and Ailean lifted it into its pot with his good hand while the other bled freely down his sleeve, and only then went in to have Lìobhan bind the wound, by which time the bleeding had slowed of its own accord and the scar it left, when it healed, sat white and puckered across the back of his hand much as the old tellings said Cormac's own scar had sat across his.

He woke the silver at the river below the house on an evening in early summer, kneeling at the same crossing Eòghann had knelt at and drinking from his cupped hands before he threw the fifth coal into the current, less from any need to test the water's taste, which every child of that hearth had known from infancy, than from a wish to do the thing whole, in the manner the telling gave it, rather than skip to the part that mattered; the coal took fire as it went under exactly as Eòghann's had taken fire, burning silver on the riverbed while the current ran over it and could not put it out, and Ailean lifted it out with a shallow wicker scoop he had made for the purpose and set it, wet and still alight, into the fifth pot.

The sixth he woke without meaning to, on a warm evening near midsummer, sitting on his own doorstone with the last fragment of the old fire coal crumbling to dust between his fingers as he turned over in his mind the whole year's work and what remained of it, thinking, as it happened, of nothing at all to do with fire; his fingers closed the way a hand closes on its own account when a man's mind has gone elsewhere, and snapped without his asking them to, and the dust on them caught and flared red-gold for the length of a breath before he beat it out against his coat from old habit though it left, as it had left Seathan, not a mark on him. He sat looking at his own open hand a good while by the last light, and then went in and told Lìobhan only that the sixth was done, and did not trouble to say how, for it seemed to him, once it was over, too small and too accidental a thing to make a telling of, though Lìobhan drew the whole of it out of him before the night was over all the same.

## V. Of the Road North

Six fires stood that summer under one roof for the first time since the making of the world, each in its own clay pot with its own lid of turf, fed morning and evening by a man who had by then, without quite noticing the change come over him, stopped sleeping a full night through, waking instead at odd hours from long habit to see that none of the six had failed. He kept them through the last weeks of that summer at Tobar dhìreach, going about the ordinary business of the herd and the house by day and tending the pots by evening, while Lìobhan watched him grow thinner and quieter across those weeks and said nothing against it, having by then no more doubt than he had that the year's work was not yet finished. Gormshuil, six years old that summer, was kept from the pots by her mother's word, though she was found more than once crouched at a safe distance watching the lids lifted and the low strange colours beneath them, gold and white and the black coal's low red glow, silver, and the deep red-brown of the fifth, with the plain wide-eyed attention of a child who knows well enough that no other house in her own memory has ever kept the like.

In the last week of an t-Iuchar he set out for the grove, carrying the six pots slung in pairs from a pole across his shoulders, three to a side, with the seventh coal, the rainbow, wrapped in its old fold of cloth inside his shirt against his chest where his father had once carried it the same way. Lìobhan walked with him as far as the last hearth before the moor, carrying Gormshuil on her hip, and said little at the parting beyond that he should mind his feet on the northern slopes, which were wet that year even in high summer, and that she would keep the house fire as she had always kept it until he came home to it. Three days he walked alone, the pole's weight settling into a rhythm across his shoulders that he found, by the second day, he no longer noticed except when he set it down, and slept each night in the lee of whatever rock or bank offered itself, tending the six fires by starlight before he lay down and again before first light, so that he came into each new day already a little short of sleep and grew no less short of it as the days went on.

He came down into Doire ghlas on the twenty-first day of an t-Iuchar, with the light already going long and gold through the oaks and no wind at all in the crowns of the trees, a stillness he had not looked for after everything the tellings said of the gale that had met Diarmad in that same grove four thousand years before. There he set the six pots down in a ring among the roots of the oldest oak he could find, and lifted their lids one after another, and stood back to watch six fires stand up together out of the leaf-litter in their six colours, gold and white and the black coal's deep red and the red-brown of his own blood and the river's silver and the clear fire-colour that had once been dust on his own hand, closer together than any six of them had stood since the day each was first found. Never in his life had he seen more than three of them burning under one roof at once, and he stood a long while looking at the ring of them before he set the rainbow down in the bare ground at its centre and sat down himself beside it to wait, for every telling that had come down to him said that this was the place Coimhdeach na Fine came, if it came at all.

It was there before the light had wholly gone, standing among the oaks the height of a tall man and made, as the old telling had it, of smoke that did not move with the smoke of his own six fires though that smoke blew past it steadily on whatever small air still stirred in the grove. Ailean looked at it a long moment, and it was Coimhdeach na Fine that spoke first.

"You have brought them all," it said.

"All I could," said Ailean. "The last will not light."

It said nothing to that for a moment, and the six fires around him burned on without a sound in the stillness of the grove, gold and white and black-red and the river's silver and the dark warm red-brown and the last clear flame that had been dust on his own fingers. Then it came forward into the ring, stooping low over the bare coal at its centre where Ailean had set it, and where it stooped the rainbow took fire.

Ailean said afterward, to the few he ever spoke of it to at all, that he could not have named the colour of that flame to save his life, for it would not hold still long enough to be named, running through every colour the six fires around it held and others besides that he had no word for; and the six fires themselves, gold and white and black and red-brown and silver and the clear fire-red, leaned in toward it all together where they stood in their ring, the way grass in six different places leans the same way in one wind, and for the first time since the making of the world all seven coals of the island burned together, each out of its own spirit and all of them now out of one flame besides.

"Stay with them," Coimhdeach na Fine said, "until they are cold."

# The Annals of the Age

## The Years VE 1 – 500

- <a id="ev-I-0001"></a>**20 am Faoilleach, VE 1** — *The mason's fire*. Neachdan, a mason splitting rock for a well, breaks into a vein of hard coal that shows every colour in the break. That night a storm comes over the hills, and lightning strikes the broken vein, and it takes fire. He carries a burning coal home and lays the first hearth: it is the first fire of the Dia-thìrich. On it he tries the other coals he broke out, and all burn alike, with a low black flame; he is glad of the fire all the same.
- <a id="ev-EI-1001"></a>**10 an Gearran, VE 1** — *The spring under the shoulder of the hill fails*. The spring that fed Neachdan's valley thins through a wet season and fails by the dark of the year, leaving four households to carry water a mile and a half by skin. The valley meets and chooses to sink a well of its own.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1002"></a>**11 an Gearran, VE 1** — *Neachdan chosen to sink the well*. The households of the failed spring choose Neachdan, the best splitter of stone among them, to dig a new well. He has already gone to mark the shaft while the others are still weighing whether the old spring might return.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1001"><em>The spring under the shoulder of the hill fails</em>, 10 an Gearran, VE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1003"></a>**17 am Màrt, VE 1** — *Neachdan's hands split at the knuckle*. Through the dead of the year Neachdan digs the new well with wedge and oak maul in sleet and frost. His hands split at the knuckle and never close between one day's work and the next, and Sorcha rubs sheep-fat into the cracks each night.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1002"><em>Neachdan chosen to sink the well</em>, 11 an Gearran, VE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1004"></a>**18 am Màrt, VE 1** — *Neachdan fills his tunic with the coloured stone*. Breaking into the black seam, Neachdan finds pieces streaked gold, white, red-brown and silver, and one that holds every colour at once. Knowing no name or use for them, he judges them too beautiful to leave in the flooding shaft and carries them home against his chest.<span class="fn fl">○ Same place <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1003"><em>Neachdan's hands split at the knuckle</em>, 17 am Màrt, VE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1005"></a>**27 an Giblean, VE 1** — *Neachdan shelters as the storm breaks*. A storm comes up the valley at dusk with a green-black sky. Neachdan caps the shaft and takes shelter under a crag above it rather than go back down into a flooding hole, and watches the light change to a thick yellow-brown before the sky breaks.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1004"><em>Neachdan fills his tunic with the coloured stone</em>, 18 am Màrt, VE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1006"></a>**28 an Giblean, VE 1** — *Neachdan finds the vein still burning under the rain*. After the lightning strikes his capped shaft, Neachdan uncovers it to find the black seam awake along its whole face, breathing heat and a dark red flame that the driving rain cannot drown, only turn to a thin white smoke off its surface.<span class="fn fl">○ Same place <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1005"><em>Neachdan shelters as the storm breaks</em>, 27 an Giblean, VE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1007"></a>**2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1** — *Neachdan weeps at the well's mouth*. Kneeling at the shaft with his hands held over the burning vein, Neachdan feels warmth reach his split and aching knuckles for the first time since the winter began, and weeps at the well's edge in the storm.<span class="fn fl">○ Same place <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1006"><em>Neachdan finds the vein still burning under the rain</em>, 28 an Giblean, VE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1008"></a>**12 an t-Iuchar, VE 1** — *The household gathers at the first hearth*. Neachdan sets the carried coal on a swept ring of earth in his house. Sorcha, the boy Conall, and three younger children watch the first flame any household on Dia-thìr has ever kept, unsure at first whether it is dangerous.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1007"><em>Neachdan weeps at the well's mouth</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1009"></a>**13 an t-Iuchar, VE 1** — *The household learns the fire can be fed, and can die*. As the first coal burns down to ash-grey crust, Neachdan breaks it open and finds it still glowing beneath. Sorcha feeds it dry heather from the bedding stack, and the household understands, in one night, that the fire must be fed or it will go out.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1008"><em>The household gathers at the first hearth</em>, 12 an t-Iuchar, VE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1010"></a>**16 an Lùnastal, VE 1** — *Sorcha burned by the fire*. Feeding the fire a second time, Sorcha brushes her palm against the ash-grey crust of the coal, mistaking it for cold stone, and is burned across the base of her fingers. It is the first hurt any hearth on the island gives.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1009"><em>The household learns the fire can be fed, and can die</em>, 13 an t-Iuchar, VE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1011"></a>**26 an t-Sultain, VE 1** — *The household sets the rule of the stick*. After Sorcha's burn, the household sets a rule kept ever after: the fire is fed with a stick's length between hand and flame, never with a bare palm. Sorcha teaches it to the younger children before dawn, showing them her reddened hand.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1010"><em>Sorcha burned by the fire</em>, 16 an Lùnastal, VE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1012"></a>**27 an t-Sultain, VE 1** — *Neachdan says the fire must not go out*. At dawn, with the storm spent and his household warm for the first time any of them can remember, Neachdan kneels by the fire with his hand on the cold earth and says it must not go out. Sorcha pledges to feed it as long as she has hands.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1009"><em>The household learns the fire can be fed, and can die</em>, 13 an t-Iuchar, VE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1013"></a>**1 an t-Samhain, VE 1** — *The well begun below the flat stone*. Neachdan sets the first wedge on a rise a little east of the dead spring, where the older men of the valley say the rock runs true, and works through the dead of the year a hand's depth at a time.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1012"><em>Neachdan says the fire must not go out</em>, 27 an t-Sultain, VE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1014"></a>**7 an t-Samhain, VE 1** — *The rock runs dark under the wedge*. By the fifteenth day of the digging the shaft is over Neachdan's head and the rock has begun to run from grey to black, ringing under the maul instead of cracking clean.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1013"><em>The well begun below the flat stone</em>, 1 an t-Samhain, VE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1015"></a>**11 an Dùbhlachd, VE 1** — *Heather first fed to the fire*. Sorcha lays a handful of dry bedding-heather against the failing coal on the first night, and the fire takes it faster and brighter than it took the stone; the household learns that the thing can be fed.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1012"><em>Neachdan says the fire must not go out</em>, 27 an t-Sultain, VE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1016"></a>**12 an Dùbhlachd, VE 1** — *The first dawn by a fire*. The household sits awake round the fire through the whole first night, and at grey dawn the children wake reddened by its glow instead of blued by the cold, for the first time in their lives.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1014"><em>The rock runs dark under the wedge</em>, 7 an t-Samhain, VE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1017"></a>**27 an Giblean, VE 2** — *Meat first set to the fire* (Tobar dhìreach). A haunch of mutton hung too low over the hearth browns in the night, and the household wakes to a smell none of them has ever smelled; within a season meat is laid on stones heated at the fire's edge.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1016"><em>The first dawn by a fire</em>, 12 an Dùbhlachd, VE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1018"></a>**30 am Faoilleach, VE 3** — *Ailbhe born by the hearth* (Tobar dhìreach). A daughter is born to Neachdan and Sorcha so close to the fire that the women turn her aside for fear of a spark. She is the first child of the hill country to open her eyes by firelight rather than daylight alone. They name her Ailbhe.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1017"><em>Meat first set to the fire</em>, 27 an Giblean, VE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1019"></a>**28 an Gearran, VE 3** — *The stone kept at the hearth's edge for meat* (Tobar dhìreach). A flat stone is kept at the edge of the mason's hearth for the cooking of meat and nothing else, and the knowing of it goes out with every coal the household gives.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1018"><em>Ailbhe born by the hearth</em>, 30 am Faoilleach, VE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1020"></a>**29 am Màrt, VE 4** — *Teine a' Chlachair begged and given* (Tobar dhìreach). A neighbouring household, its own hearth cold, comes asking for a coal of Teine a' Chlachair. Neachdan gives it freely and will not hear of any debt for it, telling his children that a fire withheld from a cold house is worse than a fire given away unthanked.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1018"><em>Ailbhe born by the hearth</em>, 30 am Faoilleach, VE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1021"></a>**28 an Gearran, VE 5** — *Fire first carried in a pot* (Tobar dhìreach). The household hearth drowns in a night of driving rain. The boy Conall runs alone in the dark to the burning vein, scrapes a live coal into a clay water-pot banked round with cold ash, and carries it home to relight the fire. It is learned that fire need not stay where it is born.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1016"><em>The first dawn by a fire</em>, 12 an Dùbhlachd, VE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1022"></a>**1 am Faoilleach, VE 6** — *The hearth dies in the wet spring* (Tobar dhìreach). Three days of driven rain come through the thatch in the fifth spring after the lightning and put out the hearth in the black hour before dawn, with Neachdan from home.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1021"><em>Fire first carried in a pot</em>, 28 an Gearran, VE 5</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1023"></a>**30 am Faoilleach, VE 6** — *Conall relights the hearth from the vein* (Tobar dhìreach). Conall, eleven years old, runs barefoot through the rain to the burning vein with his mother's water-pot, scrapes a live piece into it, and brings the fire home to the dead hearth before his mother wakes.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1022"><em>The hearth dies in the wet spring</em>, 1 am Faoilleach, VE 6</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1024"></a>**24 an t-Ògmhios, VE 12** — *The hut on the heather burns*. A near household's fire, laid on packed heather, catches unseen from beneath and breaks into open flame under a heather roof. The family escapes with nothing saved. It is the first house lost to fire since the mason carried his home.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1023"><em>Conall relights the hearth from the vein</em>, 30 am Faoilleach, VE 6</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1025"></a>**23 an t-Iuchar, VE 12** — *Conall's word: fire keeps to stone*. Watching the burned household in its ruined yard, the young Conall says plainly what he has half understood since he was eleven: that a fire kept on stone can be trusted, and a fire laid on heather waits only for a moment's neglect to remember what it is.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1024"><em>The hut on the heather burns</em>, 24 an t-Ògmhios, VE 12</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1026"></a>**26 an Cèitean, VE 15** — *Households begin laying stone under their fires*. After the hut on the heather burns, the near hearths begin laying flat stones from the burn-bed beneath their fires, and the household that lost its roof rebuilds with a stone floor under its hearth.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1025"><em>Conall's word: fire keeps to stone</em>, 23 an t-Iuchar, VE 12</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1027"></a>**27 an Giblean, VE 20** — *Ailbhe first sent out with Poit an Teine* (Tobar dhìreach). Ailbhe, still a girl, is sent alone two valleys off with a coal banked in ash in a clay pot, because her hands are steadier with a live coal than her brothers'.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1018"><em>Ailbhe born by the hearth</em>, 30 am Faoilleach, VE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1028"></a>**9 an Lùnastal, VE 25** — *Fire reaches the northern moor* (Tobar dhìreach). Ailbhe, grown sure of the ground, carries a banked coal a full day's walk north to the edge of the moor at the limit of any household's grazing. Teine a' Chlachair, walked outward hearth by hearth, now burns in dozens of houses that were once each other's strangers.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1027"><em>Ailbhe first sent out with Poit an Teine</em>, 27 an Giblean, VE 20</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1029"></a>**11 an t-Iuchar, VE 29** — *Sorcha dies* (Tobar dhìreach). Sorcha, who bore Ailbhe by the hearth and was herself the first to be burned by the fire her husband brought home, dies at Tobar dhìreach. The household keeps its fire fed through the mourning without letting it fall.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1019"><em>The stone kept at the hearth's edge for meat</em>, 28 an Gearran, VE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1030"></a>**6 an Dàmhair, VE 38** — *Neachdan dies* (Tobar dhìreach). Neachdan, An Clachair, dies old by the hearth he lit from the burning vein, having asked once more to be carried to see the well-cut still burning. The household keeps the fire through the mourning as it has kept it every night since the lightning.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1020"><em>Teine a' Chlachair begged and given</em>, 29 am Màrt, VE 4</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1031"></a>**4 an t-Samhain, VE 40** — *Conall's rule of the stone*. At a gathering of the near hearths in the dark half of the year, Conall sets down standing what he has held since the burned hut: that fire kept from the mason's line should be laid on stone and never on packed heather. The near households take it as their own law.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1026"><em>Households begin laying stone under their fires</em>, 26 an Cèitean, VE 15</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1032"></a>**3 an Dùbhlachd, VE 55** — *Conall keeps the winter watch at the vein* (Tobar dhìreach). Conall sits the dark half of every year on the two flat stones above the burning vein, and the valley's children learn not to go near them without an elder by.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1031"><em>Conall's rule of the stone</em>, 4 an t-Samhain, VE 40</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1033"></a>**1 am Faoilleach, VE 71** — *Conall dies* (Tobar dhìreach). Conall, who first carried Teine na Fèithe home in a water-pot as a boy, dies by the hearth in old age, with the vein in the well-cut still burning as it has burned since Oidhche an Dealanaich, unchanged through two of the mason's line.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1032"><em>Conall keeps the winter watch at the vein</em>, 3 an Dùbhlachd, VE 55</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1034"></a>**30 am Faoilleach, VE 71** — *The watch passed to Conall's son* (Tobar dhìreach). Without ceremony, Conall's son takes up the watch of the burning vein his father and grandfather kept before him, sitting the dark half of the year on the two flat stones above the cut, understanding it is not his to let go out.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1033"><em>Conall dies</em>, 1 am Faoilleach, VE 71</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0002"></a>**17 an Giblean, VE 76** — *Three wells claim the crack* (Tobar dhìreach). Tobar dhìreach, Tobar dhubh and Tobar òg each tell that the mason's well was theirs, and that the lightning fell there. Tobar dhìreach can show a capped shaft with a scorched stain on its lip; the other two have only the telling. Between the three no chronicler has ever judged.
- <a id="ev-EI-1035"></a>**28 an Gearran, VE 80** — *Tadhg's scorched stone*. At the black well two valleys east, Tadhg holds up a dark-faced stone before a gathering and swears the lightning struck his own family's well, not the mason's. The mason's household hears of it and answers nothing, keeping the fire rather than the argument.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0002"><em>Three wells claim the crack</em>, 17 an Giblean, VE 76</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1036"></a>**29 am Màrt, VE 82** — *Ailbhe dies* (Tobar dhìreach). Ailbhe, the fire-bearer, dies in her old age at the hearth she was born beside, having walked Teine a' Chlachair to more hearths than anyone had counted.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1028"><em>Fire reaches the northern moor</em>, 9 an Lùnastal, VE 25</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1037"></a>**27 an Giblean, VE 95** — *The young well's telling*. An old woman of the young well to the south begins to tell, softly and without a stone to prove it, that her own mother saw the lightning fall into their well and not the mason's. The telling travels further than Tadhg's louder claim and outlasts it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0002"><em>Three wells claim the crack</em>, 17 an Giblean, VE 76</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1038"></a>**16 an Gearran, VE 96** — *Three tellings held at once* (Tobar dhìreach). The high valleys settle, without any household deciding it outright, into three tellings of where the lightning fell, held side by side and never set against each other. Only the scorched lip of the mason's own shaft still shows the truth of it, plainly, to anyone who walks to see.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0002"><em>Three wells claim the crack</em>, 17 an Giblean, VE 76</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1039"></a>**17 am Màrt, VE 100** — *Conall's son keeps the watch grown grey* (Tobar dhìreach). Conall's son, grown grey at the watch his father left him, will not have the claims of the black well and the young well argued: the fire was walked to a hundred houses that do not care which valley the lightning chose.<span class="fn fl">↩ Answers <a href="#ev-I-0002"><em>Three wells claim the crack</em>, 17 an Giblean, VE 76</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1040"></a>**18 am Màrt, VE 112** — *Muirne born* (Tobar dhìreach). A daughter is born at Tobar dhìreach, a great-granddaughter of Conall's line, and is given young to the household's hearth-keeper to be raised among the fire before she is raised among words. She is named Muirne.
- <a id="ev-EI-1041"></a>**17 an Gearran, VE 128** — *Muirne takes up the watch of the well-cut* (Tobar dhìreach). Not yet grown, Muirne begins to keep the winter watch over the burning vein as the keeper before her tires of the work, sitting the dark half of the year on the two flat stones as every keeper has sat since Conall.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1040"><em>Muirne born</em>, 18 am Màrt, VE 112</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1042"></a>**15 an Cèitean, VE 130** — *Teine na Fèithe burns low* (Tobar dhìreach). Through the years of Muirne's watch the glow in the broken vein fades winter on winter, unmarked by most of the valley, whose hundred hearths no longer need it, and marked only by the one keeper who sits with it in the cold.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1041"><em>Muirne takes up the watch of the well-cut</em>, 17 an Gearran, VE 128</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1043"></a>**16 an Giblean, VE 135** — *Muirne marks Teine na Fèithe sinking* (Tobar dhìreach). Keeping a private reckoning against her own memory, Muirne comes to see what no keeper before her has said aloud: that the glow in the well-cut grows a little lower with every winter, the vein burning down like any fire that is fed by nothing but itself.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0001"><em>The mason's fire</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1042"><em>Teine na Fèithe burns low</em>, 15 an Cèitean, VE 130</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1044"></a>**22 an t-Samhain, VE 140** — *Teine na Fèithe marked lower each winter* (Tobar dhìreach). Muirne, sitting the dark half of the year on the flat stones, begins to keep a private reckoning of the glow in the well-cut against her memory of five winters before.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1043"><em>Muirne marks Teine na Fèithe sinking</em>, 16 an Giblean, VE 135</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0003"></a>**19 am Màrt, VE 151** — *The slab over the burnt vein* (Tobar dhìreach). When the fire in the vein has burned itself out, the mason's people dig no further. They lay a flat stone over the broken vein, draw no water beside it, and cut their well again a stone's throw off. In this all the tellings agree.
- <a id="ev-EI-1045"></a>**4 an Giblean, VE 151** — *The last ember* (Tobar dhìreach). In a wet spring of failed crops and standing water, Muirne sits out the last night of Teine na Fèithe in the rain and watches its pale glow go out, quietly, with no one else there to see Teine a' Chlachair die in the ground where it was struck.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0003"><em>The slab over the burnt vein</em>, 19 am Màrt, VE 151</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1044"><em>Teine na Fèithe marked lower each winter</em>, 22 an t-Samhain, VE 140</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1046"></a>**29 an Cèitean, VE 151** — *Muirne refuses the digging* (Tobar dhìreach). When talk turns to deepening the well-cut in hope of striking fire again, Muirne stands at the mouth of it and forbids the digging, saying the fire came out of the sky on one night only and is not a thing to be dug after in the ground.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0003"><em>The slab over the burnt vein</em>, 19 am Màrt, VE 151</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1045"><em>The last ember</em>, 4 an Giblean, VE 151</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1047"></a>**27 an t-Iuchar, VE 151** — *The seed rots in the wet spring*. The spring that finishes Teine na Fèithe is remembered also for rain that stands a hand deep in the low fields and rots the seed in the ground, so that hunger is abroad in the valleys.
- <a id="ev-EI-1048"></a>**30 an t-Ògmhios, VE 152** — *Leac na Fèithe laid over the vein* (Tobar dhìreach). The household levers a broad flat stone across the mouth of the mason's well-cut and packs its edge with turf, sealing the burnt vein from the weather and forbidding any water to be drawn near it again.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0003"><em>The slab over the burnt vein</em>, 19 am Màrt, VE 151</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1046"><em>Muirne refuses the digging</em>, 29 an Cèitean, VE 151</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1049"></a>**29 an t-Iuchar, VE 152** — *The new well cut* (Tobar dhìreach). A stone's throw from the covered vein, the household cuts a fresh well that gives clean water from its first day, and it is this well, not the mason's old cut, that the household draws from from that day on.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0003"><em>The slab over the burnt vein</em>, 19 am Màrt, VE 151</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1050"></a>**25 an t-Iuchar, VE 165** — *Muirne tells the covering standing* (Tobar dhìreach). Muirne tells the finding and the covering of the vein the same way every year, standing, until her telling is the one the household keeps unaltered: a wonder found, a wonder covered, and a well that gave water all the same.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0003"><em>The slab over the burnt vein</em>, 19 am Màrt, VE 151</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1048"><em>Leac na Fèithe laid over the vein</em>, 30 an t-Ògmhios, VE 152</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1051"></a>**23 an Lùnastal, VE 175** — *Grandchildren sent out to Leac na Fèithe in Muirne's stead* (Tobar dhìreach). Grown too slow for the winter walk, Muirne sends her grandchildren out to Leac na Fèithe to see that the turf at its edge still holds the rain out and that no bucket stands near it.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1050"><em>Muirne tells the covering standing</em>, 25 an t-Iuchar, VE 165</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1052"></a>**28 an Cèitean, VE 181** — *Muirne dies* (Tobar dhìreach). Muirne dies at Tobar dhìreach in old age and is buried in the ground near the house with no coal or fire laid beside her, having already given the vein's fire, whole, back to the stone. The telling of Leac na Fèithe passes to her grandchildren.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1051"><em>Grandchildren sent out to Leac na Fèithe in Muirne's stead</em>, 23 an Lùnastal, VE 175</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1053"></a>**26 an t-Ògmhios, VE 185** — *A palm laid on the cold slab* (Tobar dhìreach). The youngest of Muirne's grandchildren walks out to the covered stone in the dark half of the year and lays a bare palm on it, as she was taught, for what the stone once held.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0003"><em>The slab over the burnt vein</em>, 19 am Màrt, VE 151</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1054"></a>**18 an t-Samhain, VE 205** — *Conn born to the upper valley*. Conn is born to a herding household high up the Abhainn uaine, further inland and higher than any household of that kin cares to winter, the country from which the summer grazing is followed up onto the shrinking snowfields.
- <a id="ev-EI-1055"></a>**17 an Dùbhlachd, VE 224** — *Conn trusted to choose the high ground*. Grown to a young man, Conn reads the colour of the light on the high tops before dawn to judge whether the beasts want driving down, and is seldom wrong; the older herders of his kin begin letting him choose the summer ground himself.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1054"><em>Conn born to the upper valley</em>, 18 an t-Samhain, VE 205</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0004"></a>**14 an t-Ògmhios, VE 227** — *The high snowfields shrink* (Abhainn uaine). Meltwater off the central mountains cuts the bed that Abhainn uaine follows still. On the gravel terraces of its lower reach lie hearth-stones at three heights, each left as the water rose to it.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-1054"><em>Conn born to the upper valley</em>, 18 an t-Samhain, VE 205</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-1055"><em>Conn trusted to choose the high ground</em>, 17 an Dùbhlachd, VE 224</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1501"></a>**23 am Màrt, VE 230** — *Conn's fire-ring on the gravel terrace*. Conn lays hearth-stones on the gravel terrace above the summer bend of the Abhainn uaine, on ground his father and grandfather used before him, a coal carried up from the household's own fire in a clay pot banked in ash.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0004"><em>The high snowfields shrink</em>, 14 an t-Ògmhios, VE 227</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1055"><em>Conn trusted to choose the high ground</em>, 17 an Dùbhlachd, VE 224</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1502"></a>**21 an Giblean, VE 240** — *The flood takes Conn's lower ring*. A week of unlifting cloud on the high ground sends the Abhainn uaine over Conn's fire-ring at flood height; he saves the coal and drives the beasts to the shelf above, and the water carries off all but the flat stone at the ring's back.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0004"><em>The high snowfields shrink</em>, 14 an t-Ògmhios, VE 227</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1501"><em>Conn's fire-ring on the gravel terrace</em>, 23 am Màrt, VE 230</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1503"></a>**20 an Cèitean, VE 250** — *The white draws back up the mountain* (Abhainn uaine). Year on year of Conn's manhood the old snow draws back further up the shoulder of the central mountains, and more water comes down the Abhainn uaine than the grass alone can explain.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0004"><em>The high snowfields shrink</em>, 14 an t-Ògmhios, VE 227</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1502"><em>The flood takes Conn's lower ring</em>, 21 an Giblean, VE 240</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1504"></a>**29 an Dàmhair, VE 260** — *Conn shows his sons the three rings* (Abhainn uaine). Conn walks the terrace above the river with his sons and shows them three rings of fire-stones on three shelves, each set higher than the last by a man who judged the water would not come so far.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1503"><em>The white draws back up the mountain</em>, 20 an Cèitean, VE 250</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1505"></a>**27 an t-Samhain, VE 266** — *Conn dies among three rings*. Conn dies at his household's hearth in the low valley in his sixty-second year, having shown his sons the three fire-rings on three shelves of the one terrace, each built a little higher than the last by a man reading how far the river could be trusted.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0004"><em>The high snowfields shrink</em>, 14 an t-Ògmhios, VE 227</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1504"><em>Conn shows his sons the three rings</em>, 29 an Dàmhair, VE 260</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1506"></a>**26 an Dùbhlachd, VE 281** — *Eachna born south of Tobar dhìreach*. Eachna is born to a household some way south of Tobar dhìreach that keeps a fire carried, hearth by hearth, from the mason's own since Ailbhe first walked it outward; she grows up wanting open ground of her own rather than a corner of her father's.
- <a id="ev-EI-1507"></a>**24 am Faoilleach, VE 300** — *Eachna walks the straight field* (Achadh dhìreach). Eachna walks the level ground west of Tobar dhìreach more than once as a young woman, looking at it the way a woman looks at a thing she means to have.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1506"><em>Eachna born south of Tobar dhìreach</em>, 26 an Dùbhlachd, VE 281</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0005"></a>**16 an Cèitean, VE 303** — *The first hearths of the high valleys* (Achadh dhìreach). Hearths are made at Achadh dhìreach, of pine and heather charcoal, with scrapers of grey flint and the split bones of red deer about them. There is no coloured coal in them: those who sat there had none of it, or would not burn it.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-1506"><em>Eachna born south of Tobar dhìreach</em>, 26 an Dùbhlachd, VE 281</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1508"></a>**5 an t-Iuchar, VE 306** — *Eachna carries fire to the straight field* (Achadh dhìreach). Eachna walks a day's distance from Tobar dhìreach with a coal from the line's own hearth to settle the level, well-watered ground west of the high valleys that households call, for its lie, the straight field; the line asks nothing for the giving.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0005"><em>The first hearths of the high valleys</em>, 16 an Cèitean, VE 303</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1507"><em>Eachna walks the straight field</em>, 24 am Faoilleach, VE 300</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1509"></a>**3 an Lùnastal, VE 306** — *The first hearth of Achadh dhìreach laid on stone* (Achadh dhìreach). Eachna lays her first fire on a bed of pine and dried heather banked over flat stone, the lesson of stone under every fire carried out from the mason's own household as freely as the fire itself; grey flint and red deer bone gather round it in the seasons after.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0005"><em>The first hearths of the high valleys</em>, 16 an Cèitean, VE 303</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1508"><em>Eachna carries fire to the straight field</em>, 5 an t-Iuchar, VE 306</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1510"></a>**7 an Gearran, VE 320** — *Deer hunted by torch at Achadh dhìreach* (Achadh dhìreach). With calves lost to deer grown bold on ground still thin of houses, Eachna's sons take to hunting the moor's deer by torchlight after dark, a burning brand carried low and a spearman behind, working the herds back from the standing crop.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0005"><em>The first hearths of the high valleys</em>, 16 an Cèitean, VE 303</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1509"><em>The first hearth of Achadh dhìreach laid on stone</em>, 3 an Lùnastal, VE 306</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1511"></a>**9 am Faoilleach, VE 330** — *The straight field named* (Achadh dhìreach). The level ground between the burn and the rise where Eachna settled is called the straight field by those who first work it, and keeps the name after the households round it grow too many to count.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0005"><em>The first hearths of the high valleys</em>, 16 an Cèitean, VE 303</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1512"></a>**11 an Dùbhlachd, VE 335** — *Achadh dhìreach grows to five hearths* (Achadh dhìreach). Eachna's household becomes three hearths and then five as sons and daughters marry out and stay near rather than moving off, each new fire lit in an unbroken line from the coal Eachna herself carried from Tobar dhìreach.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0005"><em>The first hearths of the high valleys</em>, 16 an Cèitean, VE 303</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1510"><em>Deer hunted by torch at Achadh dhìreach</em>, 7 an Gearran, VE 320</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1513"></a>**12 an t-Samhain, VE 349** — *Eachna dies at her own hearth* (Achadh dhìreach). Eachna dies at Achadh dhìreach in her sixty-eighth year among her own grown children; the fire she carried from Tobar dhìreach burns on after her, tended by hands that have never seen the mason's well and owe it only the memory of it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0005"><em>The first hearths of the high valleys</em>, 16 an Cèitean, VE 303</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1512"><em>Achadh dhìreach grows to five hearths</em>, 11 an Dùbhlachd, VE 335</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0006"></a>**11 an Lùnastal, VE 378** — *The oak comes to the lowlands* (Doire ghlas). The birch and pine of the cold years give way to oak and hazel, as the pollen in the bog under Doire ghlas shows. The grove that names the place stands on ground that was open heath when the vein was first broken.
- <a id="ev-EI-1514"></a>**14 an Dàmhair, VE 390** — *The first autumn store of roasted hazel-nuts* (Achadh dhìreach). At Achadh dhìreach, under the oak and hazel now grown thick where birch once stood, Eachna's descendants roast whole nuts in the embers and lay by the first store of them against the dark months, rather than gathering only as the season allows.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0006"><em>The oak comes to the lowlands</em>, 11 an Lùnastal, VE 378</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1515"></a>**15 an t-Sultain, VE 400** — *Oak fuel holds a fire through the night* (Doire ghlas). The grandmothers of the northern heath tell that oak has come in where their own grandmothers knew only birch, and that a household with oak in reach keeps a warmer hearth for less carrying.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0006"><em>The oak comes to the lowlands</em>, 11 an Lùnastal, VE 378</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1516"></a>**17 an Lùnastal, VE 425** — *Luag born to the northern heath*. Luag is born to a herding household of the northern heath, near enough the changing country of birch and oak that he grows up on the grandmothers' telling of it, and restless in a way his own kin cannot account for.
- <a id="ev-EI-1517"></a>**19 an t-Iuchar, VE 440** — *Luag herds further out each year*. Luag of the northern heath follows the grazing past where his kin are used to follow it, until by his twenty-fifth year he has walked ground no one of his household has walked.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1516"><em>Luag born to the northern heath</em>, 17 an Lùnastal, VE 425</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1518"></a>**16 an Cèitean, VE 451** — *Luag sets out for the north-western horn*. Alone, with a coal carried in a clay pot and dried meat under a hide, Luag walks four days past the last households his own kin know of, out past the last stands of oak and hazel, meaning to see how far the land runs before it meets the sea.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1517"><em>Luag herds further out each year</em>, 19 an t-Iuchar, VE 440</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0006a"></a>**22 an Lùnastal, VE 451** — *The bare north-west*. The oak never reaches the north-western horn of the island. The gales off the north-western sea keep it bare, low heather and blanket bog behind the shore without a tree, as it is still. No hearth of that age has been found there.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-1516"><em>Luag born to the northern heath</em>, 17 an Lùnastal, VE 425</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-1518"><em>Luag sets out for the north-western horn</em>, 16 an Cèitean, VE 451</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1519"></a>**18 an Dàmhair, VE 451** — *Luag's fire will not live in the wind*. On the bare shore of the north-western horn Luag's banked fire is taken sideways along the ground faster than he can feed it, and he lets it go out rather than waste his last tinder; he finds no hearth-stone or charcoal anywhere he walks that coast.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0006a"><em>The bare north-west</em>, 22 an Lùnastal, VE 451</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1518"><em>Luag sets out for the north-western horn</em>, 16 an Cèitean, VE 451</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1520"></a>**22 an t-Sultain, VE 452** — *Luag's return and telling*. Luag walks the four days home, relighting his fire at the first hearth he reaches, and tells at his own hearth and at the dark-of-the-year gathering that the land runs out at last in the north-west, bare to a wind no fire can stand against.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0006a"><em>The bare north-west</em>, 22 an Lùnastal, VE 451</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1519"><em>Luag's fire will not live in the wind</em>, 18 an Dàmhair, VE 451</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1521"></a>**21 an Dàmhair, VE 453** — *The island is told to have an edge*. Luag's telling goes from hearth to hearth until most of the northern heath has heard that the land runs out in the north-west, bare to a wind no fire can stand against.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0006a"><em>The bare north-west</em>, 22 an Lùnastal, VE 451</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1520"><em>Luag's return and telling</em>, 22 an t-Sultain, VE 452</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1522"></a>**26 an t-Iuchar, VE 455** — *Gràinne born on the drowned neck*. Gràinne is born to a household that has kept a hearth on the low neck to Eilean dhubh since before her grandmother's grandmother, on a shelf of dry ground between two arms of shingle where the crossing to the island is narrowest and firmest underfoot.
- <a id="ev-EI-1523"></a>**24 an Lùnastal, VE 475** — *Gràinne learns to watch the tide*. Taught by her mother to set a stone at the mark each spring tide leaves on the shingle and measure it against the last, Gràinne takes up a watch on the sea's creep against the neck that she keeps, by her own habit, for the rest of her life.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1522"><em>Gràinne born on the drowned neck</em>, 26 an t-Iuchar, VE 455</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1524"></a>**10 an Cèitean, VE 480** — *Gràinne sets stones at the high-water mark* (Eilean dhubh). Gràinne's mother teaches her to walk the shingle at every high water and set a stone at the sea's mark, so that each tide can be measured against the last.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1523"><em>Gràinne learns to watch the tide</em>, 24 an Lùnastal, VE 475</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1525"></a>**8 an t-Ògmhios, VE 495** — *The crossing to Eilean dhubh dries only at the lowest ebbs* (Eilean dhubh). By the time Gràinne is grown the neck to Eilean dhubh can be crossed only within two hours either side of the lowest ebbs, and only by those who know which channels run firm.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1524"><em>Gràinne sets stones at the high-water mark</em>, 10 an Cèitean, VE 480</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1526"></a>**13 am Màrt, VE 497** — *Luag dies among his own children*. Luag dies at his own household's hearth in his seventy-second year, remembered kindly as the man who walked to the edge of the world and came back with nothing to show for it but a burnt cloak and a telling that outlived him.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0006a"><em>The bare north-west</em>, 22 an Lùnastal, VE 451</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1521"><em>The island is told to have an edge</em>, 21 an Dàmhair, VE 453</a>.</span>

## The Years VE 501 – 1,000

- <a id="ev-I-0007"></a>**13 an t-Iuchar, VE 506** — *Eilean dhubh cut off* (Eilean dhubh). The rising sea floods the low neck of land that joined Eilean dhubh to the main island. The hearths of the neck lie drowned under the sand of the sound, and the deer of the island, cut off, grow smaller in the lifetimes after.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-1522"><em>Gràinne born on the drowned neck</em>, 26 an t-Iuchar, VE 455</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-1523"><em>Gràinne learns to watch the tide</em>, 24 an Lùnastal, VE 475</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-1525"><em>The crossing to Eilean dhubh dries only at the lowest ebbs</em>, 8 an t-Ògmhios, VE 495</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1527"></a>**6 an t-Samhain, VE 506** — *Gràinne leaves the drowned neck*. The sea reaches the hearth-stones of Gràinne's house in a spring of hard westerlies; she rakes the fire into her mother's clay pot and carries it, the same day, to new hearth-ground behind the shelf that no tide of her lifetime reaches again.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0007"><em>Eilean dhubh cut off</em>, 13 an t-Iuchar, VE 506</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1525"><em>The crossing to Eilean dhubh dries only at the lowest ebbs</em>, 8 an t-Ògmhios, VE 495</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1528"></a>**3 an t-Sultain, VE 507** — *The new hearth behind the drowned shelf* (Eilean dhubh). Gràinne carries the coal herself from the flooded house to a new hearth on the dry ground behind the old shelf, and lights it there before dark on the day the sea comes in.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0007"><em>Eilean dhubh cut off</em>, 13 an t-Iuchar, VE 506</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1527"><em>Gràinne leaves the drowned neck</em>, 6 an t-Samhain, VE 506</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1529"></a>**2 an Dàmhair, VE 528** — *Oisean born to the seal-hunters of the south shore*. Oisean is born to a household that works the rocks and skerries of the south coast for grey seals, and grows up watching the greater number that haul out on Eilean mhin, further out than any boat of that coast has yet been trusted to carry a man and bring him back.
- <a id="ev-EI-1530"></a>**7 an t-Iuchar, VE 531** — *Gràinne dies at the second hearth*. Gràinne dies by her own fire on the higher ground she moved to twenty-five years before, and is buried there rather than on the shelf that had been her people's ground for longer than any teller could reckon, and that by then the sea covers at every tide.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0007"><em>Eilean dhubh cut off</em>, 13 an t-Iuchar, VE 506</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1528"><em>The new hearth behind the drowned shelf</em>, 3 an t-Sultain, VE 507</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1531"></a>**8 an t-Ògmhios, VE 540** — *The Abhainn ìseal settles into its wide bed*. After generations of shifting across the flat ground below the high valleys, the longest river of the island settles into the wide bed the households along it come to know simply as the river, the shallower side channels running gentler and thick with fish at certain seasons.
- <a id="ev-EI-1532"></a>**3 an t-Sultain, VE 545** — *The first hazel weirs driven in the side channels*. Households along the newly settled river drive the first weirs of hazel stakes across the mouths of the side channels, angled against the current with gaps left for a hand to reach through, and leave the stakes standing once the season's run is done.
- <a id="ev-EI-1533"></a>**5 an Lùnastal, VE 546** — *Oisean stitches the first hide boat*. Working alone over the better part of a season, Oisean stretches and stitches greased sealskin over a frame of bent hazel shaped to his own body, and floats it first in a calm inlet, where it holds him and does not sink.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1529"><em>Oisean born to the seal-hunters of the south shore</em>, 2 an Dàmhair, VE 528</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1534"></a>**13 am Màrt, VE 547** — *Oisean crosses to Eilean mhin and comes home*. Alone and with only a paddle and a coil of plaited hide, Oisean crosses the open water to Eilean mhin in an early summer calm and returns before dark with three seals lashed to the frame behind him, the first crossing on the island made of set purpose to a place seen but not walked to.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1533"><em>Oisean stitches the first hide boat</em>, 5 an Lùnastal, VE 546</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0008"></a>**1 an t-Iuchar, VE 551** — *Hunters on Eilean mhin* (Eilean mhin). Seal-hunters pitch camps on Eilean mhin, coming there by boat: the first sure sign that anyone on Dia-thìr crossed open water of set purpose. The camps are kept a season at a time and left.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-1529"><em>Oisean born to the seal-hunters of the south shore</em>, 2 an Dàmhair, VE 528</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-1533"><em>Oisean stitches the first hide boat</em>, 5 an Lùnastal, VE 546</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EI-1534"><em>Oisean crosses to Eilean mhin and comes home</em>, 13 am Màrt, VE 547</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1535"></a>**21 an Dàmhair, VE 552** — *The seal-bothies of Eilean mhin first thatched*. Oisean builds a larger boat and begins camping among the seal rocks of Eilean mhin for a stretch of good weather at a time rather than returning each day, raising a shelter of driftwood and hide that comes to be kept and re-thatched, season after season, by those who cross after him.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0008"><em>Hunters on Eilean mhin</em>, 1 an t-Iuchar, VE 551</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1534"><em>Oisean crosses to Eilean mhin and comes home</em>, 13 am Màrt, VE 547</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1536"></a>**10 an Cèitean, VE 553** — *Others follow Oisean across* (Eilean mhin). Oisean's brothers and then young men of the neighbouring households build boats on his pattern and follow him to Eilean mhin, until the crossing in the calm months is a thing the shore simply does.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0008"><em>Hunters on Eilean mhin</em>, 1 an t-Iuchar, VE 551</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1535"><em>The seal-bothies of Eilean mhin first thatched</em>, 21 an Dàmhair, VE 552</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1537"></a>**11 an Giblean, VE 560** — *The deer of Eilean dhubh grow smaller*. Hunters who cross to Eilean dhubh by boat, the neck no longer drying at all but the lowest ebbs, bring home carcasses lighter than their grandfathers' tellings led them to expect, the island's deer penned by the water onto ground too small to feed a herd that once ranged the length of two islands as one.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0007"><em>Eilean dhubh cut off</em>, 13 an t-Iuchar, VE 506</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1538"></a>**24 an Gearran, VE 590** — *Scàire born to the north shore*. Scàire is born into a household of the north shore that has already taken up the hide boat after the manner spreading up the coast from the south, though built heavier and lower for water that seldom runs calm even at midsummer.
- <a id="ev-EI-1539"></a>**26 am Faoilleach, VE 596** — *Oisean dies among boats of his grandsons' making*. Oisean dies at his own hearth on the mainland shore in his old age, by then one boat-builder among many of that coast, his grandsons shaping hulls beside his own with a sureness he never had, having had nothing of his own to look at when he began.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0008"><em>Hunters on Eilean mhin</em>, 1 an t-Iuchar, VE 551</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1536"><em>Others follow Oisean across</em>, 10 an Cèitean, VE 553</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1540"></a>**3 an Dàmhair, VE 600** — *The weir-stakes renewed in the same holes*. A generation on from the first driving, households of the Abhainn ìseal renew their weirs by driving fresh stakes into the holes the old ones rotted out of, so that a weir kept thirty years stands on almost the same ground it first stood on, though none of its first stakes remain.
- <a id="ev-EI-1541"></a>**1 an t-Samhain, VE 606** — *Scàire first goes out to the skerries* (Eilean fhada). Scàire goes out with her father's crew to the seal skerries off Eilean fhada from her sixteenth year, bailing in boats that ship water with every third swell.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1538"><em>Scàire born to the north shore</em>, 24 an Gearran, VE 590</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0008a"></a>**30 an t-Sultain, VE 611** — *Seals on the skerries* (Eilean fhada). Hunters of the north shore go out in skin boats in the autumn gales to the skerries off Eilean fhada, where the grey seals haul out to pup, and take them there. The seal bones in the middens of the north coast bear the same cut-marks as those of Eilean mhin. On Eilean fhada a hard year is counted by the boats the gales kept ashore.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-1538"><em>Scàire born to the north shore</em>, 24 an Gearran, VE 590</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EI-1541"><em>Scàire first goes out to the skerries</em>, 1 an t-Samhain, VE 606</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1542"></a>**30 an t-Samhain, VE 620** — *Scàire sees the grey bank from the skerries*. Master of her own boat and crew, Scàire climbs the highest of the seal skerries off Eilean fhada to judge the weather and sees, lying always along the same stretch of the northern and eastern sea, a grey that no sun burns off and no gale blows away.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0008a"><em>Seals on the skerries</em>, 30 an t-Sultain, VE 611</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1541"><em>Scàire first goes out to the skerries</em>, 1 an t-Samhain, VE 606</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1543"></a>**29 an Dùbhlachd, VE 628** — *The hard year of the kept boats*. In Scàire's thirty-eighth year the autumn gales hold five boats out of every six ashore the whole season through, the seal harvest thin enough that more than one household of the north shore goes into the winter short of oil for its lamps.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0008a"><em>Seals on the skerries</em>, 30 an t-Sultain, VE 611</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1542"><em>Scàire sees the grey bank from the skerries</em>, 30 an t-Samhain, VE 620</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1544"></a>**27 am Faoilleach, VE 640** — *Scàire master of her own boat* (Eilean fhada). After her father's death Scàire is master of his boat and crew without much argument from anyone, no one on that coast doubting that she reads a north-shore sea as well as any man alive on it.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1543"><em>The hard year of the kept boats</em>, 29 an Dùbhlachd, VE 628</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1545"></a>**25 an Gearran, VE 652** — *Scàire dies having brought her crews home whole*. Scàire dies at her own hearth in old age, remembered by her kin less for the grey bank on the northern sea, by then known to every household of that coast, than for a working life spent bringing crews home whole across water that forgave very little.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0008a"><em>Seals on the skerries</em>, 30 an t-Sultain, VE 611</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-1544"><em>Scàire master of her own boat</em>, 27 am Faoilleach, VE 640</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0009"></a>**2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 681** — *The flood-plain of Abhainn ìseal* (Abhainn ìseal). Abhainn ìseal, the longest river of the island, settles into the wide bed it keeps now. Fish-weirs of hazel stakes are set across its side channels, and the stakes are renewed in the same holes for generations.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-1531"><em>The Abhainn ìseal settles into its wide bed</em>, 8 an t-Ògmhios, VE 540</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EI-1532"><em>The first hazel weirs driven in the side channels</em>, 3 an t-Sultain, VE 545</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EI-1540"><em>The weir-stakes renewed in the same holes</em>, 3 an Dàmhair, VE 600</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1546"></a>**18 an t-Iuchar, VE 690** — *Children wade the shallows at weir-mending* (Abhainn ìseal). Children of the households along the Abhainn ìseal grow up wading the shallows at weir-mending time, knowing which hole takes a stake easily and which fights it long before they know why the holes are where they are.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0009"><em>The flood-plain of Abhainn ìseal</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 681</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1547"></a>**16 an Lùnastal, VE 700** — *The salmon run first feasted at the weirs*. Households up and down the Abhainn ìseal gather for the first time at the largest of the weirs when the salmon run stands at its thickest, sharing out the catch between more hands than any one household's own rather than guarding it apart.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0009"><em>The flood-plain of Abhainn ìseal</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 681</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0010"></a>**28 an Lùnastal, VE 751** — *The middens of Seann Dunn* (Seann Dunn). The Seann-Dhaoine begin the great mound at Seann Dunn: limpet shell, seal bone and burnt weed, laid down over many lifetimes until it stands taller than a man. It is the first sure trace of them. No tool in it is shaped as any later Dia-thìreach shaped tools.
- <a id="ev-EI-1548"></a>**14 an t-Sultain, VE 758** — *The heap's fire kept through the three-day gale* (Seann Dunn). A winter gale tears the roof from the shelter behind the shell heap at Dunn and drives the sea over the gathering-rocks for three days; the fire kept at the heap's foot is banked low and fed through the storm by whoever can be spared, and does not go out.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0010"><em>The middens of Seann Dunn</em>, 28 an Lùnastal, VE 751</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1549"></a>**13 an Dàmhair, VE 760** — *The heap worked with the foot* (Seann Dunn). A woman of Dunn keeps the heap as her mother taught her, letting each bag of shell fall where the heap wants it and working it level with her foot, with the burnt weed laid in thin.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0010"><em>The middens of Seann Dunn</em>, 28 an Lùnastal, VE 751</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1550"></a>**18 an t-Sultain, VE 765** — *The gatherer's mother dies at the tide* (Seann Dunn). An old woman of the Dunn heap, who has worked the shore pools long past when her hands were fit for it, is found sitting against a rock with the tide turning round her feet, dead as quietly as she lived; what is done with her is not carried past the household's own places.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0010"><em>The middens of Seann Dunn</em>, 28 an Lùnastal, VE 751</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1551"></a>**20 an Lùnastal, VE 766** — *A season worked alone at the heap* (Seann Dunn). Through the season after her mother's death the gatherer works the shore pools alone, going down before light and coming up after dark, and keeps the heap's fire no lower than it was kept with two pairs of hands, before her own daughter is old enough to work beside her.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0010"><em>The middens of Seann Dunn</em>, 28 an Lùnastal, VE 751</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1552"></a>**22 an t-Iuchar, VE 770** — *Eggs taken from the low cliffs at Dunn* (Seann Dunn). The gatherers of Dunn take eggs from the ledges of the low cliffs in the dry months, never so many from one ledge that the birds do not come back to it the next year.
- <a id="ev-EI-1553"></a>**23 an t-Ògmhios, VE 778** — *An old scraper turned up in the heap* (Seann Dunn). Loosening an old shoulder of the Dunn heap, a girl finds a flint scraper struck and finished unlike any tool freshly made at the heap's fire that same season; she turns it over a while and lets it fall back into the shell with everything else the heap has taken in.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0010"><em>The middens of Seann Dunn</em>, 28 an Lùnastal, VE 751</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1554"></a>**12 am Faoilleach, VE 785** — *The heap first used to watch the sea* (Seann Dunn). A boy sent to fetch fire down for the smoking of fish remarks, standing at the heap's foot, that its top gives the farthest view of the water on that stretch of coast; after that day the heap is climbed from time to time to watch for boats or weather.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0010"><em>The middens of Seann Dunn</em>, 28 an Lùnastal, VE 751</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-1555"></a>**14 an Dùbhlachd, VE 790** — *The Dunn heap stands a man's height* (Seann Dunn). The shell heap above the shore at Dunn, built shell by shell and bag by bag over more lifetimes than any one gatherer can reckon, now stands higher at its crown than a grown man can reach with his arm raised, the tallest thing on that shore.
- <a id="ev-EI-1556"></a>**15 an t-Samhain, VE 798** — *The net-maker of Cwen begins the long mesh* (Seann Chwen). At Cwen, on the sheltered bay to the south, a net-maker who has always set short nets from each shallow toward an open channel begins, over a winter's close work by the fire, twisting a mesh long enough to close the whole width of the bay's mouth.
- <a id="ev-EI-1557"></a>**17 an Dàmhair, VE 805** — *The Cwen nets first set across the bay* (Seann Chwen). The net-maker's household stakes a single unbroken net from shallow to shallow across the mouth of the bay at Cwen for the first time, the net-maker herself wading the deepest channel to sink the centre true; more fish come against it than the smoking-racks can hold.
- <a id="ev-EI-1558"></a>**8 an Cèitean, VE 806** — *Households come to see the closed net* (Seann Chwen). Word of the catch taken at the closed net travels the shore, and households from some way off come to see the long line of stakes and weights for themselves, going home to lengthen their own nets by whatever means each knows.
- <a id="ev-EI-1559"></a>**9 an Giblean, VE 810** — *The net-maker's daughter learns the groove* (Seann Chwen). The net-maker's daughter, grown old enough for close work, begins sitting beside her mother through whole afternoons at the stone weights, learning by eye alone which beach stones will split true under the pecking and which will shatter wrong.
- <a id="ev-EI-1560"></a>**11 am Màrt, VE 812** — *The daughter's first spoiled stones* (Seann Chwen). Given a stone and the small flint used for the cutting, the net-maker's daughter is set to notching the three strokes; her first attempts run too long, too short or crossing, and each spoiled stone goes back to the unworked pile without comment.
- <a id="ev-EI-1561"></a>**9 an Giblean, VE 815** — *The net-maker's eyes fail first* (Seann Chwen). The net-maker of Cwen gives the finer judging of the stones over to her daughter's sharper sight some while before her own hands fail her.
- <a id="ev-EI-1562"></a>**12 am Faoilleach, VE 818** — *The three strokes held a breath longer in the light* (Seann Chwen). The net-maker's daughter takes up a way of holding each finished weight a breath longer in the light than the work requires, as though the three strokes were worth looking at for their own sake.
- <a id="ev-I-0011"></a>**26 an t-Sultain, VE 820** — *The notched net-weights of Seann Chwen* (Seann Chwen). At Seann Chwen the Seann-Dhaoine sink their nets with beach stones, and every stone is notched with the same three strokes. It is the eldest mark on Dia-thìr made again and again of purpose.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-1556"><em>The net-maker of Cwen begins the long mesh</em>, 15 an t-Samhain, VE 798</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-1558"><em>Households come to see the closed net</em>, 8 an Cèitean, VE 806</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-1559"><em>The net-maker's daughter learns the groove</em>, 9 an Giblean, VE 810</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-1560"><em>The daughter's first spoiled stones</em>, 11 am Màrt, VE 812</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-1562"><em>The three strokes held a breath longer in the light</em>, 12 am Faoilleach, VE 818</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2001"></a>**3 an Dùbhlachd, VE 820** — *The daughter cuts the three strokes true* (Seann Chwen). On a calm morning the net-maker's daughter cuts three strokes into a finished weight and finds nothing in it her trained eye can fault; her mother takes it up, turns it in the same light, and sets down the next stone before her without a word.
- <a id="ev-EI-2002"></a>**18 am Màrt, VE 862** — *Diarmad is born at Tobar dhìreach*. Diarmad is born the third child and second son of Fionnghuala, into a household that keeps the mason's own unbroken fire and a leather bag of seven coloured pieces the children play with at the hearth.
- <a id="ev-EI-2003"></a>**16 an Giblean, VE 868** — *The aunt keeps Poit an Teine* (Tobar dhìreach). Poit an Teine at Tobar dhìreach is kept in Diarmad's childhood by his mother's aunt, called by the household only the aunt, who works wool by the hearth while the children play with the coloured pieces.
- <a id="ev-EI-2004"></a>**15 an Cèitean, VE 869** — *Diarmad first asks why the pieces are coloured*. Playing with the leather bag of coloured pieces at the hearth, Diarmad, seven years old, asks the aunt who keeps Poit an Teine why the mason's pieces hold colour and the coal of the hillside does not, and is told only that a boy who wants a better answer may go and ask the sky.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2002"><em>Diarmad is born at Tobar dhìreach</em>, 18 am Màrt, VE 862</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2005"></a>**13 an t-Ògmhios, VE 870** — *The aunt tells Diarmad to go and ask the sky* (Tobar dhìreach). Wearied by a seven-year-old's questions, the aunt tells Diarmad that the stones are coloured because the sky made them so on the night of the fire, and that a boy who wants a better answer can go and ask the sky.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2004"><em>Diarmad first asks why the pieces are coloured</em>, 15 an Cèitean, VE 869</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2006"></a>**12 an t-Iuchar, VE 871** — *Diarmad asks the elders and the fire-bearers*. Diarmad puts his question to the oldest of the line and to the fire-bearers who carry coal to the hearths of the hills, and gathers only shrugs and a fire-bearer's tale that the colour is no more real than a rainbow's, which the pieces' own unfading colour does not bear out.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2005"><em>The aunt tells Diarmad to go and ask the sky</em>, 13 an t-Ògmhios, VE 870</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2007"></a>**10 an Lùnastal, VE 872** — *Diarmad carries the rainbow piece*. From about his tenth year Diarmad keeps the piece that holds every colour and none carried loose at his belt, and takes to turning it in every light the day offers, once holding it bare in a shower of rain to see whether the wet would draw its colour out; it does not.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2006"><em>Diarmad asks the elders and the fire-bearers</em>, 12 an t-Iuchar, VE 871</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2008"></a>**8 an t-Sultain, VE 873** — *Diarmad asks it of travellers*. He begins putting his question to travellers passing through Tobar dhìreach with no stake in the household's pride, reasoning that a stranger has no cause to fob him off, and gets from most of them a shrug dressed in more words.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2007"><em>Diarmad carries the rainbow piece</em>, 10 an Lùnastal, VE 872</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2009"></a>**7 an Dàmhair, VE 874** — *The rainbow piece held out in the rain* (Tobar dhìreach). Diarmad is seen more than once sitting under the eaves in a shower with the rainbow piece held bare to the wet, watching to see whether the rain draws the colour out of it; it lies on top.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2008"><em>Diarmad asks it of travellers</em>, 8 an t-Sultain, VE 873</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2010"></a>**12 an t-Iuchar, VE 875** — *The valley names it Diarmad's question*. The asking becomes a settled joke of the high valleys, carried from hearth to hearth by the fire-bearers, half in earnest and half for a laugh, until every household near Tobar dhìreach knows Diarmad's question and no household yet has an answer for it.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2009"><em>The rainbow piece held out in the rain</em>, 7 an Dàmhair, VE 874</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2011"></a>**13 an t-Ògmhios, VE 880** — *Fionnghuala takes Poit an Teine*. On the death of the aunt who had kept it, Fionnghuala becomes keeper of the pot that holds the mason's own ember, the office passing to her at two-and-forty as it had passed through the women of the line before her.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2002"><em>Diarmad is born at Tobar dhìreach</em>, 18 am Màrt, VE 862</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2012"></a>**15 an Cèitean, VE 881** — *Fionnghuala silences the joke at her own hearth*. When a cousin by marriage mocks Diarmad's question in front of a full house, Fionnghuala answers that twenty years of one question asked is not the same as a mind that cannot let a matter drop, and the joke is not made again in her hearing.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2011"><em>Fionnghuala takes Poit an Teine</em>, 13 an t-Ògmhios, VE 880</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2013"></a>**16 an Giblean, VE 882** — *A fire-bearer brings a false answer* (Tobar dhìreach). A fire-bearer tells Diarmad that colour in a stone is no more real than colour in a rainbow and thins when looked at close; he has looked close a hundred times and the colour has never thinned.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2012"><em>Fionnghuala silences the joke at her own hearth</em>, 15 an Cèitean, VE 881</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2014"></a>**5 an t-Samhain, VE 884** — *Diarmad narrows his question* (Tobar dhìreach). Past twenty, Diarmad begins to ask a narrower question than the one he started with: not why the pieces hold colour, but whether there is anyone or anything on the island that might know.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2013"><em>A fire-bearer brings a false answer</em>, 16 an Giblean, VE 882</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2015"></a>**8 an t-Sultain, VE 886** — *A fire-bearer brings word of a grove where the wind speaks*. Returning from the longest circuit the household's fire-bearers still walk, a woman of Tobar dhìreach reports, more in passing than in earnest, an old herder's warning of an oak grove on the far northern moor where the wind does not blow as it blows anywhere else.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2014"><em>Diarmad narrows his question</em>, 5 an t-Samhain, VE 884</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2016"></a>**7 an Dàmhair, VE 886** — *Diarmad presses the fire-bearer for the herder's words*. Diarmad asks the fire-bearer more than once to repeat exactly what the northern herder had said of the grove, until, tired of the asking, she tells him to go and hear it from the herder's own mouth.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2015"><em>A fire-bearer brings word of a grove where the wind speaks</em>, 8 an t-Sultain, VE 886</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2017"></a>**10 an Lùnastal, VE 888** — *Diarmad gathers every scrap told of the grove*. Over two years he seeks out travellers from the north and west and sets together their thin, half-agreeing tellings of a grove no bird will nest in and no fire is lit within sight of, the first tale in twenty years of asking that does not simply shrug his question off.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2016"><em>Diarmad presses the fire-bearer for the herder's words</em>, 7 an Dàmhair, VE 886</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2018"></a>**31 am Faoilleach, VE 889** — *Fionnghuala gives Diarmad the rainbow piece for the road*. Told her son means to walk north to put his question to the grove itself, Fionnghuala gives him the piece that holds every colour to carry loose in his hand rather than shut in its bag, so that he may have the thing itself before him when he asks.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2012"><em>Fionnghuala silences the joke at her own hearth</em>, 15 an Cèitean, VE 881</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2019"></a>**1 am Màrt, VE 889** — *Diarmad walks north from Tobar dhìreach*.
