At seven-and-twenty, Diarmad sets out alone from Tobar dhìreach with a coal banked in a clay pot, a little food and the rainbow piece against his palm, walking three days north and a little west into country his own household has never settled.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2018"><em>Fionnghuala gives Diarmad the rainbow piece for the road</em>, 31 am Faoilleach, VE 889</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2020"></a>**5 am Màrt, VE 889** — *A gale overtakes Diarmad on the open moor*. On the second day of his walk a hard west wind rises over the high moor and does not slacken, and Diarmad pushes on through it regardless, his food too scant to spare for waiting out weather.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2019"><em>Diarmad walks north from Tobar dhìreach</em>, 1 am Màrt, VE 889</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2021"></a>**3 an Giblean, VE 889** — *Diarmad reaches the grove's edge in the gale*. On the third afternoon Diarmad comes under the first oaks of the grove he has walked three days to find, and shelters at a fallen trunk with a small fire, listening to a gale in the branches that sounds, to his tired ear, less like wind than like many voices speaking at once.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2020"><em>A gale overtakes Diarmad on the open moor</em>, 5 am Màrt, VE 889</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2022"></a>**12 am Faoilleach, VE 890** — *Diarmad reaches Doire ghlas after three days on the road* (Doire ghlas). After three days walking north-west from Tobar dhìreach, footsore and short of food, Diarmad comes down into the oak grove at Doire ghlas in the last light with a gale already roaring in the crowns of the trees.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2021"><em>Diarmad reaches the grove's edge in the gale</em>, 3 an Giblean, VE 889</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2023"></a>**30 am Faoilleach, VE 890** — *Diarmad builds his fire in the lee of a fallen oak* (Doire ghlas). In the shelter of a fallen trunk's torn roots, the one spot in the gale-driven grove where a small fire might live, Diarmad builds a fire of oak twigs from an ember he has carried the whole way from Tobar dhìreach in a moss-packed pot.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2022"><em>Diarmad reaches Doire ghlas after three days on the road</em>, 12 am Faoilleach, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0011a"></a>**17 an Gearran, VE 890** — *The Keeper in the grove* (Doire ghlas). In the oak grove at Doire ghlas a figure of grey smoke comes to Diarmad of the Mason's line, who has asked why the coal of the vein has colours. It names itself Coimhdeach na Fine, the kin's keeper, and tells him of the making of the world by Caoran, the Young God, and of the gift hidden in the coal. Asked how the colours may be opened, it gives a riddle: the sky, the earth and the sea each carry their own spirit; merge the spirits, and they become almighty. From Diarmad's line the telling of the making goes to every hearth.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2004"><em>Diarmad first asks why the pieces are coloured</em>, 15 an Cèitean, VE 869</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2015"><em>A fire-bearer brings word of a grove where the wind speaks</em>, 8 an t-Sultain, VE 886</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2018"><em>Fionnghuala gives Diarmad the rainbow piece for the road</em>, 31 am Faoilleach, VE 889</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2019"><em>Diarmad walks north from Tobar dhìreach</em>, 1 am Màrt, VE 889</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2021"><em>Diarmad reaches the grove's edge in the gale</em>, 3 an Giblean, VE 889</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2022"><em>Diarmad reaches Doire ghlas after three days on the road</em>, 12 am Faoilleach, VE 890</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2023"><em>Diarmad builds his fire in the lee of a fallen oak</em>, 30 am Faoilleach, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2024"></a>**19 an Gearran, VE 890** — *A grey figure stands still in the gale* (Doire ghlas). Across Diarmad's fire a figure of grey smoke, the height of a tall man, stands unmoving in a wind that flattens the flame and tears every leaf and branch in the grove; Diarmad does not run, and asks it what it is.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0011a"><em>The Keeper in the grove</em>, 17 an Gearran, VE 890</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2023"><em>Diarmad builds his fire in the lee of a fallen oak</em>, 30 am Faoilleach, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2025"></a>**11 am Màrt, VE 890** — *Coimhdeach na Fine names itself to Diarmad* (Doire ghlas). The figure names itself Coimhdeach na Fine, the keeper of the kin, made from the smoke of the first coal an Dia Òg woke, watching the island's people for the one who made them; it tells Diarmad it has watched his line since the mason and bids him ask his question.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0011a"><em>The Keeper in the grove</em>, 17 an Gearran, VE 890</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2024"><em>A grey figure stands still in the gale</em>, 19 an Gearran, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2026"></a>**30 an Giblean, VE 890** — *Diarmad hears Aithris a' Chruthachaidh* (Doire ghlas). Coimhdeach na Fine tells Diarmad the whole Aithris a' Chruthachaidh, from Caoran's choosing of coal to the shaping of the world and the island's own birth of fire, and of the seven spirits hidden colour by colour in the vein under the mountains.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0011a"><em>The Keeper in the grove</em>, 17 an Gearran, VE 890</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2025"><em>Coimhdeach na Fine names itself to Diarmad</em>, 11 am Màrt, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2027"></a>**7 an Cèitean, VE 890** — *Diarmad asks whether an Dia Òg was angry* (Doire ghlas). Shamed by the telling of how an Dia-shluagh once found the coloured stones and let them fall back into the heather unknown, Diarmad asks Coimhdeach na Fine whether an Dia Òg was angry at the forgetting; Coimhdeach na Fine answers that he only laughed, for a gift not opened is still given.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0011a"><em>The Keeper in the grove</em>, 17 an Gearran, VE 890</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2026"><em>Diarmad hears Aithris a' Chruthachaidh</em>, 30 an Giblean, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2028"></a>**16 an Cèitean, VE 890** — *Coimhdeach na Fine gives Diarmad Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich* (Doire ghlas). Asked why Teine a' Chlachair burned the colour out of every coal alike, Coimhdeach na Fine answers that they are burned all in one fire and none in its own, and gives Diarmad Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich of the sky, the earth and the sea, first in the old words and then in his own tongue.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0011a"><em>The Keeper in the grove</em>, 17 an Gearran, VE 890</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2027"><em>Diarmad asks whether an Dia Òg was angry</em>, 7 an Cèitean, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2029"></a>**27 an Cèitean, VE 890** — *Coimhdeach na Fine leaves Diarmad by his dying fire* (Doire ghlas). When Diarmad calls Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich no answer, Coimhdeach na Fine tells him it is the one it was given to give, and the wind that had gone round it all night long passes through the place where it stood and finds nothing there.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0011a"><em>The Keeper in the grove</em>, 17 an Gearran, VE 890</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2028"><em>Coimhdeach na Fine gives Diarmad Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich</em>, 16 an Cèitean, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2030"></a>**3 an t-Ògmhios, VE 890** — *Diarmad tries Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich alone against sky, earth and fire* (Doire ghlas). Unwilling to leave the grove, Diarmad spends two days trying gual bogha-froise by himself: held up to a gap of open sky, buried in the wet earth by the fallen trunk, and set back into his own small fire alone, with no sea near enough to try and none of the other six coals in hand.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0011a"><em>The Keeper in the grove</em>, 17 an Gearran, VE 890</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2029"><em>Coimhdeach na Fine leaves Diarmad by his dying fire</em>, 27 an Cèitean, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2031"></a>**23 an t-Iuchar, VE 890** — *Diarmad speaks Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich over the bare coal* (Doire ghlas). On the second morning Diarmad kneels and speaks Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich's words aloud over the coal laid bare on the fallen trunk's bark; nothing in it changes, and he gives up trying it alone after that.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0011a"><em>The Keeper in the grove</em>, 17 an Gearran, VE 890</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2030"><em>Diarmad tries Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich alone against sky, earth and fire</em>, 3 an t-Ògmhios, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2032"></a>**1 an Lùnastal, VE 890** — *Diarmad turns south for Tobar dhìreach* (Doire ghlas). After two days failing to open Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich alone, Diarmad banks his fire under turf, wraps gual bogha-froise back against his chest, and sets out on the three-day road home, saying the words over to himself so as not to lose them.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0011a"><em>The Keeper in the grove</em>, 17 an Gearran, VE 890</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2031"><em>Diarmad speaks Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich over the bare coal</em>, 23 an t-Iuchar, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2033"></a>**19 an Lùnastal, VE 890** — *Diarmad returns to Tobar dhìreach*. Diarmad comes down into the high valleys on the evening of the third day with Aithris a' Chruthachaidh whole in him and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich unopened, not yet sure which of the two the hearths of his own kin will find harder to believe.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0011a"><em>The Keeper in the grove</em>, 17 an Gearran, VE 890</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2032"><em>Diarmad turns south for Tobar dhìreach</em>, 1 an Lùnastal, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2034"></a>**21 an Lùnastal, VE 890** — *The dead leaves go round Coimhdeach na Fine* (Doire ghlas). In the gale at Doire ghlas the dead leaves streaming past Diarmad's fire go round the place where the smoke-figure stands, as water goes round a rock, and meet again beyond it.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0011a"><em>The Keeper in the grove</em>, 17 an Gearran, VE 890</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2033"><em>Diarmad returns to Tobar dhìreach</em>, 19 an Lùnastal, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2035"></a>**8 an Dàmhair, VE 890** — *Diarmad sees the forgotten coal* (Doire ghlas). In Aithris a' Chruthachaidh Diarmad sees a child of an Dia-shluagh carry coloured stones home in her cloak and a whole valley throw them away as the mountain's droppings, and is ashamed for them.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0011a"><em>The Keeper in the grove</em>, 17 an Gearran, VE 890</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2034"><em>The dead leaves go round Coimhdeach na Fine</em>, 21 an Lùnastal, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2036"></a>**17 an Dàmhair, VE 890** — *A wren comes to the coal* (Doire ghlas). On his second morning alone in the grove a wren hops along the fallen trunk to within a hand of gual bogha-froise, looks at it and at Diarmad, and goes about its business; Diarmad does not try Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich again that day.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2035"><em>Diarmad sees the forgotten coal</em>, 8 an Dàmhair, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2037"></a>**6 an t-Samhain, VE 890** — *Diarmad says Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich over on the road*. All the first day of the walk home Diarmad says Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich aloud, the strange words and the plain, over and over, the way a man says a name so as not to lose it before he reaches the house.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2036"><em>A wren comes to the coal</em>, 17 an Dàmhair, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2038"></a>**24 an Dùbhlachd, VE 890** — *Diarmad tells Aithris a' Chruthachaidh at his own hearth*. Home from Doire ghlas, Diarmad stands at the hearth of Tobar dhìreach and tells the household the bones of what Coimhdeach na Fine gave him: the making of the island from drops of fire, the gift buried and thrown away, and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich of the sky, the earth and the sea.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0011a"><em>The Keeper in the grove</em>, 17 an Gearran, VE 890</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2037"><em>Diarmad says Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich over on the road</em>, 6 an t-Samhain, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2039"></a>**26 an Dùbhlachd, VE 890** — *The hearth's laughter*. A kinsman of Tadhg's line by marriage laughs Aithris a' Chruthachaidh off as three days' talk with an empty grove, and the household laughs with him, gently, glad to have its world handed back the shape it always was.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2038"><em>Diarmad tells Aithris a' Chruthachaidh at his own hearth</em>, 24 an Dùbhlachd, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2040"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, VE 890** — *Niamh will not believe it*. Told Aithris a' Chruthachaidh in full, alone, Diarmad's wife Niamh hears him out and says plainly that hunger and cold on an empty moor can put much into a man's head that has no business there, and that she does not believe a word of it.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2039"><em>The hearth's laughter</em>, 26 an Dùbhlachd, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2041"></a>**17 am Màrt, VE 892** — *Diarmad begins gathering the fathers' names*. Diarmad takes up a second labour beside Aithris a' Chruthachaidh, walking hearth to hearth among the wider kin of the high valleys and the northern moor to ask each house how far back it can say its fathers' names, keeping no name a house cannot answer for.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2040"><em>Niamh will not believe it</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2042"></a>**15 an Giblean, VE 893** — *Old women give up the fathers' names*. Old women who never troubled themselves over Diarmad's question turn out to have kept four and five fathers' names back, and are glad to give them to someone willing to carry the weight of remembering them.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2041"><em>Diarmad begins gathering the fathers' names</em>, 17 am Màrt, VE 892</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2043"></a>**14 an Cèitean, VE 895** — *The first recital of the Line*. On Oidhche an Dealanaich Diarmad stands at his own hearth and says the fathers' names from Neachdan to himself without a stumble, and Niamh, unbelieving still, stands after him and says Aithris a' Chruthachaidh in full because a house should hear whole what its head carries.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2042"><em>Old women give up the fathers' names</em>, 15 an Giblean, VE 893</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2044"></a>**23 an Dàmhair, VE 895** — *Niamh says Aithris a' Chruthachaidh after the Line* (Tobar dhìreach). At the first standing of the Line Niamh stands after her husband and says Aithris a' Chruthachaidh, though she does not yet believe it, holding that a house ought to hear the whole of what its head carries.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2043"><em>The first recital of the Line</em>, 14 an Cèitean, VE 895</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2045"></a>**21 an t-Samhain, VE 897** — *Diarmad takes up Poit an Teine* (Tobar dhìreach). On his mother's death Diarmad takes the keeping of Poit an Teine alongside the keeping of the names and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich, three weights on one back.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2044"><em>Niamh says Aithris a' Chruthachaidh after the Line</em>, 23 an Dàmhair, VE 895</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2046"></a>**20 an Dùbhlachd, VE 900** — *Niamh comes to believe*. In the tenth year after Diarmad's return, Niamh tells their daughter that she has come to believe Aithris a' Chruthachaidh without ever deciding to, the way a path comes to lie worn into a hillside with no single footstep marked as the one that made it.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2044"><em>Niamh says Aithris a' Chruthachaidh after the Line</em>, 23 an Dàmhair, VE 895</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2047"></a>**18 am Faoilleach, VE 902** — *Fionnghuala dies keeping Poit an Teine*. Diarmad's mother Fionnghuala dies in her own bed with Poit an Teine within reach of her hand, as she had asked, and Diarmad takes up the keeping of the pot himself alongside the names and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2045"><em>Diarmad takes up Poit an Teine</em>, 21 an t-Samhain, VE 897</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2048"></a>**29 an t-Ògmhios, VE 903** — *The dark coals tried in driving rain*. At a standing of the Line the kin lay four dark coals bare on the hillside through a night of hard rain, on the thought that rain is the sky's own water as much as the sea's, and find them in the morning only wet, cold and themselves.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2047"><em>Fionnghuala dies keeping Poit an Teine</em>, 18 am Faoilleach, VE 902</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2049"></a>**28 an t-Iuchar, VE 904** — *The coals held up into the gale*. The kin carry the leather bag onto the ridge above Tobar dhìreach on a night of hard wind and hold the coals up bare-handed into it, on the thought that the sky's spirit might answer to its own true weather; the wind passes them by unchanged.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2048"><em>The dark coals tried in driving rain</em>, 29 an t-Ògmhios, VE 903</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2050"></a>**11 an t-Iuchar, VE 905** — *All seven burned together in one fire*. Reasoning that Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich's merging might mean the coals themselves rather than their elements, the kin burn all seven together in the hearth-fire and watch them go down black and ordinary together, no brighter for the company.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2049"><em>The coals held up into the gale</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, VE 904</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2051"></a>**9 an Lùnastal, VE 905** — *Sea-water carried inland for the trial*. A skin of true sea-water is carried the long way from the south shore to Tobar dhìreach and poured over the dark coals in a stone basin, the nearest the inland line can come to the sea itself; it wets them and leaves them cold, as the rain had.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2050"><em>All seven burned together in one fire</em>, 11 an t-Iuchar, VE 905</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2052"></a>**12 an t-Ògmhios, VE 910** — *Aithris a' Chruthachaidh carried to the northern moor*. A fire-bearer who has heard Aithris a' Chruthachaidh three times at Tobar dhìreach carries it unasked to a hearth on the northern moor, and tells it there in his own words, some pieces lost and others changed in the carrying.
- <a id="ev-EI-2053"></a>**14 an Cèitean, VE 920** — *Aithris a' Chruthachaidh reaches the eastern hearths*. By the thirtieth year after Diarmad's walk to the grove, traders carry some shape of Aithris a' Chruthachaidh to nearly every hearth of the eastern farms, garbled in a dozen small ways but keeping, in each, the one true thing: that the coal holds a gift no one has yet opened.
- <a id="ev-EI-2054"></a>**15 an Giblean, VE 925** — *A garbled riddle comes back from the east*. A trader newly down from the east gives Diarmad a telling of his own riddle in which the sea and the sky have changed places and the earth has dropped out; Diarmad sits a long while after, struck by how far a true thing can travel.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2051"><em>Sea-water carried inland for the trial</em>, 9 an Lùnastal, VE 905</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2055"></a>**17 am Màrt, VE 931** — *Diarmad dies sure the answer is near*. Diarmad dies at his hearth with Poit an Teine near him and the six dark coals and the rainbow at his side, telling Niamh he is sure the answer is nearer than it has ever been, though he cannot say what has brought the nearness home to him.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2054"><em>A garbled riddle comes back from the east</em>, 15 an Giblean, VE 925</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2056"></a>**16 an Gearran, VE 940** — *Deirbhile fixes Aithris a' Chruthachaidh word for word*. Diarmad's daughter Deirbhile, keeping Aithris a' Chruthachaidh more exactly than her father ever told it, teaches it word for word to her own children and to any of the wider kin who will learn it as strictly as she asks.
- <a id="ev-EI-2057"></a>**18 am Faoilleach, VE 945** — *Deirbhile teaches Aithris a' Chruthachaidh a section at a time* (Tobar dhìreach). Deirbhile sits each of her children down in turn and makes them say Aithris a' Chruthachaidh back to her a section at a time until they have it as clean as she does, and teaches it so to any of the kin who will sit still for the whole.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2056"><em>Deirbhile fixes Aithris a' Chruthachaidh word for word</em>, 16 an Gearran, VE 940</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2058"></a>**20 an Dùbhlachd, VE 950** — *Aithris a' Chruthachaidh said at an eastern hearth*. Three mouths removed from Deirbhile, a woman of an eastern household with no claim on the Line beyond distant kinship says Aithris a' Chruthachaidh standing on the darkest night, and tells a child who asks what Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich means that it is a question for An Clachair's own line to answer.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2057"><em>Deirbhile teaches Aithris a' Chruthachaidh a section at a time</em>, 18 am Faoilleach, VE 945</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0012"></a>**1 an t-Iuchar, VE 951** — *The mole at Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). A mole of unmortared boulders is laid out into the Abhainn naomh from the bank at Seann Skell, long enough to shelter a dozen boats from the current. Its foot lies under water still at the lowest tides, and every quay wall built there since stands on it.
- <a id="ev-EI-2501"></a>**31 an t-Iuchar, VE 951** — *The old man begins choosing stones at Skell* (Seann Skell). On the first day of the warm month an old man of the river bank at Skell walks the shingle at first light and chooses, by a judgement none of the younger men beside him can name, the boulder that will be rolled and set as the first stone of a mole into the current.
- <a id="ev-EI-2502"></a>**21 an Gearran, VE 955** — *The trying of Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich is let rest at the mason's hearth*. After coals have been carried to unceasing rain, sunk in sea-water fetched home in skins, and set together seven at once in the hottest fire the line's hands can build, and have come out of every trial the same dull stones, Clann a' Chlachair lets the trying rest, the leather bag closed and kept rather than opened again.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0011a"><em>The Keeper in the grove</em>, 17 an Gearran, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2503"></a>**23 am Faoilleach, VE 958** — *A grandson stands against the current* (Seann Skell). A boy of the old man's own kin takes to standing chest-deep at the mole's outer edge on calm summer days, bracing his feet on the last stone set and letting the river push at him without giving ground, watched from the bank by a grandfather who says nothing of it either way.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0012"><em>The mole at Seann Skell</em>, 1 an t-Iuchar, VE 951</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2504"></a>**31 an Lùnastal, VE 960** — *The mole's first winter* (Seann Skell). By the turn of the second year the low ridge of unmortared boulders reaches far enough from the bank at Skell that boats which once beached in the open now lie sheltered in its lee, a dozen at a time on a hard night, and the households along that stretch stop thinking of their landing as open water.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0012"><em>The mole at Seann Skell</em>, 1 an t-Iuchar, VE 951</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2505"></a>**2 an Lùnastal, VE 962** — *The first slab set on the worst scramble at Bral* (Seann Bhral). A woman of the grazing household above the western cliffs at Bral works a frost-loosened slab, over most of a season, into a single set step at the foot of the worst stretch of the scramble down to the shingle, wedging it level with smaller stones packed beneath.
- <a id="ev-EI-2506"></a>**28 an Dàmhair, VE 964** — *The first stone box raised for the dead of Vell* (Eilean dhearg). A household of the low south-eastern headland rows one of its own dead out to the near island for the first time in a boat built broad enough for the crossing, and raises a box of four slabs and a lid over the body, its face set toward the mainland shore rather than the open sea beyond.
- <a id="ev-EI-2507"></a>**29 an t-Sultain, VE 966** — *The flood the mole holds against* (Seann Skell). A flood the old man says he has not seen the like of in all his years on the bank takes one small boat downstream and out of reach, but drives its whole weight against the mole's upstream face without shifting a single stone the old man has set, and the ridge stands scoured clean when the water falls.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0012"><em>The mole at Seann Skell</em>, 1 an t-Iuchar, VE 951</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2508"></a>**7 an Cèitean, VE 968** — *Other households ask for the same lee* (Seann Skell). After the flood, households that had watched the mole rise from a distance come to the old man and ask to have their own landings brought under its shelter, and he sets them to the rolling and placing exactly as he learned it, so the work outgrows any one household's hands.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0012"><em>The mole at Seann Skell</em>, 1 an t-Iuchar, VE 951</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2509"></a>**8 an Giblean, VE 975** — *The old stone-judge counts the boats coming in* (Seann Skell). In his last summers, too stiff to walk the bank at first light, the old man who began the mole at Skell sits above the river of an evening and counts the boats coming in under its lee.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0012"><em>The mole at Seann Skell</em>, 1 an t-Iuchar, VE 951</a>.</span>

## The Years VE 1,001 – 1,500

- <a id="ev-EI-2510"></a>**9 am Faoilleach, VE 1,005** — *The steps reach the first shelf at Bral* (Seann Bhral). Cut a slab at a time in whatever season allows it, the steps from the shingle at Bral now run unbroken to a shelf a third of the way up the cliff, wide enough for two to pass, while above it the bare scramble still wants both hands free.
- <a id="ev-EI-2511"></a>**7 an Gearran, VE 1,012** — *A boy runs the finished stretch without a hand to the rock* (Seann Bhral). Sent down for shellfish on a morning the household is short-handed, a boy runs the whole finished stretch of the Bral steps down and up again without once touching the rock, and laughs at the top of it while the women above, none of whom has ever gone that way without a hand out, laugh with him.
- <a id="ev-I-0013"></a>**30 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,027** — *The steps of Seann Bhral* (Seann Bhral). Two hundred and twelve steps are cut up the cliff at Seann Bhral, from the shingle to the grazing above. Their treads are worn hollow in the middle. How many feet that took, none has reckoned.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2505"><em>The first slab set on the worst scramble at Bral</em>, 2 an Lùnastal, VE 962</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2510"><em>The steps reach the first shelf at Bral</em>, 9 am Faoilleach, VE 1,005</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2511"><em>A boy runs the finished stretch without a hand to the rock</em>, 7 an Gearran, VE 1,012</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2512"></a>**12 an t-Samhain, VE 1,040** — *The steps above the shelf go slower* (Seann Bhral). Above the first shelf at Bral the rock runs harder and gives up fewer slabs, and a worker of the household spends a whole season on a stretch of a dozen feet that yields three steps.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0013"><em>The steps of Seann Bhral</em>, 30 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,027</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2513"></a>**11 an Dùbhlachd, VE 1,060** — *An old woman rests her hand on the topmost step* (Seann Bhral). An old woman of Bral sits of an evening on the shelf a third of the way up the cliff and runs her hand along the edge of the topmost step then cut, saying of the rock above only that it will come when it comes.
- <a id="ev-EI-2514"></a>**5 an Cèitean, VE 1,080** — *The two hundred and twelfth step is cut at Bral* (Seann Bhral). The steps from the shingle to the grazing above Bral are finished at two hundred and twelve, cut across three generations of hands that never once all worked in the same season, the last stretch of hard rock giving up only three steps for a whole season's work.
- <a id="ev-EI-2515"></a>**3 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,090** — *The treads of Bral wear hollow* (Seann Bhral). The lower steps at Bral, cut soonest and used longest, wear a shallow dish into their middles before the upper steps have worn at all.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0013"><em>The steps of Seann Bhral</em>, 30 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,027</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0014"></a>**4 an Cèitean, VE 1,096** — *The dead of Seann Vell go to Eilean dhearg* (Eilean dhearg). The Seann-Dhaoine of Seann Vell row their dead out to Eilean dhearg and lay them in stone boxes facing the mainland. Forty boxes are counted there. No grave of theirs of this time is found on the mainland.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2506"><em>The first stone box raised for the dead of Vell</em>, 28 an Dàmhair, VE 964</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2516"></a>**8 am Màrt, VE 1,100** — *The recital said to a gathering that came unsent-for*. On the dark-of-the-year night the keeper of An Clachair's hearth stands to say the fathers' names before a gathering that has walked up from the lower valleys of its own will, without any household sending word ahead, and says Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich after as she has said it every year, and closes the bag again unopened.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0011a"><em>The Keeper in the grove</em>, 17 an Gearran, VE 890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2517"></a>**6 an Giblean, VE 1,100** — *No grave left open through a night on Eilean dhearg* (Eilean dhearg). The households of Vell will not let a stone box stand open through a night; an unfinished box is covered with brush and stone until the true lid can be rowed across.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0014"><em>The dead of Seann Vell go to Eilean dhearg</em>, 4 an Cèitean, VE 1,096</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2518"></a>**22 an Cèitean, VE 1,131** — *A woman rows her mother out, then her daughter* (Eilean dhearg). A woman of the same shore rows her own mother's body to the island one autumn and her own daughter's the spring after, and is remembered to have gone to the boat the second time with a face that told the household this crossing was not, for her, a labour like any other.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0014"><em>The dead of Seann Vell go to Eilean dhearg</em>, 4 an Cèitean, VE 1,096</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2519"></a>**20 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,169** — *The fortieth box is counted at Vell* (Eilean dhearg). By whatever reckoning that shore keeps among itself, the box set in this season is counted the fortieth to stand on the low ground of the island, its lid laid last and turned, like every lid before it, back toward the water it was rowed across.
- <a id="ev-I-0015"></a>**2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,170** — *The fish-channel of Seann Toll* (Seann Toll). At Seann Toll a channel is cut through a shelf of rock into a pool beside the Abhainn uaine, with a slot for a wattle gate. When the river falls the gate is dropped and the pool emptied by hand. The slot is sharp still.
- <a id="ev-EI-2520"></a>**19 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,175** — *The channel at Toll cut through to the pool* (Seann Toll). At Toll a household finishes widening a natural crack in a rock shelf into a channel between the still water above and a tide-fed pool below, following the crack's own line rather than cutting fresh through sound stone.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0015"><em>The fish-channel of Seann Toll</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,170</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2521"></a>**20 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,176** — *The careful cutter begins his rows at Tarr* (Seann Tarr). Along the pale cliffs above Tarr a man of that shore's trade begins cutting rows of signs into the standing rock with a flaked flint chisel and a small stone hammer, each stroke light enough to take the chisel through a shape without lifting it.
- <a id="ev-EI-2522"></a>**22 an Cèitean, VE 1,178** — *The slots cut for the wattle gate* (Seann Toll). Deep slots are picked into the rock on either side of the channel's narrowest place at Toll, true from above the river's highest mark to below its lowest, so that a woven gate can be driven home and drawn again season by season.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0015"><em>The fish-channel of Seann Toll</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,170</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2523"></a>**23 an Giblean, VE 1,180** — *The Toll gate first dropped* (Seann Toll). The wattle gate is driven home into the slots at Toll for the first time, one man in the channel to guide its foot and two above on the mallet, penning the fish left behind by the ebb in the pool below for the household to take by hand.
- <a id="ev-EI-2524"></a>**25 am Màrt, VE 1,183** — *Shell first carried out onto the sunken reed track* (Seann Warr). At the western shore of Loch chrom, after a wet season sinks the worn reed track sooner than most years, broken mussel shell is carried out and trodden into the worst of the sunken ground for the first time, rather than left by the shallows where it was worked.
- <a id="ev-EI-2525"></a>**24 an Gearran, VE 1,185** — *A child learns the channel by her feet* (Seann Toll). A child of the Toll household is led by the hand along the smoothed floor of the fish channel at low water until her feet know which stretch stands firm and which gives, without a word for it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0015"><em>The fish-channel of Seann Toll</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,170</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2526"></a>**26 am Faoilleach, VE 1,190** — *A boy watches an afternoon of the cutting* (Seann Tarr). A boy sits a whole afternoon at the foot of the Tarr cliff watching the careful cutter's hand, and counts, by a later telling, near two hundred light strokes of the hammer to finish a single sign.
- <a id="ev-EI-2527"></a>**28 an Dùbhlachd, VE 1,197** — *The carrying of shell becomes yearly work* (Seann Warr). What began as one season's answer to a bad sinking becomes, without any one choice remembered for it, a thing the loch household does each year: crushed shell carried out and packed into the worst stretches of the reed crossing on the same errand that gathers the day's mussel.
- <a id="ev-EI-2528"></a>**8 am Màrt, VE 1,198** — *A boy loses two fingers to the mallet* (Seann Toll). Misjudging the moment to clear the mallet's swing at the Toll gate, a boy of the household loses two fingers of his left hand; he goes on working the gate in the years after with the hand that remains him.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0015"><em>The fish-channel of Seann Toll</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,170</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2529"></a>**7 an Gearran, VE 1,200** — *The gate dropped three times in a dry summer* (Seann Toll). In a summer when the river falls low and stays low the Toll household drops and draws its gate three times before the autumn rains, and reckons the late summer by the droppings rather than by days.
- <a id="ev-EI-2530"></a>**26 am Faoilleach, VE 1,210** — *Shell crushed before carrying* (Seann Warr). The loch household at Warr crushes the mussel shell underfoot on a flat stone kept by the water before carrying it out, having found that crushed shell packs and holds where whole shell slides.
- <a id="ev-EI-2531"></a>**24 an Gearran, VE 1,220** — *The reed-marsh flood* (Seann Warr). A hard winter's water works thin the shell already laid on the western marsh crossing at Loch chrom, and the household spends the following spring re-packing the low places before the road can be trusted at a run again.
- <a id="ev-I-0016"></a>**7 am Màrt, VE 1,233** — *The shell causeway of Seann Warr* (Seann Warr). A road of crushed shell is laid across the reed marsh at Seann Warr, on the western shore of Loch chrom, a little over a mile long and raised a forearm above the reeds. It is the eldest made road on the island that may still be walked.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2524"><em>Shell first carried out onto the sunken reed track</em>, 25 am Màrt, VE 1,183</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2527"><em>The carrying of shell becomes yearly work</em>, 28 an Dùbhlachd, VE 1,197</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2530"><em>Shell crushed before carrying</em>, 26 am Faoilleach, VE 1,210</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2531"><em>The reed-marsh flood</em>, 24 an Gearran, VE 1,220</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2532"></a>**25 am Màrt, VE 1,236** — *A girl runs the whole shell road at once* (Seann Warr). Sent to carry word that the boats are wanted in before dark, a girl of the loch household crosses the whole finished length of the shell road at a run without once testing the ground with a toe, the first so remembered to trust it end to end.
- <a id="ev-EI-2533"></a>**23 an Giblean, VE 1,240** — *An old row cut over and broken* (Seann Tarr). Somewhere along the Tarr cliff a first cutting is found deepened and cut across by a later hand, worked with the same patient care as the row it undoes; no one of that shore is remembered ever claiming to know why.
- <a id="ev-EI-2534"></a>**2 an Dàmhair, VE 1,250** — *A northern-shore family comes to see the road* (Seann Warr). A household from further round Loch chrom's northern shore walks the finished road from end to end and home again, but goes the long way about on their own crossing rather than tread the loch household's shell a second time.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0016"><em>The shell causeway of Seann Warr</em>, 7 am Màrt, VE 1,233</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2535"></a>**31 an Dàmhair, VE 1,260** — *The road left to its builders* (Seann Warr). The household that laid the shell road keeps it as a household keeps a hearth, and a stranger's foot on another household's shell is not a thing lightly done on that shore.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0016"><em>The shell causeway of Seann Warr</em>, 7 am Màrt, VE 1,233</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0017"></a>**5 an Giblean, VE 1,301** — *The script appears at Seann Tarr* (Seann Tarr). Rows of signs are cut into the cliff above Seann Tarr, in the script that is found afterwards on the standing stones. It is not Dia-thìris, and none has read it. No sign of it has a meaning that all accept.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2521"><em>The careful cutter begins his rows at Tarr</em>, 20 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,176</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2526"><em>A boy watches an afternoon of the cutting</em>, 26 am Faoilleach, VE 1,190</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2533"><em>An old row cut over and broken</em>, 23 an Giblean, VE 1,240</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2536"></a>**14 an Dùbhlachd, VE 1,301** — *The first row cut on the cliff at Tarr* (Seann Tarr). A man of the cliff shore at Tarr finishes a row of signs cut into the standing rock with a flint chisel, each sign some two hundred light blows of the hammer, and begins a second above it.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0017"><em>The script appears at Seann Tarr</em>, 5 an Giblean, VE 1,301</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2537"></a>**28 an Dùbhlachd, VE 1,320** — *More rows cut at Tarr* (Seann Tarr). By the time the careful cutter's hand has grown unsteady with age, the rows above Tarr run further along the face than any one person standing at its foot can take in with a single turn of the head, and no later hand takes up the cutting with the same close care.
- <a id="ev-EI-2538"></a>**15 an t-Sultain, VE 1,330** — *A woman of Toll walks the coast and finds the cliff* (Seann Toll). On an errand along the coast a woman of the Toll household comes to the cliff at Tarr and stands a while in the rain watching it darken the newest of the cut rows against the paler stone around them, before going on her way without speaking of it at either household she passes between.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0017"><em>The script appears at Seann Tarr</em>, 5 an Giblean, VE 1,301</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2539"></a>**14 an Dàmhair, VE 1,344** — *Aodh born at Tobar dhìreach*. Aodh is born into Clann a' Chlachair at Tobar dhìreach, into a hearth that has by then said Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich at every recital for near five hundred years without once carrying gual òir to the sea it is said to answer.
- <a id="ev-EI-2540"></a>**5 an Lùnastal, VE 1,353** — *A traveller names the sea to Aodh*. A trader up from the eastern farms speaks in passing of grey water without a far shore, and Aodh, nine years old, asks him plainly whether he has seen it; it is the first time the boy understands the sea for more than a word said at the recital.
- <a id="ev-EI-2541"></a>**7 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,360** — *Aodh works the harvest before going* (Tobar dhìreach). Asked by Muirgheal to wait until the barley is in and the beasts settled, Aodh works that harvest with more will than any before it, as a man works to leave a thing clean behind him.
- <a id="ev-EI-2542"></a>**2 an Dàmhair, VE 1,364** — *Aodh tells Muirgheal he means to walk north*. At twenty Aodh tells Muirgheal, keeper of Poit an Teine at Tobar dhìreach, that he means to carry gual òir to the sea before another generation lets Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich lie; she does not laugh, and asks only that he wait until the harvest is in.
- <a id="ev-EI-2543"></a>**3 an t-Sultain, VE 1,369** — *Muirgheal bids Aodh take all seven* (Tobar dhìreach). Muirgheal tells Aodh to carry all seven pieces to the sea and not the gold alone, since the seven came out of the mason's tunic together and ought to go together, so that whatever answers answers among its own.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2541"><em>Aodh works the harvest before going</em>, 7 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,360</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2544"></a>**17 an Gearran, VE 1,370** — *Aodh sets out for the northern shore*. With the harvest under thatch and the beasts driven in from the high pasture, Aodh sets out alone from Tobar dhìreach with all seven coals of the vein wrapped against his chest, walking north across the moor toward a sea he has never seen.
- <a id="ev-EI-2545"></a>**6 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,370** — *Aodh's first sight of the sea* (Ceann thais). Aodh comes over the last rise of the moor and stands before the open sea for the first time in his life, understanding only then, by its slow endless heave, why no telling at any hearth had ever thought the word alone enough to carry it.
- <a id="ev-I-0017a"></a>**14 an t-Sultain, VE 1,370** — *The gold coal takes fire on the sea* (Ceann thais). Aodh of the Mason's line carries the seven coals of the vein down to the northern shore, below where Ceann thais now stands, and throws them into the sea one by one. The coal with the sheen of gold takes fire on the water and burns gold until the waves put it under; the other six sink. It is the first of the Seven Coals to be lit from its own spirit.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2539"><em>Aodh born at Tobar dhìreach</em>, 14 an Dàmhair, VE 1,344</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2540"><em>A traveller names the sea to Aodh</em>, 5 an Lùnastal, VE 1,353</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2542"><em>Aodh tells Muirgheal he means to walk north</em>, 2 an Dàmhair, VE 1,364</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2543"><em>Muirgheal bids Aodh take all seven</em>, 3 an t-Sultain, VE 1,369</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2544"><em>Aodh sets out for the northern shore</em>, 17 an Gearran, VE 1,370</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-2545"><em>Aodh's first sight of the sea</em>, 6 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,370</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2546"></a>**30 an t-Sultain, VE 1,370** — *Gual òir takes fire on the sea* (Ceann thais). Aodh throws na Seachd Guail of the vein into the sea one by one from the northern shingle; six sink as any coal sinks, and the coal with the sheen of gold takes fire on the swell and burns gold until a breaker rolls it under.
- <a id="ev-EI-2547"></a>**3 an Dàmhair, VE 1,370** — *Muirgheal weeps at the telling of the gold*. Hearing Aodh's account at the hearth of Tobar dhìreach, old Muirgheal weeps before the gathered kin, near five hundred years since the grove, and says that Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich is proved true: each coal answers to its own element.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0017a"><em>The gold coal takes fire on the sea</em>, 14 an t-Sultain, VE 1,370</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2548"></a>**7 an t-Samhain, VE 1,370** — *The name gual òir said at the recital*. For the first time since the mason's own well a new line is added to the recital after the fathers' names, telling of gual òir's lighting on the northern sea; from that night the piece is called gual òir at every telling that carries it on.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0017a"><em>The gold coal takes fire on the sea</em>, 14 an t-Sultain, VE 1,370</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2549"></a>**8 an t-Samhain, VE 1,370** — *Word of gual òir spreads from Tobar dhìreach*. Households a half-day's walk and more from Tobar dhìreach send someone to ask whether the telling of gual òir is true, and for days Poit an Teine's door stands open near the whole day to let in one more household wanting to hear it from Aodh's own mouth.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0017a"><em>The gold coal takes fire on the sea</em>, 14 an t-Sultain, VE 1,370</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2550"></a>**12 an Dùbhlachd, VE 1,370** — *Aodh sleeps a night above the tideline*. Aodh does not throw the coals on the evening he reaches the shore, but sleeps in a hollow above the tideline and listens all night to a sound he has never heard before.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2543"><em>Muirgheal bids Aodh take all seven</em>, 3 an t-Sultain, VE 1,369</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2551"></a>**13 an Dùbhlachd, VE 1,370** — *A new line added to the recital* (Tobar dhìreach). For the first time since the mason a new line is added after the fathers' names at the recital: that gual òir was thrown into the northern sea by Aodh and burned gold until the water put it under.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0017a"><em>The gold coal takes fire on the sea</em>, 14 an t-Sultain, VE 1,370</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2550"><em>Aodh sleeps a night above the tideline</em>, 12 an Dùbhlachd, VE 1,370</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2552"></a>**1 an Cèitean, VE 1,375** — *Aodh tries the six coals against ground, water and air*. In the years after the gold, Aodh carries the six unanswered coals to hilltop, black peat and standing rainwater within a day's walk of Tobar dhìreach, and once holds one to the bare air in a hard frost, and none of them answers him.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0017a"><em>The gold coal takes fire on the sea</em>, 14 an t-Sultain, VE 1,370</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2553"></a>**30 an Cèitean, VE 1,381** — *Muirgheal dies at Tobar dhìreach*. Muirgheal, keeper of Poit an Teine, dies an old woman having lived to hear the sea answer and wept for it; she is carried out and laid as her own mother was before her, the hearth-fire kept burning the whole night through.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0017a"><em>The gold coal takes fire on the sea</em>, 14 an t-Sultain, VE 1,370</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2554"></a>**4 am Màrt, VE 1,395** — *The six held up in a hard frost*. Aodh holds the six dark pieces up on an open palm in a hard frost, as Diarmad was said to have held the rainbow to the sky, and the bare air does not answer.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-2551"><em>A new line added to the recital</em>, 13 an Dùbhlachd, VE 1,370</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2555"></a>**2 an Giblean, VE 1,412** — *Aodh dies at Tobar dhìreach*. Aodh dies at eight-and-sixty years with the six unanswered coals still kept under his own hand; the recital adds his name after the fathers' names down from Neachdan, and tells that six of the seven still wait to be answered.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0017a"><em>The gold coal takes fire on the sea</em>, 14 an t-Sultain, VE 1,370</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2556"></a>**5 am Faoilleach, VE 1,420** — *New pieces of the vein found in the stream-bank*. A boy of Aodh's own house, following a strayed goat below Tobar dhìreach, finds the black vein showing bare in a stream-bank cut fresh by a hard season's rain, and the line for the first time since Neachdan holds more coal than the seven old pieces kept in the leather bag.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0017a"><em>The gold coal takes fire on the sea</em>, 14 an t-Sultain, VE 1,370</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-2557"></a>**3 an Gearran, VE 1,421** — *The new pieces passed hand to hand at the recital* (Tobar dhìreach). At the recital after the stream-bank finding the fresh pieces of the vein are passed round the gathered kin before the fire is banked, so that every soul there may hold a piece not yet tried against anything.
- <a id="ev-I-0018"></a>**17 an Giblean, VE 1,443** — *The fish-kilns of Seann Mhorn* (Seann Mhorn). Stone-lined pits with short flues are built above the beach at Seann Mhorn, to dry the catch over peat smoke. Seven are known. They are the first buildings on Dia-thìr made for a trade, and not for sleep or for the dead.
- <a id="ev-EI-3001"></a>**21 am Màrt, VE 1,446** — *The seventh kiln-pit dug at Morn* (Seann Mhorn). A household of the Seann-Dhaoine finishes a seventh stone-lined smoking pit above the shingle at Morn, each fed by a short turf-cut flue and kept for smoke and not flame, the first buildings raised on Dia-thìr for a trade rather than a hearth.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0018"><em>The fish-kilns of Seann Mhorn</em>, 17 an Giblean, VE 1,443</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3002"></a>**20 an Gearran, VE 1,450** — *The kiln smoke seen from inland* (Seann Mhorn). Herders of the inland hearths mark a grey column standing over the coast on still mornings and take it for a weather of that shore alone, not knowing for some years that it is a fire kept low and smouldering on purpose, day upon day, to dry a catch too great for one winter's eating.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0018"><em>The fish-kilns of Seann Mhorn</em>, 17 an Giblean, VE 1,443</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3003"></a>**22 am Faoilleach, VE 1,455** — *A kiln is fed with dry peat only* (Seann Mhorn). The keeper of the kilns at Morn keeps a store of dry peat under an overhang of turf for the kiln fires alone, holding that green peat flares where dry peat smokes, and a flare undoes a season's catch.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0018"><em>The fish-kilns of Seann Mhorn</em>, 17 an Giblean, VE 1,443</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3004"></a>**13 an Lùnastal, VE 1,461** — *The fourth pit drowned in a night's rain* (Seann Mhorn). A gale drives rain sideways off the bay at Morn and puts out the fourth kiln before the keeper's last round; she lets the pit stand cold rather than relight it under a soaked load, and carries the spoiled catch to the gulls at the tideline.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0018"><em>The fish-kilns of Seann Mhorn</em>, 17 an Giblean, VE 1,443</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3005"></a>**15 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,467** — *The ninth kiln set higher against the rain* (Seann Mhorn). The keeper of Morn's kilns digs a ninth pit set higher on the rise than the first seven, its flue longer and angled harder against a driving rain, after a wet night once cost the household a whole pit's catch.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0018"><em>The fish-kilns of Seann Mhorn</em>, 17 an Giblean, VE 1,443</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3006"></a>**16 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,470** — *The keeper teaches the wet-night watch to her niece* (Seann Mhorn). The keeper of the kilns teaches her niece to watch a kiln past the hour she would go to bed on a night of gathering rain, since a fire low enough to smoke is near enough to going out that a hard rain can take it.
- <a id="ev-EI-3007"></a>**18 an Cèitean, VE 1,478** — *The first ramp-slab laid at Brenn* (Seann Bhrenn). A household of skin-boat builders on the north coast begins laying flat slabs down a shelf of stone at Brenn from above the highest tide to deep water, meaning to draw down a load heavier than any hide boat's frame.
- <a id="ev-EI-3008"></a>**30 an Lùnastal, VE 1,483** — *A ramp-slab relaid twice at Brenn* (Seann Bhrenn). Twice a slab of the new ramp at Brenn settles crooked overnight where the ground beneath it runs soft, and is levered up with poles of green oak and reset on stone packed hard by hand and heel, without complaint from the household doing it.
- <a id="ev-EI-3009"></a>**1 an Lùnastal, VE 1,499** — *The first ramp at Brenn finished* (Seann Bhrenn). The first ramp at Brenn stands finished its whole length, laid true enough that a loaded sledge runs it without a check, some years before the household raises anything heavier upon it than the skin boats they had always built.

## The Years VE 1,501 – 2,000

- <a id="ev-EI-3010"></a>**4 an Cèitean, VE 1,510** — *A dog lies across the finished ramp* (Seann Bhrenn). A dog of the Brenn household lies full length on the finished ramp on warm days, and the household steps over it on the way down to the water rather than move it.
- <a id="ev-EI-3011"></a>**2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,512** — *The first plank-built hull framed at Brenn* (Seann Bhrenn). The household at Brenn frames the first hull of planks pegged and caulked over a timber frame, a make no shore of Dia-thìr had built before, and raises it on rollers along the finished ramp to wait on the tide.
- <a id="ev-I-0019"></a>**16 an Cèitean, VE 1,515** — *The slipways of Seann Bhrenn* (Seann Bhrenn). Long ramps of flat stone are laid down into the water at Seann Bhrenn, wide enough for hulls greater than any hide boat. Of the hulls nothing is left, nor any telling of where they went.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-3007"><em>The first ramp-slab laid at Brenn</em>, 18 an Cèitean, VE 1,478</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EI-3008"><em>A ramp-slab relaid twice at Brenn</em>, 30 an Lùnastal, VE 1,483</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EI-3009"><em>The first ramp at Brenn finished</em>, 1 an Lùnastal, VE 1,499</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-3011"><em>The first plank-built hull framed at Brenn</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,512</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3012"></a>**1 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,520** — *The first hull launched down the ramps* (Seann Bhrenn). The household of Brenn walks its first plank-built hull down the finished ramp on rollers and lets it take the water at the height of the tide; it floats low and steady, and hands already aboard it work it out past the last stone shelf into open water.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0019"><em>The slipways of Seann Bhrenn</em>, 16 an Cèitean, VE 1,515</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3013"></a>**30 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,521** — *The first hull goes out past the last shelf* (Seann Bhrenn). The hull launched from Brenn is worked out past the last shelf of stone into open water, and of where it went, or what it was built to reach, nothing is told.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0019"><em>The slipways of Seann Bhrenn</em>, 16 an Cèitean, VE 1,515</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3014"></a>**28 an Lùnastal, VE 1,522** — *A sail seen small from the height above Brenn* (Seann Bhrenn). A watcher on high ground along the coast near Brenn marks a dark sail standing out against the grey water and shrinking until it cannot be told from the sea it stands on, then turns back to the day's work once there is nothing left to watch.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0019"><em>The slipways of Seann Bhrenn</em>, 16 an Cèitean, VE 1,515</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3015"></a>**26 an t-Sultain, VE 1,540** — *The first platform driven at Loch chrom* (Crannagan Loch chrom). Oak piles are driven down through the shallows of Loch chrom to firmer ground beneath, and a floor of split timber raised across their tops, joined to the shore by a walk of planks lashed to crossbeams below; whose hands began it, no telling has kept.
- <a id="ev-EI-3016"></a>**25 an Dàmhair, VE 1,560** — *The planks of the lake walks listened to* (Crannagan Loch chrom). A child of the Loch chrom platforms is sent along every plank walk each morning to listen for the sound of a plank gone thin under its light weight before a grown foot finds it the hard way.
- <a id="ev-I-0020"></a>**7 am Màrt, VE 1,588** — *The lake dwellings of Loch chrom* (Loch chrom). Platforms on oak piles are raised in the shallows of Loch chrom and joined to the shore by plank walks. Whether the Seann-Dhaoine built them, or some other people of those years, is not known.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-3015"><em>The first platform driven at Loch chrom</em>, 26 an t-Sultain, VE 1,540</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EI-3016"><em>The planks of the lake walks listened to</em>, 25 an Dàmhair, VE 1,560</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3017"></a>**23 an t-Samhain, VE 1,600** — *Eels first taken from beneath the platforms* (Crannagan Loch chrom). The households of Loch chrom learn to lower baited traps through gaps left in the plank floors of their platforms, finding more eels gathered in the shade and stillness of the piles than any open bank of the loch had ever drawn to a hand's reach before.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0020"><em>The lake dwellings of Loch chrom</em>, 7 am Màrt, VE 1,588</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3018"></a>**14 an t-Sultain, VE 1,612** — *A child carries the first basket the length of the longest walk* (Crannagan Loch chrom). A child of one household at Loch chrom is trusted, for the first time, to carry a basket of the day's eels the whole length of the longest plank walk alone, watched without a word by an elder who by then counts the crossing an ordinary errand.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0020"><em>The lake dwellings of Loch chrom</em>, 7 am Màrt, VE 1,588</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3019"></a>**13 an Dàmhair, VE 1,640** — *A shared meal for a new pile* (Crannagan Loch chrom). The households of the lake platforms count a new oak pile driven and holding as an occasion for a shared meal on the nearest platform once the driving-frame is struck down.
- <a id="ev-EI-3020"></a>**25 an Cèitean, VE 1,650** — *A new pile driven at Loch chrom* (Crannagan Loch chrom). Four or five hands together drive a fresh oak pile into the mud of Loch chrom in place of one worked loose by years of current, the heaviest labour that shore's households reckon their own, and mark it, once it holds, with a shared meal on the platform.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0020"><em>The lake dwellings of Loch chrom</em>, 7 am Màrt, VE 1,588</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3021"></a>**26 an Giblean, VE 1,669** — *A second ramp begun at Brenn* (Seann Bhrenn). The household at Brenn lays a second ramp beside the first, wider and longer, and launches hulls from it in the years after the way any trade repeats what it has once learned, though none of those hulls draws the telling's eye as the first one did.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0019"><em>The slipways of Seann Bhrenn</em>, 16 an Cèitean, VE 1,515</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0021"></a>**6 an Gearran, VE 1,670** — *The whale-rib houses of Seann Dunn* (Seann Dunn). A whale strands below the southern Seann Dunn, and its ribs are raised for the frames of three round houses roofed with turf. The ribs are set up again in new houses at least twice before they rot.
- <a id="ev-EI-3022"></a>**23 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,672** — *A whale strands below the southern Dunn* (Seann Dunn). A whale comes ashore in an autumn gale below the southern Dunn, stranded beyond the tide's reach. It lives through a day and a night before its breathing stops, watched from a careful distance by the household nearest the shingle who first heard the surf change its voice.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0021"><em>The whale-rib houses of Seann Dunn</em>, 6 an Gearran, VE 1,670</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3023"></a>**22 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,672** — *The whale cut and shared along the shore* (Seann Dunn). Word of the stranding carries both ways along the shore, and households beyond the one that found it come down to Dunn to help with the cutting. The meat is salted and smoked, the blubber rendered in clay-lined pits, and no household that helped goes home with an empty basket.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0021"><em>The whale-rib houses of Seann Dunn</em>, 6 an Gearran, VE 1,670</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3024"></a>**18 an t-Sultain, VE 1,673** — *The whale's ribs driven upright for house frames* (Seann Dunn). Once the meat and the blubber are taken, the whale's bared ribs are driven upright in the turf above the shingle and lashed together at the crown. Three round houses stand roofed in turf by the year's end, taller and wider than any frame of bent branch the shore had raised before.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0021"><em>The whale-rib houses of Seann Dunn</em>, 6 an Gearran, VE 1,670</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3025"></a>**20 an Lùnastal, VE 1,675** — *Whale oil burned through two winters* (Seann Dunn). The oil rendered from the whale at the southern Dunn is kept in bladders and clay pots and burned in stone lamps through two winters at least, by more hearths than the one that first heard the surf change.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0021"><em>The whale-rib houses of Seann Dunn</em>, 6 an Gearran, VE 1,670</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3026"></a>**9 am Màrt, VE 1,678** — *The first rib found cracked through* (Seann Dunn). A rib bearing the heaviest weight of turf is found cracked through in its fifth winter, salt and rain having told on the bone faster than they tell on green wood. It is shored with a driven stake lashed alongside it rather than taken down before the roof can fall.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0021"><em>The whale-rib houses of Seann Dunn</em>, 6 an Gearran, VE 1,670</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3027"></a>**8 an Gearran, VE 1,720** — *The whale-rib houses raised a second time* (Seann Dunn). The original ribs having failed past shoring, the three houses at Dunn are raised again, this time on bone from a second, smaller stranding that had come ashore some way along the same stretch in the years between, cut by a household with no thought then of building.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0021"><em>The whale-rib houses of Seann Dunn</em>, 6 an Gearran, VE 1,670</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3028"></a>**6 an Cèitean, VE 1,731** — *A child turns up the buried foot of the first rib* (Seann Dunn). Digging in ground long since grown thick with turf, a child of the household turns up a length of bone gone soft and dark with years, and cannot say what it is until an elder names it: the foot of a rib from the first whale-rib house, sunk and near forgotten.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0021"><em>The whale-rib houses of Seann Dunn</em>, 6 an Gearran, VE 1,670</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0022"></a>**8 am Faoilleach, VE 1,734** — *The round houses of the eastern Seann Vell* (Seann Vell). At the eastern Seann Vell the Seann-Dhaoine build round houses of dry stone, each with a hearth sunk in the middle of the floor and a drain running out under the wall. Fourteen house-rings are counted there.
- <a id="ev-EI-3029"></a>**7 an Giblean, VE 1,740** — *A third raising on bone carried from the west* (Seann Dunn). The rib houses at the southern Dunn are raised a third time on bone carried along the shore from a whale cut further west, word of usable ribs travelling faster by then than word of strandings once did.
- <a id="ev-EI-3030"></a>**10 an Dàmhair, VE 1,758** — *The eastern Vell's first dry-stone round house* (Seann Vell). On ground thick with loose slabs above the eastern Vell, a household raises the first of what will become fourteen round houses, dry stone laid without mortar, each course fitted and refitted until it holds by its own weight alone, roofed at last by corbelled slabs closed with turf.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0022"><em>The round houses of the eastern Seann Vell</em>, 8 am Faoilleach, VE 1,734</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3031"></a>**8 an t-Samhain, VE 1,761** — *A hearth sunk below the sunk floor at eastern Vell* (Seann Vell). A household of the eastern Vell cuts its hearth-pit deeper than the sunk floor around it and lines it with stone set on edge, keeping the fire below any draught the door might let in, and letting the smoke find its own way out past the corbelled roof's crown.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0022"><em>The round houses of the eastern Seann Vell</em>, 8 am Faoilleach, VE 1,734</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3032"></a>**13 an Lùnastal, VE 1,766** — *The first drain cut beneath a wall at eastern Vell* (Seann Vell). A household whose floor stands wetter than its neighbours' through a wet winter takes up its own floor the following dry season and cuts a stone-lined channel under the wall to carry the water clear. Other households of the cluster, watching, take up their own floors in turn.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0022"><em>The round houses of the eastern Seann Vell</em>, 8 am Faoilleach, VE 1,734</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3033"></a>**11 an t-Sultain, VE 1,770** — *Drains cut under standing walls at Vell* (Seann Vell). Households of the eastern Vell whose houses were built without a drain take up their floors in a dry season and cut the channel in under walls already standing, having watched their neighbours' floors stand drier.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0022"><em>The round houses of the eastern Seann Vell</em>, 8 am Faoilleach, VE 1,734</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3034"></a>**16 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,773** — *The fourteenth house finished at eastern Vell* (Seann Vell). The last of the fourteen round houses stands finished on the eastern Vell's cleared ground, doors facing every way the ground allows, and every house of the cluster by now given its own dry outfall beneath the wall, a drier floor than the cluster's first years knew.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0022"><em>The round houses of the eastern Seann Vell</em>, 8 am Faoilleach, VE 1,734</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3035"></a>**15 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,796** — *A hollow-walled tower begun at the north-western Skell* (Seann Skell). A household of the north-western Skell, settled where the ground runs out to open water on three sides, begins a round tower of two dry-stone faces built together, a stair let into the gap between them, climbing the wall's own thickness rather than crossing any open floor.
- <a id="ev-EI-3036"></a>**19 an Giblean, VE 1,804** — *A winter storm throws down the unfinished outer face* (Seann Skell). With the tower a third of its final height, a winter storm throws down the outer face of the stair while the inner holds. The household clears the fallen stone from the gap and sets the cross-stones binding the two faces closer together through the whole climb of what remains to be built.
- <a id="ev-I-0023"></a>**10 an Dùbhlachd, VE 1,806** — *The tower at the north-western Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). At the least of the Seann Skell places, on the north-west coast, a single round tower of dry stone is raised, hollow-walled, with a stair in the thickness of the wall. It looks out over the water where the Sea-Watcher is afterwards seen.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-3035"><em>A hollow-walled tower begun at the north-western Skell</em>, 15 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,796</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-3036"><em>A winter storm throws down the unfinished outer face</em>, 19 an Giblean, VE 1,804</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3037"></a>**18 an Cèitean, VE 1,810** — *The first night at the tower's crown* (Seann Skell). With the stair whole and the parapet laid, a household of the north-western Skell climbs to the tower's open crown by clear starlight and sees more of the sea at once than any of that shore had seen from any roof or headland before it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0023"><em>The tower at the north-western Seann Skell</em>, 10 an Dùbhlachd, VE 1,806</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3038"></a>**20 an Gearran, VE 1,826** — *A fire lit on the parapet turns a boat from the rocks* (Seann Skell). In hard weather, a boat not of that shore is seen from the tower's crown standing in blind toward the rocks below. A fire lit on the parapet shows its crew the coast they are running for in time to bear off from the worst of it before the light fails.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0023"><em>The tower at the north-western Seann Skell</em>, 10 an Dùbhlachd, VE 1,806</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3039"></a>**21 am Màrt, VE 1,830** — *The stair walked after every storm* (Seann Skell). The household of the north-western Skell walks the tower stair from foot to crown after every storm, feeling along both faces for any stone gone slack in its bed.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0023"><em>The tower at the north-western Seann Skell</em>, 10 an Dùbhlachd, VE 1,806</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3040"></a>**31 an Dàmhair, VE 1,858** — *Stone huts built in the dune's lee at Toll* (Seann Toll). A household of Toll builds a row of low stone huts against the slope of a dune tall enough to break the worst of the sea wind before it reaches a wall, turf-roofed and set close, the sand that blows loose in an ordinary gale cleared each morning as an ordinary chore.
- <a id="ev-EI-3041"></a>**30 am Faoilleach, VE 1,879** — *A wind rises off the sea that does not settle* (Seann Toll). A wind rises off the sea and holds through a full day and into a second, driving sand off the dune's whole face until the air itself thickens to the colour and near the weight of the ground it carries, and sand mounts against the huts faster than hands can clear it.
- <a id="ev-EI-3042"></a>**4 an Gearran, VE 1,879** — *The household of Toll leaves the buried huts* (Seann Toll). Before the storm's second night closes on them, the household carries what it can and goes inland to higher ground, none of them lost or badly hurt in the leaving. The dune moves forward the width of the huts and beyond, and the row is not seen again above the sand.
- <a id="ev-I-0024"></a>**1 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,879** — *The huts of the northern Seann Toll* (Seann Toll). At Seann Toll on the north coast a cluster of stone huts is built in the lee of a dune. The dune afterwards buries them whole, and the sand keeps them.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-3040"><em>Stone huts built in the dune's lee at Toll</em>, 31 an Dàmhair, VE 1,858</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-3041"><em>A wind rises off the sea that does not settle</em>, 30 am Faoilleach, VE 1,879</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-3042"><em>The household of Toll leaves the buried huts</em>, 4 an Gearran, VE 1,879</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3043"></a>**5 an Lùnastal, VE 1,880** — *The dune moves the width of the huts* (Seann Toll). When the wind falls on the third day the dune at the northern Toll stands forward the whole width of the huts and beyond, a slope of new pale sand over ground where doors opened two days before.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0024"><em>The huts of the northern Seann Toll</em>, 1 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,879</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3044"></a>**7 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,890** — *New walls raised inland from the buried row* (Seann Toll). After digging finds the buried huts still whole but past any hope of clearing, the household of Toll gives up the digging and raises new walls further inland, on ground it judges, by the coast's own long habit of wind and sand, unlikely to be claimed again in its own lifetime.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0024"><em>The huts of the northern Seann Toll</em>, 1 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,879</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0025"></a>**2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,951** — *The eastern Seann Bhral* (Seann Bhral). At the Seann Bhral of the south-east coast the Seann-Dhaoine keep a landing and a line of fish-kilns like those of Seann Mhorn. The two places lie within a day's rowing of each other.
- <a id="ev-EI-3045"></a>**16 an Lùnastal, VE 1,951** — *Gormal takes up Poit an Teine*. Past thirty and past the birth of the one daughter who lived, Gormal takes up Poit an Teine and the leather bag of the line's an gual dathach from an aunt with no living daughter of her own, having already buried a father, an aunt and two of her own age who died saying the sky-coal would never light.
- <a id="ev-EI-3046"></a>**10 an Cèitean, VE 1,955** — *The middle kiln judged by smell* (Seann Bhral). The woman who minds the middle kiln at the eastern Bral judges the smoke by its smell at first light and dusk and the fish by the give of the flesh under one finger, and teaches both by standing a child at her elbow.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0025"><em>The eastern Seann Bhral</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,951</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3047"></a>**11 an Giblean, VE 1,960** — *Gormal's rule that the recital be kept*. Gormal rules that the fathers' names and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich after them be said standing every dark-of-the-year night whether any of the gathered kin care to hear it or not, holding that a recital kept only while it is believed is not kept at all.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-3045"><em>Gormal takes up Poit an Teine</em>, 16 an Lùnastal, VE 1,951</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3048"></a>**20 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,965** — *Gormal learns the fathers' names at nine* (Tobar dhìreach). Gormal stands the fathers' names over to the aunt who keeps Poit an Teine every evening of a whole winter until not a name comes out of its place, and asks, the first time she hears Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich whole, why no one has tried from higher ground.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-3047"><em>Gormal's rule that the recital be kept</em>, 11 an Giblean, VE 1,960</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3049"></a>**22 an Cèitean, VE 1,978** — *Three good harvests on the eastern slopes*. Word climbs to the high valleys of a third good harvest running on the farms of the eastern slopes, and the branch of the kin already drifting down toward that lower ground begins drifting faster, households following one another rather than waiting their own turn to go.
- <a id="ev-EI-3050"></a>**10 an Cèitean, VE 1,980** — *The branch leaves with no coal of the vein*. The last households of the eastern branch load their gear onto ox-sledges and go down from the high valleys for good, carrying a coal from their own daily fire and not one splinter of the mason's vein, the first households of the line ever to leave it empty-handed.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-3048"><em>Gormal learns the fathers' names at nine</em>, 20 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,965</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3051"></a>**8 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,981** — *Gormal names three hills for the sky*. At the recital after the branch's leaving, Gormal argues that the sky, like the sea, should be tried from the ground nearest it, and names three hills of her own judging, one south of the black well, one west toward Achadh dhìreach and a bare shoulder of moor she herself favours, though the kin cannot agree which of the three, or any other, truly stands highest.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-3050"><em>The branch leaves with no coal of the vein</em>, 10 an Cèitean, VE 1,980</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3052"></a>**7 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,983** — *Gormal meets the branch at the sledges* (Tobar dhìreach). Gormal walks out to the yard where the last of the going branch lash their sledges and tells them that no household has gone from the line empty of the vein before; she does not ask them to stay.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-3051"><em>Gormal names three hills for the sky</em>, 8 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,981</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3053"></a>**5 an Lùnastal, VE 1,985** — *The eastern Bral kilns kept alight in relay* (Seann Bhral). At the eastern landing three fish-kilns are kept fed at any time while three stand cold and swept, a household's whole catch never dried on the same night lest a failed wind leave it with nothing, the kilns built and worked in the same way as the sister kilns a day's rowing to the south.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0025"><em>The eastern Seann Bhral</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,951</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3054"></a>**14 am Faoilleach, VE 1,990** — *A girl reads the smoke at the eastern kilns* (Seann Bhral). A granddaughter of the woman who minds the middle kiln at the eastern landing notices, before anyone older has remarked it, that the smoke of that kiln runs paler than its neighbours in some seasons though the fire beneath is fed no differently, and is told only that the smoke says what the smoke says.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0025"><em>The eastern Seann Bhral</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,951</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3055"></a>**12 an Gearran, VE 1,993** — *Dried fish given back for a stranded beast's oil* (Seann Bhral). When a beast comes ashore dead below the southern kilns, the eastern landing sends back a share of its own dried fish by the same boat that brought the word, the giving between the two places running both ways over the years without either side keeping any closer account of it.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0025"><em>The eastern Seann Bhral</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,951</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3056"></a>**13 am Màrt, VE 1,996** — *Sìomha softens the recital for her own children*. Gormal's daughter Sìomha, unable to move her mother from the fixed words, begins saying the fathers' names and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich to her own children in gentler terms at her own hearth, without ever once letting the recital itself lapse.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-3052"><em>Gormal meets the branch at the sledges</em>, 7 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,983</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-3057"></a>**11 an Giblean, VE 1,998** — *The southern oyster mound stands taller than any household's reach* (Seann Mhorn). Along the southern headland the pile of raked and eaten oyster shell, built up by generations of the same households, comes to stand higher at its oldest end than a tall man can reach with his arm above his head, whiter at the crown where gulls have picked it clean.
- <a id="ev-EI-3058"></a>**28 an Dùbhlachd, VE 2,000** — *Gormal adds her own words at her last recital* (Tobar dhìreach). At the last recital she stands for, Gormal adds to the fixed words that the line has not yet thrown from the one hill that matters, and that whoever finds it will do the line more good in an afternoon than the branch in ten generations.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-3056"><em>Sìomha softens the recital for her own children</em>, 13 am Màrt, VE 1,996</a>.</span>

## The Years VE 2,001 – 2,500
