- <a id="ev-EI-6567"></a>**11 an Giblean, VE 5,322** — *Lìobhan names the rainbow's want* (Tobar dhìreach). Lìobhan says aloud to Ailean what he has half thought and not yet let himself say, that a coal made of every colour together may belong wholly to no single element, as a child of two households belongs wholly to neither; Ailean turns the thought over the whole of that winter until it settles into near certainty.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-6566"><em>Gormshuil born</em>, 8 an t-Ògmhios, VE 5,318</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-6568"></a>**10 an Cèitean, VE 5,323** — *Ailean tells the recital he means to light the six again* (Tobar dhìreach). At the recital in his three-and-twentieth year Ailean tells the reciters only that he means, in the year ahead, to light the six coals again by each one's own old way and carry them living to wherever the seventh might at last be answered; the reciters say they will wait to hear how it goes.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-6567"><em>Lìobhan names the rainbow's want</em>, 11 an Giblean, VE 5,322</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-6569"></a>**22 an Cèitean, VE 5,323** — *Ailean wakes the gold on the northern sea*. Ailean carries a fresh piece of the vein's gold-sheened colour the day's road north to the shore and throws it into the autumn swell as Aodh once did; it takes fire bright gold on the water, and this time he wades in after it and carries it home still burning in a clay pot with a lid of turf.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-6568"><em>Ailean tells the recital he means to light the six again</em>, 10 an Cèitean, VE 5,323</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-6570"></a>**8 an t-Ògmhios, VE 5,323** — *Ailean wakes the snowflake off the height* (Binnean a' Chlachair). Before winter closes Binnean a' Chlachair, Ailean climbs it in a bitter wind and lets gual sneachda fall from the height of his own arm as Fearghas once let it fall; it catches fire white halfway down the steep side, and he carries both fires down off the summit together.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-6569"><em>Ailean wakes the gold on the northern sea</em>, 22 an Cèitean, VE 5,323</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-6571"></a>**20 an t-Ògmhios, VE 5,323** — *Ailean wakes the black coal in the earth* (Tobar dhìreach). In the last week before the ground freezes hard Ailean digs a grave-deep hole beside the old slab at Tobar dhìreach, lays the black coal in it as Brian once did, and finds it warm and glowing at dawn; three fires now burn under his roof through the shortest days of the year.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-6570"><em>Ailean wakes the snowflake off the height</em>, 8 an t-Ògmhios, VE 5,323</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-6572"></a>**7 an t-Iuchar, VE 5,323** — *Ailean wades after the burning gold*. Where Aodh let the gold burn out on the water, Ailean wades in to the waist after it and catches it still burning between his cupped hands, and carries it home in a clay pot with a turf lid.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0017a"><em>The gold coal takes fire on the sea</em>, 14 an t-Sultain, VE 1,370</a>; ◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-6571"><em>Ailean wakes the black coal in the earth</em>, 20 an t-Ògmhios, VE 5,323</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-6573"></a>**3 am Faoilleach, VE 5,324** — *Ailean wakes the red-brown coal with his own blood* (Tobar dhìreach). In the yard behind his house on a frosted spring morning Ailean sets the red-brown coal on a stone and strikes it as Cormac once struck his; the hammer turns and lays his hand open, and where his blood runs onto the coal a deep warm flame comes up, leaving a scar to match the byname's own.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-6572"><em>Ailean wades after the burning gold</em>, 7 an t-Iuchar, VE 5,323</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-6574"></a>**24 am Faoilleach, VE 5,324** — *Ailean wakes the silver in the Abhainn ghorm* (Tobar dhìreach). At the crossing below Tobar dhìreach Ailean drinks from his own cupped hands as Eòghann once did and throws gual airgid into the current; it takes fire beneath the running water, and he lifts it out still alight with a wicker scoop made for the purpose.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-6573"><em>Ailean wakes the red-brown coal with his own blood</em>, 3 am Faoilleach, VE 5,324</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-6575"></a>**24 an Gearran, VE 5,324** — *Ailean wakes gual teine on his own doorstone* (Tobar dhìreach). Sitting on his doorstone at midsummer, thinking of nothing to do with fire, Ailean snaps his fingers over dust from the old fire coal without meaning to try anything, as Seathan once did by accident, and the dust flares red-gold and leaves no mark on him; the sixth fire is lit within the same year as the first five.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-6574"><em>Ailean wakes the silver in the Abhainn ghorm</em>, 24 am Faoilleach, VE 5,324</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-6576"></a>**17 am Màrt, VE 5,324** — *Ailean sets out north with six fires on a pole* (Tobar dhìreach). In the last week of an t-Iuchar Ailean sets out from Tobar dhìreach for Doire ghlas, carrying the six relit coals in clay pots slung from a pole across his shoulders and the dark rainbow coal wrapped against his chest, with Lìobhan and Gormshuil walking beside him as far as the last hearth before the moor.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-6575"><em>Ailean wakes gual teine on his own doorstone</em>, 24 an Gearran, VE 5,324</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-6577"></a>**24 an Giblean, VE 5,324** — *Six fires kept under one roof* (Tobar dhìreach). Through the last weeks of summer six fires burn in six clay pots under one roof at Tobar dhìreach for the first time since the making of the world, and Ailean wakes at odd hours to see that none has failed.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-6576"><em>Ailean sets out north with six fires on a pole</em>, 17 am Màrt, VE 5,324</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-6578"></a>**1 an Cèitean, VE 5,324** — *Gormshuil watches the lids lifted* (Tobar dhìreach). Gormshuil, six years old, kept from the pots by her mother's word, is found more than once crouched at a safe distance watching the lids lifted on the six low fires in their six colours.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-6576"><em>Ailean sets out north with six fires on a pole</em>, 17 am Màrt, VE 5,324</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EI-6579"></a>**22 an t-Ògmhios, VE 5,324** — *Lìobhan parts from Ailean at the last hearth*. Lìobhan walks with Ailean as far as the last hearth before the moor with Gormshuil on her hip, and tells him only to mind his feet on the wet northern slopes and that she will keep the house fire until he comes home.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EI-6577"><em>Six fires kept under one roof</em>, 24 an Giblean, VE 5,324</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0080a"></a>**21 an t-Iuchar, VE 5,324** — *The rainbow coal lit by the Keeper* (Doire ghlas). Ailean of Clann na Ceiste, having lit each of the six coals again by its own way, carries them burning to the grove at Doire ghlas with the last coal, which his kindred have tried for more than four hundred years. The Keeper comes to him there and lights the rainbow coal, and for the first time all seven burn together, each from its own spirit. It bids him stay with them until they are cold.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-6562"><em>Suibhne carries the rainbow to Doire ghlas</em>, 5 an Lùnastal, VE 5,316</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-6576"><em>Ailean sets out north with six fires on a pole</em>, 17 am Màrt, VE 5,324</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EI-6577"><em>Six fires kept under one roof</em>, 24 an Giblean, VE 5,324</a>.</span>

# A Gazetteer of the Age

#### A

**Achadh a' Chalbh** (the hill country south-west of Tobar dhìreach). Founded 7 an Dùbhlachd, VE 4,851. Achadh a' Chalbh, is the gathering-ground about Calbh Cnoc ghorm, the third of the standing stones of the saying, on a low rise in the hill country south-west of Tobar dhìreach. Ciannait, a woman of a nearby hearth, found the stone standing on the rise where she had never seen it, and put her hand to it; within two summers the rise had its name. The whole saying was said standing there for the first time, Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann, and an old woman said the sayings of the three stones together and said after them that the stone said in fewer words what Aithris a' Chruthachaidh had always said. The gathering was kept a second year and a third, and a market grew up at it, traders walking in from the northern shore with hides to trade for salt. In the years after Seathan's snap the crowd at the column grew to some hundreds on the nights of the great tellings; shelters were built about the stone and rebuilt many times, and one of Clann na Ceiste was sent to say the Line there, slowly, with a pause after each father's name long enough for it to be passed back to those at the back. At a great telling gual bogha-froise went round the crowd hand to hand through a whole night and came back at dawn as dark as it went. At the close of the age the hill country reckons its year by the gatherings at the column. Known for the gatherings at the column and the saying said standing.

**Achadh dhìreach** (the high valleys, west of Tobar dhìreach). Founded 16 an Cèitean, VE 303. Achadh dhìreach, the straight field, holds the oldest hearths of the high valleys after the mason's own. Eachna, a young woman of a household near Tobar dhìreach, walked the level ground west of the well more than once, looking at it the way a woman looks at a thing she means to have, and in the end carried fire there in a clay pot and laid the first hearth of the place on stone, as the near hearths had learned to do. The hearths were of pine and heather charcoal, with scrapers of grey flint and the split bones of red deer about them; there was no coloured coal in them. Deer were hunted by torch across the straight field, and within a generation five hearths stood there. The first autumn store of roasted hazel-nuts on the island was put by at Achadh dhìreach, in a pit lined with bark. Late in the age the households of the straight field began to rub broken coal from the vein into the wool of their dead, and it took streaks of a colour no plant dye makes. Giorsal of Achadh dhìreach was the one who began it, after her grandmother had shown her a scrap of coloured stone kept in a box three generations and called only the bright stone; when Giorsal died, her daughter rubbed a sliver into her mother's own wrapping. It is seldom done, one grave in some thirty. At the close of the age some sixty souls live at Achadh dhìreach. Known for its oldest hearths and the stained wool of its dead.

**Àirighean a' Bhealaich** (the high passes of the central mountains). Founded 13 an Lùnastal, VE 5,043. Àirighean a' Bhealaich, are the summer camps of the herders in the high passes of the central mountains, where the grass is sweet after the snow goes off it. Each household of the upland valleys keeps its own shieling there, a hut of stone and turf with a fold beside it, and goes up with its beasts when the lambs are strong enough to walk. Since the great cats of the mountains were first seen to keep their roads, crossing by fixed ways at fixed seasons, the households have learned the crossing season and keep off the passes while it lasts: the shielings stand stripped and shuttered at the same point in every year, and a crossing mark is cut on each gatepost and scraped when the season has been kept. A boy sent up to winter sheep in the crossing season, his father having lost the count of days in a wet spell, found his household's shieling already stripped by neighbours who had read the signs, and came down the same evening. The shielings are empty now in their season, and full in the rest of the summer. Known for the shielings left empty while the cats cross.

**Àth gharbh** (the high valleys, on the hill road east of Tobar dhìreach). Founded 13 an Gearran, VE 4,424. Àth gharbh, the rough ford, lies a short walk from Tobar dhìreach on the hill road, where the burn runs broad and stony and the drovers rest their beasts. Its households are kin by marriage to half the high valleys, and it was here that the valleys about the crack came to call themselves by one name: at the gathering on Oidhche an Dealanaich, an old man of the western household answered a stranger's question with a word for the whole of the gathered valleys, Clann nan Dè, and the name was said the next year at hearths that had not been at the gathering. Rathnait, born in the valleys about the crack, lived long enough to hear it in ordinary use. The households of Àth gharbh lay their dead in the ground on their side, knees drawn up, facing the central mountains, with an uncut stone at the head. It was also at Àth gharbh that an gual dathach was first burned outside the line. Barabal, a woman of a household of the ford, dropped a sliver of it into her peat fire, and it burned black-flamed like any other coal, and the hearthstone round it was stained through with colour. Her husband's mother turned the stone over at the door in daylight and said she had heard Clann a' Chlachair kept coloured stones such as this. The stained hearthstone is shown to travellers who ask after it and to children who do not. At the close of the age the ford holds some twelve households, and the drovers' beasts still churn the burn to mud at its crossing. Known for the name Clann nan Dè and the first small burning outside the line.

#### B

**Bothan a' Chaolais** (the strait of the north-western coast). Founded 5 an Cèitean, VE 3,126. Bothan a' Chaolais, the bothies of the strait, is the seal-hunters' camp on the quiet water of the north-western strait, south of the headlands, where the tide runs slow between the mainland and the near skerries. The hunters of the north-west came here when they left the open water for fear of Uilebheist na Mara, working the lee of the headlands out of its sight; the seal bones thinned in the middens of the open coast and grew here, shell on shell and bone on bone, until the middens of the strait outgrew the old grounds. An old steersman of the strait said at a net-mending that the sea had not grown smaller, only that the island's hand had drawn back from the part of it a man could no longer trust. The camp is kept through the seal season and the autumn fishing, and some households of Ros ruadh winter there now. At the close of the age it is the busiest seal-camp of the north-west, and its boats do not go out past the point. Known for the seal-hunt of the strait, out of Uilebheist na Mara's sight.

**Bothan an Fhoghair** (the skerries off Eilean fhada, on the northern coast). Founded 25 an t-Ògmhios, VE 609. Bothan an Fhoghair, the autumn bothies, is the camp of the north-shore hunters on the landward point of Eilean fhada, opposite the skerries where the grey seals haul out to pup in the autumn gales. Hunters went out in skin boats in that weather, the worst of the year, because the seals are there then and at no other time. Scàire, who went out with her father's crew from her sixteenth year and was master of his boat after his death, kept the camp in her day, and no one on that coast doubted that she read a north-shore sea as well as any man alive on it. The seal bones in the middens of the northern shore bear the same cut-marks as those of the camp. The bothies are low huts of stone and turf, roofed with hide in the season and left bare in the rest of the year. At the close of the age the autumn crossing is still made by some dozen boats, though since the loss of the boats of Ros ruadh the hunters go out only when the gulls are on the water and come home before dusk. Known for the autumn seal-hunt on the skerries.

**Bothan nan Ròn** (Eilean mhin, off the southern coast). Founded 5 an Dùbhlachd, VE 542. Bothan nan Ròn, the seal bothies, is the camp of the seal-hunters on Eilean mhin. The hunters came to the island by boat, the first on the island known to have crossed open water of set purpose: Oisean, who built his boat of hide over a frame of hazel, and his brothers after him, and then the young men of the neighbouring households, until the crossing in the calm months was a thing the shore simply did. They pitched their bothies of hide and turf on the green above the landing, kept them a season at a time, and left them standing when they went home, to be patched and roofed again the next year. The seals of Eilean mhin haul out on the flat rocks below the camp, and the hunters take them there with clubs and spears. By the close of the age the bothies have been kept every season since Oisean's own, and the ground beneath them is black with the fires of every season. Known for the first crossing of open water on purpose.

**Bral** (now Seann Bhral) (the south-eastern coast). Founded 30 an Lùnastal, VE 1,005. The eastern Bral is a landing on the south-eastern coast with a line of fish-kilns above its beach like those of Morn, within a day's rowing along the coast. The woman who minded the middle kiln judged the smoke by its smell at first light and dusk and the fish by the give of the flesh under one finger, and taught both by standing a child at her elbow; a girl of the landing learned to read the smoke well enough to tell a kiln going wrong from the far end of the beach. The kilns were kept alight in relay by the households in the busy weeks, one household taking the night and another the day. When a whale stranded on the beach, the landing gave dried fish to the southern landings for a share of its oil, and the two kept up the giving for a generation. At the close of the age the landing holds some hundred souls, and the smell of its kilns reaches the grazing above the shore in any wind off the sea. Known for its line of fish-kilns in the south-east.

**Bral** (now Seann Bhral) (the far western coast). Founded 5 an Dàmhair, VE 196. Bral sits on the far western coast at the foot of a cliff, where a strip of shingle gives on to the sea and the grazing lies above out of reach. For generations the households went up and down by a scramble no child could climb alone. Then a household set the first slab on the worst of the scramble, and after it cut steps into the rock itself, a few in a season, until the steps reached the first shelf, a third of the way up the cliff. Above the shelf the rock ran harder and gave up fewer slabs, and a worker might spend a season on a stretch that yielded three steps; an old woman used to sit of an evening on the shelf and run her hand along the edge of the topmost step then cut, saying of the rock above only that it would come when it came. It came. The two hundred and twelfth step was cut in her grandchildren's time, and the grazing above was reached by a stair. The lower treads, cut soonest and walked longest, wore a shallow dish into their middles before the upper treads had worn at all. Late in the age a chip of an gual dathach, still staining the shell about it, was thrown on the landing's midden; a household found it and kept it among its trinkets, a bright stone with no use. How it came to the western coast no one there asked. At the close of the age Bral is a landing of some eighty souls, going up and down its stair twice a day with the flocks. Known for the two hundred and twelve steps up the cliff, worn hollow.

**Brenn** (now Seann Bhrenn) (the northern coast, west of the Toll dune). Founded 12 an Giblean, VE 321. Brenn lies on the north coast where the rock shelves down into deep water in broad flat steps. Its households laid long ramps of flat stone from the shore into the sea, slab after slab, each one bedded on the one below and relaid where the sea shifted it; one slab was relaid twice before it held. When the first ramp was finished a dog of the household took to lying full length on it on warm days, and the household stepped over the dog on the way down to the water rather than move it. The ramps were wide enough for hulls greater than any hide boat, and on them the households framed the first plank-built hull on the island, launched it down the stone and watched it go out past the last shelf. A sail was seen small from the height above Brenn the next summer and not afterward. More hulls went down the ramps in the lives of their children and grandchildren, and of them nothing is left, nor any telling of where they went; a second ramp was begun beside the first when the first could not serve the work. By the close of the age the ramps stand clean and pale at low water, green-slicked at their feet, and the households use them for their own boats, which are small. Some sixty souls live there, fishing the rock ledges west of the landing. Known for the stone ramps into deep water and the hulls that left them.

**Brenn** (now Seann Bhrenn) (the north-eastern coast). Founded 15 an Lùnastal, VE 23. The second Brenn lies far to the north-east of the first, on a shore of the same shelving rock, and it has the same long ramps of flat stone laid down into deep water. The households of the north-eastern coast began their ramps after those of the northern Brenn had stood a long lifetime, and a third ramp was begun there when two would not serve. Whether the two Brenns were of one people, or only the way of building and the name were carried along the coast from landing to landing, the households themselves could not have said, and did not try. A boy of the landing stood once at the head of the twin ramps on a still evening and watched the water run up the stone and fall back, and asked his mother where the big boats had gone; she told him the sea had them, which was the answer every mother on that coast gave. No hull like those of the first Brenn is remembered to have been built here. At the close of the age the ramps serve small boats and the drying of weed, and some fifty souls live about them, fishing and gathering along the rocks on either hand. The landing lies within a day's rowing of the northern Tarr, and the two keep an eye on one another's smoke. Known for its twin ramps into the sea.

**Bruthach nan Teaghlach** (the south-eastern valleys). Founded 27 an t-Ògmhios, VE 2,574. Bruthach nan Teaghlach, is the scatter of hill-folk steadings along a long south-facing slope in the valleys of the south-east, above a river that runs down toward the coast of the kilns. The households came there from the high valleys in the lifetimes when the walls of the heights were being raised, herders looking for grazing that did not freeze, and they took the slope for its warmth and its springs. They were half a day's walk from Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh to the west, and some of their sick were carried there, and a day's walk from the empty platform of the temple in the hills to the north-east, which they did not climb. They keep a gathering of their own on Oidhche an Dealanaich, and send one of their elders to Tobar dhìreach in some years to hear the fathers' names said at the mason's hearth. At the close of the age some twenty hearths stand on the slope, and they lay their dead in the ground on the ridge above it, facing the central mountains. Known for its warm south-facing slope and its many hearths.

#### C

**Cnoc fhionn** (the north-east, in the sheltered hill farms). Founded 25 an t-Samhain, VE 3,715. Cnoc fhionn, the fair hill, is a hearth-kindred of the hill-folk in the north-east, on sheltered ground under a pale hill with deer forest to the south. Its households were hunters as much as herders, and went south in the autumns to the deer-drives of the eastern woods. Dubhghall, who drove the gully alone for the first time as a young man and took the head of the drive when his uncle's knees failed, lived his last years here. His grandson's dog died the year the boy was eleven, and the boy dug it a grave beside the family's own dead and set a shell at its head. An old woman questioned the grave; the boy's grandfather let it stand; and within a few years two more households of the hill had buried their dogs so. When Dubhghall died, his grandson set a shell at his head too, the last of the small store kept since the dog's grave, saying the old man deserved no less than a dog. Beasts had never had graves on the island before. At the close of the age some fifty souls live at Cnoc fhionn, and their burial ground holds more dogs than any other on the island. Known for the first dog graves.

**Crannagan Loch chrom** (the shallows of Loch chrom). Founded 23 am Faoilleach, VE 1,533. The lake dwellings stand in the shallows of Loch chrom: platforms of split planks on piles of oak driven into the loch floor, joined to the shore by plank walks long enough to keep a household out of reach of anything that walks on four legs. The first platform was driven by a household that had cut the oaks on the shore above and floated them down, and the driving of a pile was work for every hand, the frame raised over the water and the weight dropped on the pile's head until it stood fast. A pile driven and holding was counted an occasion for a shared meal on the nearest platform once the driving-frame was struck down. Eels were first taken from beneath the platforms in baskets let down through the planks, and a child carried the first basket the length of the longest walk. Every morning a child was sent along the walks to listen for the sound of a plank gone thin under its light weight before a grown foot found it the hard way. Who built the platforms, the people of the shell road or some other people of those years, the tellings do not agree, and the households on the platforms do not trouble to settle it. At the close of the age some twelve platforms stand in the shallows, and a new pile is driven most summers. Known for the platforms on oak piles and the plank walks.

**Creag Ruadh** (the hill above the eastern shore of Loch chrom). Founded 14 an Dàmhair, VE 3,773. Creag Ruadh is Creag Ruadh above the eastern shore of Loch chrom, a steep hill of reddish rock with a shelf of good ground about its shoulder and springs on its south face. The hill-folk of the lake shore lit their first hearths there some lifetimes on from the raising of the lake dwellings were raised, coming west out of the high valleys with fire carried in a pot from hearth to hearth, and they took the crag for the view it gave of the loch and of anyone coming across the water. They were herders more than fishers, and grazed their beasts on the slopes below the crag and down to the reeds. What passed between them and the people of the platforms, or the households of the shell road on the far shore, no telling of the crag keeps: the crag's households say they watched the smoke of the platforms of an evening, and that was all. By the close of the age some eight or nine hearths stand on the shelf of the crag, lit from Teine a' Chlachair as every hearth of the hill-folk is, and their dead are laid in the ground below the red rock, facing the central mountains. Known for its red rock and its view over Loch chrom.

**Cwen** (now Seann Chwen) (the southern coast, east of the southern Cwen). Founded 29 an Lùnastal, VE 3,488. The third Cwen is a small landing a short way along the southern coast from the second, on a harbour sheltered by a reef that breaks the swell at half tide. Its households came to it from the southern Cwen in the lifetimes when the holy woods of the east were first set aside by the hill-folk, and they carried the name with them as a household carries its fire, so that the south coast had two Cwens within a morning's rowing of each other. They fished the reef and took shellfish from the pools inside it, and hunted seal on the skerries when the seals came. After the heights were left and the south coast filled with households come down to the shore, this Cwen grew with its neighbour; its landing stones were relaid and lengthened, and a second row of houses raised behind the first. At the close of the age some sixty souls live there. Known for its reef-sheltered landing on the south coast.

**Cwen** (now Seann Chwen) (the southern coast). Founded 1 am Faoilleach, VE 1,236. The southern Cwen is a small landing on the southern shore, its boats drawn up on flat stones at the head of a sandy cove. For most of the age its midden grew slowly, a household's meals at a time. Then, once the heights were left, whole kin-groups came down from the abandoned rings and the lands about them, and some settled here; the midden began to grow as fast as the mound at the eastern Dunn had grown when it was young, and in the end outgrew it. A landing once counted by the dozen was counted by the score. The people of the landings raised no new work anywhere out of sight of salt water after that time, and the southern Cwen is the place where the turning is plainest to see. At the close of the age it holds some two hundred souls, more than any landing of the south but its namesake on the gulf, and a new row of houses stands behind the old. Known for the midden that outgrew the eastern Dunn.

**Cwen** (now Seann Chwen) (the head of the southern gulf). Founded 19 an Giblean, VE 32. Cwen is the larger of the landings on the southern gulf, a wide bay of quiet water where the fish come in on the tide in shoals. Its households fished with nets of twisted fibre and sank them with beach stones, and it was a net-maker of Cwen who began the long mesh, a net long enough to close across the bay's inner arm, and set it there with the help of every household on the shore. Households came from along the coast to see the closed net. Her weights were notched with three strokes each, cut with a hard stone into the soft beach pebble, so that a weight knew its own net; her daughter learned the groove, spoiled her first stones, and cut the three strokes true before her mother's eyes failed. The daughter took up a way of holding each finished weight a breath longer in the light than the work required, as though the three strokes were worth looking at for their own sake. Every weight of the Cwen nets was notched the same way after, and the three strokes are the eldest mark on the island made again and again of purpose. At the close of the age some hundred and fifty souls live at Cwen, the largest landing of the south coast, and the notched weights lie thick on the floor of the bay where the nets have torn. Known for the net-weights notched with three strokes, the eldest mark on the island.

#### D

**Dunn** (now Seann Dunn) (the Abhainn chaol, a little above its mouth on the south-eastern coast). Founded 5 an Cèitean, VE 642. This Dunn lies on the Abhainn chaol a little above its mouth, where the river's brown water meets the sea's green, and low cliffs on either hand give nesting to the birds. Its gatherers took eggs from the ledges of those cliffs in the dry months, never so many from one ledge that the birds did not come back to it the next year. It is the northern end of Slighe-mhara àrsaidh, the lane Seann-Dhaoine' boats kept along the south-east coast in the last lifetimes of the age, from the river mouth below Dunn round the great cape to the bay far to the south. Flat landing-stones were laid along the lane a day's rowing apart, and at Dunn the stones are grooved by keels. A father of the landing taught his son the sea-way stone by stone, naming each landing's look from the water and the look of the sky that meant a boat should lie up there. Rowers on that coast kept a plain word for anyone new to the stretch north of the cape: watch the gulls before you watch the sky. At the close of the age the landing holds some fifty souls and is busier with boats coming and going than its size would suggest. Known for the head of Slighe-mhara àrsaidh and its grooved landing-stones.

**Dunn** (now Seann Dunn) (the southern coast). Founded 28 am Faoilleach, VE 601. The southern Dunn is a landing on the southern coast at the head of a beach of fine sand, where the swell runs long and the whales go by in their seasons. A whale stranded below it one autumn, and the households of the whole shore came to cut it and share it out; its oil was kept in bladders and clay pots and burned in stone lamps through two winters at least, and its ribs were driven upright into the ground for the frames of three round houses roofed with turf. The first rib cracked through within a few years, and the houses were raised a second time on the sound bone; a child digging by the wall turned up the buried foot of the first rib and the landing kept it by the door. A third raising stood on bone carried along the shore from a whale cut further west, word of usable ribs travelling faster by then than word of strandings once had. The landing also has a short mole of heaped stone at the western end of the beach, where the boats lie in the worst weather. At the close of the age some ninety souls live there, in houses framed on whale-bone and on timber both. Known for the whale-rib houses.

**Dunn** (now Seann Dunn) (the eastern coast). Founded 22 an Dùbhlachd, VE 320. The eastern Dunn is where Seann-Dhaoine first leave a trace that can be followed: the great mound of their meals, limpet shell, seal bone and burnt weed, laid down over many lifetimes at the back of the beach until it stood taller than a man. A woman of the landing kept the heap as her mother had taught her, letting each bag of shell fall where the heap wanted it and working it level with her foot, with the burnt weed laid in thin; the heap's fire was kept through a three-day gale by a gatherer whose mother had died at the tide that same season, and she worked a season at the heap alone. An old scraper turned up in the heap one spring, of a shape no one living made, and the household that found it put it back. In time the heap stood high enough that the households climbed it to watch the sea for boats coming home. No tool in the lowest layers is shaped as any tool the hill-folk used. At the close of the age the heap runs the length of the back of the beach and more than a man's height, and the landing below it holds some sixty souls who gather, fish and hunt seal as their mothers did. Known for the great shell mound, the first sure trace of Seann-Dhaoine.

#### G

**Gleann nan Damh** (the eastern woods). Founded 4 am Màrt, VE 3,487. Gleann nan Damh, is the gully of the eastern woods into which the hill-folk of the east drive the red deer every autumn, along lines of stakes and brush set out through the trees, and kill them at the gully's throat with spears. The antlers of the greatest stags are stacked apart from the rest at the gully's mouth, and the stand of them grew higher every year. It was at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar above the glen that Sadhbh and two others first saw the white stag and none of them drew; afterward the hunters began letting the gully's beasts go when a pale one was among them, rather than risk the wrong one. Dubhghall drove the gully alone for the first time as a young man, threw wide at a young stag in his first year and practised all winter against a bundle of brush, and took the head of the drive when his uncle's knees would no longer hold him through a whole autumn morning; he was exacting in one thing only, that no young man should stand carelessly. At the close of the age the drive is kept every autumn by households from Cnoc fhionn to the edge of the woods. Known for the autumn deer-drive and the stand of antlers.

#### M

**Morn** (now Seann Mhorn) (the south-eastern coast). Founded 5 an t-Iuchar, VE 80. Morn lies above a beach on the south-eastern coast, where the catch comes in heavier than the households can eat. Its people built stone-lined pits with short flues above the beach and dried the fish over peat smoke: seven kilns in the end, the first buildings on the island made for a trade and not for sleep or the dead. The fourth pit drowned in a night's rain and was left; the ninth was set higher against the rain; the seventh was the last dug. The keeper of the kilns kept a store of dry peat under an overhang of turf for the kiln fires alone, holding that green peat flares where dry peat smokes and a flare undoes a season's catch, and she taught her niece to watch a kiln past bed on a night of gathering rain. The smoke of the kilns could be seen from inland on a still day. When the heights were left, a household that had lived within the rings came down to Morn, and the keeper of the middle kiln led the son's wife by the wrist to a smouldering kiln and held her hand over its rack until she understood what three tellings in words had not taught her. At the close of the age some sixty souls live there, and the kilns smoke through the summer. Known for the seven fish-kilns, the first buildings made for a trade.

**Morn** (now Seann Mhorn) (the southern coast, on the oyster headland). Founded 31 an Cèitean, VE 784. The southern Morn lies on a low headland of the southern coast where the oyster beds are close enough inshore to be raked from the rocks at low water, and it has little else. Its households raked oyster, whelk and cockle and heaped the shells over the whole headland, until the mound stood taller than any household's reach and the houses were built on the shell itself. A worn rake was laid on the mound by the household that had used it longest when its owner died. The raking households found that the oysters of the lowest layers of their mound were broader by half than any taken from the same water in living memory, and did not trouble over why; the beds were raked every summer and never rested. At the close of the age the landing holds some forty souls, and the white of the headland can be seen from far out to sea, whiter than any cliff on that coast. Known for its headland of heaped shell and the great oysters at the bottom of the heap.

#### N

**Na Teallaichean Falaichte** (the Doire uaine hills). Founded 13 an Giblean, VE 3,151. Na Teallaichean Falaichte, is the hamlet of the herders of the Doire uaine hills, a scatter of steadings in the folds of the hills south of Tobar dhìreach. The hill-folk found the rock faces of those hills cut all over with lines of signs, more than anywhere else on the island; Eimhir, a herder-girl following a strayed ewe up a defile before first light, found the first of them, and the elders judged the writing older than living memory. No one of the hills could read it; the tellings came to agree that it told of something that walked without breathing and fell upon any who lit a fire in its sight, and some lines were cut over and defaced by another hand. Dreams of the same shape came at several hearths, two herders saw a walker on the ridge and lived, and children went less often alone to the far pastures. Laoghaire dug the first pit-hearth, a fire under a slab at the foot of a slanting shaft bent near its foot so that no glow could climb it straight, with the smoke led out through a crack in the turf ten paces off. Other households dug the like, and within a few lifetimes the covered hearth was the hills' law. Eimhir kept her own hearth open to the last. At the close of the age no open fire shows in those hills. Known for the covered pit-hearths.

#### R

**Ros ruadh** (the north-western coast). Founded 21 an Dùbhlachd, VE 3,075. Ros ruadh is a harbour of the hill-folk on a red headland of the north-western coast, the furthest west the hearths of the north shore reach before the bare horn. Its households fished and hunted seal on the open water west of the headland, going out in skin boats in the calm months and coming home heavy. A calm summer filled its nets as no summer had, and in that same season seven boats of Ros ruadh went out on calm water and did not come home: the first on a still morning, the second eleven days after from a different stretch of the same sea, and five more before the autumn, with no storm to blame and no wreckage found. The widows named what had taken them, and Uilebheist na Mara entered the tellings of the shore by name for the first time. In the years after, the headland kept seven empty places on its shingle where seven boats had lain, and no household built on them. The hunters of the north-west afterward left the open water for the lee of the headlands and the strait, and Ros ruadh grew smaller. At the close of the age it is a landing of some thirty households who fish close inshore, keep an eye on the gulls, and do not speak of the water beyond the point after dark. Known for the seven boats lost in one calm season.

#### S

**Skell** (now Seann Skell) (the northern coast). Founded 19 an t-Samhain, VE 1,833. The northern Skell stands on a wide bay of the north coast, facing the open sea that the island's northern shore takes square on its chin. Its households knew of the great mole on the Abhainn naomh by telling long before any of them had seen it, and when they came to build their own they made it shorter and curved against the swell, since a river's push and the sea's roll are two different weights. Each stone was laid dry against the course already set and worked back and forth until it sat without rocking, and only then bedded; a swell broke over the unfinished mole in its first autumn and moved nothing, which the households took as the sea's own leave to go on. The curved mole was finished in the lifetime of the grandchildren of those who began it. A traveller from this Skell who went the long way round to the western river and stood on the first mole came home saying the two were built the same way, stone by stone without mortar, and that the western one was the longer and the northern the harder to lay. In the years when the heights were left, a household that had lived within the three rings came down to this coast and learned to live by the tide again. At the close of the age the landing is a village of several hundred, its boats in the lee of the curve, and amber from the bay's strands is kept in its houses as a thing pleasant to hold. Known for the curved mole against the open sea.

**Skell** (now Seann Skell) (the north-western horn). Founded 10 an Gearran, VE 1,404. The least of the three Skells sits on the far north-western coast, on bare ground where no tree grows and the gales off the open sea come in unbroken across low heather and bog. Its few households fished the grey water below the horn and lived close to the shore under turf, until one household raised a round tower of dry stone on the rock above the landing, with a hollow wall and a stair wound up inside its thickness. A winter storm threw down the unfinished outer face in the second year of the building, and the household set it up again course by course the next spring, feeling every stone into its bed. The first night anyone slept at the tower's crown was remembered as a night of stars and no wind at all, which on that coast is a rarer thing than a stranded whale. The household walked the stair from foot to crown after every storm, feeling along both faces for a stone gone slack, and one night a fire lit on the parapet turned a boat from the rocks below. The tower looks out over the water where Uilebheist na Mara was afterwards seen, and by the close of the age the households of the horn keep their boats out of that water as the hill-folk of the same coast do, each for their own reasons, neither knowing the other's. The landing holds a few dozen souls, the tower and some turf houses in its lee; nothing has ever grown taller than the tower there. Known for the hollow-walled round tower over the north-western water.

**Skell** (now Seann Skell) (the Abhainn naomh, above its mouth on the western coast). Founded 6 an Gearran, VE 173. The greatest landing of Seann-Dhaoine lies a short way up the Abhainn naomh from the western sea, where the river runs broad and brown past a low bank of gravel and the tide pushes up against the current twice a day. Boats lay there long before the mole, pulled up on the gravel and dragged higher at every flood. The mole was begun by an old man who chose each boulder by its weight in his hands and set it with his grandsons standing in the river to their chests against the push of the water; it was laid out from the bank without mortar, stone set against stone, and in its first winter it held against a flood that took boats from every other stretch of that bank. After that the households of the river asked for the same lee and built beside it, and the landing grew on the mole's shelter as a village grows on a spring. By the time Seann-Dhaoine held every coast of the island, Skell was the one place among them that a stranger would have called crowded: some three hundred souls at the height, every mooring behind the mole taken, smoke from forty hearths lying along the river on a still evening. A woman of the landing walked the mole's length each evening at the turn of the tide, looking for any stone the current had worked loose, and the stones she reset were set the old way. When the heights were left and the households that had gone up to the rings came down, some came here, and one grandfather of the landing never once spoke of what he had seen up there. At the close of the age the mole stands whole, its foot under water at the lowest tides, and the landing keeps to the river as it always kept. Known for the mole of unmortared boulders, the eldest work on the Abhainn naomh.

#### T

**Tarr** (now Seann Tarr) (the eastern coast, under the cut cliff). Founded 25 an Giblean, VE 1,212. The eastern Tarr is a landing under a high cliff of fine grey rock on the eastern coast, and it is the place where the script was first cut. A man of the landing began rows of signs on the standing rock above the shingle with a flint chisel, each sign some two hundred light blows of the hammer, and worked at them a long life; a boy of the landing watched an afternoon of the cutting once and was sent off before he had seen a whole sign made. After the careful cutter, others cut more rows beside and above his, and an old row was cut over and broken by a later hand with the same kind of tool, for what reason the landing never gave. The first row cut on the cliff runs straight and even, and the rows above it less so. The signs are not the speech of the hill-folk, and none of the hill-folk could have read them; the landing's own people say only that the cliff has been cut. A woman of the midland Toll walked the coast once as far as this cliff and found the rows, and went home with nothing to tell but that they were there. At the close of the age some seventy souls live at the landing, fishing the eastern water, and the rows stand pale on the grey rock over their roofs. Known for the rows of signs cut on the cliff, the first of the script.

**Tarr** (now Seann Tarr) (the north-eastern headlands). Founded 30 an Cèitean, VE 884. At the Tarr of the north-eastern headlands a household built a single long house into a cleft of the cliff, with the living rock for its back wall and a roof of turf and driftwood across the cleft's mouth. The hearth stood against the rock, and the rock above it blackened year on year to the height of a man. A child of the house stood with her back to the soot-stain each midwinter to see how far up it her crown reached, until the year she stood as tall as the stain. The house was built for the wind and it kept the wind out: in the hard winter that the whole north-east remembered, when the sea froze in the rock pools and no boat put out from that stretch the whole season, the household lived on what it had put by and came out on the calm morning after with every soul alive. In the darkest months, when the cliff kept the sun from the doorway, a second small fire was kept lit just inside the door, more for its light than its warmth. At the close of the age some thirty souls live in and about the long house and the huts below it, and the stain behind the hearth reaches higher than any of them. Known for the long house built into the cliff, black with soot behind the hearth.

**Tarr** (now Seann Tarr) (the north-eastern coast, below the headlands). Founded 17 an Lùnastal, VE 4,706. The lesser Tarr of the north-east is one of the last landings Seann-Dhaoine made, laid down once the heights were left, when every new work of theirs was made within sight of salt water. It lies on a small inlet below the headlands, a short row along the coast from the older Tarr, and it was settled by households that had outgrown the cleft-house and its huts. Its landing stones are flat slabs set into the shingle at the water's edge, bedded the way the stones of Slighe-mhara àrsaidh in the south-east are bedded, so that a laden boat may be drawn up on them without grinding its hide on the stones beneath. The households fish, gather weed, and trade dried fish along the coast to the older Tarr for what the cliff's shelter can give. At the close of the age it is a landing of a dozen households, young beside its neighbours, and its people still call it by the same root as the landing up the coast, as though the one name were enough for both. Known for its landing stones, among the last of Seann-Dhaoine' works.

**Teallaichean a' Chladaich** (the southern shore, below the southern hills). Founded 23 an t-Sultain, VE 4,983. Teallaichean a' Chladaich, are the households of the hill-folk on the southern shore, a string of steadings on the slope above the beach, with barley in the small fields and boats on the shingle. They were lit from Teine a' Chlachair like every hearth of the hill-folk, carried south over the mountains in a pot. It was from here that a party of eleven, with Cairbre at their head, went up into the southern hills in the crossing season, the harvest inland having failed and the geese of the coast not yet gone over in their numbers, reading the season as a slow one. They did not come home. Cairbre's wife kept the twelfth day on the rise above the steadings, and the fourteenth and the twentieth, and by the thirtieth had stopped telling herself anything, and only watched. Their bones were found years afterward along the line the cats use, and were buried where they were found. At the close of the age the households of the shore keep the crossing season as strictly as any in the passes, and cut their gateposts deep. Known for the eleven who went up in the crossing season.

**Tobar dhìreach** (the high valleys, on the north side of the central mountains). Founded 25 an t-Iuchar, VE 42. Tobar dhìreach, the straight well, is the hearth of Clann a' Chlachair and the place where fire came to the hill-folk. The well it is named for runs along a straight channel cut in the rock, and the old telling says it was on this ground, in the dead of a winter, that Neachdan the mason set his wedge in a seam he had not seen and broke into a vein of hard coal that showed every colour in the break; that the lightning struck the broken vein that night and it took fire; and that he carried a burning piece home, and his household sat by the first fire any of them had seen. From that hearth the fire was begged and given, carried in a clay pot banked with ash to the near hearths and then to the far ones, until there was no hearth of the hill-folk that was not lit from it, by one borrowing or another. The vein burned in its cut through the lives of the mason's son and grandson and beyond, watched through the dark half of every year from two flat stones above it. When it burned out, Muirne of the line would not let it be dug further: a flat slab was laid over the broken vein, no water was drawn beside it, and the well was cut again a stone's throw off. The black well and the young well, in the valleys on either side, each tell that the mason's well was theirs; Tobar dhìreach can show the capped shaft with a scorched stain on its lip, and the other two have only the telling. No house stands beside Leac na Fèithe. The household keeps two things for the line: Poit an Teine, the clay pot said to hold the mason's first fire, kept alight by the women of the line from mother to daughter and aunt to niece; and a leather bag of coloured pieces broken from the vein before it was covered, with fresh pieces taken in each lifetime from where the vein shows in a stream bank above the well. Here Diarmad asked why the coal had colours, and came home from the grove with Aithris a' Chruthachaidh and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich; here the fathers' names are said standing on Oidhche an Dealanaich, and the lightings of the coals are told as they come: gold on the sea, the snowflake in the air, the black coal in the ground by Leac na Fèithe, the red-brown in blood, the silver in the river below the house, gual teine on the doorstone in Seathan's fingers. From the lifetime of Colla the line is called Clann na Ceiste by the valleys. At the close of the age some ninety souls live at Tobar dhìreach, and Ailean son of Suibhne has gone north to the grove with six fires on a pole, leaving Lìobhan and the child Gormshuil to keep the house fire until he comes home. Known for Teine a' Chlachair, Leac na Fèithe over the burnt vein, and the bag of na Seachd Guail.

**Toll** (now Seann Toll) (the Abhainn uaine, in the midlands). Founded 8 an Gearran, VE 92. The midland Toll is a landing of Seann-Dhaoine inland, on the Abhainn uaine, where a shelf of rock runs out into the river and the water pools behind it. Its households cut a channel through the shelf into a pool beside the river, with slots at the channel's mouth for a wattle gate; when the river fell the gate was dropped and the pool emptied by hand, and the fish left stranded in it were taken with baskets. A boy of the landing lost two fingers to the mallet in the cutting of the slots. A child of the landing learned the floor of the channel by her feet at low water, which stretch stood firm and which gave, long before she had a word for it. In a summer when the river fell low and stayed low the gate was dropped three times before the autumn rains, and the households reckoned the late summer by the droppings. A woman of Toll walked the coast once as far as the cut cliff at Tarr, and came home saying the signs were there and no more. At the close of the age some sixty souls live at the landing, one of the two landings of Seann-Dhaoine a day's walk from salt water that were not left when the heights were, since their rivers run to the sea. Known for the fish-channel and the gate-slot cut in the rock.

**Toll** (now Seann Toll) (the northern coast, under the dune). Founded 8 an t-Samhain, VE 1,033. The northern Toll takes its name from the sea-caves under its headland, where the water booms at the turn of the tide. Its households raised a cluster of stone huts in the lee of a great dune, which kept the wind off them for a lifetime. Then a wind rose off the sea that did not settle for three days, and the household left the huts with what they could carry; when the wind fell the dune stood forward the whole width of the huts and beyond, a slope of new pale sand over ground where doors had opened two days before. No one dug for the huts. New walls were raised inland of the buried row within the season, and the sand has kept the old huts whole ever since, hearths, doors and all. The households of the new walls keep a strict eye on the dune's face and plant marram on its brow, and children are told early not to dig in it. At the close of the age Toll is a fishing landing of some fifty souls, living inland of the sand, with the caves below the headland for shelter from the worst weather and for the drying of nets. Known for the huts the dune buried whole.

**Toll** (now Seann Toll) (the north-eastern coast, in a cleft of the rock). Founded 19 an Giblean, VE 2,319. The north-eastern Toll is a harbour in a cleft of the rock, a narrow inlet between two walls of stone where the sea runs in quiet even when the open water beyond is white. Its households found the cleft in the generations when the rings and Làrach an Dùin-fhaire were still lived in, and made it a landing by cutting the lowest shelf of the rock level with the water, dressing it flat with stone tools over many summers until a boat could lie alongside it and be unloaded dry-shod. The cutting of that shelf is the work the landing is known for, and it is cut in a manner of its own, the face of the rock taken down in long straight strokes. The households are few, fishing the rocks at the cleft's mouth and hunting seal in the season on the skerries to the south. Word of the northern Toll's buried huts came to them along the coast, and they built nothing in the lee of any sand. At the close of the age the landing holds a few households, perhaps forty souls, and its quay is the plainest and most lasting thing on that coast. Known for its quay cut level in the living rock.

#### V

**Vell** (now Seann Vell) (the western coast, among the dunes). Founded 16 an Dàmhair, VE 1,197. The western Vell is a small landing on a coast of dunes and wide sand, where the fishing is good in autumn and poor in the late winter. Its households learned to put the autumn by for the lean months. A woman of the landing dug the first pit in the dune's flank, lined it with clay carried from a bank upstream and lidded it with a slab, and stored dried fish in it through a winter; the fish came out sound. She set her later pits a full body's length apart, holding that a pit dug too near another drew damp, and the households after her kept the spacing without asking why. A younger household once cut the lining clay out of turn and spoiled a season's store, and the landing kept the turns strictly after. The pits run in a line along the dune now, dozens of them, and some that were forgotten when a household died out still hold fish bones under their slabs. Late in the age the doors of the landing were turned from the sea toward the dune, for the wind. At the close of the age some forty souls live there on fish and the store-pits. Known for the clay-lined store-pits in the dune.

**Vell** (now Seann Vell) (the Abhainn fhionn, above the lake country). Founded 1 an t-Ògmhios, VE 3,673. The inland Vell is a landing on a river of the midlands, reached by Seann-Dhaoine' boats poling up from the coast. Its households came to it in the lifetimes when the holy woods of the east were first let alone, settling on a shelf of gravel where the river runs slow and the eels are thick, and raised a few round houses there in the manner of the coast. They lived on eels and on what the river brought, and kept their boats on the gravel. When the heights were left and every new work of Seann-Dhaoine was made by salt water, the inland Vell was not abandoned, since the river runs to the sea and the landing's boats go down it every season; but it did not grow, and its young people went down to the coast. At the close of the age it holds a few households only, some twenty souls. Known for its gravel landing on the river.

**Vell** (now Seann Vell) (the south-eastern coast, opposite Eilean dhearg). Founded 4 an t-Ògmhios, VE 396. The eastern Vell lies on the south-eastern coast facing Eilean dhearg across a short sound. Its households built round houses of dry stone, each with a hearth sunk in the middle of the floor and, beneath that, a drain running out under the wall; the first house was raised on a knoll above the landing, and the first drain cut beneath a wall came after the floor had stood wet through a winter. Households whose houses were built without a drain took up their floors in a dry season and cut the channel in under walls already standing, having watched their neighbours' floors stand drier. Fourteen houses were finished in the end. The dead of the Vell were rowed across the sound to Eilean dhearg and laid in stone boxes facing the mainland, and no box was left standing open through a night: an unfinished one was covered with brush and stone until its lid could be rowed across. Forty boxes are counted on the island. At the close of the age some hundred souls live in the house-rings, and the boats that carry the dead still go out from the same stone. Known for its round houses with sunk hearths and drains, and its dead on Eilean dhearg.

**Vell** (now Seann Vell) (the Abhainn bheag, above its mouth in the north-east). Founded 1 an Gearran, VE 1,698. This Vell stands a short way above the mouth of the Abhainn bheag in the north-east, where the ground slopes steeply to the water and each household had to cut its own level ground into the slope before it could raise a wall. Four houses were raised there and a boat-shed, and the households built a flat-bottomed hull for the river that could be poled up the shallows where a sea-boat would ground. A spring flood once reached the boat-shed and lifted the hull off its blocks, and the households hauled it back with ropes and raised the shed a step higher up the slope. The river gave the landing what the open sea further along the coast could not always give: eels in their seasons, trout, and water that never failed. The eel-trap pattern was known only in one pair of hands until an old man taught it to two children at once, lest one bad season lose it to the whole landing. A girl grown up at the Vell stood at the river's mouth one evening looking at the open sea and went no further, holding that a river's own child had no business beyond its mouth. No dwelling of Seann-Dhaoine on the main island is known further to the north-east. At the close of the age some thirty souls live there. Known for its four houses and boat-shed, the furthest north-east of Seann-Dhaoine' landings.

#### W

**Warr** (now Seann Warr) (the southern shore of the gulf). Founded 15 an Gearran, VE 2,245. The eastern Warr is a small landing on the southern shore of the gulf, across the water from the eastern Bral and in sight of its kiln smoke. Its households were fishers and weed-gatherers who came to it from the west of the gulf in the lifetimes when the long house was built into the cliff at the north-eastern Tarr, and they carried with them the name of the shell-road landing on Loch chrom, though no road was ever made here. They fish the quiet water inside the gulf and dry their catch on racks rather than in kilns, and trade what they dry across the water. At the close of the age it is a landing of some thirty souls, content with the gulf's shelter, whose boats go out in weather that keeps the open-sea landings ashore. Known for its sheltered landing on the gulf.

**Warr** (now Seann Warr) (the western shore of Loch chrom). Founded 27 am Màrt, VE 725. Warr lies on the western shore of Loch chrom, behind a broad marsh of reeds that stood between the dry ground and the open water. Its households fished the loch and gathered mussels in the shallows, and crossed the marsh on a track of trodden reed that sank a little every year. A household first carried shell out onto the sunken track and found that it held a foot where reed would not; within a generation the carrying of shell was yearly work for every household, and the shell was crushed underfoot on a flat stone by the water before it was carried out, since crushed shell packs and whole shell slides. A flood of the reed-marsh in a wet year drowned the road's middle length and the households raised it again a forearm above the reeds. The road runs a little over a mile, white in the sun, from the dry ground to the water's edge, and a girl of the landing was the first to run its whole length at once without stopping. A family of the northern shore came once to see it, having heard of a road made of shells, and went home saying it was so. The road is kept as a household keeps a hearth: a stranger's foot on another household's stretch is not a thing lightly done. At the close of the age the landing holds some seventy souls. Known for the shell road across the reed marsh.

# Appendix A — Sloinneadh a' Chlachair

The only roll this age kept was a roll of names said aloud. Sloinneadh a' Chlachair is the pedigree of the mason's line from An Clachair himself down to the father then living, said standing at the hearth of Tobar dhìreach on Oidhche an Dealanaich, the dark of the year when the vein first took fire. Diarmad fixed its form in the years after he came home from the grove, gathering the names from old women who had kept four and five fathers back without being asked, and from then on it was said the same way every winter, with nothing added but the name of each father as he died and the line for each coal as it answered. This appendix gives what the line let strangers hear, the named fathers with their deeds, and the women who kept Poit an Teine. The years beside each name are the years of the annals of this volume; no one living in the age counted them so, and Appendix C tells how they did count.

## The rule of the recital

The recital is said standing, by the father who holds the bag, or by one he chooses when he cannot stand. It opens with the mason and closes with the father living. Between the two it gives every father's name, but to strangers the line gives only the named fathers, each with his deed, and says of the rest only how many stood between: *and so many fathers whose names we keep*. The counts between are said as numbers and the names are kept. After the Line comes the telling of the coals, one line for each lighting as it came, and after that Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich, said once in the old words and once in plain speech, and left unanswered. In Gormal's day the recital was softened, at her daughter Sìomha's asking, so that a small child might leave the fire when the fathers' names were done instead of being held through Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich; the full recital was kept for the grown. In the lifetimes of the gatherings at the column, the recital came to be said there too, slowly, with a pause after each named father long enough for the name to be passed back through the crowd.

## The short form

This is the Line as it was given to strangers at the close of the age, in plain speech:

> Neachdan the mason, who broke the vein and carried the fire home; Conall his son, who kept the vein burning.
> Thirty-four fathers whose names we keep. Diarmad, who asked, and heard Aithris a' Chruthachaidh in the grove. Eighteen fathers
> whose names we keep. Aodh, who gave the seven to the sea, and the gold burned. Thirty-one fathers whose names we
> keep. Fearghas, who let the six fall from the height, and the snowflake burned in the air. Twenty-eight fathers
> whose names we keep. Brian, who gave the five to the ground, and the black coal was warm. Thirty fathers whose
> names we keep. Cormac of the Misstrike, whose blood lit the red-brown. Twenty-one fathers whose names we keep.
> Eòghann, who tasted the river, and the silver burned under the water. Fifteen fathers whose names we keep.
> Colla, in whose days we were called Clann na Ceiste. Ten fathers whose names we keep.
> Seathan, who snapped his fingers, and the fire came. Fifteen fathers whose names we keep. Suibhne, who carried
> the rainbow to the grove. Ailean his son, who lives.

## The named fathers

**Neachdan, An Clachair** (died VE 38). A mason of the high valleys north of the central mountains, splitting rock for a well in the dead of a winter when the old spring had failed. His wedge went into a seam he had not seen and the rock broke open on a vein of hard coal that showed every colour in the break. The lightning struck the broken vein that night and it took fire, and he carried a burning piece home in his hands wrapped in a sodden hide. His wife Sorcha was the first to be burned by a hearth and the first to feed one heather. He died in the thirty-eighth winter after the lightning, an old man for that age, and is the first of the dead buried within sight of the vein.

**Conall mac Neachdain** (died VE 71). The mason's son, eleven when he ran barefoot through the rain with his mother's water-pot to bring fire home from the vein to the dead hearth. He kept the winter watch at the burning vein from two flat stones above it for most of his life, and gave fire to any hearth that sent for it. His sister Ailbhe carried it to the hearths further off. He is the last father named before the long count of kept names.

**Diarmad** (VE 862–931), the thirty-sixth father. A boy who would not stop asking why the pieces in the bag held colours, and a young man who went north three days alone to the oak grove at Doire ghlas with gual bogha-froise and asked Coimhdeach na Fine, which came to his fire out of the smoke of the gale. He came home with Aithris a' Chruthachaidh and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich, and fixed the recital: the Line said standing, then Aithris a' Chruthachaidh, then Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich. He died in his seventieth year at Tobar dhìreach. His wife Niamh said Aithris a' Chruthachaidh at his hearth before she believed it; his daughter Deirbhile kept it word for word and taught it.

**Aodh** (VE 1,344–1,412), the fifty-fourth father. At Muirgheal's bidding he carried all seven coals down to the northern shore, slept a night above the tideline, and threw them into the sea one by one. Gual òir took fire on the water and burned gold until the sea put it under, and a new line was added to the recital for the first time since the mason. He brought the other six home and tried them against everything in reach for the rest of his life. In his last years he first took fresh pieces of the vein from where it shows in a stream bank above the well.

**Fearghas** (VE 2,138–2,199), the eighty-sixth father. With his brother Mathan he walked the ridges south for two summers until there was no taller hill behind the one they stood on, and on the summit of Binnean a' Chlachair he let the six unlit coals fall one by one. Gual sneachda took fire as it fell and burned white; they left it burning where it lay. Mathan set the first stone of the summit cairn. Fearghas died at sixty-one.

**Brian** (VE 2,858–2,921), the hundred and fifteenth father. The grave-digger of the high valleys, who dug through frozen ground for other households' dead without cursing it. The old widow Sireadh, who had kept the bag sixty years, gave him the five dark coals, and he buried them deep beside Leac na Fèithe with the words said over every grave in the valleys. When he dug them up the next day the black coal was warm in his hand and smouldered as the air reached it. He kept it burning at his own hearth and taught the grave-digger's trade to younger men, and died at sixty-three. The black coal burned at his burial. His wife was Caoimhe.

**Cormac of the Misstrike** (VE 3,640–3,712), the hundred and forty-sixth father. The keeping fell to him at fifteen when both his elder brothers died in one season. He carried the four unlit coals to the grove at Doire ghlas to break them there, reasoning that the grove might hold some leaving that would answer; on the last morning of a month under the oaks the maul turned on the red-brown coal and opened the back of his hand, and where his blood fell on it the coal took fire. He came home with his hand bound and held it up at the next recital. His wife was Aoibheann. He died at seventy-two at his own hearth.

**Eòghann** (VE 4,196–4,262), the hundred and sixty-eighth father. A younger son who came to the keeping at twenty when his sister and father died in one season. He carried gual airgid to river after river, and one evening, kneeling to drink at the crossing below Tobar dhìreach, said that the water tasted different from the sea water, and threw in the three unlit coals. The silver caught under the current and burned there, a low pale light any traveller could kneel and see; the two dark coals were found again on a gravel bar downstream. His wife was Dearbhail, of the lake-shore line. He died at sixty-six.

**Colla** (VE 4,590–4,655), the hundred and eighty-fourth father. He held the bag when the valleys, half in jest, began to call the line by a long name for its long questioning of the two dark coals, and he gave the long name back to a traveller without the laughter, and the short form, Clann na Ceiste, with it. It stuck. He died at sixty-five, and the old name Clann a' Chlachair was heard for the last time as the line's own name within a generation of him.

**Seathan** (VE 4,862–4,934), the hundred and ninety-fifth father. He took the bag at twenty and kept it more than fifty years, and handled gual teine every day of them, and put it at last into the pot itself. On a doorstone at the age of forty-three he snapped his fingers when a thought struck him, and the coal-dust on his hand took fire; he beat it out against his coat and was not burned, and laughed until Caitir his wife came to the door with her hands floury from the baking. With her he tried the rainbow at the sea and the river. The bag passed to his eldest son. He died at seventy-two.

**Suibhne** (VE 5,272–5,318), the two hundred and eleventh father. He learned the Line standing as a boy and tried the rainbow by the sea, the height, the river and the earth, but would not try it by blood. In his forty-fourth year he walked the three days north to Doire ghlas with it and sat a night by his own small fire in the grove; nothing answered. He said at the next recital that he doubted the rainbow would answer him, and died of a fever two years later, at forty-six.

**Ailean mac Shuibhne** (born VE 5,300), the two hundred and twelfth father, living at the close of the age. A big young man, slow of speech and broad of hand, who sat by Poit an Teine for whole mornings as a child. He married Lìobhan at seventeen. At twenty-three he told the recital he meant to light the six again, each by its own way, and over the better part of a year he did it: the black coal in the earth, the gold out of the sea where Aodh let it burn, the snowflake on the height, the red-brown with his own blood, the silver in the Abhainn ghorm, gual teine on his own doorstone. In the last week of an t-Iuchar, at twenty-four, he set out north with six fires in six clay pots slung on a pole, and on the evening of the twenty-first day, in the grove at Doire ghlas, Coimhdeach na Fine came and lit the rainbow, and all seven burned together. Lìobhan and their daughter Gormshuil, then six, were at Tobar dhìreach.

## The women of the pot

Poit an Teine, the clay pot said to hold the mason's first fire, was never in the keeping of the father who held the bag. It passed among the women of the line, most often from a woman to her brother's daughter or her sister's, to whoever of the household had the steadiest hands with a live coal and the patience to rise in the night. The recital does not name them; the tellings of the hearth name some.

- **Ailbhe nic Neachdain** (VE 3–82), the mason's daughter, first child born by a hearth, who walked the fire in its pot to more hearths than anyone counted.
- **Muirne** (VE 112–181), who kept the watch of the vein when it burned low, would not let it be dug further, and bade them lay Leac na Fèithe.
- **Fionnghuala** (VE 838–897), Diarmad's mother, who took the pot from the old aunt the household called only the aunt.
- **Deirbhile nic Dhiarmaid** (VE 894–968), who kept Aithris a' Chruthachaidh word for word and made every child of the line say it back to her a section at a time.
- **Muirgheal** (VE 1,290–1,381), who bade Aodh take all seven to the sea and wept at the telling of the gold.
- **Gormal** (VE 1,930–2,004), who kept the pot and the recital in the lean years when a branch of the line went away from the vein, and added her own words at her last recital.
- **Sìomha** (VE 1,958–2,030), Gormal's daughter, who softened the recital for the children.
- **Sireadh** (VE 2,825–2,895), who kept the bag sixty years as a widow and gave Brian the five dark coals.
- **Mòrnait** (VE 4,785–4,850), of Clann na Ceiste though not of the narrow line, who kept fire at the ring about Colbh Cnoc chiar.
- **Caitir** (VE 4,868–4,940), Seathan's wife, the only keeper's wife remembered to have gone with the rainbow to the sea and not stayed by the pot.
- **Lìobhan** (born VE 5,302), Ailean's wife, who named what the rainbow wanted, and kept the house fire while he went north.
