# Appendix B — The Telling, the Riddle and the Lightings

Three things were said at the hearth of Tobar dhìreach on Oidhche an Dealanaich, and the whole faith of the high valleys in this age grew out of them: the Line of the fathers (Appendix A), Aithris a' Chruthachaidh, and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich. To these the line added, one at a time over more than four thousand years, a line for each coal as it answered. This appendix tells how Aithris a' Chruthachaidh was kept, gives Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich, sets out the lightings in order, and describes the other reverences of the hearths, which were kept by households that had never heard Aithris a' Chruthachaidh whole. It ends with what is not known of the holy things of Seann-Dhaoine.

## How the Telling was kept

Aithris a' Chruthachaidh came to the island in one night. Coimhdeach na Fine gave it whole to Diarmad in the oak grove at Doire ghlas, in the gale, sitting by his fire under a fallen trunk: the gods and their line, each god making a world of what was dearest to him; Caoran an Dia Òg, youngest son of an Dagda and Danu, who chose coal; the making of the stars and the sun and the moon out of its sparks and ash, and last of all the island, born out of the sea from drops of fire; An Dia-shluagh grown up out of the heather; Na Seachd Guail laid under the mountains, each colour locked with its own key; the Tuath Dè who came down to see the island, and what each of them loves; Coimhdeach na Fine itself, the smoke of the first coal given a mind and a charge; and the forgetting of the coal by an Dia-shluagh, who threw the coloured stones away as the mountain's droppings.

Diarmad walked home saying Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich over and over to keep it; Aithris a' Chruthachaidh he carried home in his head unspoken, and it took him most of a winter to lay it out at the hearth in the order Coimhdeach na Fine had given it. His wife Niamh said it after him at the first standing of the Line, though she did not yet believe it. His daughter Deirbhile learned it from him word for word and made each of her own children say it back to her a section at a time until they had it as clean as she did, and taught it so to any of the kin who would sit still for the whole. From her the line has it. It is said sitting, unlike the Line, and it is said by whoever of the household says it best. A trader who had heard it once told it back to Diarmad, some years after, with the sea and the sky changed places and the earth dropped out; the line took this as a warning, and never let Aithris a' Chruthachaidh be said at the hearth in any words but the kept ones.

Outside the line Aithris a' Chruthachaidh went out in pieces. Every hearth of the high valleys knew by the close of the age that the island was born of fire from a young god's hand, and that the colours in the coal were his gift, locked; fewer knew the names of the Tuath Dè in their order; hardly any outside Tobar dhìreach could have said the whole. At the gatherings at the column, from Seathan's time, the line's reciter said Aithris a' Chruthachaidh to crowds of some hundreds, and many heard it whole there for the first time.

## The riddle

Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich was given last, after Aithris a' Chruthachaidh, when Diarmad asked whether an Dia Òg had been angry at the forgetting. Coimhdeach na Fine answered that he was not, and gave Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich, and would give nothing more:

> *Tha spiorad fa leth san speur, san talamh agus sa mhuir. Meascaich na spioradan agus bidh iad uile-chumhachdach.*
> The sky, the earth and the sea each carry their own spirit. Merge the spirits, and they become almighty.

The line said it at every recital after Aithris a' Chruthachaidh, once in the old words and once in plain speech, and left it unanswered. For eighteen fathers after Diarmad they tried the coals against the three things Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich names as they understood them: held to the sky, pressed into the earth, dropped into sea water carried home in skins; in the hearth, in the rain, all seven together. Nothing answered. What no one of the line understood until Aodh was that each coal wanted its own element in the element's own body, the whole sea and not a skin of it, and that each lighting would be a step of that kind: the coal taken to what it holds. Even then Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich's last line stayed shut. Lìobhan, Ailean's wife, is remembered as the one who first said at the hearth what the rainbow wanted: the other six, burning, together.

## The lightings

Each lighting added a line to the recital. A coal once lit burned until it burned out, and the line relit from the bag, which held pieces of every colour broken from the vein before it was covered and, from Aodh's time, fresh pieces taken from where the vein shows in a stream bank above the well, a handful a life.

| Coal | Holds | Lit by | Where | How | Annals |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| the vein | fire of the lightning | the storm | the mason's well, Tobar dhìreach | lightning on the broken vein | VE 1 |
| gual òir, the gold | the sea | Aodh | the northern shore | thrown into the sea; burned gold on the water | VE 1,370 |
| gual sneachda, the snowflake | the air | Fearghas | Binnean a' Chlachair | let fall from the summit; took fire falling and burned white | VE 2,170 |
| gual dubh, the black | the earth | Brian | beside Leac na Fèithe, Tobar dhìreach | buried a night deep in the ground; warm when dug up | VE 2,885 |
| gual donn-ruadh, the red-brown | life | Cormac | the grove at Doire ghlas | the maul turned; his blood fell on it | VE 3,670 |
| gual airgid, the silver | river water | Eòghann | the Abhainn ghorm below Tobar dhìreach | thrown into the river; burned under the current | VE 4,225 |
| gual teine, the fire | fire | Seathan | his own doorstone, Tobar dhìreach | the dust on his fingers caught at a snap | VE 4,905 |
| gual bogha-froise, the rainbow | spirit | Coimhdeach na Fine | the grove at Doire ghlas | the six burning in a ring about it | VE 5,324 |

Ailean relit the six over the better part of his twenty-fourth year, each by its own way: the black coal in the earth by Leac na Fèithe; the gold where Aodh let it burn, wading after it and catching it still burning between his cupped hands; the snowflake on the height; the red-brown with his own blood; the silver in the Abhainn ghorm; Gual teine on his own doorstone. Six fires stood in six clay pots under one roof at Tobar dhìreach through the last weeks of summer, and on the twenty-first day of an t-Iuchar they stood in a ring under the oaks.

## The bag and the pot

Two things were kept at Tobar dhìreach for the whole line. Poit an Teine, is a squat clay pot with a turf lid, said to hold the mason's first fire; it has been remade more than once as clay pots crack, and each time the fire was moved from the old pot to the new before the old was broken up, so that the fire in it has never been let go dark. It stood by the hearth and was kept by the women of the line (Appendix A). The bag is a pouch of greased leather on a peg by the door, holding the pieces of an gual dathach: pieces of every colour broken from the vein before Leac na Fèithe was laid, and fresh pieces taken in each life from where the vein shows in a stream bank above the well. Children of the line played with the pieces when they were small enough not to know better, and learned the colours so. The bag passed from father to son with the Line, and the father who held it said the recital.

A coal that answered was left to burn where it had answered, as the gold burned on the sea and the silver under the river, or kept in a pot of its own, as Brian kept the black coal, until it burned out. The line did not grieve a coal that went out; the bag held more of the same colour, and the way of lighting it was now known. What the line guarded was the knowing, and the knowing was in the recital.

## The reverences of the hearths

These were kept by the hill-folk at large, most of them by households that knew Aithris a' Chruthachaidh only in pieces.

**Leac na Fèithe.** When Teine na Fèithe burned out, Muirne of the line would not have it dug further. A flat stone was laid over the broken vein, no water was drawn beside it, and the well was cut again a stone's throw off. No house stands by Leac na Fèithe, no bucket is set near it, and the turf at its edge is kept whole against the rain. Children of the line are brought to lay a bare palm on it in the dark half of the year.

**The fire given.** Every hearth of the hill-folk was lit from Teine a' Chlachair, by one borrowing or another, carried in a clay pot banked with ash. A fire was never sold. A household whose hearth died begged a coal from the nearest living one, and was never refused.

**The dead in the ground.** The hill-folk lay their dead in the ground, on the side, knees drawn up, facing the central mountains, with an uncut stone set on end at the head and no mark on it. At Tuam Cnoc dhìreach on the south coast the graves came to be laid in rows, heads toward the mountains; the first rows are straight, the later ones bend round older graves no one will disturb. At Achadh dhìreach, in one grave in some thirty, coal of the vein is rubbed into the wool the dead are wrapped in. At Tuam Cnoc dhìreach a child was buried with a sliver of an gual dathach closed in one hand, and there were words between two households over it.

**The covered hearth.** In the Doire uaine hills the fire is kept in pits under slabs, with a blind bend in the shaft, against the thing that walks without breathing (Appendix E). The line at Tobar dhìreach would not cover its own fire, holding Teine a' Chlachair owed better than to hide.

**The uncut woods.** Two woods were let alone: Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, from whose edge no household cut a branch, and Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag in the west, never walked from end to end, where three paths stop at a line of set stones.

**The stones and their sayings.** Three standing stones were found in the west and south-west within some two hundred years, each bearing words in the tongue of the hill-folk: Carragh Cnoc bheag, *Bha teine sa chloich*, "there was fire in the stone," cut low beneath a line of the unread script; Colbh Cnoc chiar, *Cuimhnich an teine*, "remember the fire"; and Calbh Cnoc ghorm, *Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann*, "we did not come; we were here." None of the hill-folk could read a letter. How the words came to be known at every hearth is a riddle the tellings leave as they found it; known they were, and said the same way at every hearth that told of them. At Colbh Cnoc chiar a ring of ground was trodden hard and paved with fire-cracked stones, and fires the size of hearths were kept there. At the column the saying was said standing, and the gatherings grew.

**Oidhche an Dealanaich.** The dark of the year, when the vein first took fire, was kept at every hearth that had heard of it with a fire built high and the fathers' names said by whoever knew them. At Tobar dhìreach it was the night of the recital. By the close of the age, in the hill country about the column, it was the night of the great telling.

## What is not known of the Old Ones' holy things

Of the faith of Seann-Dhaoine only what they built remains, and what they built does not explain itself. They rowed their dead to Eilean dhearg and laid them in stone boxes facing the mainland, and no box was left open through a night. They raised a stepped platform of fitted stone in the eastern hills with an altar block on its top step, set square to the central mountains, with its back to the sea; the top stone of the altar was prised off and carried away, and the platform left. Two shafts were cut straight down through the rock at the two Toll-dubhs, far apart, smooth-walled, with no spoil beside them; stones thrown into either are not heard to land. A script was cut on the cliff above their landing at Tarr; the same script stands on the rocks of the Doire uaine hills and on the upper face of Carragh Cnoc bheag, and who cut those is not known. No one of the hill-folk could read a sign of it. They notched their net-weights with three strokes. Whether any of these things was holy to them, and to what, no telling of the hill-folk says, and Seann-Dhaoine' own tellings, if they had any, are not known.

# Appendix C — Cunntas nan Athraichean

No one in this age counted years. There was no tally, no notched stick kept for the purpose, no stone cut with marks, and no number of years from any beginning was said at any hearth. The dates in the annals of this volume, from 20 am Faoilleach VE 1 at the breaking of the vein to 21 an t-Iuchar VE 5,324 in the grove, are the dates of the annals of the island, set against its master record; the people of the age would not have understood them. This appendix tells how they knew time instead: by Cunntas nan Athraichean, by the turning of the year, by Oidhche an Dealanaich, and by the beasts and birds that keep their own seasons.

## The count of fathers

The only long measure the age had was Cunntas nan Athraichean, and only the mason's line kept it whole. A father, in this count, is a span as much as a man: the time from a father's taking the bag to his son's. Asked how long ago a thing was, an elder of the line answered in fathers, *so many fathers back*, and a listener who wanted it closer could ask *in whose father's time*, and be told a name if the name was one the line gave to strangers, or a count if it was not. The line itself reckoned a father at about the time it takes a boy to grow and have a son of his own grown, and the count held true enough that the named fathers, set against the years of the annals, stand spaced as the recital says (Appendix A).

Other households counted fathers too, but shorter. Most hearths of the hill-folk could give four or five fathers back, and a few old women could give eight or nine; past that a household said *long ago*, or *in the mason's time*, or *before the fire*, which meant the same as *never*. Diarmad, gathering the names for the Line, found that old women who had never troubled over his question had kept names back without being asked, and were glad to give them to someone willing to carry the weight of remembering them. Among Seann-Dhaoine no count of any kind is known.

Cunntas nan Athraichean made spans easy to say and dates hard. The line could say that Aodh gave the seven to the sea eighteen fathers after Diarmad went to the grove, but not how many winters Aodh had seen, except by counting them in his own lifetime at his own hearth. Ages were known within a household by the winters a person had lived through, counted on the fingers and remembered by the hard ones: *she was born the winter the seed rotted*; *he was a boy of ten winters when the whale came ashore*. The ages given in this volume for the people of the line are the annals' ages; the households themselves would have said them in winters, and would not always have agreed.

## The turning of the year

The year was known by its halves and its marks. The dark half ran from the first frosts to the lambing, and the light half from the lambing to the frosts. Within them each household knew the year by its own work: the peat cut and stacked, the barley sown in the small fields and cut, the flocks taken up to the shielings and brought down, the seals hauling out on the skerries in the autumn gales, the eels running in the rivers, the kilns smoking on the south-east coast through the summer. A woman of the shore might say a thing happened *at the second hauling-out* and be understood along the whole of that coast and nowhere else.

The dates of the annals name the months, from am Faoilleach in the dead of winter to an Dùbhlachd at the year's close. The hill-folk of the age named stretches of the year and not fixed counts of days, and a stretch began when the weather that named it began. The shortest day was marked at the temple platform in the eastern hills by Seann-Dhaoine, who climbed the steps in the dark and stood about the great stone the whole hour the light took to cross it; the hill-folk marked it, if at all, by a fire.

## The night of the lightning

The one night of the year that the whole of the high valleys kept on the same night was Oidhche an Dealanaich, in the dark of the winter, when the vein first took fire. At Tobar dhìreach the Line was said standing that night, Aithris a' Chruthachaidh after it and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich after that, and any new line for a coal was added. At other hearths the fire was built high and the fathers' names said by whoever knew them. As the age went on the night gathered other things to it: the gathering at Àth gharbh where the valleys first named themselves Clann nan Dè; the ring of fires about Colbh Cnoc chiar; and, from Seathan's time, the great telling at the column, to which some hundreds walked from every quarter of the hill country. By the close of the age the hill country about the column reckoned its year by the gatherings there, one in the dark of the year and one at midsummer, and a thing done between them was said to be done *between the gatherings*.

## The beasts that keep their seasons

Where Cunntas nan Athraichean was too long and the year too short, the hill-folk measured by the beasts.

**The salmon** came up the rivers in their great runs at much the same season each year, and the weirs on the Abhainn ìseal were renewed in the same holes for the runs, so that the households along that river knew the late summer by the salmon before they knew it by anything else.

**The geese** of Eilean ghorm came in with the first storm of the winter and left with the last, and households that watched them close enough learned to read the turn of the winter in their leaving, which came a day or two ahead of the year's last storm. The geese of the southern coast, going over in their numbers in the autumn, told the southern households that the season had turned; in the year the eleven went up from Teallaichean a' Chladaich, the geese were late, and the shore read the season as a slow one.

**The seals** hauled out to pup on the skerries off Eilean fhada in the autumn gales, and on Eilean mhin in their own season, and the hunters went out when the seals were there.

**The great cats** of the mountains crossed the high ground by fixed ways at fixed seasons, and from Beithir's time the households learned the crossing season and kept off the passes while it lasted. A crossing mark was cut on each shieling's gatepost when the season came, and scraped bare when it had been kept, so that a latecomer knew the season had been kept there before. It was the nearest thing to a tally the hill-folk made, and it counted one thing only: that the cats had passed.

**The white stag** of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar was seen at long intervals, and the hunters who saw it did not draw. A household of the east might say a thing happened *the year the stag was seen*, and be understood.

## The span of a life

No one in this age lived long. A child who lived past its fifth winter might hope for fifty or sixty more; a man or woman of seventy was old, and one of eighty was a wonder spoken of along a whole valley. The named fathers of the line died between sixty and their early seventies, most at their own hearths; Suibhne died of a fever at forty-six. Many children died before they could walk, and fevers took the young in bad seasons along whole shores. A household reckoned its strength by how many of its children had lived to be grown, and a woman who had lost children young and trusted, at last, that one would live, sewed it a coat cut to its own growing.

Because lives were short and Cunntas nan Athraichean long, the tellings of this age are a relay: no one lived to see more than one or two of the lightings, and the line's knowledge of the coals passed from hand to hand across two hundred fathers with no one to say from memory how a thing had first been done. What a keeper knew of the lightings before his own was what the recital gave him, and what the recital gave him was what the fathers before him had chosen to keep.

## Spans in this volume

Because the age had no count, spans in the Books of this volume are given as the tellers of the age would have given them: in fathers, in lifetimes, in winters, or in the seasons of the beasts. Where the annals give a year, it is the annals' own year. The two do not quarrel: a father in the recital is about twenty-five of the annals' years, a lifetime some sixty to seventy, and the line's own boast that the bag had waited *longer than any stone in the south* means a little over four thousand of them.

# Appendix D — The Peoples of the Shore and the Hills

Two peoples lived on the island in this age, and no telling of either says that they met. The hill-folk, who called themselves Clann nan Dè from the time of the gathering at Àth gharbh, had fire from the mason's vein, buried their dead in the ground, and cut no script. Seann-Dhaoine kept every coast, rowed their dead to the islands, built in stone, and cut a script of their own that the hill-folk could not read. Things passed between them, a chip of an gual dathach on a midden at Bral, a second hand on a standing stone, but how is not told. This appendix sets out what is known of each: where they lived, how many they were, and what they made.

## Numbers

At the breaking of the vein there were perhaps a few thousand souls on the whole island. By the time the walls of the heights were raised there were some ten thousand, and at the close of the age some eighteen thousand, of whom Seann-Dhaoine were perhaps a third. No one of the age counted them. The largest place on the island was Skell on the Abhainn naomh, with some three hundred souls at its height; Tobar dhìreach held some ninety at the close; most hearth-kindreds of the hill-folk were of twenty to eighty souls, and most landings of Seann-Dhaoine of thirty to a hundred. The three rings of Làrach an Dùin were built with room for four hundred people and their beasts, and are the only place of the age made for more than a landing's worth. A crowd at the column on the night of a great telling was some hundreds.

## The Old Ones

Seann-Dhaoine left their first sure trace at the eastern Dunn, in the great mound of shell, seal bone and burnt weed that the households there laid down over many lifetimes. From there, by the evidence of what they built, they came to hold every coast of the island, and at their widest reach they had landings at every good harbour from the north-western horn to the south-eastern cape. The hill-folk of the close of the age did not say *Seann* before the landings' names, and called each by its bare root, the only words of Seann-Dhaoine' speech that have come down.

**The ten roots.** The landings go under ten names, several landings to a name:

| Root | Landings in this age | Known for |
|---|---|---|
| Skell | on the Abhainn naomh in the west; the north-western horn; the northern coast | the mole; the hollow-walled tower; the curved mole |
| Dunn | the eastern coast; the Abhainn chaol in the south-east; the southern coast | the shell mound; the head of the sea-way; the whale-rib houses |
| Cwen | the head of the southern gulf; two on the southern coast | the notched net-weights; the midden that outgrew Dunn's |
| Bral | the far western coast; the south-eastern coast | the two hundred and twelve steps; the fish-kilns |
| Morn | the south-eastern coast; the southern coast | the seven fish-kilns; the headland of heaped shell |
| Brenn | the northern coast; the north-eastern coast | the stone ramps and the great hulls |
| Toll | the northern coast; the Abhainn uaine; the north-eastern cleft | the buried huts; the fish-channel; the quay cut in the rock |
| Vell | the south-east; the Abhainn bheag; the western dunes; an inland river | the round houses; the four houses and boat-shed; the store-pits |
| Warr | the western shore of Loch chrom; the southern shore of the gulf | the shell road |
| Tarr | the eastern cliff; the north-eastern headlands; a north-eastern inlet | the cut script; the cliff-house; landing stones |

**Their works.** Seann-Dhaoine built in stone without mortar, stone set against stone, and their building held: the mole at Skell stands with its foot under water at the lowest tides; the steps at Bral are worn hollow; the round houses at the eastern Vell stand in their rings. They made the first buildings on the island for a trade, the fish-kilns at Morn; the first made road, the shell causeway at Warr; the first quay, the mole; the first ramps for hulls greater than hide boats, at Brenn. They sank their nets with notched stones, the eldest mark on the island made again and again of purpose, and they cut a script on the cliff at Tarr.

**The heights.** In the middle lifetimes of the age some of Seann-Dhaoine went up from the shore. They raised the walled outpost of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire on a spur above the southern lowland, its stones dressed on the outer face only and its single gate looking inland; the three rings of Làrach an Dùin on a height some way from it, with a cistern cut into the bedrock; a kerbed way paved with flat slabs toward both; the stepped platform of Làrach an Teampaill in the eastern hills, its altar set square to the central mountains; and the two shafts of the Toll-dubhs, south-east and west, cut straight down and smoothed. Whether the builders of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and of the rings were the same people is not known.

**The going down.** Then the gate of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire was walled up with rubble from within, and Làrach an Dùin-fhaire left; the cistern of the rings was choked with the bones of cattle thrown in whole, and the rings left; the top stone of the altar was prised off and carried away, and the temple left. The households of the heights came down to the shore, to Skell and Morn and the southern Cwen and the northern Skell, and after that Seann-Dhaoine made no new work anywhere out of sight of salt water. Their last lifetimes in this age were lifetimes of the shore: the middens of the south grew as fast as Dunn's once had, landings once counted by the dozen were counted by the score, and a lane of flat landing-stones a day's rowing apart ran along the south-east coast from the river mouth below Dunn round the great cape. Who walled the gate, who fouled the cistern, who took the altar stone, and why, is not known.

**Their dead.** Seann-Dhaoine of the eastern Vell rowed their dead to Eilean dhearg and laid them in stone boxes facing the mainland; forty boxes are counted there. No grave of theirs of this age is found on the main island.

## The hill-folk

The hill-folk were the people of Teine a' Chlachair: every hearth of theirs was lit from the vein, by one borrowing or another. They lived in households of twenty to eighty, herding sheep and cattle, hunting deer, growing barley in small fields, and gathering; they built in turf and timber and laid their hearths on stone. They buried their dead in the ground facing the central mountains. They cut no script and read none. They had no king, no chief over more than a household, no war and no walled place; a quarrel between households was settled by the elders of both, or not at all.

**The high valleys**, about the crack on the north side of the central mountains, were the heart of them: Tobar dhìreach, the black well and the young well, Achadh dhìreach, Àth gharbh and the hearths between. Here the Line was said and Aithris a' Chruthachaidh kept, here the valleys first named themselves Clann nan Dè, and from here the fire went out.

**The Doire uaine hills**, south of the high valleys, were herding country, full of rock faces cut with lines of the unread script. After the hollow thing was first told of there, the households of those hills put their fires under the ground (Appendix E), and kept them there to the close of the age. Na Teallaichean Falaichte is their largest hamlet.

**The east** was deer country. The households of the eastern woods drove the red deer into Gleann nan Damh each autumn and stacked the antlers of the greatest stags apart; they let Coille Naomh Muileann chiar alone, and there the white stag was first seen. At Cnoc fhionn they first buried their dogs beside their people.

**The south-east valleys**, the slope of Bruthach nan Teaghlach above the river running down toward the kilns, were settled by herders from the high valleys in the lifetimes of the heights; some of their sick were carried to Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh.

**The south-west hill country**, about the column, was the country of the three stones and, from the finding of Calbh Cnoc ghorm, of the gatherings at Achadh a' Chalbh.

**The northern shore** was seal country. Its households hunted seal on the skerries off Eilean fhada from Bothan an Fhoghair in the autumn gales, fished from skin boats, and watched the grey on the northern and eastern sea that never lifts. The north-western coast, from Ros ruadh to the strait, was Uilebheist na Mara's country after the seven boats were lost, and its hunters moved into the lee of the headlands and the strait at Bothan a' Chaolais. A warning fire was kept on the north-western headland.

**The southern shore** was the country of the first boats: Oisean crossed to Eilean mhin from it, and the seal-camp of Bothan nan Ròn was kept there every season after. Teallaichean a' Chladaich, the households from which the eleven went up into the hills, lay on this coast, and the burial-ground of Tuam Cnoc dhìreach grew above it.

**The lake shore** about Loch chrom held the lake dwellings of Crannagan Loch chrom, whose builders are not known, and the hearths of the hill-folk on Creag Ruadh above the eastern shore. Eòghann's wife Dearbhail was of the lake-shore line.

## How the households lived

No one on the island in this age worked metal. The hill-folk and Seann-Dhaoine alike cut with flint and chert, split with wedges of antler and hard stone, and dressed stone by pecking it with harder stone; a maul was a rounded cobble lashed to a haft of ash. A household's wealth was its beasts, its store of food against the dark half of the year, its boats if it had any, and the skill in its members' hands.

**Houses.** The hill-folk built round and oval houses of turf on a footing of stones, roofed with heather thatch over a frame of birch or, as the oak came in, of oak; the hearth stood in the middle of the floor on a flat stone, and the smoke went out through the thatch. Seann-Dhaoine built in dry stone where they could and in turf and driftwood where they could not: round houses with sunk hearths and drains at the eastern Vell, a long house in a cleft of the cliff at Tarr, huts in the lee of a dune at the northern Toll, and, where a whale gave them the chance, frames of rib. On the lake shore the platforms stood on oak piles over the water.

**Food.** The hill-folk ate mutton and beef, venison, barley bread and porridge, milk and curds, hazel-nuts roasted and stored, berries and roots in their seasons, and fish where they had water. Meat was cooked on stones heated at the fire's edge from the first years of the mason's hearth, and in pits of heated stones for a gathering. Seann-Dhaoine ate from the sea: shellfish above all, as their middens show, and fish, seal, seabirds and their eggs, and whale when one came ashore; they dried and smoked fish in their kilns and stored it in clay-lined pits.

**Fire.** Every fire of the hill-folk was Teine a' Chlachair, lent from hearth to hearth and carried in clay pots banked with ash. A household that let its hearth die begged a coal from the nearest living one. Hearths burned wood, peat and heather; before the first small burning at Àth gharbh no household outside the line burned an gual dathach, and after it very few did. How Seann-Dhaoine came by fire the tellings do not say.

**Boats.** The first boats were of hide stretched on a frame of bent hazel, greased against the wet; Oisean's was of that kind, and the north-shore hunters went out to the skerries in the like. Seann-Dhaoine built bigger boats of the same kind and, at Brenn, the first plank-built hulls, launched down stone ramps; of those hulls nothing is left. River landings kept flat-bottomed hulls for poling up the shallows.

**Cloth.** The hill-folk wove wool from their sheep and wore sealskin and deerskin cloaks in the cold; at Achadh dhìreach, late in the age, the wool of the dead was streaked with the colour of the vein. What Seann-Dhaoine wore the tellings do not say.

## What passed between them

No telling keeps a meeting. The tellings keep three things that passed. A chip of an gual dathach, still staining the shell about it, was thrown on the midden at Bral on the far western coast, late in the age: by gift, by trade or by theft, a piece of the vein came to Seann-Dhaoine. On the upper face of Carragh Cnoc bheag runs a line of the unread script, and the four words of the hill-folk lie lower on the same face, cut with a narrower tool by another hand; which hand came first is not known. And the same script that Seann-Dhaoine cut on the cliff at Tarr stands on the rock faces of the Doire uaine hills among the hill-folk's pastures. Whether the two peoples shared the island knowingly, no telling knows.

# Appendix E — Of Fears, Beasts and Holy Places

The hill-folk of this age feared few things by name, and named them late. For most of the age a fear was a place a household did not go, a thing a child was told not to do, or a custom kept without a reason given; only toward its close did the fears gather names, and even then the names were few. This appendix gathers the fears, the beasts that the tellings keep, and the places that were let alone or kept holy, with what the tellings say of each and what they do not.

## The fears

**Uilebheist na Mara.** Old sailors of the north-western coast told of a vast creature dwelling in the water off the north-western horn. Four men of that coast saw it rise once, and the youngest of them kept the telling word for word into his old age, adding nothing and taking nothing away; the coast counted this for more than any argument of the doubters. No wreck was ever brought up to prove the tellers wrong. For a long while Uilebheist na Mara was feared only in general, as a thing out there; then, in one calm season, seven boats of Ros ruadh went out on still water and did not come home, and the widows of Ros ruadh named it. It was the first loss laid at its door by name. After that the hunters of the north-west left the open water for the lee of the headlands and the strait, where the seal bones grew in the middens of Bothan a' Chaolais, and Criomthann kept a fire on the north-western headland, from a peat bank cut for it alone, to warn boats off the water where Uilebheist na Mara was seen. The fire was never lit to bring boats in. Its ash lies a man's height deep. What Uilebheist na Mara is, the tellings do not say; the households of Seann-Dhaoine' tower on the north-western horn kept their boats out of the same water, and no one knows why.

**Marbh-bheò.** In the Doire uaine hills, where the rock faces are cut with lines of the unread script more thickly than anywhere else on the island, the tellings came to agree that the writing told of something that walked without breathing and fell upon any who lit a fire in its sight. How the hills came to know what the writing said, when none of them could read a sign, is a riddle; known it was, and told the same way at every hearth. Some lines were cut over and defaced by another hand with the same kind of tool. Two or three people of the hills dreamed, without having spoken to one another, of something walking the ridges without breath; two herders saw a walker on a ridge and lived. The hills' answer was the covered hearth: Laoghaire dug the first pit-hearth, the fire under a slab at the foot of a slanting shaft bent near its foot so that no glow could climb it straight, and within a few lifetimes no open fire showed in those hills. Eimhir, who found the first cut stone, kept her hearth open to her death. Whether Marbh-bheò is, or was, the tellings do not say. The hills say only that a fire built where the ridge can see it is a fire built carelessly.

**The camp of the nine.** At a hill camp nine people were found dead inside one hut, lying where they fell beside a hearth of fresh ash, with no wound on any of them. The hut was never opened again and none was buried from it; the camp was left for good. The hills did not agree on a cause. Some laid it at Marbh-bheò's door, some at the fire itself, burning in a shut hut; the tellings keep both and choose neither.

**The line of stones.** Children of the country about Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag were told early and plainly: go as far as the stones and no further, and whatever crosses the line ahead of you, a ball or a lamb or a hound, let it go. A girl named Muireall went past the stones after a young deer and was never found. After her no household let its children watch for deer at that stretch without a grown hand near enough to close on a small arm.

**The grey on the sea.** On the northern and eastern sea lies a grey bank that never lifts. Scàire of the north shore saw it first from the skerries and would not steer toward it. Bran, a steersman of the north-west, sailed west with the grey bank on his right hand in search of an isle of the blessed, and did not come back; one of his crew came home, and died within days. The hill-folk name the western lands of the dead from Aithris a' Chruthachaidh: Tìr nan Òg, Magh Meall, Taigh Dhuinn. What lies in the grey, no telling says.

## The beasts

**The great cats.** The great cats of the mountains were known from the beginning of the age as a danger to flocks and lone walkers. From the time of Beithir, a herder of the high shoulders who first read their road in the snow, the tellings say that the cats keep their roads, crossing the mountains by fixed ways at fixed seasons. The households learned the crossing season and kept off the passes while it lasted, leaving the shielings of Àirighean a' Bhealaich stripped and shuttered and cutting a mark on each gatepost that was scraped when the season had been kept. Eleven of Teallaichean a' Chladaich went up into the southern hills in the crossing season, reading the geese as late and the season as slow, and did not come home; their bones were found years after along the line the cats use, and were buried where they lay. Why the cats keep their roads, no one has learned.

**The white stag.** Three hunters of the east, Sadhbh and her cousin Ruadhan and one other, saw a white stag at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, and none of them drew. It was seen again at long intervals, and the hunters of the gully began letting a beast go if a pale one was among the drove, sooner than risk the wrong one. Aithris a' Chruthachaidh says that Flidais keeps the wild things and that the white stag of the wood is hers; no one of this age tied the stag at the wood's edge to that line of Aithris a' Chruthachaidh, and in this age the stag has no god.

**The red deer.** The deer of the eastern woods were driven each autumn into Gleann nan Damh and killed at the gully's throat; the antlers of the greatest stags were stacked apart. The deer of Eilean dhubh, cut off when the sea drowned the neck, grew smaller in the lifetimes that followed.

**The seals.** The grey seals haul out to pup on the skerries off Eilean fhada in the autumn gales, and on Eilean mhin in their season. They were the first quarry for which anyone on the island crossed open water of set purpose.

**The whales.** A whale stranded below the southern Dunn was cut and shared along the whole shore, its oil burned through two winters and its ribs raised for house frames. Word of usable ribs travelled faster, by the end, than word of strandings once had.

**The geese.** The grey geese that winter on Eilean ghorm came in with the first storm and left with the last, and none hunted them there. A young man who sailed for Eilean ghorm to hunt them is told three ways at three hearths, and remembered as a warning.

**The dogs.** At Cnoc fhionn a boy buried his dog beside his family's dead with a shell at its head, and within a few years two more households of that hill buried their dogs so. No beast had had a grave on the island before.

**The crows and the wrens.** The crows of the island are as black as the black coal, and Aithris a' Chruthachaidh gives them to the Morrìgan; the hill-folk let them be. A wren came along the fallen trunk to within a hand of gual bogha-froise on Diarmad's second morning in the grove, looked at it and at him, and went about its business; the line tells it at the recital as a sign of nothing, and keeps it all the same.

## The holy places

**Leac na Fèithe over the vein** at Tobar dhìreach, with no house beside it and no water drawn near it (Appendix B).

**The grove at Doire ghlas**, three days north of Tobar dhìreach, where the oaks came in on ground that had been open heath when the vein was broken. Coimhdeach na Fine came to Diarmad there, Cormac's blood lit the red-brown there, Suibhne sat a night there with the rainbow, and Ailean brought the six there at the close of the age. The line did not build there.

**Binnean a' Chlachair**, the highest ground of the island, where Fearghas let the six fall and the snowflake burned; herders passing the summit each lay a stone on the cairn Mathan began.

**Coille Naomh Muileann chiar**, from which no household cut a branch; the households at its edge carried their fuel from beyond the far shoulder of open ground, two journeys where one would serve.

**Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag**, the second wood, older-seeming than the first, never settled, never felled, never walked from end to end; three paths stop short of it at a low line of set stones.

**Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh**, Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh south of the high valleys, where stone basins were set into the springs and the sick of the island were first brought for healing. The keeper of the basins judged a wound by its colour and its smell, and in a dry summer heated stones were laid in the third basin to bring back its warmth. The dead buried near the springs have old breaks that knitted clean.

**The three stones** and their sayings: Carragh Cnoc bheag, Colbh Cnoc chiar with its ring of fire-cracked stones, and Calbh Cnoc ghorm with the gathering-ground of Achadh a' Chalbh about it (Appendix B).

**Tuam Cnoc dhìreach**, the burial-ground on the south coast that none remembers hallowing, where the rows bend round older graves.

**Seann-Dhaoine' places.** The platform of Làrach an Teampaill in the eastern hills; the two shafts of the Toll-dubhs, into which a youth of the south-east was once let down on a plaited rope and came up silent; the boxes on Eilean dhearg. The hill-folk of this age did not go to them. What they were to their makers is not known.
